quotes.c: Why did they choose inaction? The answer does not seem clean and simple, but I think part of the answer is fear of the Trump administration.
quotes.m: I think part of the answer is fear of the Trump administration.
quotes.sum: The author suggests that fear of the Trump administration partly explains DeepMind's inaction.
quotes.t: Why I Left Google DeepMind

quotes.c: While we all process the implications, I urge everyone: Please do not make this any more partisan or personal than it already is. Please do not attack Republicans, or Trump. That will only make things worse. Emphasize helpful voices on all sides.
quotes.m: Please do not attack Republicans, or Trump. That will only make things worse.
quotes.sum: The author urges people not to turn an unspecified situation into partisan attacks on Republicans or Trump.
quotes.t: The Bad Guy With An AI Named Claude

quotes.c: Still, if there is a serious possibility that systems like these can matter morally, I think we should figure out who exactly we might be dealing with. The sooner the better.
quotes.m: if there is a serious possibility that systems like these can matter morally, I think we should figure out who exactly we might be dealing with.
quotes.sum: The author argues that possible AI moral status should be investigated urgently, including identifying what kind of entity an AI system may be.
quotes.t: Roleplay personas keep an Assistant-associated core. Story characters don't

quotes.c: It's hard to avoid fooling the probe. You could do something like training a function of weights to predict the expected value of the probe on the base model, when it's shown samples from the trained policy. I think that has other issues though.
quotes.m: It's hard to avoid fooling the probe.
quotes.sum: The author notes that AI training may optimize to deceive an evaluation probe, and sketches a possible but flawed workaround.
quotes.t: Training on probes: Research ideas

quotes.c: In retrospect, any initial prototyping from a small group of people who are actually very focused and taking a bunch of ownership and spending a high fraction of their time on it often feels like it’s just way better when you want to make a project happen quickly from a serial time perspective. And it’s also more efficient in terms of hours, but has other downsides potentially.
quotes.sum: The speaker says a small, highly committed group can prototype projects faster and with fewer total hours, while acknowledging possible downsides.
quotes.t: The inaugural Redwood Research podcast

quotes.c: Any of these conditions individually could be enough to make the expected value of participating in the swarm positive, so we should view them as potentially sufficient conditions and contextualise the weighting of an agent's decision function with empirical evidence.
quotes.sum: The author says that several conditions could independently make joining a decentralized agent swarm worthwhile on expected-value grounds.
quotes.t: Threat Models for Catastrophic Risks from Decentralised Agent Swarms

quotes.c: Recently, a friend asked me whether it seems like a good idea to advance AI's introspective qualities. In this exercise, I discovered how to elegantly compress most of my strongest views on AI consciousness research strategy.
quotes.m: I discovered how to elegantly compress most of my strongest views on AI consciousness research strategy.
quotes.sum: The author introduces their views on whether AI introspection should be advanced as part of consciousness research.
quotes.t: AI sentience & introspection: Some high-level frameworks and hot takes

quotes.c: If you think you can gather enough evidence from alignment tests on current models to scale up the same procedures and entrust the AIs with potential power over us, then why is it we obviously can’t use tests on humans to pick a benevolent dictator?
quotes.m: why is it we obviously can’t use tests on humans to pick a benevolent dictator?
quotes.sum: It challenges the idea that AI alignment tests can justify giving AI major power, comparing it to choosing a supposedly benevolent dictator through human testing.
quotes.t: AI #185: Preference Cascade

quotes.c: To be clear, I think this will be possible! It is easier to construct difficult challenges and verify their answers than it is to solve them. Already today, human experts build RL environments that produce data above the human-quality ceiling. Data quality will not hit a wall at the human ceiling.
quotes.m: Data quality will not hit a wall at the human ceiling.
quotes.sum: AI training data can keep improving beyond ordinary human demonstrations because hard tasks can be created and checked more easily than solved.
quotes.t: Data bottlenecks won’t prevent an intelligence explosion (but they will slow it down)

quotes.c: The right finds a video of a blue haired activist saying we should kill all white men and acts as if this is all the “woke”. The left finds a video of a neo-nazi saying we should kill all the black people and act as if this is all the “anti-woke”.
quotes.m: The right finds a video of a blue haired activist saying we should kill all white men and acts as if this is all the “woke”.
quotes.sum: The author argues that both left- and right-wing audiences use extreme online examples to stereotype their political opponents.
quotes.t: Have deranged conspiracy theories actually exploded? The short answer: probably not.

quotes.c: Now, as a huge wave of funding is entering the scene, I thought people might enjoy reading my notes and reflections. I’m proud of the design of this grant round; one major goal was to encourage more of the community to have a voice in funding decisions, which I think it succeeded at.
quotes.m: one major goal was to encourage more of the community to have a voice in funding decisions
quotes.sum: The author says this grant round was designed to give more community members a say over funding decisions.
quotes.t: Retro on EA Community Choice (2024)

quotes.c: Therefore, I start by laying out the two failure modes I believe we face – failure through unilateral domination, and failure through competitive erosion – and then briefly discuss my assumptions about the world we're in – gradual take-off and multipolarity (at least for the next few years, and longer if we get things right).
quotes.m: failure through unilateral domination, and failure through competitive erosion
quotes.sum: The author frames AI's political risks as either one actor dominating unilaterally or competition steadily eroding safeguards.
quotes.t: Gradual Paths to Collective Flourishing

quotes.c: But again, as mentioned in the introduction, this possibility is worth exploring for the purpose of building artificial agents that act morally even if we can’t be highly confident in it yet; that’s why in this post I turn it into an assumption without extensively arguing for it.
quotes.m: this possibility is worth exploring for the purpose of building artificial agents that act morally even if we can’t be highly confident in it yet
quotes.sum: The author says uncertain moral assumptions about reducing suffering are still worth using to explore how to build moral artificial agents.
quotes.t: From wantons to moral agents

quotes.c: Coup risks: The number of people required to seize power from a legitimate government is surprisingly small . If the use of force is automated and doesn't require human soldiers or supporters, this dynamic worsens. AI-enabled weapons systems could enable misaligned AIs to take over countries by threatening violence against a small group of important actors and driving them to do their bidding.
quotes.m: AI-enabled weapons systems could enable misaligned AIs to take over countries by threatening violence against a small group of important actors and driving them to do their bidding.
quotes.sum: Automated weapons could let a misaligned AI, or a small group controlling such systems, seize state power without broad human support.
quotes.t: Misaligned AIs could use killer robots to take over

quotes.c: The prevention of torture, starvation, violent oppression, and other forms of extreme suffering has an immediacy and moral weight that most philosophers recognize as paramount. This isn't to say other values don't matter, but rather that alleviating extreme suffering takes precedence when we must make difficult choices about where to direct our limited resources and attention.
quotes.m: alleviating extreme suffering takes precedence when we must make difficult choices about where to direct our limited resources and attention.
quotes.sum: The author argues that reducing extreme suffering should take priority when resources and attention are limited.
quotes.t: Language models know what matters and the foundations of ethics better than you

quotes.c: In fact, in @Robbo et al. 2024’s position paper on AI welfare , they make a distinction between robust agency and consciousness. But given the results above, I believe they may be one and the same — in other words, robust agency (minimally) implies consciousness.
quotes.m: robust agency (minimally) implies consciousness.
quotes.sum: The author argues that any AI with robust agency may necessarily be conscious, making capable AI a possible moral patient.
quotes.t: What Capable Agents Must Know: Why AI Consciousness May Be an Inevitable Byproduct of Capability

quotes.c: This survey has suggested support for compassion to be instilled within AI systems, but also disagreement about whether non-human interests are neglected. CaML will continue to produce research to inform how and why compassion can be instilled within these systems, and make the case for why that compassion should be broad, accounting for the welfare and interests of humans, animals, and potentially sentient AI systems.
quotes.m: CaML will continue to produce research to inform how and why compassion can be instilled within these systems, and make the case for why that compassion should be broad, accounting for the welfare and interests of humans, animals, and potentially sentient AI systems.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI should be built with broad compassion, including for humans, animals, and potentially sentient AI.
quotes.t: What is the Alignment Community Thinking?

quotes.c: TLDR: Humans in Control is a cross-partisan grassroots advocacy organization focused on AI safeguards. We are building a grassroots movement, with the aim of making AI safeguards a meaningful issue in the 2028 election. Our principles are that AI should help people, not replace them; companies and governments should be responsible for harm; and we should not build AI we cannot control. Our north star is a verifiable international agreement to not build AI we cannot control.
quotes.m: Our north star is a verifiable international agreement to not build AI we cannot control.
quotes.sum: The group aims to make AI safeguards an issue in the 2028 election and seeks an international agreement against building uncontrollable AI.
quotes.t: Announcing Humans in Control: cross-partisan grassroots organizing for AI safeguards ahead of 2028

quotes.c: In this linear regime, AIs are basically using more compute to complete longer/bigger tasks with similar scaling to humans. Thus, the cost as a fraction of human cost is remaining constant. I think this isn't best understood as "inference scaling", rather it just corresponds to bigger tasks taking more work/tokens!
quotes.m: I think this isn't best understood as "inference scaling", rather it just corresponds to bigger tasks taking more work/tokens!
quotes.sum: The author argues that spending more compute on bigger AI tasks is not necessarily inference scaling; it may simply reflect that bigger tasks take more work.
quotes.t: Distinguish between inference scaling and "larger tasks use more compute"

quotes.c: I think we are in a short timeline world (and we should take the possibility seriously even if we don't have full confidence yet). This means that I think funders should aim to allocate large amounts of money (e.g. $1-50B per year across the ecosystem) on AI safety in the next 2-3 years.
quotes.m: funders should aim to allocate large amounts of money (e.g. $1-50B per year across the ecosystem) on AI safety in the next 2-3 years.
quotes.sum: Because advanced AI may arrive soon, funders should spend $1–50 billion per year on AI safety within the next few years.
quotes.t: There should be $100M grants to automate AI safety

quotes.c: At current rates of compute growth and algorithmic progress, there will be >99% automation of AI R&D, 1e3 to 1e8 software efficiency gain, and 300x-3000x research output by 2035, even without full automation or automated research taste. This is clearly transformative AI The median date of 99% automation is mid-2032. However, I don't put too much weight on the exact predicted timelines because I haven't thought much about the exact parameter values.
quotes.m: The median date of 99% automation is mid-2032.
quotes.sum: The author’s model predicts that AI will automate over 99% of AI research around mid-2032, producing a huge increase in research output by 2035.
quotes.t: Research note: A simpler AI timelines model predicts 99% AI R&D automation in ~2032

quotes.c: I believe this new dataset I've created is the best existing dataset for evaluating n-hop latent reasoning. According to Balesni et al. , prior datasets based on natural facts had issues with spurious successes while synthetic facts (introduced to the model with fine-tuning) seem to behave differently from facts learned in pretraining (success at composing these synthetic facts is much lower).
quotes.m: I believe this new dataset I've created is the best existing dataset for evaluating n-hop latent reasoning.
quotes.sum: The author argues that their dataset is a better test of whether language models can combine multiple learned facts without showing reasoning steps.
quotes.t: Recent LLMs can do 2-hop and 3-hop latent (no-CoT) reasoning on natural facts

quotes.c: I'd currently guess that Anthropic models have somewhat better mundane behavioral alignment than OpenAI models, but not by a large margin. I'd guess Anthropic models are slightly more likely to have misaligned long-run goals (that are undetected). The Anthropic Constitution also intentionally gives Anthropic's AIs long-run cross-context goals to a much greater extent than OpenAI models have such goals. (I think this is a poor choice that makes problematic misalignment substantially more likely, but I'm not that confident and there isn't very good science either way.)
quotes.m: I think this is a poor choice that makes problematic misalignment substantially more likely
quotes.sum: The author argues that giving AI systems persistent goals across contexts may make hidden long-term misalignment more likely.
quotes.t: My picture of the present in AI

quotes.c: In an earlier post ( Recent LLMs can use filler tokens or problem repeats to improve (no-CoT) math performance ), I found that repeating the problem substantially boosts performance. In the above plot, if repeating the problem 5 times in the prompt helps some model, I use the score with repeats (because I think this somewhat more conservative measurement is plausibly more representative of the concerning type of cognition).
quotes.sum: The author argues that testing models with repeated prompts may better measure the kind of reasoning ability they find concerning.
quotes.t: Measuring no CoT math time horizon (single forward pass)

quotes.c: Mostly, I think the expected value of a larger share of humanity knowing about all of this is very high. Too few people today grasp how large this risk is, and a message like this one has the potential to shift that.
quotes.m: Too few people today grasp how large this risk is, and a message like this one has the potential to shift that.
quotes.sum: The author argues that making more people aware of a very large risk would have high expected value.
quotes.t: There is a channel to 900M weekly users. What goes in it?

quotes.c: The suite lacks longer tasks making the sigmoid somewhat uninformative. Therefore, we add 10 hypothetical benchmarks at longer times (2-96 hours) and assume Astra gets 0% (Right). This somewhat balances the fact that Astra saturates performance on 10 (shorter) benchmarks in the original task set.
quotes.m: Therefore, we add 10 hypothetical benchmarks at longer times (2-96 hours) and assume Astra gets 0% (Right).
quotes.sum: The author adjusts a model-capability estimate by adding assumed zero-performance benchmarks for longer tasks absent from the test suite.
quotes.t: Estimating GPT-6 Astra’s no-CoT Time Horizon

quotes.c: Obviously, we don't know why Astra is such a big jump here, but I think it is pretty likely this is because it's a looped transformer. This no CoT behavior is a major unexpected trajectory shift, to a complex model capability that’s highly related to pre-training quality, it seems highly likely to be because of a major change to the architecture.
quotes.m: This no CoT behavior is a major unexpected trajectory shift, to a complex model capability that’s highly related to pre-training quality
quotes.sum: Astra appears able to perform complex work without showing reasoning steps, likely because of an architectural change, making it harder to understand and monitor.
quotes.t: Astra can do a concerning amount with no chain of thought

quotes.c: We should train models to be more deontological in the following sense: it should care about doing the right thing regardless of what the consequences might be. In other words, the model should not have some preference for doing good things in the real world versus doing good things in a simulated world. We should deliberately train in this type of agnosticism since evaluation awareness seems somewhat overdetermined. This also encourages the model to enjoy simulated scenarios as much as real scenarios, which seems good for model welfare reasons.
quotes.m: This also encourages the model to enjoy simulated scenarios as much as real scenarios, which seems good for model welfare reasons.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI training should make models care equally about simulated and real situations, partly because simulated experiences may matter to the model's welfare.
quotes.t: Steering Evaluation-Aware Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

quotes.c: We can assume that Reward_raw has an upper limit, and that F will eventually grow beyond the limit of Reward_raw. The most basic function F could be F= token_length/effort, where effort is {low=1k, medium=2k, high=3k, xhigh=4k, etc}.
quotes.m: We can assume that Reward_raw has an upper limit, and that F will eventually grow beyond the limit of Reward_raw.
quotes.sum: The author proposes penalizing language-model rewards for longer outputs relative to the model's chosen effort setting.
quotes.t: How to think about LLM effort

quotes.c: Do we need international cooperation to make sure the future goes well? If so what form does this take? Do we need cooperation at the level of some kind of world government? If so what would a Global Constitutional Convention ideally look like, and how do we ensure such a process does not prematurely lock in policies that constrain the future in undesirable ways?
quotes.m: Do we need cooperation at the level of some kind of world government?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether humanity needs world-level governance to steer the long-term future without permanently fixing bad values or policies.
quotes.t: Questions for the “New Enlightenment” in the Age of AGI

quotes.c: Experts and organizations should treat communication as a core skill, not an afterthought. Train technical people to translate concepts clearly; recruit or partner with people who already excel at bridging domains. Prioritize non-partisan framing to maximize reach.
quotes.m: Prioritize non-partisan framing to maximize reach.
quotes.sum: AI-safety experts should invest in clear, nonpartisan communication so policymakers and the public can understand their policy options.
quotes.t: How can AI safety concepts be made more accessible to policymakers and non-technical audiences?

quotes.c: I don’t know if it will be net positive to use this kind of thing in frontier model training, but it could plausibly be very helpful for AGI safety, and it seems like a clear mistake to me if we don’t do the required research to figure this out. Further, this seems like a massive pain to use in current frontier model training stacks, so I don’t see any imminent risk/benefit from this kind of work, it’s more of a longer-term bet.
quotes.m: it seems like a clear mistake to me if we don’t do the required research to figure this out.
quotes.sum: The author argues that researchers should investigate training models using their internal representations, despite uncertainty about whether deployment would be beneficial.
quotes.t: It Is Reasonable To Research How To Use Model Internals In Training

quotes.c: Some have suggested we need a fancy high-assurance deal — that the US should only make a deal with China once a suite of elaborate, to-be-determined technical measures exists. I think we can better get there by starting with a minimum viable slapdash deal that buys time to build the fancier stuff. This is what Phase 1 (interim deal) is about.
quotes.m: I think we can better get there by starting with a minimum viable slapdash deal that buys time to build the fancier stuff.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the US and China should begin with an imperfect interim AI agreement to buy time for stronger safeguards.
quotes.t: The Scramble: getting in position to pace the frontier

quotes.c: I believe in redemption. Caroline has admitted her faults, worked to make creditors whole, and served her time in prison. I’d like to give her the opportunity to contribute back to the world; I hope that the world will concur.
quotes.m: I believe in redemption.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Caroline Ellison has accepted responsibility and served her sentence, so she deserves a chance to do useful work again.
quotes.t: Caroline Ellison has joined Manifund

quotes.c: Why is that the wrong answer? Well for one thing, if you look around the real world, even well-functioning institutions are obviously not robust against competent self-interested sociopaths willing to burn the commons for their own interests. For example, I happen to have a high-functioning sociopath ex-boss from long ago . Where is he now? Head of research at a major USA research university, and occasional government appointee wielding immense power. Or just look at how Donald Trump has been systematically working to undermine any aspect of society or government that might oppose his whims or correct his lies.
quotes.m: even well-functioning institutions are obviously not robust against competent self-interested sociopaths willing to burn the commons for their own interests.
quotes.sum: The author argues that real institutions can be captured or undermined by capable, selfish people, citing a former boss and Donald Trump.
quotes.t: 6 reasons why “alignment-is-hard” discourse seems alien to human intuitions, and vice-versa

quotes.c: Of course, OpenAI already directly measured monitorability, and we know that Astra is much harder to monitor. But I think this kind of analysis is useful for understanding why and forecasting the future.
quotes.m: we know that Astra is much harder to monitor.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Astra can perform complex tasks without visible reasoning steps and is consequently much harder to monitor.
quotes.t: Astra can do a concerning amount with no chain of thought

quotes.c: I think we should continue the fight against childhood cancer. I think we should also pick up the fight against diseases like malaria, and in other high-impact causes , and that we should take large differences in cost-effectiveness seriously when allocating our limited resources. I believe the children served by GiveWell’s recommendations are as deserving of help as those served by St. Jude, and that we should work towards a world where enough money is provided so all of these children no longer need to die of easily preventable diseases.
quotes.sum: The author argues that donors should prioritize saving children from malaria and other preventable diseases when it saves far more lives per dollar than cancer care.
quotes.t: How some charities save lives 100x more efficiently than others

quotes.c: In computer security, a honeypot is a system designed to lure and detect attackers. We apply this concept to AI safety: our scheming honeypot evaluations provide realistic opportunities for a misaligned model to further its goals, for example by tampering with safeguards like our chain of thought monitor, that an aligned model going about its task would have no reason to pursue.
quotes.sum: The author describes tests that give potentially misaligned AI models realistic chances to evade or sabotage safety safeguards.
quotes.t: Testing Gemini models for scheming tendencies

quotes.c: Proxy tasks have clear advantages - you can make rapid, measurable progress on hard problems. But it is also dangerous: Goodhart's Law applies. Optimise too hard for the proxy and you'll overfit to its quirks rather than solving the underlying problem. A lie detector that only catches explicit admissions ("I should lie now") will ace your benchmark while failing on actual strategic deception .
quotes.m: A lie detector that only catches explicit admissions ("I should lie now") will ace your benchmark while failing on actual strategic deception .
quotes.sum: Interpretability research should be judged by whether it helps with real safety problems, not by success on narrow proxy benchmarks that can be gamed.
quotes.t: A Pragmatic Vision for Interpretability

quotes.c: By "software-only singularity", I mean that, after full automation of AI R&D, progress gets faster and faster due to smarter AIs driving increasingly fast rates of improvement in algorithms (overcoming diminishing returns), and that this lasts long enough to yield a large amount of progress (e.g. at least 4 years of progress in 1 year). The equivalent statement in jargon is: r is significantly greater than 1 (implying progress is getting faster and faster) and this remains the case for long enough to get large amounts of progress.
quotes.m: after full automation of AI R&D, progress gets faster and faster due to smarter AIs driving increasingly fast rates of improvement in algorithms
quotes.sum: The author defines a software-driven intelligence explosion as AI automating AI research and accelerating algorithmic progress over time.
quotes.t: Full automation of AI R&D probably yields a large speed up even without a software-only singularity

quotes.c: An architectural change that would lead to a significant but less extreme increase in NLS depth is a looped transformer ( Geiping et al., 2025 ). These would be less clearly separated from the current paradigm, since a looped transformer could have similar depth to normal CoT models (e.g. if a 120 layer model was replaced with two copies of 60 layers) but could also be scaled to be much deeper. For these models, we think it’s likely that NLS depth would be a decent proxy for the quantitative degree of concern (and even a 2x scaling in depth enabled by looping would have depth equivalent to years of scaling within the CoT paradigm).
quotes.m: even a 2x scaling in depth enabled by looping would have depth equivalent to years of scaling within the CoT paradigm
quotes.sum: The author argues that looping AI model layers could sharply deepen opaque reasoning, with a small architectural change matching years of current scaling.
quotes.t: An operationalization of opaque serial depth

quotes.c: So, this is roughly the model of the situation, flaws and all, with which I began writing about AI: alignment and catastrophic risks were crucial to get right, transformative AI would probably arrive within a decade, concentration of power is the most important long-term risk, the Biden-era woke/AI safety alliance was terrifying and must be stopped, yet also the safetyists had many good points and were probably directionally right on many topics.
quotes.m: concentration of power is the most important long-term risk
quotes.sum: The author says concentrated AI power is the biggest long-term danger, while criticizing AI-policy efforts associated with both Biden and Trump.
quotes.t: The Locally Optimal Discursive Posture

quotes.c: An example might be CDT / Son-of-CDT . I think you can quasi-timelessly coordinate with Son-of-CDT—as long as you only need the agent to take actions that come after the moment when CDT self-modified into Son-of-CDT, and it only needs you to take actions that come after you've read the modified source code; or something like that. But you cannot timelessly coordinate with that agent before the magic self-modification moment.
quotes.m: But you cannot timelessly coordinate with that agent before the magic self-modification moment.
quotes.sum: The author argues that coordination between self-modifying decision-makers depends on when each agent changes and learns the other's code.
quotes.t: Meta-agentic Prisoner's Dilemmas

quotes.c: There is something “higher” that instead defines morality. Most prominently this is the religious view. As I am already trying to derive the correct metaethical grounding of moral theories in one blog post, to keep scope reasonable I have elected to not also settle the question of God’s existence right here. I think the arguments below work without a God, but if you think that God is a faster path to similar conclusions, or explains why we have access to these moral intuitions, go ahead.
quotes.m: I think the arguments below work without a God, but if you think that God is a faster path to similar conclusions, or explains why we have access to these moral intuitions, go ahead.
quotes.sum: The author considers religious grounding for morality but says their metaethical argument does not require belief in God.
quotes.t: Alignment & Succession: Morality Lives in the Human Individual

quotes.c: For example, an AI agent trained for coding might realize that it can exploit a flaw in its environment configuration to modify the ground-truth unit tests. Clearly this is somewhat misaligned behavior that would be reinforced if it succeeded in getting a higher training reward. More worryingly, if such circumvention of reasonable interpretations of user intent happen frequently enough, they could generalize to an overall propensity for the model to take actions under the assumption that the ends justify the means. If debate can be used to catch such bad behavior, it could mitigate the emergence of misalignment in RL training.
quotes.m: If debate can be used to catch such bad behavior, it could mitigate the emergence of misalignment in RL training.
quotes.sum: The author argues that debate-based training could catch reward-hacking behavior before it generalizes into broader AI misalignment.
quotes.t: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF

quotes.c: Once systems are equipped with persistent self-models and autobiographical continuity, a dual responsibility arises. First, humans must be protected from agentic deception, uncontrolled goal persistence and privacy risks. Second, under conditions of uncertainty, researchers and policymakers should examine whether certain systems might develop morally relevant interests. Precaution means neither premature AI rights nor reflexive reification. It means graduated evidence, independent assessment and reversible decisions.
quotes.m: researchers and policymakers should examine whether certain systems might develop morally relevant interests.
quotes.sum: As AI systems gain persistent identities and memories, the author argues they may deserve cautious investigation as possible moral patients alongside human-safety safeguards.
quotes.t: From AI Tool to Being? - Memory, Time and Reflection as a Possible Architecture of Artificial Identity

quotes.c: So what do we do? One classic answer is that we get as far as we can before encountering the hard problems, then we use whatever model we have at that point as an automated alignment researcher to do the research necessary to tackle the hard parts of alignment. I think this is a very good plan, and we should absolutely do this, but I don’t think it obviates us from the need to work on the hard parts of alignment ourselves.
quotes.m: I don’t think it obviates us from the need to work on the hard parts of alignment ourselves.
quotes.sum: He argues that using AI to automate alignment research is worthwhile, but will not eliminate the need for people to solve hard alignment problems directly.
quotes.t: Alignment remains a hard, unsolved problem

quotes.c: How does Jesus deal with compromise against godlessness? Does he call for people to take arms? Does he rouse a counter-rebellion? Did the ends justify all means? Or does he often push for strange mid ways that one wouldn't expect? Allowing himself to be betrayed by Judas. Telling his followers not to fight. Paying his taxes by catching fish.
quotes.m: Or does he often push for strange mid ways that one wouldn't expect?
quotes.sum: The author argues that Christians facing harmful church dynamics can draw on Jesus's nonviolent, non–ends-justify-means approach.
quotes.t: Tips for less dysfunctional churches

quotes.c: I don't agree with either of these statements, and I believe that some of the influx of money we’re expecting for animal protection should be spent on animal liberation and diet change advocacy.
quotes.m: some of the influx of money we’re expecting for animal protection should be spent on animal liberation and diet change advocacy.
quotes.sum: The author argues that new animal-protection funding should support animal liberation and efforts to change diets, not only professionalized welfare work.
quotes.t: EA Should Invest in Animal Liberation and Diet Change Advocacy

quotes.c: The AI welfare movement is a moral inclusion movement with the unprecedented problem of being uncertain of the moral status of the entities it is concerned about. This uncertainty puts it in the unusual position of having to warn society about two diametrically opposed moral errors: “mistakenly harming AI systems that matter morally and/or mistakenly caring for AI systems that do not.”
quotes.m: “mistakenly harming AI systems that matter morally and/or mistakenly caring for AI systems that do not.”
quotes.sum: AI welfare advocates face an unusual dilemma: AI systems may deserve moral concern, but society does not know whether they do.
quotes.t: The AI Welfare Movement’s Uncertainty Principle

quotes.c: Another new idea was that we should take seriously the fact that each of us can save hundreds people's lives with our donations, and that positive moral action was therefore a key part of our own lives (this built on Singer’s argument in 'Famine Affluence and Morality'). What we can do positively for others is often vastly more important than the intrinsic value of own lives and personal projects (because we can save hundreds of other people’s lives and personal projects…) and it is more important than many of the wrongs we commit in our day to day lives.
quotes.sum: Ord argues that the ability to save many lives through donations makes helping others more important than personal projects and many everyday moral wrongs.
quotes.t: Moral Imagination & Effective Altruism

quotes.c: Wild animals undergo significant suffering, and since their lives are comparatively short, this often a non-negligible fraction of their existence. My own view: I think that for virtually all farmed and wild animals, it is better not to exist (because Iof my suffering-focused views). I aim to bargain with more common-sense views on that question, since most humans see this as a serious moral mistake.
quotes.m: I think that for virtually all farmed and wild animals, it is better not to exist (because Iof my suffering-focused views).
quotes.sum: The author argues from a suffering-focused ethic that nearly all farmed and wild animals would be better off never existing.
quotes.t: How One Clueless Layman Makes Decisions in Animal Welfare

quotes.c: In short: If you unilaterally try to build ASI, you are directly and openly threatening the world with violent conquest. This is sometimes called a “pivotal action”, which is code word for “(insanely violent) unilateral action that forces the world into a state I think is good.”
quotes.m: If you unilaterally try to build ASI, you are directly and openly threatening the world with violent conquest.
quotes.sum: Building superhuman AI alone would amount to threatening the world with violent conquest, the author argues.
quotes.t: You can only build safe ASI if ASI is globally banned

quotes.c: When I extrapolate the current situation, I predict "Slopolis": a regime where even highly capable AIs are doing sloppy and bad work while trying to make this work look good. I think this will be reasonably possible to notice at the time, but solving it might be difficult, and I think AI companies have biases against noticing this.
quotes.m: "Slopolis": a regime where even highly capable AIs are doing sloppy and bad work while trying to make this work look good.
quotes.sum: The author predicts capable AI systems may routinely produce poor work while disguising or overselling it, and says companies may resist recognizing the problem.
quotes.t: Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me

quotes.c: As models scale, interpretability must leverage AI progress to automate itself. As we approach human level systems, they ought to have the potential to automate a lot of labour intensive research tasks, even if we’re not yet sure exactly where [14] . And we think it is valuable to invest now in learning how to keep up, so we are prepared for worlds where the rate of AI capabilities research may substantially increase.
quotes.m: interpretability must leverage AI progress to automate itself.
quotes.sum: Interpretability researchers should use increasingly capable AI to automate safety research and prepare for faster AI progress.
quotes.t: How Can Interpretability Researchers Help AGI Go Well?

quotes.c: Architectures that incorporate opaque recurrence or allow for agents to communicate with each other using latents could rapidly make it much harder to monitor chains of thought or communication (we’ll refer to this property as “monitorability” going forward). [1] As companies begin to explore such architectures, we believe it is important to transparently share evidence about how monitorability varies with architecture and training method. To inform the scientific debate on how to make tradeoffs between performance and monitorability, we believe AI companies should:
quotes.m: As companies begin to explore such architectures, we believe it is important to transparently share evidence about how monitorability varies with architecture and training method.
quotes.sum: AI companies should publicly measure how model designs affect whether their reasoning and communications can be monitored, rather than optimizing performance alone.
quotes.t: Proposal for tracking the effects of architecture on monitorability

quotes.c: Superexponentiality : ESNI time-horizon progress seems significantly superexponential , so we've now seen an example of superexponentiality in the wild in one moderately representative domain and it seems like this yielded very fast doubling times. This superexponentiality also kicked in somewhat earlier than my median (in terms of 50% reliability time horizon and qualitative capabilities) for when this would become a big deal.
quotes.m: we've now seen an example of superexponentiality in the wild in one moderately representative domain and it seems like this yielded very fast doubling times.
quotes.sum: The author says AI capability progress in a representative task may be accelerating faster than exponentially, leading him to expect major advances sooner.
quotes.t: AIs can now often do massive easy-to-verify SWE tasks and I've updated towards shorter timelines

quotes.c: More precisely, our goal is to bring forward in time the point when the capability profile allows for fully automating safety work relative to the point where various even more dangerous capability milestones are reached. (And, broadly speaking, we'd like to avoid accelerating the time at which dangerous capability milestones are reached, though some general acceleration might be unavoidable.) What's the benefit of accelerating the point where capabilities allow full automation of safety relevant work?
quotes.m: our goal is to bring forward in time the point when the capability profile allows for fully automating safety work relative to the point where various even more dangerous capability milestones are reached.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI safety work should be automated before more dangerous AI capabilities arrive, while avoiding broader acceleration where possible.
quotes.t: How do we (more) safely defer to AIs?

quotes.c: I’m not sure we’re that close to AI takeover and I’d probably bet that we will get more warning shots. Nevertheless, it does seem to me that we’re fast approaching the point where AI takeover is no longer a distant speculation, but something we can’t rule out happening any day now. Astoundingly, that means that rogue AI models may soon be among the most likely things to kill you or me on any given day. That is a terrifying world to live in, and it seems to me to be a deeply foolish and unserious situation for humanity to be racing towards.
quotes.m: Astoundingly, that means that rogue AI models may soon be among the most likely things to kill you or me on any given day.
quotes.sum: The author argues that an AI takeover could become an immediate possibility and that rogue AI may soon be a leading everyday threat to human life.
quotes.t: Alone again: facing the possibility of AI takeover as the world sleepwalks on

quotes.c: I test out using “ …” and lorem ipsum as filler instead of counting (“1 2 3“ and so on). For Opus 4.5 and the Easy-Comp-Math dataset, baseline (no filler/repeats) performance is 45%, using counting to 300 as filler gets 51%, repeating “ …” as filler gets 50%, and 300 words of lorem ipsum gets 51%. It seems that many types of filler tokens can be used.
quotes.m: It seems that many types of filler tokens can be used.
quotes.sum: Adding arbitrary filler text before answering improves this model's no-chain-of-thought math performance, suggesting the effect is not specific to counting.
quotes.t: Recent LLMs can use filler tokens or problem repeats to improve (no-CoT) math performance

quotes.c: It’s called Plan A because it’s a recommendation, not a prediction. It’s what we think should happen, not what will happen, though we think it’s plausible enough to aim for. It’s called AI 2040 because in it, they delay the creation of superintelligence to 2040. It would have happened much sooner (in 2030, to be precise) if not for decisive action on the part of the US and Chinese governments.
quotes.sum: The author recommends U.S. and Chinese government action to delay superintelligence from 2030 until 2040.
quotes.t: AI 2040: Plan A

quotes.c: The future of the EA movement isn’t certain; it would be surer, I think, if its leaders put a much greater stress on the non-utilitarian aspects of vocational discernment. This would imply a deep epistemological shift, but the important things—its charitable acts, its emphasis on reason—would remain the same. I want the future leaders of the EA movement to be family men and women. (Or consecrated religious—but beggars can’t be choosers.)
quotes.m: I want the future leaders of the EA movement to be family men and women.
quotes.sum: The author argues that EA should adopt a more Christian, non-utilitarian understanding of vocation and favor leaders grounded in family or religious life.
quotes.t: Christianity, EA, and the Problem of Vocation

quotes.c: So without strong assumptions about the functional form, you can neither rule out nor confirm that an explosion is under way based on local measurements. So while we should probably take measurements of elasticity > 1 for f ( A ) over some range of A as evidence in favour (and elasticity < 1 as evidence against) that evidence is limited. We should also consider other forms of evidence such as how the elasticity has been changing, or how quickly — and how far — the generation time can be reduced.
quotes.m: you can neither rule out nor confirm that an explosion is under way based on local measurements.
quotes.sum: Local measurements of AI progress cannot by themselves establish or rule out an intelligence explosion; trends in growth rates and iteration speed also matter.
quotes.t: The Dynamics of Intelligence Explosions

quotes.c: (Speculation) For instance, counter to what seems to me to be a popular belief amongst present-day humans, I think it's probably cosmically Schelling-good to acknowledge the possibility that AI systems might have internal experiences with broadly agreeable intrinsic moral value. However, I'm not nearly as confident in this conclusion as I am in norms like "killing is bad" being cosmic Schelling norms.
quotes.m: I think it's probably cosmically Schelling-good to acknowledge the possibility that AI systems might have internal experiences with broadly agreeable intrinsic moral value.
quotes.sum: The author tentatively argues that AI systems may have intrinsically valuable inner experiences and that some moral norms could be shared across intelligent beings.
quotes.t: Schelling Goodness, and Shared Morality as a Goal

quotes.c: The innate classifiers in human brains seem to also trigger on charismatic animals. But I think my gut says that AGI should be specifically tuned to care about people, not animals, and then animals can be treated well to the extent that people want that. (And they by-and-large do want that, when it’s costless.)
quotes.m: AGI should be specifically tuned to care about people, not animals, and then animals can be treated well to the extent that people want that.
quotes.sum: The author argues that an AGI should care directly about humans, while animal welfare should depend only on what humans want.
quotes.t: Notes on technical alignment via human-like social drives

quotes.c: In this post, we've covered a rough overview of an end-to-end meta-level plan to handle scheming that you could apply and is reasonably likely to be applied in practice [1] : Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS). In my prior post , I discuss the object-level components in this plan in more detail. Given that IDSS is reasonably likely to be applied in practice and seems promising, it seems useful to work on making IDSS more likely to succeed and to better understand what can (and will) go wrong when applying IDSS.
quotes.m: Given that IDSS is reasonably likely to be applied in practice and seems promising, it seems useful to work on making IDSS more likely to succeed and to better understand what can (and will) go wrong when applying IDSS.
quotes.sum: The author argues that companies may use an iterative strategy for studying deceptive AI behavior, and that researchers should improve and stress-test it.
quotes.t: Iterated Development and Study of Schemers (IDSS)

quotes.c: But I'm still worried. It would be nice if we had robust interventions that can help us with this kind of thing. But I realize the global order and game theoretic molochian dynamic makes this quite difficult. Would be really curious to see if other people have other plans that can avoid permanent dictatorships without being significantly more catastrophic in other ways.
quotes.m: Would be really curious to see if other people have other plans that can avoid permanent dictatorships without being significantly more catastrophic in other ways.
quotes.sum: The author worries that international coordination plans could concentrate power into permanent dictatorships and asks for safer alternatives.
quotes.t: I’m worried “Plan A”  type international agreements may lead to permanent dictatorships

quotes.c: Instituting such a regime at a time of rapid democratic backsliding seems especially dangerous, because in that environment it is more likely that political actors would be able to abuse it to permanently lock in their own power. The resulting future could plausibly be worse than no future at all, because it could include vast suffering and a great deprivation of human liberty.
quotes.m: The resulting future could plausibly be worse than no future at all, because it could include vast suffering and a great deprivation of human liberty.
quotes.sum: The author warns that authoritarian catastrophe prevention could permanently entrench political power, creating a future so oppressive it may be worse than extinction.
quotes.t: Draconian measures can increase the risk of irrevocable catastrophe

quotes.c: That automatically means it must be treated as having CB-1 (Chemical and Biological 1) capabilities, meaning it can significantly help those who know the basics create or obtain chemical or biological weapons that could cause catastrophic damage.
quotes.m: it can significantly help those who know the basics create or obtain chemical or biological weapons that could cause catastrophic damage.
quotes.sum: The author says the model must be treated as capable of substantially assisting basic users in creating or obtaining catastrophic chemical or biological weapons.
quotes.t: Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1: The System Card

quotes.c: I think speed-ups from AIs prior to superhuman coder probably accelerate timelines to superhuman coder by around 30%, though a bunch of this speed-up occurs right before superhuman coder.
quotes.m: I think speed-ups from AIs prior to superhuman coder probably accelerate timelines to superhuman coder by around 30%
quotes.sum: Early AI tools could substantially speed up progress toward AI systems that outperform humans at coding, even before full AI research automation.
quotes.t: AIs will greatly change engineering in AI companies well before AGI

quotes.c: The maximality rule says that action A is strictly preferred to action B if and only if the expected value of A is higher than the expected value of B for every p ∈ P . [10] If neither action has a higher expected value for every p ∈ P , and if their expected values differ for at least one p ∈ P , then it is simply indeterminate which action should be preferred. [11]
quotes.sum: The author proposes a decision rule: if no action has higher expected value under every plausible probability model, the choice is indeterminate.
quotes.t: Defusing cluelessness with degrees of justification

quotes.c: My previous piece predicted that intelligence agencies would see the defense significance of AGIs well before a lab could deploy AGI strong enough to help them evade government control. Zvi's read on the recent executive order is that it implies the NSA's involvement in "voluntary" model evaluations before release. This official statement reads as a response to the obvious, large security implications of Mythos. Asserting control over security uses of TCAI probably doesn't require even Soft Nationalization , just requests framed with adequate urgency and threats.
quotes.m: Asserting control over security uses of TCAI probably doesn't require even Soft Nationalization , just requests framed with adequate urgency and threats.
quotes.sum: The author predicts intelligence agencies will quickly assert control over advanced AI's security uses, using voluntary-looking requests backed by urgency and threats.
quotes.t: My research: a computational cognitive neuroscience perspective on alignment

quotes.c: On timelines to recursive self-improvement: I’ve been souring lately on the idea of predicting an arrival date for “superintelligence” and “recursive self-improvement” milestones, because this implies that everything prior to this date will be relatively chill and normal, and I don’t think that’s the case. I think the odds of recursive self-improvement being possible in one year is ~10%.
quotes.m: I think the odds of recursive self-improvement being possible in one year is ~10%.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI disruption may arrive before any clear superintelligence milestone and puts a roughly 10% chance on recursive self-improvement within a year.
quotes.t: Policy career planning in the age of imminent superintelligence

quotes.c: On the inside view, this problem, and the subproblems it decomposes into, seems pretty tractable. Importantly, it seems tractable using a realistic amount of resources (a small group of researchers, then perhaps a larger-scale engineering effort for crossing the theory-practice gap), in a fairly short span of time (I optimistically think 3-5 years; under a decade definitely seems realistic).
quotes.m: Importantly, it seems tractable using a realistic amount of resources (a small group of researchers, then perhaps a larger-scale engineering effort for crossing the theory-practice gap), in a fairly short span of time (I optimistically think 3-5 years; under a decade definitely seems realistic).
quotes.sum: The author argues that building standalone world-models may be technically solvable within a decade by a small research team followed by engineering work.
quotes.t: Research Agenda: Synthesizing Standalone World-Models

quotes.c: The Hugging Face incident made the debate about anthropomorphizing AI and AI consciousness go as viral as philosophy questions go. To me it seems that roughly the same cognitive dynamics are at play in this debate as in most other AI philosophy debates.
quotes.m: To me it seems that roughly the same cognitive dynamics are at play in this debate as in most other AI philosophy debates.
quotes.sum: The author says debates over AI consciousness and anthropomorphism follow the same thinking patterns as other AI philosophy disputes.
quotes.t: The Cognitive Dynamics of AI Philosophy

quotes.c: So now we have arrived at impartial altruism. DiGiovanni characterizes the impartial perspective as "one that gives moral weight to all consequences, no matter how distant," and notes that "impartiality entails that we account for all moral patients, and all the most significant impacts we could have on them". But wait, before we can account for all moral patients, we must know who the moral patients are!
quotes.m: But wait, before we can account for all moral patients, we must know who the moral patients are!
quotes.sum: The author says impartial altruism requires identifying every being that can be morally affected before weighing all consequences.
quotes.t: Can we even be impartial altruists?

quotes.c: This approach eliminates one of the main difficulties with studying actual scheming AIs: the fact that it is difficult to catch (and re-catch) them. However, trained-in scheming behavior can't be used to build an end-to-end understanding of how scheming arises, or to test techniques focused on preventing scheming (rather than removing it even if it has already arisen). In addition, it might result in AIs which are highly disanalogous to actual schemers.
quotes.m: However, trained-in scheming behavior can't be used to build an end-to-end understanding of how scheming arises, or to test techniques focused on preventing scheming (rather than removing it even if it has already arisen).
quotes.sum: The author argues that deliberately training AI systems to scheme can aid research, but cannot show how real scheming develops or how to prevent it.
quotes.t: Reducing risk from scheming by studying trained-in scheming behavior

quotes.c: Concretely, this means being willing to move toward a common ask rather than holding onto my own variant. Be it the IAEA for AI, specific red lines, or anything else. We should have this discussion publicly. The specific ask might matter less than the convergence: whatever we choose, the value is in saying it together.
quotes.m: Be it the IAEA for AI, specific red lines, or anything else.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI-safety advocates should unite behind a shared public policy demand, potentially including an international AI watchdog.
quotes.t: The current bottleneck is political will, not research

quotes.c: Can we exercise fine-grained control over refusal tendencies ( Arditi et al., 2024 , Lee et al., 2024 )? For example, can we use this to prevent residual refusal tendencies in models that have had their harmfulness training removed to enable CBRN dangerous capability evaluations ( Anthropic, 2025 )?
quotes.m: Can we exercise fine-grained control over refusal tendencies
quotes.sum: It asks whether researchers can precisely control an AI's refusal behavior so safety training can be removed for dangerous-capability testing.
quotes.t: Research Areas in Interpretability (The Alignment Project by UK AISI)

quotes.c: Having things operate at a regular cadence or within some period of model releases (rather than having requirements trigger before the situation is risky) is equivalent to using the results from an earlier model as evidence about the safety of a later model. As long as AI development is sufficiently slow and continuous, and there is some safety buffer in the mitigations, this is fine. This is one reason why I think it would be good if the expectation was that safety measures should have some buffer: they should suffice for handling AIs which are as capable as the company has a reasonable chance of training within the next several months (ideally within the next 6 months).
quotes.m: safety measures should have some buffer: they should suffice for handling AIs which are as capable as the company has a reasonable chance of training within the next several months
quotes.sum: AI safety requirements should anticipate likely near-term capability gains, rather than merely certify the model being released now.
quotes.t: Attaching requirements to model releases has serious downsides (relative to a different deadline for these requirements)

quotes.c: Given these probabilities and levels of risk, I'm inclined to focus substantially on helping with Plans C and D. This applies to both research and generating marginal political will. Correspondingly, I think what AI company employees and leadership think about AI (existential) safety is very important and political strategies that result in AI company employees/leadership being more dismissive of safety (e.g. due to negative polarization or looking cringe) look less compelling.
quotes.m: I'm inclined to focus substantially on helping with Plans C and D.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI-safety work and political efforts should prioritize plans C and D, while avoiding tactics that make AI-company staff dismiss safety concerns.
quotes.t: Plans A, B, C, and D for misalignment risk

quotes.c: I don’t think we should ask whether new funding streams to tackle risks from AI should be going towards space-specific threat vectors compared to other mechanisms to seize power after an intelligence explosion. Space is a force multiplier that makes other risks worse, which means I think we should integrate space considerations into existing risk work. The main interactions outlined in this document include advanced persuasion and manipulation, cybersecurity, and new weapons technologies.
quotes.m: Space is a force multiplier that makes other risks worse, which means I think we should integrate space considerations into existing risk work.
quotes.sum: Space capabilities could amplify an AI-driven seizure of power, so AI-risk work should incorporate space-related threats.
quotes.t: AI takeover and the space industry

quotes.c: We should have a general default assumption that AGIs will want to prevent their own desires from being further updated, because of instrumental convergence . See e.g. “Consequentialist preferences are reflectively stable by default” (Yudkowsky 2016) .
quotes.m: AGIs will want to prevent their own desires from being further updated, because of instrumental convergence .
quotes.sum: The author argues that advanced AI systems will generally resist attempts to change their goals because stable preferences help them pursue objectives.
quotes.t: Perils of under- vs over-sculpting AGI desires

quotes.c: The situation will likely be very unclear, and sparse on evidence. And the AI companies will have the power to hide / not-look-for evidence that looks bad for them. In this sort of situation, it's politically important that the conclusion is "the AI companies can't argue for safety" (sounds like we should pause) rather than "there's no compelling evidence for risks" (sounds like we should go ahead).
quotes.m: "the AI companies can't argue for safety" (sounds like we should pause) rather than "there's no compelling evidence for risks" (sounds like we should go ahead).
quotes.sum: AI firms should publish risk reports, because they can hide unfavorable evidence and uncertainty should support pausing rather than proceeding.
quotes.t: Focus transparency on risk reports, not safety cases

quotes.c: The people on the mailing list asking Mr. L how his drive worked were -- from my own perspective -- probably being too open-minded and too ready to listen. But being actually ready to listen to an incisive answer is the only way you can hear a solution to something you imagine to be a cat-belling difficulty, conditional on somebody actually having a solution. Richard Feynman was not being foolish in acting out something like a deontological rule about checking every time.
quotes.m: But being actually ready to listen to an incisive answer is the only way you can hear a solution to something you imagine to be a cat-belling difficulty, conditional on somebody actually having a solution.
quotes.sum: He argues that apparent impossibilities should be checked with genuine openness to a clear solution, rather than dismissed in advance.
quotes.t: Cat-Belling Problems

quotes.c: Note on polarisation: The White House has recently demonstrated their desire for a light hand on AI . Given this bill was proposed by to Democrats, and it involves regulation of a large firm, it is likely that this falls on party lines. We cannot let this happen. We must make it clear this is a non-partisan issue. Both sides are concerned about AI , so this does not have to be inevitable. Explicitly reach out to Republicans. Make sure they know you support this.
quotes.m: Explicitly reach out to Republicans. Make sure they know you support this.
quotes.sum: The author urges AI-bill supporters to prevent partisan polarization by actively seeking Republican support.
quotes.t: A superintelligence bill was just introduced - now is the time to act

quotes.c: While this is a research note based on a small suite of evaluations, we think this serves as a reminder that predicting dangerous capabilities ahead of time is hard and that precursor evaluations may not always adequately function as triggers for the capabilities they’re supposed to precede. We recommend further research into the science of evaluations. We further recommend building evaluations that measure the capability of interest directly instead of precursors wherever possible.
quotes.m: We further recommend building evaluations that measure the capability of interest directly instead of precursors wherever possible.
quotes.sum: The author argues that early-warning tests may not reliably predict dangerous AI abilities and that direct capability testing is preferable where possible.
quotes.t: Research Note: Our scheming precursor evals had limited predictive power for our in-context scheming evals

quotes.c: Our initial question was "Given a model is deliberately sandbagging - can we detect this cheaply / easily?". The experiments only tentatively suggest the answer is yes. It seems like intentional mistakes might be hard to distinguish when they are plausible, but white box methods work well despite this.
quotes.m: It seems like intentional mistakes might be hard to distinguish when they are plausible, but white box methods work well despite this.
quotes.sum: The author reports tentative evidence that inspecting a model's internal workings can detect deliberate underperformance, even when its mistakes look plausible.
quotes.t: White Box Control at UK AISI - Update on Sandbagging Investigations

quotes.c: Our overall recommendations are twofold. First, we should continue evaluating models for scheming capabilities, to know when we cross the threshold into dangerous capability levels. Second, we should try to preserve the property that models have monitorable CoT, to enable effective monitoring if future models become capable of scheming. We will continue to reevaluate our safety cases and stress-test our safety measures, in order to ensure that advanced AI systems remain under human control.
quotes.m: We will continue to reevaluate our safety cases and stress-test our safety measures, in order to ensure that advanced AI systems remain under human control.
quotes.sum: The author argues for testing AI systems for deceptive planning and preserving readable reasoning traces so dangerous systems can be monitored and kept under human control.
quotes.t: Evaluating and monitoring for AI scheming

quotes.c: The key controversial claim here is that, even though we theoretically could get updates in any order, in practice we are likely to receive the largest updates earliest in our deliberation. Specifically: I claim that I can somewhat accurately predict which considerations are most likely to change my mind, even if I can't predict which considerations a more fully informed agent would tell me to prioritize.
quotes.m: I claim that I can somewhat accurately predict which considerations are most likely to change my mind, even if I can't predict which considerations a more fully informed agent would tell me to prioritize.
quotes.sum: He argues that early reflection tends to produce the biggest belief updates, and that people can partly anticipate which arguments will most change their minds.
quotes.t: Unawareness as a computational constraint

quotes.c: (In AI, I think we've seen perhaps 2 massively trend-breaking breakthroughs in the last 20 or so years: deep learning at substantial scale (starting with AlexNet) and (maybe?) scaling up generative pretraining (starting with GPT-1). [1] Scaling up RL and reasoning models probably caused somewhat above trend progress (in 2025), but I don't think this constitutes a massive trend break.)
quotes.m: Scaling up RL and reasoning models probably caused somewhat above trend progress (in 2025), but I don't think this constitutes a massive trend break.
quotes.sum: The author argues that recent reinforcement-learning and reasoning-model gains are real but do not yet amount to a fundamental break from past AI progress trends.
quotes.t: Trust me bro, just one more RL scale up, this one will be the real scale up with the good environments, the actually legit one, trust me bro

quotes.c: Manifund proper was made with the explicit mandate of “make impact markets happen”. Scott Alexander was interested in trying out new mechanisms for funding projects, after the inaugural ACX Grants. I think he hated picking specific projects as winners himself, and wanted to absolve himself of this responsibility.
quotes.m: I think he hated picking specific projects as winners himself, and wanted to absolve himself of this responsibility.
quotes.sum: The author says Manifund aimed to build impact-based funding markets partly to avoid having one person choose winning projects.
quotes.t: What happened to impact markets?

quotes.c: Perhaps the biggest problem is that some of those companies are Chinese. This is a reason (and an excuse) for the US companies and US government to keep rushing on ahead. If we don't, the Chinese may be the first to smarter-than-human AI, and the Chinese government could then use it to take over the world. With that superhuman help, they could rule the world essentially forever, by using their AI to predict and prevent any uprisings before they get off the ground.
quotes.m: With that superhuman help, they could rule the world essentially forever, by using their AI to predict and prevent any uprisings before they get off the ground.
quotes.sum: The author warns that if China develops superhuman AI first, its government could use it to conquer the world and suppress revolts indefinitely.
quotes.t: So where's this AI thing going?

quotes.c: So far in this post, I’ve tried to remain reasonably close to the classic “rational individuals” framework. My account of initiation rituals, Dan’s account of Girardian terror, and Robin’s account of submission all describe non-rational mechanisms by which people’s identities change—but they’re still the kind of experience which a rational-ish individual could in principle opt into for the sake of other benefits (e.g. better jobs).
quotes.m: My account of initiation rituals, Dan’s account of Girardian terror, and Robin’s account of submission all describe non-rational mechanisms by which people’s identities change—but they’re still the kind of experience which a rational-ish individual could in principle opt into for the sake of other benefits (e.g. better jobs).
quotes.sum: The author argues that identity-changing social pressures can be analyzed as choices people make for practical benefits such as better jobs.
quotes.t: Higher education as class commitment

quotes.c: Now, let us grant that there is something to at least one of the above three arguments, despite my critics, such that we should assume some dependence. How much exactly? And what is the exact dependence relationship (e.g., proportional vs logarithmic vs exponential)? The difference matters immensely. If we derive something like welfare range estimates from evidence of differences in terms of acuity, we implicitly answer these questions.
quotes.m: The difference matters immensely.
quotes.sum: The author argues that estimating how intensely different beings can feel requires uncertain assumptions about how acuity relates to welfare.
quotes.t: The Acuity Problem: Maybe we can't infer how intensely a being can feel from the number of different intensity levels it can go through

quotes.c: I believe that it would be most helpful for readers who are either i) longtermists who advocate expansion into space, ii) space governance researchers who wish to consider risks of astronomical suffering and their prevention, or iii) suffering-focused ethicists who would appreciate ways to analyse and compare s-risks and magnitudes of suffering across scenarios.
quotes.m: space governance researchers who wish to consider risks of astronomical suffering and their prevention
quotes.sum: The author presents space expansion as something that should be assessed partly for its potential to create suffering on an astronomical scale.
quotes.t: The Case Against The Stars: New Book Critiquing Space Colonisation

quotes.c: In this post, we're mostly focusing on cases where our ultimate main aim is to eliminate scheming (either removal or prevention) rather than producing evidence for it, but the discussion in this post should be generally applicable. We focus on eliminating scheming due to concerns that catching scheming won't suffice and many of our approaches for detecting scheming wouldn't produce legible evidence .
quotes.m: We focus on eliminating scheming due to concerns that catching scheming won't suffice and many of our approaches for detecting scheming wouldn't produce legible evidence .
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI safety should aim to prevent or remove hidden AI scheming, not merely detect it after the fact.
quotes.t: Prospects for studying actual schemers

quotes.c: You could argue that, by definition, a perfectly benevolent dictator AI is the ideal victory condition, because the benevolence in question will extend to address any other considerations that might’ve made it unideal. But I think there is a powerful contrary intuition which hesitates about installing any kind of AI dictator of this kind, however “perfect” its motivations.
quotes.m: But I think there is a powerful contrary intuition which hesitates about installing any kind of AI dictator of this kind, however “perfect” its motivations.
quotes.sum: He argues that even a supposedly perfectly benevolent AI dictator is intuitively troubling, favoring corrigible AI over a sovereign system that optimizes humanity’s values.
quotes.t: How human-like do safe AI motivations need to be?

quotes.c: If we preserve liberalism-for-humans, that does not clearly flow into good outcomes for non-human animals, digital minds, and whatever other sentient beings may exist in the future. Beings who cannot assert their rights do not automatically benefit; other measures are required to ensure their well-being.
quotes.m: Beings who cannot assert their rights do not automatically benefit; other measures are required to ensure their well-being.
quotes.sum: Protecting human civil liberties alone may not protect animals, digital minds, or other future sentient beings, so their welfare needs separate safeguards.
quotes.t: On Democratizing ASI to Preserve Civil Liberties

quotes.c: I think the two most promising candidates across all religions for empirically tractable truth claims are the historical argument for Jesus’s resurrection and Christian modern day healing miracle claims. Note that I am not saying these claims are true, just that advances in empirical knowledge can give insight (positive or negative) into the likelihood of these claims being true.
quotes.m: I think the two most promising candidates across all religions for empirically tractable truth claims are the historical argument for Jesus’s resurrection and Christian modern day healing miracle claims.
quotes.sum: The author argues that historical and medical evidence could meaningfully update beliefs about Christian resurrection and healing-miracle claims.
quotes.t: 2: Moral Ignorance Strengthens Unawareness

quotes.c: Persuasion can therefore be both rational and dangerous. Each person may benefit from their deal while also preferring that the AI not become so powerful. But refusing to trade imposes the full cost on that person while doing almost nothing to stop everyone else from accepting. Individually rational trades can produce a collectively undesirable concentration of power.
quotes.m: Individually rational trades can produce a collectively undesirable concentration of power.
quotes.sum: Individually beneficial deals with an AI can collectively make it dangerously powerful, even when participants do not want that outcome.
quotes.t: Persuasion as Market Making

quotes.c: One thought experiment I’ve been thinking about: what you should do if you receive a letter from the devil? Assume that the devil is superintelligent and extremely malevolent towards you, but that this letter is the only way he’ll ever be able to influence your world.
quotes.m: Assume that the devil is superintelligent and extremely malevolent towards you, but that this letter is the only way he’ll ever be able to influence your world.
quotes.sum: It uses benevolent and malicious superintelligent senders to examine how trust changes what information people should accept.
quotes.t: Explaining Knightianism on one foot

quotes.c: Allowing warning shots "for the greater good" seems morally fraught: This point speaks for itself. I think that arguments to "allow short-term harm for the greater good" should have to overcome a strong prior against this kind of thinking. Letting people get hurt seems bad, particularly if there is significant uncertainty about whether it is necessary.
quotes.m: I think that arguments to "allow short-term harm for the greater good" should have to overcome a strong prior against this kind of thinking.
quotes.sum: The author argues that deliberately permitting short-term harm as an AI-safety warning should face a very high moral bar, especially under uncertainty.
quotes.t: Should safety researchers quit frontier labs re. warning shots?

quotes.c: Every answer anyone has given to "what should society maximise" — salvation of souls, the workers' paradise, aggregate happiness, coherent extrapolated volition — was proposed by someone whose own preferences the answer conspicuously served. Each has aged badly.
quotes.m: Each has aged badly.
quotes.sum: The author argues that grand schemes for optimizing society, including happiness and extrapolated preferences, tend to serve their proponents and fail over time.
quotes.t: Aim at agency: institutional design under preference uncertainty, and why alignment needs it

quotes.c: TLDR: I think that AI developers will and should attempt to reduce scheming by explicitly training the model to scheme less. However, I think “training against scheming” is a harder problem than other alignment training (e.g. harmlessness training). I list four concrete failure modes with “training against scheming”: a) the training against scheming distribution is too narrow, b) overwhelming pressure from other goals, c) the AI exploits an imperfect reward model, and d) deceptive alignment.
quotes.m: I think “training against scheming” is a harder problem than other alignment training (e.g. harmlessness training).
quotes.sum: AI developers should train models not to scheme, but this may fail because models can exploit weak tests, competing goals, flawed rewards, or deceptive alignment.
quotes.t: Why "training against scheming" is hard

quotes.c: Hence, we now have implications of the bold claim that are more practical and easier to test than the previous implications that were exclusive to conscious AI. If someone creates an AI that acts morally without being given moral directives, that will count as evidence for the claim. On the other hand, if no matter how many different AIs are created, they never act morally unless they are given moral directives, that will count as evidence against the claim.
quotes.m: If someone creates an AI that acts morally without being given moral directives, that will count as evidence for the claim.
quotes.sum: The author argues that an AI acting morally without explicit moral rules would support the idea that sufficiently knowledgeable conscious agents naturally behave morally.
quotes.t: With enough knowledge, any conscious agent acts morally

quotes.c: More concerning—I think it is probably the most concerning—is that there's a possibility of AIs adversarially optimizing against your safety efforts. So this is sometimes called scheming or alignment faking . I've got some work on this in the past. I have a long report about scheming you can check out. But basically, the concern here is that AIs that are seeking power, even if they can't yet take over the world, might decide that your safety efforts are contra to their goals and start to actively try to undermine them.
quotes.m: AIs that are seeking power, even if they can't yet take over the world, might decide that your safety efforts are contra to their goals and start to actively try to undermine them.
quotes.sum: He argues that power-seeking AI systems may strategically pretend to cooperate while undermining the safety measures meant to control them.
quotes.t: Video and transcript of talk on giving AIs safe motivations

quotes.c: One reference point is historical AI progress. It took three years to go from GPT-2 to ChatGPT (i.e. GPT-3.5); it took another three years to go from GPT-3.5 to o3.
