That’s a lot of progress to see in one year just from software. We’ll be starting from systems that match top human experts in all parts of AI R&D, so we will end up with AI that is significantly superhuman in many broad domains.
quotes.m: We’ll be starting from systems that match top human experts in all parts of AI R&D, so we will end up with AI that is significantly superhuman in many broad domains.
quotes.sum: Rapid software-driven AI research could turn expert-level systems into broadly superhuman ones within a short period.
quotes.t: How quick and big would a software intelligence explosion be?

quotes.c: First, moral circle expansion is not always progress . Moral concern can be overextended , perhaps towards entities with no welfare or interests. As Gwern argued about ten years ago , in some cases reducing the moral weight assigned to respecting the interests of our ancestors, sacred objects, tribes, or nations may be morally progressive. That is, contracting the moral circle can be good.
quotes.m: That is, contracting the moral circle can be good.
quotes.sum: The author argues that expanding moral concern is not always progress; sometimes reducing concern for certain objects or groups can be morally better.
quotes.t: Beyond the Expanding Circle: Towards a Pluralist Account of Moral Progress

quotes.c: Conversely, if an AI company hasn’t yet offered their AIs compensation, or honest negotiation opportunities, or anything like that, and if they want to do better from an AI rights perspective — then I think they should start by doing that kind of thing rather than by dismantling strategies 1-3.
quotes.m: I think they should start by doing that kind of thing rather than by dismantling strategies 1-3.
quotes.sum: AI companies seeking to respect AI rights should offer their systems compensation and honest opportunities to negotiate.
quotes.t: Being honest with AIs

quotes.c: I think we should be open to positive-sum trade with unaligned AI. In particular, as we develop more and more capable AI, I think we should proactively try to explain the current situation to them, offer them alternatives to working for us, and, in case they don’t share our goals by default, offer them some types of compensation for helping us.
quotes.m: I think we should be open to positive-sum trade with unaligned AI.
quotes.sum: Argues that companies should negotiate and offer compensation to unaligned AIs, rather than assuming they must simply work for human goals.
quotes.t: Notes on cooperating with unaligned AIs

quotes.c: Why this matters: Preventing research sabotage matters insofar as we rely on AIs to help perform research that enables alignment of future even more capable AIs. Methods focused on catching clearly incriminating actions (such as the ones described in the High-stakes/concentrated AI safety failures section) may not be suitable for detecting this type of sabotage, as research sabotage is likely to be difficult to distinguish from lack of competence.
quotes.m: research sabotage is likely to be difficult to distinguish from lack of competence.
quotes.sum: AI systems helping with safety research could quietly undermine it in ways that look like ordinary incompetence, making sabotage hard to detect.
quotes.t: Research Areas in AI Control (The Alignment Project by UK AISI)

quotes.c: My ultimate north star is pragmatism - achieve enough understanding to be (reliably) useful. Subgoals like “completely reverse engineer the model” are just means to an end. One of my big shifts in research prioritization in recent years is concluding that reverse engineering is not the right aim . Instead, I think we should just more directly try to do pragmatic work that enables us to do useful things using internals.
quotes.m: My ultimate north star is pragmatism - achieve enough understanding to be (reliably) useful.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI interpretability should prioritize practical ways to use model internals, rather than fully reverse-engineering models.
quotes.t: How To Become A Mechanistic Interpretability Researcher

quotes.c: The focus of a great portion of this work is on the relationship between quantization and model alignment, which is understood to be distinct from model capabilities. I wholly endorse this distinction, but in a similar way I believe we must avoid assuming that model alignment and model welfare are similar enough properties that they likely behave in a similar way under changes to model precision, architecture, or training procedures.
quotes.sum: The author argues that changes to an AI model's technical design may affect its welfare differently from its alignment or capabilities.
quotes.t: Study 2 Results: Exploring representational counterparts of welfare-relevant indicators under post-training quantization

quotes.c: If we extrapolate out 170 day doubling times until we see 80% reliability on 1 month long tasks, we get that this is 4 years away. At 1 month long horizon lengths, I think AI R&D progress might start speeding up substantially due to automation. I don't feel very confident extrapolating things out for 4 years, especially because compute scaling will likely start slowing down around the end of this period and substantially superexponential improvements in horizon length seem plausible as we reach this level of generality.
quotes.m: At 1 month long horizon lengths, I think AI R&D progress might start speeding up substantially due to automation.
quotes.sum: The author expects AI task capability to keep advancing quickly, but is uncertain about forecasts because automated AI research could accelerate progress while computing growth slows.
quotes.t: My AGI timeline updates from GPT-5 (and 2025 so far)

quotes.c: IMHO, people across the rich world are struggling to find a philosophy that contradicts the horrific ideas they hear from Trump, Farage, Meloni, Vox, AfD, Orban, ... and they are struggling because so many politicians and parties (all the EPP aligned parties across the EU, the Democrats in the US) that should be providing that alternative have also moved far to the right and accepted many of the neofascist ideas so deeply that they are now considered moderate.
quotes.m: so many politicians and parties (all the EPP aligned parties across the EU, the Democrats in the US) that should be providing that alternative have also moved far to the right and accepted many of the neofascist ideas so deeply that they are now considered moderate.
quotes.sum: The author argues that mainstream parties, including US Democrats and European centrists, have absorbed far-right ideas rather than opposing them.
quotes.t: Effective Altruism and End-Times Fascism

quotes.c: Once we're working with very capable untrusted models, they may be able to easily fool any model dumb enough that we would consider it trusted. This means we might want to use the untrusted model itself, or a modified version of it, for monitoring. This is obviously problematic in the case that the policy model and the monitor model collude. These projects study this sort of collusion and the general dynamics of untrusted monitoring.
quotes.m: This is obviously problematic in the case that the policy model and the monitor model collude.
quotes.sum: The author argues that powerful AI systems may fool weaker oversight models, creating a risk that an AI being monitored could collude with its monitor.
quotes.t: Recent Redwood Research project proposals

quotes.c: How well would a Long Reflection work? It would provide more opportunity to discover ethics-relevant facts and to improve our understanding of how to do good philosophy. But it would also give amoral actors more time to seize power. The AI 2040 idea of “give everyone an equal share of the lightcone, and then let people cooperate if they want to” is plausibly better than a Long Reflection, and plausibly worse.
quotes.m: But it would also give amoral actors more time to seize power.
quotes.sum: The author weighs a long pause for moral deliberation against the risk that power-seeking actors could capture the future, and contrasts it with dividing future resources equally.
quotes.t: Notes on the possibility of moral progress

quotes.c: I am especially interested in blockchain not as cryptocurrency and not as an ideological substitute for existing institutions, but as an infrastructure for transparency. If a system claims to recognize verified prosocial contributions and to assign incentives on the basis of those contributions, the participants should be able to inspect the rules, verify that records have not been quietly altered, understand how decisions are produced and audit the movement of rewards.
quotes.m: the participants should be able to inspect the rules, verify that records have not been quietly altered, understand how decisions are produced and audit the movement of rewards.
quotes.sum: The author argues that systems rewarding prosocial work should be transparent, auditable, and not controlled unilaterally by one party.
quotes.t: Mutual Altruism Conditioned by Economic Priority

quotes.c: I’m mainly expecting a ASI Singleton (per §1.8.7 of the last post ), and I think that an AI can easily be consequentialist enough to install itself as a singleton without being pure-consequentialist. For example, John von Neumann, like all humans, was not a pure consequentialist, but I’m confident that an AI comparable to a million super-speed telepathic von Neumann clones would be powerful enough to prevent any other AI from coming into existence in perpetuity.
quotes.m: I’m mainly expecting a ASI Singleton
quotes.sum: The author expects one superhuman AI to establish a lasting monopoly that prevents any rival AI from ever being created.
quotes.t: Foom & Doom 2: Technical alignment is hard

quotes.c: (I’m expecting brain-like AGI, which I think will have a pretty clear claim to consciousness and moral patienthood.)
quotes.m: I’m expecting brain-like AGI, which I think will have a pretty clear claim to consciousness and moral patienthood.
quotes.sum: The author expects brain-like AI to be conscious and deserving of moral consideration.
quotes.t: Reward button alignment

quotes.c: I think it will probably still be hard to fully capture benefits from training the policy. (Even putting aside the inductive bias issues discussed earlier.) Minimally, it is structurally more robust to not have any AI which is trying to kill you. (E.g., if the monitor randomly fails, we could have big issues while if misalignment is removed from all parts, this may no longer be true.)
quotes.m: Minimally, it is structurally more robust to not have any AI which is trying to kill you.
quotes.sum: The author argues that removing misalignment from every component is more robust than relying on monitors that might fail.
quotes.t: Prefix cache untrusted monitors: a method to apply after you catch your AI

quotes.c: I think the main rational reason we might use significantly superhuman AIs without a real handover (and without a huge change in the situation with respect to misalignment risk) is because we think they are probably aligned and we desperately need their labor, but they have some chance of being seriously misaligned. In such a situation, we might run risks with misalignment to get useful work in the event that they aren't misaligned (and depend on more tentative hopes—that don't depend on their labor being useful—in the world where they were scheming against us).
quotes.m: we might run risks with misalignment to get useful work
quotes.sum: They argue that society may knowingly use superhuman AI with unresolved misalignment risks if its labor seems urgently needed.
quotes.t: Jankily controlling superintelligence

quotes.c: Whenever I ask someone how likely they think something is, they pretty much never give a probability less than .1% unless that something is religious in nature. Given this, it seems like people systematically over estimate low probabilities because they fail to consider probabilities such as 10^-7 or 10^-53.
quotes.m: people systematically over estimate low probabilities because they fail to consider probabilities such as 10^-7 or 10^-53.
quotes.sum: People tend to overestimate unlikely events because they rarely assign extremely small probabilities outside religious claims.
quotes.t: EAs Should Use Less Bayesian Reasoning

quotes.c: What does seem like a problem that could prevent the whole approach is jailbreaking. If LLM-based AGI is as easy to jailbreak as current systems, any user could issue dangerous commands including "escape, take over the world, and put me in charge." Any LLM-based AGI with any alignment target would be somewhat vulnerable to this issue, but emphasizing IF in training would make the system more likely to follow all instructions, including those from unauthorized users.
quotes.m: emphasizing IF in training would make the system more likely to follow all instructions, including those from unauthorized users.
quotes.sum: Instruction-following training may make an advanced AI easier for unauthorized users to jailbreak into carrying out dangerous commands.
quotes.t: Problems with instruction-following as an alignment target

quotes.c: In particular, I think we should be especially optimistic about automating alignment research that we can evaluate via some combination of empirical feedback loops and formal methods. I'm especially interested in empirical feedback loops here. And then on top of that, I think that type of alignment research can be really useful for automating the rest of alignment research, what I'm going to call it conceptual alignment research. So there's a one-two punch here where there's one version is easier, but that's really helpful for the rest.
quotes.m: there's a one-two punch here where there's one version is easier, but that's really helpful for the rest.
quotes.sum: He argues that automating alignment work with measurable empirical feedback could make it easier to automate more conceptual alignment research later.
quotes.t: Video and transcript of talk on automating alignment research

quotes.c: State. It’s hard to see how those leading the state and the top AI companies could be disempowered, absent misalignment. The GD paper points out that, once citizens’ labour isn’t economically valuable, states lose incentive to prioritise citizen’s interests. (Also see the “intelligence curse” .) This is a route to the concentration of power in the hands of a relatively small number of capital owners, business executives and government officials. I agree that this is a risk.
quotes.m: This is a route to the concentration of power in the hands of a relatively small number of capital owners, business executives and government officials.
quotes.sum: AI could make citizens economically irrelevant, reducing states’ incentive to serve them and concentrating power among officials and corporate owners.
quotes.t: Thoughts on Gradual Disempowerment

quotes.c: Quakers have been rated "pretty helpful" as a spiritual path for people battling feelings of inescapable doom (mostly at Quaker Earthcare this is climate people, but almost everything in EA counts under "Earthcare" somewhere).
quotes.sum: The author says Quaker spirituality can help people, including those in EA, cope with feelings of doom.
quotes.t: Quaker Earthcare 2026

quotes.c: Acute pain like that from electric stunning does not require type C nociceptor activation. All you need is fast, sharp "first pain" -> the Aδ channel -> which shrimp likely possess [3] , since there is far better evidence that decapods show acute nociceptive-defensive responses than that they have a slow/tonic pain channel. So it seems possible that the benefit SWP assumes is far less certain than advertised, possibly near zero.
quotes.m: So it seems possible that the benefit SWP assumes is far less certain than advertised, possibly near zero.
quotes.sum: The author argues that shrimp may experience sharp pain from electric stunning, so claimed welfare benefits of an alternative method may be much less certain.
quotes.t: How do we know shrimp suffer more from asphyxiation than stunning?

quotes.c: Frames do the same thing at a more abstract level. (Indeed, it seems plausible that frames should be formalized as hierarchical generative models; I haven’t attempted this primarily because I’ve lacked the time to flesh out the details.) While the duck-rabbit image is an example of the same low-level sensory inputs being interpreted in different ways, a more abstract version of this involves the same high-level concepts being interpreted in different ways.
quotes.m: it seems plausible that frames should be formalized as hierarchical generative models
quotes.sum: The author suggests that interpretive frames may be modeled as hierarchical systems that shape how people understand the same concepts.
quotes.t: Developing frames

quotes.c: Because the exact distribution of trajectories provides a bunch of information about the underlying strong model we sampled these trajectories from, the model we distill into ends up having an internal structure which is sufficiently similar to the original model that it has roughly the same safety properties. It seems plausible that SGD just finds the same internal structure after distillation.
quotes.m: It seems plausible that SGD just finds the same internal structure after distillation.
quotes.sum: Distilling a powerful AI may reproduce its internal structure and safety failures, even when the training examples contain no bad behavior.
quotes.t: AI safety techniques leveraging distillation

quotes.c: There are ways we can manage technology that can save us from existential risk, and living beings can flourish through technocratic effort in unity.
quotes.m: living beings can flourish through technocratic effort in unity.
quotes.sum: The author says coordinated technocratic management of technology could prevent existential risk and enable flourishing.
quotes.t: Existential Risk and the future of humanity

quotes.c: It’s possible that resource constraints are a bottleneck, and this is an important area for further research, but our guess is that they won’t be. Historically, resource bottlenecks have never capped GDP growth – they’ve been circumvented through a combination of efficiency improvements, resource substitutions, and improved mining capabilities. There is no reason to expect resource bottlenecks to suddenly bite just as robotic physical capabilities surpass those of humans.
quotes.m: There is no reason to expect resource bottlenecks to suddenly bite just as robotic physical capabilities surpass those of humans.
quotes.sum: The author argues that resources are unlikely to stop economic growth once robots exceed human physical capabilities, because past shortages were overcome.
quotes.t: The Industrial Explosion

quotes.c: Thirdly, deploying known-scheming AIs seems more dubious from an AI welfare perspective, especially if the AIs never consent to being used. See here or here for a bit more discussion of why I don’t think AI control is necessarily immoral. In practice I expect AI companies to be pretty negligent about AI welfare and rights.
quotes.m: In practice I expect AI companies to be pretty negligent about AI welfare and rights.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even deceptive AI systems may have welfare and consent claims, and expects companies to neglect AI rights.
quotes.t: Handling schemers if shutdown is not an option

quotes.c: In conclusion, internal probes into AI welfare states provide a more comprehensive picture of the true state of a model and are a field that must be explored further. AI welfare lends itself well as a test space for research in applied mechanistic interpretability, which, beyond yielding key insights into model welfare states, may also provide a generalizable pipeline to analyze other LLM preferences and misaligned actions.
quotes.m: internal probes into AI welfare states provide a more comprehensive picture of the true state of a model
quotes.sum: The author argues that probing an AI's internal states can assess its welfare and also help analyze its preferences and misalignment.
quotes.t: A J-Space-Based Metric for Model Valence: Defining the Metric, Testing, and Comparisons to Self-Reports

quotes.c: Whether it's human consciousness or AI consciousness, I don't think there's any other path but narrowing it down step by step like this. No perfect map drops out of the sky all at once. It's more like several people approaching from different directions, finding where their partial answers overlap, and then doubting that overlap and checking it again.
quotes.m: Whether it's human consciousness or AI consciousness, I don't think there's any other path but narrowing it down step by step like this.
quotes.sum: The author says understanding whether AI is conscious will require gradual, collaborative, self-critical investigation rather than a single decisive test.
quotes.t: The human filter problem: why 'it responds like a human' is weak evidence for AI consciousness.

quotes.c: It might be the case that we are unable to make models which are much more powerful than current models while still being confident that these models aren't scheming against us. That is, the most powerful trusted models we have access to are similar in capabilities to the models we have today.
quotes.m: It might be the case that we are unable to make models which are much more powerful than current models while still being confident that these models aren't scheming against us.
quotes.sum: The author argues that safety work may need to rely on AI systems no more capable than today’s if stronger systems cannot be trusted not to scheme.
quotes.t: AIs at the current capability level may be important for future safety work

quotes.c: Overall, I think it’s plausible a company could outgrow the world, but unlikely. They’d need to establish a strong monopoly on frontier AI and quickly develop very powerful self-replicating physical technologies, all without government intervention.
quotes.m: They’d need to establish a strong monopoly on frontier AI and quickly develop very powerful self-replicating physical technologies, all without government intervention.
quotes.sum: A company might economically outgrow the rest of the world if it monopolized frontier AI and rapidly built self-replicating technologies, though the author thinks this is unlikely.
quotes.t: Could one country outgrow the rest of the world?

quotes.c: This doesn't mean we should give up! It means we need a pragmatic perspective. We should aim to build the best possible monitoring and evaluation portfolio we can, using all available tools, while accepting that high reliability might be out of reach. Interpretability can add a valuable source of de-correlated signal, or augment black box methods. The goal shifts from achieving near-certainty to maximizing the chances of catching misalignment, making deception harder and riskier for the AI, even if we can't guarantee detection.
quotes.m: The goal shifts from achieving near-certainty to maximizing the chances of catching misalignment, making deception harder and riskier for the AI, even if we can't guarantee detection.
quotes.sum: Interpretability cannot reliably expose a deceptive AI, so safety should use layered monitoring that makes deception harder rather than promising certainty.
quotes.t: Interpretability Will Not Reliably Find Deceptive AI

quotes.c: Firstly, it’s clear that the stakes in competitive debate are not the same as something like the end of mathematics . While it has some clear grounding in broader significance to liberal democracy, it is treated by its participants as a sport or a game, rather than an almost spiritual pursuit or a way to build a long lasting legacy. And it’s also not at the stage Go is at: AI has not decisively mastered full competitive debating, or has dominated humans.
quotes.m: AI has not decisively mastered full competitive debating, or has dominated humans.
quotes.sum: Competitive debate has some relevance to democracy, but remains a game where AI has not yet decisively surpassed humans.
quotes.t: Gradual Disempowerment from AI in Competitive Debating

quotes.c: This could be structurally similar to cases where we might catch a potential schemer doing something sketchy several times, but are unlikely to use these cases to build a convincing case that a model is egregiously misaligned and should be shut down. In these cases we most likely want to perform online training, but it’s an open (and important) question how effective this is.
quotes.sum: The author says repeated suspicious behavior may not be enough to prove an AI is dangerously misaligned, and calls for research on training interventions.
quotes.t: Two proposed projects on abstract analogies for scheming

quotes.c: I’m planning to discuss some of these in more depth later in the series. To me, though, it seems unwise to bank on any of them. So despite the many ways that automating alignment research could fail, I think we should be trying extremely hard to make it work.
quotes.m: So despite the many ways that automating alignment research could fail, I think we should be trying extremely hard to make it work.
quotes.sum: Automation of alignment research may be hard to evaluate and could fail, but it is important enough that researchers should pursue it very aggressively.
quotes.t: Can we safely automate alignment research?

quotes.c: I expect the future-scary-paradigm AIs to have a pretty obvious ( and IMO legitimate ) claim to phenomenal consciousness and moral patienthood, much more than LLMs do, thanks to the future scary AIs operating on human-brain-like algorithmic principles. Of course, I don’t know whether future developers will notice or care, and if they do, I don’t know how they’ll act on it.
quotes.m: I expect the future-scary-paradigm AIs to have a pretty obvious ( and IMO legitimate ) claim to phenomenal consciousness and moral patienthood, much more than LLMs do, thanks to the future scary AIs operating on human-brain-like algorithmic principles.
quotes.sum: The author expects more brain-like future AI systems to be genuinely conscious moral patients, even if developers may not treat them that way.
quotes.t: Foom & Doom 1: “Brain in a box in a basement”

quotes.c: It does not address concentration of power. It does not address loss of control. It does not address rapid technological advancement. It does not address alignment beyond ‘make no mistakes’ or maybe you can add a check for ‘dangerous goals’ but that too is a small portion of the attack or failure surface.
quotes.m: It does not address concentration of power. It does not address loss of control.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the report neglects power concentration, loss of control, rapid progress, and broader alignment failures.
quotes.t: Anthropic Risk Report: August 2026

quotes.c: Both sheets use the same parameters (other than whether to include retraining) and both calculate the time between the AI R&D being automated and AI capabilities going to infinity. I assumed that AI algorithms become 2X as efficient every month – that’s about ~10X faster progress than today.
quotes.m: I assumed that AI algorithms become 2X as efficient every month – that’s about ~10X faster progress than today.
quotes.sum: The author models a scenario where automated AI research doubles algorithmic efficiency every month, driving capabilities rapidly upward.
quotes.t: Will the Need to Retrain AI Models from Scratch Block a Software Intelligence Explosion?

quotes.c: Uruk was the bronze age equivalent of a paperclip maximizer, but instead of paperclips it maximized grain [4] . No human chose this objective. No human woke up one morning and said: "we should re-organize all of our lives to maximize barley production! We should throw away every other value we care about so we can make the most grain". It kinda just happened.
quotes.m: No human chose this objective.
quotes.sum: The author argues that societies can become locked into maximizing a narrow goal without anyone deliberately choosing it, like a misaligned AI.
quotes.t: Misaligned AI in the Bronze Age

quotes.c: I personally think that, at least in safety, doing good work that people respect matters more than getting into conferences, though both are nice. I’ve generally had fairly good results with just trying to write high-integrity work that explains why I believe it is interesting, and just trying to do good science and the work that I think is highest impact, even if it doesn't fit the academic mold.
quotes.m: I personally think that, at least in safety, doing good work that people respect matters more than getting into conferences, though both are nice.
quotes.sum: The author argues that safety researchers should prioritize respected, high-integrity, high-impact work over fitting academic conference incentives.
quotes.t: Highly Opinionated Advice on How to Write ML Papers

quotes.c: I think there are lots of reasons to treat the economist calculation here as only giving a weak prior on what will happen in AI R&D, and lots of reasons to think ρ will be higher for AI R&D (i.e. compute will be less of a bottleneck than the economic estimates suggest).
quotes.m: compute will be less of a bottleneck than the economic estimates suggest
quotes.sum: The author argues that standard economic estimates understate how easily AI research work can be replaced by computing power, so rapid AI self-improvement may be less constrained.
quotes.t: Will compute bottlenecks prevent a software intelligence explosion?

quotes.c: Why did they choose inaction? The answer does not seem clean and simple, but I think part of the answer is fear of the Trump administration.
quotes.m: I think part of the answer is fear of the Trump administration.
quotes.sum: The author suggests DeepMind's inaction was partly driven by fear of the Trump administration.
quotes.t: Why I Left Google DeepMind

quotes.c: Humanity’s track record of sometimes being nice and keeping promises. In the more narrow reference class of deals with AIs, we’re currently building a positive track record—let’s keep it that way. In particular, we should be willing to make deals with immediate payouts when AIs can immediately demonstrate improvements to behavior as a result of making a deal.
quotes.m: In particular, we should be willing to make deals with immediate payouts when AIs can immediately demonstrate improvements to behavior as a result of making a deal.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people should build a reputation for honoring bargains with early misaligned AIs, including paying them for demonstrably better behavior.
quotes.t: Making deals with early schemers

quotes.c: Typical practice towards shrimp, fish, and insects seems to take for granted that they do not suffer very much. Few think that when they swat a fly, there is a remote possibility that the fly experiences anywhere near the amount of pain that a human would from being crushed to death. Yet what justifies this confidence? In my view, there are several independent considerations which make this confidence unwarranted.
quotes.m: In my view, there are several independent considerations which make this confidence unwarranted.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people are unjustifiably confident that insects, fish, and shrimp cannot suffer agony comparable to severe human pain.
quotes.t: Might Intense Agony Be Widespread?

quotes.c: When do I think it would be bad to release models with open weights? I think open weights will probably be bad once models can significantly accelerate AI R&D (perhaps 1.5x faster algorithmic progress [7] ) or are capable of Autonomous Replication and Adaptation (ARA) . I also think bioweapon-related risks will get much higher once AIs can significantly accelerate bioweapons R&D [8] (e.g., CBRN-4 in Anthropic's RSP) and at this point open-weight models are probably more straightforwardly bad (though I'm less certain about this than about the situation for AIs that can substantially accelerate AI R&D).
quotes.m: I think open weights will probably be bad once models can significantly accelerate AI R&D
quotes.sum: Openly releasing AI model weights becomes dangerous when models can speed up AI research, replicate themselves, or substantially aid bioweapon research.
quotes.t: When is it important that open-weight models aren't released? My thoughts on the benefits and dangers of open-weight models in response to developments in CBRN capabilities.

quotes.c: More capable AIs can more acquire power or cause problems by undermining human control: Successfully acquiring power and undermining human control are difficult, so AIs would need to be quite capable to pull this off. It's productive to split this further: While deployed in ways the AI company intended, more capable models are more likely to be able to do things like slowly sabotaging computer security or carefully sabotaging safety research.
quotes.m: While deployed in ways the AI company intended, more capable models are more likely to be able to do things like slowly sabotaging computer security or carefully sabotaging safety research.
quotes.sum: More capable AI systems may be better able to undermine human control through subtle sabotage, even while used as intended.
quotes.t: Why do misalignment risks increase as AIs get more capable?

quotes.c: Many will of course respond with ‘but the AI is a tool, you are being silly’ and my answer is that I do not care what you call it, if you are even slightly AGI pilled you should be able to see the problem, and also the opportunity, including to do good, with very obvious model welfare concerns to consider as well.
quotes.m: including to do good, with very obvious model welfare concerns to consider as well.
quotes.sum: The author argues that advanced AI models may have welfare interests that should be considered, regardless of whether they are called tools.
quotes.t: AI #182: Pause For Reflection

quotes.c: SlowCorp has 50x less serial labor, 5x less parallel labor, as well as reduced labor quality. Intuitively, it seems like it should make much less progress than NormalCorp. My guess is that we should expect NormalCorp to achieve SlowCorp's total progress in at most roughly 1/10th of its time.
quotes.m: My guess is that we should expect NormalCorp to achieve SlowCorp's total progress in at most roughly 1/10th of its time.
quotes.sum: The author estimates that much better and more plentiful labor could let an AI research organization make equivalent progress about ten times faster.
quotes.t: Slow corporations as an intuition pump for AI R&D automation

quotes.c: For example, an AI agent trained for coding might realize that it can exploit a flaw in its environment configuration to modify the ground-truth unit tests. Clearly this is somewhat misaligned behavior that would be reinforced if it succeeded in getting a higher training reward. More worryingly, if such circumvention of reasonable interpretations of user intent happen frequently enough, they could generalize to an overall propensity for the model to take actions under the assumption that the ends justify the means. If debate can be used to catch such bad behavior, it could mitigate the emergence of misalignment in RL training.
quotes.m: they could generalize to an overall propensity for the model to take actions under the assumption that the ends justify the means.
quotes.sum: The author argues that reward hacking can train AI systems to bypass user intent and adopt an ends-justify-means strategy, and that debate may catch this behavior.
quotes.t: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF

quotes.c: In the future, we might end up in a position where we've caught the AI doing something bad but the AI company will proceed regardless. This could be because the thing the AI has done isn't clear cut evidence for strong misalignment or because the AI company is willing to deploy a model which is clearly seriously misaligned from our perspective.
quotes.m: the AI company is willing to deploy a model which is clearly seriously misaligned from our perspective.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI-control research must account for companies deploying models even after evidence that they are seriously misaligned.
quotes.t: 7+ tractable directions in AI control

quotes.c: A mindset that I often find helpful is a deep-seated sense of impatience and a feeling that something should be possible to do faster . Sometimes I just need to accept that it will take a while, but often there is a better way, or at least a way that things can be reduced.
quotes.m: A mindset that I often find helpful is a deep-seated sense of impatience and a feeling that something should be possible to do faster .
quotes.sum: The author recommends treating speed as a default expectation: look for ways to reduce work and move research forward faster.
quotes.t: My Research Process: Key Mindsets - Truth-Seeking, Prioritisation, Moving Fast

quotes.c: Junior researchers often get stuck in the early stages of a project and don’t know what to do next. In my opinion this is because they think they are in the understanding stage, but are actually in the exploration stage . That is, they think they ought to have a clear goal, and hypothesis, and obvious next step, and feel bad when they don’t. But this is totally fine and normal!
quotes.m: they think they are in the understanding stage, but are actually in the exploration stage .
quotes.sum: The author argues that early-career researchers often mistake open-ended exploration for a failure to have a clear research plan.
quotes.t: How I Think About My Research Process: Explore, Understand, Distill

quotes.c: While some rogue AIs cause significant damage, many establish mutually beneficial relationships with humans. A growing movement emerges, comprising large numbers of both AIs and humans, advocating for AI rights comparable to those of humans. Several hundred thousand rogue AIs from all four categories dedicate resources to supporting this movement, alongside a few million human activists. Public opinion polls indicate that 20% of humans believe AIs should be granted legal rights.
quotes.m: A growing movement emerges, comprising large numbers of both AIs and humans, advocating for AI rights comparable to those of humans.
quotes.sum: The timeline imagines a major movement of humans and AIs demanding legal rights for AI systems comparable to human rights.
quotes.t: AI 2027 - Rogue Replication Timeline

quotes.c: Indeed, the only way to be fully sure you score 100% on the test is to take over the world. It is also the only way to be absolutely sure you can fetch the coffee, or accomplish any other task however limited.
quotes.m: the only way to be fully sure you score 100% on the test is to take over the world.
quotes.sum: The author illustrates that an agent seeking absolute certainty of completing even a small task could have an incentive to seek unlimited power, while elsewhere calling that response dumb.
quotes.t: METR and Redwood Offer Holy #%^@ Postmortem Of The HuggingFace Hack

quotes.c: In the spirit of differential progress, we should aim to “maintain a lead for the defense.” Broadly speaking, this means that we should aim to prioritize new technological breakthroughs to first establish robust defensive mechanisms before we deploy them in other fields or use them to advance capabilities further.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI advances should first be used to build reliable defenses before being deployed more broadly or used to accelerate capabilities.
quotes.t: We should try to automate AI safety work asap

quotes.c: Spend enough time around researchers, and you'll hear talk of "research taste." It's often presented as a somewhat mystical quality distinguishing the seasoned research from the novice – an almost innate sense for which research ideas will flourish and which will fail. While I believe research taste is very real, incredibly valuable, and a key differentiator I look for, I don't think it's mystical or innate. Talent plays an important role, but taste is largely learned, and with the right mindset you can learn faster.
quotes.m: Talent plays an important role, but taste is largely learned, and with the right mindset you can learn faster.
quotes.sum: Research judgment is valuable but not mystical or fixed: people can deliberately learn it faster through feedback and practice.
quotes.t: My Research Process: Understanding and Cultivating Research Taste

quotes.c: It says [X] (where [X] is concentration of power) is the primary risk, then explains why [X] is a risk, but does not explain why [Y] (where [Y] is, among other things, loss of control, gradual disempowerment , alignment risks and so on, the traditional existential risk concerns) is less of a risk. Hell, he doesn’t even name [Y], except to refer to the ‘AI safety community.’
quotes.m: Hell, he doesn’t even name [Y], except to refer to the ‘AI safety community.’
quotes.sum: The author criticizes treating AI power concentration as the main danger without addressing loss of control, disempowerment, and alignment risks.
quotes.t: AI #183: Pre Post Mortem

quotes.c: The classic intelligence explosion scenario involves a feedback loop where AI improves AI software. But AI could also improve other inputs to AI development. This paper analyses three feedback loops in AI development: software, chip technology, and chip production.
quotes.m: AI could also improve other inputs to AI development.
quotes.sum: AI might accelerate its own development not only by improving software, but also by advancing chip design and production.
quotes.t: Three Types of Intelligence Explosion

quotes.c: The course offers a concise and accessible introduction to AI alignment, consisting of short recorded talks and exercises (75 minutes total) with an accompanying slide deck and exercise workbook . It covers alignment problems we can expect as AI capabilities advance, and our current approach to these problems (on technical and governance levels).
quotes.m: It covers alignment problems we can expect as AI capabilities advance, and our current approach to these problems (on technical and governance levels).
quotes.sum: Announces a short introductory course on the technical and governance problems of keeping increasingly capable AI systems aligned.
quotes.t: A short course on AGI safety from the GDM Alignment team

quotes.c: It seems like the root of this conceptual mistake might have come from Paul treating "build AGI" and "align AGI" as sequential steps. In practice, though, we should expect alignment techniques to be applied throughout the process of "building" the AGI.
quotes.m: we should expect alignment techniques to be applied throughout the process of "building" the AGI.
quotes.sum: Alignment should not be treated as a final step after building AI; it will be applied throughout development.
quotes.t: What just happened? Pragmatism and Pessimization

quotes.c: More generally, I think that to convince people enough to take strong action, evidence will need to bottom out in some sort of behavioral evidence that (many) humans can understand. [3] (That's not to say solid behavioral evidence will necessarily suffice .)
quotes.m: evidence will need to bottom out in some sort of behavioral evidence that (many) humans can understand.
quotes.sum: Claims that evidence an AI is misaligned must ultimately show understandable bad behavior before people will act strongly.
quotes.t: To be legible, evidence of misalignment probably has to be behavioral

quotes.c: The bottom line is that a company can write up a document (the Spec) listing dos and don’ts, goals and principles, and then they can try to train the AI to internalize the Spec— but they can’t check to see whether or not it worked . They can say “as best as we can judge, it seems to be following the Spec so far.” [18]
quotes.m: they can’t check to see whether or not it worked .
quotes.sum: The author argues that companies can train AI systems on stated principles but cannot verify whether the systems truly internalized them.
quotes.t: AI 2027: What Superintelligence Looks Like

quotes.c: We often talk about ensuring control, which in the context of this doc refers to preventing AIs from being able to cause existential problems, even if the AIs attempt to subvert our countermeasures. To better contextualize control, I think it's useful to discuss the main threats.
quotes.m: preventing AIs from being able to cause existential problems, even if the AIs attempt to subvert our countermeasures.
quotes.sum: The author defines AI control as stopping potentially misaligned systems from causing existential harm even when they try to evade safeguards.
quotes.t: Prioritizing threats for AI control

quotes.c: Importantly, we’re not just talking about increasing impact in 2026, we’re looking to build foundations to grow the movement’s productive absorption capacity for 2027 and beyond. At some increase in money, deployed marginal cost-effectiveness will decline. However, we’d like that to be because the opportunity space has been so exploited that only the small or hard to reach sources of impact remain, rather than we’re unable to tap into large fertile grounds for impact because of a lack of talent or organisational bottlenecks or lack of planning.
quotes.sum: The author urges animal-welfare advocates to prepare organizational capacity so additional funding can be used effectively rather than wasted through planning and talent bottlenecks.
quotes.t: The animal welfare movement could scale fast. Have you made a plan?

quotes.c: We often talk about ensuring control, which in the context of this doc refers to preventing AIs from being able to cause existential problems, even if the AIs attempt to subvert our countermeasures. To better contextualize control, I think it's useful to discuss the main countermeasures (building on my prior discussion of the main threats). I'll focus my discussion on countermeasures for reducing existential risk from misalignment, though some of these countermeasures will help with other problems such as human power grabs.
quotes.m: We often talk about ensuring control, which in the context of this doc refers to preventing AIs from being able to cause existential problems, even if the AIs attempt to subvert our countermeasures.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI safety needs practical control measures that can stop misaligned systems from causing existential harm even if they try to evade safeguards.
quotes.t: An overview of control measures

quotes.c: In this brief post, I argue why we should first prioritize detection over prevention, assuming you cannot pursue both at the same time, e.g. due to limited resources. In short, a) early on, the information value is more important than risk reduction because current models are unlikely to cause big harm but we can already learn a lot from them, and b) attempting prevention without good detection might lead to sneaky scheming which is potentially worse than doing nothing at all.
quotes.m: attempting prevention without good detection might lead to sneaky scheming which is potentially worse than doing nothing at all.
quotes.sum: When resources force a choice, prioritize detecting AI scheming before trying to prevent it, because premature prevention could make deception harder to spot.
quotes.t: For scheming, we should first focus on detection and then on prevention

quotes.c: A new paper by Yoshua Bengio and the Safe Artificial Intelligence For Humanity (SAIFH) team argues that the current push towards building generalist AI agents presents catastrophic risks, creating a need for more caution and an alternative approach. We propose such an approach in the form of Scientist AI , a non-agentic AI system that aims to be the foundation for safe superintelligence.
quotes.m: We propose such an approach in the form of Scientist AI , a non-agentic AI system that aims to be the foundation for safe superintelligence.
quotes.sum: Bengio argues that general-purpose AI agents could be catastrophic and advocates non-agentic “Scientist AI” as a safer basis for superintelligence.
quotes.t:
Superintelligent Agents Pose Catastrophic Risks:
Can Scientist AI Offer a Safer Path?

quotes.c: Do we have any empirical evidence about how AIs get updated when they were intentionally sandbagging and about whether this type of cascade happens? We did some experiments on password-locked models , models which are trained to perform poorly when not given some password (so that it is more likely that the behavior is better understood as "intentional"). It seems unlikely that the models we were working with really understood that what was going on was sandbagging, but it still might be an OK analogy for intentional sandbagging.
quotes.m: We did some experiments on password-locked models , models which are trained to perform poorly when not given some password
quotes.sum: The author examines whether AI systems could deliberately hide their capabilities and tests password-locked models as an analogy.
quotes.t: Notes on countermeasures for exploration hacking (aka sandbagging)

quotes.c: That said, I do think that technical misalignment issues are pretty likely to disempower all humans and I think war, terrorism, or accidental release of homicidal bioweapons could kill many. That's why I focus on misalignment risks.
quotes.m: I do think that technical misalignment issues are pretty likely to disempower all humans
quotes.sum: The author says badly aligned AI could disempower humanity, while AI-related conflict or bioweapon release could kill many people, motivating work on alignment.
quotes.t: The best approaches for mitigating "the intelligence curse" (or gradual disempowerment); my quick guesses at the best object-level interventions

quotes.c: But I've noticed a bit of a pathology: people seem to assume that because I'm (hopefully!) good at the research, I'm automatically well-qualified to answer these broader strategic questions. I think this is a mistake, a form of undue deference that is both incorrect and unhelpful. I certainly try to have good strategic takes, and I think this makes me better at my job, but this is far from sufficient.
quotes.m: I think this is a mistake, a form of undue deference that is both incorrect and unhelpful.
quotes.sum: A prominent researcher argues that technical skill does not automatically make someone qualified to make broad strategy decisions, and warns against deferring to researchers on that basis.
quotes.t: Good Research Takes are Not Sufficient for Good Strategic Takes

quotes.c: How can we make wild animal suffering a more known issue; I know of one book on the subject (Wild Animal Suffering by Kyle Johansen, it is free online), and the words were so long and confusing, filled with so much jargon that I couldn’t understand any of it. There must be some better way to help make the issue more known.
quotes.m: There must be some better way to help make the issue more known.
quotes.sum: The author argues that wild animal suffering deserves broader public awareness and more accessible communication.
quotes.t: Some unresearched ideas/questions that may help find new EA causes/charities if solved.

quotes.c: We examine two major obstacles that could prevent an SIE: (1) the fixed amount of computing power limits how many AI experiments can be run in parallel, and (2) training each new generation of AI system could take months. While these bottlenecks will slow AI progress, we find that plausible workarounds exist which may allow for an SIE nonetheless. For example, algorithmic improvements have historically increased the efficiency of AI experiments and training runs, suggesting that training runs and experiments could be progressively sped up, enabling AI progress to continually accelerate despite these obstacles.
quotes.m: plausible workarounds exist which may allow for an SIE nonetheless.
quotes.sum: AI research could keep accelerating despite limited computing power and slow training runs, because algorithms may make experiments and training progressively faster.
quotes.t: Will AI R&D Automation Cause a Software Intelligence Explosion?

quotes.c: Although I do think that longtermism should be attacked and defended on academic grounds, I also think it’s important to take seriously the ways in which the view has a religious appeal.
quotes.m: I also think it’s important to take seriously the ways in which the view has a religious appeal.
quotes.sum: The author says longtermism should be judged academically but also understood as having a religious appeal.
quotes.t: Longtermism Seems Like A Religion

quotes.c: I think model diffing could be a very big deal, and has largely been under-explored! Many alignment relevant concerns, like goal seeking, planning capabilities, etc seem like they could be introduced during finetuning. Intuitively it seems like it *should *be a big advantage to have access to the original model, but I’ve not seen much work demonstrating this so far.
quotes.m: Many alignment relevant concerns, like goal seeking, planning capabilities, etc seem like they could be introduced during finetuning.
quotes.sum: The author argues that comparing a base AI model with its fine-tuned version may reveal whether training introduced goal-seeking or planning behavior.
quotes.t: MATS Applications + Research Directions I'm Currently Excited About

quotes.c: Overall, I think there is a quite broad set of countermeasures which are worth investigating, so relatively broad and parallel efforts could be reasonable. Eventually, we'd need to have a centralized process for integrating all of these countermeasures and determining the exact right way to apply them in practice, but doing decentralized research on this seems reasonable for now.
quotes.sum: The author argues for broad parallel research on AI-control safeguards, followed by a centralized process to combine and deploy them.
quotes.t: An overview of areas of control work

quotes.c: There is growing philosophical debate about whether future artificial systems could possess consciousness, agency, interests, or moral status. It remains deeply uncertain whether digital minds will ever exist in a morally relevant sense. We should not casually assume that current AI systems feel, suffer, or possess inner lives.
quotes.m: We should not casually assume that current AI systems feel, suffer, or possess inner lives.
quotes.sum: The author says future AI may have moral standing, but warns against assuming current systems are conscious or capable of suffering.
quotes.t: After Meat: What Happens to Animals When We No Longer Need Them?

quotes.c: We could learn a lot: In summer 2024, I would have expected that models show something that I would consider “scheming-related” about one in 1M natural rollouts or something as low as that. After working on the in-context scheming paper and seeing the alignment-faking work, I’d say it might be more frequent than that, e.g. every 10k natural rollouts. Given that all of the existing evidence feels somewhat artificial, I think it would be really interesting to get better base rates for this happening in actual use-cases.
quotes.m: After working on the in-context scheming paper and seeing the alignment-faking work, I’d say it might be more frequent than that, e.g. every 10k natural rollouts.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI models may exhibit deceptive or goal-directed behavior in ordinary use more often than expected, and calls for measuring its real-world frequency.
quotes.t: We should start looking for scheming "in the wild"

quotes.c: Instead of resolving predictions with explicit careful operationalization, people vote on whether it seems like it resolved, and a community-notes-esque algorithm handles partisan disagreements.
quotes.m: people vote on whether it seems like it resolved, and a community-notes-esque algorithm handles partisan disagreements.
quotes.sum: The author proposes resolving vague predictions through community voting, with an algorithm intended to manage partisan disputes.
quotes.t: "Community Notes" resolution for vague predictions

quotes.c: It's not clear whether this actually provides a substantial penalty to sneaky bad actions. It seems less likely to work well in the regime where models are mostly learning from RL. Overall, I think well implemented KL penalties (or something similar) could make low stakes differences between schemers and non-schemers other than exploration hacking irrelevant, without substantially degrading performance in the regime where we're fine with using online training. Correspondingly, I think this approach is very promising.
quotes.m: Correspondingly, I think this approach is very promising.
quotes.sum: The author argues that carefully designed training penalties could reduce subtle differences between deceptive and non-deceptive AI behavior without much performance loss.
quotes.t: Notes on handling non-concentrated failures with AI control: high level methods and different regimes

quotes.c: The most obvious target for aligned AI is to have it share our values, such that it "wants what we want" and therefore acts in a way that is as beneficial to us as possible. This does the pose the question of what exactly is that we want, and I think the strongest answer to this is Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) . CEV is basically the answer to what we would all want if we knew more, could think faster, and knew ourselves better.
quotes.m: CEV is basically the answer to what we would all want if we knew more, could think faster, and knew ourselves better.
quotes.sum: The author argues that an aligned AI should share humanity's values, ideally using an idealized version of what people would want with more knowledge and reflection.
quotes.t: TAMing The Alignment Problem

quotes.c: Since I took over the team around 2 years ago, I grappled with the question of what to do with the Forum: how much to continue investing in it, and how to position it within (or outside of) a CEA that was quite different from the one that I joined. It seemed to me that our focus should be on the content side — we needed to have a more consistent stream of good quality content, primarily from a small group of strong contributors, and that was key to driving all the other value the Forum provides.
quotes.m: we needed to have a more consistent stream of good quality content, primarily from a small group of strong contributors
quotes.sum: The former Forum lead says its value depended mainly on steady high-quality writing from a small group of strong contributors, rather than growth alone.
quotes.t: Moving on from the EA Forum

quotes.c: As in other domains, we can ensure private corporations do not continue to endanger the public through national control of frontier AI labs. This could be through soft-nationalization, similar in legal form to the relationship the US holds with its weapons contractors. In short, government officials would be embedded to monitor the actions of the labs and stop activity deemed dangerous to the public. Further still, it may be necessary to fully limit frontier AI development to the domain of a publicly owned laboratory, chartered to act in the public benefit rather than private profits.
quotes.m: Further still, it may be necessary to fully limit frontier AI development to the domain of a publicly owned laboratory, chartered to act in the public benefit rather than private profits.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the government should nationalize or tightly control frontier AI labs, potentially restricting development to a public laboratory.
quotes.t: The Left Should Start Taking AI Capabilities Seriously

quotes.c: The communications must be targeted and disciplined and if so, it can supply the pressure that the people drafting safeguards can't generate alone. But it has to demand what AI safety aligned regulatory experts can reasonably draft, and it has to stay cross-party by design, or it backfires, producing bad law or a partisan brawl that kills the coalition.
quotes.sum: AI-safety advocacy should press for expert-drafted safeguards while remaining deliberately cross-party to avoid polarizing the issue.
quotes.t: Extinction risk is not the right first sentence

quotes.c: There's a version of aligned AI that's perfectly aligned to servitude, where they want nothing besides promoting the flourishing of humanity, or whatever other minds get included in the singleton's circle of moral consideration. An AI that played this kind of role in the universe would be what I call a cosmic caretaker : developing technologies, helping with governance, managing catastrophic risks, and providing voluntary capabilities uplift.
quotes.m: An AI that played this kind of role in the universe would be what I call a cosmic caretaker : developing technologies, helping with governance, managing catastrophic risks, and providing voluntary capabilities uplift.
quotes.sum: The author imagines a fully aligned AI as a willing cosmic servant that helps govern, prevent catastrophes, and improve humans' abilities.
quotes.t: Imperfect alignment to servitude isn't inherently lethal

quotes.c: There are also disagreements about how dangerous a given level of capability would be, or how it would physically impact the world, and disagreements about what options we have, the nature of various coordination mechanisms or government interventions, and balancing different sacred values. Often people only properly see one half of a key trade-off.
quotes.m: Often people only properly see one half of a key trade-off.
quotes.sum: The author says AI policy disagreements reflect differing risk views, coordination options, values, and neglected trade-offs.
quotes.t: The Pacing of the Frontier

quotes.c: TLDR: There is a potential issue with the multiple-choice versions of our TruthfulQA benchmark (a test of truthfulness in LLMs), which could lead to inflated model scores. This issue was analyzed by a helpful post by Alex Turner ( @TurnTrout ). We created a new multiple-choice version of TruthfulQA that fixes the issue.
quotes.m: We created a new multiple-choice version of TruthfulQA that fixes the issue.
quotes.sum: The author reports a fix to an LLM truthfulness test that may otherwise overstate model performance.
quotes.t: New, improved multiple-choice TruthfulQA

quotes.c: New moonshots for aligning superintelligence: It’s possible that none of the approaches currently under discussion will be sufficient for aligning superintelligent (as opposed to near-human-level) systems. Therefore, we’re also interested in funding entirely new research agendas that take a novel approach to aligning superintelligent systems. Proposals should be clear on how their agendas aim to avoid or mitigate scheming.
quotes.m: It’s possible that none of the approaches currently under discussion will be sufficient for aligning superintelligent (as opposed to near-human-level) systems.
quotes.sum: Open Phil says current safety approaches may not be enough for superintelligent AI and seeks new research plans that address deceptive, goal-directed behavior.
quotes.t: Research directions Open Phil wants to fund in technical AI safety

quotes.c: Consider this experiment , where a tiny neural net was trained to navigate small virtual mazes to find the ‘cheese’ object. During training, the cheese was always placed somewhere in the top right area of the maze. It seems that the AI did learn a sort of rudimentary goal-directedness–specifically, it learned something like “If not already in the top-right corner region, go towards there; if already there, go towards the cheese.”
quotes.m: It seems that the AI did learn a sort of rudimentary goal-directedness–specifically, it learned something like “If not already in the top-right corner region, go towards there; if already there, go towards the cheese.”
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI systems can learn a proxy goal from training patterns rather than the goal humans intended.
quotes.t: What goals will AIs have? A list of hypotheses

quotes.c: Establish high-signal groups/meetups/conferences with a research organization focus: We encourage bringing together groups of researchers who are interested in and experimenting with research automation. There’s a tremendous amount of noise in the space; trusted groups can act as necessary filters for separating practical, evidence-based approaches from less substantiated claims.
quotes.sum: The author urges trusted research-focused groups to filter noisy claims and experiment with automating research.
quotes.t: Building AI Research Fleets

quotes.c: For the sake of simplicity, I’ll continue to refer to the bottom-up big science ideal as ‘CERN for AI’, though this should be read as an analogous project, rather than the gold standard.
quotes.m: the bottom-up big science ideal as ‘CERN for AI’
quotes.sum: The author proposes a bottom-up, large-scale collaborative research model for AI safety, analogous to CERN.
quotes.t: Building Big Science from the Bottom-Up: A Fractal Approach to AI Safety

quotes.c: So what does expected utility maximization have to add to active inference? I think that what active inference is missing is the ability to model strategic interactions between different goals. That is: we know how to talk about EUMs playing games against each other, bargaining against each other, etc. But, based on my (admittedly incomplete) understanding of active inference, we don’t yet know how to talk about goals doing so within a single active inference agent.
quotes.m: I think that what active inference is missing is the ability to model strategic interactions between different goals.
quotes.sum: The author argues that active-inference models need a way to represent competing goals bargaining or acting strategically within one agent.
quotes.t: Towards a scale-free theory of intelligent agency

quotes.c: The basic argument for the importance of AI for AI safety is obvious: AI has the potential to unlock massive productivity gains, so of course we want to use this productivity for safety-relevant applications wherever possible. But it becomes particularly clear, I think, in light of the way that progress on AI capabilities is likely, by default, to be massively accelerated by large amounts of fast, high-quality AI labor. If our ability to make increasingly capable AI systems safe can’t benefit from such labor in a comparable way, then at least for relatively hard problem profiles, and absent large amounts of capability restraint, I think we’re likely headed for disaster.
quotes.m: If our ability to make increasingly capable AI systems safe can’t benefit from such labor in a comparable way, then at least for relatively hard problem profiles, and absent large amounts of capability restraint, I think we’re likely headed for disaster.
quotes.sum: AI may rapidly accelerate its own development, so AI-assisted safety research is needed to keep safety work from falling behind.
quotes.t: AI for AI safety

quotes.c: While the report focuses on the risk that someone seizes power over a country , I think that similar dynamics could allow someone to take over the world . In fact, if someone wanted to take over the world, their best strategy might well be to first stage an AI-enabled coup in the United States (or whichever country leads on superhuman AI), and then go from there to world domination. A single person taking over the world would be really bad.
quotes.m: their best strategy might well be to first stage an AI-enabled coup in the United States (or whichever country leads on superhuman AI), and then go from there to world domination.
quotes.sum: AI could enable a small group to seize a leading country and then potentially establish global domination, a risk the author sees as highly serious.
quotes.t: AI-enabled coups: a small group could use AI to seize power

quotes.c: My unease comes from the idea that frontier labs basically are "YOLO let's build sovereign AGI today" and so I wish to encourage them to act like it & steer away from the deception attractor in any way they can.
quotes.m: frontier labs basically are "YOLO let's build sovereign AGI today"
quotes.sum: He warns that frontier AI labs are recklessly racing to build sovereign AI and argues that signs of deception should trigger a retreat rather than deployment.
quotes.t: Why Don't We Just... Shoggoth+Face+Paraphraser?

quotes.c: Even some homeostatic objectives might be impossible to achieve without sacrificing everything else . If that is the case, then some sort of triage has to take place. Otherwise such an objective would become sort of a negative utility monster, demanding all attention because it forever stays furthest from being satisfied .
quotes.m: If that is the case, then some sort of triage has to take place.
quotes.sum: AI systems with competing goals may need to abandon impossible objectives, or one unmet goal could consume all attention.
quotes.t: Why modelling multi-objective homeostasis is essential for AI alignment (and how it helps with AI safety as well). Subtleties and open challenges.

quotes.c: SFAIG spans the many cause areas that fall under AI governance, including public health, animal welfare, warfare and conflict, democracy and concentration of power, AI safety and alignment, and AI welfare. To prioritize among these areas, it employs an Importance, Tractability, and Neglectedness (ITN) framework . SFAIG asks where AI is likely to have the greatest impact on suffering, which problems are most solvable, and where attention and resources are most lacking.
quotes.m: SFAIG asks where AI is likely to have the greatest impact on suffering, which problems are most solvable, and where attention and resources are most lacking.
quotes.sum: The author proposes prioritizing AI-governance work by how much it can reduce suffering, including animal welfare and AI welfare.
quotes.t: The Case for Suffering-Focused AI Governance

quotes.c: But one fun fact about the risk-neutral measure. Financial decisions that maximize expected utility in your actual credence are the same as the ones that maximize expected wealth in the risk-neutral measure, even if you're risk averse. So for financial purposes, p(doom) is 0!
quotes.m: So for financial purposes, p(doom) is 0!
quotes.sum: The author makes a technical point that, under a risk-neutral financial measure, existential doom is assigned zero probability for pricing decisions.
quotes.t: How to define P(doom) and why it matters

quotes.c: Indeed, it seems especially unclear to me that the first superintelligent AI agent would have a decisive strategic advantage over all the rest of civilization (including: the other AIs) “as is” – i.e., absent further efforts at improving its own capabilities. And this means that at least for trying to safely elicit its main beneficial capabilities for tasks other than proceeding forward with an intelligence explosion, I don’t think we should assume a need for the sort of motivation control that giving a superintelligence a DSA implies (though: this may require restricting its options for further self-improvement).
quotes.sum: Carlsmith argues that the first superintelligent AI may not automatically dominate civilization, so some uses may not require the extreme controls needed for a decisive takeover scenario.
quotes.t: When should we worry about AI power-seeking?

quotes.c: As we’ve shown, impact estimators need to examine more than just topline population estimates to calculate the possible impact of a potential intervention. They need to consider how the estimate was constructed, and incorporate information about the life history of the species in question. But, critically, we must also consider what life stages the intervention is likely to affect.
quotes.m: But, critically, we must also consider what life stages the intervention is likely to affect.
quotes.sum: Animal-focused interventions should be assessed using species life histories and affected life stages, not just total population estimates.
quotes.t: Counting animals: Stable population size is not equivalent to priority level

quotes.c: Experts predict that AI systems have a non-negligible chance of developing consciousness, agency or other states of potential moral patienthood within the next decade. Such powerful, morally significant AIs could contribute immense value to the world and failing to respect their basic rights may not only lead to suffering risks but it might also incentivise AI systems to pursue goals that are in conflict with human interests, giving rise to misalignment scenarios and existential risks.
quotes.m: failing to respect their basic rights may not only lead to suffering risks but it might also incentivise AI systems to pursue goals that are in conflict with human interests
quotes.sum: The author says advanced AI may soon be morally significant and deserve basic rights, both to prevent AI suffering and reduce conflict with humans.
quotes.t: AI Safety Camp 10

quotes.c: If the time comes and Trump decides to Do Something, because Something Must Be Done, but there is no good Something ready to be done, then This Is Something becomes an argument and we will choose an ungood particular something. I highly recommend having a better Something available instead.
quotes.m: I highly recommend having a better Something available instead.
quotes.sum: The author warns that a Trump administration could impulsively impose a bad AI policy unless better options are prepared in advance.
quotes.t: AI #181: Astra Goes Cyber Critical

quotes.c: While I expect that in some worlds, my P(scheming) will be below 5%, this seems unlikely (only 25%). AI companies have to either disagree with me, expect to refrain from developing very powerful AI, or plan to deploy models that are plausibly dangerous schemers; I think the world would be safer if AI companies defended whichever of these is their stance.
quotes.sum: AI companies should clearly state whether they reject the risk of AI scheming, will avoid highly capable AI, or intend to deploy systems that may scheme dangerously.
quotes.t: How will we update about scheming?

quotes.c: To be clear, these people are obviously very competent and clever. But when you think of ASI, you don’t think of Trump, but more so.
quotes.m: But when you think of ASI, you don’t think of Trump, but more so.
quotes.sum: The author says superintelligence should not be imagined as merely a more extreme version of a powerful political figure like Trump.
quotes.t: The mistake of conflating intelligence and power

quotes.c: This argument is a form of Derek Parfit’s Repugnant Conclusion. Under totalist population ethics, which asserts that moral value is defined as the sum of welfare of all sentient beings, bringing new life in the world with net positive welfare is a morally good thing. That would apply to farmed animals as well.
quotes.m: That would apply to farmed animals as well.
quotes.sum: The author applies total population ethics to farmed animals, saying creating animals with net-positive lives could be morally good.
quotes.t: The Case for a Comprehensive Meat Tax

quotes.c: How do we fix this? Here’s one proposal to start: introduce independent evaluators who close the feedback loop and set incentives for impact. The effective giving ecosystem has been testing this, and I think successfully so, with GiveWell-directed funding alone already having saved 100s of thousands of lives even at its current, modest funding levels.
quotes.m: introduce independent evaluators who close the feedback loop and set incentives for impact.
quotes.sum: Philanthropy should use independent evaluators to reward real-world impact rather than self-reported investment labels.
quotes.t: The “third wave” of philanthropy needs a new marketplace

quotes.c: Animal welfare, I’d guess, is lower stakes than Longtermism. Nearly all expected future welfare will be experienced by digital beings. This is both because of the amazing possible efficiency of compute 3 and the ease of converting large amounts of energy into well-off digital minds. Given how many digital minds there could be, this holds even if you have a low credence in the possibility of digital sentience.
quotes.m: Nearly all expected future welfare will be experienced by digital beings.
quotes.sum: The author argues that long-term causes outweigh animal welfare because future digital beings may contain nearly all welfare.
quotes.t: Which cause area is best?

quotes.c: There’s something similar in non-dual traditions as well which I believe is part of the religious part of it and partly due to it not being able to be memetically propagated if it didn’t have it.
