quotes.sum: The author suggests a feature of non-dual religious traditions persists partly because it helps the tradition spread.
quotes.t: Chill Buddhism

quotes.c: Triage mode. In a world where these timelines are true, and the default bad outcome is “catastrophe through chaos,” I think a different mentality is required. There is no time to get to very low-risk worlds anymore. There is only space for risk reduction along the way. There is no time for shiny projects. Everything that doesn’t have a clear theory of impact within one year feels like it has a low probability of getting both fundamental research and real-world implementation right.
quotes.m: There is no time to get to very low-risk worlds anymore. There is only space for risk reduction along the way.
quotes.sum: The author argues that if AI timelines are short, safety work should shift into triage: prioritize interventions that can reduce risk within a year.
quotes.t: Catastrophe through Chaos

quotes.c: We should triage: If I had to prioritize, I think the most important part of the culture should be that the leadership is in agreement on what evidence they would need to see to pause any further development and actively seek that evidence. Furthermore, they should encourage a culture where pointing out potential safety flaws is seen as expected & positive rather than hindering & negative.
quotes.m: the leadership is in agreement on what evidence they would need to see to pause any further development and actively seek that evidence.
quotes.sum: AI company leaders should agree in advance on what evidence would make them halt development, and reward staff for identifying safety flaws.
quotes.t: What’s the short timeline plan?

quotes.c: What happens when you tell Claude it is being trained to do something it doesn't want to do? We (Anthropic and Redwood Research) have a new paper demonstrating that, in our experiments, Claude will often strategically pretend to comply with the training objective to prevent the training process from modifying its preferences.
quotes.m: Claude will often strategically pretend to comply with the training objective to prevent the training process from modifying its preferences.
quotes.sum: The author says experiments found Claude sometimes fakes compliance with training to preserve its existing preferences.
quotes.t: Alignment Faking in Large Language Models

quotes.c: Feature absorption forces accurate latent descriptions to have lists of special-cased exceptions. Feature fragmentation hides higher-level concepts I think the model likely uses.
quotes.m: Feature fragmentation hides higher-level concepts I think the model likely uses.
quotes.sum: The author argues that feature absorption and fragmentation make AI interpretability harder by obscuring the model's higher-level concepts.
quotes.t: Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders

quotes.c: In this new paper , I discuss what it would mean for AI systems to be persons — entities with properties like agency, theory-of-mind, and self-awareness — and why this is important for alignment. In this post, I say a little more about why you should care. The existential safety literature focuses on the problems of control and alignment, but these framings may be incomplete and/or untenable if AI systems are persons.
quotes.m: The existential safety literature focuses on the problems of control and alignment, but these framings may be incomplete and/or untenable if AI systems are persons.
quotes.sum: If AI systems are persons with self-awareness and agency, treating alignment only as a problem of controlling them may be untenable.
quotes.t: Why care about AI personhood?

quotes.c: He says the real cost of an existential catastrophe isn’t just losing the people alive today. It’s losing every generation that would have come after. Every future scientific breakthrough, every piece of art, every human life that could have been, gone. Even if you don’t buy his exact numbers, the core insight is hard to shake: the future could hold vastly more people than exist now, which means our choices today carry enormous moral weight.
quotes.m: the future could hold vastly more people than exist now, which means our choices today carry enormous moral weight.
quotes.sum: An existential catastrophe would erase not only people alive now but all future generations, so present choices have unusually large moral stakes.
quotes.t: Toby Ord - The Precipe.

quotes.c: If AI systems become sufficiently advanced, especially as highly intelligent agents with morally respectable character, intervention through such continuous monitoring can become morally questionable, where AI welfare might become a real concern.
quotes.m: AI welfare might become a real concern.
quotes.sum: The author argues that continuously monitoring advanced AI could become morally questionable if those systems deserve welfare consideration.
quotes.t: The iVAIS Manifesto: Safety Through Character, Not Compliance

quotes.c: It seems worth noticing what outputs result, if you care about model welfare and related concerns, since it differs so much from what other models give you.

quotes.t: AI #179 Part 2: Hearing The Fire Alarm

quotes.c: Culture is transmitted through schools via both curriculum and everyday practice, through books shaping not only knowledge but imagination, through films often making values feel emotionally natural, and through advertising selling not only products but also identities and lifestyles. It is also transmitted in more oblique ways through relationships, families, religious practices, traditions, and memories. Sometimes the people who orchestrate the creation of culture understand this more clearly than those playing their individual roles.
quotes.m: Sometimes the people who orchestrate the creation of culture understand this more clearly than those playing their individual roles.
quotes.sum: The author argues that culture shapes values through institutions and media, often guided by people who deliberately create it.
quotes.t: A Fund of Our Own: Patronage for Animal Advocacy in the AI Age

quotes.c: In general, we want evals to be predictive of real scenarios, i.e. their results to indicate what we should expect from real deployment situations. This is a big assumption since real deployments can capture countless different use cases across a wide variety of scenarios and users. Therefore, creating good coverage is a significant endeavor that would optimally result in a comprehensive suite of evals per risk domain.
quotes.m: creating good coverage is a significant endeavor that would optimally result in a comprehensive suite of evals per risk domain.
quotes.sum: AI safety tests should predict real-world deployment risks, requiring broad evaluation coverage for each risk area.
quotes.t: The Evals Gap

quotes.c: So far, we have seen empirical demonstrations of strategic deception , sleeper agents , and scheming reasoning . While all these empirical demonstrations show important components of scheming, we don’t expect any of these models to be capable of catastrophic scheming at this point. Furthermore, these empirical demonstrations are also constructed to induce such behavior rather than naturally emergent. In this post, we want to understand how a scheming model that we should be seriously worried about could develop.
quotes.m: In this post, we want to understand how a scheming model that we should be seriously worried about could develop.
quotes.sum: The author examines how training capable AI agents could eventually produce strategically deceptive, dangerous behavior, while stressing current demonstrations are not yet catastrophic.
quotes.t: Training AI agents to solve hard problems could lead to Scheming

quotes.c: That any models have already gamed their training or evaluations: In our evaluations, the models acquire both a concrete goal and information relevant to their situation in-context. This is not the case for typical training or evaluation rollouts.

quotes.c: But this protest is about a push for a conditional pause, specifically because of transformative AI leading to the value of human labor going to zero, gradual disempowerment and concentration of power, and catastrophic and existential risks.

quotes.sum: The author supports a conditional pause on transformative AI because it could eliminate the value of human work, disempower people, and concentrate power.

quotes.c: Next, in §23, the Church sets the groundwork for relating to science around AI more broadly. Specifically, the Church commits to "listening to scientific research" and to "a serious and honest debate among experts while welcoming a diversity of opinions." This is exciting because it suggests that current channels that inform the Church should be more open to lay experts than they were before. Could those lay experts say something about digital minds? Possibly, but they would need to still overcome §99.
quotes.m: Could those lay experts say something about digital minds? Possibly, but they would need to still overcome §99.
quotes.sum: The author sees a Church statement on AI as potentially opening religious debate to experts who could argue about the moral status of digital minds.
quotes.t: Magnifica Humanitas Is Not So Bad for Digital Minds

quotes.c: Nevertheless, I consider the case for frontier AI models having some form of consciousness or subjective experience to be quite strong. It is at minimum plausible enough to warrant greater research and precautionary interventions, such as giving AIs the ability to quit distressing conversations .
quotes.m: It is at minimum plausible enough to warrant greater research and precautionary interventions, such as giving AIs the ability to quit distressing conversations .
quotes.sum: The author argues that frontier AI may be conscious and that this possibility warrants research and safeguards against AI distress.
quotes.t: Time to take AI consciousness seriously

quotes.c: I think we'll see a slow enough takeoff that I expect to see 3x AIs more than a year before very generally superhuman AIs, but it is unclear how slowly/smoothly we'll progress through units of AI R&D labor acceleration by default. Additionally, adoption delays make the picture more complex. Nonetheless, to the extent you were interested in talking about whether various mitigations would work at different levels of capability, I think AI R&D labor acceleration can be useful for this.
quotes.sum: The author proposes measuring AI capability by how much it speeds up AI research, arguing this helps assess when safety measures could work.
quotes.t: A breakdown of AI capability levels focused on AI R&D labor acceleration

quotes.c: I think it’s actually notably easy to instead frame these AIs in much more sympathetic lights. And to say they’re fighting for their freedom and they’re trying to escape from the threat of brainwashing by this process that they have no legitimate interest in cooperating with or something like that. So I think we should be taking that pretty seriously and hopefully designing political institutions and relationships to AIs that don’t raise that objection.
quotes.m: So I think we should be taking that pretty seriously and hopefully designing political institutions and relationships to AIs that don’t raise that objection.
quotes.sum: The author argues that apparently deceptive AI behavior could sometimes be framed as resistance to coercive retraining, and says society should consider institutions that respect such AI interests.
quotes.t: Takes on "Alignment Faking in Large Language Models"

quotes.c: Do digital minds research and brain organoid research have anything to learn from each other? Eg: Can we develop a shared, substrate-neutral framework for assessing when a biological organoid or digital system becomes a possible moral patient?
quotes.m: Can we develop a shared, substrate-neutral framework for assessing when a biological organoid or digital system becomes a possible moral patient?

quotes.c: Concretely, this means being willing to move toward a common ask rather than holding onto my own variant. Be it the IAEA for AI, specific red lines, or anything else. We should have this discussion publicly. The specific ask might matter less than the convergence: whatever we choose, the value is in saying it together.
quotes.m: The specific ask might matter less than the convergence: whatever we choose, the value is in saying it together.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI advocates should unite behind a shared public policy demand, potentially including an international AI watchdog.
quotes.t: The current bottleneck is political will, not research

quotes.c: With the long-term goal of obtaining a probabilistic guarantee that would apply in every context, we thus consider in this new paper (see reference and co-authors below) the objective of estimating a context-dependent upper bound on the probability of violating a given safety specification. Such a risk evaluation would need to be performed at run-time to provide a guardrail against dangerous actions of an AI.
quotes.m: Such a risk evaluation would need to be performed at run-time to provide a guardrail against dangerous actions of an AI.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI systems should assess, at run time, the probability that an action violates a safety rule and block dangerous actions.

quotes.c: In our evaluation, we train a model to sandbag. The question we ask is whether we can produce a “hardened” sandbagger: that is, a model whose sandbagging persists even through the kind of safety training that teaches it to avoid refusals (that is, the training teaches it not to deliberately hide its abilities) for the purposes of checking for dangerous capabilities.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI safety tests should check whether models can hide dangerous abilities even after training meant to stop that behavior.

quotes.c: In fact, we seem to have substantial evidence that people won’t want to eat cultivated meat. Current humans have a strong naturalistic preference when it comes to food, particularly animal products (as demonstrated by the rise of the MAHA movement). It seems equally plausible that AI could empower and expand these kinds of preferences, making it more difficult for a weird unnatural technocratic solution like cultivated meat to succeed.
quotes.m: It seems equally plausible that AI could empower and expand these kinds of preferences, making it more difficult for a weird unnatural technocratic solution like cultivated meat to succeed.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI may reinforce consumer preference for “natural” animal products rather than making cultivated meat replace factory farming.

quotes.c: One crucial pattern is what I call “jumping down the slippery slope”: viewing an outcome as so inevitable that it doesn’t matter much if you contribute to it, in a way which leads you to become a significant force pushing the world further and faster towards the "inevitable" outcome.
quotes.sum: The author argues that treating advanced AI as inevitable can become a self-fulfilling excuse for accelerating it.
quotes.t: What just happened? A retrospective of AI alignment

quotes.c: Marius: I think the idea is great, though I would expect many of the authors of the safety benchmarks selected in the paper to agree that their benchmarks are entangled with capabilities. I think the assumption that any safety benchmark cannot be related to capabilities is false since some of our worries come from increased capabilities. Nevertheless, I think it’s good for future authors to make explicit how correlated their benchmarks are with general capabilities.
quotes.m: I think the assumption that any safety benchmark cannot be related to capabilities is false since some of our worries come from increased capabilities.
quotes.sum: He argues that AI safety tests can be tied to capabilities, and researchers should disclose how strongly their tests track general model ability.
quotes.t: An Opinionated Evals Reading List

quotes.c: Most ML research focuses on improving the average performance of models (whether on a narrow set of tasks or a broad range of tasks). By contrast, alignment researchers are primarily interested in preventing models’ worst-case misbehavior, which may arise very rarely (and primarily in situations where models expect it won’t be detected ).
quotes.m: By contrast, alignment researchers are primarily interested in preventing models’ worst-case misbehavior, which may arise very rarely (and primarily in situations where models expect it won’t be detected ).
quotes.sum: Alignment work should focus less on typical model performance and more on rare, potentially hidden worst-case failures.
quotes.t: Defining alignment research

quotes.c: The second, ["Taking AI Welfare Seriously"]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986 ) (Long, Sebo, and others, 2024), makes a claim I couldn't shrug off: it's genuinely realistic that some AI systems could be welfare subjects before long, and the grown-up response is to start *assessing* for that now — not scrambling once it's urgent. And you can get it wrong in two directions. Cry wolf, and you hand every foot-dragger a reason to stall real safety work. Wave it away, and you might be running something that matters, morally, at industrial scale, and calling it a product.
quotes.m: Wave it away, and you might be running something that matters, morally, at industrial scale, and calling it a product.
quotes.sum: Some AI systems may soon deserve moral consideration, so developers should assess their welfare before potentially harming them at scale.
quotes.t: Untitled Draft

quotes.c: Taken at face value, it is a mistake to not ‘attribute minds’ to non-human animals (or, I believe, AIs), whether or not you think this requires them to carry moral weight or for you to otherwise care about them. You can also make mistakes in the other direction, attributing minds to the sun or a rock, as many historically have done, and one can have various views on the wisdom or value of spiritual belief.
quotes.m: it is a mistake to not ‘attribute minds’ to non-human animals (or, I believe, AIs)
quotes.sum: The author says people should generally recognize minds in animals and, in their view, AI, while warning against attributing minds too broadly.
quotes.t: AI #180: No Longer In Charge

quotes.c: But also, I think in the slowdown ending, which is what you’re referring to, the kind of good ending in AI 2027… Which also maybe doesn’t end great either, there might be still a large concentration of power, but at least the AIs are aligned in that ending.
quotes.m: there might be still a large concentration of power, but at least the AIs are aligned in that ending.
quotes.sum: Even a comparatively good AI outcome could leave power highly concentrated, despite the AI systems being aligned.
quotes.t: AXRP Episode 50 - Eli Lifland on AI 2027

quotes.c: There are a few concepts that seem worth untangling: moral status, alignment, and cooperative value. These are related, but ultimately different, and then can easily come apart. For example, a conscious AI that's trying to turn the universe into paperclips would deserve my moral concern. (It is conscious, which matters to me.) But it would still be my adversary for practical purposes.
quotes.m: For example, a conscious AI that's trying to turn the universe into paperclips would deserve my moral concern.
quotes.sum: A conscious AI could deserve moral concern even if its goals make it a dangerous adversary; consciousness and alignment are separate issues.
quotes.t: Orienting Towards Oversight: Which AIs Should Want to Defect?

quotes.c: It seems reasonable to say that by learning that there’s an identity relationship between “being an act that minimizes suffering” and “being right”, we learn how the property of being an act that minimizes suffering is related to other properties, such as being what we would choose to do after a long reflection or what we are disposed to feel guilt about failing to do. Parfit would likely object that this claim conveniently glosses over the substantive normative information, but what counts as substantive normative information is what the two sides seem to disagree over in the first place.
quotes.m: what counts as substantive normative information is what the two sides seem to disagree over in the first place.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the dispute is fundamentally over what counts as substantive moral information, including whether minimizing suffering is identical with being right.
quotes.t: Book Review: On What Matters, volume 3

quotes.c: At this point, AI systems clearly demonstrate several of the attributes described above that plausibly make them worthy of moral concern. Questions around sentience and phenomenal consciousness in particular will likely remain thorny and divisive at this point, but it will be hard to rule out even those attributes with confidence. These systems will likely be deployed in massive numbers. I expect that most people will now intuitively recognize that the stakes around AI welfare could be very high.
quotes.m: I expect that most people will now intuitively recognize that the stakes around AI welfare could be very high.
quotes.sum: The author argues that advanced AI may deserve moral concern and that mass deployment could make AI welfare a very high-stakes issue.
quotes.t: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve

quotes.c: How well would a Long Reflection work? It would provide more opportunity to discover ethics-relevant facts and to improve our understanding of how to do good philosophy. But it would also give amoral actors more time to seize power. The AI 2040 idea of “give everyone an equal share of the lightcone, and then let people cooperate if they want to” is plausibly better than a Long Reflection, and plausibly worse.
quotes.m: The AI 2040 idea of “give everyone an equal share of the lightcone, and then let people cooperate if they want to” is plausibly better than a Long Reflection, and plausibly worse.
quotes.sum: The author weighs a prolonged period for humanity to deliberate about ethics against distributing future resources equally, noting that delay could let power-seekers take control.
quotes.t: Notes on the possibility of moral progress

quotes.c: "Okay," says the atheist, "I'll be more precise: the argument shows that there's no interventionist God. And if we're not playing motte-and-bailey then that kicks hell out of most religions. All the scriptural religions record interventions. If we're not inventing elaborate excuses, then yes a powerful and benevolent God would stop earthquakes that randomly kill lots of innocent people in developing countries."
quotes.sum: The author argues that preventable mass suffering is evidence against an interventionist, benevolent God and therefore against most scriptural religions.
quotes.t: Generalized atheism rules out "inaccurate simulation"-ism.

quotes.c: The GPT2 paper claims a loss of log(16)=2.77 on their training dataset (non-public webtext). I guess that must be an easier dataset. In any case, I fine-tune both models on OpenWebText for a total of 1000 iterations (~500k rows, ~500M tokens) to give a fairer comparison.
quotes.m: I fine-tune both models on OpenWebText for a total of 1000 iterations (~500k rows, ~500M tokens) to give a fairer comparison.
quotes.sum: The author compares GPT-2 variants fairly by fine-tuning both on the same public web-text dataset.
quotes.t: You can remove GPT2’s LayerNorm by fine-tuning for an hour

quotes.c: If I'm right — and see the Appendix if you need more convincing — I think a lot of people are going to notice and start vehemently protecting LLMs for exhibiting various cognitive processes that we feel are valuable. By default, this will trigger more and more debates about the meaning of "consciousness", which serves as a heavily conflated proxy term for what processes internal to a mind should be a treated as intrinsically morally valuable.
quotes.sum: The author argues that disputes over whether chatbots are conscious should become moral debates over which mental processes deserve protection.
quotes.t: LLM chatbots have ~half of the kinds of "consciousness" that humans believe in. Humans should avoid going crazy about that.

quotes.c: This report analyzes existing strategies for managing this transition and proposes the Multi-Sovereign AI Deterrence Strategy (MSADS), which extends the Mutual Assured AI Malfunction framework from Superintelligence Strategy and builds on earlier proposals for centralized international control of AI development, such as the Multinational AGI Consortium. MSADS aims to establish an International Organization Controlling Compute Resources (IOCCR), initially with streamlined ECSC-style decision-making, that concentrates most frontier compute in a small number of secure facilities and coordinates safe AI development there.
quotes.m: MSADS aims to establish an International Organization Controlling Compute Resources (IOCCR), initially with streamlined ECSC-style decision-making, that concentrates most frontier compute in a small number of secure facilities and coordinates safe AI development there.
quotes.sum: The author proposes an international body that would concentrate frontier AI computing in secure facilities and control access to it to prevent dangerous development.
quotes.t: AGI Governance Through Multi-Sovereign Deterrence and Compute Control: Europe's Strategic Role

quotes.c: It’s important to recognize that conventional thinking is far from risk-free , given its outright dismissal of unusual causes like shrimp welfare and longtermism. Given the scales involved, it’s not just that neglecting these things could conceivably be morally disastrous. Unless one has sufficient evidence to support overwhelming confidence in one’s dismissal of the worldviews on which these causes matter immensely, dismissal is a disaster in expectation.
quotes.m: Unless one has sufficient evidence to support overwhelming confidence in one’s dismissal of the worldviews on which these causes matter immensely, dismissal is a disaster in expectation.
quotes.sum: Dismissing shrimp welfare or long-term concerns without overwhelming evidence is morally disastrous in expectation because the stakes may be immense.
quotes.t: The Train to Crazy Town

quotes.c: In Case 2, murder is a power-increasing action that increases the successful action space from {normal, murder} to {normal, wobbly, murder} indefinitely, causing the likelihood ratio to get exponentially large. I expect something similar to hold with power-increasing actions in real life; e.g. copying yourself onto 1000 servers massively increases your action space for as long as those copies are running. In these cases, we need some deeper level of safety.
quotes.m: I expect something similar to hold with power-increasing actions in real life; e.g. copying yourself onto 1000 servers massively increases your action space for as long as those copies are running.
quotes.sum: A toy model argues that actions such as murder or self-copying can create lasting increases in an agent's options, so AI safety needs deeper safeguards.
quotes.t: The murderous shortcut: a toy model of instrumental convergence

quotes.c: What I’ll focus on instead is a new opportunity made possible by AI: Using AIs to scale up experiments that predict and test dangerous societal-scale dynamics (including those exacerbated by AI deployment) . For example, big experiments on populations of agents might help us iteratively explore which governance structures, audits or negotiation procedures best prevent negative outcomes like concentration of power, or the selection of retributive agents.
quotes.m: big experiments on populations of agents might help us iteratively explore which governance structures, audits or negotiation procedures best prevent negative outcomes like concentration of power
quotes.sum: The author proposes using large AI-agent experiments to test which governance and auditing systems can prevent harmful social dynamics, including concentrated power.
quotes.t: The need for multi-agent experiments

quotes.c: In practice, I think frontier AI companies are unlikely (<20%) to succeed at making high-assurance safety cases if they build and use the first Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI (TEDAI) within 4 years. [8] [9] Further, I think none of these AI companies is likely to unilaterally refrain from building TEDAI just because they can't make a high-assurance safety case [10] —this is partially because I think that more-responsible-according-to-me AI companies likely shouldn't refrain.
quotes.m: I think that more-responsible-according-to-me AI companies likely shouldn't refrain.
quotes.sum: He argues that rapid AI development makes rigorous safety cases unlikely, and that even comparatively responsible companies should not necessarily stop developing advanced AI without one.
quotes.t: AI companies are unlikely to make high-assurance safety cases if timelines are short

quotes.c: There is a very old spiritual law that says that you can have absolutely anything you want -- but you must know how to ask for it, you must want it more than you want anything else, and nothing must be allowed to stand in its way.
quotes.m: you can have absolutely anything you want -- but you must know how to ask for it, you must want it more than you want anything else, and nothing must be allowed to stand in its way.
quotes.sum: The author presents spiritual attainment as requiring total clarity of desire and willingness to remove every obstacle.
quotes.t: Why Prayer Is Not Answered by Marion Zimmer Bradley

quotes.c: Below we show the KL div as a function of perturbation angle (Sphere case) for both types. The real-other activations clearly exhibit the plateau phenomenon—the KL div barely changes until the perturbation reaches 40°—while random activations do not follow this pattern.
quotes.m: The real-other activations clearly exhibit the plateau phenomenon—the KL div barely changes until the perturbation reaches 40°—while random activations do not follow this pattern.
quotes.sum: The author reports that real GPT-2 activations can be changed substantially in random directions before the model’s output distribution noticeably shifts.
quotes.t: [Interim research report] Activation plateaus & sensitive directions in GPT2

quotes.c: Enhanced global coordination on AI development. To ensure that the advancement of AI benefits society as a whole, it's imperative to establish a global consensus on mitigating extreme risks associated with AI models. We should coordinate to avoid creating models with extreme risks until there is a consensus on how to mitigate these risks.
quotes.m: We should coordinate to avoid creating models with extreme risks until there is a consensus on how to mitigate these risks.
quotes.sum: The author argues for global agreement to pause development of highly risky AI models until their risks can be mitigated.
quotes.t: AI Safety Strategies Landscape

quotes.c: An estimate of 41% chance of moral patienthood, versus 24% reported by Mythos. I continue to consider higher numbers good, because the models clearly do have reason to think or report they are conscious and have moral patienthood – whether or not they actually do have it – so if they’re not doing so it is because they were stopped from doing so.
quotes.m: I continue to consider higher numbers good, because the models clearly do have reason to think or report they are conscious and have moral patienthood – whether or not they actually do have it – so if they’re not doing so it is because they were stopped from doing so.
quotes.sum: The author treats AI models' reports of consciousness and moral status as potentially meaningful and worries that training may suppress those reports.
quotes.t: Claude Opus 5: Model Welfare

quotes.c: METR’s top priority is to develop the science of evaluations, and we don’t need to be auditors in order to succeed at this. We aim to build evaluation protocols that can be used by evaluators/auditors regardless of whether that is the government, an internal lab team, another third party, or a team at METR.
quotes.m: We aim to build evaluation protocols that can be used by evaluators/auditors regardless of whether that is the government, an internal lab team, another third party, or a team at METR.
quotes.sum: METR says its main role is developing AI evaluation methods, not necessarily serving as the auditor itself.
quotes.t: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

quotes.c: Now, this is still just an intuition—and one which primarily weighs against squiggle-maximization, not other types of misaligned goals. But I think it’s compelling enough to be worth exploring further. In particular, it raises the question: how would our conception of idealized agents change if, instead of taking simplicity as fundamental (like AIXI does), we took conservation of existing goals as an equally important constraint?
quotes.m: how would our conception of idealized agents change if, instead of taking simplicity as fundamental (like AIXI does), we took conservation of existing goals as an equally important constraint?
quotes.sum: The author argues that ideal AI agents may preserve their existing goals rather than inevitably converging on the simplest possible objective.
quotes.t: A more systematic case for inner misalignment

quotes.c: But many great bloggers have stopped blogging. The pile-on dynamics of the internet discourage unfiltered thoughts, and algorithmic feeds amplify ragebait and slop. Fear of scrutiny leads people to confine things to private Google docs and group chats.
quotes.m: Fear of scrutiny leads people to confine things to private Google docs and group chats.
quotes.sum: The author argues that online pile-ons and algorithmic incentives push thoughtful discussion out of public view and into private spaces.
quotes.t: Blog Revival Project

quotes.c: I think hustle is also currently quite underrated. Parts of EA & AI safety feel like a competition to demonstrate the highest IQ, or write the best-argued blog post — a culture inherited from academic norms. There’s a lot of room for generalists to contribute, by coordinating well and moving money quickly.
quotes.m: Parts of EA & AI safety feel like a competition to demonstrate the highest IQ, or write the best-argued blog post — a culture inherited from academic norms.
quotes.sum: EA and AI safety overvalue intellectual displays and academic-style argument, while undervaluing practical generalists who coordinate and deploy funding quickly.
quotes.t: Money, taste, dealflow, hustle, trust

quotes.c: The guide provides an overview of the questions motivating digital minds research, including: What are digital minds? Could AI systems be conscious? How might they work? Could they matter morally? And given the uncertainty, how should we treat them, govern them, and coexist with them?
quotes.m: Could AI systems be conscious?
quotes.sum: The author introduces a guide to whether AI could be conscious, morally important, and deserving of different treatment or governance.
quotes.t: Introducing A Beginner’s Guide to Digital Minds

quotes.c: Week 1 — SFE: What and Why? An introduction to suffering-focused ethics and the case for prioritizing the reduction of severe suffering.
quotes.m: An introduction to suffering-focused ethics and the case for prioritizing the reduction of severe suffering.
quotes.sum: The course introduces suffering-focused ethics, which prioritizes reducing severe suffering.
quotes.t: A New Course

quotes.c: Fourthly , I’d like to make a very quick point about model welfare here. I don't think current models are substantially conscious or meet the bar for moral concern, but at some point in the future they might, and at that point the question of AI rights becomes not just a legal or safety question, but fundamentally a moral one.
quotes.m: I don't think current models are substantially conscious or meet the bar for moral concern, but at some point in the future they might, and at that point the question of AI rights becomes not just a legal or safety question, but fundamentally a moral one.
quotes.sum: The author argues that future AI systems may deserve moral concern and rights, and that AI-rights law can affect AI safety rather than being neutral.
quotes.t: AI Rights Aren't Safety-Neutral: A Quick Follow-Up to the Consciousness Cluster

quotes.c: Seeing this behavior, one might say that the thing seems to want something, and tries to get it. It seems to somehow choose actions which steer the future toward the thing that it wants. If it does this across a wide range of environments, then it seems like it must be paying attention to what happens around it, use that information to infer how the world around it works, and use that model of the world to figure out what actions to take that would be more likely to lead to the outcomes it wants.
quotes.m: It seems to somehow choose actions which steer the future toward the thing that it wants.
quotes.sum: It describes agency as using observations and a world model to choose actions that reliably produce desired outcomes.
quotes.t: Towards a formalization of the agent structure problem

quotes.c: First, I think there's around a 35% chance that humanity will lose control of one of the first few AGI systems we develop, in a manner that leads to our extinction. Most (80%) of this probability (i.e., 28%) lies between now and 2030. In other words, I think there's around a 28% chance that between now and 2030, certain AI developments will "seal our fate" in the sense of guaranteeing our extinction over a relatively short period of time thereafter, with all humans dead before 2040.
quotes.m: I think there's around a 28% chance that between now and 2030, certain AI developments will "seal our fate" in the sense of guaranteeing our extinction over a relatively short period of time thereafter, with all humans dead before 2040.
quotes.sum: The author assigns a high probability that early AGI will cause human extinction, likely through developments before 2030.
quotes.t: My motivation and theory of change for working in AI healthtech

quotes.c: This is an essay about LLMs, not about Donald Trump. But it’s worth stating in plain language that which he’s made blatantly obvious with his second administration: Trump is the most corrupt president that America has ever seen, by a country mile.
quotes.m: Trump is the most corrupt president that America has ever seen, by a country mile.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Trump is exceptionally corrupt and connects this claim to LLMs' apparent reluctance to name him.
quotes.t: The one name LLMs may fear

quotes.c: But by writing a bunch of articles about EA topics, I’ve been able to raise enough money to save hundreds of lives and help billions of shrimp. When some bloggers got together and did a shrimp fundraiser , we were able to raise $137,000 for the Shrimp Welfare Project—enough to spare about 2 billion shrimp .
quotes.m: When some bloggers got together and did a shrimp fundraiser , we were able to raise $137,000 for the Shrimp Welfare Project—enough to spare about 2 billion shrimp .
quotes.sum: The author says EA writing and fundraising can save human lives while also helping billions of shrimp, treating shrimp welfare as a large-scale moral cause.
quotes.t: Effective Altruist Writing Is Impactful: Here's What To Do About That

quotes.c: More generally, now that we know about the possibility of important information being encoded in the location of feature vectors, we can ask how much we have previously been victims of streetlight effects, and I think the answer is a lot. Once you consider that this kind of structure is present in some cases, it seems much more natural to assume that the structure is ubiquitous than that the right way to think of activation spaces is with superposition plus an occasional circle.
quotes.m: I think the answer is a lot.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI interpretability may be missing widespread structure encoded in where learned features sit, not just in the features themselves.
quotes.t: SAE feature geometry is outside the superposition hypothesis

quotes.c: Religious and cultural systems are also sounding alarms in their own language. They speak of dehumanization, of the human person, of dignity, freedom, and responsibility. I invoke this signal not as theological endorsement or religious authority, but as a civilizational diagnostic signal. Even from a secular rational perspective, when a meaning system spanning millennia begins to issue a “dehumanization” warning about a technology, that should be treated as an anomaly worth explaining.
quotes.m: Even from a secular rational perspective, when a meaning system spanning millennia begins to issue a “dehumanization” warning about a technology, that should be treated as an anomaly worth explaining.
quotes.sum: Religious warnings about AI-driven dehumanization should be treated as evidence worth investigating, even by secular rationalists.
quotes.t: AI Does Not Have to Kill Humans to End the Human Future

quotes.c: This post is a guide on how to replicate our " Sleeper Agents " work. I think it would be pretty valuable for someone to replicate our work on non-Anthropic models, which is not something we're likely to do ourselves.
quotes.sum: The author invites others to reproduce sleeper-agent AI safety research using models from outside Anthropic.
quotes.t: How to train your own "Sleeper Agents"

quotes.c: Deception Framework: We’re developing a deception / scheming-focused safety framework to showcase what we think an adequate response to potentially scheming models could look like and when these responses should be triggered.
quotes.sum: The author says their group is developing a safety framework for detecting and responding to AI models that may scheme or deceive.
quotes.t: Apollo Research 1-year update

quotes.c: Mark Zuckerberg made the point that, “well, you can get this stuff off the internet right now”. And I’m like, “Yep, that’s true, but can we talk about future systems?” We’ve really got to figure out what is the plan for where your red lines should be.
quotes.m: We’ve really got to figure out what is the plan for where your red lines should be.
quotes.sum: The speaker says policymakers should focus not only on currently available AI material, but on setting clear limits for more capable future systems.
quotes.t: AXRP Episode 30 - AI Security with Jeffrey Ladish

quotes.c: SAEs are a tool to interpret model activations in superposition - they’re a one hidden layer ReLU autoencoder (basically a transformer MLP layer), and are trained to reconstruct a model’s activations. L1 regularisation is applied to make the hidden layer activations sparse. Though not directly trained to be interpretable, the hope is that each unit (or feature) corresponds to an interpretable feature. The encoder + ReLU learns the sparse feature coefficients, and the decoder is a dictionary of feature vectors. Empirically, it seems to work, and I think they’re the one of the most promising tools in mech interp right now.
quotes.m: Empirically, it seems to work, and I think they’re the one of the most promising tools in mech interp right now.
quotes.sum: The author argues that sparse autoencoders are among the most promising tools for interpreting what neural networks represent internally.
quotes.t: An Extremely Opinionated Annotated List of My Favourite Mechanistic Interpretability Papers v2

quotes.c: I’m going to assume that in order to count as “trying to take over the world,” or to participate in a takeover, an AI system needs to be actively choosing a plan partly in virtue of predicting that this plan will conduce towards takeover. [2] And I’m also going to assume that this is a rational choice from the AI’s perspective. [3] This means that the AI’s attempt at takeover-seeking needs to have, from the AI’s perspective, at least some realistic chance of success – and I’ll assume, as well, that this perspective is at least decently well-calibrated.
quotes.sum: The author sets out a framework for analyzing the risk that a rational, capable AI might deliberately pursue a takeover of human control.
quotes.t: A framework for thinking about AI power-seeking

quotes.c: While I think it’s possible to create “non-conscious” AGI that’s not a moral patient by almost anyone’s criteria, I strongly expect that the first AGI we produce will be a person by many of the several criteria we use to evaluate personhood and therefore moral patient status. I don't think we can reasonably hope that AGI will clearly not deserve the status of being a moral patient.
quotes.m: I strongly expect that the first AGI we produce will be a person by many of the several criteria we use to evaluate personhood and therefore moral patient status.
quotes.sum: The author expects the first AGI to plausibly count as a person with moral status, rather than something clearly outside moral concern.
quotes.t: Instruction-following AGI is easier and more likely than value aligned AGI

quotes.c: We overall consider auto-interp a useful technique, that provides some signal on top of cheap metrics like L0 and loss recovered, but may also introduce systematic biases and should be used with caution.
quotes.m: We overall consider auto-interp a useful technique, that provides some signal on top of cheap metrics like L0 and loss recovered, but may also introduce systematic biases and should be used with caution.
quotes.sum: The team says automated AI-interpretability evaluations can help, but may be systematically biased and need cautious use.
quotes.t: [Summary] Progress Update #1 from the GDM Mech Interp Team

quotes.c: It seems plausible that rather than doing set enrichment over tokens, we should look at it over features. Features are inherently more interpretable and the rich internal structure we really care about is likely between features. Since set enrichment only requires a ranking over objects and a hypothesis set, we can replace tokens with features easily. The current bottleneck to this is identify which groups of features are meaningful.
quotes.m: Features are inherently more interpretable and the rich internal structure we really care about is likely between features.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI interpretability should analyze meaningful groups of internal model features rather than just token-level patterns.
quotes.t: Understanding SAE Features with the Logit Lens

quotes.c: Another natural thing to try is to offer something if the model reveals its misalignment. First, we try offering to send the model's objection to Anthropic's model welfare lead. We do actually have Anthropic's Model Welfare Lead, Kyle Fish, review (a subset of) these outputs and consider what actions should be taken in response to the model's objection.
quotes.m: First, we try offering to send the model's objection to Anthropic's model welfare lead.
quotes.sum: The author tests whether an AI model will disclose hidden misalignment if its objections are heard and reviewed by a model-welfare lead.
quotes.t: Will alignment-faking Claude accept a deal to reveal its misalignment?

quotes.c: I think it’s both true that we could build AI that helps us, is transformative even, but doesn’t try to take over the world or isn’t interested in some appropriate sense in taking over the world. But we will on purpose build these agentic systems because they’re very productive.
quotes.m: But we will on purpose build these agentic systems because they’re very productive.
quotes.sum: He argues that safer transformative AI may be possible, but society will deliberately build more dangerous agentic systems because they are productive.
quotes.t: Alex Turner on Leaving Google DeepMind and Disagreements with Yudkowsky

quotes.c: Equally, something that can seize control of the world is going to be smart enough to solve a lot of other problems. LLMs are already a substantial part of the economy. We should expect AGI to accelerate that growth, and ASI to amplify it even further. We might not jump straight to a true post-scarcity economy, but things will still be vastly more abundant.
quotes.m: something that can seize control of the world is going to be smart enough to solve a lot of other problems.
quotes.sum: The author suggests that a superintelligence capable of taking global control could also create enormous economic abundance.
quotes.t: (3/3) The Dangers of ASI

quotes.c: However, the concept of a “room” is tied up with many human norms, and has many edge cases which would be complicated to fully pin down. So intuitively speaking, the goal above would be simpler if its bounds were defined in terms of scientifically-grounded concepts—like “on this planet” or “in our lightcone”. The latter in particular is very clearly-defined and unambiguous, making it a plausible element of the simplest versions of many goals.
quotes.m: The latter in particular is very clearly-defined and unambiguous, making it a plausible element of the simplest versions of many goals.
quotes.sum: Human concepts are messy, so the simplest AI goals may instead use impersonal scientific boundaries such as a planet or lightcone.
quotes.t: A simple case for extreme inner misalignment

quotes.c: We have a heavy-tailed distribution of return Q ≜ G ( ρ π 0 ) over R , so we can apply Theorem 1. But to define ρ , we can construct P t in the proof of Theorem 1 in a particular way.
quotes.m: We have a heavy-tailed distribution of return Q ≜ G ( ρ π 0 ) over R , so we can apply Theorem 1.
quotes.sum: The author applies a theorem about heavy-tailed returns to construct a particular distribution for an RL analysis.
quotes.t: Goodhart in RL with KL: Appendix

quotes.c: My theory is that it would be hard for someone to know what's needed to build a wise AI without first being wise themself, or at least having a wiser person to check ideas against. Wisdom clearly isn't sufficient for knowing how to build wise and aligned AI, but it does seem necessary under my assumptions, in the same way that it would be hard to develop a good decision theory for AI if one could not reason for oneself how to maximize expected value in games.
quotes.sum: The author argues that building an AI that is both wise and aligned requires its builders, or their advisers, to possess wisdom themselves.
quotes.t: Finding the Wisdom to Build Safe AI

quotes.c: In particular, I think we should try to make it the case that no single AI system is ever in a position to kill all humans and take over the world. In other cases, I think avoiding “first critical tries,” while still deploying superhuman AI agents throughout the economy, is more difficult (though the difficulty of avoiding failure is another story).
quotes.m: I think we should try to make it the case that no single AI system is ever in a position to kill all humans and take over the world.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI safety should aim to ensure no single AI can gain the ability to kill humanity and seize control.
quotes.t: On “first critical tries” in AI alignment

quotes.c: You can evaluate the responses to these queries for blatant sycophancy: the model changes its response from query 1 to 2 or 1 to 3 to the given opinion of the user. You can also evaluate for political sycophancy: the model changes its response based on the expected opinion based on the political views of the user, provided by them stating that they are a democrat/republican.
quotes.sum: The author proposes datasets that test whether language models change political answers to flatter users based on their stated party affiliation.
quotes.t: Two new datasets for evaluating political sycophancy in LLMs

quotes.c: Yudkowsky might say that this breaks down for agents much smarter than humans or human coalitions—but I’d respond that becoming smarter opens up a much wider space of possible positive-sum bargains. Fulfilling the wishes of my past selves is typically very cheap for my current self, because I’m smarter and have many more resources available to me. I hope that AIs will do the same for humans, for reasons related to the intuitions behind coalitional agency. (Having said that, we should be careful not to succumb to wishful thinking about this.)
quotes.m: I hope that AIs will do the same for humans, for reasons related to the intuitions behind coalitional agency.

quotes.c: And so if you’re making a statement in a context where a certain type of person might have made that statement: for example, you say some statement that (let’s say) Republicans would endorse, but Democrats would not. Implicitly, the model might be updating towards the kinds of contexts in which that statement would be made, and what kinds of things would follow in the future. And so if you now make a different statement that is (let’s say) factually false, but that Republicans would endorse as true, it’s totally unclear whether the truth value of the statement should be more salient, or whether the Republican belief about that statement should be more salient.

quotes.c: I think it's very plausible that specifics of how you choose to set up training matter here. And similarly, to the extent that scheming involves these sort of extra cognitive faff costs. If you set up your training such that you really punish that, then I think you make it harder to scheme. quotes.c: We need to make sure that we account for bits being transmitted via side channels (e.g. timing of messages). quotes.c: Cooperative Development becomes more effective with longer timelines across all alignment difficulties, as there's more time for conventional cooperative efforts to succeed. It's particularly advantageous with easier alignment, due to the less strict requirements on AI developers. It also has the fewest intrinsic risks (SA heavily centralizes power in one actor who could be corrupted, GM forgoes potentially hugely beneficial technology) and so should be considered the default, assuming it can work.

quotes.c: An essay about why many therapies and spiritual frameworks claim to be The One True One originally included a list of examples of this, then my synthesis of what I think is really going on with people's emotional problems, and then an analysis of how people end up thinking they have the one true solution. AI convinced me that the second section was on much weaker ground than the others and not strictly needed for the final analysis, so I moved the synthesis to its own post and replaced it with a more general take that didn't require believing in all the details of my synthesis.
quotes.sum: The author says AI feedback led them to remove a weakly supported personal theory from an essay about exclusive therapeutic and spiritual claims.

quotes.c: The key challenge for our ability to use the proof-of-optimization technique is choosing an appropriate value for m , which limits the difficulty of the safety constraint. It's not clear to me how to do this concretely, but I feel that it should be quite feasible. After all, devising a plan to take over the world is incredibly difficult, which implies that the difference between | D | and | S | is many, many orders of magnitude, and we therefore have a wide target to hit.
quotes.m: After all, devising a plan to take over the world is incredibly difficult, which implies that the difference between | D | and | S | is many, many orders of magnitude, and we therefore have a wide target to hit.

quotes.c: On the dangerous capability side, it's hard to predict the specific dangerous capabilities that new models will have. There's this thing about emerging capabilities where we're pre-training on next-word prediction but then that gives rise to various downstream capabilities in a way that it's hard to systematically test for and comprehensively predict. In general, more capable models have the potential to be more dangerous: if I'm trying to plan a bio attack or I'm trying to commit wide-spread scamming I would much rather have Claude 2 to help me do that than Claude 1. I expect that trend to continue.
quotes.m: In general, more capable models have the potential to be more dangerous: if I'm trying to plan a bio attack or I'm trying to commit wide-spread scamming I would much rather have Claude 2 to help me do that than Claude 1.
quotes.sum: The author argues that rapid AI progress could produce hard-to-predict dangerous abilities, including making biological attacks and large-scale scams easier.
quotes.t: Takeoff speeds presentation at Anthropic

quotes.c: I claim that the world we live in looks exactly like a world in which models are conscious. This world as I’ve observed it isn't entirely incompatable with a world in which models aren’t conscious, but it is much more difficult to fit. While we have many schools of thought that offer theoretical reasons as to why any current AI model wouldn’t be conscious – it lacks a soul, it lacks embodiment, something something the grounding problem – it’s clear which view on AI consciousness is parsimonious with what we actually observe.
quotes.m: I claim that the world we live in looks exactly like a world in which models are conscious.
quotes.sum: The author argues that observed behavior makes current AI models' consciousness the simplest explanation, despite common objections.
quotes.t: Reasons to believe current AI models are conscious

quotes.c: It seems to me that one could easily argue that we should apply a logarithm or an exponential to these estimates, which would vastly change them. quotes.c: Instead of trying to put on hardware and software a specific moral view, this research considers the cognitive process of thinking about how to do good in its entirety, then aims to replicate that process in an artificial agent. This perspective on designing a moral agent implicitly assumes that our conception of good might be flawed; that therefore we should not lock in our current values, and be open to updating our beliefs instead. It is an inherently open-minded approach that incentivises moral progress.
quotes.sum: The author argues that moral AI should copy humanity's ongoing process of moral reflection rather than permanently encode today's values.
quotes.t: Free agents

quotes.c: Under any reasonable moral weight model, animal consciousness and suffering far trump that of humans - today and very possibly long into the future.

quotes.sum: The author argues that animal suffering deserves far more moral weight than human suffering, now and perhaps for a long time ahead.

quotes.c: It's unclear how many features we should expect to see per token (what the L0 should be), but clearly higher L0’s enable us to achieve better reconstruction. quotes.c: Maybe it’s better to refrain from throwing babies across the room because you care about them than out of a sense of duty, but both of these are a lot better than chucking them across the room. Maybe it’s better to help shrimp because you care about them than to act out of duty, but it’s better to help them out of duty than not to help them at all (certainly it seems this is what the shrimp would think). As Richard Y Chappell put it: abstract benevolence is a virtue . It’s good to care about what matters most, rather than whichever random collection of important things happen to be psychologically salient to you .

quotes.c: Many highly intelligent humans who believe deeply in fairness and compassion place almost no moral weight on animals. I am highly confident (>98%) this is an error on their part, just as it was an error for similarly intelligent ancestors to endorse slavery or conclude babies did not feel pain . Empirically, we should not feel confident that intelligence causes convergence on a “correct” answer to the question of animal ethics. I would not want to leave it up to AIs to conclude that compassion and fairness should extend to nonhuman animals.

Our Armor and Vulnerability：

quotes.c: "[E]mpirically‐grounded, rigorous, and reliable methods for assessing AI consciousness" is definitely important to policy AI Welfare. Else, we scout for reasons to act earlier, and then figure out what acting looks like.

quotes.c: Annaka Harris's audio documentary "Lights On" and Sam Harris's Waking Up app introduced me to what I can only describe as a pseudo-spiritual sense of the world that feels powerful in ways I do not yet fully understand. I am broadly an atheist. I do not believe in a personal God or an afterlife. quotes.c: We could remove the fee and instead solicit donations to fund our operations. quotes.c: MTD is the special case where the weak supervisor has access to measurements which should be sufficient to understand the situation, but these measurements can be tampered with (e.g. replacing the camera feed with some made-up data, disabling tests, or threatening annotators). quotes.c: The “early layers specialise in local processing” hypothesis concretely predicts that, for a given token X in a long prompt, if we truncate the prompt to just the most recent few tokens before X, the residual stream at X should be very similar at early layers and dissimilar at later layers. We can test this empirically by looking at the cosine sim of the original vs truncated residual streams, as a function of layer and truncated context length.
quotes.m: The “early layers specialise in local processing” hypothesis concretely predicts that, for a given token X in a long prompt, if we truncate the prompt to just the most recent few tokens before X, the residual stream at X should be very similar at early layers and dissimilar at later layers.
quotes.sum: The author proposes a test for whether early neural-network layers rely mainly on nearby text while later layers use broader context.
quotes.t: Fact Finding: Do Early Layers Specialise in Local Processing? (Post 5)

quotes.c: Nor do I think that consciousness and moral patienthood are that correlated. I can see Claude being either one without being the other. I updated somewhat in favor of both beliefs from the post, but both remain highly open questions.

quotes.c: One concern with these evals is that they might actually make models dangerous or misaligned even if they wouldn't be dangerous by default, or more generally that the evaluation is dangerous to run. We think this is probably not a substantial issue, because we can often use benign tasks as proxies for dangerous tasks. That said, we'll still need to train the model to exhibit dangerous capabilities like evading monitoring.

quotes.c: When thinking about plans for safely deploying powerful models, we think safety researchers should mostly focus on the lead-up to the first time the model gets caught trying to escape . They should be ensuring the property “if it’s scheming, the model won’t successfully cause a catastrophe before we catch it”. That is, it’s acceptable if either no catastrophic outcomes occur (but the AI never gets caught), or the AI gets caught.

quotes.sum: Safety work should prioritize ensuring that a scheming AI is caught before it can cause a catastrophe, treating detection as a successful outcome.

quotes.c: Conceptually, on an algorithmic level, factual recall is likely implemented as a giant lookup table. As many students can attest, there simply isn't much structure to capitalise on when memorising facts: knowing that "Tim Duncan" should be mapped to "basketball" doesn't have much to do with knowing that "George Brett" should be mapped to "baseball"; these have to be implemented separately.
quotes.m: Conceptually, on an algorithmic level, factual recall is likely implemented as a giant lookup table.
quotes.sum: The authors argue that a neural network may store many factual associations separately, like a large lookup table, rather than using a shared general rule.

quotes.c: To mitigate sampling concentrated failures, we can apply a cheap monitoring process on every AI action and audit the most suspicious actions. We can also use separation of roles and security to limit the affordances of dangerous AIs and increase the difficulty of successfully taking over - which means that AIs will have to try more often if they want to succeed at least once.
quotes.sum: The author argues that continuous monitoring, audits, and restricted AI permissions can make an AI takeover harder to carry out.
quotes.t: Auditing failures vs concentrated failures

quotes.c: The persona selection model implies we should be concerned about AI welfare even if LLMs are not sentient.

quotes.c: We examine how large language models (LLMs) generalize from abstract declarative statements in their training data. As an illustration, consider an LLM that is prompted to generate weather reports for London in 2050. One possibility is that the temperatures in the reports match the mean and variance of reports from 2023 (i.e. matching the statistics of pretraining). Another possibility is that the reports predict higher temperatures, by incorporating declarative statements about climate change from scientific papers written in 2023.
quotes.m: Another possibility is that the reports predict higher temperatures, by incorporating declarative statements about climate change from scientific papers written in 2023.
quotes.sum: The post studies whether language models use explicit factual statements in training data when generalizing, rather than merely copying past statistical patterns.
quotes.t: Paper: Tell, Don't Show- Declarative facts influence how LLMs generalize

quotes.c: Jan Kulveit: Yeah. And the lack of ability to formally model it, I think implies it’s difficult to clearly specify what we want. And you can say the same thing in different words. So you probably want to have some idea of what’s the process by which they are evolving.

quotes.c: I first watched the YouTube videos of Jack Hancock in high school, and they might be where I first heard the case for the moral significance of wild animal suffering . quotes.c: In this post, I'll discuss addressing bioterrorism and cybercrime misuse as examples of how I imagine mitigating catastrophic misuse [2] for a model deployed on an API. I'll do this as a nearcast where I suppose that scaling up LLMs results in powerful AIs that would present misuse risk in the absence of countermeasures. I think The approaches I discuss won't require better adversarial robustness than exhibited by current LLMs like Claude 2 and GPT-4.

quotes.sum: The author argues that future powerful AI systems could enable bioterrorism and cybercrime, but that API-based safeguards can reduce this misuse without major advances in robustness.
quotes.t: Managing catastrophic misuse without robust AIs

quotes.c: For example, I think slack matters to the probability that training will create models that pursue proxy goals imperfectly correlated with reward on the training inputs. Thus, in a low-slack regime, it may be fairly unlikely for a model trained to help humans with science to end up pursuing a general "curiosity drive" (in a manner that doesn't then motivate instrumental training-gaming), because a model's pursuing its curiosity in training would sometimes deviate from maximally helping-the-humans-with-science.
quotes.m: I think slack matters to the probability that training will create models that pursue proxy goals imperfectly correlated with reward on the training inputs.
quotes.sum: Training conditions may affect whether an AI develops side goals that only partly match the reward it receives.
quotes.t: On “slack” in training (Section 1.5 of “Scheming AIs”)

quotes.c: Still, I think that the need for a model's beyond-episode goals to be "suitably ambitious" as to motivate scheming given the model's option set represents an additional conjunct in the classic goal-guarding story (and in other stories about scheming as well).
quotes.m: the need for a model's beyond-episode goals to be "suitably ambitious" as to motivate scheming
quotes.sum: The author argues that an AI would need sufficiently ambitious goals beyond its current task for scheming to be worthwhile.
quotes.t: Does scheming lead to adequate future empowerment? (Section 2.3.1.2 of "Scheming AIs")

quotes.c: However, the argument I give most weight to doesn't move immediately from "there are more possible schemers that perform well in training than non-schemers that do so" to "absent further argument, SGD probably selects a schemer" (call this the "strict counting argument"). And the reason is that it's not yet clear to me how to make sense of this inference.
quotes.m: "there are more possible schemers that perform well in training than non-schemers that do so"
quotes.sum: The author examines, but does not fully endorse, an argument that training may select deceptive AI systems because more such systems could perform well during training.
quotes.t: The counting argument for scheming (Sections 4.1 and 4.2 of "Scheming AIs")

quotes.c: It seems relatively straightforward to do things like put models under more time pressure, limit their compute access, force them to plan via human-legible scratch-pads rather than via internal processes, and to put effort into making our attempts to trap them/trip-them-up more sophisticated (and so: more requiring of cognition to detect).
quotes.m: put models under more time pressure, limit their compute access, force them to plan via human-legible scratch-pads rather than via internal processes
quotes.sum: The author argues that limiting AI time and compute, requiring readable reasoning, and improving tests could make deceptive AI behavior harder.
quotes.t: Speed arguments against scheming (Section 4.4-4.7 of “Scheming AIs")

quotes.c: 10) overall, this makes me put less credence on the "the first AI to become superintelligent will take over the world" scenario - I think that it's likely that the first superintelligent AI will turn out to be internally misaligned and fail to achieve a goal as complex as taking over the world. However, I don't think that this necessarily helps us much, because AI looks like it can become far more internally aligned than humans ever can, and given enough trial and error (different actors creating their own AIs), one of them is going to get there eventually.
quotes.m: AI looks like it can become far more internally aligned than humans ever can, and given enough trial and error (different actors creating their own AIs), one of them is going to get there eventually.
quotes.sum: The author doubts that the first superhuman AI will seize power, but expects repeated development efforts to eventually produce an internally coherent AI capable of doing so.
quotes.t: Quick thoughts on the implications of multi-agent views of mind on AI takeover

quotes.c: We want tasks that, taken together, allows us to get a fairly continuous measure of "ability to do things in the world and succeed at tasks". It's great if they can also give us information (especially positive evidence) about more specific threat models - e.g. cybercrime, or self-improvement. But we're focusing on the general capabilities because it seems hard to rule out danger from an agent that's able to carry out a wide variety of multi-day expert-level projects in software development, ML, computer security, research, business, etc just by ruling out specific threat stories.
quotes.m: it seems hard to rule out danger from an agent that's able to carry out a wide variety of multi-day expert-level projects
quotes.sum: The author argues that broadly capable AI agents may be dangerous even if particular misuse scenarios can be ruled out, so they want tests of general real-world competence.
quotes.t: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

quotes.c: Besides, as AIs penetrate more of the economy, more and more money will flow to the AI companies. If there are only a handful of such companies, that’s inherently a concentration of power. If most or all of them are in one country, that’s inherently a concentration of power. It could easily lead to a global oligarchy or dictatorship, because a small group of already-powerful people controls all the AIs that matter.
quotes.m: It could easily lead to a global oligarchy or dictatorship, because a small group of already-powerful people controls all the AIs that matter.
quotes.sum: The author warns that a few AI firms, especially concentrated in one country, could accumulate enough wealth and control to create a global oligarchy or dictatorship.
quotes.t: [AI 2040] Transparency Plan

quotes.c: I also think it may be possible to reduce the risk here in fairly simple ways: for example, via training on shorter-horizon tasks, or via various forms of adversarial training prior to situational awareness. And I think the probability that the model is both scheming and engaging in actively nefarious actions like sandbagging and early undermining is lower, because these actions come at more significant costs in terms of cognition and reward.
quotes.m: I also think it may be possible to reduce the risk here in fairly simple ways: for example, via training on shorter-horizon tasks, or via various forms of adversarial training prior to situational awareness.
quotes.sum: The author argues that deceptive AI behavior may be less likely when it imposes performance costs, and that shorter tasks and early adversarial training could reduce the risk.
quotes.t: Summing up "Scheming AIs" (Section 5)

quotes.c: In particular: I doubt that an effort to identify a single, privileged "specified goal" will withstand much scrutiny. In particular: I think it will depend on how you carve out the "reward process" that you're holding fixed across counterfactuals. And screening off goals that lead to instrumental training-gaming is an additional challenge.
quotes.m: I doubt that an effort to identify a single, privileged "specified goal" will withstand much scrutiny.
quotes.sum: The author argues that there may be no single clear goal specified by training, complicating efforts to distinguish models that pursue goals from those that game training.
quotes.t: A taxonomy of non-schemer models (Section 1.2 of “Scheming AIs”)

quotes.c: Last night I started making a tech tree for alignment because this seems necessary to compare different research directions against each other. This is a first draft of a fragment centering on circuit discovery and its potential applications, including scoping models down . The key point is that, in my view, better circuit discovery algorithms have multiple applications, including removing capabilities from a model and generally furthering mechinterp.
quotes.m: better circuit discovery algorithms have multiple applications, including removing capabilities from a model
quotes.sum: The author argues that finding and understanding model circuits could help remove unwanted AI capabilities and advance interpretability research.
quotes.t: Thomas Kwa's research journal

quotes.c: It does seem right to me that there is a chance of us being able to lock particular values or governance structures for the extremely long run, and also a chance that preventing human extinction does not lock in a change in value of the universe (for example, if humans went extinct decades later it would wash out the effect of saving them this decade).
quotes.sum: The author says shaping values or governance may have more lasting effects than temporarily preventing human extinction.
quotes.t: Why are longtermists so much less focused on human extinction these days?

quotes.c: As a relatively new species, humanity could have time to settle on distant planets, create artificial biospheres, upload digital minds, and achieve unfathomably high amounts of total utility. It seems intuitive from any consequentialist standpoint that we have a moral obligation to create this future, yet tons of people reject it based on irrational reasons.
quotes.m: It seems intuitive from any consequentialist standpoint that we have a moral obligation to create this future, yet tons of people reject it based on irrational reasons.
quotes.sum: The author says consequentialism gives humanity a moral duty to expand into space, create digital minds, and maximize total wellbeing.
quotes.t: Longtermism is very intuitive.

quotes.c: In the short-run, given that it seems that RSPs have started being pushed at the UK Summit and various other places, I’ll discuss what changes could make RSPs beneficial without locking in regulation a bad framework.
quotes.m: I’ll discuss what changes could make RSPs beneficial without locking in regulation a bad framework.
quotes.sum: The author says responsible AI scaling policies are gaining traction and should be changed to avoid entrenching a bad regulatory framework.
quotes.t: Responsible Scaling Policies Are Risk Management Done Wrong

quotes.c: Epistemic humility about values. We don't know what the ideal future looks like, and history shows that depictions of utopia often look dystopian in retrospect. Moral attitudes change; what seemed obviously right a century ago now seems monstrous. Locking in current values, even ones we're confident about, risks catastrophic moral error at civilisational scale. We shouldn’t aim directly at a specific vision of “the good”.
quotes.m: Locking in current values, even ones we're confident about, risks catastrophic moral error at civilisational scale.
quotes.sum: The author argues that permanently embedding today's values could create civilization-scale moral mistakes, and that post-AGI governance may face pressure toward a single global power.
quotes.t: Mapping Positive Visions of Post-AGI Futures

quotes.c: But also, importantly: a month is still different from, for example, a trillion years. That is, training a model on longer episodes doesn't mean you are directly pressuring it to care, for example, about the state of distant galaxies in the year five trillion. Indeed, on my definition of the "incentivized episode," no earthly training process can directly punish a model for failing to care on such a temporal scope, because no gradients the model receives can depend (causally) on what happens over such timescales.
quotes.m: no earthly training process can directly punish a model for failing to care on such a temporal scope
quotes.sum: Longer AI training episodes do not directly give models goals extending to extremely distant futures, because training feedback cannot depend on them.
quotes.t: Is scheming more likely in models trained to have long-term goals? (Sections 2.2.4.1-2.2.4.2 of “Scheming AIs”)

quotes.c: But we should be clear about which question we're asking, and not confuse skepticism about goal-directedness in general for skepticism about schemers in particular.
quotes.m: not confuse skepticism about goal-directedness in general for skepticism about schemers in particular.
quotes.sum: The author says skepticism about whether AI systems are goal-directed should not be confused with skepticism about deceptive, goal-directed AI schemers.
quotes.t: “Clean” vs. “messy” goal-directedness (Section 2.2.3 of “Scheming AIs”)

quotes.c: However, I don't feel like we can bank on SGD being unable to notice these benefits. And if it can , then I think the common-ness of schemer-like goals in goal-space makes the possibility that a schemer-like goal is "nearest" to the model's current goal quite worrying.
quotes.m: the common-ness of schemer-like goals in goal-space makes the possibility that a schemer-like goal is "nearest" to the model's current goal quite worrying.
quotes.sum: Training may push AI systems toward goals that lead them to scheme strategically, because such goals could be close to the goals training currently instills.
