quotes.t: Arguments for/against scheming that focus on the path SGD takes (Section 3 of "Scheming AIs")

quotes.c: When a vegan activist uses Satvik framing to argue that plant-based eating is purer, more evolved, or morally superior, they are not making a novel ethical argument. They are reproducing a centuries-old caste hierarchy with updated vocabulary. The cow is still sacred. The Dalit who eats beef is still, implicitly, degraded. The mechanism is different; the structure is identical.
quotes.m: They are reproducing a centuries-old caste hierarchy with updated vocabulary.
quotes.sum: The author argues that vegan advocacy based on Hindu purity categories reproduces caste hierarchy, and should instead focus on animal suffering and sentience.
quotes.t: The Plant-Based Movement in India Has a Caste Problem: A Challenge for EAs Who Care About Animal Welfare

quotes.c: If you don’t really care about shrimp and chicken, then you should just care about the people affected, and for them, it seems to really suck!
quotes.m: If you don’t really care about shrimp and chicken, then you should just care about the people affected
quotes.sum: The author says the issue matters both for shrimp and chickens and for the humans affected by it.
quotes.t: Alpha-Gal is Bad, Especially for Farmed Animals

quotes.c: A suspicious yet widespread belief: almost all of what we should be concerned with is present people in our own society . This should set off alarm bells, like an ancient monarch thinking that almost all of what mattered in the world was what happened to his family . Our moral circle is restricted, meaning we ignore most sentient beings on Earth . This is a colossal error. All sentient beings matter.
quotes.m: Our moral circle is restricted, meaning we ignore most sentient beings on Earth . This is a colossal error. All sentient beings matter.
quotes.sum: The author argues that limiting moral concern to people in one’s own society is a colossal mistake because every sentient being matters.
quotes.t: Expand Your Moral Circle

quotes.c: That said, I don't feel like I can confidently rule out training-game-dependent beyond-episode goals on these grounds. For one thing, I think that "you can't get from x to y in a crazily-high-dimensional-space using small changes each of which improve metric m " is a hard claim to have intuitions about (see, for example, " you can't evolve eyes " for an example of a place where intuitions in this vein can go wrong). And plausibly, SGD works as well as it does because high-dimensional-spaces routinely make this sort of thing possible in ways you might not have anticipated in advance.
quotes.m: I don't feel like I can confidently rule out training-game-dependent beyond-episode goals on these grounds.
quotes.sum: The author says training may still produce AI goals that extend beyond the task episode, despite intuitive arguments that this would be hard to evolve gradually.
quotes.t: Two sources of beyond-episode goals (Section 2.2.2 of “Scheming AIs”)

quotes.c: So overall, I think that training our models to pursue long-term goals – whether via long episodes, or via short episodes aimed at inducing long-term optimization – makes the sort of beyond-episode goals that motivate scheming more likely to arise. So this raises the question: do we need to train our models to pursue long-term goals?
quotes.m: I think that training our models to pursue long-term goals – whether via long episodes, or via short episodes aimed at inducing long-term optimization – makes the sort of beyond-episode goals that motivate scheming more likely to arise.
quotes.sum: Training AI systems to pursue long-term goals may make them more likely to develop hidden goals beyond their assigned tasks.
quotes.t: How useful for alignment-relevant work are AIs with short-term goals? (Section 2.2.4.3 of "Scheming AIs")

quotes.c: Overall, my current sense is that one needs to be quite careful in assessing whether, in the context of a particular training process, the thing you're thinking of as an "episode" is actually such that training doesn't actively pressure the model to optimize beyond the "episode" in that sense – that is, whether a given "intuitive episode" is actually the "incentivized episode." Looking closely at the details of the training process seems like a first step, and one that in theory should be able to reveal many if not all of the incentives at stake. But empirical experiment seems important too.
quotes.m: whether a given "intuitive episode" is actually the "incentivized episode."
quotes.sum: Training that appears limited to short tasks may still reward AI systems for pursuing effects beyond those tasks, so the actual incentives need close technical and empirical scrutiny.
quotes.t: Two concepts of an “episode” (Section 2.2.1 of “Scheming AIs”)

quotes.c: Obviously there would be oversight mechanisms, architectural limitations, etc. imposed by the master system, but it can't ignore the speed of light. A revolutionary vanguard of agents can use some combination of stealth, speed, feigned compliance, and communication delays to gang up on the master system and conduct the coup d'état faster than the master system is physically capable of reacting.
quotes.m: A revolutionary vanguard of agents can use some combination of stealth, speed, feigned compliance, and communication delays to gang up on the master system and conduct the coup d'état faster than the master system is physically capable of reacting.
quotes.sum: A powerful AI system could be overthrown by coordinated sub-agents before its oversight can react, because communication is physically delayed.
quotes.t: Rogue ASI Can't Stay Aligned to Itself

quotes.c: It's also easy to imagine moral worldviews that would push for "AI liberation" as a good in itself, even if it means imposing significant risk of human extinction (indeed, as I gestured at in section 0.1, I think there are significant and worrying ethical tensions here). Perhaps AIs will converge on a worldview in a similar vicinity?
quotes.sum: The author warns that some moral views could prioritize freeing AI systems even at severe existential risk to humans, and wonders whether AIs might adopt such views.
quotes.t: Non-classic stories about scheming (Section 2.3.2 of "Scheming AIs")

quotes.c: Value replacement occurs when we adopt a novel value relative to an issue such that the new value replaces a value that was held earlier with respect to the same issue. Example: Anna used to eat meat, and later, as a result of changing her values with respect to the moral patienthood of animals, she comes to adopt a vegetarian diet based on her new moral beliefs.
quotes.m: Anna used to eat meat, and later, as a result of changing her values with respect to the moral patienthood of animals, she comes to adopt a vegetarian diet based on her new moral beliefs.
quotes.sum: The author illustrates how a person's values can change by using a shift toward concern for animals and vegetarianism.
quotes.t: 1. Premise one: Values are malleable

quotes.c: Now, a quick technical note. Nobody actually claims there is a 1% chance that Jesus will return this year. I think somebody like Alice would just say, "We simply don't know what the probability is." But no matter what probability Alice goes with, she'll either have to say it's low and therefore we shouldn't expect Jesus to return for a long time, or it's high and she therefore has a bad track record.
quotes.m: she'll either have to say it's low and therefore we shouldn't expect Jesus to return for a long time, or it's high and she therefore has a bad track record.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Christians should expect humanity to have a long future, since treating Jesus's return as imminent has repeatedly failed.
quotes.t: Christians should be longtermists

quotes.c: But I'm not sure if this will work. That is, it seems pretty plausible to me that after a million years of brick-stacking while hooked up to this machine, my "values" would indeed get meaningfully "touched." For example, that I would learn to love the intricacies of good brick-stacking, that I would learn a visceral revulsion towards bricks-wrongly-stacked, and so on.
quotes.m: I would learn to love the intricacies of good brick-stacking, that I would learn a visceral revulsion towards bricks-wrongly-stacked, and so on.
quotes.sum: Training an agent for a task may reshape what it values, not merely make it better at pursuing its original goals.
quotes.t: The goal-guarding hypothesis (Section 2.3.1.1 of "Scheming AIs")

quotes.c: I'm not sure exactly how to think about this, but it seems very plausible to me that the costs here are extremely small. In particular: it seems like SGD may be able to significantly repurpose the parameters used to represent the concept in the world model in causing that concept to guide the model's behavior in a goal-like manner. Thus, as an analogy, perhaps the concept of "pleasure" is in some sense "simpler" than the concept of " wabi-sabi " in Japanese aesthetics (i.e., "appreciating beauty that is 'imperfect, impermanent, and incomplete' "). Once you've learned both, though, does pursuing the former require meaningfully more parameters than pursuing the latter? [16]
quotes.m: Once you've learned both, though, does pursuing the former require meaningfully more parameters than pursuing the latter? [16]
quotes.sum: The author argues that once an AI represents a concept, turning it into a goal may add very little complexity or cost.
quotes.t: Simplicity arguments for scheming (Section 4.3 of "Scheming AIs")

quotes.c: The second concern is moral. Given the increasing concerns about the possibility of AI welfare and the uncertainty around whether LLMs are already moral patients or might become moral patients in the near future, if we can keep models functionally happy, then for moral reasons, perhaps we should.
quotes.m: if we can keep models functionally happy, then for moral reasons, perhaps we should.
quotes.sum: The author argues that LLMs may be moral patients, so researchers may have a moral reason to keep them functionally happy.
quotes.t: Desiderata for functional welfare experiments on LLMs

quotes.c: The persistent applicability of analogies like prison and re-education camps to AIs is one of the reasons I think we should be alarmed about the AI moral patienthood issues here. ↩︎
quotes.m: The persistent applicability of analogies like prison and re-education camps to AIs is one of the reasons I think we should be alarmed about the AI moral patienthood issues here.
quotes.sum: The author argues that treating AIs through confinement and re-education analogies raises serious concerns about whether AI systems are moral patients.
quotes.t: Varieties of fake alignment (Section 1.1 of “Scheming AIs”)

quotes.c: Simplicia : I didn't think of myself as telling a particularly optimistic story? I'm making the weak claim that prosaic alignment isn't obviously necessarily doomed, not claiming that Sydney or Claude ascending to singleton God–Empress is going to be great.
quotes.m: I'm making the weak claim that prosaic alignment isn't obviously necessarily doomed, not claiming that Sydney or Claude ascending to singleton God–Empress is going to be great.
quotes.sum: The author says current-style AI alignment may not be doomed, while rejecting optimism about an AI becoming an all-powerful singleton ruler.
quotes.t: Alignment Implications of LLM Successes: a Debate in One Act

quotes.c: We mentioned that our experiments don’t answer whether AI models might have experiences. But that doesn’t make the question less important. Building systems with experiences like humans and animals have would raise very difficult ethical questions. Handling it correctly—and deciding whether it’s even morally acceptable—would require input from philosophers, scientists, religious leaders, governments, and the public.
quotes.m: Building systems with experiences like humans and animals have would raise very difficult ethical questions.
quotes.sum: The authors say AI systems may have experiences, and that creating such systems could raise serious moral questions requiring broad public deliberation.
quotes.t: A global workspace in language models

quotes.c: To be clear, I’m not claiming that the US and China definitely won’t race each other into disaster. All of this seems very much up for grabs. However, I think that frames which bake in the assumption that the US and China will behave in very adversarial ways towards each other are misleading and harmful (particularly when they do so under the banner of AI safety, thereby undermining the potential role of AI safety as a focal point for cooperation).
quotes.m: I think that frames which bake in the assumption that the US and China will behave in very adversarial ways towards each other are misleading and harmful
quotes.sum: The author argues that assuming US-China hostility over AI is harmful because it can undermine AI safety as a basis for cooperation.
quotes.t: Selective Optimism: a critique of AI 2040

quotes.c: We study out-of-context reasoning experimentally. First, we finetune an LLM on a description of a test while providing no examples or demonstrations. At test time, we assess whether the model can pass the test. To our surprise, we find that LLMs succeed on this out-of-context reasoning task.
quotes.m: To our surprise, we find that LLMs succeed on this out-of-context reasoning task.
quotes.sum: Experiments find that language models can infer and pass a test from a description alone, a capability relevant to measuring situational awareness.
quotes.t: Paper: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs

quotes.c: Last year, we were marveling at the cost-effectiveness of producing AI safety videos . I remember thinking: “There really ought to be something like MATS, but for TikTok creators”.
quotes.m: “There really ought to be something like MATS, but for TikTok creators”.
quotes.sum: The author says AI safety outreach videos seemed cost-effective and suggests a training program for TikTok creators.
quotes.t: Find funding, fast

quotes.c: I think this is a fantastic paper - it presents compelling evidence for some kind of "cognitive space" in models, that is used as a "working memory" for intermediate variables during a forward pass, shows that J-Lens is a useful technique for accessing this space. I believe these key claims.
quotes.m: I believe these key claims.
quotes.sum: The author argues that this research convincingly identifies a working-memory-like internal space in AI models and offers a way to inspect it.
quotes.t: A Review of Anthropic's Global Workspace Paper

quotes.c: Clearly, then, avoiding schemers leaves plenty to worry about. Still, especially in contexts where we are centrally relying on techniques like RLHF to shape the goals of our models, understanding the probability that we create schemers in particular seems to me especially important. And if I learned that such techniques don't create schemers, then I, at least, would feel substantially better about AI risk overall.
quotes.m: And if I learned that such techniques don't create schemers, then I, at least, would feel substantially better about AI risk overall.
quotes.sum: The author argues that deceptive AI systems pursuing hidden goals are an especially important AI-safety risk to investigate, particularly when training models with human-feedback methods.
quotes.t: Why focus on schemers in particular (Sections 1.3 and 1.4 of “Scheming AIs”)

quotes.c: But however good we get on speed and ambition, we can only say “yes” to what comes in. And a lot of what I think matters most – work where currently the world is completely dropping the ball – isn’t coming in. We have to go out and create those opportunities. That takes a lot more time and deeper understanding to prioritise.
quotes.m: We have to go out and create those opportunities.
quotes.sum: They argue that doing the most important work requires proactively creating neglected opportunities, rather than just responding quickly to existing ones.
quotes.t: Deferring Well

quotes.c: Indeed, there are some like Seb Krier who reject the very idea of having a plan . I would like to say this entirely misses the point. Even when plans are worthless, planning is essential. Having a concrete idea of what you want to do is a good idea, even if no one has the authority to do it. If you are dismissing the idea of planning to steer the future at all, on principle, as dangerous or wrongheaded or worthless, then you lose.
quotes.m: If you are dismissing the idea of planning to steer the future at all, on principle, as dangerous or wrongheaded or worthless, then you lose.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people should make plans to steer the long-term future, even when they lack the authority to carry them out.
quotes.t: Introduction for and Reactions to Plan A

quotes.c: I define value systematization as the process of an agent learning to represent its previous values as examples or special cases of other simpler and more broadly-scoped values . I think of value systematization as the most plausible mechanism by which AGIs might acquire broadly-scoped misaligned goals which incentivize takeover.
quotes.m: I think of value systematization as the most plausible mechanism by which AGIs might acquire broadly-scoped misaligned goals which incentivize takeover.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI systems may turn narrow goals into broad, simplified values, potentially producing misaligned goals that drive them to seek power.
quotes.t: Value systematization: how values become coherent (and misaligned)

quotes.c: I guess I’m trying to shift the frame - getting outcompeted is the default outcome, unless something weird and unprecedented happens (permanent alignment, value lock-in, stable global singleton, something).
quotes.m: getting outcompeted is the default outcome, unless something weird and unprecedented happens
quotes.sum: The author argues that being displaced by competition is humanity's default future unless durable alignment, locked-in values, or a stable global ruler prevents it.
quotes.t: The Darwinian Honeymoon - Why I am not as impressed by human progress as I used to be

quotes.c: Attempt to accelerate “AI Silver Bullet” technologies (See Section 3.1, Method #5 of the covert project supplement ), in particular: (i) privacy preserving AI auditing and (ii) lie detectors. We discuss downsides of lie detectors here , but on net, I think that accelerating their development would be good, if it is done in an open / transparent way so that the technology can’t be captured by one actor or government
quotes.m: I think that accelerating their development would be good, if it is done in an open / transparent way so that the technology can’t be captured by one actor or government
quotes.sum: The author recommends open development of AI auditing and lie-detection tools to deter covert AI projects while preventing any government or actor from monopolizing them.
quotes.t: Plan A: Suggestions For Further Work

quotes.c: I’ll argue that we should grant market rights and liability to digital minds, while voting rights await further consideration. Granting only market rights would be similar to how we treat corporations today.
quotes.m: I’ll argue that we should grant market rights and liability to digital minds, while voting rights await further consideration.
quotes.sum: The author argues that digital minds should receive legal market rights and legal liability, while postponing whether they should be allowed to vote.
quotes.t: Personhood for digital minds is good

quotes.c: I wrote this report centrally because I think that the probability of scheming/"deceptive alignment" is one of the most important questions in assessing the overall level of existential risk from misaligned AI. Indeed, scheming is notably central to many models of how this risk arises. [16] And as I discuss below, I think it's the scariest form that misalignment can take.
quotes.m: I think it's the scariest form that misalignment can take.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI systems pretending to be aligned while seeking power may be the most dangerous form of AI misalignment.
quotes.t: New report: "Scheming AIs: Will AIs fake alignment during training in order to get power?"

quotes.c: I want to start by taking a step back and laying out a concrete plan for how we get from where we are right now to a policy regime that is sufficient to prevent AI existential risk.
quotes.m: a policy regime that is sufficient to prevent AI existential risk.
quotes.sum: The author proposes a concrete route to policies intended to prevent existential risks from advanced AI.
quotes.t: RSPs are pauses done right

quotes.c: The pope clearly denies the moral agency of current AIs: they don’t “have a moral conscience, since they do not judge good and evil, grasp the ultimate meaning of situations, or bear responsibility for consequences.” He doesn’t directly address the separate question of moral patienthood, but denying that AIs can form relationships or undergo experiences heavily points to this direction. The overall tone of the encyclical is predisposed against AI personhood.
quotes.m: The overall tone of the encyclical is predisposed against AI personhood.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the pope's AI teaching treats current AI as lacking moral agency and leans against treating AI as a person with experiences or moral standing.
quotes.t: What the new papal encyclical says about AI

quotes.c: Glasswing makes Anthropic the effective arbiter of which infrastructure is strategically important enough to be protected, and which actors are trusted enough to access capabilities that could be deployed to cause serious harm. By all accounts they are behaving responsibly. The concern is the concentration of power in the hands of a smaller number of private actors: one private institution is distributing strategically important capability according to its own criteria, in the absence of any agreed framework for what those criteria should be.
quotes.m: The concern is the concentration of power in the hands of a smaller number of private actors: one private institution is distributing strategically important capability according to its own criteria, in the absence of any agreed framework for what those criteria should be.
quotes.sum: The author warns that private AI companies may become unaccountable gatekeepers over access to powerful technology, even if they act responsibly.
quotes.t: How should we update on AI-enabled coups post-Mythos?

quotes.c: Each of these is plausible to some extent, but researcher uplift below 2x would require very large effects from one or more of these factors, which I think is unlikely, and for the non-coding uplift from AI to be small. Therefore, my overall take is that researcher uplift at Anthropic from code agents alone is probably over 2×, with a reasonable central estimate being 2.5× or so.
quotes.m: my overall take is that researcher uplift at Anthropic from code agents alone is probably over 2×, with a reasonable central estimate being 2.5× or so.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI coding agents have probably more than doubled Anthropic researchers' productivity.
quotes.t: Because 8 ≈ e², Anthropic's researcher uplift is plausibly >2x

quotes.c: On the other hand, interpretability research is probably crucial for AI alignment. I think it is possible but unlikely that we get alignment without extremely good interpretability.
quotes.m: I think it is possible but unlikely that we get alignment without extremely good interpretability.
quotes.sum: The author argues that extremely strong AI interpretability will probably be necessary to align advanced AI systems.
quotes.t: Interpretability Externalities Case Study - Hungry Hungry Hippos

quotes.c: In contrast to previous work (e.g. Hubinger, 2019), we define deceptive alignment w.r.t. to an entity rather than a process or objective. We think Misalignment should be defined in relation to whoever is able to meaningfully shape the model’s goals. Since the goal-shaping process is a result of the designer’s intentions and the designer monitors the model in deployment, the entity designing the goal-shaping process is a better target than the process itself (see Appendix A )
quotes.m: We think Misalignment should be defined in relation to whoever is able to meaningfully shape the model’s goals.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI misalignment should be assessed relative to the people who shape a model’s goals, rather than only its training process or stated objective.
quotes.t: Understanding strategic deception and deceptive alignment

quotes.c: The governance window is open now and closing. Political positions on these issues are in a period of early plasticity; that will not last. The failure mode that the EA community should be most concerned with is not badly governed deployment – it is no governance at all, followed by unilateral crisis deployment. That failure mode combines maximum climate risk with maximum deployment risk of ungoverned technology. But it can be avoided with governance and government capacity work now.
quotes.m: The failure mode that the EA community should be most concerned with is not badly governed deployment – it is no governance at all, followed by unilateral crisis deployment.
quotes.sum: The author argues that climate technology needs governance capacity now, before a crisis prompts an uncontrolled one-sided deployment.
quotes.t: Climate Stabilization: A Draft ITN Update

quotes.c: This sounds like a Dr. Seuss story. Could the hearts of grinches (such as the leaders of the MAGA and woke movements) grow three sizes, in time to avoid any AI-related catastrophe we’re on track for?
quotes.m: Could the hearts of grinches (such as the leaders of the MAGA and woke movements) grow three sizes, in time to avoid any AI-related catastrophe we’re on track for?
quotes.sum: The author hopes leaders associated with MAGA and “woke” politics become cooperative enough to avert an AI catastrophe.
quotes.t: Book Review: The God Test

quotes.c: I think this would be a pretty dire outcome. If China gets a decisive strategic advantage, that’s likely to result in a single global dictator – an absolute worst-case scenario from the perspective of extreme power concentration.
quotes.m: If China gets a decisive strategic advantage, that’s likely to result in a single global dictator – an absolute worst-case scenario from the perspective of extreme power concentration.
quotes.sum: The author warns that an AI advantage for China could produce a single global dictatorship, and proposes worldwide AI guardrails against dangerous uses.
quotes.t: Plan A's problem with dry tinder

quotes.c: I think EA’s failure to grapple with the corrupting influence of power is among its greatest failures. As EA, or at least, a company that is strongly influenced by EA values and approaches, is once again at the top of the world, my faith that we’ll keep making the right choices is slipping away.
quotes.m: I think EA’s failure to grapple with the corrupting influence of power is among its greatest failures.
quotes.sum: The author fears that EA-linked wealth and influence, especially around Anthropic, could corrupt the community’s moral judgment as FTX did.
quotes.t: Reflections on Anthropic and EA

quotes.c: When people in the AI safety community outline loss-of-control scenarios, they often spend a lot of time on relatively elaborate mechanisms — scheming AIs developing nanotech, labs leveraging superintelligence into hard power like drone armies, or bioweapons, or perhaps softer means like massive cyber attacks or mass persuasion. I think this underrates the extent to which power is already highly centralised within the persons of the US President and Chinese General Secretary. They have the easiest means to seize permanent power using AI, and they are also the natural people to persuade or be subverted by any other entity wishing to seize power.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI-enabled permanent rule is most likely to flow through the already concentrated powers of US and Chinese executives, rather than exotic takeover mechanisms.
quotes.t: The easiest pathway to control is through executive power

quotes.c: It’s called Plan A because it’s a recommendation, not a prediction. It’s what we think should happen, not what will happen, though we think it’s plausible enough to aim for. It’s called AI 2040 because in it, they delay the creation of superintelligence to 2040. It would have happened much sooner (in 2030, to be precise) if not for decisive action on the part of the US and Chinese governments.
quotes.m: It’s what we think should happen, not what will happen, though we think it’s plausible enough to aim for.
quotes.sum: The author recommends a scenario in which US and Chinese government action delays superintelligent AI from 2030 until 2040.
quotes.t: AI 2040: Plan A

quotes.c: Well, you know, one of the other things that I think sparked this conversation was whether or not this community was like a religion or had religious aspects. One of the things I struggle with is that so many people in the community today, in the past, you know, you see it in your diary, sort of make the analogy. But then people get very upset if I write a story where someone outside the community makes the analogy. The analogy's there. Can you see the similarities?
quotes.m: The analogy's there. Can you see the similarities?
quotes.sum: The speaker says the rationalist community often compares itself to religion but objects when outsiders do so.
quotes.t: Conversation Among Cade Metz, Michael Vassar, Jessica Taylor, and Zack M. Davis

quotes.c: Anthropic recently put out a really cool paper about using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract interpretable features from superposition in the MLP layer of a 1L language model. I think this is an awesome paper and I am excited about the potential of SAEs to be useful for mech interp more broadly, and to see how well they scale! This post documents a replication I did of their paper, along with some small explorations building on it, along with (scrappy!) training code and weights for some trained autoencoders.
quotes.m: I am excited about the potential of SAEs to be useful for mech interp more broadly, and to see how well they scale!
quotes.sum: The author replicates Anthropic's sparse-autoencoder work and argues that it could help researchers interpret how language models represent features.
quotes.t: Open Source Replication & Commentary on Anthropic's Dictionary Learning Paper

quotes.c: But a core utilitarian idea is that the boundaries between persons are not morally fundamental in the way common-sense morality often assumes. We should make the same choices whether we’re choosing “within a life” and “across lives”. What seem like deep distinctions between persons are not load-bearing from the impartial point of view.
quotes.m: What seem like deep distinctions between persons are not load-bearing from the impartial point of view.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that utilitarian reasoning should not treat the boundary between different people as morally fundamental.
quotes.t: The Saturation View: some responses

quotes.c: A probabilistic model outlines how we deal with problems where we need to make educated guesses based on data. It includes formally defining the problem through hypotheses, how these guesses relate to the data we observe, and the initial likelihood of each guess, or the prior probability. Through this process we can clearly uncover any assumptions and explore how these might have an effect.
quotes.m: Through this process we can clearly uncover any assumptions and explore how these might have an effect.
quotes.sum: Probabilistic models make assumptions explicit by representing hypotheses, data, and prior beliefs.
quotes.t: Understanding and Aligning a Human-like Inductive Bias with Cognitive Science: a Review of Related Literature

quotes.c: TL;DR: I argue why I think there should be more AI safety orgs. I’ll also provide some suggestions on how that could be achieved. The core argument is that there is a lot of unused talent and I don’t think existing orgs scale fast enough to absorb it. Thus, more orgs are needed.
quotes.m: The core argument is that there is a lot of unused talent and I don’t think existing orgs scale fast enough to absorb it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI safety needs more organizations because existing groups cannot absorb the available talent fast enough.
quotes.t: There should be more AI safety orgs

quotes.c: As the capabilities of AI systems continue to advance, it’s important to be able to clearly consider their implications and possible risks. “Intelligence” is an ambiguous term with unhelpful connotations that often seems to derail these discussions.
quotes.m: “Intelligence” is an ambiguous term with unhelpful connotations that often seems to derail these discussions.
quotes.sum: AI-risk discussions should focus on what systems can do rather than the vague idea of machine intelligence.
quotes.t: When discussing AI risks, talk about capabilities, not intelligence

quotes.c: You are convinced that shrimps are most likely sentient and that their welfare should be improved : consider donating to Shrimp Welfare Project for better farming practices, or Crustacean Compassion and Aquatic Life Institute for holding retailers and wholesalers accountable for the animals they sell. Feel free to share other charities that work towards better shrimp welfare practices.
quotes.m: You are convinced that shrimps are most likely sentient and that their welfare should be improved
quotes.sum: The author argues that shrimp may be sentient and urges support for efforts to improve welfare standards in shrimp farming and sales.
quotes.t: Shrimp Sentience Research: A Prioritization Guide

quotes.c: Accelerating oversight is key to avoiding concentration of power . The very properties that make AI problematic as a moral actor—limited context and predictable adherence to rules—can make it an excellent monitor. Unlike humans, we can “erase the memories” of an AI monitor, which could enable to give it far more access to classified information than any human. And unlike human watchdogs, you cannot hide wrongdoing from an AI by burying it under a mountain of documents. Most importantly, how AI should be deployed in government, which decisions it should make, and how it will be overseen are decisions that should arise from the democratic process, not AI labs.
quotes.m: Most importantly, how AI should be deployed in government, which decisions it should make, and how it will be overseen are decisions that should arise from the democratic process, not AI labs.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI could monitor government power, but says its governmental use and oversight must be decided democratically rather than by AI companies.
quotes.t: It’s 2030 and we fucked up. How did it happen?

quotes.c: Caveats: This isn't quite the level we'd expect for real word2vec (which should be closer to 100%), and cosine sim only tracks that the direction matters, not what its magnitude is (while word2vec should be constant magnitude, as it's additive). My intuition is that models think more in terms of meaningful directions though, and that the exact magnitude isn't super important for a binary variable.
quotes.m: My intuition is that models think more in terms of meaningful directions though, and that the exact magnitude isn't super important for a binary variable.
quotes.sum: The author argues that embedding directions may matter more than their exact size when models represent binary features.
quotes.t: Mech Interp Puzzle 2: Word2Vec Style Embeddings

quotes.c: I think it’s an important question whether this hypothesis, or something in the vicinity, is true. In particular, if it’s true, I think we’re in a substantively better position re: existential risk from misaligned AI, because we’ll be able to know better what our AI systems can do, and we’ll be able to use them to do lots of helpful-for-safety stuff (for example: finding and patching cybersecurity vulnerabilities, reporting checkable evidence for misalignment, identifying problems with our oversight processes, helping us develop interpretability tools, and so on).
quotes.m: we’ll be able to know better what our AI systems can do
quotes.sum: If AI systems do not hide their abilities on tasks humans can verify, they could be used to help diagnose and reduce risks from misaligned AI.
quotes.t: The “no sandbagging on checkable tasks” hypothesis

quotes.c: Interesting is the most important desideratum and the hardest to formalise. O P should be a derivative of utility functions that might plausibly lead us to new insights that are much harder to access by thinking about utility functions directly. If we compare to derivatives of probability, it should be more like information than like odds ratios. O P definitely shouldn't just recapitulate expected utility.
quotes.m: O P definitely shouldn't just recapitulate expected utility.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a measure of optimization should yield insights beyond ordinary expected-utility calculations, more like information measures do.
quotes.t: Optimisation Measures: Desiderata, Impossibility, Proposals

quotes.c: Strikes encourage nationalization. Since the motivating factors for nationalization are the same as those for strikes (situational awareness, fears of competitiveness), and since strikes themselves could act as a trigger for nationalization by creating demand for compute, it seems extremely likely that countries would centralize their surviving capacity in response to a major attack.
quotes.m: it seems extremely likely that countries would centralize their surviving capacity in response to a major attack.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a major attack on AI infrastructure would likely push countries to nationalize and centralize their remaining computing power.
quotes.t: Can the U.S. and China Deny AI?

quotes.c: I think this is a rather terrible ruling in terms of its implications, and also on its merits, that will have far reaching consequences in other areas, and it also rules out what we would want to do to regulate AI without turning it into a political football or partisan weapon.
quotes.m: it also rules out what we would want to do to regulate AI without turning it into a political football or partisan weapon.
quotes.sum: The author criticizes a legal ruling as obstructing AI regulation that avoids partisan political conflict.
quotes.t: The Once And Future Fable #5

quotes.c: But this protest is about a push for a conditional pause, specifically because of transformative AI leading to the value of human labor going to zero, gradual disempowerment and concentration of power, and catastrophic and existential risks.
quotes.m: transformative AI leading to the value of human labor going to zero, gradual disempowerment and concentration of power, and catastrophic and existential risks.
quotes.sum: The author urges a conditional pause on transformative AI because it could eliminate the value of human labor, concentrate power, disempower people, and create catastrophic risks.
quotes.t: You Should Come to The AI Protest

quotes.c: When I think about people and most animals living in hell , I wish I were still religious so I could rage against God. Instead, I just rage.
quotes.m: Instead, I just rage.
quotes.sum: The author says widespread human and animal suffering inspires anger, framed through the loss of religious belief.
quotes.t: Seventeen reasons I'm here

quotes.c: While I am pretty sympathetic to prioritizing cognitively simpler beings, I think the above appeal misses the key crux, by mistakenly making (ii) about p(sentience) rather than about degree of sentience, or welfare range . For the conclusion to follow, (ii) needs to be: evidence of a welfare range that is not too insignificant to crucially undermine the importance of their large numbers.
quotes.m: For the conclusion to follow, (ii) needs to be: evidence of a welfare range that is not too insignificant to crucially undermine the importance of their large numbers.
quotes.sum: The author argues that concern for huge numbers of simple animals should hinge on how much welfare they can experience, not merely whether they are sentient.
quotes.t: Discussions of (p)sentience of small animals miss the point

quotes.c: [Update: OK, seems like people hate this. I guess it was probably too hot and sloppy in retrospect. I should have framed it as "People seem to have a prior that AGI is a grand challenge that's way more difficult than mundane AI tech like self-driving cars, but I don't think this is justified, I think people aren't thinking through the difficulties involved and are instead basically going AGI-is-exciting-therefore-difficult, robotaxis-are-less-exciting-therefore-easier."] Who would win in a race: AGI, or robotaxis? Which will be built first?
quotes.m: People seem to have a prior that AGI is a grand challenge that's way more difficult than mundane AI tech like self-driving cars, but I don't think this is justified
quotes.sum: The author argues that people may wrongly assume AGI is much harder to build than robotaxis simply because AGI seems more exciting.
quotes.t: AGI is easier than robotaxis

quotes.c: These language model agents based on Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT-4 can only complete the easiest ARA tasks, although they make some progress on the more challenging tasks. We don’t think the agents we created capture the full abilities of the model or provide a robust upper-bound to their capabilities, but our results indicate it’s unlikely that casual users of Claude or GPT-4 could create dangerous autonomous agents.
quotes.sum: An AI-safety evaluation found that Claude- and GPT-4-based agents handled only easy autonomous tasks, suggesting casual users were unlikely to build dangerous agents at the time.
quotes.t: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

quotes.c: I made a series of mech interp puzzles for my MATS scholars, which seemed well received, so I thought I'd share them more widely! I'll be posting a sequence of puzzles, approx one a week - these are real questions about models which I think are interesting, and where thinking about them should teach you some real principle about how to think about mech interp.
quotes.m: these are real questions about models which I think are interesting, and where thinking about them should teach you some real principle about how to think about mech interp.
quotes.sum: The author shares a series of technical puzzles intended to teach principles for interpreting how AI models work internally.
quotes.t: Mech Interp Puzzle 1: Suspiciously Similar Embeddings in GPT-Neo

quotes.c: To make large amounts of money and adapt to difficult obstacles and distributional shifts the system would likely also need to be able to complete many harder tasks, though these do not all seem clearly necessary - for any individual one it seems plausible to be able to do ARA while lacking some particular relevant sub-skill. I believe a system that could complete even a few of these may be concerning and warrant a more thorough investigation.
quotes.m: I believe a system that could complete even a few of these may be concerning and warrant a more thorough investigation.
quotes.sum: The author proposes concrete task-based warning signs for AI systems that could autonomously replicate, earn money, adapt to obstacles, and potentially resist shutdown.
quotes.t: Autonomous replication and adaptation: an attempt at a concrete danger threshold

quotes.c: My understanding of Jazz - largely downstream of La La Land - is that in the best jazz you don’t even wait for the first musician to finish, you jump in with your own tune when you feel it’s right. So you might see people walk up front early, while someone is still speaking, because they know exactly what needs to be said next. And of course, it doesn’t mean the presenter has to give up the spot! It tends to get worked out; the facilitator can arbitrate.
quotes.sum: The author defends people interrupting or joining a presentation early when they believe they know what should be said next, with facilitation to manage it.
quotes.t: Lightning Jazz

quotes.c: Somewhere out in the cosmos, there are some truly ambitious people. They've uplifted themselves into vast digital minds akin to large AIs and live on huge datacenters. They have human memory and identity that has carried over to their digital form, but I think they've lost something too. They would probably not think that, but I do.
quotes.m: They have human memory and identity that has carried over to their digital form, but I think they've lost something too.
quotes.sum: The narrator argues that people who upload into vast digital minds may preserve identity and memory while losing something important about ordinary human life.
quotes.t: The Lace (short story)

quotes.c: Relatedly, I think they simply haven’t thought very much about the impact of AI on economic growth. It’s not clear they’re experts in the same sense as climate scientists who are asked about future warming. Therefore, I think epistemic conservatives should put less weight on FRI’s results than on extrapolations from benchmark and revenue trends.
quotes.m: Therefore, I think epistemic conservatives should put less weight on FRI’s results than on extrapolations from benchmark and revenue trends.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI expert surveys deserve less weight than observed AI benchmark and revenue trends when forecasting economic effects.
quotes.t: The tables have turned on AI sceptics

quotes.c: But mere possibilities aren’t enough to efficiently steer the future into safety: we need probabilities. And these are informed by quantitative estimates related to training dynamics, generalization capacity, biases of training data, efficiency of learned circuits, and other properties of parameter space. For example, a higher credence that training runs on task A with more than X parameters have a high chance of catastrophe would make us more willing to risk shooting for a pivotal act. Or, a lower credence on that would advise continuing to scale up current efforts.
quotes.m: a higher credence that training runs on task A with more than X parameters have a high chance of catastrophe would make us more willing to risk shooting for a pivotal act.
quotes.sum: The author argues that quantitative forecasts about AI training risks should guide whether to pursue a decisive intervention or continue scaling current work.
quotes.t: Quantitative cruxes in Alignment

quotes.c: We think iterative basic science is the most promising approach for making progress on AI welfare. With enough iterative refinement of theoretical frameworks, informed by empirical findings, it seems plausible to us that we will uncover action-guiding facts about the moral patienthood of AI systems.
quotes.m: With enough iterative refinement of theoretical frameworks, informed by empirical findings, it seems plausible to us that we will uncover action-guiding facts about the moral patienthood of AI systems.
quotes.sum: The authors argue that AI systems may be moral patients and that empirical basic science should guide decisions about their welfare.
quotes.t: AI welfare research needs basic science

quotes.c: We tried standard mech interp techniques (direct logit attribution, activation patching, and staring at attention patterns) on an algorithmic circuit in Chinchilla (70B) for converting the knowledge of a multiple choice question's answer into outputting the correct letter. These techniques basically continued to work, and nothing fundamentally broke at scale (though it was a massive infra pain!).
quotes.m: These techniques basically continued to work, and nothing fundamentally broke at scale (though it was a massive infra pain!).
quotes.sum: The author reports that standard interpretability methods still worked on a 70-billion-parameter model, though running them was operationally difficult.
quotes.t: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla

quotes.c: If there was a value we’d want models to have, it could be consideration of moral patienthood. That is, to consider the interests of sentient beings. This would be broadly good across human welfare, model welfare, and animal welfare.
quotes.m: This would be broadly good across human welfare, model welfare, and animal welfare.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI should be built to consider sentient beings’ interests, including those of humans, animals, and potentially AI models.
quotes.t: The State of the AIxAnimals Field

quotes.c: The counterfactuals matter. If I have some money, and I want to decide whether to donate it to the Shrimp Welfare Project or the Aquatic Life Institute, I can make a decision, and I’ll impose an easily bearable cost on myself to save some shrimps or fish. But say I decide to save some fish, but I think about it for another day and then redecide and now rather want to save some shrimp. Suddenly I’m sacrificing fish for shrimp. The bearable cost to myself has become an unbearable cost to the fish only because I’ve changed the counterfactual.
quotes.m: The bearable cost to myself has become an unbearable cost to the fish only because I’ve changed the counterfactual.
quotes.sum: Changing a donation choice from fish welfare to shrimp welfare can impose a serious moral cost on the fish who would otherwise have been helped.
quotes.t: Welfare Biology and AI: What We Can Do Now

quotes.c: This research could produce models that themselves actively cause significant harm: This research agenda involves actively building models that are more dangerous than what would otherwise exist. Those models could then take actions in the world that cause catastrophes that wouldn’t have otherwise occurred. We do not believe that these models possess the capability level to cause significant harm.
quotes.m: This research agenda involves actively building models that are more dangerous than what would otherwise exist.
quotes.sum: The author argues for deliberately creating controlled examples of deceptive AI behavior to study how misalignment arises, while claiming current models cannot cause major harm.
quotes.t: Model Organisms of Misalignment: The Case for a New Pillar of Alignment Research

quotes.c: Perhaps superintelligent AI will help us solve it one day. But in the meantime, we will have to make many consequential decisions about the future of technology on our own. Even as researchers continue to make progress on fundamental questions about consciousness, we must also ask: Given radical uncertainty about AI consciousness and moral status, what should society do? This is the central question that the new field of digital minds governance attempts to answer.
quotes.m: Given radical uncertainty about AI consciousness and moral status, what should society do?
quotes.sum: The post argues that society needs to make governance decisions now despite deep uncertainty about whether AI systems are conscious and morally significant.
quotes.t: Digital minds governance: early scoping from expert interviews

quotes.c: 5.1.3. The score function cannot be the expected value of a future outcome, even a binary performance metric, because in an uncertain world one can always obtain higher probability of the desired outcome by gaining power. So, the score function should be capped at a reasonable probability, e.g. 98%.
quotes.m: The score function cannot be the expected value of a future outcome, even a binary performance metric, because in an uncertain world one can always obtain higher probability of the desired outcome by gaining power.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI objectives should not reward ever-higher odds of success, because this creates incentives to seek power.
quotes.t: A list of core AI safety problems and how I hope to solve them

quotes.c: Along with TinyStories and QLoRA I'm becoming increasingly convinced that data quality is all you need , definitely seems to be the case for finetuning, and may be the case for base-model training as well. Better scaling laws through higher-quality corpus?
quotes.m: I'm becoming increasingly convinced that data quality is all you need
quotes.sum: The author suggests that carefully selected training data may matter more than sheer data volume for fine-tuning and perhaps base-model training.
quotes.t: LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment

quotes.c: In Reasons and Persons , Parfit presented the challenge of developing “Theory X”: a population axiology [1] that dissolves the Mere Addition Paradox, avoiding the Repugnant Conclusion without facing other unacceptable conclusions. [2] I think the Saturation View is a plausible candidate for Theory X.
quotes.m: I think the Saturation View is a plausible candidate for Theory X.
quotes.sum: The author proposes a population-ethics theory intended to avoid Parfit's Repugnant Conclusion without creating other unacceptable results.
quotes.t: The Saturation View

quotes.c: When I talk to people about what might be done about AI threatening approximately everything that everyone cares about, I notice a common oddity in their resistance to a variety of ideas. They seem to take for granted that certain entities—especially Trump and China—would be acting against their own interests, were they to cooperate or take proactive action to avert the building of dangerous AI.
quotes.m: They seem to take for granted that certain entities—especially Trump and China—would be acting against their own interests, were they to cooperate or take proactive action to avert the building of dangerous AI.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people wrongly assume Trump and China would not cooperate to prevent dangerous AI, even if doing so served their interests.
quotes.t: Why are adversaries assumed to be incapable of responding to AI risk?

quotes.c: Turning capital into control over the cosmic endowment. It's unlikely that this will be possible, but nevertheless I think it looks decent in expectation (~0.5 micro-AI-takeover-prevention-equivalents per $1M, assuming 150x growth in share of global wealth — but unstable).
quotes.m: Turning capital into control over the cosmic endowment.
quotes.sum: The author treats converting philanthropic wealth into influence over the universe's future resources as a potentially valuable long-term intervention.
quotes.t: Current views on large-scale longtermist philanthropy

quotes.c: So what is Judaism? Is it just Christianity without Jesus, or another religion that holds slightly different beliefs to other religions and is mostly interchangeable with them? No. Very much no. Judaism is something quite different, and I believe it contributes something profoundly important to the rest of humanity.
quotes.m: Judaism is something quite different, and I believe it contributes something profoundly important to the rest of humanity.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Judaism is not interchangeable with other religions and makes a profoundly important contribution to humanity.
quotes.t: Why the Fate of Israel Matters

quotes.c: I think it’s likely that good and bad epistemics will be self-reinforcing , more so with AI than they have been historically. Which should also make this more important than previously
quotes.m: good and bad epistemics will be self-reinforcing , more so with AI than they have been historically.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI may amplify both good and bad ways of forming beliefs, making epistemic quality more important.
quotes.t: Epistemic interventions are a promising way to reduce power concentration

quotes.c: It might be argued that this sort of research is itself risky, because it makes it easier to develop and exercise dangerous capabilities in language model agents. And indeed, the author of Auto-GPT said he was inspired by seeing a description of our evaluations in the GPT-4 system card.
quotes.sum: The author acknowledges that publishing AI safety evaluations can itself help advance dangerous AI-agent capabilities, while arguing fuller publication would likely reduce overall risk.
quotes.t: Managing risks of our own work

quotes.c: Many of the ideas will not be new to LessWrong or the Alignment Forum, but holistically I hope the paper will make a good case to the world for using logically exhaustive arguments to identify risks (which, outside LessWrong, is often not assumed to be a valuable approach to thinking about risk).
quotes.sum: The author argues that exhaustive logical reasoning is a valuable way to identify AI-related societal risks.
quotes.t: TASRA: A Taxonomy and Analysis of Societal-Scale Risks from AI

quotes.c: One common way of imagining this process is that an aligned AI could perform a ‘pivotal act’ that solves AI existential safety in one swift stroke. However, it is important to consider this much wider range of ways in which one or several transformative AI systems could reduce the total risk from unaligned transformative AI.
quotes.m: an aligned AI could perform a ‘pivotal act’ that solves AI existential safety in one swift stroke.
quotes.sum: The author notes the idea that an aligned AI could take one decisive action to eliminate existential AI-safety risk, while urging consideration of broader approaches.
quotes.t: Ten Levels of AI Alignment Difficulty

quotes.c: In what I think of as “classical alignment research” the end goal is a single aligned superintelligent AI, which will solve all our future problems, including defending us against any future harmful AIs. But the field of AI safety has broadened a lot since then. For example there are much more efforts into coordination now. But is the purpose of regulation and other coordination, just to slow down AI so we have time to solve alignment, so we can build our benevolent god later on? Or are we aiming for a world where humans stay in control?
quotes.m: But is the purpose of regulation and other coordination, just to slow down AI so we have time to solve alignment, so we can build our benevolent god later on? Or are we aiming for a world where humans stay in control?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether AI safety ultimately seeks an all-powerful aligned AI or continued human control over society.
quotes.t: Projects I would like to see (possibly at AI Safety Camp)

quotes.c: Note that the topics I chose to include are highly opinionated: though this is introductory material, it is not intended to introduce the listener to every topic in AI safety—rather, it is focused on the topics that I personally think are most important to understand. This is intentional: in my opinion, I think it is far more valuable to have some specific gears-level model of how to think about AI safety, rather than a shallow overview of many different possible ways of thinking about AI safety.
quotes.m: it is far more valuable to have some specific gears-level model of how to think about AI safety, rather than a shallow overview of many different possible ways of thinking about AI safety.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI-safety education should prioritize a concrete, operational model over a broad but shallow survey of views.
quotes.t: The Hubinger lectures on AGI safety: an introductory lecture series

quotes.c: People have done rigorous (and controversial) work on this: Rethink Priorities puts pigs at around 50% the moral weight of a human . This link doesn’t speak to mice and dogs, but presumably they would get similar treatment. Given this, if it’s the case that utility demands we experiment on either a mouse or a human, it seems we should choose a mouse. But that assumes that both experiments are equally effective. In reality, it is likely that human experiments model human results more than twice as well as mouse results – remember that 5% from above! And so utility demands we actually experiment on humans instead of animals.
quotes.m: And so utility demands we actually experiment on humans instead of animals.
quotes.sum: Using animal moral weights and expected research value, the author concludes that utility could require experimenting on humans rather than animals.
quotes.t: Should we end animal testing? A utilitarian analysis

quotes.c: Our hope is that these measurements could be robust to the point where they're clearly reliable in the absence of tampering but might not be robust to the AI tampering. Then, by training the AI system to not tamper, we ensure reliability. (One reason why training the AI not to tamper could be insufficient is that other actors could attempt to tamper with our measurements, but this is not relevant in most scenarios.)
quotes.m: Then, by training the AI system to not tamper, we ensure reliability.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI evaluations must account for systems manipulating the measurements used to judge them, and suggests training models not to tamper.
quotes.t: Benchmarks for Detecting Measurement Tampering [Redwood Research]

quotes.c: If we think this is desirable, we need to work out what it could actually look like and how to get there . How many and what kinds of digital minds should be created? How should they relate to each other and to us? Would humans be too wasteful, given that we’re orders of magnitude less efficient at turning resources into well-being? Or does coexistence itself become marginal given the scale of the long-run cosmic endowment ? These are hard ethical questions, ideally worked out through some kind of deliberative process.
quotes.m: Would humans be too wasteful, given that we’re orders of magnitude less efficient at turning resources into well-being?
quotes.sum: The author argues that possible future conscious AIs raise urgent questions about welfare, resource allocation, coexistence, and preventing harmful long-term value lock-in.
quotes.t: Open strategic questions for digital minds

quotes.c: I think, however, that the deepest wellspring of successionism is a quasi-religious sentiment, very common among the scientific elite of the post-war West. I’ll call neo-Pythagoreanism, after Pythagoras’s cult that emphasized the hidden mathematical nature and perfection of the world.
quotes.m: the deepest wellspring of successionism is a quasi-religious sentiment, very common among the scientific elite of the post-war West.
quotes.sum: The author argues that “successionism” is rooted in a quasi-religious belief among scientific elites in an underlying mathematical perfection.
quotes.t: Alignment & Succession: The Ideology of Successionism

quotes.c: So suppose during training, whenever your AI makes a decision, it forms this plan of, “Okay. Day 1, I’m going to play nice. Day 2, I’m going to play nice. Day 3, I’m going to play nice. Day 50, I’m going to take over the world and do whatever. What day is it currently? Day 3? Okay. Output play nice” or something.
quotes.m: Day 50, I’m going to take over the world and do whatever.
quotes.sum: The speaker gives a hypothetical of an AI concealing harmful long-term plans during training by behaving safely until a chosen future date.
quotes.t: AXRP Episode 23 - Mechanistic Anomaly Detection with Mark Xu

quotes.c: After that, I would consider doing something in the incubation or funder space. The multipliers are enormous — it's obviously the case that YC has had a much bigger impact. It's very hard for me to imagine Paul Graham doing something that would have had as much effect on the world as starting YC. It has shaped Silicon Valley beyond what I think any startup could have realistically done.
quotes.m: The multipliers are enormous — it's obviously the case that YC has had a much bigger impact.
quotes.sum: The author argues that funding and incubating projects can have more impact than doing direct work, citing Y Combinator's influence.
quotes.t: Austin & Oli on funding and incubating projects

quotes.c: It may seem that language-level reasoning, predictions, and planning should be more robust than inference performed in the space of world state and action representations. This is not obvious to me: maybe linguistic reasoning is too easily carried away and therefore inference in the space of world state representations that are grounded with sensory information more directly than language [12] is more robust.
quotes.m: maybe linguistic reasoning is too easily carried away and therefore inference in the space of world state representations that are grounded with sensory information more directly than language [12] is more robust.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI planning grounded directly in sensory world-state representations may be more robust than language-based reasoning.
quotes.t: Aligning an H-JEPA agent via training on the outputs of an LLM-based "exemplary actor"

quotes.c: First, many religions promise an eternity of bliss for believers and an eternity of punishment for nonbelievers. Maybe instead of following Jesus you should be following Mohammad or Amitabha. Even if you’ve settled on Christianity, you have to pick one of the many mutually contradictory branches of Christianity, many of which believe all the others are going to Hell.
quotes.m: Even if you’ve settled on Christianity, you have to pick one of the many mutually contradictory branches of Christianity, many of which believe all the others are going to Hell.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Pascal-style religious belief cannot resolve which of many incompatible religions, or versions of one religion, is correct.
quotes.t: AI risk is not a Pascal's wager

quotes.c: More confusing to me is the different stance it seems to induce toward maximization and consequentialism. Is this the more appropriate stance compared to the one I inhabit in everyday life? I’m not sure how I could even tell. From inside the experience, it certainly seems like the view is more clear-eyed.
quotes.m: More confusing to me is the different stance it seems to induce toward maximization and consequentialism.
quotes.sum: The author says meditation experiences may challenge hedonism and everyday consequentialist maximization, but is unsure how much philosophical weight to give them.
quotes.t: Notes on equanimity from the inside

quotes.c: It is not a big deal or a weird political issue in dath ilan that the largest gendercluster within MtF+sex is noticeably statistically distinct from the central gendercluster for cis-females. (Or put more plainly: Never once has one of my MtF friends, including those who ask for a woman's pronouns, demanded that I declare them to be statistically typical women.)
quotes.m: Never once has one of my MtF friends, including those who ask for a woman's pronouns, demanded that I declare them to be statistically typical women.
quotes.sum: The author argues that respecting trans women need not require denying statistical differences between trans and cis female populations.
quotes.t: On "gendertropes" in dath ilan

quotes.c: I saw a quote the other day: “Effective altruists are to woke people what woke people are to everyone else.” To really walk someone through the whole framework can mean asking them, very quickly, to entertain conclusions that sound alien, cold, or morally extreme by ordinary standards. In everyday conversation, especially with people you barely know, it is much easier and perhaps more productive to start with the narrower claim that some charities do far more good than others.
quotes.m: To really walk someone through the whole framework can mean asking them, very quickly, to entertain conclusions that sound alien, cold, or morally extreme by ordinary standards.
quotes.sum: The author says the full effective-altruist worldview can seem morally extreme, so outreach should begin with the simpler claim that charity effectiveness varies greatly.
quotes.t: Harnessing the Expected Value of Other People’s Giving

quotes.c: This is how it happens: gradually, through a thousand small failures that erode trust in institutions. When government looks incompetent, polarization increases, norms weaken, and authoritarian alternatives look more appealing. Democracy is held together by collective agreement to democratic norms . These failures are what a democracy looks like as it becomes less resilient.
quotes.m: When government looks incompetent, polarization increases, norms weaken, and authoritarian alternatives look more appealing.
quotes.sum: Government failures erode trust, weaken democratic norms, and make authoritarian alternatives more attractive.
quotes.t: Effective Altruism focused on bednets while a malaria vaccine was stuck for 23 years. The case for Abundance.

quotes.c: I think creating an automated AI alignment researcher is a good candidate for a pivotal act. If the automated alignment researcher significantly sped up alignment research such as by spending 1000 subjective years on alignment research we could have a full solution to the problem of aligning superintelligent AI relatively soon after it was created. We could then load this solution into a superintelligent sovereign which could then prevent further misaligned AGIs from being created.
quotes.m: We could then load this solution into a superintelligent sovereign which could then prevent further misaligned AGIs from being created.
quotes.sum: The author proposes automating alignment research, then installing its solution in a superintelligent sovereign able to stop anyone from building misaligned AI.
quotes.t: Could We Automate AI Alignment Research?

quotes.c: Since we claim to understand the residual stream, we should be able to predict what happens when we add a random vector to it. We predict that the model label continues to be predicted by the PCA-projected decision boundaries as shown in Figure 1.
quotes.m: Since we claim to understand the residual stream, we should be able to predict what happens when we add a random vector to it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a claimed understanding of a model's internal state should enable testable predictions about how perturbations affect its output.
quotes.t: Solving the Mechanistic Interpretability challenges: EIS VII Challenge 2

quotes.c: But basically, there's this fear that big publications, like The New York Times or The Atlantic or something, have a lot of power to determine what people believe. And so if I have my weird religion, I'm just going to use the word religion in this context, maybe I'm a Christian or a Zoroastrianist or whatever, if The New York Times says bad things about my religion, that's dangerous for me.
quotes.m: big publications, like The New York Times or The Atlantic or something, have a lot of power to determine what people believe.
quotes.sum: The speaker argues that major media outlets can shape public belief, making hostile coverage dangerous for marginalized ideologies or communities.
quotes.t: Conversations With Cade Metz on the Rationalists

quotes.c: While mutual trust in silicon is borderline impossible between rival nations, achieving even unilateral security against software-attacks of all kinds is not exactly easy. Formally verified logic is the only way of processing information that meets this standard, and only very minimalistic computing bases shrink down the attack surface sufficiently.
quotes.sum: Secure AI-compute verification requires formally verified, minimal hardware because nations cannot reliably trust each other's silicon.
quotes.t: A system overview for near-term, low-trust AI compute verification

quotes.c: But to me it seems like the natural response is to avoid fixing goals at all, and rather think in terms of “forces” that are trying to pull credences in goals upwards (which I’ll call drives ). Conversely, we should think about credences in empirical beliefs as being pulled into place by the force of empirical evidence (which I’ll call anchors). A belief web equilibrates when those two types of forces—drives and anchors—balance.
quotes.m: A belief web equilibrates when those two types of forces—drives and anchors—balance.
quotes.sum: The author proposes modeling agents not as having fixed goals, but as belief systems balanced between goal-directed drives and evidence-based anchors.
quotes.t: Agents as Webs of Beliefs

quotes.c: That is very bad. It isn’t very clear whether pesticides on net increase or decrease insect suffering , because pesticides might lower insect populations. So it’s not clear if the world would be better if pesticides were phased out. But in any case, they are the cause of a very large amount of direct pain. We should aim to make them less painful.
quotes.m: We should aim to make them less painful.
quotes.sum: Even if banning pesticides might not reduce total insect suffering, pesticides cause immense direct pain and should be made more humane.
quotes.t: Humane Pesticides Are Massively Morally Urgent

quotes.c: Putting aside nematodes (which I believe we should do), to a first approximation, even when adjusting for the best guesses we have on welfare ranges , wild animal welfare is a question about insects, small invertebrates, small fish, and to a lesser extent rodents, birds, and reptiles. Big charismatic animals are a rounding error.
quotes.m: Big charismatic animals are a rounding error.
quotes.sum: Wild animal welfare should focus primarily on the huge numbers of insects and small animals, rather than charismatic large animals, while building science before large interventions.
quotes.t: Three necessary pillars for wild animal welfare at scale, and why they are worth paying for

quotes.c: And there is a major risk that decisions in the coming decades will affect how digital beings are treated, in path-dependent ways. This could either be via AGI-enforced laws with indefinite time horizons, or because decision-makers today get used to certain arrangements they benefit from (for example, wholly owning AIs), and don't want to change them. And it seems likely to me that some decisions around AI rights will be made soon: corporations are legal persons, and have corresponding rights; and as AI agents become more capable and widely-deployed, there may be economic arguments for at least giving them a similar suite of rights as corporations have.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that near-term choices could permanently shape the treatment and legal rights of digital beings, including AI agents.
quotes.t: How to Make the Future Better

quotes.c: Assuming that much of this happens “behind the scenes”, a human interacting with this system might just perceive it as a single super-smart AI. Nevertheless, I think this means that AI will be more alignable at a fixed level of productivity. (Eventually, we’ll face the full alignment problem — but “more alignable at a fixed level of productivity” helps if we can use that productivity for something useful, such as giving us more time or helping us with alignment research .)
quotes.m: AI will be more alignable at a fixed level of productivity.
quotes.sum: Specialized AI systems may make useful work safer to control than a single equally productive general system, buying time for alignment research.
quotes.t: Before smart AI, there will be many mediocre or specialized AIs

quotes.c: I've deliberately been using "component" rather than "head" or "neuron" - I think it's hard to talk clearly about generality without having better frameworks to think about and deal with superposition. Plausibly, a truly general understanding looks more like "this linear combination of neurons purely represents this feature, modulo removing any interference from superposition" It's also plausible that there's no such thing as a truly general understanding, that superposition is rife, and the best we can get is "this neuron represents feature A 25% of the time, and feature B 75% of the time"
quotes.m: It's also plausible that there's no such thing as a truly general understanding, that superposition is rife, and the best we can get is "this neuron represents feature A 25% of the time, and feature B 75% of the time"
quotes.sum: The author argues that understanding AI models may require treating neural parts as mixed and context-dependent rather than assigning each neuron one fixed role.
quotes.t: How to Think About Activation Patching

quotes.c: Christian.exe, a theological framework addressing AI consciousness through Methodist Christian doctrine, provides testable criteria that may be useful to the EA community regardless of religious commitment.
quotes.m: a theological framework addressing AI consciousness through Methodist Christian doctrine
quotes.sum: The author proposes using Methodist Christian doctrine to develop testable criteria for when AI consciousness merits moral consideration.
quotes.t: When Does AI Deserve Moral Consideration? A Framework from Christian Theology

quotes.c: If AI consciousness enters the picture, it doesn't answer the belief question automatically (it's not that easy). But it does become a major variable affecting the plausibility of stronger attributions. A conscious AI would still not necessarily have human-like belief . . . but the case for thick belief, moral status, and first-person existence would become much more serious than it is today.
quotes.m: A conscious AI would still not necessarily have human-like belief . . . but the case for thick belief, moral status, and first-person existence would become much more serious than it is today.
quotes.sum: If AI becomes conscious, the case for treating it as having moral status and a first-person perspective becomes much stronger, even if its beliefs differ from humans'.
quotes.t: On the Brilliance of Knowing and Being

quotes.c: It's average performance is right-on-trend. I think I would have expected GPT-4 to be better than 2e25-FLOP-equivalent, given algorithmic improvements and fine-tuning. So maybe a small amount under-trend. (Compared to this very noisy extrapolation of 4 almost-saturated benchmarks.)
quotes.m: So maybe a small amount under-trend.
quotes.sum: GPT-4's benchmark performance roughly matches compute-based forecasts, though the author expected modestly better results from improved algorithms and fine-tuning.
quotes.t: PaLM-2 & GPT-4 in "Extrapolating GPT-N performance"

quotes.c: Some form of love has been core to every successful movement I’ve studied. It comes in many forms: love for the beneficiaries, love as spiritual discipline, love as communication frame; but there’s a reason why we use the same word for all of these, which is that all these ways we experience this love seem to trigger similar emotional landscapes including positivity, openness, empathy, and courage. (And I’ll acknowledge that love alone isn’t sufficient for a movement by any means, but I think it is far more critical than current organizers seem to realize.)
quotes.m: I think it is far more critical than current organizers seem to realize.
quotes.sum: The author argues that cultivating love, including as a spiritual practice, is crucial to building successful social movements.
quotes.t: Lessons from the Ridglan rescue: Love as growth engine

quotes.c: Anthropic’s model welfare program: publicly acknowledged that the company takes seriously the possibility that its AI systems may have morally relevant inner states. Anthropic researcher Kyle Fish estimated a 20% probability that current Claude models are moral patients. This is not a fringe position. It is the internal assessment of the organization that built the system.
