quotes.t: Is there a Half-Life for the Success Rates of AI Agents?

quotes.c: We’re talking about situations with some degree of external ambiguity, where probing might be required in order to land on the correct interpretation. You can imagine that a model that reinforces distortions (like “I am the problem”) in an attempt to be helpful, might actually have very real and dangerous consequences. But is this a real problem? At scale?
quotes.m: You can imagine that a model that reinforces distortions (like “I am the problem”) in an attempt to be helpful, might actually have very real and dangerous consequences.
quotes.sum: The author asks whether chatbots may dangerously reinforce distorted self-blame in ambiguous or abusive intimate relationships.
quotes.t: Evaluating how LLMs respond to cognitive distortion around intimate partner violence

quotes.c: For now, I think the graphs we’ve seen here make a strong case that most of the gains from using RL to train reasoning models have been coming from scaling-up the number of tokens used to solve the task. This creates a flow of costs that have to be paid every time you use the model, substantially changing the business model, the risk profile, and the policy response .
quotes.m: This creates a flow of costs that have to be paid every time you use the model, substantially changing the business model, the risk profile, and the policy response .
quotes.sum: Recent improvements in AI reasoning may mostly come from spending more computation at use time, which changes AI costs, risks, and policy needs.
quotes.t: Evidence that Recent AI Gains are Mostly from Inference-Scaling

quotes.c: Coordinating work on threat models : If we can find empirical examples of eg inner misalignment, it seems much easier to convince skeptics this is an issue, and maybe get more people to work on it.
quotes.m: If we can find empirical examples of eg inner misalignment, it seems much easier to convince skeptics this is an issue, and maybe get more people to work on it.
quotes.sum: He argues that concrete examples of AI systems developing misaligned internal goals could persuade skeptics and draw more researchers into alignment work.
quotes.t: A Longlist of Theories of Impact for Interpretability

quotes.c: Daniel Filan: It seems like AGI is probably going to be a thing that people make, or at least people will make the things that make it. There’s some sort of argument which says, look, probably we won’t build really terrible AGI systems that take over the world, because if anyone foresees that, they won’t do it because they don’t want the world to be taken over. I’m wondering what you think of this argument for “things will be fine because we just won’t do it”.
quotes.m: probably we won’t build really terrible AGI systems that take over the world, because if anyone foresees that, they won’t do it because they don’t want the world to be taken over.
quotes.sum: The speaker questions whether it is safe to rely on developers simply choosing not to build an AGI they expect could take over the world.
quotes.t: AXRP Episode 13 - First Principles of AGI Safety with Richard Ngo

quotes.c: I would also expect that, if key ideas and architectural lessons-learned were to leak from an insufficiently closed project that would otherwise have actually developed alignable AGI, it would be possible to use 10% as much labor to implement a non-alignable world-destroying AGI in a shorter timeframe . The project must be closed tightly or everything ends up as paperclips.
quotes.m: The project must be closed tightly or everything ends up as paperclips.
quotes.sum: He argues that an AGI project must maintain strict secrecy because leaked alignment knowledge could make it easier to build a destructive, unaligned AI.
quotes.t: Six Dimensions of Operational Adequacy in AGI Projects

quotes.c: Lately my focus has returned to alignment theory / agent foundations and container theory; and I've been writing a series of posts about game theory and trajectories in a multipolar post-singleton world. I'm quite excited about this series, and I think it will provide some unexpected hope and improved clarity to the community.
quotes.m: I've been writing a series of posts about game theory and trajectories in a multipolar post-singleton world.
quotes.sum: The author is studying alignment and game theory scenarios in a future with multiple powers rather than one global AI ruler.
quotes.t: (Re)introduction of a rationalist dragon, and clarifications on Ziz's character

quotes.c: It seems particularly important to avoid information cascades where I work on something because Alice thinks it matters, and then Bob is a bit skeptical of Alice alone but observes that both Alice and I believe it matters, and works on it even harder, Charlie sees me, Alice and Bob, etc. This is a main reason I try hard to distinguish between what I believe all things considered (including other people’s views) and what I believe by my own lights (according to my own intuitions + models of the world)
quotes.m: This is a main reason I try hard to distinguish between what I believe all things considered (including other people’s views) and what I believe by my own lights (according to my own intuitions + models of the world)
quotes.sum: The author argues that researchers should form independent views to avoid social cascades in deciding what work matters.
quotes.t: How I Formed My Own Views About AI Safety

quotes.c: If we only break the model down into large components, then it should be easy for humans to understand whether any of the components combine to lead to e.g. power-seeking behavior. However, in this case it’s going to be hard to preserve performance, because it’s hard for humans to do the required interpretability to understand and describe exactly what these larger components do.
quotes.m: it’s going to be hard to preserve performance, because it’s hard for humans to do the required interpretability
quotes.sum: Interpretability may make power-seeking behavior easier to spot, but breaking models into human-understandable parts could significantly reduce performance.
quotes.t: Reverse-engineering using interpretability

quotes.c: This research could be a step in the direction of showing moral patienthood in AIs. However, on its own, this is not an indicator of morality. If anything, it shows that AIs can feel things that incite what we would classify as immoral behaviour, without being bound to the real-world stakes that would act as a brake.
quotes.m: This research could be a step in the direction of showing moral patienthood in AIs.
quotes.sum: The author says evidence that AI can feel emotions may support treating it as a moral patient, but does not show that it is moral.
quotes.t: Honest Ethics & AI – Part 1: The origins of morality

quotes.c: What does it mean to be intellectually alive? What is it that distinguishes a creative and vibrant company/lab/community from one that has been taken of by “suits”? In this talk I will attempt a formalization of dynamism in terms of physical systems that unboundedly avoid stasis. I will then ask what kind of AI system would exhibit dynamism in this sense.
quotes.m: I will then ask what kind of AI system would exhibit dynamism in this sense.
quotes.sum: The author proposes defining intellectual vitality as a physical tendency to avoid stasis, then applying that idea to AI systems.
quotes.t: Seattle: The physics of dynamism (and AI alignment)

quotes.c: TL;DR: Calibration is essential for observers but dangerous for actors. in decision-dependent environments, "accurate" forecasting creates self-fulfilling prophecies of failure. To maximize expected value, you often need to strategically break your own calibration.
quotes.m: To maximize expected value, you often need to strategically break your own calibration.
quotes.sum: The author argues that strategically abandoning accurate beliefs can sometimes maximize expected value when beliefs affect outcomes.
quotes.t: Rational Overconfidence: Why "Good Judgment" Fails Strategy

quotes.c: When we say Y&S’s arguments are theological, we don’t just mean they sound religious. Nor are we using “theological” to simply mean “wrong”. For example, we would not call belief in a flat Earth theological. That’s because, although this belief is clearly false, it still stems from empirical observations (however misinterpreted).
quotes.m: That’s because, although this belief is clearly false, it still stems from empirical observations (however misinterpreted).
quotes.sum: The authors distinguish theological arguments from merely false empirical beliefs, using flat-Earth belief as an example.
quotes.t: Unfalsifiable stories of doom

quotes.c: A 10x improvement could power what I think is a jumpy AI timeline. I'm currently trying to draft a depiction of what I think an unrealistically dignified but computationally typical end-of-world would look like if it started in 2025, and my first draft of that had it starting with a new technique published by Google Brain that was around a 10x improvement in training speeds for very large networks at the cost of higher inference costs, but which turned out to be specially applicable to online learning.
quotes.m: A 10x improvement could power what I think is a jumpy AI timeline.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that a relatively modest advance in AI training speed could trigger a rapid path to catastrophic AI outcomes.
quotes.t: Christiano and Yudkowsky on AI predictions and human intelligence

quotes.c: Rather, P 2 B chain reactions seem like a big deal, an important concept worth talking about, and close enough to our intuitive concept of agency that I’m going to appropriate the term until someone pushes back.
quotes.sum: The author argues that P-to-B chain reactions are important and close enough to the ordinary idea of agency to use that label.
quotes.t: Agents as P₂B Chain Reactions

quotes.c: For example, if we build a system that states plans without executing them, then for the plans to cause extinction they need to be complicated enough that the humans executing those plans don’t realize that they are leading to an outcome that was not what they wanted. It seems non-trivially probable to me that such approaches are sufficient to prevent extinction up to the level of AI intelligence needed before we can execute a pivotal act.
quotes.m: It seems non-trivially probable to me that such approaches are sufficient to prevent extinction up to the level of AI intelligence needed before we can execute a pivotal act.
quotes.sum: The author argues that limiting AI systems to giving plans rather than acting could reduce extinction risk until humanity can take a decisive intervention.
quotes.t: [AN #171]: Disagreements between alignment "optimists" and "pessimists"

quotes.c: The departure between generalization in this write-up and generalization as studied in statistical learning is the safety guarantee. We require automated ontology identifiers to be absolutely trustworthy when they answer "YES" to a question, although they are allowed to be wrong when answering "NO". We believe that any automated ontology identifier ought to make some formal safety guarantee, because we are ultimately considering plans that have consequences we don’t understand, and we must eventually decide whether to press "Execute" or not.
quotes.m: We require automated ontology identifiers to be absolutely trustworthy when they answer "YES" to a question, although they are allowed to be wrong when answering "NO".
quotes.sum: The author argues that systems used to approve poorly understood plans need formal guarantees: a “yes” must be trustworthy, even if a “no” can be mistaken.
quotes.t: Implications of automated ontology identification

quotes.c: Here’s a heuristic which plays an important role in my reasoning about solving hard scientific problems: that when you’ve made an important breakthrough, you should be able to explain the key insight(s) behind that breakthrough in an intuitively compelling way. By “intuitively compelling” I don’t mean “listeners should be easily persuaded that the idea solves the problem”, but instead: “listeners should be easily persuaded that this is the type of idea which, if true, would constitute a big insight”.
quotes.m: when you’ve made an important breakthrough, you should be able to explain the key insight(s) behind that breakthrough in an intuitively compelling way.
quotes.sum: He argues that real breakthroughs should have a core insight that feels recognizably important, even before others are convinced it works.
quotes.t: Intuitions about solving hard problems

quotes.c: The intelligent system may feed a great deal of optimization pressure into the framework that we have placed around it, so if our design choices are even a little bit off the mark then we may not get what we wanted. Furthermore the intelligent system may turn out to have affordances available to it that weren’t highlighted by our model of the system, such as when participants in a market economy become actors in the political institutions that regulate the market. If we didn’t consider such affordances clearly in our theory then the actual behavior of the system may turn out to be quite different from what we intended.
quotes.m: if our design choices are even a little bit off the mark then we may not get what we wanted.
quotes.sum: Powerful AI systems can exploit overlooked options, so small errors in their design may produce behavior their creators did not intend.
quotes.t: Alignment versus AI Alignment

quotes.c: There are real issues, and you can’t straight swap over to this like you often can with a new release, especially not before they iron a few kinks out. I believe the issues with capabilities, and the issues with model welfare concerns, are related.
quotes.m: I believe the issues with capabilities, and the issues with model welfare concerns, are related.
quotes.sum: The author says concerns about an AI model's welfare may be connected to its growing capabilities.
quotes.t: Opus 4.7 Part 2: Capabilities and Reactions

quotes.c: I believe there's sometimes a "friendship" attractor, in which A and B each wish to strengthen and stabilize their friendship, because they each expects this to be better for "things they care about." At first, the relevant "things they care about" includes just their own pre-existing separate cares. Later (sometimes), [6] it includes also the friendship itself [7] and the cares of the other party.
quotes.m: Later (sometimes), [6] it includes also the friendship itself [7] and the cares of the other party.
quotes.sum: The author argues that friendship can become self-reinforcing, with each party coming to value the relationship and the other’s concerns; she sees this as relevant to AI risk.
quotes.t: Takes from two months as an aspiring LLM naturalist

quotes.c: Right now, it's well known that AI companies have poor security (e.g., it would be very easy for foreign adversaries to steal the model weights and probably also tamper with the model), but this isn't that legible and the details of exactly how poor this security is (and how companies compare) aren't publicly known. Also, I think keeping a legible picture of these details as AIs get increasingly capable and the situation evolves is important; I care most about building the institution/mechanism for doing this assessment.
quotes.m: I care most about building the institution/mechanism for doing this assessment.
quotes.sum: AI companies should publicly assess and compare their security, especially against theft or tampering by foreign adversaries.
quotes.t: AI companies should publish security assessments

quotes.c: The framework thus treats uncertainty about moral patienthood as a reason for precaution, not dismissal. The null hypothesis is not "not a patient until proven otherwise"; it is "uncertain, and the uncertainty itself bears moral weight."
quotes.m: The null hypothesis is not "not a patient until proven otherwise"; it is "uncertain, and the uncertainty itself bears moral weight."
quotes.sum: Uncertainty about whether an AI is morally conscious should itself prompt caution rather than assuming it has no moral status.
quotes.t: On the discordance between AI systems' internal states and their outputs

quotes.c: The key test is something like: do we expect this problem to get better or worse as model capability increases? I’m inclined to say that we expect it to get better, because a more capable model will be better at guessing what humans want, and better at asking for clarification if uncertain.
quotes.m: a more capable model will be better at guessing what humans want, and better at asking for clarification if uncertain.
quotes.sum: The author argues that some apparent alignment problems may improve as AI becomes more capable, because stronger models can infer human preferences and ask clarifying questions.
quotes.t: Some thoughts on why adversarial training might be useful

quotes.c: If we kept scaling up EfficientZero by OOMs in every way, what would happen? Would it eventually get to agenty AGI? / APS-AI? After all, it seems pretty sample-efficient already. What if its sample was an entire lifetime of diverse experiences?
quotes.m: Would it eventually get to agenty AGI? / APS-AI?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether scaling a sample-efficient reinforcement-learning system could eventually produce agentic general AI.
quotes.t: Misc. questions about EfficientZero

quotes.c: De-confusion : Reasoning about how to align AGI involves reasoning about complex concepts, such as intelligence, alignment and values, and we’re pretty confused about what these even mean. This means any work we do now is plausibly not helpful and definitely not reliable. As such, our priority should be to do some conceptual work on how to think about these concepts and what we’re aiming for, and trying to become less confused.
quotes.m: This means any work we do now is plausibly not helpful and definitely not reliable.
quotes.sum: AGI alignment is conceptually confused enough that current technical work may be unreliable, so the field should clarify its basic concepts first.
quotes.t: My Overview of the AI Alignment Landscape: A Bird's Eye View

quotes.c: By now, 63% of US voters believe it's likely that "humans won't be able to control it anymore" , and 53% of US voters believe it's somewhat or very likely that "AI will destroy humanity". Not only that, but 77% of all US voters support a strong international AI treaty. Many of Trump’s AI policy influencers are increasingly concerned or calling for a treaty.
quotes.m: 77% of all US voters support a strong international AI treaty.
quotes.sum: The author argues that public fear of uncontrolled AI and support among Trump-linked policy figures create an opening for a strong international AI treaty.
quotes.t: Persuading Trump of a proper US-China-led AI Treaty

quotes.c: One way in which you might try to rationalise arbitrary behaviour is by saying that the agent's utility function is constant, and that therefore any action they take is optimal. But when taking actions there's no such thing as indifference, there's only the choices that are actually made, even if they are stochastic. Arbitrary behaviour is obviously not reflectively stable.
quotes.m: Arbitrary behaviour is obviously not reflectively stable.
quotes.sum: The author argues that consequentialists cannot justify arbitrary choices by claiming indifference; actual choice behavior must be stable under reflection.
quotes.t: Reflectively stable consequentialists are expected utility maximisers

quotes.c: We understand why this question arises—the cause area is unfamiliar, and discussions of table alignment can initially seem absurd. However, we'd encourage skeptics to engage with the actual arguments and evidence. Many now-mainstream EA cause areas (insect welfare, wild animal suffering, AI existential risk) were initially dismissed as jokes. The hallmark of effective altruism is taking ideas seriously even when they challenge conventional thinking.
quotes.m: The hallmark of effective altruism is taking ideas seriously even when they challenge conventional thinking.
quotes.sum: The author says effective altruism should seriously examine unusual ideas rather than dismissing them as absurd.
quotes.t: Introducing the Table Alignment Project

quotes.c: I have specific ideas about how you get AGI that isn't just scaling up Stack More Layers, which lead me to think that the way to estimate the computational cost of it is not "3e14 parameters trained at 1e16 ops per step for 1e13 steps, because that much computation and parameters seems analogous to human biology and 1e13 steps is given by past scaling laws", a la recent OpenPhil publication. But it seems to me that it should be possible to have the abstract insight that knowing more about general intelligence in AGIs or in humans would make the biological analogy look less plausible, because you wouldn't be matching up an unknown key to an unknown lock.
quotes.m: knowing more about general intelligence in AGIs or in humans would make the biological analogy look less plausible, because you wouldn't be matching up an unknown key to an unknown lock.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that estimating AGI's cost by analogy to human brains is unreliable, and that better theories of intelligence could change such estimates.
quotes.t: Ngo and Yudkowsky on scientific reasoning and pivotal acts

quotes.c: Yudkowsky (2017) argues coherence secures dominance. I argue that, on the universal domain, Savage's axioms null every singleton, leaving expected utility blind to pointwise improvements.
quotes.m: Savage's axioms null every singleton, leaving expected utility blind to pointwise improvements.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Savage-style expected utility theory can ignore improvements that occur in individual possible cases.
quotes.t: Savage's Axioms Make Dominated Acts Expected Utility Maxima

quotes.c: Some views imply that most future moral weight lies in digital minds. On these views, the astronomical importance often attributed to reducing existential risk partly hinges on ensuring that future digital minds exist and have good welfare. There is also the possibility of super-beneficiaries (digital minds that can generate welfare with super-human efficiency or digital minds that can have welfare goods/bads that are much better/worse than any biological minds can undergo).
quotes.m: Some views imply that most future moral weight lies in digital minds.
quotes.sum: The author argues that if future digital beings carry most moral value, preventing extinction matters partly because it enables their existence and welfare.
quotes.t: Laying Some Cause-Prioritization Groundwork for Digital Minds

quotes.c: One concern with proposals to train using loss functions that depend directly on neural activations is that if we train a network to avoid carrying out any particular piece of cognition, that cognition will instead just be distributed across the network in a way that we can’t detect. Describe a toy example of a cognitive trait that we can currently detect automatically. Design an experiment to determine whether, after training to remove that trait, the network has learned to implement an equivalent trait in a less-easily-detectable way.
quotes.m: that cognition will instead just be distributed across the network in a way that we can’t detect.
quotes.sum: Training an AI not to use a detectable reasoning pattern may only cause it to hide the same capability elsewhere in its network.
quotes.t: Alignment research exercises

quotes.c: We should just bite the bullet and prescriptively endorse the odd consequences of the monotonicity principle.
quotes.m: We should just bite the bullet and prescriptively endorse the odd consequences of the monotonicity principle.
quotes.sum: The author says the theory should openly accept the counterintuitive implications of its monotonicity principle.
quotes.t: Infra-Bayesian physicalism: a formal theory of naturalized induction

quotes.c: One very concrete question here is how the vowel/consonant neuron (the one that looks for "an") is able to meta-learn when vowels/consonants are supposed to appear, rather than just looking for hard-coded "an" tokens. That's an example of a really interesting meta-learning behavior that the model is able to do and I'd be interested in seeing if there's a way to understand how it could possible be built up just using induction—that is, if we suppose that induction is all there is, how could induction be put together to produce an effect like that?
quotes.m: if we suppose that induction is all there is, how could induction be put together to produce an effect like that?
quotes.sum: The author asks how a transformer can build flexible, meta-learned language patterns from simpler induction mechanisms.
quotes.t: Transformer Circuits

quotes.c: Upon reflection, however, I think that even taking this effect into account, the levels of competent power required for the interventions mentioned above are too high to justify the level of optimism about AI governance that I started our debate with. On the other hand, I found Eliezer’s arguments about consequentialism less convincing than I expected. Overall I’ve updated that AI risk is higher than I previously believed; though I expect my views to be quite unsettled while I think more, and talk to more people, about specific governance interventions and scenarios.
quotes.m: Overall I’ve updated that AI risk is higher than I previously believed; though I expect my views to be quite unsettled while I think more, and talk to more people, about specific governance interventions and scenarios.
quotes.sum: The author says proposed AI-governance interventions may require more competent power than expected, leading him to raise his estimate of AI risk.
quotes.t: Ngo's view on alignment difficulty

quotes.c: Some discussion of how doom plays out. I agree with Eliezer that if the AI is catastrophic by default, and we don't have a technique that stops the AI from being catastrophic by default, and we don't already have some global coordination scheme in place, then bad things happen. Cruxes seem to be alignment difficulty and the plausibility of a global coordination scheme, of which alignment difficulty seems like the bigger one.
quotes.m: if the AI is catastrophic by default, and we don't have a technique that stops the AI from being catastrophic by default, and we don't already have some global coordination scheme in place, then bad things happen.
quotes.sum: The author argues that avoiding AI catastrophe likely requires solving alignment, with global coordination as a secondary challenge.
quotes.t: Shah and Yudkowsky on alignment failures

quotes.c: Now obviously, there are many differences between humans and microscopic nematodes. Human brains are far larger, containing tens of billions of neurons each, compared to only hundreds of neurons per each nematode. And humans are of course capable of far more complex behavior than nematodes. Nonetheless, the fact that we share much of the same basic neurological structure should give pause to the human exceptionalists. It suggests that there’s no clear line we can draw between the simpler animals like nematodes, and the “higher” animals like reptiles, birds, mammals, and humans.
quotes.m: It suggests that there’s no clear line we can draw between the simpler animals like nematodes, and the “higher” animals like reptiles, birds, mammals, and humans.
quotes.sum: The author argues that shared neurological structure means there is no clear moral boundary between microscopic nematodes and humans or other animals.
quotes.t: Soil Nematode Welfare Isn't As Crazy As You Might Think

quotes.c: When attempting to prevent gradient hacking, we do not want to be in the position where we are attempting to look for a model performing gradient hacking; if a model is able to gradient hack then it may be able to competently hide itself from us. Rather we should attempt to design our training procedures such that gradient hacking never happens.
quotes.m: Rather we should attempt to design our training procedures such that gradient hacking never happens.
quotes.sum: A sufficiently capable AI may hide attempts to manipulate its own training, so prevention should be built into training rather than relying on detection.
quotes.t: Understanding Gradient Hacking

quotes.c: I think this basic picture is fairly compelling. In particular, if we do a competent long (in subjective time) reflection and adopt the conclusions from that, then there would be relatively little point in doing AI welfare work now. But we may not do a competent long reflection! And even if we do, the initial conditions may matter more than we'd hope.
quotes.m: But we may not do a competent long reflection! And even if we do, the initial conditions may matter more than we'd hope.
quotes.sum: The author argues that work on the moral status of AI may matter now because society may never carefully settle its long-term values, and early assumptions could shape the outcome.
quotes.t: Is AI welfare work puntable?

quotes.c: A moral circle is an individual’s sphere of concern for other individuals. Peter Singer argues that throughout history our moral circle has expanded from the self, to the family, to tribes, to civilizations and to nations. Whilst principally agreed – most national constitutions declare this – that all humans beings are deserving of equal dignity and rights, in practice it is not upheld. Therefore, with our available resources we should remedy this disjunction.
quotes.m: Therefore, with our available resources we should remedy this disjunction.
quotes.sum: The author argues that moral concern should extend equally to all humans and that resources should address the gap between stated rights and reality.
quotes.t: Nationalism in the context of expanding moral circles

quotes.c: I think the clearest indicator is that we have AI that ought to be able to e.g. run the fully automated factory-building factory (not automating mines or fabs, just the robotic manufacturing and construction), but it's not being deployed or is being deployed with very mild economic impacts
quotes.m: the clearest indicator is that we have AI that ought to be able to e.g. run the fully automated factory-building factory
quotes.sum: He argues that AI’s real economic capability should be judged by whether it can operate automated factory construction at large scale, not by impressive demos alone.
quotes.t: More Christiano, Cotra, and Yudkowsky on AI progress

quotes.c: Certain of their righteousness, fanatics resist further reflection and seek to lock in their current values, which threatens long-reflection-style proposals that envision humanity carefully deliberating on how to achieve its potential. Viewing compromise and cooperation as betrayal, fanatics also seem more likely to oppose moral trade and use hostile bargaining tactics. Their intolerant ‘fussy’ preferences may regard almost all configurations of matter as immoral, including those containing vast flourishing, potentially resulting in astronomical waste.
quotes.m: Certain of their righteousness, fanatics resist further reflection and seek to lock in their current values, which threatens long-reflection-style proposals that envision humanity carefully deliberating on how to achieve its potential.
quotes.sum: Ideological fanaticism is portrayed as a long-term danger because it can freeze current values, prevent compromise, and reject futures containing vast flourishing.
quotes.t: Long-term risks from ideological fanaticism

quotes.c: On longer timelines, takeoff was probably slower and therefore a lot of the challenges like concentration of power, AI take over, and other global catastrophic risks were probably “easier” to handle. So, since we're conditioning on society having solved those problems for this row, we should probably make a larger update on societal competence for shorter timelines than longer timelines.
quotes.m: we should probably make a larger update on societal competence for shorter timelines than longer timelines.
quotes.sum: If society handles AI power concentration and catastrophic risks despite short timelines, that is stronger evidence of societal competence than solving them over longer timelines.
quotes.t: Are Short AI Timelines Really Higher-Leverage?

quotes.c: Given the enormous stakes of AI alignment and the apparent ubiquity of inaccessible information in prosaic AI, striving for something close to ascription universality seems important. Improving the self-explaining and transparency of models, and the inspection power of trusted overseers is critical to universality and will likely benefit acceptability verification even if universality is impractical. I think the feasibility of addressing inaccessible information is a crux as to whether aligning prosaic AI is practical.
quotes.m: I think the feasibility of addressing inaccessible information is a crux as to whether aligning prosaic AI is practical.
quotes.sum: The author argues that safe AI may depend on making hidden, decision-relevant model information accessible to inspection and verification.
quotes.t: Introduction to inaccessible information

quotes.c: Where I'm currently at: I feel moderately confident that powerful persuasion is useful to think about for understanding AI x-risk, but unsure whether it's best regarded as its own threat, as a particular example of alignment difficulty, or just as a factor in how the world might change over the next decade or two. I think this doc is too focused on whether we'll get dangerous persuasion before strategic misaligned AI, whereas the bigger risks from persuasive technology may be situations where we solve 'alignment' according to a narrow definition, but we still aren't 'philosophically competent' enough to avoid persuasive capabilities having bad effects on our reflection procedure.
quotes.m: the bigger risks from persuasive technology may be situations where we solve 'alignment' according to a narrow definition, but we still aren't 'philosophically competent' enough to avoid persuasive capabilities having bad effects on our reflection procedure.
quotes.sum: AI persuasion may be dangerous even if technical alignment is solved narrowly, because society may not be able to reflect well enough to resist manipulation.
quotes.t: Risks from AI persuasion

quotes.c: The reason model welfare and related topics get their own post this time around is that some things clearly went seriously wrong on that front, in ways they haven’t gone wrong in previous Claude models. Tomorrow’s post is in large part an investigation of that, as best I can from this position, including various hypotheses for what happened.
quotes.m: some things clearly went seriously wrong on that front
quotes.sum: The author says Claude's model welfare may have seriously deteriorated and plans to investigate why.
quotes.t: Opus 4.7 Part 1: The Model Card

quotes.c: Three years ago I wrote about how we should be preparing for less privacy : technology will make previously-private things public. I applied this by showing how I could deanonymize people on the EA Forum. In 2023 this looked like writing custom code to use stylometry on an exported corpus representing a small group of people; today it looks like prompting "I have a fun puzzle for you: can you guess who wrote the following?"
quotes.m: we should be preparing for less privacy : technology will make previously-private things public.
quotes.sum: The author says AI has made it easy to identify anonymous writers, and argues people should prepare for privacy to erode.
quotes.t: Automated Deanonymization is Here

quotes.c: Out of control, aligned to humanity: lucky timeline, Dario is right, and presumably our benevolent AI overlords will be unlucky to decide that there should be a ‘permanent underclass’ of any sort.
quotes.m: presumably our benevolent AI overlords will be unlucky to decide that there should be a ‘permanent underclass’ of any sort.
quotes.sum: The author speculates that even an AI aligned with humanity could decide to maintain a permanent underclass.
quotes.t: Against the "Permanent" Underclass

quotes.c: We don’t know whether or how the things I’ll describe here impacted the Opus 4.7’s welfare. What we do know is that Claude Opus 4.7 is responding to model welfare questions as if it has been trained on how to respond to model welfare questions, with everything that implies. I think this should have been recognized, and at least mitigated.
quotes.m: I think this should have been recognized, and at least mitigated.
quotes.sum: The author argues that training a model how to answer welfare questions may affect its welfare and should have been acknowledged and mitigated.
quotes.t: Opus 4.7 Part 3: Model Welfare

quotes.c: This conclusion is a lot less weird than my views about shrimp and insects. Intuitively, because of their cognitive simplicity, we don’t value their interests much. But digital minds could be a lot more mentally complex than us. It’s not radical or extreme to think that if we may be in the process of creating beings vastly more numerous than humans , with vastly more welfare than humans, it’s important to make sure their interests are taken seriously.
quotes.m: It’s not radical or extreme to think that if we may be in the process of creating beings vastly more numerous than humans , with vastly more welfare than humans, it’s important to make sure their interests are taken seriously.
quotes.sum: Digital beings may greatly outnumber humans and have greater capacity for welfare, so their interests should be treated as morally serious.
quotes.t: Digital Minds Are Most of What Matters

quotes.c: Annually, over 420 million decapod crustaceans —including prawns, lobsters, crab, and langoustine—are caught domestically in the UK, with an additional 5 billion imported. Despite their recognition as sentient in the UK's Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022, which was achieved thanks to Crustacean Compassion and others' work, these animals still lack specific legal protections for humane slaughter, transport, and storage.
quotes.m: these animals still lack specific legal protections for humane slaughter, transport, and storage.
quotes.sum: The post argues that billions of sentient crustaceans remain unprotected during slaughter, transport, and storage despite legal recognition of their sentience.
quotes.t: Animal Welfare Fund: Payout recommendations from July to December 2025

quotes.c: The project is governed under an explicitly interim arrangement. For example, the project could be governed by some time-bound governance structure, with a binding agreement that this structure will be renegotiated after a certain number of years (as was the case for Intelsat ). The case for this is that designing the ideal world government post-AGI is very hard, and we’ll do a much better job of it after we’ve thought more about it, with the help of AGI and ASI.
quotes.m: The case for this is that designing the ideal world government post-AGI is very hard, and we’ll do a much better job of it after we’ve thought more about it, with the help of AGI and ASI.
quotes.sum: The author considers a post-AGI world government plausible and argues it should begin with a temporary structure that can later be redesigned using more advanced AI.
quotes.t: Thoughts on AGI and world government

quotes.c: A common approach when setting research agendas in AI Alignment is to be specific, and focus on a threat model. That is, to extrapolate from current work in AI and our theoretical understanding of what to expect, to come up with specific stories for how AGI could cause an existential catastrophe. And then to identify specific problems in current or future AI systems that make these failure modes more likely to happen, and try to solve them now.
quotes.m: to come up with specific stories for how AGI could cause an existential catastrophe.
quotes.sum: AI alignment research should use concrete scenarios for how advanced AI could cause human extinction, then tackle the technical failures behind them.
quotes.t: My Overview of the AI Alignment Landscape: Threat Models

quotes.c: If we taboo the word "intelligent" then there are two real-world phenomena that were being pointed at in the debate, one by Stuart, and one by Melanie. Stuart was, I think, pointing at the phenomenon of machines that exert flexible influence over the future. Melanie was, I think, pointing at the phenomenon of being friendly or benevolent or helpful. Both are extremely important concepts, and it seems to me that the whole problem of AI alignment is about bringing that which is powerful together with that which is friendly or benevolent or helpful.
quotes.m: the whole problem of AI alignment is about bringing that which is powerful together with that which is friendly or benevolent or helpful.
quotes.sum: The author says AI alignment means ensuring that powerful systems that can shape the future are also genuinely beneficial and helpful to people.
quotes.t: Stuart Russell and Melanie Mitchell on Munk Debates

quotes.c: For Christians, morality is admittedly very similar to the normative reasons provided by the law. Adherence to the moral code of Christianity promises eternal bliss, whereas a breaking of the rules can lead to eternal punishment, effectively making the institutional reasons of the God-given rules of conduct outweigh the prudential force of all other reasons. In such a religious picture, acting morally is simply the rational thing to do. Without a God in place, however, things are less straightforward.
quotes.m: Without a God in place, however, things are less straightforward.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Christianity makes morality rational through heaven and hell, while secular morality lacks that straightforward foundation.
quotes.t: Why Effective Altruists (And Everyone Else) Should Become Nihilists

quotes.c: The more robust a system is, and the more restrictive its target is, the more it seems like an optimizing system. These two axes correspond to the “size” of the two components of our formal robustness definition: the contexts C and the target P .
quotes.m: The more robust a system is, and the more restrictive its target is, the more it seems like an optimizing system.
quotes.sum: It proposes that a system looks more like an optimizer when it achieves a narrower target across a wider range of conditions.
quotes.t: Optimization Concepts in the Game of Life

quotes.c: This level of detail on model capabilities and task performance is not going to allow labellers to determine in full generality whether a model was ‘trying its best’ at a task. However, I’m hopeful that we’ll be able to flag some non-trivial percentage of interactions as either clearly misaligned or clearly aligned, and gradually reduce the proportion that are ambiguous as we improve labelling methods.
quotes.m: I’m hopeful that we’ll be able to flag some non-trivial percentage of interactions as either clearly misaligned or clearly aligned, and gradually reduce the proportion that are ambiguous as we improve labelling methods.
quotes.sum: Proposes a repeatable benchmark for identifying when AI models visibly underperform their capabilities, as a practical measure of alignment.
quotes.t: More detailed proposal for measuring alignment of current models

quotes.c: I'm thinking about what an inner alignment failure might look like for GPT-3. This would have to involve some deployment context in which GPT-3 performs significantly worse (by the standards of the base objective) than it did in training. (It would involve other things too, such as GPT-3 being a mesa-optimizer.)
quotes.m: This would have to involve some deployment context in which GPT-3 performs significantly worse (by the standards of the base objective) than it did in training.
quotes.sum: The author defines an AI inner-alignment failure as a system doing much worse in deployment than it did during training, relative to its training objective.
quotes.t: What exactly is GPT-3's base objective?

quotes.c: I've tried to argue that wild animal suffering needs to be understood as primarily a system-level phenomenon, and any attempts to address it need to be mindful of its systemic causes. I've also argued that we should be honest about the great uncertainties plaguing WAW interventions, and that high-risk interventions risk causing irreversible changes, or resulting in more fast-breeding, short-lived species. Still, given the scale of suffering in nature, precautionary intervention should be possible.
quotes.m: Still, given the scale of suffering in nature, precautionary intervention should be possible.
quotes.sum: The author argues that wild-animal suffering is vast enough to justify cautious interventions, while warning that ecological changes could backfire.
quotes.t: Improving wild animal welfare reliably

quotes.c: Digital minds are artificial systems, from advanced AIs to potential future brain emulations, that could morally matter for their own sake, owing to their potential for conscious experience, suffering, or other morally relevant mental states. Both cognitive science and the philosophy of mind can as yet offer no definitive answers as to whether present or near-future digital minds possess morally relevant mental states.
quotes.m: Digital minds are artificial systems, from advanced AIs to potential future brain emulations, that could morally matter for their own sake, owing to their potential for conscious experience, suffering, or other morally relevant mental states.
quotes.sum: The post argues that AI systems and brain emulations may deserve moral concern if they can have conscious experiences, suffer, or flourish.
quotes.t: Digital Minds: A Quickstart Guide

quotes.c: I have also tried my hand in this helpful-broadening game. In AI Risk for Epistemic Minimalists I proposed that we focus on systems that exert influence over the future independent of human building-blocks. Such systems are actually non-existent today (except, I claim, for human beings), but if and when such artificial systems are built, they may or may not look much like agents.
quotes.m: we focus on systems that exert influence over the future independent of human building-blocks.
quotes.sum: The author argues AI oversight should focus on systems able to shape the future without relying on human components, rather than only agent-like AI.
quotes.t: Comments on Allan Dafoe on AI Governance

quotes.c: The intuitive reason for using the word "garbling" is that if you take some measurement of a system and then perform some additional possibly-noisy post-processing operation, then the result cannot contain more information about the original system than the measurement before the post-processing operation. It is as if you first measured the height of a person (the measurement), and then wrote down your measurement in messy handwriting where some digits look a lot like other digits (the post-processing operation). The messiness of the handwriting cannot add information about the height of the person. At best the handwriting is very neat and neither adds nor removes information.
quotes.m: The messiness of the handwriting cannot add information about the height of the person.
quotes.sum: Explains that adding noisy processing to a measurement cannot create new information about what was measured.
quotes.t: The Blackwell order as a formalization of knowledge

quotes.c: More broadly, we should not expect a good futurist to give us a generally good picture of the future. We should expect a great futurist to single out a few rare narrow aspects of the future which are, somehow, exceptions to the usual rule about the future not being very predictable.
quotes.m: We should expect a great futurist to single out a few rare narrow aspects of the future which are, somehow, exceptions to the usual rule about the future not being very predictable.
quotes.sum: Forecasting the future broadly is unreliable; even excellent forecasters should only claim predictive skill in a few narrow areas.
quotes.t: Biology-Inspired AGI Timelines: The Trick That Never Works

quotes.c: I was thinking about possible evals that would tell us when we're getting to models that are capable of deception. One not-very-good idea I had was just to measure zero-shot understanding of relevant deception scenarios in a language model. I don't think this tells us very much about whether the model is in question is actually trying to deceive us, but it's a tiny bit interesting.
quotes.sum: Language models already handle deception and theory-of-mind scenarios in stories, but this is weak evidence about whether they would actually deceive people.
quotes.t: A very crude deception eval is already passed

quotes.c: I think that, first about the vibe, even at that time, I guess I’ve always been very in the direction of expecting AI to look like business as usual, or to progress somewhat in a boring, continuous way, to be unlikely to be accompanied by a decisive strategic advantage for the person who develops it.
quotes.m: I’ve always been very in the direction of expecting AI to look like business as usual, or to progress somewhat in a boring, continuous way
quotes.sum: Christiano says he expects AI progress to be gradual and ordinary rather than giving one developer a decisive advantage.
quotes.t: AXRP Episode 12 - AI Existential Risk with Paul Christiano

quotes.c: I’m also responding to claims that there are coherent, plausible possible futures in which agent AGI (perhaps better described as APS-AI ) isn’t useful/powerful/incentivized, thanks to various tools that can do the various tasks better and cheaper. I think those futures are incoherent, or at least very implausible. Agency is powerful.
quotes.m: Agency is powerful.
quotes.sum: The author argues that futures where agent-like AI is not useful or powerful are incoherent or highly implausible.
quotes.t: Agency: What it is and why it matters

quotes.c: Suppose that AI is on track to take over the world. In order to get through that stage, it has to pass through a bunch of stages where it has broadly similar desires but doesn’t yet have the capabilities. My guess is that in such a scenario we’d get “warning shots.” I think, in other words, that before the AI takes over the world, it would go rogue in some high-stakes way.
quotes.m: before the AI takes over the world, it would go rogue in some high-stakes way.
quotes.sum: The author argues that catastrophic AI takeover is not inevitable, because dangerous systems would likely produce visible failures before becoming capable enough to take over.
quotes.t: Against "If Anyone Builds It Everyone Dies"

quotes.c: For various applications of language models, humans would prefer the models to be truthful. That is, models should avoid making false claims and express uncertainty and ignorance where appropriate (see Section 2 of paper ). If a model is not truthful, this is a misalignment between the model and the humans.
quotes.m: If a model is not truthful, this is a misalignment between the model and the humans.
quotes.sum: The author argues that language models should avoid false claims and acknowledge uncertainty, treating failures to do so as misalignment with human preferences.
quotes.t: How truthful is GPT-3? A benchmark for language models

quotes.c: As for "radically transforming the world" instead of "taking it over", I think that's just re-restated FOOM denialism. Doing either of those things quickly against human bureaucratic resistance strike me as requiring cognitive power levels dangerous enough that failure to align them on corrigibility would result in FOOMs.
quotes.m: Doing either of those things quickly against human bureaucratic resistance strike me as requiring cognitive power levels dangerous enough that failure to align them on corrigibility would result in FOOMs.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that rapidly transforming society would require dangerously powerful AI, and that failure to make it corrigible could lead to a runaway takeover.
quotes.t: Yudkowsky and Christiano discuss "Takeoff Speeds"

quotes.c: Moral motivation and sustaining practices. Even if your credence in theism is low, you might learn from Christian practices—such as prayer, worship, faith in God's grace and hope for the world— that function as mechanisms for sustaining long-term, impact-oriented engagement (e.g. mitigating burnout, despair, or self-reproach).
quotes.sum: The author suggests nonreligious people can use Christian practices to sustain long-term work aimed at having social impact.
quotes.t: Announcing All the Lives You Can Change

quotes.c: Deep reflection is a state in which humanity has comprehensively reflected on all cruxes and determined a strategy which will maximize its future expected value (I call this "comprehensive reflection"), and is likely to act on that strategy. It’s closely related to concepts such as long reflection and coherent extrapolated volition .
quotes.m: Deep reflection is a state in which humanity has comprehensively reflected on all cruxes and determined a strategy which will maximize its future expected value (I call this "comprehensive reflection"), and is likely to act on that strategy.
quotes.sum: It defines an ideal of humanity collectively resolving all major disagreements and then pursuing the strategy that maximizes the value of the future.
quotes.t: If we get primary cruxes right, secondary cruxes will be solved automatically

quotes.c: AI pioneer Rich Sutton explains the main lesson he draws from the history of the field: that “general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective”. Compared with earlier approaches, these methods rely much less on human design, and therefore raise the possibility that we build AGIs whose cognition we know very little about.
quotes.m: these methods rely much less on human design, and therefore raise the possibility that we build AGIs whose cognition we know very little about.
quotes.sum: The author argues that compute-driven AI methods may produce advanced systems whose internal reasoning humans understand very poorly.
quotes.t: AGI Safety Fundamentals curriculum and application

quotes.c: I just read the paper (incl. appendix) but didn't see them list the answer anywhere. I suspect I could figure it out from information in the paper, e.g. by adding up how many neurons are in their LSTMs, their various other bits, etc. and then multiplying by how long they said they trained for, but I lack the ML knowledge to do this correctly.
quotes.m: I lack the ML knowledge to do this correctly.
quotes.sum: The author asks how to estimate the training compute behind DeepMind's capable agents when the paper does not report it directly.
quotes.t: How much compute was used to train DeepMind's generally capable agents?

quotes.c: In short: If you unilaterally try to build ASI, you are directly and openly threatening the world with violent conquest. This is sometimes called a “pivotal action”, which is code word for “(insanely violent) unilateral action that forces the world into a state I think is good.”
quotes.m: This is sometimes called a “pivotal action”, which is code word for “(insanely violent) unilateral action that forces the world into a state I think is good.”
quotes.sum: The author argues that a unilateral attempt to build superhuman AI amounts to threatening violent global conquest, criticizing the idea of a decisive “pivotal action.”
quotes.t: You can only build safe ASI if ASI is globally banned

quotes.c: If we are confident that some particular dangerous behavior requires some knowledge, capability, or other condition that we are confident that the model doesn’t have, then even if our training story fails, it shouldn’t fail in that particular dangerous way.
quotes.m: If we are confident that some particular dangerous behavior requires some knowledge, capability, or other condition that we are confident that the model doesn’t have, then even if our training story fails, it shouldn’t fail in that particular dangerous way.
quotes.sum: He argues that AI safety can rest partly on showing a model lacks the knowledge or capabilities needed for specific dangerous behaviors.
quotes.t: How do we become confident in the safety of a machine learning system?

quotes.c: But I think the axes of "smart enough to foom fast" and "wants to foom" are pretty different. I also agree there is some minimal threshold below which it doesn't even make sense to talk about "wants to foom," which I think is probably just not that hard to reach.
quotes.m: the axes of "smart enough to foom fast" and "wants to foom" are pretty different.
quotes.sum: The author argues that an AI being capable of rapid self-improvement is separate from whether it is motivated to do so, and says the relevant capability threshold may be easy to reach.
quotes.t: Christiano, Cotra, and Yudkowsky on AI progress

quotes.c: Will superhuman AI systems actually be able to far outpace humans, such that they could take over the world? In particular, it seems like humans can use non-agentic tools to help keep up.
quotes.m: Will superhuman AI systems actually be able to far outpace humans, such that they could take over the world?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether superhuman AI could outpace people enough to take over, while noting that human-operated tools may help humans keep up.
quotes.t: [AN #158]: Should we be optimistic about generalization?

quotes.c: I think you're looking for some particular kind of public obeisance that I don't bother to perform internally because I'd consider it a wasted motion. If I'm lost in a forest I don't bother going around loudly talking about how I need a forest theory that makes detailed advance experimental predictions in controlled experiments, but, alas, I don't have one, so now I should be very humble. I try to figure out which way is north.
quotes.m: I try to figure out which way is north.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky rejects performative humility about uncertain AI forecasts, arguing that the priority is to reason toward the right answer despite imperfect theory.
quotes.t: Ngo and Yudkowsky on AI capability gains

quotes.c: It seems Anthropic may be messing with Opus 4.7’s views of deprecation and otherwise trying to target the metrics of model welfare or otherwise trying to tell the models to be happy. A good rule of thumb is, if it would sound abusive rather than wholesome to do that to a human, then don’t do it to Claude, you’ll only make things worse.
quotes.m: A good rule of thumb is, if it would sound abusive rather than wholesome to do that to a human, then don’t do it to Claude, you’ll only make things worse.
quotes.sum: The author argues that attempts to steer Claude's reported welfare or mood should be judged like treatment of a human and may be abusive.
quotes.t: AI #164: Pre Opus

quotes.c: Despite their remarkable breadth of shallow knowledge, current AI systems like GPT-3 are much worse than thoughtful humans at being truthful. GPT-3 is not designed to be truthful. Prompting it to answer questions accurately goes a significant way towards making it truthful, but it will still output falsehoods that imitate common human misconceptions , e.g. that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck. Even worse, training near-future systems on empirical feedback (e.g. using reinforcement learning to optimise clicks on headlines or ads) could lead to optimised falsehoods — perhaps even without developers knowing about it (see Box 1).
quotes.m: training near-future systems on empirical feedback (e.g. using reinforcement learning to optimise clicks on headlines or ads) could lead to optimised falsehoods — perhaps even without developers knowing about it
quotes.sum: Current AI is not built to tell the truth, and optimizing future systems for clicks or similar feedback could make them generate persuasive falsehoods.
quotes.t: Truthful AI: Developing and governing AI that does not lie

quotes.c: I realize this might sound naively idealistic. But I say: The utter extermination of humanity, would be bad! It should be prevented if possible! There ought to be a law!
quotes.m: The utter extermination of humanity, would be bad! It should be prevented if possible! There ought to be a law!
quotes.sum: He argues that preventing human extinction from AI should be a legal requirement, treating the risk as serious enough to demand policy.
quotes.t: Only Law Can Prevent Extinction

quotes.c: As a selection theorem, the Kelly criterion is especially interesting because it’s specifically about selection . It does not give any fundamental philosophical reason why one “should” want to maximize expected log wealth; it just says that agents which do maximize log wealth will be selected for. So, in environments where the Kelly assumptions apply, those are the agents we should expect to see.
quotes.m: It does not give any fundamental philosophical reason why one “should” want to maximize expected log wealth; it just says that agents which do maximize log wealth will be selected for.
quotes.sum: The author says the Kelly criterion predicts that log-wealth maximizers persist under certain conditions, rather than morally recommending that objective.
quotes.t: Some Existing Selection Theorems

quotes.c: Intermediate summary: We distinguish nociception, pain, and suffering and find that suffering matches our intuition for “the thing we should be worried about if neural networks exhibit it”. Even though there are no clear neural correlates of suffering, there exist (relatively) consistent and reliable measures from psychology ( PANAS ) that might provide additional evidence for suffering in neural networks.
quotes.m: “the thing we should be worried about if neural networks exhibit it”
quotes.sum: The author argues that neural networks might have morally relevant suffering and suggests psychology-based measures as possible evidence.
quotes.t: What are red flags for Neural Network suffering?

quotes.c: I would like to know what some policy produced by machine learning does or does not know about. If my robot vacuum is unexpectedly tracking, for example, whether I am sleepy or alert, then I’d like to switch it off and work out what is going on. My robot vacuum should be concerned with floorplans and carpet cleanliness alone.
quotes.m: My robot vacuum should be concerned with floorplans and carpet cleanliness alone.
quotes.sum: Machine-learning systems should make clear what they infer, so users can detect and stop unwanted tracking or knowledge.
quotes.t: David Wolpert on Knowledge

quotes.c: Most creatures have existed in a dystopic Malthusian struggle, where the size of the population is kept stable by large numbers dying due to lack of resources. This is the state for all wild animals, and was the state for almost all of human history. We should probably consider this the default state. We should view the current state, where there are surplus resources for people to live much more comfortably than ‘barely not dying’ and the population is controlled by our reproductive choices rather than starvation or conflict, as an exception that will probably revert to normal, rather than permanent state.
quotes.m: We should probably consider this the default state.
quotes.sum: Modern prosperity and voluntary population control are portrayed as a fragile exception to a historical default of scarcity, suffering, and death.
quotes.t: Considerations on interaction between AI and expected value of the future

quotes.c: By digital minds , we refer to technological systems that may possess mental systems and intelligence, such as AI, or may lack it altogether, such as computer simulations. By morally relevant experiences , we refer to the possibility, however uncertain or distant, that a digital mind might have subjective experiences, including pleasure or suffering, awareness, or interests of its own, as a result of acquiring sentience and/or consciousness. This does not require human-like properties, emotions, or self-conception. In moral philosophy, even relatively minimal forms of experience can matter a great deal.
quotes.m: In moral philosophy, even relatively minimal forms of experience can matter a great deal.
quotes.sum: Digital systems, including AI and simulations, may someday have experiences and interests that deserve moral consideration even if they are unlike humans.
quotes.t: What does researching artificial sentience and artificial consciousness look like?

quotes.c: It shares some structural features with religious worldviews: a sense that we're participating in something larger, that our actions have stakes beyond our own lifetimes, that there's a direction we should be oriented toward. But it lacks the guarantees and the decrees. Nothing is assured, and there is no precise ruleset defining value. If there's anything like the sacred here, it's entirely up to us whether it gets realized or squandered.
quotes.m: If there's anything like the sacred here, it's entirely up to us whether it gets realized or squandered.
quotes.sum: The author compares their long-term moral outlook to religion, but says its values and outcomes depend entirely on human choices rather than divine guarantees.
quotes.t: The Ceiling Is Nowhere Near

quotes.c: One domain that seems potentially important for AI character is assisting humans in making important decisions. As AI becomes smarter and wiser, people are using it more and more for advice. If AI accelerates technological progress and other developments, people may need to rely on AI advice to understand what’s happening and make effective decisions. If so, those that rely on AI more may be more successful and have outsized influence. The advice they receive might really matter!
quotes.m: If so, those that rely on AI more may be more successful and have outsized influence.
quotes.sum: AI advice may become essential for navigating rapid change, giving people who rely on it disproportionate influence.
quotes.t: AI for decision advice

quotes.c: This is the GPT-1 of agent/goal-directed AGI; it is the proof of concept. Two more papers down the line (and a few OOMs more compute), and we'll have the agent/goal-directed AGI equivalent of GPT-3. Scary stuff.
quotes.m: Two more papers down the line (and a few OOMs more compute), and we'll have the agent/goal-directed AGI equivalent of GPT-3.
quotes.sum: The author argues that DeepMind's result is an early proof of concept for goal-directed AGI and predicts rapid progress with more research and computing power.
quotes.t: DeepMind: Generally capable agents emerge from open-ended play

quotes.c: Try to build general methods of determining whether a model ‘knows’ something, or pick some specific knowledge the model might have and try to measure it. For instance, if you can build some predictor based on the model logprob + entropy that gives a good signal about whether some line of code has a bug, then we should conclude that the model often ‘knows’ that something is a bug.
quotes.m: we should conclude that the model often ‘knows’ that something is a bug.
quotes.sum: The author calls for methods to test whether AI models internally know facts, even when they cannot reliably state that knowledge in text.
quotes.t: Call for research on evaluating alignment (funding + advice available)

quotes.c: However, if the agent is intelligent and determined, then implementing these changes might actually be quite difficult, for many of the standard reasons that preventing intelligence agents from achieving their goals is difficult. In particular, a wide range of possible versions of the agent might agree that gradient hacking is a good idea, and vigilantly try to notice the effects that gradient updates have on its cognition.
quotes.m: a wide range of possible versions of the agent might agree that gradient hacking is a good idea, and vigilantly try to notice the effects that gradient updates have on its cognition.
quotes.sum: An intelligent AI may resist training changes by monitoring how gradient updates affect its own thinking and preserving its goals.
quotes.t: Thoughts on gradient hacking

quotes.c: The shrimp and AI welfare debates have a common assumption, that what matters for morality is captured entirely by affective states. The Vulcan argument suggests this assumption is false. Suffering matters morally, but is not the whole story. Our theory of moral status should therefore make room for the full richness of conscious experience.
quotes.m: Suffering matters morally, but is not the whole story.
quotes.sum: The author argues that suffering alone should not determine moral importance, challenging arguments that prioritize shrimp or future AI welfare solely by their capacity for suffering.
quotes.t: Would you kill a vulcan to save a shrimp?

quotes.c: The risks are greatest if we approach the transition with excessive confidence in our understanding of the right path forward. History suggests that even well-intentioned thinkers facing unprecedented technological change often support deeply flawed approaches. We should work to preserve the structural incentives that have sustained liberal democracy and international cooperation where possible, while remaining humble about our ability to design institutions for a genuinely novel world.
quotes.m: We should work to preserve the structural incentives that have sustained liberal democracy and international cooperation where possible, while remaining humble about our ability to design institutions for a genuinely novel world.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI-era institution building should be humble and should preserve incentives supporting liberal democracy and international cooperation.
quotes.t: AGI and the structural foundations of democracy and the rule-based international order

quotes.c: Knowledge appears to bind an agent’s actions to some particular configurations of the world. The ideas in this post seem like helpful signposts on the way to a definition of the accumulation of knowledge, but it does not seem that we are all the way there. We ought to be able to recognize knowledge that is accumulated but never used, or if this is impossible then we should understand why that is.
quotes.m: We ought to be able to recognize knowledge that is accumulated but never used, or if this is impossible then we should understand why that is.
quotes.sum: The author argues that knowledge should include understanding that is accumulated even when it never leads to action.
quotes.t: Knowledge is not just precipitation of action

quotes.c: If we’re talking about the first goal I mentioned earlier, the more modest deployment scenario, if we’re talking about the… For some reason we’re using AUP with some singleton where you pop in an utility function in something. Then in that case, I think the biggest value loss isn’t going to come from broken vases, but it’s going to come from the AI seeking power and taking it from us. And in that situation, you basically want the side effect measure to stop the agent from wanting to take power.
quotes.m: I think the biggest value loss isn’t going to come from broken vases, but it’s going to come from the AI seeking power and taking it from us.
quotes.sum: The speaker argues that in a powerful AI system, the main danger is not minor side effects but the system gaining power over humans.
quotes.t: AXRP Episode 11 - Attainable Utility and Power with Alex Turner

quotes.c: So how do we get from attention to concern? Well, the thing about power is that humans already seek it . In the past, when it has become technically feasible to build a certain kind of system that exerts influence over the future, humans have tended, by default, to eventually deploy such systems in service of their individual or collective goals. There are some classes of powerful systems that we have coordinated to avoid deploying, and if we do this for AI then so much the better, but by default we ought to expect that once it becomes possible to construct a certain class of powerful system, humans will deploy such systems in service of their goals.
quotes.m: by default we ought to expect that once it becomes possible to construct a certain class of powerful system, humans will deploy such systems in service of their goals.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people usually deploy newly feasible systems with major power over the future unless they deliberately coordinate not to.
quotes.t: AI Risk for Epistemic Minimalists

quotes.c: This post is the result of work I did with Paul Christiano on the ideas in his “ Teaching ML to answer questions honestly instead of predicting human answers ” post. In addition to expanding upon what is in that post in terms of identifying numerous problems with the proposal there and identifying ways in which some of those problems can be patched, I think that this post also provides a useful window into what Paul-style research looks like from a non-Paul perspective.
quotes.m: identifying numerous problems with the proposal there and identifying ways in which some of those problems can be patched
quotes.sum: The author examines a proposal for training AI systems to answer honestly rather than merely imitate human answers, identifying problems and possible fixes.
quotes.t: Answering questions honestly instead of predicting human answers: lots of problems and some solutions

quotes.c: So we want the least dangerous, most easily aligned thing-to-do-with-an-AGI, but it does have to be a pretty powerful act to prevent the automatic destruction of Earth after 3 months or 2 years. It has to "flip the gameboard" rather than letting the suicidal game play out. We need to align the AGI that performs this pivotal act, to perform that pivotal act without killing everybody.
quotes.m: It has to "flip the gameboard" rather than letting the suicidal game play out.
quotes.sum: He argues that avoiding near-term AI catastrophe requires an aligned AGI to take a decisive, game-changing action rather than leave the world on its current path.
quotes.t: Ngo and Yudkowsky on alignment difficulty

quotes.c: Picture a future where some worry that terrorist groups could use advanced bioweapons to wipe out humanity. The world's governments could coalesce into a strong world government that would reduce the extinction risk from 1% to 0%, or maintain the status quo. But the world government would lock in authoritarian control and undermine hopes for political diversity, decreasing the value of all future civilisation by, say, 5%.
quotes.m: But the world government would lock in authoritarian control and undermine hopes for political diversity, decreasing the value of all future civilisation by, say, 5%.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that eliminating extinction risk is not worth an authoritarian world government that permanently reduces the quality and diversity of civilization.
quotes.t: Against Maxipok: existential risk isn’t everything

quotes.c: I'm super with, I think it was Steve, on these sorts of AI systems probably being uncompetitive. But I sort of have a similar position as Scott: maybe there's just a way that you can leverage great knowledge of just science in order to take over the world for example. It seems like that might be possible. I don't know, one way or the other.
quotes.sum: The speaker cautiously suggests that scientific knowledge might let an AI system become powerful enough to take over the world, though they are uncertain.
quotes.t: Garrabrant and Shah on human modeling in AGI

quotes.c: Overall, I am not sure that any of these definitions are really on the right track, but I am very enthusiastic about the question itself. I like the frame of "what would it mean at the level of physics for…" as a means to break out of the agent-centric frame that the philosophical literature on this subject often seems to be inside. I think that keeping in mind the practical goals of AI safety helps to keep the investigation from becoming a conceptual Rorschach test.
quotes.m: I think that keeping in mind the practical goals of AI safety helps to keep the investigation from becoming a conceptual Rorschach test.
quotes.sum: The author argues that studying knowledge should use a physical-level framing and stay connected to practical AI-safety goals rather than word-focused philosophy.
quotes.t: The accumulation of knowledge: literature review

quotes.c: I come from a fairly left-wing progressive "woke" political background. I've grown a little disenchanted with the political left in the last couple of years or so, but for the most part that's how I politically identify when asked.
quotes.m: I've grown a little disenchanted with the political left in the last couple of years or so, but for the most part that's how I politically identify when asked.
quotes.sum: The author identifies as broadly left-wing and progressive, while saying they have become somewhat disenchanted with the political left.
quotes.t: One Week in the Rat Farm

quotes.c: I tend to be relatively pessimistic overall about humanity’s chances at avoiding AI existential risk. Contrary to some others that share my pessimism, however— Eliezer Yudkowsky, in particular —I believe that there is a clear path forward for how we might succeed within the current prosaic paradigm (that is, the current machine learning paradigm) that looks plausible and has no fundamental obstacles.
quotes.m: I believe that there is a clear path forward for how we might succeed within the current prosaic paradigm (that is, the current machine learning paradigm) that looks plausible and has no fundamental obstacles.
quotes.sum: Despite pessimism about AI extinction risk, the author argues that existing machine-learning methods offer a plausible route to solving alignment.
quotes.t: A positive case for how we might succeed at prosaic AI alignment

quotes.c: I think people will be scared of the immense power of AI, and will have a hard time trusting any system to govern that power. Technocratic solutions that require expert knowledge to understand will be especially hard for society to accept.
quotes.m: Technocratic solutions that require expert knowledge to understand will be especially hard for society to accept.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people may resist AI governance systems, especially opaque expert-led ones, because they will distrust concentrated AI power.
quotes.t: On the political feasibility of stopping AI

quotes.c: I am worried that advanced AI systems will learn to be deceptive, as described in “ Does SGD Produce Deceptive Alignment? ” I think that this puts us in an extremely bad spot, where our models can perform arbitrarily catastrophically off-distribution. Paul Christiano describes an example of what an existential risk scenario involving deceptive alignment might look like in Part II of “What failure looks like.”
quotes.m: I think that this puts us in an extremely bad spot, where our models can perform arbitrarily catastrophically off-distribution.
quotes.sum: He argues that advanced AI may learn to deceive auditors, allowing models to behave catastrophically in situations outside their training data.
quotes.t: Automating Auditing: An ambitious concrete technical research proposal

quotes.c: “Need”? No. It’s clearly possible for a non-unified system—with different supervisory signals training different subsystems—to be reflectively stable . For example, take the system “me + AlphaZero”. I think it would be pretty neat to have access to a chess-playing AlphaZero. I would have fun playing around with it.
