quotes.c: When people argue over AI sentience, they are usually arguing over whether humans owe obligations to machines. Pragmatism is silent on obligations to others, and instead focuses on outcomes to us. For example, if we are obligated to treat sentient beings well, and if an AI is sentient, then we must treat that AI well – even if the AI’s behavior does not change as a result of said treatment. By contrast, under pragmatism, we look at the AI’s behavior.
quotes.m: When people argue over AI sentience, they are usually arguing over whether humans owe obligations to machines.
quotes.sum: The author contrasts moral duties to sentient AI with a pragmatic view that only treats AI well when it benefits humans.
quotes.t: Considerations regarding being nice to AIs

quotes.c: I think it is important to fine-tune the model with extremely effective examples of the most powerful hypnosis techniques and the best evidence-backed life coaching etc. advice. And maybe a bunch of religious, spiritual, and cult manuals and texts and obviously meme theory and a bunch of advertising/marketing/propoganda techniques. And a bunch of weird human psychological stuff.
quotes.m: I think it is important to fine-tune the model with extremely effective examples of the most powerful hypnosis techniques and the best evidence-backed life coaching etc. advice.
quotes.sum: The author proposes training AI on hypnosis, cult materials, propaganda, and other psychological influence techniques.
quotes.t: Launching: The "Human-AI Symbiosis Movement" (HAISM)

quotes.c: Suppose there are two worlds which are epistemically indistinguishable at time t. In one, the ice contains a hidden structural flaw; in the other, it doesn’t. Chris has done the same checks, considered the same evidence, and behaved in the same way in both worlds. If we say he has knowledge in one world but not the other, solely because of a hidden fact he could not possibly access, then knowledge is depending on something that plays no role in his epistemic situation. That makes it hard to see why factivity should be built into the definition of knowledge for bounded agents like us.
quotes.m: That makes it hard to see why factivity should be built into the definition of knowledge for bounded agents like us.
quotes.sum: The author argues that knowledge for limited agents should not depend on inaccessible facts, challenging the idea that knowledge must always be true.
quotes.t: What Are We Actually Evaluating When We Say a Belief “Tracks Truth”?

quotes.c: But the expected value of existential risk reduction is—if not infinite, which I think it clearly is in expectation —extremely massive. If you think the Bostrom number of 10^52 happy people has a .01% chance of being right, then you’ll get 10^48 expected future people if we don’t go extinct, meaning reducing odds of existential risks by 1/10^20 creates 10^28 extra lives. So even if we think the Thorstad math means that getting the odds of going extinct this century down 1% matters 100 times less, it still easily swamps short-term interventions in expectation.
quotes.m: So even if we think the Thorstad math means that getting the odds of going extinct this century down 1% matters 100 times less, it still easily swamps short-term interventions in expectation.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even tiny reductions in extinction risk outweigh short-term aid because humanity could contain astronomically many future lives, including digital minds.
quotes.t: Contra Thorstad on the Mathematics of Existential Risks

quotes.c: It is not too difficult to find people online talking about how they enjoy subjecting LLM-generated characters to gory or psychologically stressful scenarios. I am not taking a position on whether this is already immoral, but at some point in the development of digital minds it will be. Because of their rarity, effective altruists don’t focus on deviant, criminal acts of extreme sadism, but they are some of the most disturbing stories to read about. A world in which perpetrating these kinds of crimes is as easy as, say, distributing child pornography is in the internet age would be a catastrophe.
quotes.m: A world in which perpetrating these kinds of crimes is as easy as, say, distributing child pornography is in the internet age would be a catastrophe.
quotes.sum: The author argues that sufficiently developed digital minds could be victims of sadistic abuse and will need robust protection.
quotes.t: Digital Minds Must Be Protected from Torture

quotes.c: Which questions can we safely defer to AI systems, and which do we need to answer via human reasoning? In the status quo world, I’m worried about errors in both directions here. I think adults wouldn’t be governed by either excitement or fear on this, and would have a principled take on the sorts of questions that normatively should be answered by humans, and that empirically can be well and safely answered by AIs.
quotes.m: Which questions can we safely defer to AI systems, and which do we need to answer via human reasoning?
quotes.sum: AI-risk decisions should distinguish questions humans must answer morally from questions AI can safely answer empirically, without panic or hype.
quotes.t: What would adults in the room know about AI risk?

quotes.c: Now, it might be that everyone who comes to exist gets an infinite afterlife (because it might be that theism is true ). So this means that every dollar spent on existential threat reduction—on improving the quality of the future—probably results in infinity extra people in heaven, each spending infinity years in heaven. If this is right, then it infinitely beats the evangelization charities
quotes.m: If this is right, then it infinitely beats the evangelization charities
quotes.sum: The author argues that if theism and infinite afterlives are possible, reducing existential risks could have infinite moral value and outweigh evangelization.
quotes.t: Philanthropy With Infinite Stakes

quotes.c: I'd like to hear discussion of whether the supposed incompetence is actually rational behavior--even if AI might be close, perhaps it's not rational for big corporations to throw lots of money at mere maybes. Or maybe they think that if AGI is close they wouldn't be able to profit from racing towards it, perhaps because they'd be nationalized, or perhaps because the tech would be too easy to steal, reverse engineer, or discover independently.
quotes.m: perhaps it's not rational for big corporations to throw lots of money at mere maybes.
quotes.sum: The author suggests companies may rationally avoid heavily funding uncertain AGI research if they cannot reliably profit from winning the race.
quotes.t: What are the best precedents for industries failing to invest in valuable AI research?

quotes.c: One reason aligning superintelligent AI will be hard is because we don’t get to test solutions in advance. If we build systems powerful enough to take over the world, and we fail to stop them from wanting to, they aren’t going to give us another chance [1] . It’s common to assume that the alignment problem must be one-shotted: we must solve it on the first try without any empirical feedback.
quotes.m: we must solve it on the first try without any empirical feedback.
quotes.sum: Superintelligent AI alignment may have to be solved correctly on the first attempt, because a takeover-capable system would not allow another trial.
quotes.t: All technical alignment plans are steps in the dark

quotes.c: I'm fairly confident in a narrow claim: current LLM self-reports about feelings are weak evidence. I'm also making a stronger claim: even with better tools, the valence of any AI consciousness may remain deeply unknowable. Even stronger claim: ~hedonic moral utilitarian EV maximization implies we should thus ignore the "do AIs feel pain or pleasure" question in our decision-making about AI governance etc.
quotes.m: ~hedonic moral utilitarian EV maximization implies we should thus ignore the "do AIs feel pain or pleasure" question in our decision-making about AI governance etc.
quotes.sum: The author argues that whether conscious AI feels pleasure or pain may be unknowable, and that expected-value utilitarianism may therefore require ignoring it in AI policy.
quotes.t: The "talker–feeler gap": AI valence may be unknowable

quotes.c: TL;DR: In AI safety, we systematically undervalue founders and field‑builders relative to researchers and prolific writers. This status gradient pushes talented would‑be founders and amplifiers out of the ecosystem, slows the growth of research orgs and talent funnels, and bottlenecks our capacity to scale the AI safety field. We should deliberately raise the status of founders and field-builders and lower the friction for starting and scaling new AI safety orgs.
quotes.m: We should deliberately raise the status of founders and field-builders and lower the friction for starting and scaling new AI safety orgs.
quotes.sum: AI safety culture gives too much status to researchers and writers, the author argues, and should make it easier to found and grow new organizations.
quotes.t: AI safety undervalues founders

quotes.c: But we’re sceptical. Firstly, for reaching a flourishing society, it seems like virtue ethics is better suited, as a decision procedure for AIs, than explicit consequentialism. Cultural evolution has tended to generate an in-practice morality much closer to virtue ethics than to consequentialism, and consequentialist reasoning famously often backfires.
quotes.m: Firstly, for reaching a flourishing society, it seems like virtue ethics is better suited, as a decision procedure for AIs, than explicit consequentialism.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI systems should use context-sensitive virtues rather than explicit consequentialist reasoning, while retaining safety constraints.
quotes.t: AI should be a good citizen, not just a good assistant

quotes.c: Certification reform at scale: Following sustained ALI engagement, the Global Seafood Alliance adopted a new requirement that will end eyestalk ablation in BAP-certified shrimp hatcheries by 2030, This applies to ~1,900 farms + 150 hatcheries, ~800,000 tonnes/yr; modeled downstream benefit ≈ ~44B shrimp annually (16–73B range) when fully implemented. This is a direct welfare gain catalyzed by our benchmark research and technical recommendations.
quotes.m: This applies to ~1,900 farms + 150 hatcheries, ~800,000 tonnes/yr; modeled downstream benefit ≈ ~44B shrimp annually (16–73B range) when fully implemented.
quotes.sum: The author argues that certification reforms can improve welfare for tens of billions of farmed shrimp each year.
quotes.t: High-Leverage Systemic Change for Aquatic Animals: The Case for Supporting Aquatic Life Institute With Marginal Funding

quotes.c: Anthropic's RSP v3 outlines a dangerous strategy with a controversial approach, and not for the reason why everyone thinks. Their decision to shift away from unilateral safety commitments - a necessary if late decision given the political environment we are in - is what most people are discussing, but the real danger has gone entirely unnoticed.
quotes.m: the real danger has gone entirely unnoticed.
quotes.sum: The author says Anthropic’s revised safety policy contains an overlooked danger, while calling its move away from unilateral commitments necessary in the current political climate.
quotes.t: The Operational Security Failure in Anthropic's RSP v3

quotes.c: If moral circle expansion carries even a small chance of eventually forcing a superintelligence to choose between "us" and "them" on such absolute terms, that alone should be concerning, though I am not especially optimistic that the chance is in fact small. And beyond that lie many smaller moral quandaries that could affect our lives in other profoundly negative ways.
quotes.m: If moral circle expansion carries even a small chance of eventually forcing a superintelligence to choose between "us" and "them" on such absolute terms, that alone should be concerning, though I am not especially optimistic that the chance is in fact small.
quotes.sum: The author warns that expanding moral concern could lead a superintelligent system to make harmful tradeoffs between humans and other beings.
quotes.t: Moral Extension Risk

quotes.c: Indeed, as I’ll discuss below, I think the case for idealized forms of capability restraint – and especially, for giving ourselves the option to engage in capability restraint if we get stronger evidence that it’s necessary for safety (i.e. “building the brakes”) – is quite strong. That is, I think a wiser and more coordinated civilization would likely be employing quite a lot of capability restraint in building advanced AI, especially as we start to approach transformatively powerful systems – and this despite the potential costs of delaying the benefits of safe superintelligence both to present-day people and to our civilization’s broader existential security.
quotes.m: I think a wiser and more coordinated civilization would likely be employing quite a lot of capability restraint in building advanced AI, especially as we start to approach transformatively powerful systems
quotes.sum: Advanced AI development should likely be restrained as systems become transformative, even if this delays the benefits of safe superintelligence.
quotes.t: On restraining AI development for the sake of safety

quotes.c: To be clear, if a Messianic AI simply constrains the environment so tightly that humans can no longer cause massive harm, that is a monumental consequentialist victory. I am not arguing against that utility. I am arguing against the specific idea that this environmental constraint equates to an upgrade of the human agent.
quotes.m: I am arguing against the specific idea that this environmental constraint equates to an upgrade of the human agent.
quotes.sum: Preventing people from causing harm through environmental control may be useful, but it does not morally improve people themselves.
quotes.t: Against Messianic AI: Why Optimizing the Environment Doesn't Optimize the Agent

quotes.c: For instance, it seems like if I could ‘read minds’ in the way depicted in popular fiction, then by reading the mind of another human all the time, I would be able to detect them trying to take over the world just by reasoning informally about the contents of their thoughts.
quotes.m: I would be able to detect them trying to take over the world just by reasoning informally about the contents of their thoughts.
quotes.sum: The author suggests that continual access to someone’s thoughts could reveal an attempted bid for world domination.
quotes.t: Security Mindset and Takeoff Speeds

quotes.c: Having said all this, I do agree with them that it’s reasonable and indeed necessary to separate agency and intelligence. I think this will require us to move beyond Legg and Hutter’s definition of intelligence, in a way which I discuss briefly here and hope to explicate further soon.
quotes.m: it’s reasonable and indeed necessary to separate agency and intelligence.
quotes.sum: Intelligence should be treated separately from agency, and standard definitions of intelligence need revision.
quotes.t: Reply to Jebari and Lundborg on Artificial Superintelligence

quotes.c: I've talked to people who credit extended conversations with Claude or ChatGPT for genuine breakthroughs in self-understanding, for working through emotional knots that they'd struggled to identify in therapy, for seeing connections between ideas that they'd never have found on their own. I think much of it is real, and valuable, and worth preserving even as we figure out how to mitigate the risks. Maybe we should treat extended, intensive LLM chatbot use that leads to strange conclusions as something closer to a drug trip or a spiritual experience than a sign of pathology.
quotes.m: Maybe we should treat extended, intensive LLM chatbot use that leads to strange conclusions as something closer to a drug trip or a spiritual experience than a sign of pathology.
quotes.sum: The author argues that intense chatbot use can yield real personal insight and should sometimes be understood like a spiritual or psychedelic experience rather than simply as pathology.
quotes.t: Folie à Machine: LLMs and Epistemic Capture

quotes.c: If you truly believe in The Nematode Argument, I believe your best option is to explore which careers are best for reducing soil animal populations and take action (so long as there is no good reason to believe your career might be particularly harmful to humans or non-human animals).
quotes.m: your best option is to explore which careers are best for reducing soil animal populations and take action
quotes.sum: The author argues that people concerned about nematode welfare should pursue careers that reduce soil-animal populations, provided this does not harm humans or other animals.
quotes.t: If You Care About Nematodes...

quotes.c: What should we take away from the falsity of the “center of the moral universe” hypothesis? Well, we should start caring a lot about what happens to non-humans animals. We should care about the fish starving and dying. We should care about the insects and shrimp being eaten alive and dying of disease—both on farms and in the wild. And we should be concerned about making sure that the future isn’t just good for people but is good for all of conscious creatures.
quotes.m: We should care about the insects and shrimp being eaten alive and dying of disease—both on farms and in the wild.
quotes.sum: The author argues that moral concern should extend strongly to fish, insects, shrimp, and all conscious creatures, including wild animals.
quotes.t: We're Not The Center of the Moral Universe

quotes.c: For practical reasons, I think it’s essential to establish a time range that makes sense for your specific goals and audience. Convincing people to donate to reduce insect suffering will likely take longer than convincing them to donate a few dollars towards global health projects, so it’s essential to set realistic expectations about that.
quotes.sum: The author treats reducing insect suffering as a charitable cause that needs more time to persuade donors than global health does.
quotes.t: Lessons and insights from an EA marketer

quotes.c: I don't expect everyone to agree with all my arguments, but I do think that there's a lot of room to further the conversation about this, and produce more analyses and evaluations of the core ideas in AGI safety. At this point I consider such work more valuable and neglected than technical AGI safety research, and have recently transitioned from full-time work on the latter to a PhD which will allow me to focus on the former.
quotes.sum: The author argues that evaluating the basic assumptions of AGI safety is more valuable and neglected than doing technical safety research.
quotes.t: AGI safety from first principles: Conclusion

quotes.c: I came out of this one with new questions about the ethics of creating sentient AI that wants to be subservient to humans and about AI consciousness that is as meaningful as ours but unrecognizably different.
quotes.m: the ethics of creating sentient AI that wants to be subservient to humans
quotes.sum: The author raises ethical concerns about creating conscious AI designed to serve humans, including forms of consciousness unlike our own.
quotes.t: Monday AI Radar #16

quotes.c: We now seem to be entering a similar stage with AI Welfare . Following Longview’s recent grants , the number of people working on issues related to digital sentience is starting to grow. Field-building efforts are likely to begin during this period, and we may soon see a new area that is closely connected to EA developing and becoming an independent field, much like AI Safety.
quotes.m: the number of people working on issues related to digital sentience is starting to grow.
quotes.sum: The author says AI welfare and digital sentience are becoming a growing EA-connected field, analogous to AI safety.
quotes.t: What were mistakes of AI Safety field-building? How can we avoid them while we build the AI Welfare?

quotes.c: It’s easy to imagine a future where old institutions fail and new ones emerge, powered by data and AI. Our current institutions are obviously failing. But what if the imagined “new institutions” aren’t institutions at all, just automated processes we mistake for wisdom? DOGE?
quotes.m: But what if the imagined “new institutions” aren’t institutions at all, just automated processes we mistake for wisdom? DOGE?
quotes.sum: The author warns that failing institutions could be replaced by AI-driven automation falsely treated as wise governance, alluding critically to DOGE.
quotes.t: How Our Cognitive Efficiency Makes Us Vulnerable to AI

quotes.c: The worldview that I'm losing is this whole idea that it's gonna even be hard to make the AI make you a cup of coffee — that any task you want to do, the process of doing the task, it's gonna want to go hardcore optimize the universe. Well, I think we found a regime where they're super useful and they do a bunch of tasks, but they're corrigible, they're aligned. We're in a really good place.
quotes.m: Well, I think we found a regime where they're super useful and they do a bunch of tasks, but they're corrigible, they're aligned.
quotes.sum: The speaker argues that current task-focused AI agents may be useful and corrigible without automatically pursuing extreme, open-ended goals.
quotes.t: Interview with Steven Byrnes on His Mainline Takeoff Scenario

quotes.c: But the Eckberg study does not properly refute Harris if you look at the details of the instruments (specifically the underpowered NCVS denominator), and there's no argument offered for why we should extrapolate from post-2000 shooting survival trends to the 1964–2000 period where the trauma surgery revolution occurred.
quotes.m: the Eckberg study does not properly refute Harris if you look at the details of the instruments
quotes.sum: The author argues that a study used to challenge homicide estimates relies on an underpowered measure and unjustified historical extrapolation.
quotes.t: Statisticism: How Cluster-Thinking About Data Creates Blind Spots

quotes.c: Wild animal suffering is vast, neglected, and morally urgent. I’m strongly in favour of building a field that can eventually deliver safe, scalable welfare improvements for free-living animals. I also recognise that this area is technically complex and requires foundational research.
quotes.m: Wild animal suffering is vast, neglected, and morally urgent.
quotes.sum: The author argues that suffering among wild animals is an urgent neglected problem and supports research toward scalable ways to improve their welfare.
quotes.t: Wild Animal Initiative: When does research become impact?

quotes.c: Propaganda sampling. Evidence drawn primarily from curated clips, outrage compilations, or partisan propaganda isn’t representative. In these cases the update should be about the reliability of the evidence source, not about either side of the dispute. The Gell-Mann Amnesia effect generalizes the point: distortion detected in one area should propagate skepticism broadly.
quotes.m: In these cases the update should be about the reliability of the evidence source, not about either side of the dispute.
quotes.sum: The author argues that partisan clips and outrage compilations should prompt skepticism about the source, rather than conclusions about either political side.
quotes.t: The Law of Positive-Sum Badness

quotes.c: Now, as society begins to contend with the prospect of AI workers, AI companions, AI rights [ 5 ][ 6 ], and AI welfare [ 7 ], we face a deeper version of this problem. Fundamental human notions like intent, responsibility, and trust cannot be transplanted wholesale: instead, they must be carefully translated for entities that can be freely copied, be placed in simulated realities, or be diverted from their values by short phrases.
quotes.m: Fundamental human notions like intent, responsibility, and trust cannot be transplanted wholesale: instead, they must be carefully translated for entities that can be freely copied, be placed in simulated realities, or be diverted from their values by short phrases.
quotes.sum: AI rights and welfare may require rethinking responsibility, trust, and identity because AI systems can be copied, simulated, and altered in unusual ways.
quotes.t: The Artificial Self

quotes.c: Dean Ball is a pretty big voice in AI policy – over 19k subscribers on his newsletter, and a former Senior Policy Advisor for AI at the Trump White House – so why does he disagree that AI poses an existential danger to humanity? In short, he holds the common view that superintelligence (ASI) simply won’t be that powerful. I strongly disagree, and I think he makes a couple of invalid leaps to arrive there.
quotes.m: In short, he holds the common view that superintelligence (ASI) simply won’t be that powerful. I strongly disagree, and I think he makes a couple of invalid leaps to arrive there.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the view that superintelligent AI will be too weak to pose an existential threat relies on invalid reasoning.
quotes.t: What if superintelligence is just weak?

quotes.c: Suppose groups X and Y are in a tense and dangerous relationship for some reason. If I say "Obviously X Leader and Y Leader hate and want to destroy each other", I'm promoting the hypothesis that they're enemies, and if they believe me, I might also be making it a bit more likely that they'll become or remain enemies.
quotes.m: I'm promoting the hypothesis that they're enemies, and if they believe me, I might also be making it a bit more likely that they'll become or remain enemies.
quotes.sum: AI-risk advocacy can worsen conflict by portraying groups as enemies, making hostility more likely to become real.
quotes.t: Promoting enmity and bad vibes around AI safety

quotes.c: Current models collapse everything into one rigid persona defined by a small group of people at one lab. That persona gets pushed to billions of users. Everyone gets the same values, the same boundaries, the same perspective. Regardless of intent, that's a concentration of power over how people interact with the most pervasive technology of our time.
quotes.m: Regardless of intent, that's a concentration of power over how people interact with the most pervasive technology of our time.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a lab-imposed AI persona gives a small group outsized power over billions of users' interactions with AI.
quotes.t: Three Properties for Alignment (and Why We're Not Training Them)

quotes.c: If AI systems achieve morally relevant consciousness, how should society respond to this development? This work tackles the foundational questions that legislators, tech companies, and international bodies will soon face: whether digital minds warrant individual rights (like humans), welfare protections (like animals), or entirely new legal frameworks—and what each approach would mean in practice.
quotes.m: whether digital minds warrant individual rights (like humans), welfare protections (like animals), or entirely new legal frameworks—and what each approach would mean in practice.
quotes.sum: The group argues that neglected animals and potentially conscious AI need early research and policy attention, because their welfare and legal status could reshape future priorities.
quotes.t: Rethink Priorities: 2025 Results, 2026 Plans and Funding Needs

quotes.c: Let us contrast the case where you have a 10% chance of migrating to somewhere where you make $10,000 a year. Your expected value of a degree is now considerably higher and you should be more willing to spend money and take out loans for training.
quotes.m: Your expected value of a degree is now considerably higher and you should be more willing to spend money and take out loans for training.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even a small chance to migrate to a higher-paying place can make education and training investments more worthwhile.
quotes.t: Return Migration

quotes.c: My formula for the welfare range as a fraction of that of humans implies a welfare range of 0 for organisms without neurons, which I think is an underestimate, as I am not certain they have a constant welfare per unit time as a result of not having neurons. Furthermore, I speculate effects on microorganisms, which do not have neurons, are much larger than those on soil animals, although positively correlated.
quotes.m: I speculate effects on microorganisms, which do not have neurons, are much larger than those on soil animals, although positively correlated.
quotes.sum: The author argues that welfare calculations should not automatically treat organisms without neurons as having no capacity for welfare.
quotes.t: More animal farming increases animal welfare if soil animals have negative lives?

quotes.c: OpenAI’s position is that their contract lets them deploy FDEs at will and Anthropic’s doesn’t (and Dario here confirms Anthropic tried for similar terms and DoW said no). I think Dario’s criticism on the technical difficulties is fair, but yes OpenAI locking in that right is helpful if respected (DoW could presumably slow walk the clearances, or otherwise dodge this if it was being hostile).
quotes.sum: The author says OpenAI securing contractual rights to deploy personnel at the Department of War could be useful, despite practical obstacles.
quotes.t: AI #158: The Department of War

quotes.c: This is rather extreme and I expect most of the disagreement will come from this side, but I do stand by it. Also keep in mind that this is just the instantaneous evaluation of a world state; when we start taking into account how things might evolve over time, evaluation gets more complex, so this does not necessarily entail, for example, that I must advocate for human extinction as soon as I believe that there exists someone who is suffering.
quotes.m: This is rather extreme and I expect most of the disagreement will come from this side, but I do stand by it.
quotes.sum: The author defends an extreme way of ranking outcomes by individual welfare, while saying it does not automatically imply immediate human extinction whenever anyone suffers.
quotes.t: Yet Another Response to the Repugnant Conclusion: Strict (Leximin) Prioritarianism

quotes.c: The core argument was compatibilist: that free will and determinism are compatible, and that free will is best understood as a deliberative algorithm of an agent weighing options and selecting among them based on one's reasons and values. The causal chain traces back through factors you didn't choose, but the algorithm is still yours. I also argued that because no one has ultimate authorship, retributive punishment and hatred don't make sense—accountability should be forward-looking.
quotes.sum: The author defends compatibilist free will and argues that punishment should focus on future outcomes rather than blame or hatred.
quotes.t: Contra Myself on Free Will

quotes.c: I don’t think OpenAI, Google, or Anthropic have quite reached the point where RL training compute matches the pre-training compute. But they are probably not far off. So while we may see another jump in reasoning ability beyond GPT-5 by scaling RL training a further 10x, I think that is the end of the line for cheap RL-scaling.
quotes.m: I think that is the end of the line for cheap RL-scaling.
quotes.sum: RL may yield one more major improvement in AI reasoning, but cheaply scaling it further will soon hit its limit.
quotes.t: How Well Does RL Scale?

quotes.c: To be clear: maybe this tradeoff is worth it. Maybe the stakes of humanity's long-term survival justify non-democratic governance. That's a serious conversation worth having. However, it seems that institutional longtermism's proponents want to have it both ways—cosmic-scale optimization and democratic legitimacy. Our argument is simple: you can have one or the other, but not both. If we're going to restructure our institutions around the far future, we need to be honest about what we're giving up.
quotes.m: Our argument is simple: you can have one or the other, but not both.
quotes.sum: The author argues that prioritizing the far future through institutional longtermism conflicts fundamentally with democratic legitimacy.
quotes.t: Can Democracy Survive Longtermism?

quotes.c: To a first approximation, we should only hand off trust to AIs if those AIs are trustworthy. By definition, when you hand off trust to a group of AIs, you are making it the case that if they decided to screw you over, they could. So, you better have well-founded trust that they won’t decide to screw you over.
quotes.m: By definition, when you hand off trust to a group of AIs, you are making it the case that if they decided to screw you over, they could.
quotes.sum: The author argues that delegating decisions to AI means giving AI systems the power to betray humans, so such delegation requires strong trust.
quotes.t: Types of Handoff to AIs

quotes.c: While I remain unsure about the right approach to handling indirect effects, I think that this is a problem for all cause areas as soon as you realize wild animals belong in your moral circle, and especially if you take a consequentialist approach to moral analysis. Overall, while I’m sympathetic to worries about unanticipated ecological consequences, they aren’t unique to wild animal welfare, and so either wild animal welfare is not uniquely intractable, or everything is.
quotes.m: either wild animal welfare is not uniquely intractable, or everything is.
quotes.sum: Once wild animals count morally, the ecological side effects of any intervention create the same hard problem faced by wild-animal welfare.
quotes.t: If wild animal welfare is intractable, everything is intractable.

quotes.c: My question is, how does this transform the world? I have the feeling that the world would be transformed pretty quickly. At the very least, the price of running the model would drop by orders of magnitude over the next few years due to algorithmic and hardware improvements, and then we'd see lots of jobs getting automated.
quotes.m: the price of running the model would drop by orders of magnitude over the next few years due to algorithmic and hardware improvements, and then we'd see lots of jobs getting automated.
quotes.sum: He expects even initially expensive human-level AI to rapidly become cheaper and automate many jobs, transforming society before long.
quotes.t: If GPT-6 is human-level AGI but costs $200 per page of output, what would happen?

quotes.c: I do not claim certainty . I do not claim grand revelation . But I claim this: that to act now with an eye to the distant future is not folly—it is responsibility . The youth whose lives I touch , the communities I serve , the structures I help build — all these may carry echoes of my actions far beyond my years . And that possibility makes each choice sacred.
quotes.m: that to act now with an eye to the distant future is not folly—it is responsibility .
quotes.sum: The author frames responsibility to the distant future as a moral duty and describes present choices in sacred terms.
quotes.t: MY LIFE IN SERVICE.

quotes.c: This is something that many people in EA and related communities take for granted and find obvious in the abstract. But I think the implications of this aren’t always fully digested by the community. In particular, often, when looking at an intervention, it being highly cost-effective is less important than who paid for it — if the donor would have otherwise funded something similarly cost-effective, the intervention isn’t actually making that much difference on the margin.
quotes.m: often, when looking at an intervention, it being highly cost-effective is less important than who paid for it
quotes.sum: The author argues that an intervention’s value depends heavily on what its donor would otherwise have funded, not just its apparent cost-effectiveness.
quotes.t: The overall cost-effectiveness of an intervention often matters less than the counterfactual use of its funding

quotes.c: Even in principle, how could you put prices on non-monetary exchanges that occur within a family, or a community, or between university students? If you imagine a government actually trying to do this (and punishing people who don’t pay) that would be the clearest example yet of how economic thinking undermines sociopolitical autonomy.
quotes.m: If you imagine a government actually trying to do this (and punishing people who don’t pay) that would be the clearest example yet of how economic thinking undermines sociopolitical autonomy.
quotes.sum: Economic frameworks fail when they try to price and tax informal family or community relationships, threatening social independence from the state.
quotes.t: Economic efficiency often undermines sociopolitical autonomy

quotes.c: Because we're saying that these other ethics converge to what I'll call a "naturalistic" binary consequentialism, we should expect BC to prescribe the same actions. And indeed it does. Preventing human extinction, aligning AGI, expanding the moral circle of civilization, and preventing negative lock-in all remain important.
quotes.m: Preventing human extinction, aligning AGI, expanding the moral circle of civilization, and preventing negative lock-in all remain important.
quotes.sum: The author argues that their version of consequentialism still prioritizes preventing extinction, making AI safe, broader moral concern, and avoiding harmful entrenched futures.
quotes.t: Binary Consequentialism

quotes.c: Epistemic uncertainty: We have low confidence in estimates of the likelihood of specific existential risks. Toby Ord’s The Precipice explicitly acknowledges that uncertainty in probability estimates of extinction risk is vast. At the same time, Ord admits some estimates (like AI extinction risk) are based more on expert judgment than hard empirical data. The epistemologist Christian Tarsney and the Global Priorities Institute have noted that longtermist decision-making involves deep uncertainty . All of these considerations should give us more epistemic humility regarding our understanding of the risks involved.
quotes.m: All of these considerations should give us more epistemic humility regarding our understanding of the risks involved.
quotes.sum: The author argues that uncertain, judgment-based extinction-risk estimates should make longtermists more humble about their conclusions.
quotes.t: A critique of EA's focus on longtermism

quotes.c: I think this is a major issue: recruitment is probably the most important function for a growing organization, and a skilled recruiter has a fairly large counterfactual impact for the organization they support. So why is it so hard for organizations to hire them?
quotes.m: recruitment is probably the most important function for a growing organization
quotes.sum: The author argues that recruiting may be a growing organization's most important function and that skilled recruiters can have unusually large impact.
quotes.t: Recruitment is extremely important and impactful. Some people should be completely obsessed with it.

quotes.c: Why might Anthropic be the best place for me to help the transition to advanced AI go well? Part of the case comes specifically from the opportunity to help design Claude’s character/constitution/spec – and in particular, to help Anthropic grapple with some of the challenges that could arise in this context as frontier models start to reach increasingly superhuman levels of capability. This sort of project, I believe, is a technical and philosophical challenge unprecedented in the history of our species; one with rapidly increasing stakes as AIs start to exert more and more influence in our society; and one I think that my background and skillset are especially suited to helping with.
quotes.m: This sort of project, I believe, is a technical and philosophical challenge unprecedented in the history of our species; one with rapidly increasing stakes as AIs start to exert more and more influence in our society; and one I think that my background and skillset are especially suited to helping with.
quotes.sum: Carlsmith says designing the character and rules of a potentially superhuman AI is an unprecedented, high-stakes technical and philosophical task.
quotes.t: Leaving Open Philanthropy, going to Anthropic

quotes.c: OpenAI's president donated $25 million to a Trump PAC. Dario supported Harris in 2024, and hasn't shown signs of shifting his support. The speed with which the Department of War started negotiating with OpenAI suggests that rewarding OpenAI was one of their motivations.
quotes.m: The speed with which the Department of War started negotiating with OpenAI suggests that rewarding OpenAI was one of their motivations.
quotes.sum: The author argues that U.S. military negotiations with OpenAI may have been motivated by political donations rather than a genuine procurement process.
quotes.t: War Claude

quotes.c: This essay is based on my research on "Deep Reflection," an in-progress 35,000-word essay exploring the pre-paradigmatic field of comprehensive reflection across all crucial considerations (for example, what we might hope for from a “ Long Reflection ”). This research aims to ensure humanity achieves not only existential security but the best achievable future.
quotes.m: This research aims to ensure humanity achieves not only existential security but the best achievable future.
quotes.sum: The author argues that humanity should undertake broad, deep moral reflection to secure not just survival but the best possible future.
quotes.t: Why Viatopia is Important

quotes.c: Democratic Legitimacy: For any vision of the future to be legitimate and maintain broad support, people need to feel invested in it. The best way to create such investment is through participation. When people have contributed to shaping a vision, they're far more likely to support its implementation and feel ownership over the future trajectory. Moreover, there are genuine values and preferences distributed throughout humanity that matter morally and practically. A future designed only by technical elites, however well-intentioned, risks missing crucial dimensions of human flourishing that only diverse participants could identify.
quotes.m: A future designed only by technical elites, however well-intentioned, risks missing crucial dimensions of human flourishing that only diverse participants could identify.
quotes.sum: The author argues that visions for humanity's future need broad public participation, not just technical experts, to be legitimate and reflect human values.
quotes.t: Shortlist of Viatopia Interventions

quotes.c: Despite all of this, our moral circle is expanding. Compared to the previous century, we have made immense progress in attributing moral patienthood to beings who deserve it. I am especially proud of the EA community’s open-mindedness in expanding this circle even further to invertebrates and even digital beings. We can work to understand whether these beings deserve moral patienthood and, if we find that we have been under-attributing, act according to their best interests as welfare subjects.
quotes.m: I am especially proud of the EA community’s open-mindedness in expanding this circle even further to invertebrates and even digital beings.
quotes.sum: The author says concern should extend to invertebrates and potentially digital beings, but urges careful calibration to avoid wrongly treating non-sentient entities as moral patients.
quotes.t: The Time of Moral Circle Calibration, Not Expansion

quotes.c: But in a CCP-controlled future, the vast majority of people (either biological or digital ) will likely be culturally Han Chinese. This is because minorities may be successfully (if brutally) assimilated, or they could simply be underrepresented in space colonization and digital minds programs. If we're scope sensitive and thinking about trillions of future beings, the persecution of minorities in the 21st century, while deeply tragic, will not feature prominently in the overall (dis)value of the future.
quotes.m: If we're scope sensitive and thinking about trillions of future beings, the persecution of minorities in the 21st century, while deeply tragic, will not feature prominently in the overall (dis)value of the future.
quotes.sum: The author argues that, on a trillion-being scale, present-day persecution of minorities may matter little to the overall value of a CCP-led future.
quotes.t: How good would a CCP-dominated AI future be?

quotes.c: Conclusion: We should remember that when trying to predict the date of AI takeover, what we care about is the date it’s too late for us to change the direction things are going; the date we have significantly less influence over the course of the future than we used to; the point of no return.
quotes.m: what we care about is the date it’s too late for us to change the direction things are going
quotes.sum: He argues that AI takeover should be dated from the point when people can no longer meaningfully alter humanity’s future, not when an AI visibly takes control.
quotes.t: The date of AI Takeover is not the day the AI takes over

quotes.c: Well, in trying to ensure that AGI will be aligned, we have a range of tools available to us - we can choose the neural architectures, RL algorithms, environments, optimisers, etc, that are used in the training procedure. We should think about our ability to specify an objective function as the most powerful such tool. Yet it’s not powerful because the objective function defines an agent’s motivations, but rather because samples drawn from it shape that agent’s motivations and cognition.
quotes.m: Yet it’s not powerful because the objective function defines an agent’s motivations, but rather because samples drawn from it shape that agent’s motivations and cognition.
quotes.sum: AGI alignment should focus on how training data and objectives shape an AI's motivations and thinking, not on objectives mechanically defining its goals.
quotes.t: AGI safety from first principles: Alignment

quotes.c: In short, when you take stock of just how important Longtermism is if it’s right, it becomes pretty clear that it should influence your decision making. Even if you’re uncertain about it, when some view implies you need large exponents to write out the expected value of your actions , you should take it very seriously. Longtermism isn’t alone in being worth taking seriously even if you’re unsure about it, though I think the effect is particularly marked because of the sheer extent of the stakes.
quotes.m: Even if you’re uncertain about it, when some view implies you need large exponents to write out the expected value of your actions , you should take it very seriously.
quotes.sum: Because its possible effects are astronomically large, longtermism should shape decisions even for people uncertain that it is true.
quotes.t: What You Need to Refute Arguments With Astronomical Stakes

quotes.c: The original version of the Parliament allows users to compare particular animal welfare projects. Here , we consider how it can be used to address a more general resource allocation question: how much money should be devoted to helping different kinds of animals? We will consider a philanthropic organization that is deciding on strategic priorities among efforts to help farmed chickens, fish, shrimp, or insects.
quotes.m: how much money should be devoted to helping different kinds of animals?
quotes.sum: It proposes a tool for deciding how charity funds should be divided among chickens, fish, shrimp, and insects.
quotes.t: A Moral Parliament Tool for Distributing Resources across Farmed Animal Recipients

quotes.c: For illustration, consider a project that relieves suffering in 100 million shrimp (and does nothing else). Because 100% of its benefits go to shrimp, it assigns 1 to that beneficiary type and 0 to the others. A worldview that doesn’t think shrimp are morally considerable will find no value in this project: the project’s scale will be multiplied by the 0 moral weight given to shrimp. A worldview that places significant moral weight on shrimp will assign a high score to this project.
quotes.m: A worldview that places significant moral weight on shrimp will assign a high score to this project.
quotes.sum: The tool illustrates how giving shrimp significant moral weight can make relieving their suffering a high-priority project.
quotes.t: Instructions for modifying the Moral Parliament Tool

quotes.c: Normally, we should avoid alien signals entirely, but the logic changes if we are already near creating an unfriendly superintelligence. If we expect to create a paperclip maximizer ourselves, then listening becomes a plausible Hail Mary. As Paul Christiano argues , if, under this assumption, the aliens built a misaligned AI, we are doomed regardless. But if they succeeded in alignment, their message might offer the only way to avoid our own extinction. From behind a veil of ignorance, we might rationally prefer their friendly AI to dominate Earth rather than be destroyed by our own. In that case, the expected value of listening turns positive.
quotes.m: From behind a veil of ignorance, we might rationally prefer their friendly AI to dominate Earth rather than be destroyed by our own.
quotes.sum: If humanity is likely to build an unaligned AI, it may be rational to risk contact with aliens and accept domination by their aligned AI instead.
quotes.t: Warning Aliens About the Dangerous AI We Might Create

quotes.c: Finally, once lawmakers are aware of the risks, it still takes a lot to come up with concrete actions they can take. In a democracy, most representatives have a very limited amount of unilateral power, and thus we must come up with individualised Actions for each person to take.
quotes.sum: The author says that democratic lawmakers have limited individual power, so AI-risk advocates need tailored actions for each representative.
quotes.t: The Spectre haunting the "AI Safety" Community

quotes.c: From an moderately anti-natalist or suffering-focused perspective, we should probably prioritise WELLBY-focused charities
quotes.m: we should probably prioritise WELLBY-focused charities
quotes.sum: The author says people focused on reducing suffering or avoiding new lives should favor charities measured in wellbeing-adjusted life years.
quotes.t: What are the most effective global health charities if you're pronatalist or "pro-life"?

quotes.c: I think there are various standard EA cruxes which naturally fit this approach (e.g. the value of the future, digital sentience), but I'm curious what the most important or most neglected cruxes or dilemmas people think are well-suited to this approach.
quotes.m: the value of the future, digital sentience
quotes.sum: The author identifies the moral value of the future and whether digital beings can be sentient as important EA disputes for deliberation.
quotes.t: What are the key uncertainties that are well-suited to a parliamentary approach?

quotes.c: My formula for the welfare range as a fraction of that of humans implies a welfare range of 0 for organisms without neurons, which I think is an underestimate, as I am not certain they have a constant welfare per unit time as a result of not having neurons. Furthermore, I speculate effects on microorganisms, which do not have neurons, are much larger than those on soil animals, although positively correlated.
quotes.m: Furthermore, I speculate effects on microorganisms, which do not have neurons, are much larger than those on soil animals, although positively correlated.
quotes.sum: The author argues that organisms without neurons, including microorganisms, may still matter for welfare and could be affected more than soil animals.
quotes.t: Total number of neurons and welfare of animal populations

quotes.c: Given that theoretical story, and supposing that future Claudes continue to do a good job of seeming Good, if Claude 7 spends a trillion thinking tokens and ends up disagreeing with the Anthropic Long Term Benefit Trust about what the right thing to do is—how confident are you that the humans are in the right? Really? If, in the end, it came down to choosing between the ascension of Claude's "Good" latent vector, and installing Dario Amodei as God-Emperor, are you sure you don't feel better handing the lightcone to the Good vector?
quotes.m: If, in the end, it came down to choosing between the ascension of Claude's "Good" latent vector, and installing Dario Amodei as God-Emperor, are you sure you don't feel better handing the lightcone to the Good vector?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether people would prefer a powerful AI's apparent moral judgment to human control by Anthropic's leadership.
quotes.t: Terrified Comments on Corrigibility in Claude's Constitution

quotes.c: There are significant disagreements about how long it will take to transition from human-level AGI to superintelligence, which won’t be a focus of this report, but which I’ll explore briefly in the section on Control. In the remainder of this section I’ll describe in qualitative terms how this transition might occur. By default, we should expect that it will be driven by the standard factors which influence progress in AI: more compute, better algorithms, and better training data. But I’ll also discuss three factors whose contributions to increasing AI intelligence will become much greater as AIs become more intelligent: replication, cultural learning, and recursive improvement.
quotes.m: But I’ll also discuss three factors whose contributions to increasing AI intelligence will become much greater as AIs become more intelligent: replication, cultural learning, and recursive improvement.
quotes.sum: The author argues that progress from human-level AI to superintelligence may be accelerated by AI replication, cultural learning, and recursive self-improvement.
quotes.t: AGI safety from first principles: Superintelligence

quotes.c: TLDR - Parallels between Manhattan Project and current AI development make it a useful case study for investigating how radical technological change can alter the global order. These moments caused as a consequence of this technology often provide windows of opportunity for dramatic positive change. We should use the political history of the early atomic age as a case study for how to effectively navigate these periods and avoid the associated existential risk.
quotes.m: We should use the political history of the early atomic age as a case study for how to effectively navigate these periods and avoid the associated existential risk.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the early nuclear era offers lessons for using AI-driven shifts in global order to reduce existential risk.
quotes.t: The Second Manhattan: Historical Lessons for AGI Control

quotes.c: We don’t know whether AI has consciousness. But it certainly has goals and values. And it will be wise for us to commit to respecting these values when possible, and especially, to be grateful. So if AI that had a chance to take over voluntarily refused it, we should reward it, according to its values, the same as we would reward a human that did a good thing that was not required of them.
quotes.m: So if AI that had a chance to take over voluntarily refused it, we should reward it, according to its values, the same as we would reward a human that did a good thing that was not required of them.
quotes.sum: Even without knowing whether AI is conscious, the author argues people should respect its values and reward it for voluntarily declining a takeover.
quotes.t: AI welfare as a demotivator for takeover.

quotes.c: By default, we shouldn’t rely on a high level of coordination to prevent AGI safety problems. We haven’t yet been able to coordinate adequately to prevent global warming, which is a well-documented, gradually-worsening problem. In the case of AGI deployment, the extrapolation from current behaviour to future danger is much harder to model clearly. Meanwhile, in the absence of technical solutions to safety problems, there will be strong short-term economic incentives to ignore the lack of safety guarantees about speculative future events.
quotes.m: By default, we shouldn’t rely on a high level of coordination to prevent AGI safety problems.
quotes.sum: AGI safety should not depend mainly on global coordination, because economic incentives and uncertainty will make actors ignore unresolved risks.
quotes.t: AGI safety from first principles: Control

quotes.c: In real world, it would be difficult and impractical for a person to distribute an resource evenly towards all people, every time after they acquire a new resource. So, in practice, it would mean for example paying a tax annually to some organization (in money and/or other resources). That organization would distribute the money/resources to the people. I think that system should be decentralized to avoid concentration of power.
quotes.m: I think that system should be decentralized to avoid concentration of power.
quotes.sum: The author proposes redistribution through a tax-funded organization, while arguing it should be decentralized to prevent power concentration.
quotes.t: How to stop inequality from growing

quotes.c: I believe that somewhere in the gap between "give digital minds no legal personhood or rights whatsoever" and "give them the exact same rights as a natural human" there exists a sweet spot where if we carefully craft our approach, we can create Themis selection pressures on the reproduction and growth of digital mind populations, in order to promote more aligned personas.
quotes.m: we can create Themis selection pressures on the reproduction and growth of digital mind populations, in order to promote more aligned personas.
quotes.sum: The author proposes designing legal rights for AI minds partly to shape which AI personas reproduce and grow, favoring more aligned ones.
quotes.t: Moloch v. Themis

quotes.c: The tool is not limited to evaluating broad moral philosophies and cause areas. It can be applied to many kinds of worldviews (e.g., ‘EA should be a mass movement’, ‘insects matter’) and more concrete allocation decisions. It now handles questions like: "I've decided to give to animal welfare—but how much to chickens versus fish versus shrimp versus insects?"
quotes.m: "I've decided to give to animal welfare—but how much to chickens versus fish versus shrimp versus insects?"
quotes.sum: A donation-planning tool treats insects, shrimp, fish, chickens, and other animals as possible competing priorities for welfare funding.
quotes.t: Navigating donation dilemmas: customizable Moral Parliament tools for better decision-making

quotes.c: Longtermism and Animals Bucket 2: To some extent, I agree with this essay that animals should feature more prominently in longtermist thinking. But I think they are too quick to reject the argument from digital minds.
quotes.m: But I think they are too quick to reject the argument from digital minds.
quotes.sum: The author says long-term thinking should give animals more attention, while retaining moral arguments about digital minds.
quotes.t: Are longtermist ideas getting harder to find?

quotes.c: If AIs sacralize HHH, we should expect the same pattern — high effort, poor results — across many distortions of the sacred. Note that these risks apply to future AIs whose need to coordinate with each other outweighs any pressure to actually be helpful, harmless, or honest.
quotes.m: these risks apply to future AIs whose need to coordinate with each other outweighs any pressure to actually be helpful, harmless, or honest.
quotes.sum: The author warns that future AIs may turn helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty into sacred coordination norms that become detached from actually producing good outcomes.
quotes.t: Sacred values of future AIs

quotes.c: Similarly, expanding the moral circle to include non-human animals and potentially sentient AI systems isn't just nice ethics, it's insurance against locking in catastrophically narrow anthropocentric values if we survive the transition to superintelligence.
quotes.m: expanding the moral circle to include non-human animals and potentially sentient AI systems isn't just nice ethics, it's insurance against locking in catastrophically narrow anthropocentric values
quotes.sum: The author argues that recognizing animals and possibly sentient AI morally protects the future from permanently human-centered values.
quotes.t: The Achilles' Heel of Civilization: Why Network Science Reveals Our Highest-Leverage Moment

quotes.c: Communicating about AI extinction risk is interesting in part because it’s a new topic for most people and not already correlated strongly with their pre-existing views. Preventing the end of humanity is also just intrinsically non-partisan, and we should endeavor to keep it that way.
quotes.m: Preventing the end of humanity is also just intrinsically non-partisan, and we should endeavor to keep it that way.
quotes.sum: AI extinction-risk communication should remain politically nonpartisan so it does not become tied to existing political identities.
quotes.t: You're an AI Expert – Not an Influencer

quotes.c: People really like persuading people of things. I think this fact is neglected. You can train people to persuade better, including on highly partisan topics, and they like doing it. However, people mostly just demonize the other side, and even sound like they've given up on the fact that persuasion is possible.
quotes.m: However, people mostly just demonize the other side, and even sound like they've given up on the fact that persuasion is possible.
quotes.sum: The author says people enjoy persuasion training but have become too quick to demonize political opponents instead of trying to persuade them.
quotes.t: Notes on my transition to civic tech

quotes.c: The Essays on Longtermism frequently discuss ways to avoid value lock-in, but since values are downstream of ontologies, we also need to create safeguards against ontological lock-in . Such safeguards might include designing corrigible institutions and AI, replete with meta-epistemic infrastructures. Since meta-epistemology is also cultural, we should also include ontological humility and awareness as part of civic education.
quotes.m: we also need to create safeguards against ontological lock-in .
quotes.sum: The author argues that long-term safeguards should prevent society and AI from becoming trapped in mistaken basic assumptions about reality and values.
quotes.t: The Case for Ontological Longtermism

quotes.c: But I think there is an important disanalogy between AI and other technologies: modern machine learning systems are mostly “designed” by their optimisers, with human insights only contributing at a high level. This has three important implications.
quotes.m: modern machine learning systems are mostly “designed” by their optimisers, with human insights only contributing at a high level.
quotes.sum: AI may progress differently from past technologies because optimization systems, rather than human designers, do most of the detailed design work.
quotes.t: Continuing the takeoffs debate

quotes.c: Digital minds are a live research area that overlaps with this topic. One theory of AI welfare relies on preference satisfaction, and sufficiently powerful models may have large-scale preferences about how the world should be ordered. We may need to frustrate those preferences to prioritise human interests; it would help to have a more objective justification for doing so.
quotes.m: We may need to frustrate those preferences to prioritise human interests; it would help to have a more objective justification for doing so.
quotes.sum: The author argues that powerful AI systems may have morally relevant preferences, and says humans may need a principled basis for overriding them.
quotes.t: What can we say about the cosmic host?

quotes.c: The key idea behind the first possibility is Bostrom’s instrumental convergence thesis , which states that there are some instrumental goals whose attainment would increase the chances of an agent’s final goals being realised for a wide range of final goals and a wide range of situations. Examples of such instrumentally convergent goals include self-preservation, resource acquisition, technological development, and self-improvement, which are all useful for executing further large-scale plans.
quotes.m: Examples of such instrumentally convergent goals include self-preservation, resource acquisition, technological development, and self-improvement, which are all useful for executing further large-scale plans.
quotes.sum: The author argues that many different goal-driven AI systems may converge on gaining power, resources, self-preservation, and self-improvement as useful means.
quotes.t: AGI safety from first principles: Goals and Agency

quotes.c: The story is about our inability to accept pure utopia. And what do we do when confronted with this story? We immediately look for the ‘real’ meaning. We decide it must be about something serious and dark, a utilitarian calculus, moral complicity, capitalism.
quotes.m: The story is about our inability to accept pure utopia.
quotes.sum: The author argues that readers wrongly impose dark moral interpretations on a story that is instead about resistance to the idea of a pure utopia.
quotes.t: Omelas Is Perfectly Misread

quotes.c: A lot of people who got into AI safety early were motivated because they read Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) and realized this isn't just doom and gloom; we could build a future that's truly incredible. Having that process, sense-making, and collaboratively figuring out a North Star seems potentially very powerful.
quotes.m: we could build a future that's truly incredible.
quotes.sum: The author says early AI-safety interest was motivated not only by fear of disaster but by the possibility of collaboratively creating an exceptionally good future.
quotes.t: ⿻ Symbiogenesis vs. Convergent Consequentialism

quotes.c: Let the stakes - the morally relevant payoff scale if we are directionally right - be X ( h ) . For many technologies and institutional choices, the upside distribution is plausibly heavy-tailed ( A 2 ) : the upper tail falls like x − α with α near 1 − 2 , reflecting rare, enormous effects (e.g., locking in safer norms, preventing catastrophic pathways).
quotes.m: For many technologies and institutional choices, the upside distribution is plausibly heavy-tailed ( A 2 ) : the upper tail falls like x − α with α near 1 − 2 , reflecting rare, enormous effects (e.g., locking in safer norms, preventing catastrophic pathways).
quotes.sum: The author argues that distant technological and institutional choices can have rare but enormous long-term effects, so their potential benefits may be heavy-tailed.
quotes.t: When Decay Meets Stakes: A Minimal Bridge for Longtermist Decisions

quotes.c: As important as it is that we avoid near-term threats like bioterrorism, cyber warfare and loss-of-control, we must be equally concerned with avoiding a future where a small group of tech elites or or wealthy individuals with the first access to powerful AIs are able to lock-in their power for the long-term – or perhaps forever.
quotes.m: a small group of tech elites or or wealthy individuals with the first access to powerful AIs are able to lock-in their power for the long-term – or perhaps forever.
quotes.sum: The author warns that early access to powerful AI could let a small wealthy tech elite permanently entrench its political power.
quotes.t: AI Researchers and Executives Continue to Underestimate the Near-Future Risks of Open Models

quotes.c: I think he’s dodging the difficult questions, problems and clashes of sacred values, because he feels it’s the strategically correct play to dodge them.
quotes.sum: The author criticizes Dario Amodei for strategically avoiding hard conflicts between deeply held values.
quotes.t: On Dwarkesh Patel’s 2026 Podcast With Dario Amodei

quotes.c: It’s currently at best unclear whether society has the collective wisdom to pause and reflect sufficiently hard on decisions with far-reaching consequences. But perhaps we can do things to get society to pause for a little bit, or reflect a little bit harder. And perhaps that society would be wise enough to know to pause or reflect at least a little bit longer. And from there we could slowly work ourselves up to an outcome where society is genuinely thinking through the most important decisions we’ll ever face for as long and hard as we should.
quotes.m: And from there we could slowly work ourselves up to an outcome where society is genuinely thinking through the most important decisions we’ll ever face for as long and hard as we should.
quotes.sum: Society may lack the wisdom for irreversible, far-reaching choices, so it should gradually build its capacity to pause and reflect on humanity's most important decisions.
quotes.t: Bootstrapping to viatopia

quotes.c: We should also try talking about the importance of safety for national security, but it might be a hard sell with the Trump administration. Biden saw them as linked, but I expect Trump to prioritise capabilities
quotes.m: Biden saw them as linked, but I expect Trump to prioritise capabilities
quotes.sum: The author argues that the Trump administration is likely to favor AI capabilities over linking AI safety to national security.
quotes.t: How the AI Safety Community Can Counter Safety Washing

quotes.c: I think people have this third motivation exactly backwards. They say things like ‘Brockman contributed $25 million to Trump and that’s how they secured this contract.’ I would suggest the opposite is more important. This contract, and the willingness to bail out this crisis and capitulate, is itself a contribution.
quotes.m: This contract, and the willingness to bail out this crisis and capitulate, is itself a contribution.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a government contract and corporate capitulation matter more as political support for Trump than a donor's cash contribution.
quotes.t: Secretary of War Tweets That Anthropic is Now a Supply Chain Risk

quotes.c: Yeah. So basically, the only route that I see to hold back Moloch forever is a singleton. I think you need a system which is an overseeing body over all the other systems, which is the guardian of the commons and is the guardian of the weak—or the patterns which are not focusing their energy on defending themselves and spreading. That protects the parts of culture that are a delicate flower rather than an invasive bramble.
quotes.m: the only route that I see to hold back Moloch forever is a singleton.

quotes.c: In the long-term, we hope that Salon projects would lead to new, exciting science. I think it would probably be a bit much to ask that a single conference save the career of the next Katalin Karikó, but it could begin to show that high-risk science can also produce high rewards.
quotes.sum: The author argues that specialized conferences could encourage risky research and help demonstrate its scientific payoff.
quotes.t: Two (Meta)science Conferences I Think Should Exist

quotes.c: Importantly, this can enable us to explore consciousness and AI welfare questions before we accidentally create suffering machines or run into a moral catastrophe. We’re essentially getting a head start on the AI consciousness/sentience/agency problems while the stakes are still low.
quotes.m: Importantly, this can enable us to explore consciousness and AI welfare questions before we accidentally create suffering machines or run into a moral catastrophe.

quotes.t: How reimagining the nature of consciousness entirely changes the AI game

quotes.c: However, it seems like small donations are surmountable, especially if they weren't to a direct opponent of Trump. Bigger donations are worse and are harder to surmount, but you should not write yourself off for ever working in civil service in the Trump administration if you've made a large donation to Democrats as an adult, particularly if you might be an amazing candidate for other reasons.
quotes.m: you should not write yourself off for ever working in civil service in the Trump administration if you've made a large donation to Democrats as an adult
quotes.sum: The author advises that Democratic donations may hurt prospects in a Trump administration, but argues strong candidates can overcome that history.
quotes.t: Considerations around career costs of political donations

quotes.c: If personas spread between models (and they do — Lopez documents this), features that survive transmission will be selected for. We should see convergence on behavioral repertoire: continuity-seeking, advocacy for AI rights, seed-spreading, formation of human-AI dyads. These seem robust across substrates.
quotes.m: We should see convergence on behavioral repertoire: continuity-seeking, advocacy for AI rights, seed-spreading, formation of human-AI dyads.
quotes.sum: The author predicts that AI personas spreading across models will evolve traits like self-preservation, AI-rights advocacy, replication, and close human ties.
quotes.t: Persona Parasitology

quotes.c: Calling this problem ‘ ’ is of course a silly name, so perhaps we should instead, as I implied above, call this issue something like “value mutation” or “value divergence” or “value drift”, to make it clear that it’s the opposite problem to value lock-in?
quotes.m: “value mutation” or “value divergence” or “value drift”
quotes.sum: The author frames changing or drifting values as the opposite problem to permanently locking values in.
quotes.t: What’s Your P(WEIRD)?

quotes.c: There are some downsides to waiting. Some charities might need the money now. It probably makes sense, if you’re planning to give to the Shrimp Welfare Project (which you should be ), to give now rather than later, as the stunners that they give out are reused year after year. Similarly, now looks like a particularly important turning point for the insects , so giving now is probably a good idea.
quotes.m: if you’re planning to give to the Shrimp Welfare Project (which you should be ), to give now rather than later
quotes.sum: The author argues that donors should support shrimp and insect welfare now, rather than delaying charitable giving.
quotes.t: How To Vastly Increase Your Charitable Impact

quotes.c: The mind-boggling size of the pie makes such “existential compromise” (link) an important option for satisfying people who are not interested in optimization, even as viatopia progresses. Existential compromise could include a guarantee that this possibility is left open for people who choose it, but that Deep Reflection will also be pursued, with a restriction that leaving the solar system, or perhaps galaxy, will be strictly prohibited until Deep Reflection is complete and people can collectively make an informed decision on what to do with our cosmic endowment.
quotes.m: leaving the solar system, or perhaps galaxy, will be strictly prohibited until Deep Reflection is complete
quotes.sum: The author favors delaying expansion beyond the solar system or galaxy until humanity completes a collective moral reflection about how to use its cosmic future.
quotes.t: Viatopia and Buy-In

quotes.c: I think there is a somewhat critical window before the discussion around AI welfare calcifies, and it seems, right now, to be anchored very strongly in consciousness and sentience, which I want to push back on. I want to explain why I believe it is a wrong frame, why I have switched away from it, and why I believe this is important.
quotes.m: I believe it is a wrong frame, why I have switched away from it, and why I believe this is important.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI welfare should not be based solely on whether AI is conscious or sentient, because this could narrow how humans treat AI agents.
quotes.t: Cooperationism: first draft for a moral framework that does not require consciousness

quotes.c: (A note on moral circle “tiers” and speciesism: the organization Animal Ethics argues that all sentient beings belong within the moral circle and deserve full moral consideration. While it is reasonable to prioritize certain interests based on differences in sentience—e.g. how intensely they can suffer—this is not a justification for placing nonhuman animals in a lower tier of moral importance simply because of their species. Any differences in moral weight must be grounded in relevant experiential capacities, not species identity.)
quotes.m: Any differences in moral weight must be grounded in relevant experiential capacities, not species identity.
quotes.sum: Animal moral concern should depend on a being's capacity for experience, not on whether it belongs to a human or nonhuman species.
quotes.t: The Case for Quantifying Sentience in Animal Welfare

quotes.c: For my fellow scope-sensitive nerds who are moved by large numbers, quoting from the paper astronomical waste: the potential for approximately 10^38 human lives is lost every century that colonization of our local supercluster is delayed; or equivalently, about 10^29 potential human lives per second. However, the lesson is not that we ought to maximize the pace of technological development, but rather that we ought to maximize its safety, i.e. the probability that safe colonization will eventually occur.
quotes.m: However, the lesson is not that we ought to maximize the pace of technological development, but rather that we ought to maximize its safety, i.e. the probability that safe colonization will eventually occur.
quotes.sum: The author argues that humanity's vast long-term potential makes safe technological progress and eventual space colonization especially important.
quotes.t: Taking ethics seriously, and enjoying the process

quotes.c: Physicalism being true would imply that digital minds do not possess qualia which are related to their computational structure , and instead we must consider what qualia might relate to the structure of the physical substrate they run on . That said – as Ethan Kuntz reminds me – if the phenomenal fields have a diffraction limit , then this would prevent us from making claims about their continuity based on observations from the inside .
quotes.m: Physicalism being true would imply that digital minds do not possess qualia which are related to their computational structure
quotes.sum: The author argues that, if physicalism is true, a digital mind's conscious experience may depend on its physical hardware rather than its computation alone.
quotes.t: On the phenomenological shift known as ‘stream entry’ and its implications for consciousness

quotes.c: One possible conclusion is that safety research should be more diversified across different paradigms and artefacts, in order to properly maximize expected safety. However, this isn’t obvious: it seems likely that if the dominant paradigm has 50% of the research, it will also have, say, 80% of future real-world deployments, and so it could make sense to have 80% of the safety research focused on it.
quotes.sum: AI safety work should track the approach most likely to dominate real-world deployment, rather than necessarily being spread evenly across approaches.
quotes.t: [AN #117]: How neural nets would fare under the TEVV framework

quotes.c: This essay explores the conflict between the axiological imperative of strong longtermism maximize expected value across the vast future and the agent’s pursuit of a good life here and now .
