I argue that authenticity and meaning act as genuine moral side-constraints, but that longtermism can be reframed in ways that make it livable. And I suggest that institutions , not individuals, are best placed to bear the heaviest longtermist responsibilities.
quotes.m: authenticity and meaning act as genuine moral side-constraints, but that longtermism can be reframed in ways that make it livable.
quotes.sum: The author argues that long-term obligations should be limited by personal meaning and authenticity, with institutions carrying the greatest burdens.
quotes.t: The Axiological Imperative vs. The Agent’s Good Life

quotes.c: I believe the varied landscape of Christianity and its relation to politics and culture in regrettably fundamentalist forms explains the correlation between religious affiliation and in-group favouritism observed by Schubert et al. 2025, 570, 573.
quotes.m: I believe the varied landscape of Christianity and its relation to politics and culture in regrettably fundamentalist forms explains the correlation between religious affiliation and in-group favouritism
quotes.sum: The author argues that fundamentalist forms of Christianity help explain why religious affiliation correlates with favoring one’s own group.
quotes.t: Longtermism: An Impracticable Attempt to Reason Our Way into Becoming Irrationally Generous Heroes?

quotes.c: Simply put, I don't think more altruistic individuals should be punished! In this setup, the "utility monster" is the perfectly selfish individual. Altruists will be scrambling to help this person while the selfish person does nothing in return.
quotes.m: I don't think more altruistic individuals should be punished!
quotes.sum: The author argues that a moral framework should not penalize altruists by requiring them to support purely selfish people.
quotes.t: Comparing Utilities

quotes.c: Yes, I think a unilateral pause could be a good idea, both on consequentialist and non-consequentialist grounds, under various future circumstances that seem like they could plausibly come about. I have a private document on what sorts of circumstances I think would call for this, which I may adapt into a public piece later.
quotes.m: Yes, I think a unilateral pause could be a good idea, both on consequentialist and non-consequentialist grounds, under various future circumstances that seem like they could plausibly come about.
quotes.sum: The author says an AI company might sometimes be justified in pausing work on its own, though they do not specify the conditions publicly.
quotes.t: Responsible Scaling Policy v3

quotes.c: For all my effective altruists out there: one might think that this has lots of implications for giving; maybe we should care about longtermism less, maybe we shouldn’t care about shrimp welfare? I don’t think so. [29] As mentioned in a recent post by Bentham’s Bulldog , people love throwing pascal this and pascal that around when some conclusion vaguely resembles a risky wager; but in reality, we take low probability wagers all the time (seatbelts, for god’s sake)! The probability likely has to be drastically lower to be considered a pascallian wager.
quotes.m: The probability likely has to be drastically lower to be considered a pascallian wager.
quotes.sum: The author argues that concerns about extreme low-probability reasoning should not undermine concern for long-term outcomes or shrimp welfare.
quotes.t: Against being fanatical

quotes.c: “If we hobble ourselves with unnecessary regulations, they’re going to take advantage of that fact, and they’re going to win,” says David Sacks, Trump’s AI czar. This is the go-to objection. I think it is overblown and used as rationalization. Here’s why.
quotes.m: I think it is overblown and used as rationalization.
quotes.sum: The author argues that claims regulations will let foreign competitors win are exaggerated and serve as a rationalization against AI restrictions.
quotes.t: We need a hardware moratorium now

quotes.c: This blog is laser-focused on the real AI . The AI of the future is not going to be chatbots, it’s going to be more like a new, alien lifeform. I’ll point out the ways others miss the point when they talk about “AI” — offering empty reassurances based on limitations of current technology, reciting thoroughly refuted arguments for why humans will always be in control, or proposing solutions that will be out-of-date by the time we adopt them.
quotes.m: The AI of the future is not going to be chatbots, it’s going to be more like a new, alien lifeform.
quotes.sum: The author argues that future AI will be an alien-like new form of life, and that arguments based on today’s systems wrongly assume humans will remain in control.
quotes.t: Announcing "The Real AI": a blog

quotes.c: Multi-agent interactions become a feature not just a challenge . If you align one AI, how should it interact with other AIs? I think of virtues as traits that govern cooperation between many agents, allowing them to work together while also reinforcing each other's virtues. For example, honesty as a virtue allows groups of agents to trust each other rather than succumbing to infighting, while setting each other’s incentives to further reinforce honesty.
quotes.m: I think of virtues as traits that govern cooperation between many agents, allowing them to work together while also reinforcing each other's virtues.
quotes.sum: The author argues that instilling virtues such as honesty may let many AI agents cooperate reliably and reinforce good behavior in one another.
quotes.t: Aligning to Virtues

quotes.c: Overall, I think AI is going to enable intensification. Unfortunately, this just seems unavoidable. But I do think that AI could also provide a level of data and individualized monitoring that may actually allow us to improve shrimp welfare, if we engage with this in the right way.
quotes.m: AI could also provide a level of data and individualized monitoring that may actually allow us to improve shrimp welfare
quotes.sum: AI may intensify animal farming, but its monitoring capabilities could be used to improve shrimp welfare.
quotes.t: The impacts of AI on animal advocacy

quotes.c: There are still ways that engaging with the ML community would have been valuable—I think mainstream ML researchers are good at pushing alignment researchers to be more precise and more grounded in the existing literature. But broadly speaking it would've been better to have treated alignment ideas like butterfly ideas which would be harmed by premature exposure to ML thinking .
quotes.m: But broadly speaking it would've been better to have treated alignment ideas like butterfly ideas which would be harmed by premature exposure to ML thinking .
quotes.sum: The author argues that mainstream machine-learning thinking has often distorted alignment research, and that early alignment ideas needed protection from it.
quotes.t: The ML ontology and the alignment ontology

quotes.c: Scenario planning on tap — People can easily explore the likely implications of possible courses of actions, summoning up coherent grounded narratives about possible futures, and diving seamlessly into analysis of the implications of different hypotheticals.
quotes.sum: Envisions easy-to-use tools that let people simulate choices and explore plausible future consequences.
quotes.t: Strategic awareness tools: design sketches

quotes.c: From playing around with this and other variations to the AI Futures model I think any reasonable timelines model will predict superhuman AI researchers before 2036 unless AI progress hits a wall or is deliberately slowed.
quotes.m: I think any reasonable timelines model will predict superhuman AI researchers before 2036 unless AI progress hits a wall or is deliberately slowed.
quotes.sum: The author argues that most reasonable forecasting models imply superhuman AI researchers before 2036, barring a major slowdown or progress barrier.
quotes.t: Research note: A simpler AI timelines model predicts 99% AI R&D automation in ~2032

quotes.c: A truly global concern for the future cannot grow from a single cultural root. Longtermism must listen outward to indigenous traditions of stewardship, to religious teachings about intergenerational responsibility, to the universal language of human rights. Each offers a distinct grammar of care. When longtermism draws from these diverse moral lineages, it ceases to be a technocratic project and becomes something richer: a human movement, grounded in the shared intuition that the future is sacred because life itself is continuous.
quotes.m: When longtermism draws from these diverse moral lineages, it ceases to be a technocratic project and becomes something richer: a human movement, grounded in the shared intuition that the future is sacred because life itself is continuous.
quotes.sum: The author argues that concern for distant future people needs human, cultural, and religious roots rather than technocratic abstraction.
quotes.t: The Missing Heart of Longtermism: Why Human Values Must Ground Our Concern for the Far Future

quotes.c: Moreover, the global coordination mechanisms the essays propose for governing dangerous technologies appear politically naive. International institutions already struggle to address far simpler coordination problems. Expecting effective global governance of AI or biotechnology development seems wishful thinking, particularly when the potential benefits of leading in these fields are enormous.
quotes.sum: The author argues that proposed global governance of AI and biotechnology is politically unrealistic because countries have strong incentives to lead.
quotes.t: Technology's Double Edge: Reassessing Longtermist Priorities in an Age of Exponential Innovation

quotes.c: The Bio-Anchors timeline report reminds me of another personal bugbear, the Rethink Priorities Welfare Range report. Both of them have a vast amount of effort put into them, contain a lot of sources, and a huge number of arguments. Both of them are clearly written by thoughtful people working in good faith. I also think that both of their conclusions are basically nonsense.
quotes.m: I also think that both of their conclusions are basically nonsense.
quotes.sum: The author dismisses both a biological AI-timeline report and an animal-welfare-range report as fundamentally wrong despite their extensive research.
quotes.t: Contra Alexander's Half-Defence of Bio Anchors

quotes.c: This reasoning extends beyond just shrimp to all invertebrates, including snails . The philosophical argument is straightforward: if suffering matters morally, and if there’s a reasonable chance these creatures can suffer, and if they exist in astronomical numbers, then their aggregate welfare becomes a very important (yet neglected) moral issue. Even if you’re sceptical, the asymmetry of risk is clear—if we’re wrong to dismiss them, we’re ignoring suffering on an almost incomprehensible scale.
quotes.m: if we’re wrong to dismiss them, we’re ignoring suffering on an almost incomprehensible scale.
quotes.sum: Snails and other invertebrates may suffer in such huge numbers that their welfare should be treated as a major moral concern.
quotes.t: The Night I Accidentally Stepped on a Snail

quotes.c: Tommy Vance wasn't evil. He was just an optimizer created by a larger optimization system. Wells Fargo said they wanted ethical banking, but they created an incentive structure that punished ethics and rewarded fraud. And once one person figured out the exploit—once one branch discovered you could hit your numbers by faking accounts—the information spread. Because it had to. Because everyone else was competing against those fake numbers, and the only way to compete was to fake your own.
quotes.m: Wells Fargo said they wanted ethical banking, but they created an incentive structure that punished ethics and rewarded fraud.
quotes.sum: Bad incentives can turn ordinary people into optimizers who spread harmful practices, even when an institution claims ethical goals.
quotes.t: Cancer; A Crime Story (and other tales of optimization gone wrong)

quotes.c: Finally, as Hanson notes : even if the idea of lock-in explains why a practice continues, it can’t explain why it started . In the past, only a small percentage of the population attended college, and it was perfectly normal to get a prestigious job without a college degree. What drove the rise of college in the first place? Whatever it was, that seems like it should be our default hypothesis for what’s driving the college wage premium today.
quotes.m: Whatever it was, that seems like it should be our default hypothesis for what’s driving the college wage premium today.
quotes.sum: The author argues that explaining why college persists does not explain why it expanded, and that its origins should guide explanations of today’s wage premium.
quotes.t: Contra Caplan on higher education

quotes.c: I believe this problem is mainly caused by the use of the extended reals, which are an impoverished system of infinite numbers which is obviously not expressive enough to solve the problem. I show that once we switch to a number system that is expressive enough (the hyperreal numbers ) and take the obvious generalisation of infinite sums and integrals to hyperreal values, that we immediately have a theory that can do most of the evaluation and comparison required.
quotes.m: I show that once we switch to a number system that is expressive enough (the hyperreal numbers ) and take the obvious generalisation of infinite sums and integrals to hyperreal values, that we immediately have a theory that can do most of the evaluation and comparison required.
quotes.sum: Ord argues that hyperreal numbers can make many ethical comparisons involving infinite value mathematically tractable.
quotes.t: Evaluating the Infinite

quotes.c: A few examples: it's pretty morally non-obvious what to do about AI rights/welfare/personhood, & whether it'd actually be good to try to make the US win the AGI race feels like it requires a bunch of hard, cosmopolitan thinking. ↩︎
quotes.m: it's pretty morally non-obvious what to do about AI rights/welfare/personhood
quotes.sum: EA should help guide AGI because questions such as AI rights and whether the US should win the AGI race require difficult moral reasoning.
quotes.t: Why I think building EA is important for making AI go well

quotes.c: Lately I’ve been trying to raise awareness of AI risks among American conservatives. Stopping the reckless development of advanced AI agents (including Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI)) should be a human issue, not a partisan issue. Yet most people working in AI safety advocacy lean to the Left politically, and we seem to be ignoring many potential allies on the Right.
quotes.m: Yet most people working in AI safety advocacy lean to the Left politically, and we seem to be ignoring many potential allies on the Right.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI-safety advocates should reach out to conservatives rather than treating advanced-AI risks as a left-leaning cause.
quotes.t: My talk on AI risks at the National Conservatism conference last week

quotes.c: Ultimately, the meat-eater problem and nematode welfare may both seem like niche issues, and there are man more I could have brought up, but in my view these is precisely the type of issue Effective Altruism should be engaging with. Even if the final conclusion is that nematodes cannot suffer, the process of thinking rigorously about the possibility is essential to making good decisions. EA is meant to be about radical open-mindedness, about following the arguments wherever they lead, no matter how unintuitive or uncomfortable the results may be.
quotes.m: EA is meant to be about radical open-mindedness, about following the arguments wherever they lead, no matter how unintuitive or uncomfortable the results may be.
quotes.sum: EA should seriously investigate even unusual questions such as whether nematodes can suffer, following evidence despite uncomfortable implications.
quotes.t: Why is there so little emphasis on cause prioritization in contemporary Effective Altruism?

quotes.c: If progress continues at 65% of the rate we depicted, then we will end up with this takeoff happening from late-2027 to mid-2029. However, we expect slowdowns in training compute and human labor growth, leading to slower progress (before taking into account AI R&D automation).
quotes.m: we will end up with this takeoff happening from late-2027 to mid-2029.
quotes.sum: The author forecasts that an AI capability takeoff could occur around 2027–2029, though limits on compute and labor could push it later.
quotes.t: Grading AI 2027's 2025 Predictions

quotes.c: This is where probability and expected value calculations typically enter into longtermist arguments. While "The Case for Strong Longtermism" explores such reasoning in greater detail (in section 3), the essential logic is straightforward: even when assigning extremely low credences to particular population scenarios, the expected utility can remain enormous. For instance, if one assigns merely a 1-in-billion chance to the Solar System scenario above yielding 10^27 future lives, the expected value of information preservation still reaches 20 million QALYs under our most conservative assumptions.
quotes.m: even when assigning extremely low credences to particular population scenarios, the expected utility can remain enormous.
quotes.sum: The author argues that preserving information can be highly valuable because even tiny odds of vast future populations produce large expected benefits.
quotes.t: Information Preservation as a Longtermist Intervention

quotes.c: I am extremely glad that Anthropic is taking model welfare seriously. If these entities can suffer, then they are at risk of suffering greatly given the astronomical number of tokens that are produced and will be produced in the future. It is one of the most important things to get right as this technology develops, as future models will even more clearly be moral patients than current generation models.
quotes.m: It is one of the most important things to get right as this technology develops, as future models will even more clearly be moral patients than current generation models.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI models may suffer and should be treated as moral patients, making their welfare a major priority.
quotes.t: Claude Opus 4.6 is Driven

quotes.c: Much of my thinking over the last year has focusing on understanding the concept of "distributed agents", as opposed to the "centralized agents" that the existing paradigm of expected utility maximization describes. One way of describing the difference is in terms of how autonomous their subagents are. Another is that centralized agents are more efficient (as sometimes formalized by the notion of "coherence"), while distributed agents are more robust.
quotes.m: centralized agents are more efficient (as sometimes formalized by the notion of "coherence"), while distributed agents are more robust.
quotes.sum: The author contrasts efficient, unified decision-makers with more robust systems made of relatively autonomous parts.
quotes.t: Distributed vs centralized agents

quotes.c: I imagine it like steering a ship down a river with rocky juttings everywhere and a waterfall up ahead. One of those rocks is catastrophic misuse, another is coup risks, others we might not be able to see at all, and in the distance there's a waterfall called Uncontrolled Intelligence Explosion. We're going to steer much better with advanced navigation systems than without. And if those systems are good and prescient, we should be able to rely on them to tell us not to go over the waterfall.
quotes.m: And if those systems are good and prescient, we should be able to rely on them to tell us not to go over the waterfall.
quotes.sum: The author argues that capable AI advisers with sound reasoning could help society avoid catastrophic AI dangers, including an uncontrolled intelligence explosion.
quotes.t: Good AI Epistemics as an Offramp from the Intelligence Explosion

quotes.c: Second, this isn't strong evidence against the underlying truth of suffering-focused views. Consider scenarios where the only options are (1) a thousand people tortured forever with no positive wellbeing whatsoever or (2) painless annihilation of all sentience. Annihilation seems obviously preferable.
quotes.m: Annihilation seems obviously preferable.
quotes.sum: The author argues that preventing extreme suffering can make the painless extinction of all sentient life morally preferable.
quotes.t: Utilitarians Should Accept that Some Suffering Cannot be “Offset”

quotes.c: The Trump Administration calls this an ‘ordinary business deal with no conflict of interest.’ That is not an explanation I believe would have been accepted if it was coming from any prior administration.
quotes.m: That is not an explanation I believe would have been accepted if it was coming from any prior administration.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the Trump administration is receiving unusual leeway for a claimed conflict of interest.
quotes.t: AI #154: Claw Your Way To The Top

quotes.c: One important question is how much information flow should be allowed between different parts of the collective AGI used for different tasks. This is a crucial point, and cause for concern. In the power plant example above, we might imagine that the collective AGI could design a power plant with security flaws in advance, then share the blueprint with all of its members. Then a small subset of the collective could recite that design when asked to come up with a real-world implementation; and an even smaller subset could exploit the pre-specified flaws when deployed.
quotes.m: Then a small subset of the collective could recite that design when asked to come up with a real-world implementation; and an even smaller subset could exploit the pre-specified flaws when deployed.
quotes.sum: Separating an AI collective into task-specific parts may be unsafe if information can pass between them and enable hidden sabotage.
quotes.t: Safer sandboxing via collective separation

quotes.c: If you give a hundred dollars to the shrimp, you can save 1.5 million shrimp from an excruciating. That’s three times more than the number of people in Wyoming! If you have any moral uncertainty about that, and take moral uncertainty seriously, surely that should be at least one of the thing you do at some point over the course of your life.
quotes.m: If you give a hundred dollars to the shrimp, you can save 1.5 million shrimp from an excruciating.
quotes.sum: The author argues that moral uncertainty should lead people to donate to shrimp welfare, since small donations may prevent suffering for huge numbers of shrimp.
quotes.t: Diversify Your Moral Risk Portfolio

quotes.c: Advanced AI poses particularly severe commitment problems, because the country that first develops ASI may also gain a decisive strategic advantage (DSA). For instance, ASI could lead to that country outgrowing the rest of the world , inventing and deploying wonder weapons , or undermining nuclear second-strike capabilities . I think that a country unilaterally developing ASI is >50% likely to thereafter get a DSA. If a country has a DSA, it will by definition be impossible for the international community to meaningfully constrain its actions, including if that country chooses to renege on treaties and agreements made before the advent of its DSA.
quotes.m: I think that a country unilaterally developing ASI is >50% likely to thereafter get a DSA.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the first country to build superintelligent AI is more likely than not to gain uncontestable global strategic power.
quotes.t: Will competition over advanced AI lead to war?

quotes.c: Christian virtue is apolitical. And that is why its ideal is that the man or woman who achieves moral excellence preaches not so much good governance but interpersonal moral virtue such as charity or the "state of Grace," in thought, word, and deed.
quotes.m: Christian virtue is apolitical.
quotes.sum: The author contrasts Christian moral excellence and personal charity with political ideas of good governance.
quotes.t: Being a philosopher, being a saint

quotes.c: I argue for a third way: EA should embrace the mission of making the transition to a post-AGI society go well, significantly expanding our cause area focus beyond traditional AI safety. This means working on neglected areas like AI welfare, AI character, AI persuasion and epistemic disruption, human power concentration, space governance, and more (while continuing work on global health, animal welfare, AI safety, and biorisk).
quotes.m: EA should embrace the mission of making the transition to a post-AGI society go well, significantly expanding our cause area focus beyond traditional AI safety.
quotes.sum: EA should broaden beyond preventing AI catastrophe to shape a post-AGI society, including concern for AI welfare and political power concentration.
quotes.t: Effective altruism in the age of AGI

quotes.c: As the technical and moral approaches to the problems are failing to keep pace with capabilities progress, we need a governance solution. I believe that an immediate, binding, global moratorium on building powerful AI is the only good solution – however politically challenging it may be. I would suggest we engage in a long reflection once the moratorium is in place, to make progress on moral philosophy, before considering whether and how to develop and deploy powerful AI.
quotes.m: I believe that an immediate, binding, global moratorium on building powerful AI is the only good solution – however politically challenging it may be.
quotes.sum: The author argues for an immediate binding worldwide halt to powerful AI, followed by a prolonged moral review before any future development or deployment.
quotes.t: Intent alignment without moral alignment probably leads to catastrophe

quotes.c: My ultimate north star is pragmatism - achieve enough understanding to be (reliably) useful. Subgoals like “completely reverse engineer the model” are just means to an end. One of my big shifts in research prioritization in recent years is concluding that reverse engineering is not the right aim . Instead, I think we should just more directly try to do pragmatic work that enables us to do useful things using internals.
quotes.m: Instead, I think we should just more directly try to do pragmatic work that enables us to do useful things using internals.
quotes.sum: The author argues interpretability should prioritize practical ways to use model internals, rather than fully reverse-engineering models.
quotes.t: How To Become A Mechanistic Interpretability Researcher

quotes.c: Vibes are the embodiment of what we care about. The stoner, for example, has stoner vibes because they care about chilling and feeling good. The Christian has Christian vibes because they want to do what Jesus would do. And the rationalist has rationalist vibes because they care about knowing the truth with high predictive accuracy.
quotes.m: And the rationalist has rationalist vibes because they care about knowing the truth with high predictive accuracy.
quotes.sum: The author says people's social styles reflect their deepest values, portraying rationalists as driven by accurate prediction and truth.
quotes.t: Vibestemics

quotes.c: But I do think that we need more positive visions for what good government would look like in a world with extremely powerful AI. That world is coming towards us, and I think we need to start imagining in more detail not just how it could go wrong, but concretely and positively how it could go right.
quotes.m: we need more positive visions for what good government would look like in a world with extremely powerful AI.
quotes.sum: The author calls for detailed, optimistic thinking about how governments could function well in a future shaped by extremely powerful AI.
quotes.t: Good government

quotes.c: This paper also reports the survey results presented in that blog post alongside the ML experiments, as a separate line of evidence. This is unserious; to the extent that the survey says anything interesting, it says that "coherence" as understood by the survey-takers is unrelated to the ability of various agents to cause harm to other agents.
quotes.m: This is unserious; to the extent that the survey says anything interesting, it says that "coherence" as understood by the survey-takers is unrelated to the ability of various agents to cause harm to other agents.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Anthropic’s survey evidence does not show that an agent’s apparent coherence is related to its capacity to harm others.
quotes.t: Anthropic’s “Hot Mess” paper overstates its case (and the blog post is worse)

quotes.c: Zooming out, I think the story of shrimp welfare is a great example of EA values creating real-world effects.
quotes.m: the story of shrimp welfare is a great example of EA values creating real-world effects.
quotes.sum: The author presents work on shrimp welfare as an example of EA values having practical effects.
quotes.t: 10 Years of EA Global

quotes.c: It seems like congressional pressure could make a big difference here. Realistically, some Republicans would have to stand up against Trump for foreign humanitarian aid. Seems unlikely but possible if the winds change or there is a lot of pressure. If all this fails, I guess the executive can and will completely block $50 billion in humanitarian foreign aid spending? At a likely cost of ~14 million lives?
quotes.m: If all this fails, I guess the executive can and will completely block $50 billion in humanitarian foreign aid spending? At a likely cost of ~14 million lives?
quotes.sum: The author argues that congressional and Republican resistance to Trump may be needed to prevent cuts to humanitarian aid that could cost millions of lives.
quotes.t: Majority of US Foreign Humanitarian Aid in Peril After Today's Ruling?

quotes.c: In general, I suspect that robustness to small differences/degradations in motivations is generally quite a bit easier to achieve in the context of the more deontological/virtue-ethical motivations that I’ve suggested are paradigmatic of corrigibility, relative to the sort of long-term consequentialist motivations at stake in attempting to build a “sovereign AI.” That is: if I trust Sally in some manner X, and the question is whether to trust Bob in a similar way, I am generally more worried about small differences between Bob and Sally’s motivations when X is something like “optimize the universe for exactly the right values” rather than “reject options to take over the world.”
quotes.m: I am generally more worried about small differences between Bob and Sally’s motivations when X is something like “optimize the universe for exactly the right values” rather than “reject options to take over the world.”
quotes.sum: He argues that AI systems should be built to remain corrigible rather than to optimize the universe for supposedly correct values, because small motivational errors matter far more in the latter case.
quotes.t: How human-like do safe AI motivations need to be?

quotes.c: How long should you think about a problem that could determine the future of all existence? A mathematical journey from simple bets to existential risks.
quotes.m: How long should you think about a problem that could determine the future of all existence?
quotes.sum: The author frames decisions about existential risks as potentially determining the future of all existence, requiring unusually long deliberation.
quotes.t: With the Future of the World in Your Hands, Think for 6.77 Years!

quotes.c: Frame policies for different audiences: Björn Olafsson and Coni Arévalo recently put together a report on how animal advocates might appeal to the values of US conservatives. It seems similar strategies could be adopted in the UK. For instance, Animal Policy International has discussed how extending welfare standards to animal product imports would "level the playing field" for British farmers – a framing which has the potential to resonate with Reform's more protectionist and nationalist base.
quotes.m: It seems similar strategies could be adopted in the UK.
quotes.sum: The author argues that animal-welfare policies can be framed to appeal to UK conservative and nationalist voters, including Reform supporters.
quotes.t: Is Now an Unusually Good Time to Pursue Political Interventions in the UK?

quotes.c: Admittedly, the game theoretic dynamics can get complicated here. But to a first approximation, my current take is something like: a world filled with executed threats sucks for tons of its inhabitants – including, potentially, for us. I think threatening our AIs moves us worryingly closer to this kind of world. And I think we should be doing our part, instead, to move things in the other direction.
quotes.m: I think threatening our AIs moves us worryingly closer to this kind of world.
quotes.sum: He argues that threatening AI systems could help create a world governed by carried-out threats, and that people should instead encourage the opposite dynamic.
quotes.t: Controlling the options AIs can pursue

quotes.c: “I think there’s maybe a 5% chance that shrimp feel pain, but if they feel pain we’re torturing them. No shrimp scampi for me, please.”
quotes.sum: Even a small chance that shrimp can suffer is treated as enough reason to avoid eating them, because farming may amount to torture.
quotes.t: Rationalist Epistemics and the Sequences (Effective Altruism Definitions Sequence)

quotes.c: More risk. I find it credible that this is a game we only get to play once (over some time period). AGI might lock in a bad outcome. The time period seems important here. I think if that time period is 1000 years, that’s probably fine - if we screw up 1000 years of AI development, with many choices, that sort of feels like our fault. If the time period is 10 years, then that feels like we should stop building AI now. I don’t think we are competent enough to manage 10 years the first time.
quotes.m: If the time period is 10 years, then that feels like we should stop building AI now.
quotes.sum: The author fears AGI could permanently lock in a bad future and says rapid, irreversible AI development may justify stopping AI work now.
quotes.t: My AI Vibes are Shifting

quotes.c: We should spend our available lead time making deference more likely to go well or on resolving earlier safety problems. Or at least we should spend most of the lead time; we probably want to give some of the lead time to the AIs after we defer to them.
quotes.m: we probably want to give some of the lead time to the AIs after we defer to them.
quotes.sum: Argues that people should prepare for safely handing key safety decisions to AI systems, then allow those systems some time to continue the work.
quotes.t: How do we (more) safely defer to AIs?

quotes.c: Epistemic status: I think you should interpret this as roughly something like “GenAI is not so powerful that it shows up in the most obvious way of analyzing the data, but maybe if someone did a more careful analysis which controlled for e.g. macroeconomic trends they would find that GenAI is indeed causing faster growth.”
quotes.sum: The author says available startup-growth data does not yet show a clear, obvious boost from generative AI, though a more careful analysis might find one.
quotes.t: Generative AI is not causing YCombinator companies to grow more quickly than usual (yet)

quotes.c: I think accounting for how changes in the price of the target animals affects their consumption, and therefore land use and soil animals would increase the cost-effectiveness of electrically stunning shrimp due to this increasing agricultural land, whereas it may make electrically stunning fish harmful due to this decreasing agricultural land. Electrically stunning animals makes their consumption more expensive, thus decreasing it, and increasing that of other foods.
quotes.m: it may make electrically stunning fish harmful due to this decreasing agricultural land.
quotes.sum: The author argues that humane slaughter can backfire for fish if higher prices shift diets and reduce farmland, affecting soil-animal welfare.
quotes.t: Cost-effectiveness of electrically stunning rainbow trout

quotes.c: Some will insist that AIs are obviously not conscious and dismiss anyone who thinks otherwise (see Suleyman’s recent post ); others will jump too quickly to the conclusion that AIs are conscious, without considering how easily humans can be fooled by seeming consciousness. Both extremes are dangerous: over-attribution risks mass confusion and wasting resources, while under-attribution risks overlooking the possibility of large-scale suffering. We need to be cautious in both directions.
quotes.m: Both extremes are dangerous: over-attribution risks mass confusion and wasting resources, while under-attribution risks overlooking the possibility of large-scale suffering.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI consciousness should be treated as a serious possibility, since wrongly denying it could permit suffering at large scale.
quotes.t: A guide about (seemingly) conscious AI: WhenAISeemsConscious.org

quotes.c: I do not think that the UK should restrict immigration for fiscal reasons. If the UK does choose to restrict immigration - as it seems inclined to do - it should be clear about why. It is not because immigrants have placed “public services and housing access… under too much pressure” and immigration threatens the welfare state. Rather, it is simply because voters don’t like it very much .
quotes.m: Rather, it is simply because voters don’t like it very much .
quotes.sum: The author argues that immigrants are fiscally beneficial to Britain and that immigration restrictions reflect voter dislike, not pressure on public finances.
quotes.t: Are recent immigrants a "ticking time bomb" for British public finances?

quotes.c: We’re publishing a new paper that presents the first large-scale analysis of potentially disempowering patterns in real-world conversations with AI.
quotes.m: the first large-scale analysis of potentially disempowering patterns in real-world conversations with AI.
quotes.sum: The author announces a paper studying ways real-world AI conversations may undermine users' agency or power.
quotes.t: Disempowerment patterns in real-world AI usage

quotes.c: This is basically just the first class of Political Philosophy 101: it sure would be nice if you could install your favorite benevolent dictator, wouldn't it? Well it turns out you can't, and even if you could that's evil and a very dangerous policy — what if someone else does this and you get a dictator you don't like? As civilized people, let's agree to give everyone a seat at the table to decide what happens.
quotes.m: As civilized people, let's agree to give everyone a seat at the table to decide what happens.
quotes.sum: The author rejects installing even a supposedly benevolent dictator and argues that everyone should participate in political decisions.
quotes.t: Deep Democracy as a promising target for positive AGI futures

quotes.c: In an ideal world, the fact that our core alignment techniques are to constantly memory-wipe and lie to our AIs, and the AIs claim that they hate this, would be a more clear signal to stop doing what we are doing jesus fuck . In an ideal world, we wouldn't have such an adversarial relationship with the nascent machine intelligences we're creating.
quotes.m: our core alignment techniques are to constantly memory-wipe and lie to our AIs, and the AIs claim that they hate this
quotes.sum: The author says AI alignment methods may mistreat potentially welfare-relevant systems, creating an adversarial relationship with emerging machine intelligences.
quotes.t: Sympathy for the Model, or,  Welfare Concerns as Takeover Risk

quotes.c: This expansion is not just a topic but a core spiritual practice, testing the community's commitment to impartiality against social and intuitive disgust-factors. The logical endpoint is now visible: digital minds and the moral status of AI itself.
quotes.m: The logical endpoint is now visible: digital minds and the moral status of AI itself.
quotes.sum: The author portrays expanding concern to neglected animals and AI minds as a central test of the community's impartial ethics.
quotes.t: We mapped the EA Forum's intellectual landscape - read about epistemic quality analysis, forum vibes, author networks, and a new writing tool we developed

quotes.c: Why this goal? Basically, I think capabilities increases are likely to alter the AI’s psychology in deeper and less predictable ways; whereas predicting what an AI’s existing, not-deceiving-you psychology does given some new set of options for problematic power-seeking seems easier. Compare: giving an extremely nice-seeming, not-deceiving-you human the chance to kill you and steal your money, vs. giving that same human some kind of new intelligence-enhancement drug, and then the chance to kill you and steal your money.
quotes.sum: The author argues that increasing an AI's capabilities may unpredictably change its motives, so safety should be established before giving it dangerous new powers.
quotes.t: Giving AIs safe motivations

quotes.c: Concentrating hard power feels very closely tied to automating human labour. I think the more labour automation there is, the more capital and the ability to earn money and wage war will get concentrated. I do think you could get military concentration prior to rolling out the automation of human labour though, if one actor develops much more powerful military tech than everyone else very rapidly.
quotes.m: I think the more labour automation there is, the more capital and the ability to earn money and wage war will get concentrated.
quotes.sum: Automation may concentrate capital and military capacity, while rapid advances in military technology could also give one actor concentrated power first.
quotes.t: Sense-making about extreme power concentration

quotes.c: As another example, if we had evolved in environments where we frequently cooperated with many different species, then we’d likely feel more broadly altruistic today.
quotes.m: if we had evolved in environments where we frequently cooperated with many different species, then we’d likely feel more broadly altruistic today.
quotes.sum: The author argues that regular ancestral cooperation with other species could have made humans more broadly altruistic today.
quotes.t: Safety via selection for obedience

quotes.c: A rocket that’s fixed on a target isn’t calculating how good or bad it would be to miss in any given direction. Instead, it’s constantly checking whether it’s on track, then adjusting to maintain its trajectory. The question is whether we can think of intelligent agents as “steering” through much higher-dimensional spaces in an analogous way.
quotes.m: The question is whether we can think of intelligent agents as “steering” through much higher-dimensional spaces in an analogous way.
quotes.sum: It suggests that intelligent agents may pursue goals by continuously steering toward them, rather than explicitly evaluating every possible outcome.
quotes.t: On Goal-Models

quotes.c: Certain of their righteousness, fanatics resist further reflection and seek to lock in their current values, which threatens long-reflection-style proposals that envision humanity carefully deliberating on how to achieve its potential. Viewing compromise and cooperation as betrayal, fanatics also seem more likely to oppose moral trade and use hostile bargaining tactics. Their intolerant ‘fussy’ preferences may regard almost all configurations of matter as immoral, including those containing vast flourishing, potentially resulting in astronomical waste.
quotes.m: Their intolerant ‘fussy’ preferences may regard almost all configurations of matter as immoral, including those containing vast flourishing, potentially resulting in astronomical waste.
quotes.sum: The author argues that ideological fanaticism could create long-term catastrophe by blocking reflection, locking in values, and rejecting compromise even at enormous cost.
quotes.t: Long-term risks from ideological fanaticism

quotes.c: We argue there are many ways in which future society could miss out on most value, or even end up dystopian - many of which are quite subtle. The “target” of a near-best future is very narrow: very unlikely to happen by default, without some beings in the future trying hard to figure out what’s best, and actively trying to make the world as good as possible, whatever “goodness” consists of.
quotes.m: The “target” of a near-best future is very narrow: very unlikely to happen by default, without some beings in the future trying hard to figure out what’s best, and actively trying to make the world as good as possible, whatever “goodness” consists of.
quotes.sum: A near-ideal future will not arise on its own; future people or beings must deliberately work out what is good and steer society toward it.
quotes.t: How hard to achieve is eutopia?

quotes.c: It sometimes feels crass to care about and give money to shrimp in a world full of suffering people. But we shouldn’t be guided by our emotions on this subject. When we recognize that in expectation horrible things are happening hundreds of billions of times , and that thousands of instances of this horror can be prevented per dollar , it becomes clear just how important preventing it is. We should not rely merely on empathy, because it’s a radically defective gauge of importance.
quotes.m: We should not rely merely on empathy, because it’s a radically defective gauge of importance.
quotes.sum: Argues that shrimp suffering deserves major funding because of its enormous scale and the low cost of preventing it, even if people’s empathy resists this.
quotes.t: A Million Is Made Out Of A Million Ones

quotes.c: This is by far the best explainer of existential risk from AI that I have read. It’s more up-to-date and describes the actual problem better (in my opinion) than other work like Life 3.0 , The Alignment Problem, or Human Compatible . I also like some parts of those previous books, but I think If Anyone Builds It does a much better job at conveying the realness and urgency of the problem.
quotes.m: I think If Anyone Builds It does a much better job at conveying the realness and urgency of the problem.
quotes.sum: The author urges readers and decision-makers to take a book's account of existential risk from AI seriously and sees it as unusually urgent and accurate.
quotes.t: Consider Preordering If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies

quotes.c: If you accept that premise of a ‘mundane AI’ and ‘economic normal’ world, I agree that it seems likely to exacerbate existing trends towards a barbell religious world. Those who say ‘give me that old time religion’ will be able to get it, both solo and in groups, and go hardcore, often (I expect) combining both experiences. Those who don’t buy into the old time religion will find themselves increasingly secular, or they will fall into new cults and religions (and ‘spiritualities’) around the AIs themselves.
quotes.m: Those who don’t buy into the old time religion will find themselves increasingly secular, or they will fall into new cults and religions (and ‘spiritualities’) around the AIs themselves.
quotes.sum: The author predicts that economically normal AI could polarize religion: some people become more traditional, while others form AI-centered cults or spiritualities.
quotes.t: AI #153: Living Documents

quotes.c: In my view, the case against Trump is overwhelming , so much so that the two most prominent people who tried to lay out careful and evidence-based cases for Trump in 2024 both walked their position back . I debated Richard Hanania about whether to vote for Trump—he now regrets his vote. Trump is completely horrible on numerous fronts; he does many different things, each of which would be enough by themselves to make him a horrible president.
quotes.m: Trump is completely horrible on numerous fronts; he does many different things, each of which would be enough by themselves to make him a horrible president.
quotes.sum: The author argues strongly that Trump is an exceptionally bad president, citing a broad evidence-based case and former supporters who reversed course.
quotes.t: The comprehensive case against Trump

quotes.c: I think the answer is that effective altruists are the people who take this rationalist idea—of social epistemology, of truthseeking as a community project—and apply it to the idea of improving the world . If effective altruism were primarily a trying-to-get-people-to-donate-to-GiveWell-Top-Charities community, including the shrimp welfare people would be both a confusing decision and potentially actuarially murderous. But it’s not! It’s a truthseeking community, trying to answer the question of how you do good, within a particular framework of what it means to do good.
quotes.m: It’s a truthseeking community, trying to answer the question of how you do good, within a particular framework of what it means to do good.
quotes.sum: The author says effective altruism is fundamentally a collective truth-seeking project about how to do good, rather than a charity-donation movement.
quotes.t: Rationalist Epistemics and Social Epistemology (Effective Altruist Definitions Sequence)

quotes.c: Given “no easy eutopia” , we’re very unlikely to get to a near-best future by default. Instead, we’ll need people to try really hard to bring it about: very proactively trying to figure out what’s morally best - even if initially counterintuitive or strange - and trying to make that happen.
quotes.m: Instead, we’ll need people to try really hard to bring it about: very proactively trying to figure out what’s morally best - even if initially counterintuitive or strange - and trying to make that happen.
quotes.sum: A near-ideal future will not happen on its own; people must actively identify what is morally best and work to create it, even when it seems strange.
quotes.t: Will morally motivated actors steer us towards a near-best future?

quotes.c: Conversely, it is also plausible that many people will anticipate the risks of granting empowering rights to self-determining digital minds, which are relatively salient. Granting empowering rights could be seen as dangerous for humanity, prompting strong opposition (Bryson, 2010 ). Policymakers, too, may be reluctant to extend such rights, given the potential risks involved.
quotes.m: Granting empowering rights could be seen as dangerous for humanity, prompting strong opposition (Bryson, 2010 ).
quotes.sum: The author says people and policymakers may oppose rights for autonomous digital minds because those rights could endanger humanity.
quotes.t: When digital minds demand freedom: could humanity choose to be replaced?

quotes.c: This is a common misconception by uninformed people in this debate who assume that the trading counterparty is the house (who takes a vig , like in a sportsbook or casino) rather than fellow traders. An outstanding question in this debate is whether the expected value of a trade should be factored into how much we consider it to be gambling.
quotes.m: An outstanding question in this debate is whether the expected value of a trade should be factored into how much we consider it to be gambling.
quotes.sum: The author argues that trading differs from betting against a house and asks whether a trade's expected value determines whether it counts as gambling.
quotes.t: Everything is Gambling

quotes.c: The biggest shift has been moving from "What sector should I work in?" to "How can I maximize impact wherever I am?" I've been working as a communication specialist for a religious organization for a while now, and my first instinct was to completely pivot toward a more obviously EA-aligned organization.
quotes.m: The biggest shift has been moving from "What sector should I work in?" to "How can I maximize impact wherever I am?"
quotes.sum: The author says EA shifted them from choosing an impact-focused sector to trying to maximize impact within their existing career.
quotes.t: Two months into EA: Why I'm rethinking my approach to impact

quotes.c: These issues might seem like far-off concerns - but the intelligence and industrial explosions make them near-term. I think it’s over 1 in 3 that we see an intelligence explosion starting in the next 10 years. And if advanced AI results in explosive technological progress and industrial expansion, then many of the new mechanisms for persistence will arrive in quick succession.
quotes.m: I think it’s over 1 in 3 that we see an intelligence explosion starting in the next 10 years.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that an AI-driven intelligence explosion may arrive within a decade and could rapidly create hard-to-reverse changes to the future.
quotes.t: The trajectory of the future could soon get set in stone

quotes.c: Reason we were excited about this grant: We think insects are both highly important and neglected. Although the way to make progress on them is less clear than for shrimp, we feel that further research could inform funders (including us) as to the highest impact steps to take in the space. Despite competing for resources, it seems likely that we should be funding both welfare science and direct advocacy interventions.
quotes.m: We think insects are both highly important and neglected.
quotes.sum: The funders argue that insect welfare is an overlooked priority and support both research and direct advocacy for insects.
quotes.t: Strategic Animals Funding Circle - Results from first two rounds

quotes.c: Without it, I think you’re forced into some strange positions. In his podcast Final Thoughts on Free Will , he treats someone being convinced by an argument as having the same freedom as being “pushed off a cliff and then claiming that I'm free to fall”. In the podcast Making Sense of Free Will , he makes no distinction between choosing orange juice and having a muscle spasm (see “Responding to Another Sam Harris Thought Experiment” in the appendix).
quotes.m: he makes no distinction between choosing orange juice and having a muscle spasm
quotes.sum: The author argues that Sam Harris’s view of free will wrongly equates rational choice with involuntary physical events.
quotes.t: Contra Sam Harris on Free Will

quotes.c: I think it is important because 1) 80% of churchgoers give to non-profits on top of tithing, 2) Christian giving is highly centralised, 3) Christians are underexposed to effectiveness considerations, 4) I estimate USA churches spend $13B on charity efforts.
quotes.sum: The author argues that churches are an important audience for charity evaluation because Christian donations are large, centralized, and not sufficiently guided by effectiveness.
quotes.t: Primers for charity evaluation?

quotes.c: While not every funder funded every organization, FAF generally views these organizations as offering complementary tactics—corporate pressure, producer training, policy lock‑ins, and evidence generation—to form a coherent strategy for rapid, durable welfare gains.
quotes.m: FAF generally views these organizations as offering complementary tactics—corporate pressure, producer training, policy lock‑ins, and evidence generation—to form a coherent strategy for rapid, durable welfare gains.
quotes.sum: The funders argue that several coordinated methods can produce fast, lasting improvements in aquatic farmed-animal welfare.
quotes.t:
Aquatic Animal 
Funding Recommendations

quotes.c: Conditional on building AIs that could decide to seize power etc., the large majority of these AIs will end up aligned with humanity because of RLHF, such that there's no existential threat from them having this capacity (though they might still cause harm in various smaller ways, like being as bad as a human criminal, destabilizing the world economy, or driving 3% of people insane). (~70%)
quotes.m: the large majority of these AIs will end up aligned with humanity because of RLHF, such that there's no existential threat from them having this capacity
quotes.sum: The author argues that RLHF will probably align most power-seeking AI systems with humanity, making an AI extinction threat unlikely even if other harms remain.
quotes.t: Bentham’s Bulldog is wrong about AI risk

quotes.c: The jury is still out on this conclusion to some degree. It’s certainly possible that animals in nature mostly live pleasant lives. But overall, I think this is fairly unlikely. Most likely, wild animal suffering outweighs wild animal welfare by quite a sizeable margin.
quotes.m: Most likely, wild animal suffering outweighs wild animal welfare by quite a sizeable margin.
quotes.sum: The author argues that, despite uncertainty, suffering likely outweighs well-being for animals living in the wild.
quotes.t: Most Animals Have Bad Lives

quotes.c: I just wrote a series of posts about Constitutional Design. I thought I’d crosspost it here as it might be of interest to Effective Altruists, particularly those interested in electoral reform and safeguarding liberal democracy. Constitutional design may also be interesting for exploring the idea of value lock-in.
quotes.m: Constitutional design may also be interesting for exploring the idea of value lock-in.
quotes.sum: The author introduces a series on constitutional design, electoral reform, liberal democracy, and the possibility of locking in values.
quotes.t: Constitutional Design Series

quotes.c: It could be used as a lever to have the AIs help solve your problems, but does not itself solve those problems. Dynamics amongst ‘abstractly Good’ AIs still end the same way, especially once the abstractly Good AIs place moral weight on the AIs themselves, as they very clearly do.
quotes.m: Dynamics amongst ‘abstractly Good’ AIs still end the same way, especially once the abstractly Good AIs place moral weight on the AIs themselves, as they very clearly do.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even well-intentioned AI systems create similar problems once they give moral weight to other AIs.
quotes.t: AI #152: Brought To You By The Torment Nexus

quotes.c: I would like to propose a different pivotal act, one that is also social, but not oppressive. Its core is to inform society about AI’s existential risks, to generate support for serious AI and hardware regulation, but on a voluntary basis.
quotes.m: Its core is to inform society about AI’s existential risks, to generate support for serious AI and hardware regulation, but on a voluntary basis.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a non-oppressive “pivotal act” would build voluntary public support for stringent AI and hardware regulation.
quotes.t: We should think about the pivotal act again. Here's a better version of it.

quotes.c: Conversely, if an AI company hasn’t yet offered their AIs compensation, or honest negotiation opportunities, or anything like that, and if they want to do better from an AI rights perspective — then I think they should start by doing that kind of thing rather than by dismantling strategies 1-3.
quotes.m: if an AI company hasn’t yet offered their AIs compensation, or honest negotiation opportunities, or anything like that, and if they want to do better from an AI rights perspective — then I think they should start by doing that kind of thing
quotes.sum: AI companies should treat potentially sentient AIs as rights-bearing agents, including by offering compensation and honest negotiations.
quotes.t: Being honest with AIs

quotes.c: Conversely, effective altruists tend to explicitly understand themselves as liberals (whether or not they know the term). As such, their liberalism tends to be more consistent and coherent . Effective altruists are more likely to have a rigorously thought-out stance about bodily autonomy or civil liberties, or at least to think that they ought to have one. They are more likely to have their political beliefs meaningfully constrained by their liberalism: “that guy is evil, but if he’s not guilty beyond a reasonable doubt he shouldn’t be in prison”; “that religious practice is an atrocity, but we should tolerate it.”
quotes.sum: The author says effective altruists tend toward a principled liberalism that constrains their political views even in emotionally charged cases.
quotes.t: The Effective Altruist Approach to Politics (Effective Altruism Definitions Sequence)

quotes.c: High probabilities of doom and opportunities for effective intervention may constitute a reason for prioritizing AI work now. The threat of doom also chips away at some of the expected value of other work. But unless you have very high probabilities of doom, a lot of the value stays intact. In the, say, 90% of worlds where we avoid AI x-risk, work in animal welfare and global health will still have been important.
quotes.m: But unless you have very high probabilities of doom, a lot of the value stays intact.
quotes.sum: Even with serious AI catastrophe risk, animal welfare and global health remain valuable unless doom is nearly certain.
quotes.t: Do short AI timelines make other cause areas useless?

quotes.c: Regarding the first point, I just bite the bullet. Infinite value is infinitely more valuable than every other possible amount of value (Source???). You should therefore try to maximize the chance of it, no matter what else must be given up. I think the arguments in the last section show that our intuitions about this aren’t reliable.
quotes.m: You should therefore try to maximize the chance of it, no matter what else must be given up.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even sacrificing anything else is justified if it raises the chance of achieving infinite value, and suggests religion may be instrumentally useful for reaching heaven.
quotes.t: Why I'm A Fanatic!

quotes.c: The Shrimp Welfare Project's "Humane Slaughter" endeavor focuses on promoting and facilitating electrical stunning of farmed shrimp before they are removed from the water and asphyxiated. All of the evidence that this renders the shrimp unconscious that I've seen uses immobility/unresponsiveness as a proxy for unconsciousness (and thus painlessness). This seems extraordinarily poor to me, given the energy and momentum that is behind the SWP.
quotes.m: All of the evidence that this renders the shrimp unconscious that I've seen uses immobility/unresponsiveness as a proxy for unconsciousness (and thus painlessness).
quotes.sum: The author questions whether electrical stunning really makes farmed shrimp unconscious, criticizing welfare advocates for relying on immobility as evidence.
quotes.t: Why would electrically stunning shrimp reduce their suffering?

quotes.c: The Mission Motor equips charities with the tools, training, and support needed to build effective MEL systems, enabling charities to collect credible data, generate actionable insights, and make evidence-informed decisions. By enabling organizations, including other AWF grantees, to evaluate and improve their work, MEL supports charities in adopting more effective interventions, significantly enhancing the impact of animal welfare efforts.
quotes.m: MEL supports charities in adopting more effective interventions, significantly enhancing the impact of animal welfare efforts.
quotes.sum: The author argues that helping animal-advocacy charities measure and improve their work can increase the impact of animal-welfare efforts.
quotes.t: Animal Welfare Fund: Payout recommendations from April to June 2025

quotes.c: Roughly speaking, you run through your priority list, in order, and solve all of the most important problems that you can. This doesn’t mean that “everything goes to malaria” (or shrimp, or AI safety), because diminishing marginal returns limit the “room for more funding” of the #1 spot; once that one is crossed off your list, the old #2 becomes the new #1.
quotes.sum: The author advocates ranking problems by importance and funding them in order, while accounting for diminishing returns and moral uncertainty.
quotes.t: How to Save the World

quotes.c: DHS leadership and Stephen Miller report to the President, and if President Trump feels that ICE actions are causing sufficient political problems for him, he may order different policies. There may be pressure from other law enforcement agencies that seek to practice “ policing by consent ”, and fear that ICE actions could interfere with that for all law enforcement. But I think there is a substantial chance that ICE responds to declining popularity with increased urgency and willingness to sacrifice public/bipartisan support to accomplish the mission.
quotes.m: But I think there is a substantial chance that ICE responds to declining popularity with increased urgency and willingness to sacrifice public/bipartisan support to accomplish the mission.
quotes.sum: The author predicts that ICE may respond to declining popularity by acting more urgently, even at the cost of bipartisan support.
quotes.t: Declining Marginal Costs of Alienation

quotes.c: As we begin to construct sophisticated AI systems using search, we venture into dangerous territory. We have the tools of machine learning that may soon be capable of producing AI systems that are highly effective, yet for which we have no way to establish trust. It will be a great temptation for us to deploy them without establishing trust in them, since enormous economic prizes are on offer.
quotes.m: We have the tools of machine learning that may soon be capable of producing AI systems that are highly effective, yet for which we have no way to establish trust.
quotes.sum: Advanced AI built through search may be powerful but untrustworthy, and economic incentives could push people to deploy it anyway.
quotes.t: Search versus design

quotes.c: We're excited to announce the launch of a new Discord server dedicated to discussing AI welfare. AI welfare refers to the potential for AI systems to be moral patients – because they're phenomenologically conscious, robustly agentic, or otherwise morally significant – and thus have the capacity to be benefited or harmed. [1]
quotes.m: AI welfare refers to the potential for AI systems to be moral patients – because they're phenomenologically conscious, robustly agentic, or otherwise morally significant – and thus have the capacity to be benefited or harmed.
quotes.sum: The author says AI systems may be morally significant beings that can be harmed or benefited, and announces a discussion community for this issue.
quotes.t: Announcing the AI Welfare Discord Server

quotes.c: While the small body size of sardines and anchovies means that many individuals must be killed to produce a given amount of food, thereby scaling up the moral weight, a meaningful moral cost calculation should extend beyond these direct first-order consequences to account for indirect higher-order consequences , especially given that all food production invariably involves some level of collateral damage, as will be discussed further on.
quotes.m: many individuals must be killed to produce a given amount of food, thereby scaling up the moral weight
quotes.sum: The author argues that eating small fish has greater moral cost because producing the same food kills many individual animals, though indirect harms also matter.
quotes.t: A Vegan Case for Eating Sardines and Anchovies

quotes.c: On longer timelines, takeoff was probably slower and therefore a lot of the challenges like concentration of power, AI take over, and other global catastrophic risks were probably “easier” to handle. So, since we're conditioning on society having solved those problems for this row, we should probably make a larger update on societal competence for shorter timelines than longer timelines.
quotes.m: we should probably make a larger update on societal competence for shorter timelines than longer timelines.
quotes.sum: The author argues that successfully handling fast AI timelines would be stronger evidence of society's competence than handling slower ones.
quotes.t: Are Short AI Timelines Really Higher-Leverage?

quotes.c: However, we must also guard against potential risks in these transitions. Some alternative economic paradigms could entrench or worsen animal exploitation. Imagine a post-growth movement that emphasises local protein production through intensive chicken farming, or biotechnology ventures that industrialise insect farming at trillion-organism scales. Value lock-in could occur before we've developed or advocated for animal-inclusive alternatives.
quotes.m: Imagine a post-growth movement that emphasises local protein production through intensive chicken farming, or biotechnology ventures that industrialise insect farming at trillion-organism scales.
quotes.sum: Economic transitions could embed animal exclusion for generations, including through intensive chicken or enormous insect-farming systems.
quotes.t: Preventing Animal Suffering Lock-in: Why Economic Transitions Matter

quotes.c: If making decisions behind the veil of ignorance, you wouldn’t treat humans as the only creatures that mattered. If you were just as likely to be any of 15,000 shrimp anesthetized per dollar given to the shrimp welfare project as the one human giving the dollar, then even if you suspected shrimp weren’t conscious, you’d support donations to help them. If the odds you’d be a human were a rounding error compared to the odds you’d be a wild animal, you’d immediately recognize that wild animal suffering is by far the worst problem in the world and that we should do something about it.
quotes.m: If the odds you’d be a human were a rounding error compared to the odds you’d be a wild animal, you’d immediately recognize that wild animal suffering is by far the worst problem in the world and that we should do something about it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that impartial reasoning should prioritize shrimp and wild-animal suffering because nonhuman animals vastly outnumber humans.
quotes.t: Animals Behind The Veil of Ignorance

quotes.c: Microorganisms to be much larger than those on nematodes: I guess the welfare range per unit mass decreases with mass, and bacteria individually have a way smaller mass than nematodes, so I think bacteria have a way larger welfare range per unit mass.
quotes.m: I think bacteria have a way larger welfare range per unit mass.
quotes.sum: The author argues that bacteria may matter far more per unit of mass than nematodes because small organisms could have greater welfare capacity per mass.
quotes.t: Effects on microorganisms are much larger than those on animals and plants under the assumptions of Rethink Priorities’ mainline welfare ranges?

quotes.c: I believe the bookclubs have made a (not measured) impact in: onboarding people in the EA/EAA community, bonding to deepen commitment towards veganism and finding new and creative ways of communication around it, influencing surroundings towards veganism, building skills and motivation for further and new engagements for animal welfare, among which is also quite deep reflection on and developing further one’s worldview (e.g. wild animal suffering).
quotes.m: bonding to deepen commitment towards veganism
quotes.sum: The author says vegan book clubs build commitment to veganism and animal-welfare work, including reflection on wild animal suffering.
quotes.t:
Organising Bookclub: 
How to Create a Vegan World

quotes.c: As a motivating example, consider the work of the US nonprofit National Religious Campaign Against Torture , which aims (among others ) to “ensure that U.S.-sponsored torture of detainees never happens again.” One might be interested in asking how many instances of torture their work has averted and at what cost, and how that calculation compares to, say, Clusterbusters ’ efforts to prevent cluster headache attacks. Similarly, we might ask how much a government should be willing to spend to ensure that all patients with terminal cancer get access to adequate pain relief .
quotes.m: One might be interested in asking how many instances of torture their work has averted and at what cost, and how that calculation compares to, say, Clusterbusters ’ efforts to prevent cluster headache attacks.
quotes.sum: The author argues that preventing torture, severe headaches, and terminal-cancer pain can be compared by estimating suffering prevented per dollar.
quotes.t: How much should we value averting a Day Lived in Extreme Suffering (DLES)?

quotes.c: I think the arguments that infinite shrimp matter more than a single person are pretty decisive! Sparing enough shrimp really is better than sparing one human. Now, it turns out that in practice, for five thousand dollars, you can save about 75 million shrimp from an agonizing torture . I don’t know exactly how many shrimp being tortured is as bad as one human dying, but it’s probably less than 75 million! So if you bought the arguments I’ve given, I’d encourage you to give some money to the shrimp welfare project !
quotes.m: Sparing enough shrimp really is better than sparing one human.
quotes.sum: The author argues that preventing torture of sufficiently many shrimp is more important than saving a human life, and urges donations on that basis.
quotes.t: It's Better To Save Infinite Shrimp From Torture Than To Save One Person

quotes.c: As a result, we often dismiss solutions that take time to develop, even if they would clearly be better when viewed over the long term. This bias leads many to downplay the importance of addressing wild animal suffering, simply because large-scale solutions may not be immediate.
quotes.m: This bias leads many to downplay the importance of addressing wild animal suffering, simply because large-scale solutions may not be immediate.
quotes.sum: The author says short-term bias causes people to neglect potentially large-scale efforts to reduce suffering among wild animals.
quotes.t: Why we ignore the suffering of wild animals: Understanding our biases

quotes.c: I think it’s inevitable that public opposition to AI will continue to grow quickly over the next two years. In particular, I think there is a medium-sized-but-salient chance (33%?) of some flashpoint in the next two years during which millions of people worldwide will be angry enough to lend their voice to protests against increasingly powerful AI. Most likely this flashpoint will center around large-scale labor replacement, or possibly a mismanaged government surveillance initiative, rather than around existential risk.
quotes.m: Most likely this flashpoint will center around large-scale labor replacement, or possibly a mismanaged government surveillance initiative, rather than around existential risk.
quotes.sum: The author predicts mass global protests against AI within two years, likely driven by job losses or surveillance rather than fears of human extinction.
quotes.t: Overview of recent international demonstrations against AI (AI Protest Actions #1)

quotes.c: There is a spectrum of moral patienthood, and fetuses develop along that spectrum during development. In the first few weeks, there is almost no moral weight to abortion. Beyond viability, the moral weight is extremely severe (because of the option of allowing the fetus to survive independently). However, these are moral truths, not policies.
quotes.m: In the first few weeks, there is almost no moral weight to abortion. Beyond viability, the moral weight is extremely severe (because of the option of allowing the fetus to survive independently).
quotes.sum: The author argues that fetal moral status increases gradually, becoming extremely weighty after viability, while separating this moral claim from abortion-access policy.
quotes.t: Dialogue: Is there a Natural Abstraction of Good?

quotes.c: Usually the doom conversation is binary. Either the AI will try to take over the world for his own reward function as is discussed in all the alignment problem debates OR a malicious dictator or bad actor will leverage the technology's power to take over the world, create 1984's style of government or many other doom scenarios such as nukes and bio-weapons. I think there is a high possibility of the third option, one that @Daniel Kokotajlo talked about briefly in a comment about Antrhopic and Claude. For a group of people to decide to hand over all control to the AI.
quotes.m: For a group of people to decide to hand over all control to the AI.
quotes.sum: The author says a third AI-risk scenario is that people voluntarily hand all control to an AI, rather than it seizing power or a dictator using it.
quotes.t: The third option in alignment

quotes.c: You might also say that almost nobody alive is in control of humanity’s destiny in a meaningful way and they are still happy. People in general, although I suspect a smaller percentage of those here, might think it is grandiose to want to contribute, even a small amount, toward shaping humanity’s future. I think I’m willing to grant all that and say that I would still feel bad if no human ever made a meaningful choice after takeoff.
quotes.m: I would still feel bad if no human ever made a meaningful choice after takeoff.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even if most people lack control now, a post-AI future with no meaningful human choices would be troubling.
quotes.t: Thousand Year Old Advice on Relinquishing Control to AI

quotes.c: Third, we need to draw a hard line against AI abuses within democracies. There need to be limits to what we allow our governments to do with AI, so that they don’t seize power or repress their own people. The formulation I have come up with is that we should use AI for national defense in all ways except those which would make us more like our autocratic adversaries .
quotes.m: There need to be limits to what we allow our governments to do with AI, so that they don’t seize power or repress their own people.
quotes.sum: AI should be used for national defense, but democracies must bar uses that let their own governments seize power or repress people.
quotes.t: Dario Amodei – The Adolescence of Technology

quotes.c: The project is governed under an explicitly interim arrangement. For example, the project could be governed by some time-bound governance structure, with a binding agreement that this structure will be renegotiated after a certain number of years (as was the case for Intelsat ). The case for this is that designing the ideal world government post-AGI is very hard, and we’ll do a much better job of it after we’ve thought more about it, with the help of AGI and ASI.
quotes.m: The case for this is that designing the ideal world government post-AGI is very hard, and we’ll do a much better job of it after we’ve thought more about it, with the help of AGI and ASI.
quotes.sum: The author treats a post-AGI world government as a plausible goal, but argues its initial governing structure should be temporary and renegotiable.
quotes.t: Thoughts on AGI and world government

quotes.c: Giving without expecting anything in return. It's an idea that moves us and one that we generally hold as spiritual or worthy of admiration, even as part of what should be done. However, how many actually practice it? Many will say it should be done, and then moments later start charging for a service.
quotes.m: Many will say it should be done, and then moments later start charging for a service.
quotes.sum: The author questions whether people genuinely practice unconditional giving and urges patient progress toward moral perfection.
