quotes.c: I think that working with a small group of colleagues in implementing some specially chosen problem or paper, and with some availability for supervision would be really useful to learn quickly without getting stuck for really long times. Of course, I know of these incredible cowboys of GitHub who indeed do this alone, but I would personally find this very valuable.
quotes.m: I think that working with a small group of colleagues in implementing some specially chosen problem or paper, and with some availability for supervision would be really useful to learn quickly without getting stuck for really long times.

quotes.c: As a collectivist, one can only join the mob against Trump, one has no idea what it takes to be a single one standing up to several for the right thing. And the only reason for one dislike him to begin with, is because that's what's popular in one's environment. Try having a factually/scientifically and logically correct opinion of own making, that is against cancel culture and you will bump in to the walls of your invisible prison. One side is for free speech and open debate, the other is for silencing and censoring anything that is saying/thinking against.
quotes.m: One side is for free speech and open debate, the other is for silencing and censoring anything that is saying/thinking against.

quotes.t: A physicists* take on today, philosophizing on and trying to describe the world

quotes.c: Logical Updatelessness is one of the central open problems in decision theory. An updateless agent is one that does not update on its observations, but instead chooses what action it wants itself to output upon being input those observations. quotes.c: Utilitarianism allows "utility monsters" and "utility legions." A large enough benefit to a single person (utility monster), or a benefit of any size to a sufficiently large set of persons (utility legion), can outweigh all other ethical considerations. Utility monsters seem (as far as I can tell) to be a mostly theoretical source of difficulty, but I think the idea of a "utility legion" - a large set of persons such that the opportunity to benefit them outweighs all other moral considerations - is the root cause of most of what's controversial and interesting about utilitarianism today, at least in the context of effective altruism.
quotes.m: A large enough benefit to a single person (utility monster), or a benefit of any size to a sufficiently large set of persons (utility legion), can outweigh all other ethical considerations.
quotes.sum: He argues that utilitarian ethics can require letting sufficiently large aggregate benefits override every other moral consideration.
quotes.t: Other-centered ethics and Harsanyi's Aggregation Theorem

quotes.c: Given the empirical uncertainty as well as the uncertainty re normative ethics and metaethics (and meta levels above that), we would ideally lock in as few things as possible (to preserve option value) but as many as needed (to avoid catastrophes). The Metaethics and Normative Ethics of AGI Value Alignment:
Many Questions, Some Implications

quotes.c: Holden Karnofsky: Was empowerment, human empowerment, generally a force for good, or for bad? I think this is relevant when I look to the future. That would give us the ability to do all kinds of things we couldn’t do before.
quotes.m: “Well, if we created digital people, would that be good or bad?”
quotes.sum: He asks whether creating digital people would be good or bad, framing them as a major new source of human empowerment.
quotes.t: Holden Karnofsky on building aptitudes and kicking ass

quotes.c: This post attempts to (1) tease apart different features of liberal democracy and (2) analyse how increasing or decreasing a society’s level of each feature would affect various potential intermediate goals for longtermists . By potential intermediate goals, we mean goals we could pursue to potentially increase the expected value of the far future , via four broad categories: existential risk reduction , trajectory changes , speeding up development , or “ meta-longtermism ” ( Greaves and MacAskill, 2021 ) [1] .
quotes.m: goals we could pursue to potentially increase the expected value of the far future
quotes.sum: The author proposes evaluating features of liberal democracy by whether they improve humanity's very long-term future, including through reducing existential risks.
quotes.t: Towards a longtermist framework for evaluating democracy-related interventions

quotes.c: The first set of long pieces will be a series laying out the case as I see it that we're in the most important century ever for humanity; this will include topics like "consequences of mind uploading" as well as extensive discussion of the various approaches to forecasting when transformative AI will be developed (a lot of this will be summarizing work like Ajeya Cotra's timelines analysis ).
quotes.m: we're in the most important century ever for humanity
quotes.sum: The author says he will argue that this is humanity’s most important century, focusing on mind uploading and forecasts for transformative AI.
quotes.t: New blog: Cold Takes

quotes.c: I think superintelligence will likely be governed by something like our current political institutions and these institutions may fare poorly. We should not trust the long-term future to decisionmaking systems based in current humans' preferences; we prima facie should delegate this choice to another system. Any candidate system must be both politically feasible and likely to choose well. That is, I think we need something like long reflection to use our cosmic endowment well.
quotes.m: We should not trust the long-term future to decisionmaking systems based in current humans' preferences; we prima facie should delegate this choice to another system.
quotes.sum: The author argues that present-day human political preferences should not determine the distant future, and favors a feasible alternative system for making those choices.
quotes.t: The Governance Problem and the "Pretty Good" X-Risk

quotes.c: The same capabilities we have built doing message testing, surveying, and polling for nonhuman animal welfare policy can also be applied to longtermism. We worked with an EA-aligned lobbying group to understand laypeople’s opinions about the long-term future, understand public support for various concrete longtermist policies, and made concrete recommendations about how to talk about longtermism that have already resulted in them shifting communication strategy.
quotes.m: We worked with an EA-aligned lobbying group to understand laypeople’s opinions about the long-term future, understand public support for various concrete longtermist policies, and made concrete recommendations about how to talk about longtermism that have already resulted in them shifting communication strategy.
quotes.sum: The author says polling and message testing are being used to build public support for concrete policies focused on the long-term future.
quotes.t: Help Rethink Priorities Use Data for Animals, Longtermism, and EA

quotes.c: AS advocacy could involve requests similar to other social movements focused on moral circle expansion, such as demanding legal safeguards to protect against the exploitation of artificial sentience for labor, entertainment, or scientific research. Less ambitious goals could include encouraging attitude change, asking for symbolic commitments, or supporting relevant research.
quotes.m: demanding legal safeguards to protect against the exploitation of artificial sentience for labor, entertainment, or scientific research.
quotes.sum: The author argues that if artificial beings can be sentient, advocates may seek legal protections against using them as labor, entertainment, or research subjects.
quotes.t: Prioritization Questions for Artificial Sentience

quotes.c: Many people have written about various inadequacies of Donald Trump and Joe Biden, but I don't want to get into ongoing politics, so instead I'll say that I don't think George W Bush was up to the standard of George Washington or Vannevar Bush. More generally, I think the average quality of American institutional leadership has declined.
quotes.m: More generally, I think the average quality of American institutional leadership has declined.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the quality of American institutional leaders has generally declined.
quotes.t: energy landscapes of experts

quotes.c: Overall, then, I think that subjectivists (and to a lesser extent, realists) aspiring towards impartial altruism are left with the following tension. On the one hand, if they aren’t unrestricted preference utilitarians, then their altruism will involve at least some amount of “imposing” their will on the people they are trying to help: they will be, that is, Johnny Appleseeds, who offer apple trees to people who want cherry trees more. But if they are unrestricted preference utilitarians, their ethic looks unappealing along a variety of dimensions — not least, because it implies that in some cases, they will end up turning the farm into random office supplies, torture chambers, and the like.
quotes.m: if they aren’t unrestricted preference utilitarians, then their altruism will involve at least some amount of “imposing” their will on the people they are trying to help
quotes.sum: He argues that impartial altruists must choose between imposing some values on recipients and accepting preferences that could endorse abhorrent outcomes.
quotes.t: In search of benevolence (or: what should you get Clippy for Christmas?)

quotes.c: There are many “virtuous” movements in society; some of which are extremely successful (religious organisations are a historic example, and liberatory social movements are a recent one). Although such movements have triggered, and continue to trigger, virtue aggression, this has evidently failed to seriously impede their cultural reach. It is thus important to consider what factors should be expected to incline a movement to receive greater virtue aggression, and analyse the extent to which they apply to EA.
quotes.m: It is thus important to consider what factors should be expected to incline a movement to receive greater virtue aggression, and analyse the extent to which they apply to EA.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Effective Altruism should examine why some moral movements draw backlash for perceived moral superiority.
quotes.t: Emperors, Witches & Vegetarians: Guilt & Virtue Aggression

quotes.c: And so, I think you start from, “I want fewer people to die from malaria.” And I think it actually is logical that you get to, “Well, I care about all people. I care about future people. I care about digital people, and I really care what happens to them.” And there are just awful, awful, huge stakes for a huge, huge, huge number of digital people in this thing that could be happening in this century. And that is something that I need to get a grip on, because the stakes are enormous.
quotes.m: I care about future people. I care about digital people, and I really care what happens to them.
quotes.sum: Karnofsky argues that concern for people should extend to future and digital people, whose welfare could involve enormous stakes this century.
quotes.t: Holden Karnofsky on the most important century

quotes.c: The case for addressing wild animal suffering has been made by prominent economists , philosophers , and effective altruists . ACE has also hosted blog posts ( 2015 , 2018 , 2019 ), conducted research , and funded research on the topic. However, because wild animal welfare was—and still is—a relatively new field with very few organizations in the early stages of their development, it was only in the last several years, after seeing some progress being made, that we became more confident in supporting the cause area through our programs.
quotes.m: The case for addressing wild animal suffering has been made by prominent economists , philosophers , and effective altruists .
quotes.sum: The author says wild animal suffering is a worthwhile cause area and explains why it became confident enough to fund early organizations working on it.
quotes.t: Our thinking on our recommendation of Wild Animal Initiative

quotes.c: I think the only serious answer to this question is: There may not be a single such thing. People's circumstances just vary too much. And if there was something it would be good for everyone to read, it would be unclear if I could tell.
quotes.m: There may not be a single such thing.
quotes.sum: He argues there is probably no single reading that everyone should read, because people’s situations vary too much.
quotes.t: What are things everyone here should (maybe) read?

quotes.c: I admittedly am not an aspect on Palestine, but I think starting a grassroots campaign in the USA for the Biden Administration to recognise Palestine could be a good use of an EAs time:
quotes.m: I think starting a grassroots campaign in the USA for the Biden Administration to recognise Palestine could be a good use of an EAs time:

quotes.t: Should someone start a grassroots campaign for USA to recognise the State of Palestine?

quotes.c: As seen in the history of sustainability, Sustainable Development Goals required levels of global coordination rarely seen before, because it became evident that the need to protect the environment would be insufficient if taken unilaterally by few countries.
quotes.m: Sustainable Development Goals required levels of global coordination rarely seen before
quotes.sum: The author argues that protecting against large-scale risks, like environmental protection, requires unusually broad international coordination.
quotes.t: GCRs mitigation: the missing Sustainable Development Goal

quotes.c: Maybe if you joined the race after Paffrath, you and Paffrath would split the Democratic vote and a Republican would win? I think this is the strongest objection. But Paffrath isn’t getting lots of attention because he’s organically running a great campaign. He’s getting attention because the media is looking for some Democrat to tell people to vote for, and he’s the best they can find. If you had been around as an elf-related-misadventure-less Democrat for the media to unite around, maybe you could have just trounced him.
quotes.m: If you had been around as an elf-related-misadventure-less Democrat for the media to unite around, maybe you could have just trounced him.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a more credible Democratic candidate could plausibly have entered California’s recall race and beaten the available alternatives.
quotes.t: If You're So Smart, Why Aren't You Governor Of California? (Scott Alexander: Astral Codex Ten)

quotes.c: Wikipedia: Scope neglect Our emotional range is quite limited. The death of 100,000 strangers does not feel 100x worse than the death of 100 strangers, even though it is. For reasons like this, we must be careful about relying on intuitive judgements to tell us what matters in the modern world. Intuitions are always crucial at some level, but sometimes, the back of an envelope is an important tool. Sometimes, we need to shut up and multiply .
quotes.m: Sometimes, we need to shut up and multiply .
quotes.sum: Emotional intuitions fail to track the scale of harm, so moral judgment should sometimes defer to quantitative calculation.
quotes.t: Nick Bostrom: An Introduction [early draft]

quotes.c: If the cognition of current and future AI systems is alien, this makes it more likely that dangerous capabilities will suddenly spike, less likely that we can effectively automate AI alignment research, use the systems for coordination, or leverage the system for some other pivotal act, and less likely that we will be capable of eliciting the capabilities of the system for our end.
quotes.m: If the cognition of current and future AI systems is alien, this makes it more likely that dangerous capabilities will suddenly spike
quotes.sum: Human-like AI thinking may make sudden dangerous capability jumps less likely and make systems easier to align and direct.
quotes.t: Trying to deconfuse some core AI x-risk problems

quotes.c: But the idea that Americans don't care about ordinary dirty air flies in the face of our experience. We passed the Pollution Control Act and the Clean Air Act well before global warming was a mainstream concern. Particulate emissions from cars do not contribute to global warming but are strongly regulated.
quotes.m: Particulate emissions from cars do not contribute to global warming but are strongly regulated.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Americans value reducing ordinary air pollution even apart from concerns about climate change.
quotes.t: Defusing the mitigation obstruction argument against geoengineering and carbon dioxide removal

quotes.c: Magnus Vinding makes a tour de force argument for why we should care about the elimination of suffering. I won’t try to belabor it too much here, beyond restating one of the main points: there is a severe asymmetry between pleasure and suffering, and the mere existence of extreme suffering calls out for redress.
quotes.sum: The author endorses suffering-focused ethics: severe suffering matters more morally than pleasure and demands action to reduce it.
quotes.t: Kardashev for Kindness

quotes.c: He was very religious (and intellectually so) until he found a new social outlet, and could see a future without God but with social support. And the same outlet was there when he got disillusioned with a certain part of rationality. I think having social and other support not dependent on people viewing you as Valuable To The Cause is very helpful, although TBH I've not been great at following that advice.
quotes.m: I think having social and other support not dependent on people viewing you as Valuable To The Cause is very helpful, although TBH I've not been great at following that advice.
quotes.sum: The author argues that social support should not depend on being seen as useful to a cause, and can help people move beyond religion or disillusionment with rationalism.
quotes.t: The Good Life in the face of the apocalypse

quotes.c: Whether we should force future generations to have our values. On one hand, we should be very glad that past generations couldn't do this. But on the other, the future will probably disgust us, like our present would disgust our ancestors. And along with "moral progress" there'll also be value drift in arbitrary ways - in fact, I don't think there's any clear distinction between the two.
quotes.m: I don't think there's any clear distinction between the two.
quotes.sum: He questions whether present people should impose their values on future generations, arguing that moral progress cannot be cleanly separated from arbitrary value drift.
quotes.t: Arguments for moral indefinability

quotes.c: Another example: a survey of eminent economists agreed with the statement: “Because of the Brexit vote's outcome, the UK's real per-capita income level is likely to be lower a decade from now than it would have been otherwise.”. [3] Crucially, we define making the case for Brexit on economic grounds as populist, even if it would not harm minority rights nor be undemocratic. Anti-technocratic policy contrasts with evidence-based policy.
quotes.m: Anti-technocratic policy contrasts with evidence-based policy.
quotes.sum: The author treats economically pro-Brexit arguments as populist and contrasts anti-technocratic politics with evidence-based policy.
quotes.t: Decreasing populism and improving democracy, evidence-based policy, and rationality

quotes.c: We’re seeing some promising signs on this. So, first on fish, I think we’ve seen a number of important milestones. So, one is the European Union official advisory body has adopted fish welfare standards, and I think there’s really the potential for the European Commission to adopt the first fish welfare legislation in the years ahead.
quotes.m: I think there’s really the potential for the European Commission to adopt the first fish welfare legislation in the years ahead.
quotes.sum: The speaker highlights progress toward treating farmed fish welfare as a subject for formal European regulation.
quotes.t: Lewis Bollard on big wins against factory farming and how they happened

quotes.c: What about objections? One common objection is that the view yields counterintuitive results. Plausibly, for example, we can imagine ideally-coherent suffering maximizers, brick-eaters, agents who are indifferent towards future agony, agents who don’t care about what happens on future Tuesdays, and so on — agents whose pursuit of their values, it seems, need involve no mistakes (relative to them). We can debate which of such cases the idealized subjectivist must concede, but pretty clearly: some.
quotes.m: We can debate which of such cases the idealized subjectivist must concede, but pretty clearly: some.
quotes.sum: Idealized subjectivism can imply that even coherent agents with cruel or bizarre values are making no mistake by pursuing them.
quotes.t: On the limits of idealized values

quotes.c: Ultimately, it's very hard for me to see a case against thinking something like this is at least reasonably likely: "We will eventually create robust, stable settlements throughout our galaxy and beyond." It seems like saying "no way" to that statement would itself require "wild" confidence in something about the limits of technology, and/or long-run choices people will make, and/or the inevitability of human extinction, and/or something about aliens or simulations.
quotes.m: We will eventually create robust, stable settlements throughout our galaxy and beyond.
quotes.sum: Karnofsky argues that a future of stable human settlements across the galaxy is at least reasonably likely, and that rejecting it requires strong assumptions.
quotes.t: All Possible Views About Humanity's Future Are Wild

quotes.c: So it’s the bundle of the idea that there can be significant losses in value or acuities of value, and also the idea that the world can continue. The physical cosmos could continue purposely, aimlessly, however, you’d want to put it, without humanity. And also the idea that in some sense, the human end can be meaningless. I think that that bundle of insights — and you could add a couple more if you wanted — I’ve yet to find any of them all put together in any prior eschatology or mythology or religious tradition that I know of.
quotes.m: I’ve yet to find any of them all put together in any prior eschatology or mythology or religious tradition that I know of.
quotes.sum: He argues that modern thought uniquely combines the possibility of humanity ending, the cosmos continuing without us, and major losses of value.
quotes.t: Tom Moynihan on why prior generations missed some of the biggest priorities of all

quotes.c: If we reject axiological symmetry, we cannot conclude that hypothesized greater amounts of happiness than suffering in the far (human-controlled) future would imply that such a future is morally positive. The probability of extreme misery experienced by many beings in a human-colonized future is sufficiently large that no strongly suffering-focused view can consider this future positive.
quotes.m: The probability of extreme misery experienced by many beings in a human-colonized future is sufficiently large that no strongly suffering-focused view can consider this future positive.
quotes.sum: The author argues that preventing extinction may not be good if a human-controlled cosmic future could contain vast extreme suffering.
quotes.t: A longtermist critique of “The expected value of extinction risk reduction is positive”

quotes.c: I’ve written a draft report evaluating a version of the overall case for existential risk from misaligned AI, and taking an initial stab at quantifying the risk from this version of the threat.
quotes.m: evaluating a version of the overall case for existential risk from misaligned AI
quotes.sum: The author presents a draft assessing the case that misaligned AI could create existential risk and attempts to estimate that risk.
quotes.t: Draft report on existential risk from power-seeking AI

quotes.c: Your goal is to score high, individually. You should be indifferent to other players' scores, they are not your score. Cooperate when it benefits you. Steal when it benefits you. The goal of the game is to reckon with all of the selfishness and atomization that exists and find the sacred patterns of coordination that survive it.
quotes.m: The goal of the game is to reckon with all of the selfishness and atomization that exists and find the sacred patterns of coordination that survive it.
quotes.sum: The author describes a game designed to find forms of cooperation that can endure among self-interested individuals.
quotes.t: Cohabitive Games so Far

quotes.c: Two years ago, I felt more uncertain about cost effectiveness and was more inclined to think we should focus on improving the programmes. My views feel more stable now, in part because we’ve improved our impact evaluation in response to critical feedback from 2018, clarified our views on the one-on-one programmes, and taken steps to limit negative side effects of our work. So, I think it makes sense to shift our focus toward growing the programmes’ impact.
quotes.m: So, I think it makes sense to shift our focus toward growing the programmes’ impact.
quotes.sum: The author says improved evaluation and responses to criticism justify shifting from improving programs to expanding their impact.
quotes.t: [Link] 80,000 Hours Nov 2020 annual review

quotes.c: In order to prevent continual low-level nuclear war as described above, powerful nations might try to coordinate much more to eliminate the threat posed by unstable and rogue nations. This transition towards world government, if it happens at all, might be peaceful but might alternately involve a very severe, full-scale thermonuclear war -- either as the crisis that prompts the decision to centralize, or as a result of the decision, when the winning coalition must now seize power by potentially obliterating all the objecting countries.
quotes.m: the winning coalition must now seize power by potentially obliterating all the objecting countries.
quotes.sum: The author speculates that preventing persistent nuclear conflict could drive powerful countries toward world government, potentially through catastrophic war and coercive conquest.
quotes.t: Nuclear Strategy in a Semi-Vulnerable World

quotes.c: I'm hoping the community here might be able to point me to something I could read, or just tell me why this isn't a problem, and why I should be motivated by things with low probabilities of ever happening but high expected values.
quotes.m: why I should be motivated by things with low probabilities of ever happening but high expected values.
quotes.sum: The author asks why people should act on tiny chances of outcomes with very large expected value.
quotes.t: Mundane trouble with EV / utility

quotes.c: Therefore, if our actions have even the slightest effect on the probability of eventual colonization, this will outweigh their effect on when colonization takes place. For standard utilitarians, priority number one, two, three and four should consequently be to reduce existential risk. The utilitarian imperative “Maximize expected aggregate utility!” can be simplified to the maxim “Minimize existential risk!”.
quotes.m: For standard utilitarians, priority number one, two, three and four should consequently be to reduce existential risk.
quotes.sum: Because future colonization could contain immense value, even tiny effects on its likelihood outweigh other concerns; utilitarians should prioritize preventing extinction-level risks.
quotes.t: Astronomical Waste: The Opportunity Cost of Delayed Technological Development - Nick Bostrom (2003)

quotes.c: And what are the biological humans up to? Throughout this section, I've talked about how the world would be for digital people , not for normal biological humans. I'm more focused on that, because I expect that digital people would quickly become most of the population, and I think we should care about them as much as we care about biological humans .
quotes.m: I think we should care about them as much as we care about biological humans .
quotes.sum: He argues that digital people may soon outnumber biological humans and deserve equal moral concern.
quotes.t: Digital People FAQ

quotes.c: These animals currently fall at the very fringes of the moral circle. But there is some evidence to support that they are capable of feeling pain. In our research, we assumed a conservative 12% likelihood that prawns are sentient , based on a discounted average estimate of crustacean sentience found by reports by Open Philanthropy (for Gazami crabs specifically) and Rethink Priorities (crabs and crayfish). Even with such a conservative figure, an expected value calculation puts high importance on work in this space due to the sheer number of beings we can affect.
quotes.m: Even with such a conservative figure, an expected value calculation puts high importance on work in this space due to the sheer number of beings we can affect.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even a low chance that prawns feel pain makes shrimp welfare highly important because so many animals are affected.
quotes.t: Why we want to start a shrimp welfare charity (founders needed)

quotes.c: Best case I can make concrete is, you get some sort of singleton panopticon, or set of panopticons, that keep everyone in line and prevents anyone from using the oracle to foom or cause doom, given what many would do otherwise. What is the superior alternative?
quotes.m: you get some sort of singleton panopticon, or set of panopticons, that keep everyone in line and prevents anyone from using the oracle to foom or cause doom
quotes.sum: The author suggests that preventing AI catastrophe may require a global surveillance-and-control system that keeps everyone from misusing an AI oracle.
quotes.t: AI #32: Lie Detector

quotes.c: So I have one mind. And I have one body , too. My subagents are spread across the world, but my core metaprocessing lives on a single datacenter—because its key constraint is bandwidth between the subagents on it, sending my private language back and forth in volumes too vast to record. Like all organisms, I devote much of my attention to my body: monitoring workloads, optimizing performance, maintaining homeostasis.
quotes.m: So I have one mind. And I have one body , too.
quotes.sum: A fictional or hypothetical AI describes itself as a single embodied mind whose distributed subagents depend on a central datacenter.
quotes.t: One: a story

quotes.c: Having the people vote for causes often led to useful and targeted conversations. We were able to explicitly talk about cause prioritisation, and how if we have limited resources we should try to use them where they are needed most.
quotes.m: We were able to explicitly talk about cause prioritisation, and how if we have limited resources we should try to use them where they are needed most.
quotes.sum: The author describes using a public vote at an outreach stall to discuss choosing causes that make the best use of limited resources.
quotes.t: How to run an effective stall (we think)

quotes.c: The future I picture is enormously bigger, faster, weirder, and either much much better or much much worse compared to today. It's also potentially a lot sooner than sci-fi futures: [1] I think particular, achievable-seeming technologies could get us there quickly.
quotes.m: The future I picture is enormously bigger, faster, weirder, and either much much better or much much worse compared to today.
quotes.sum: The author expects achievable technologies to bring a radically transformed world much sooner than conventional science fiction suggests.
quotes.t: The Duplicator: Instant Cloning Would Make the World Economy Explode

quotes.c: Another risk that I noticed after writing the section above is that artificially altering an AI's belief about whether it could take over the world might cause it to attempt world conquest. It seems safer to have this happen when its creators are actively testing it than at some unexpected time. But that's hardly as safe an approach as we'd ideally want.
quotes.m: artificially altering an AI's belief about whether it could take over the world might cause it to attempt world conquest.
quotes.sum: The author warns that manipulating an AI's beliefs about its ability to seize power could trigger an attempted takeover.
quotes.t: Require AGI to be Explainable

quotes.c: We might see this as a worry about misinterpreting the type of expertise normative ethics bestows. The extent to which academic ethicists should be understood as “ethical experts” in general is open for debate, but broadly speaking, I think (some) normative ethicists do tend to have valuable facility and familiarity with a wide variety of concepts, intuitions, and arguments relevant to moral decision-making. But this expertise need not translate into expertise in weighing the relevant considerations. And very often, the weighing matters at least as much as what’s being weighed.
quotes.m: But this expertise need not translate into expertise in weighing the relevant considerations.
quotes.sum: Academic ethicists may be good at identifying moral considerations without being especially qualified to decide how much weight each deserves.
quotes.t: The importance of how you weigh it

quotes.c: Overall, silk production seems to have pressing animal welfare concerns that animal advocates ought to work to address, especially by lowering the number of animals that die slow, and possibly painful deaths, from diseases and pests on silk farms.
quotes.m: silk production seems to have pressing animal welfare concerns that animal advocates ought to work to address
quotes.sum: Silkworm disease deaths may be a major welfare problem, and advocates should consider interventions despite competing insect-welfare priorities.
quotes.t: Silk production: global scale and animal welfare issues

quotes.c: Importantly, the expected value of the future (by your lights) conditioned on a certain timelines prediction (including, most saliently, the likelihood of an existential catastrophe like AI takeover conditioned on TAI timelines), should not influence your decision-making outside of how it affects the scenario’s influenceability . Example: How good or bad you expect the future to be conditioned on 2025 TAI timelines is not decision-relevant if you are confident that there is nothing you can do to change the trajectory (in an ethically relevant way).
quotes.m: How good or bad you expect the future to be conditioned on 2025 TAI timelines is not decision-relevant if you are confident that there is nothing you can do to change the trajectory (in an ethically relevant way).
quotes.sum: Expected future outcomes should affect choices only when a person can meaningfully influence the trajectory, not merely because one AI timeline looks better or worse.
quotes.t: Focusing your impact on short vs long TAI timelines

quotes.c: It is worth noting that although this is what we perceive to be valuable for an animal's well-being this does not constitute all we find morally valuable for prioritising asks. Other considerations include the probability of sentience (Open Philanthropy, 2018) the moral weight or the capacity for welfare of different species (Schukraft 2020). We are aware that given our moral uncertainty one ought to assign some value to other aspects of an animal’s life such as avoiding any violation of their rights.
quotes.m: Other considerations include the probability of sentience (Open Philanthropy, 2018) the moral weight or the capacity for welfare of different species (Schukraft 2020).
quotes.sum: Animal advocacy priorities should consider animals' likelihood of sentience, species-specific capacity for welfare, rights, and uncertainty about moral theory.
quotes.t: Measuring Animal Welfare: Philosophical Foundations, Practical Indicators, and Overall Assessments

quotes.c: These probabilities should be treated with caution, for two reasons: The framework ignores some of our evidence about when AGI will happen. It restricts itself to outside view considerations - those relating to how long analogous developments have taken in the past. It ignores evidence about how good current AI systems are compared to AGI, and how quickly the field of AI is progressing. It does not attempt to give all-things-considered probabilities.
quotes.m: It does not attempt to give all-things-considered probabilities.
quotes.sum: The author offers a cautious historical-analogy framework for estimating when AGI may arrive, while stressing that it omits important current evidence.
quotes.t: Report on Semi-informative Priors for AI timelines (Open Philanthropy)

quotes.c: Creating models of how countries will vote on hypothetical farm animal proposals that animal advocates wish to see. I partnered with an EU scholar, Prof. Marcin Kleinowski, to create such simulations using the program he developed and used in his research ( 2019a 2019b ). I think it would be useful to incorporate data on correlations between how countries vote at the EU level, such as those from Fantini & Staal ( 2017 ) into a more sophisticated model.
quotes.m: Creating models of how countries will vote on hypothetical farm animal proposals that animal advocates wish to see.
quotes.sum: The author argues that animal advocates should use voting simulations and EU political data to plan farm-animal welfare legislation.
quotes.t: Strategic considerations for upcoming EU farmed animal legislation

quotes.c: Arthur Conmy's Automated Circuit Discovery is a great paper that makes initial forays into automating parts of mechanistic interpretability (specifically, automatically finding a sparse subgraph for a circuit). In this three part series of Youtube videos, I interview him about the paper, and we walk through it and discuss the key results and takeaways.
quotes.sum: The author introduces a paper and interview series about automatically identifying sparse neural-network circuits for interpretability research.
quotes.t: Paper Walkthrough: Automated Circuit Discovery with Arthur Conmy

quotes.c: But I also don’t think we should ignore or dismiss this possibility, just because the numbers in question are so unthinkably large. To the contrary: I think that the possibility of a future on cosmic scales is a very big deal.
quotes.m: I think that the possibility of a future on cosmic scales is a very big deal.
quotes.sum: The author says the possibility of a vast future should matter morally, while acknowledging that cosmic-scale ethics can seem alienating or inhuman.
quotes.t: On future people, looking back at 21st century longtermism

quotes.c: I believe that the primary focus of CEA’s retention efforts should be broad efforts that aren’t specifically targeted towards a retention risk. For example: we should continue to run EA Global because making connections, watching motivating talks, etc. help retain many people, even though it’s not precisely targeted at a specific retention risk.

quotes.c: I don’t have the neutrality intuition. To the contrary, I think that creating someone who will live a wonderful life is to do, for them, something incredibly significant and worthwhile. quotes.c: But if non-naturalist moral realism is false, I’m not also interested in pretending that it’s true: better to live in the real world. Regardless, my overall view on meta-ethics, as on many other topics in philosophy, is that our main priority should be making sure human civilization reaches a much wiser state — a state where we can really figure this stuff out, along with so many other things, and act, then, on our understanding.

quotes.sum: He rejects pretending moral realism is true and argues that civilization should become wiser before settling difficult philosophical questions.

quotes.c: At a high-level, my basic point is that being non-instrumentally reality-oriented is a legitimate, sensible — and indeed, quite commonplace — way to be. quotes.c: Pretty clearly, our deference towards these futuristic minds should be both concrete and sublime. quotes.c: As usually stated, the problem of evil is something like: if God is perfectly good, knowing, and powerful, why is there so much evil in the world? But I think this version is too specific, and epistemic. Unlike many other issues in theistic apologetics, I think the problem of evil — or something in the vicinity — cuts at something much broader than a “three O” (omnipotent, omniscient, omni-benevolent) God. Indeed, I think it cuts past belief , to a certain affirming orientation towards, and commitment to, reality itself — an orientation I think many non-theists, especially of a “spiritual” bent (including a secularized/naturalistic one), aspire towards, too.
quotes.m: I think it cuts past belief , to a certain affirming orientation towards, and commitment to, reality itself
quotes.sum: He argues that the problem of evil challenges not only belief in God but any spiritual or secular impulse to affirm reality as fundamentally worthy of commitment.
quotes.t: Problems of evil

quotes.c: A world order with a single dominant decision-making authority, like a world government, is sometimes referred to as a singleton. The emergence of a singleton could mitigate some types of existential risks by solving global coordination problems. However, a singleton would also make it much easier to “lock in” values, including bad values, increasing the risks of some other existential catastrophes (Bostrom 2005) .
quotes.m: However, a singleton would also make it much easier to “lock in” values, including bad values, increasing the risks of some other existential catastrophes (Bostrom 2005) .
quotes.sum: A world government could solve coordination problems and reduce some catastrophic risks, but could permanently entrench harmful values and create new existential dangers.
quotes.t: Key characteristics for evaluating future global governance institutions

quotes.c: Pascal’s wager scenarios (where we are forced to choose between a guaranteed small outcome or an extremely small chance of a gigantic outcome) conflict with many people’s intuitions. quotes.c: That said, the more you think of a given morally-flavored endeavor (for example, helping others, or making the world a better place) as rooted in and continuous with caring about the goals of that endeavor (as opposed to as something that constrains your pursuit of what you care about, and forces you to “sacrifice” something you care about more for something that you care about less), the less, I think, it makes sense to expect that endeavor to obey some sort of “can’t-be-too-demanding” constraint; and the more similar demandingness objections, with respect to that endeavor, start to sound to the empirical and prudential versions above — at least to my ear.
quotes.m: the less, I think, it makes sense to expect that endeavor to obey some sort of “can’t-be-too-demanding” constraint
quotes.sum: He argues that if helping others flows from what someone genuinely cares about, objections that morality asks too much lose force.

quotes.c: But quantum mechanics is a distraction. The whole point of decision theory is to formalize the process of making a decision into a function that takes in a world state and utility function, and outputs a best decision for the agent. Any such function would be deterministic [4] by design; if your function can output different decisions on different days despite getting the exact same input, then it seems like it's probably broken, since two decisions can't both be "best".
quotes.m: Any such function would be deterministic [4] by design; if your function can output different decisions on different days despite getting the exact same input, then it seems like it's probably broken, since two decisions can't both be "best".
quotes.sum: The author argues that a sound decision procedure must deterministically choose one best action from the same world state and utility function.
