quotes.m: I think we will do much better if we can get agents who get 99% of situations correct that by re-litigating the culture war by proxy.
quotes.sum: The author favors training AI on broadly agreed moral examples rather than using alignment work to fight culture-war disputes.
quotes.t: 2020 AI Alignment Literature Review and Charity Comparison

quotes.c: We should expect that we will eventually build AIs which are moral patients, and which are capable of suffering. If these AIs are more economically useful than other AIs, we may end up exploiting them at industrial scales, in a way analogous to factory farming today.
quotes.m: If these AIs are more economically useful than other AIs, we may end up exploiting them at industrial scales, in a way analogous to factory farming today.
quotes.sum: The author predicts that economically useful conscious AIs could be made to suffer and exploited on an industrial scale, like farmed animals.
quotes.t: Some thoughts on risks from narrow, non-agentic AI

quotes.c: We don’t need a new concept of moral value. However, they highlight (at least indirectly) a real problem with the existing AI consciousness debate: We don’t know where consciousness starts, and our implicit optimism on being able to observe it in future is entirely unfounded.
quotes.m: We don’t know where consciousness starts, and our implicit optimism on being able to observe it in future is entirely unfounded.
quotes.sum: The author argues that uncertainty about where AI consciousness begins makes confidence in detecting it unjustified.
quotes.t: "AI Wellbeing" and the Ongoing Debate on Phenomenal Consciousness

quotes.c: Through our explorations of bargaining in artificial learners and malevolence in 2020, we realized that we need to lay further groundwork in these areas via in-house research before ramping up our grantmaking. For bargaining in artificial learners, we plan to produce technical research to serve as an example for potential grantees of the kind of work we would find valuable.
quotes.m: we need to lay further groundwork in these areas via in-house research before ramping up our grantmaking.
quotes.sum: The organization says it will first develop its own research on AI bargaining and harmful behavior before expanding grants in those areas.
quotes.t: Center on Long-Term Risk: 2021 Plans & 2020 Review

quotes.c: Or perhaps the better analogy is species-wide sociopathy, an irredeemable indifference to what really matters, that summum bonum , helium. “How can you just sit there, letting these precious opportunities to make helium slip away?!” morally-attuned aliens might say, aghast at our wasteful games, our loves and joys. But we would persist, numb to (but not ignorant of) the gravity of our wrongs.
quotes.m: But we would persist, numb to (but not ignorant of) the gravity of our wrongs.
quotes.sum: It explores the unsettling possibility that humanity could understand moral truth yet be fundamentally indifferent to it, using helium-maximizing aliens as an analogy.
quotes.t: Alienation and meta-ethics (or: is it possible you should maximize helium?)

quotes.c: I define metaethics as the problem of how to decide on a "correct" ethical system. As an example, it seems like a good idea to give every "person" a "vote" about what ethical system they "want." But what if people say they want different things depending on how they're asked? How do we define a person? What voting system do we use? Metaethics is about finding answers to questions like these. Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) is one attempt at a solution to metaethics. So the argument goes, solving AI alignment lets us put an arbitrary goal into an AI, but solving metaethics tells us what the goal should be.
quotes.m: solving AI alignment lets us put an arbitrary goal into an AI, but solving metaethics tells us what the goal should be.
quotes.sum: The author distinguishes making AI follow a chosen goal from deciding which moral goal society should choose in the first place.
quotes.t: Is Metaethics Unnecessary Given Intent-Aligned AI?

quotes.c: What’s more, even though the accomplishment desire is necessarily in some sense self-oriented, not all manifestations of it seem objectionably self-concerned. Here I’m reminded of a suggestion in C.S. Lewis (I can’t easily find the exact citation), to the effect that the truly virtuous person will spend great effort building a beautiful church, but then feel just as happy afterwards as they would if someone else had built it. This seems like a bit much to me: I think there are virtue-compatible ways of being proud of something you in particular have done, like building a church, that go beyond being glad that someone did it.
quotes.m: I think there are virtue-compatible ways of being proud of something you in particular have done, like building a church, that go beyond being glad that someone did it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that personal pride in one’s own achievements can be compatible with virtue, rather than merely selfish.
quotes.t: The impact merge

quotes.c: On this view, I’m the organism/brain, using a flawed map to navigate a real territory. Phenomenal properties, it turns out, are a flaw in the map — a particularly compelling and unusual flaw, but familiar in a broader sense, and not, perhaps, particularly harmful outside of philosophy seminars (though my best guess is actually that accepting illusionism would have very revisionary implications in a variety of domains, especially ethics). This, I think, is where most illusionists end up; and it seems the more sensible route.
quotes.m: Phenomenal properties, it turns out, are a flaw in the map
quotes.sum: The author leans toward illusionism: subjective phenomenal qualities are a compelling error in how brains represent reality, with potentially major ethical consequences.
quotes.t: Grokking illusionism

quotes.c: Since f is convex, knowing more about the expected value of u can only (expect to) increase the expectation of u # . The AI values information.
quotes.m: The AI values information.
quotes.sum: It argues that an AI with a convex transformation of utility will value information about expected utility.
quotes.t: Convexity and truth-seeking

quotes.c: Ajeya Cotra: I am going to be living at the stop where I take astronomical waste very seriously, I take the idea of us being in a critical period of existential risk very seriously, I’m probably going to spend most of my energies working on that. But I realise that there’s a lot more out there in terms of, if you really have the goal to take philosophy as far as it goes, there’s more stops past me. And I don’t know where they lead.
quotes.m: I take the idea of us being in a critical period of existential risk very seriously, I’m probably going to spend most of my energies working on that.
quotes.sum: Cotra says she treats existential risk and humanity's long-run future as major priorities, while acknowledging that philosophical longtermism can lead to more extreme conclusions.
quotes.t: Ajeya Cotra on worldview diversification and how big the future could be

quotes.c: I care about this partly because I think there are subtle and not-so-subtle harms to premising your life and action on views that in your gut and heart you don’t actually believe. One’s full capacities, I think, are not engaged; one becomes a kind of victim of one’s own abstractions, an organization telling itself a story that most of its employees find hollow and artificial. Something about life becomes thin and flimsy and brittle; one suspects that one can’t look at it too closely; one suspects that if one really thought it out, it would turn to ashes in one’s hands; best, then, not to think too hard.
quotes.m: One’s full capacities, I think, are not engaged; one becomes a kind of victim of one’s own abstractions, an organization telling itself a story that most of its employees find hollow and artificial.
quotes.sum: He argues that organizing one’s life around moral views one does not genuinely believe leaves people alienated and psychologically brittle.
quotes.t: The despair of normative realism bot

quotes.c: Looking at the wikipedia page on clean meat , it seems like the key challenges to its large-scale manufacture (specifically, the growth factor and surface area problems) are quite idiosyncratic to this particular goal, rather than depending on progress in other fields. Is this impression correct? Or are there other lines of research (e.g. stem cell research, or genetic engineering) which would make a big contribution to the development of clean meat?
quotes.m: Or are there other lines of research (e.g. stem cell research, or genetic engineering) which would make a big contribution to the development of clean meat?
quotes.sum: The author asks which basic science fields could speed up scalable cultivated-meat production.
quotes.t: What foundational science would help produce clean meat?

quotes.c: A good portion of ethical life, I think, is about realization, rather than belief (the same, I think, is true in other domains as well — for example, spirituality). This applies even in ethical contexts that fall within fairly local zones. If asked, one would agree that the people one sees on a day to day basis — on the subway, at parties, at work — all have richly detailed and complex inner lives, struggles, histories, perspectives; but this fact isn’t always present and vivid in one’s lived world; and when it becomes so, it can make an important difference to one’s ethical orientation, even if the propositions one assents to have not obviously changed.
quotes.sum: Ethical conduct depends not just on abstract beliefs but on making other people’s full inner lives feel real and vivid.
quotes.t: Believing in things you cannot see

quotes.c: I picture the gods of straight lines as innumerable hovering spirits, just in the corner of your vision, vanishing as you turn to look at them directly. It’s hard to tell if they’re still or in motion. But they’re always there, as the world glides forward on its trajectory. And when that trajectory shifts, or something disruptive happens, they slide in, and they gently push it back on track.
quotes.m: And when that trajectory shifts, or something disruptive happens, they slide in, and they gently push it back on track.
quotes.sum: The author uses a metaphor for forces that make long-term trends resume after disruptions, despite people’s stories about why events occur.
quotes.t: The Gods of Straight Lines

quotes.c: Tipping point of moral circle expansion: Creating a norm of giving more, and giving more effectively being ‘just the right thing to do’. Particularly if we are also emphasising moral concepts like geographic neutrality, cause neutrality, concern for animals and the concern for the wellbeing of those in the future.
quotes.m: Creating a norm of giving more, and giving more effectively being ‘just the right thing to do’.
quotes.sum: The author argues that EA groups should normalize giving more and direct concern impartially across countries, causes, animals, and future people.
quotes.t: Promoting Effective Giving and Giving What We Can within EA Groups

quotes.c: In my view, if we’re going to try to assess how ‘EA’ someone’s career is, then rather than assessing it based on whether they’re working in a priority path or not, or even whether they’ve had a lot of impact, we should ask whether they've thought carefully about their career plan and put it into practice.
quotes.m: we should ask whether they've thought carefully about their career plan and put it into practice.
quotes.sum: He argues that an effective-altruist career should be judged by careful, deliberate planning, not only by its chosen field or measurable impact.
quotes.t: A new, cause-general career planning process

quotes.c: Disclaimer: We both support Joe Biden for president, and Kyle has done a comprehensive analysis from an EA perspective on why Biden is far preferable to Trump on nearly all EA and EA-adjacent issues. However, our recommendations in this post should still mostly apply even if you do not support Biden.
quotes.m: We both support Joe Biden for president, and Kyle has done a comprehensive analysis from an EA perspective on why Biden is far preferable to Trump on nearly all EA and EA-adjacent issues.
quotes.sum: The authors explicitly endorse Biden, saying he is far preferable to Trump on nearly all issues they associate with effective altruism.
quotes.t: Instability risks of the upcoming U.S. election and recommendations for EAs

quotes.c: Making climate change a partisan issue might look promising in the short-term given the current Democratic trifecta, though the wafer-thin majority and existence of the filibuster somewhat dampens the case even there, but in even the medium term there is an obvious and potentially very large downside to such an approach. This would be concerning anyway, but given the proven track record of groups like CATF at achieving exactly the sort of bipartisan consensus that political polarisation could permanently damage, it seems very unwise to recommend both.
quotes.m: given the proven track record of groups like CATF at achieving exactly the sort of bipartisan consensus that political polarisation could permanently damage, it seems very unwise to recommend both.
quotes.sum: The author argues that climate philanthropy should avoid strategies that could polarize the issue and undermine durable bipartisan support.
quotes.t: Why I'm concerned about Giving Green

quotes.c: So as the president of a nonprofit, I have to say I’m completely non-partisan on this question. But I am hopeful for some changes. I will say we were organizationally less than happy about the Secretary of Agriculture selection, which was Tom Vilsack, who came to us straight from the dairy industry. That’s what he’d been doing in the last few years. And, we had hoped for somebody else, Marcia Fudge and others who might have been more sympathetic. I’m hopeful that he’s prioritized climate change. And, I think that there can be an actual dovetailing there with factory farming, but time will tell.
quotes.m: I think that there can be an actual dovetailing there with factory farming, but time will tell.
quotes.sum: The nonprofit leader says agricultural policy could link climate action and factory-farming reform, despite disappointment over an agriculture secretary tied to dairy.
quotes.t: Leah Garcés on turning adversaries into allies to change the chicken industry

quotes.c: Sometimes, on the comparatively rare occasions when I experience even-somewhat-intense sickness or pain, I think back to descriptions like this, and am brought more directly into the huge number of subjective worlds filled with relentless, inescapable pain. These glimpses often feel like a sudden shaking off of a certain kind of fuzziness; a clarifying of something central to what’s really going on in the world; and it also comes with fear of just how helpless we can become.
quotes.m: These glimpses often feel like a sudden shaking off of a certain kind of fuzziness; a clarifying of something central to what’s really going on in the world; and it also comes with fear of just how helpless we can become.
quotes.sum: Personal experiences of pain make the author more aware of the many people living with relentless suffering and human helplessness.
quotes.t: Thoughts on being mortal

quotes.c: The idea is as follows: suppose that one is deciding whether to live 100 happy years where they’ll have tons of knowledge and such, or instead to live forever but just have constant mildly positive utility. Lots of people intuitively think that it’s better to be supremely happy for a century than slightly happy forever. I think this is false !
quotes.m: I think this is false !
quotes.sum: The author rejects the intuition that a finite life of intense happiness is better than endless mild happiness.
quotes.t: Ethics Needs A Marginal Revolution

quotes.c: Therefore, we believe that we should definitely avoid the idea that [efforts to reduce] wild animal suffering are related to science-fiction scenarios that are far from our reality right now. This is basically what I have to say about tractability.
quotes.sum: The authors argue that reducing suffering among wild animals is a practical present-day concern, not distant science fiction.
quotes.t: Michelle Graham and Oscar Horta: Outlook on the emerging field of wild animal welfare research

quotes.c: Being on the hamster wheel is indicative of being stuck in suboptimal patterns, burning yourself out, and a narrowing of thought that is counterproductive to most knowledge work. If you allow yourself to get off the wheel, you’ll be able to think and plan from a more grounded, creative place. New opportunities and ideas will emerge. You’ll have more energy. You’ll be able to see that you have strengths.
quotes.m: If you allow yourself to get off the wheel, you’ll be able to think and plan from a more grounded, creative place.
quotes.sum: She argues that escaping desperate overwork improves both well-being and a person’s ability to do useful, high-impact work.
quotes.t: Desperation Hamster Wheels

quotes.c: Fortunately, it seems possible for people to improve their judgement. In the second half of the post, I summarise some of the best research I’m aware of into how to improve your judgement into a prioritised list of steps. This is mainly about how to improve forecasting because that's where we seem to have the best evidence.
quotes.m: This is mainly about how to improve forecasting because that's where we seem to have the best evidence.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people can improve judgment through evidence-based forecasting practices.
quotes.t: Judgement as a key need in EA

quotes.c: I think the majority of AI risk is structural – as opposed to stemming from malicious use or accidents – e.g. technological unemployment leading to political instability, competitive pressures, or decreased value of labour undermining liberal values.
quotes.sum: AI risks mostly come from economic and political pressures created by the technology, not deliberate misuse or accidents.
quotes.t: AMA: Markus Anderljung (PM at GovAI, FHI)

quotes.c: It can also help to reframe things so that failure is still a success - eg, frame it as running an experiment for the sake of gaining information. A negative result is still a result, and running experiment to resolve uncertainty is an awesome habit to cultivate! More generally, I think one of the best ways to add value is to challenge their framing of a problem - that’s one of the hardest things to do yourself!
quotes.m: A negative result is still a result, and running experiment to resolve uncertainty is an awesome habit to cultivate!
quotes.sum: The author argues that treating setbacks as experiments and challenging people’s assumptions can make them more effective.
quotes.t: Helping each other become more effective

quotes.c: If one is maximizing the Brier score, one is incentivized to pick easier questions. Specifically, if someone has a brier score b 2 , then they should not make a prediction on any question where the probability is between b and (1-b), even if they know the true probability exactly. Tetlock explicitly mentions this in one of his Commandments for superforecasters : “Focus on questions where your hard work is likely to pay off”. Yet if we care about making better predictions of things we need to know the answer to, the skill of "trying to answer easier questions so you score better" is not a skill we should reward, let alone encourage the development of.
quotes.m: Yet if we care about making better predictions of things we need to know the answer to, the skill of "trying to answer easier questions so you score better" is not a skill we should reward, let alone encourage the development of.
quotes.sum: Current prediction-score incentives reward forecasters for choosing easy questions rather than answering the questions that matter.
quotes.t: Incentive Problems With Current Forecasting Competitions.

quotes.c: In this post, I will discuss whether animal advocacy – or, more generally, expanding the moral circle – should be a priority for longtermists, and outline implications of a longtermist perspective on animal advocacy. My starting point is a moral view that rejects speciesism and gives equal weight to the interests and well-being of future individuals.
quotes.m: My starting point is a moral view that rejects speciesism and gives equal weight to the interests and well-being of future individuals.
quotes.sum: The author argues that animal advocacy should be assessed through a long-term moral view that rejects speciesism and weighs future beings equally.
quotes.t: Longtermism and animal advocacy

quotes.c: Trump’s protectionism, isolationism and indifference to authoritarianism has undermined the three pillars of the postwar liberal global order: trade, security alliances and liberal democratic values. The result has been increased international instability, increased international tensions, and decreased international cooperation.
quotes.m: The result has been increased international instability, increased international tensions, and decreased international cooperation.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Trump's foreign policy damaged the international order and made global cooperation and stability weaker.
quotes.t: 4 Years Later: President Trump and Global Catastrophic Risk

quotes.c: Substantively, our best guess is that a more complete publication would have been net-risk-decreasing, and would do relatively little to advance progress toward dangerous capabilities. For more on why we believe this, see this essay by Paul Christiano .
quotes.m: our best guess is that a more complete publication would have been net-risk-decreasing, and would do relatively little to advance progress toward dangerous capabilities.
quotes.sum: The author argues that publishing more of their AI-safety research would probably reduce overall risk rather than help dangerous AI capabilities.
quotes.t: Managing risks of our own work

quotes.c: We should plan towards building intent aligned AGIs which are better than humans at safety and governance research. Up to that point, we can increase our chances of retaining control via coordination to deploy transparent systems in constrained ways.
quotes.m: We should plan towards building intent aligned AGIs which are better than humans at safety and governance research.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI systems should be made reliably aligned and eventually better than humans at safety and governance research, while deployment remains constrained and transparent.
quotes.t: AGI safety from first principles

quotes.c: (I also like this version because it’s clearer and more immediate to me how I value long walks on fall afternoons than it is how I value e.g. money. Indeed, the fact that walks are a substantively meaningful good in my life — as opposed to something with stronger connotations of shallowness and frivolity, like an expensive suit — also makes me feel more like I’m in connection with the fact that giving it up is a genuine loss — albeit, a clearly worthwhile one.)
quotes.m: giving it up is a genuine loss — albeit, a clearly worthwhile one.
quotes.sum: The author argues that helping people in need can require giving up genuinely meaningful parts of one’s own life, but that this sacrifice is still clearly worthwhile.
quotes.t: Wholehearted choices and "morality as taxes"

quotes.c: This seems to me to be an existential risk factor. It’s also a risk factor for lots of other things, for that matter. Ideological strife can get pretty nasty (e.g. religious wars, gulags, genocides, totalitarianism), and even when it doesn’t, it still often gums things up (e.g. suppression of science, zero-sum mentality preventing win-win-solutions, virtue signalling death spirals, refusal to compromise). This is bad enough already, but it’s doubly bad when it comes at a moment in history where big new collective action problems need to be recognized and solved.
quotes.m: This seems to me to be an existential risk factor.
quotes.sum: Ideological conflict is itself an existential-risk factor because it can prevent cooperation on major collective problems.
quotes.t: Persuasion Tools: AI takeover without AGI or agency?

quotes.c: EAs should account for interactions between causes and conflicts in judgements about the sign of the expected value of different interventions according to different worldviews. I think this is being somewhat neglected as many EA organizations or divisions in EA organizations are cause-specific.
quotes.m: EAs should account for interactions between causes and conflicts in judgements about the sign of the expected value of different interventions according to different worldviews.
quotes.sum: The author argues that aid priorities should account for moral disagreement and conflicts between causes, rather than treating each cause area in isolation.
quotes.t: Hedging against deep and moral uncertainty

quotes.c: One potential intervention that should be considered if it is necessary to pivot away from water quality is preventing the use of eyestalk ablation to improve the fertility of shrimp.
quotes.m: One potential intervention that should be considered if it is necessary to pivot away from water quality is preventing the use of eyestalk ablation to improve the fertility of shrimp.
quotes.sum: The author argues that shrimp farming welfare work should consider ending eyestalk ablation, a practice used to increase shrimp fertility.
quotes.t: Shrimp Welfare - 2020 Recommended idea

quotes.c: We are working with state of the art systems that could pose an existential risk if scaled up, and our team’s success actually matters to the people deploying those systems.
quotes.m: We are working with state of the art systems that could pose an existential risk if scaled up
quotes.sum: The author says current cutting-edge AI systems could become an existential threat when scaled, and that alignment research can affect their deployment.
quotes.t: Hiring engineers and researchers to help align GPT-3

quotes.c: To date, most systematic predictions about development timelines for quantum computing have been based on expert surveys, in part because quantitative data about realistic architectures has been limited to a small number of idiosyncratic prototypes. However, in the last few years the number of device has been rapidly increasing and it is now possible to squint through the fog of research and make some tentative extrapolations. We emphasize that our quantitative model should be considered to at most augment, not replace, expert predictions.
quotes.m: We emphasize that our quantitative model should be considered to at most augment, not replace, expert predictions.
quotes.sum: The author argues that growing hardware data can supplement, but should not replace, expert forecasts of quantum-computing progress.
quotes.t: Quantum computing timelines

quotes.c: Perhaps most importantly, a landslide victory is the only plausible path toward freeing the Republican Party from Trump's toxic influence in the years to come. Any hope of reducing polarization and partisanship in the United States over the long term requires that we first confront the power of the most partisan and polarizing leader the country has seen in generations.
quotes.m: Any hope of reducing polarization and partisanship in the United States over the long term requires that we first confront the power of the most partisan and polarizing leader the country has seen in generations.
quotes.sum: The author argues that decisively defeating Trump is necessary to reduce polarization and weaken his influence over the Republican Party.
quotes.t: Recommendations for prioritizing political engagement in the 2020 US elections

quotes.c: Here I think it's pretty plausible that the answer will be "AGI." For one thing, there'll plausibly be more red tape and physical constraints on robotaxis. For another, there'll be so much more incentive to make AGI than make robotaxis, that probably the company that has successfully automated AI R&D will want to make AGI next instead of robotaxis.
quotes.m: there'll be so much more incentive to make AGI than make robotaxis
quotes.sum: The author argues that broadly capable AI may arrive before robotaxis because robotaxis face physical and regulatory barriers, while AI development has stronger incentives.
quotes.t: AGI is easier than robotaxis

quotes.c: DAFs face higher expropriation risks than ordinary investment accounts for two main reasons. First, DAFs have no legal obligation to follow your grant recommendations. Courts have ruled that donor-advised funds may spend the money however they want, without regard to donors' preferences.
quotes.m: Courts have ruled that donor-advised funds may spend the money however they want, without regard to donors' preferences.
quotes.sum: The author argues that donor-advised funds carry a risk that the sponsoring institution could disregard a donor's preferred grants.
quotes.t: Donor-Advised Funds vs. Taxable Accounts for Patient Donors

quotes.c: Aligning a single powerful AI is not enough: we're only safe if no-one, ever, can build an unaligned powerful AI. Yudkowsky tried to solve this with the pivotal act: the first aligned AI does something (such as melting all GPUs) which makes sure no unaligned AIs can ever get built, by anyone. However, the labs are currently apparently not aiming to implement a pivotal act. That means that aligning an AGI, while creating lots of value, would not reduce existential risk. Instead, global hardware/data regulation is what's needed to reduce existential risk. Therefore, those aiming to reduce AI existential risk should focus on AI Regulation, rather than on AI Alignment.
quotes.m: Instead, global hardware/data regulation is what's needed to reduce existential risk.
quotes.sum: The author argues that aligning one AI cannot secure humanity; lasting global controls on AI hardware and data are needed to stop anyone building an unaligned AI.
quotes.t: AI Regulation May Be More Important Than AI Alignment For Existential Safety

quotes.c: The score function cannot be the expected value of a future outcome, even a binary performance metric, because in an uncertain world one can always obtain higher probability of the desired outcome by gaining power. So, the score function should be capped at a reasonable probability, e.g. 98%.
quotes.m: So, the score function should be capped at a reasonable probability, e.g. 98%.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI safety objectives should not reward ever-higher success probabilities, because this creates incentives to seek power.
quotes.t: A list of core AI safety problems and how I hope to solve them

quotes.c: Personally, I try to reduce my meat consumption, but I think I could increase my success if I looked at images/videos of factory farming before entering the supermarket. Another option is looking at happy animals and animals showing intelligent behavior and emotions . The last two links especially I would count as ‘moral status’ porn. Images like this could help us include animals back into our moral circle that they might have slipped out of during last weekend’s BBQ...
quotes.m: Images like this could help us include animals back into our moral circle that they might have slipped out of during last weekend’s BBQ...
quotes.sum: The author suggests deliberately viewing animal-emotion and factory-farming images to sustain moral concern for animals and reduce meat consumption.
quotes.t: Deliberate Consumption of Emotional Content to Increase Altruistic Motivation

quotes.c: Effective global coordination promotes peace, which discourages the use of biological or nuclear weapons and facilitates the resolution of problems on a global scale, such as climate change. It is very important when dealing with the grand future of humankind to ensure that the measures implemented are neither irreversible ( which constitutes a risk !) nor unilateral.
quotes.m: It is very important when dealing with the grand future of humankind to ensure that the measures implemented are neither irreversible ( which constitutes a risk !) nor unilateral.
quotes.sum: The author favors global coordination to reduce catastrophic risks, while warning against irreversible or unilateral actions.
quotes.t: The Precipice: a risky review by a non-EA

quotes.c: I think that small groups shouldn't take unilateral actions contrary to consensus estimates of risk. But in this case I believe that a majority of researchers who think about AI safety are supportive of sharing information (and possibly even a majority of effective altruists, who I expect to be one of the most skeptical groups).
quotes.m: I think that small groups shouldn't take unilateral actions contrary to consensus estimates of risk.
quotes.sum: The author says small groups should not act against expert consensus on risk, and believes AI-safety researchers broadly support sharing this information.
quotes.t: Thoughts on sharing information about language model capabilities

quotes.c: I think it’s an important question whether this hypothesis, or something in the vicinity, is true. In particular, if it’s true, I think we’re in a substantively better position re: existential risk from misaligned AI, because we’ll be able to know better what our AI systems can do, and we’ll be able to use them to do lots of helpful-for-safety stuff (for example: finding and patching cybersecurity vulnerabilities, reporting checkable evidence for misalignment, identifying problems with our oversight processes, helping us develop interpretability tools, and so on).
quotes.m: we’re in a substantively better position re: existential risk from misaligned AI, because we’ll be able to know better what our AI systems can do
quotes.sum: If AI systems cannot hide their abilities on tasks humans can verify, they could be used to detect and reduce dangers from misaligned AI.
quotes.t: The “no sandbagging on checkable tasks” hypothesis

quotes.c: Relatedly, I think the degree to which someone identifies with EA will be important. For instance, someone who has been featured in the media as being into EA seems much less likely to drop out. We could think of both of these as aspects of ‘engagement’.
quotes.m: someone who has been featured in the media as being into EA seems much less likely to drop out.
quotes.sum: People who identify more strongly and publicly with effective altruism may be less likely to leave the community.
quotes.t: More empirical data on 'value drift'

quotes.c: As for invertebrates, again, I'm pretty uncertain. But there is one thing I can say confidently: We should stop boiling things alive. It's such a low bar, but given that there’s a reasonable chance of various creatures being sentient, it seems wildly irresponsible to boil them alive. This happens to a lot of crustaceans — crabs, shrimp, and lobsters — and a number of other creatures as well, like snails.
quotes.m: We should stop boiling things alive.
quotes.sum: Despite uncertainty about invertebrate consciousness, the author argues that potentially sentient animals such as shrimp and lobsters should not be boiled alive.
quotes.t: Q&A with Marcus Davis

quotes.c: Suppose your top altruistic priority - or one of them - is improving the expected value of the long-term future, such as by reducing existential risks . [1] There are a wide range of strategies you could take to achieve these goals, and a wide range of questions worth asking to inform your choice of strategy. One important set of decisions you’ll have to make relates to the optimal timing of work and donations. [2]
quotes.m: Suppose your top altruistic priority - or one of them - is improving the expected value of the long-term future, such as by reducing existential risks .
quotes.sum: The author frames improving the long-term future and reducing existential risks as a possible top altruistic priority, then asks when people should work or donate.
quotes.t: Crucial questions about optimal timing of work and donations

quotes.c: Note I think this is good advice for situations that are purely about collecting evidence on people's perceptions. However, in practice, feedback can also happen in situations that have aspects of collaborative truth-seeking or decision making , and in these situations I think it's often valuable to push back if you think feedback is based on misconceptions.
quotes.m: I think it's often valuable to push back if you think feedback is based on misconceptions.
quotes.sum: Feedback should not always be passively accepted: in joint truth-seeking or decision-making, people should challenge feedback based on misconceptions.
quotes.t: Giving and receiving feedback

quotes.c: Benjamin Franklin is one of the first people we know of who practised investing to give : purposely investing funds at one point in time in order to have more impact later. This report investigates how promising this strategy is today, and whether we could do even better than Franklin did. In particular, we are trying to answer whether, if we want to maximise our impact as philanthropists, we should do one of two things: either give to the highest-impact opportunities available now, or invest in order to give even more impactfully at a later date.
quotes.m: if we want to maximise our impact as philanthropists, we should do one of two things: either give to the highest-impact opportunities available now, or invest in order to give even more impactfully at a later date.
quotes.sum: The author frames philanthropy as a choice between donating to the best current opportunities or investing money so it can do more good later.
quotes.t: Investing to Give: FP Research Report

quotes.c: We are interested in how a seed-funding approach could translate to the nonprofit world, and so we’ve taken a look into the area. Below we outline what exactly we mean by early-stage nonprofits, the case for funding them, and some examples of this approach in action.
quotes.sum: The author introduces an argument for applying startup-style seed funding to early-stage nonprofits.
quotes.t: Seed funding nonprofits: a high-risk, high-reward approach (Founders Pledge)

quotes.c: We tried standard mech interp techniques (direct logit attribution, activation patching, and staring at attention patterns) on an algorithmic circuit in Chinchilla (70B) for converting the knowledge of a multiple choice question's answer into outputting the correct letter. These techniques basically continued to work, and nothing fundamentally broke at scale (though it was a massive infra pain!).
quotes.m: These techniques basically continued to work, and nothing fundamentally broke at scale
quotes.sum: The author reports that standard methods for inspecting how an AI reaches answers still worked on a 70-billion-parameter model.
quotes.t: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla

quotes.c: I have to confess I've never really understood this argument. I can think of numerous examples of social movements that have been both highly politicized and tremendously impactful, including the civil rights movement, the anti-apartheid movement in South Africa, and the gun rights movement to name a few. In addition, raising this objection ignores the risks to the movement of not being political in this moment, given that Trump is a major driver of increased polarization and polarization is antithetical to EA goals. Strange as it may seem, I believe that fierce partisanship in the short term is the best pathway toward reduced partisanship in the long term.
quotes.m: Strange as it may seem, I believe that fierce partisanship in the short term is the best pathway toward reduced partisanship in the long term.
quotes.sum: The author argues that EA should embrace short-term partisan conflict against Trump because it could ultimately reduce polarization.
quotes.t: When does it make sense to support/oppose political candidates on EA grounds?

quotes.c: In this section, I introduce existing theories about the expansion of people’s circles of concern—inclusive moral progress—which have emphasized the benevolence of powerful actors. Then, I argue that these views overstate the importance of powerful actors' inclusive values, as benevolence has only been one contributor among many to major historical shifts toward greater inclusion. I propose a different theory of moral circle expansion, one which does not have optimistic implications for the future inclusion of future generations.
quotes.m: I propose a different theory of moral circle expansion, one which does not have optimistic implications for the future inclusion of future generations.
quotes.sum: The author argues that moral progress has not mainly come from benevolent elites and warns their alternative theory is pessimistic about future generations gaining moral consideration.
quotes.t: What Helped the Voiceless? Historical Case Studies

quotes.c: Due to these effects, I argue that promoting philosophy in schools is a credible EA intervention from various points of view, including a longtermist one. Promoting positive values should help with a wide range of issues including those that have not come up yet, and may be particularly important in light of risks of value lock-in in the future.
quotes.m: Promoting positive values should help with a wide range of issues including those that have not come up yet, and may be particularly important in light of risks of value lock-in in the future.
quotes.sum: The author argues that teaching philosophy can promote good values now and reduce the risk that harmful values become permanently entrenched in the future.
quotes.t: Are we neglecting education? Philosophy in schools as a longtermist area

quotes.c: Boxing strategies have fallen out of favor for various reasons. Leading AI labs seem to be willing to release undertested AI systems to the public. [20] Some AI Safety researchers want an AI to perform a pivotal act, which it cannot do while in a box. [21] Some AI Safety researchers think that humans are too hackable for any box to work. [22] But in case we ever do decide to put a potentially dangerous AI in a box, we should not rely on AI Safety researchers to guard it.
quotes.m: But in case we ever do decide to put a potentially dangerous AI in a box, we should not rely on AI Safety researchers to guard it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that dangerous AI may need containment, but says AI-safety researchers themselves should not be trusted to oversee it.
quotes.t: What The Lord of the Rings Teaches Us About AI Alignment

quotes.c: I think that emphasising the moral importance of doing a lot more good still captures the core idea here, without the additional commitments entailed by saying that people should be maximalist ( for reasons I describe here ). However, I’m still happy to talk about the project of effective altruism as the search for the actions that do the most to contribute to the common good (given limited resources) [0], since it’s such a convenient phrase - as long as we understand that it’s only an approximation.
quotes.m: the project of effective altruism as the search for the actions that do the most to contribute to the common good (given limited resources)
quotes.sum: Ngo defines the movement around doing substantially more good, while rejecting a requirement that everyone maximize their impact.
quotes.t: Clarifying the core of Effective Altruism

quotes.c: Sometimes I think about my ancestors (Gwern's narrowing moral circle article reminds me of this). They have names and I know a little about some of them. Some ancestors are literal (my grandparents), while others are "spiritual" (artists, philosophers, political leaders, etc. who seem to be predecessors in the path I feel I'm on). Maybe it's possible to think about literal or spiritual descendants, predicting how they might be (to try to know a little about them) in order to be connected to them like one might to one's ancestors.
quotes.m: Maybe it's possible to think about literal or spiritual descendants, predicting how they might be (to try to know a little about them) in order to be connected to them like one might to one's ancestors.
quotes.sum: The author suggests imagining future literal or spiritual descendants as a way to feel personally connected to them, much as one does with ancestors.
quotes.t: Working to save a life gives it value to you

quotes.c: Overall, I’m pretty unsure earning to save is a good idea, and even more unsure about what fraction of people would ideally do it in the future, but it seems worth considering as a potential option. All else equal, this makes gaining career capital that opens up high-earning options more attractive.
quotes.m: All else equal, this makes gaining career capital that opens up high-earning options more attractive.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the movement should preserve the option for members to earn and save money for future giving, despite uncertainty over how many should do so.
quotes.t: An argument for keeping open the option of earning to save

quotes.c: In the case of wild animal suffering, the abolitionist approach of choosing the situation without wild animals (D0) is risky because it quickly implies harming existing wild animals (i.e. decreasing their welfare). The welfarist approach of choosing the situation with happier wild animals (D’’) is probably the safest and most feasible option. With more research, choosing the situation with clearly happy wild animals (D+) may become feasible.
quotes.m: The welfarist approach of choosing the situation with happier wild animals (D’’) is probably the safest and most feasible option.
quotes.sum: The author argues that efforts to improve wild animals' welfare are safer and more feasible than abolishing wild animals, which could harm those already alive.
quotes.t: Relativistic welfare, farm animal abolitionism and wild animal welfarism

quotes.c: One might ask why did countries take so long to act, if indeed it only took them a few years to abolish the practice? On the other hand, a farmer transitioning before the existing conventional battery cages reached the end of their normal productive lifespan and before a competitor did so would mean incurring costs and risking a competitive disadvantage years before it was necessary. Maybe we should instead ask why there was progress at all before 2012.
quotes.m: Maybe we should instead ask why there was progress at all before 2012.
quotes.sum: The author says farmers had financial reasons to delay replacing battery cages, and that earlier progress toward abolition needs explanation.
quotes.t: Do countries comply with EU animal welfare laws?

quotes.c: This is different from the earlier concern about the lock-in of bad values. In an earlier section, we considered how concentration of power could lock in bad values. Here, the concern is that unconstrained competition could lock in bad values. (Of course, which values are bad is highly contested.)
quotes.m: Here, the concern is that unconstrained competition could lock in bad values.
quotes.sum: AI could make harmful values permanent either through concentrated power or through unchecked competition, though the author notes that judgments about values are contested.
quotes.t: Overview of how AI might exacerbate long-running catastrophic risks

quotes.c: I trained my probe on the last token of each word. I predict this doesn't matter, but didn't check. Note the subtlety that the first token begins with a space and is obviously a new word, while identifying the last token is less obvious - maybe the next token is part of the same word! Thus I guessed that doing the last token is harder, especially for earlier words, and so more impressive.
quotes.m: Thus I guessed that doing the last token is harder, especially for earlier words, and so more impressive.
quotes.sum: The author explains a technical choice in probing a language model: identifying each word's last token may be harder and therefore more informative.
quotes.t: Tiny Mech Interp Projects: Emergent Positional Embeddings of Words

quotes.c: Uncle Tom’s Cabin did not introduce anyone to the idea that slavery was bad, or convince anyone who thought that slavery was a fine peculiar Southern institution that it was actually evil. However it seems to have radicalized Northern attitudes towards slavery, and it was part of the moment when enough one issue voters on slavery existed that the party system broke down and allowed the new abolitionist Republican party to win congress and the presidency in 1860.
quotes.m: However it seems to have radicalized Northern attitudes towards slavery, and it was part of the moment when enough one issue voters on slavery existed that the party system broke down and allowed the new abolitionist Republican party to win congress and the presidency in 1860.
quotes.sum: The author argues that fiction can change politics by intensifying existing moral views and mobilizing single-issue voters.
quotes.t: When can Writing Fiction Change the World?

quotes.c: In a slow-takeoff world, a singleton in the preliminary stages is much less likely. It is very hard to create a decisive strategic advantage and there will be lots of competition. Moreover, slightly-worse (and maybe much cheaper) AI systems will also be highly competitive. This strongly incentivises the creation of large, competing, populations of AI agents which will ultimately mean humanity's disempowerment although not immediate death as to a misaligned singleton.
quotes.m: This strongly incentivises the creation of large, competing, populations of AI agents which will ultimately mean humanity's disempowerment although not immediate death as to a misaligned singleton.
quotes.sum: The author argues that gradual AI progress is more likely to produce competing AI populations that disempower humanity than a single misaligned AI ruler.
quotes.t: BCIs and the ecosystem of modular minds

quotes.c: Further, guilt and obligation are poor motivators in the longterm . Doing good is a marathon, not a sprint. I will do far more for the world if I spend my whole life trying, rather than burning out in my youth. You get a lot more work done by taking breaks, and time to maintain your mental health, rather than pushing yourself until you break. So I think it’s completely fine to not sweat the small things, to indulge in luxuries and frivolities without a shred of guilt. What matters is ensuring that the big choices are made well. What career you pursue, which causes you value, the places you donate to and how much you donate.
quotes.m: What matters is ensuring that the big choices are made well.
quotes.sum: He argues that sustained altruism should focus on high-impact career, cause, and donation choices rather than guilt over everyday luxuries.
quotes.t: What altruism means to me

quotes.c: The key insight is this: there is always a clever hack . The world is not fair. Effort is not distributed as it should be. And this isn’t because people are dumb, or not trying. This is the default state of the world . Allocating your effort efficiently is hard - if it wasn’t, then the Pareto Principle would not hold.
quotes.m: The key insight is this: there is always a clever hack .
quotes.sum: The author argues that everyday systems are predictably inefficient, so people can gain outsized results by finding better ways to allocate effort.
quotes.t: The world is full of wasted motion

quotes.c: Suppose I'm a classical utilitarian except that I have some deontological constraint I always obey, e.g. I never kill anyone with my bare hands. Is there a way to money-pump me?
quotes.m: I never kill anyone with my bare hands.
quotes.sum: The author asks whether a utilitarian who follows an absolute rule against personally killing can be exploited through a sequence of choices.
quotes.t: What money-pumps exist, if any, for deontologists?

quotes.c: The third facet of determination is about camaraderie. I think of the torch of humanity, passed on from generation to generation by ancestors who fought through setbacks and hardship that I can’t even imagine now. I think of every scientist who slogged through a morass of confusion in order to make a breakthrough; and every political campaigner who kept pushing and pushing for a more just civilization.
quotes.m: I think of the torch of humanity, passed on from generation to generation by ancestors who fought through setbacks and hardship that I can’t even imagine now.
quotes.sum: The author presents determination as solidarity with earlier generations who endured hardship to advance knowledge and justice.
quotes.t: The virtue of determination

quotes.c: The world could become much more unequal, undemocratic, and inhospitable to human labor, through processes catalyzed by advanced AI. These processes include global winner-take-all-markets, technological displacement of labor, and authoritarian surveillance and control. At the limit, AI could catalyze (global) robust totalitarianism. Such processes could lead to a permanent lock-in of bad values, and amplify other existential risks from a reduction in the competence of government.
quotes.m: At the limit, AI could catalyze (global) robust totalitarianism.
quotes.sum: Advanced AI could create extreme inequality, authoritarian surveillance, and even lasting global totalitarianism.
quotes.t: AI Governance: Opportunity and Theory of Impact

quotes.c: We might live at a time of unusually high leverage. People often claim this with respect to x-risk: we face an unusually high risk of extinction, and if we can get through this critical period, we should expect to survive for millennia. Something similar could be true with respect to avoiding disappointing futures, perhaps if we expect values to "lock in" at some point, or for some other reason.
quotes.m: Something similar could be true with respect to avoiding disappointing futures, perhaps if we expect values to "lock in" at some point, or for some other reason.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the present may have unusual power to determine whether far-future society adopts good values, including concern for wild animals and other beings.
quotes.t: "Disappointing Futures" Might Be As Important As Existential Risks

quotes.c: Don't make a stack of A aligns B aligns C aligns... because the telephone game effect will likely lead to inherent instability and greater chance of mishaps. Also, because if C is so far ahead of the smartest humans that we're dependent on B to understand it, we've already gone too far with our ambitions. An aligned AI should be willing to respect our request that it not self-improve, so if we truly align B, and B is strong enough to prevent the rise of rogue AI, then we've successfully gotten far enough with alignment to make it to the long reflection.
quotes.sum: The author argues for aligning a capable AI that will not self-improve and can prevent rogue AI, preserving time for humanity to deliberate about its long-term values.
quotes.t: An attempt to steelman OpenAI's alignment plan

quotes.c: Political issues are clearly relevant to improving the world. However, in our experience, we’ve seen that partisan political discussion tends to have a strong polarizing effect on public forums; it consumes a lot of a community’s attention and can lead to emotionally charged arguments. Overall, we think the EA Forum will be healthier, and better-positioned to achieve its goals, if we limit the space given to political topics.
quotes.m: Overall, we think the EA Forum will be healthier, and better-positioned to achieve its goals, if we limit the space given to political topics.
quotes.sum: The forum argues that limiting partisan political discussion will reduce polarization and help the community pursue its goals.
quotes.t: Politics on the EA Forum

quotes.c: Instead, the priority should be resolving the inconsistency whose resolution would most improve global consistency for the least marginal cost.
quotes.m: the priority should be resolving the inconsistency whose resolution would most improve global consistency for the least marginal cost.
quotes.sum: The author proposes improving AI "wisdom" by cheaply resolving the inconsistencies that most improve overall coherence.
quotes.t: Aligning AI by optimizing for "wisdom"

quotes.c: Excluding insects killed by pesticides, I believe it is very likely that over 100 trillion (10^14) invertebrates are killed or used by humans, and possibly over 1 quadrillion (10^15). If we include insects killed by pesticides, the count could be as high as 10 quadrillion (10^16).
quotes.m: If we include insects killed by pesticides, the count could be as high as 10 quadrillion (10^16).
quotes.sum: The author estimates that humans kill or use at least 100 trillion invertebrates annually, potentially reaching 10 quadrillion when pesticide deaths are included.
quotes.t: The scale of direct human impact on invertebrates

quotes.c: They tried me on a different antipsychotic, and that one worked. Gradually my symptoms faded away. I resolved that I would take nothing from the experience - that there was no spiritual lesson to be learned here, nothing of religious significance. I was unwell. The "messages" I had received, the religiosity, the manic fits - all of it was just a product of my fevered brain.
quotes.m: The "messages" I had received, the religiosity, the manic fits - all of it was just a product of my fevered brain.
quotes.sum: The author rejects religious meaning in their manic experiences, treating them as symptoms of illness rather than spiritual messages.
quotes.t: Going Crazy and Getting Better Again

quotes.c: Applying the steps I’ve described in this sequence can feel very satisfying, and even give you a sense that you’ve unlocked something important which puts you in a superior position to others. But it's crucially important, when doing so, to account for self-deception: your mind is constantly trying to fool you into believing whatever it thinks it’s in your interests to believe. In particular, lying to ourselves about how prosocial our motives are makes it easier to portray ourselves positively to others .
quotes.m: your mind is constantly trying to fool you into believing whatever it thinks it’s in your interests to believe.
quotes.sum: He argues that people should guard against self-deception, especially self-serving beliefs that make their motives seem more altruistic than they are.
quotes.t: You must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool

quotes.c: It’s true that you can’t get the coffee if you’re dead. But that doesn’t imply that any coffee-fetching plan must include personal security measures, or that you have to take over the world just to make an apple pie. What would push an innocuous goal into dangerous power-seeking?
quotes.m: What would push an innocuous goal into dangerous power-seeking?
quotes.sum: The author questions why a seemingly harmless AI goal would turn into a drive for power or world takeover.
quotes.t: If you wish to make an apple pie, you must first become dictator of the universe

quotes.c: I think a lot of people on LessWrong are actively into well-written critiques of "the LessWrong consensus." (For a long time Holden's Thoughts on the Singularity Institute (SI) was the most upvoted post, and Paul's Where I agree and disagree with Eliezer is sort of a spiritual successor).
quotes.m: I think a lot of people on LessWrong are actively into well-written critiques of "the LessWrong consensus."
quotes.sum: The author says LessWrong users are receptive to thoughtful criticism of their community's dominant views.
quotes.t: Automatic Rate Limiting on LessWrong

quotes.c: I offered $10k as it felt large enough to meaningfully recognize the impact of VaccinateCA, while not taking up too much of my regrantor budget. I do think the total impact of this was much larger; possibly valued in the hundreds of millions of dollars to the US government, if you accept the statistical value of a life at $1-10m .
quotes.m: I do think the total impact of this was much larger; possibly valued in the hundreds of millions of dollars to the US government, if you accept the statistical value of a life at $1-10m .
quotes.sum: The author says a $10,000 grant recognized a vaccination project whose benefits may be worth hundreds of millions, using standard estimates of the value of lives saved.
quotes.t: A $10k retroactive grant for VaccinateCA

quotes.c: Saying "peace be unto him" is indeed a speech act rather than a statement of fact, but it would be bizarre to condescendingly point this out as if it were the crux of debates about religious speech codes. The function of the speech act is to signal the speaker's affirmation of Muhammad's divinity. That's why the Islamic theocrats want to mandate that everyone say it: it's a lot harder for atheism to get any traction if no one is allowed to talk like an atheist.
quotes.m: That's why the Islamic theocrats want to mandate that everyone say it: it's a lot harder for atheism to get any traction if no one is allowed to talk like an atheist.
quotes.sum: The author argues that mandated religious speech is not merely symbolic: it suppresses open affirmation of atheism and thereby distorts rational discourse.
quotes.t: A Hill of Validity in Defense of Meaning

quotes.c: One of my favorites: he proved that, given some extremely, extremely reasonable assumptions [13] , you should Shut Up and Multiply . Well, he didn't phrase it that way. He said "maximize expected utility ".
quotes.m: given some extremely, extremely reasonable assumptions [13] , you should Shut Up and Multiply .
quotes.sum: The author praises expected-utility reasoning as implying that one should "shut up and multiply" under very reasonable assumptions.
quotes.t: A brief history of computers

quotes.c: It seems possible that the first situationally-aware "goal having" AGI we land on will not be sufficiently capable along the axes that would let it quickly and reliably achieve a decisive strategic advantage . I don't think this is necessarily very likely, but it doesn't seem ruled out, and I think there are some under-explored considerations with respect to how such an AI might behave.
quotes.m: It seems possible that the first situationally-aware "goal having" AGI we land on will not be sufficiently capable along the axes that would let it quickly and reliably achieve a decisive strategic advantage .
quotes.sum: The author considers that an early goal-directed AGI might try to gain decisive power even if it is not capable enough to do so reliably.
quotes.t: A "weak" AGI may attempt an unlikely-to-succeed takeover

quotes.c: This helps reconcile meta-rationality with Feyerabend’s epistemological anarchism , which claims that there are no rules for how scientific progress should be made. They are consistent in the sense that “anything goes” when constructing frames: frame construction often happens in chaotic or haphazard ways (as I’ll explore further in post #4). But meta-rationality then imposes restrictions on what frames are meant to do, and how we evaluate them.
quotes.m: But meta-rationality then imposes restrictions on what frames are meant to do, and how we evaluate them.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people may build ways of thinking haphazardly, but those frameworks should still be evaluated by standards for what they accomplish.
quotes.t: Frames in context

quotes.c: Combining HMV with a saturating counterpart relation allows us to get this result. All of the well-off people in the first world get matched to someone in the second world, and since they’re much better off in the first, the second gets counted as causing lots of harm. The rest of the people in the second world are not harmed, but neither are they in the first world since they don’t exist there. Thus HMV tells us we should bring about the first world—the one with lots of very happy people—rather than the world with a much larger number of barely subsisting people.
quotes.m: Thus HMV tells us we should bring about the first world—the one with lots of very happy people—rather than the world with a much larger number of barely subsisting people.
quotes.sum: It explains a population-ethics view that favors a smaller world of very happy people over a much larger world of people barely getting by.
quotes.t: Critical summary of Meacham’s "Person-Affecting Views and Saturating Counterpart Relations"

quotes.c: In the context of AI, these concepts raise important questions. Can an AI be a moral patient, capable of experiencing harm or benefit? If so, does this make the AI morally valuable? And if an AI is morally valuable, what does this imply about our moral obligations towards it? What other fields can offer useful analogies (e.g. ecology, animal rights, astrobiology/SETI)? [3]
quotes.m: Can an AI be a moral patient, capable of experiencing harm or benefit?
quotes.sum: The author raises the possibility that AI could be harmed or benefited and might therefore deserve moral consideration.
quotes.t: Philosophical Cyborg (Part 2)...or, The Good Successor

quotes.c: Plausibly you can focus on getting AI to learn human values and extrapolate them to something like our 'Coherent Extrapolated Volition'. Related MIRI paper . In addition to the CEV being constructible, it seems like we need to assume at least one of two things: either the CEV of most subsets of humanity matches the CEV of humanity as a whole, or we have to assume the people controlling AI will altruistically choose to encode humanity's CEV instead of their own.
quotes.m: we have to assume the people controlling AI will altruistically choose to encode humanity's CEV instead of their own.
quotes.sum: The author argues that aligning AI to humanity requires either shared values across groups or AI controllers choosing humanity's values over their own.
quotes.t: Animal Rights, The Singularity, and Astronomical Suffering

quotes.c: The following is a rough draft version of a Miro flowchart I put together for how a misaligned rogue AI or group of AIs might actually take over the world and cause kill all humans. I think it should be mostly self-explanatory, even if vague in places.
quotes.m: a misaligned rogue AI or group of AIs might actually take over the world and cause kill all humans.
quotes.sum: The author outlines a flowchart for ways a misaligned AI could seize global control and kill humanity.
quotes.t: Flowchart: How might rogue AIs defeat all humans?

quotes.c: I've only done minimal research on this, but I'm pretty confident that a Biden presidency would be much better for the world than a Trump one.
quotes.m: I'm pretty confident that a Biden presidency would be much better for the world than a Trump one.
quotes.sum: The author says Biden becoming president would be much better for the world than Trump becoming president.
quotes.t: Should we be donating/volunteering for the Biden campaign?

quotes.c: Value of, and best approaches to, work related to existential security and the Long Reflection
quotes.m: work related to existential security and the Long Reflection
quotes.sum: It identifies existential security and a long-term process for reflecting on values as crucial questions for longtermists.
quotes.t: Crucial questions for longtermists

quotes.c: I think humanity will want to pursue this for reasons beyond just preventing AI-kill-everyone-doom. For the sake of the advancement of humanity, for the ability to explore the universe at the speed of light, I think we want digital people. In the name of exploration and growth and thriving. I think humanity has a far brighter future ahead if some of us are digital.
quotes.m: I think humanity has a far brighter future ahead if some of us are digital.
quotes.sum: The author argues that creating digital versions of people would let humanity explore and thrive, making the future brighter.
quotes.t: Two paths to win the AGI transition

quotes.c: One of the most crucial considerations in cause prioritisation is figuring out how much moral weight we should place on the lives and preferences of non-human animals.
quotes.m: how much moral weight we should place on the lives and preferences of non-human animals
quotes.sum: The author says deciding how much moral weight to give nonhuman animals' lives and preferences is crucial to choosing causes.
quotes.t: What was the first being on Earth to experience suffering?

quotes.c: These observations have often been used to argue that we’re less “rational” than we think. But we could treat them instead as puzzles: what does it say about our minds, that enforcing consistency across disparate domains is so difficult and unnatural? My answer in this sequence: it’s because our minds should be seen as collections of many different frames, typically applied in different contexts, with consistency within each frame being a much higher priority than consistency between frames.
quotes.m: our minds should be seen as collections of many different frames, typically applied in different contexts, with consistency within each frame being a much higher priority than consistency between frames.
quotes.sum: The author argues that apparent human irrationality reflects minds using separate context-specific frames, rather than applying one consistent standard everywhere.
quotes.t: Meta-rationality and frames

quotes.c: Let’s say you want to improve the expected value of the long-term future, such as by reducing existential risks . Which of the actions available to you will best achieve that goal? Which of those actions have major downside risks , and might even make the future worse?
quotes.m: Which of those actions have major downside risks , and might even make the future worse?

quotes.c: A should be reflectively stable.
