quotes.t: Ben's expenses in 2016

quotes.c: It is taken as a given that stopping humanity from going extinct is a good thing, and I tend to agree, though not as strongly as some (I hold uncertainty about the expected value of the future assuming humanity/life in general survive). However, if we consider different ethical theories, we find that many come up with different answers to the question of what we ought to do in this case.
quotes.sum: The author says preventing extinction is usually assumed to be good, but they are uncertain that a surviving future is necessarily valuable.
quotes.t: The need for convergence on an ethical theory

quotes.c: I'd be keen to see more people take ideas that we think we already know, but haven't ever been put down in writing, and write them up in a thorough and even-handed way; for example, why existential risk from anthropogenic causes is greater than the existential risk from natural causes, or why global health is a particularly promising area within global development.
quotes.m: why existential risk from anthropogenic causes is greater than the existential risk from natural causes
quotes.sum: He calls for careful written arguments supporting EA cause priorities, including the view that human-caused extinction risks outweigh natural ones.
quotes.t: Projects I'd like to see

quotes.c: This means, in turn, that the effective altruism movement should think through carefully whether those end-states are indeed desirable. That depends on host of considerations. We have addressed some of them here, but individual strategic decisions must be decided on a case-by-case basis. If the movement decides that a particular end-state is undesirable, it should reflect on what can be done to prevent us from ending up in it, e.g., through unilateral action.
quotes.m: If the movement decides that a particular end-state is undesirable, it should reflect on what can be done to prevent us from ending up in it, e.g., through unilateral action.
quotes.sum: The author argues that EA should anticipate the long-term outcomes of its growth and strategy, and act to avoid undesirable paths that may become hard to reverse.
quotes.t: Hard-to-reverse decisions destroy option value

quotes.c: For me, taking the pledge wasn’t primarily an act of self-binding (restricting my future self). It was an act of self-determination (choosing which of my potential future selves actually came about). I think it changed my life in a positive way. If I hadn’t taken it, I think it’s very likely that my primary goal now wouldn’t be helping people.
quotes.m: It was an act of self-determination (choosing which of my potential future selves actually came about).
quotes.sum: The author argues that a public charitable pledge can help a person deliberately become someone whose central aim is helping others, rather than merely restricting their future freedom.
quotes.t: The Giving What We Can Pledge: self-determination vs. self-binding

quotes.c: Effective altruists focussed on shaping the far future face a choice between different types of interventions. Of these, efforts to reduce the risk of human extinction have received the most attention so far. In this talk, Max Daniel makes the case that we may want to complement such work with interventions aimed at preventing very undesirable futures ("s-risks"), and that this provides a reason for, among the sources of existential risk identified so far, focussing on AI risk.
quotes.m: we may want to complement such work with interventions aimed at preventing very undesirable futures ("s-risks")
quotes.sum: The post argues that preventing vast future suffering deserves attention alongside preventing extinction, and says this strengthens the case for focusing on AI risk.
quotes.t: Why s-risks are the worst existential risks, and how to prevent them

quotes.c: If the default course of humanity is to be ethical, our prior should be that the future will be good, and the burden of proof shifts to those who believe that the future will be bad.
quotes.m: our prior should be that the future will be good, and the burden of proof shifts to those who believe that the future will be bad.
quotes.sum: The author argues that if humanity is basically ethical by default, we should presume the long-term future is good unless pessimists show otherwise.
quotes.t: An Argument for Why the Future May Be Good

quotes.c: With my donations to additional EA and x-risk organizations, I aim to support groups pursuing other types of work that I think are likely helpful in the cause to address AI x-risk. Some of these include awareness-building, strategic research, political research or activities, or other ways of attacking the problem. I also intend to support work on other existential risks through this bucket.
quotes.m: I aim to support groups pursuing other types of work that I think are likely helpful in the cause to address AI x-risk.
quotes.sum: The author explains that part of her giving supports varied efforts intended to reduce AI and other existential risks.
quotes.t: EAs write about where they give

quotes.c: The movement has some very impressive people, and it can be easy to feel lacking in comparison. While drawing inspiration from other EAs can be motivating, we should remember that what comes easily for one person may be much harder for another. We should try to recognize when comparing ourselves to others becomes counterproductive.
quotes.m: We should try to recognize when comparing ourselves to others becomes counterproductive.
quotes.sum: EA members should avoid unhelpful comparisons with high-achieving peers, since different things come easily to different people.
quotes.t: Making EA groups more welcoming

quotes.c: Donating to the DNC or the Obama/Holder redistricting campaign : This is based on the idea that (1) Democrats are much better than Republicans for global stability / good U.S. policy, and (2) Republicans should be punished for helping Trump to become president. I basically agree with both, and could see myself donating to the redistricting campaign in particular in the future, but this intuitively feels less tractable/underfunded than non-partisan efforts like the Carnegie Endowment or Blue Ribbon Study Panel.
quotes.m: Democrats are much better than Republicans for global stability / good U.S. policy, and (2) Republicans should be punished for helping Trump to become president.
quotes.sum: The author favors Democrats over Republicans for global stability and considers political donations, but prefers nonpartisan policy efforts as more effective.
quotes.t: My Donations for 2016

quotes.c: I believe that invoking “the ends justify the means” (justifying near and clear harms by pointing to their further-out effects) is sometimes the right thing to do, and is sometimes not. Specifically, I think that the worse the “means,” the more robust (and not just large in claimed magnitude) one’s case for “the ends” ought to be.
quotes.m: I believe that invoking “the ends justify the means” (justifying near and clear harms by pointing to their further-out effects) is sometimes the right thing to do, and is sometimes not.
quotes.sum: The author says harmful means can sometimes be justified by distant benefits, but the case must become more robust as the harm gets worse.
quotes.t: Sequence thinking vs. cluster thinking

quotes.c: The Field Foundation had previously worked with Bob Greenstein on a smaller project, and this was apparently an important input into its confidence in him. I think this is a good example of how grantmaking can improve one’s networks and lay the groundwork for future work.
quotes.m: I think this is a good example of how grantmaking can improve one’s networks and lay the groundwork for future work.
quotes.sum: Grantmaking can build relationships and confidence that make later, larger philanthropic work possible.
quotes.t: History of Philanthropy Case Study: The Founding of the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities

quotes.c: 2. Moral concern for animals. If you believe the wellbeing of animals is morally important, then there will probably be pond-like actions. This is because animals have no economic or political power, so are unable to protect their own interests. This will mean we should expect there to be ways to benefit lots of animals with small costs. One simple example is going vegetarian. The average American eats about 100 animals per year, almost all of which live in factory farms, so by going vegetarian you prevent 100 animals from living in terrible suffering each year for a small cost to yourself.
quotes.m: The average American eats about 100 animals per year, almost all of which live in factory farms, so by going vegetarian you prevent 100 animals from living in terrible suffering each year for a small cost to yourself.
quotes.sum: The author argues that animals lack political power, creating unusually cheap opportunities to prevent large amounts of suffering, such as becoming vegetarian.
quotes.t: If you want to disagree with effective altruism, you need to disagree one of these three claims

quotes.c: First, one or more large (and false) propositions are made that provide solid foundation for an ideology , a basket of social reforms justified by the Big Lie(s). Most misconceptions are insufficient tinder for ideologies. An incorrect belief about plumbing doesn't justify a Department for the Correctness of Plumbing, and more importantly isn't very memetic outside of some plumbing association. On the other hand, if you're a first century peasant who believes in the holy origins of Jesus, you've got a lot of work to do.
quotes.m: First, one or more large (and false) propositions are made that provide solid foundation for an ideology , a basket of social reforms justified by the Big Lie(s).
quotes.sum: The author argues that ideologies spread when broad false beliefs give followers a basis for demanding social reform and criticizing others.
quotes.t: Acolytes, reformers, and atheists

quotes.c: Several governance ideas will require that policymakers, industry leaders, and other groups have a strong understanding of the dangers and potential catastrophic risks of advanced AI systems. How can we communicate ideas and threat models clearly and responsibly to these audiences?
quotes.m: Several governance ideas will require that policymakers, industry leaders, and other groups have a strong understanding of the dangers and potential catastrophic risks of advanced AI systems.
quotes.sum: Advanced AI governance depends on helping policymakers and industry leaders understand catastrophic AI risks and threat models.
quotes.t: AI Governance & Strategy: Priorities, talent gaps, & opportunities

quotes.c: While flow-through effects will still require significant analysis, it is important to make sure they do not paralyze our decisions. Thus, in the meantime, I suggest five non-exclusive potential ways to handle flow-through effects going forward.
quotes.m: it is important to make sure they do not paralyze our decisions.
quotes.sum: Flow-through consequences matter, but uncertainty about them should not stop people from making decisions.
quotes.t: Five Ways to Handle Flow-Through Effects

quotes.c: But I think it's a real possibility now. I think we actually can think, “Wow, yeah, maybe we can achieve this.” Maybe over the long run, if we keep working on this, this actually is within our power. And it might well be that a significant fraction of the expected value of what we're doing today, as well as having this direct benefit, comes from this long-run potential to really change the mindset of people all around the world.
quotes.sum: The author argues that current work may matter largely because it could eventually shift moral attitudes worldwide.
quotes.t: Moral progress and "Cause X"

quotes.c: When I try to model all these factors out in the following Guesstimate model , I get an estimate that the total efforts of our team (including senior staff, non-senior staff, and volunteers) are roughly equal to, in expectation, the work of a team of full-time equivalent people each earning to give $400K a year to GiveWell top charities, with our 95% confidence interval ranging from $220K/yr to $720K/yr. This compares favorably, as $400K donated per year is, I think, higher than what a typically ambitious and skilled EA could be expected to earn to give and is much higher than the earning to give levels found in 80,000 Hours 2014 report .
quotes.sum: The author estimates that creating a high-performing global-health charity can be more valuable than a typical ambitious person's donation-based career.
quotes.t: What is the expected value of creating a GiveWell top charity?

quotes.c: We looked into the possibility of forming a community panel to serve this purpose. But after exploring the idea further, we decided that this might be overstepping CEA’s bounds, and that such a panel might put the community at risk of being dominated by a few groups or interests. We don’t think the effective altruism community should be controlled by any one organization, and don’t want to set CEA up to be that organization.
quotes.m: We don’t think the effective altruism community should be controlled by any one organization, and don’t want to set CEA up to be that organization.
quotes.sum: CEA rejected creating a community advisory panel because it could centralize influence and let a few interests dominate EA.
quotes.t: Advisory panel at CEA

quotes.c: Note: for simplicity, this article talks about how to increase the number of votes to a major party candidate via vote pairing, but it does not consider the value of that increase. In 2016 vote pairing helped the Democrats, but I expect that the effectiveness should be similar if/when the tables are turned and vote pairing benefits Republicans.
quotes.m: In 2016 vote pairing helped the Democrats, but I expect that the effectiveness should be similar if/when the tables are turned and vote pairing benefits Republicans.
quotes.sum: The author evaluates vote pairing as a cost-effective way to increase a major-party candidate’s votes, regardless of which party benefits.
quotes.t: Vote Pairing is a Cost-Effective Political Intervention

quotes.c: The area I know in most depth is funding of effective altruism community-building. In this area, all of the considerations above weigh on my mind; I think it would be a very precarious position (both for insurance and impartiality reasons) if the EA community were heavily dependent on a single donor, or a small number of donors. I wouldn’t be that surprised if in a few years we switched to emphasising how funding-constrained rather than people-constrained we are (though I’m aware that other people disagree with me on the likelihood of this).
quotes.m: I think it would be a very precarious position (both for insurance and impartiality reasons) if the EA community were heavily dependent on a single donor, or a small number of donors.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that earning to give can remain valuable and warns that EA community-building should not rely on only a few major donors.
quotes.t: Should you switch away from earning to give? Some considerations.

quotes.c: People already have legitimate and very severe societal concerns about things that models are doing today and you can call them mundane relative to all the existential risk. But I think they're already serious concerns about concentration of power, fairness and bias in these models, making sure that they benefit everyone, which I don't think that they do yet.
quotes.m: But I think they're already serious concerns about concentration of power, fairness and bias in these models, making sure that they benefit everyone, which I don't think that they do yet.
quotes.sum: The speaker says current AI systems already raise serious concerns about concentrated power, bias, fairness, and whether their benefits are broadly shared.
quotes.t: Podcast Transcript: Daniela and Dario Amodei on Anthropic

quotes.c: Insofar as they support or fail to challenge the equation of wild animal protection with “ecological balance”, animal activists may enable the continuation and extension of wild animal suffering. When working to reduce both domestic and wild animal suffering we should remember that, as I argued above, antispeciesist progress in one domain does not necessarily transfer to others.
quotes.m: animal activists may enable the continuation and extension of wild animal suffering.
quotes.sum: The author argues that protecting wild ecosystems for “ecological balance” can perpetuate suffering among wild animals, which activists should address.
quotes.t: Lessons from the history of animal rights

quotes.c: Empirical work is more tractable. Working out tough problems like quantifying the amount of existential risk that currently exists are difficult problems that not only are unlikely to be resolved soon, but are unlikely to even find frameworks for resolution that are satisfying. While empirical work is challenging, we at least already have a framework for how progress can be made[6].
quotes.m: While empirical work is challenging, we at least already have a framework for how progress can be made[6].
quotes.sum: The author argues that cause prioritization should give more weight to empirical research because it has clearer ways to make progress than abstract analysis of existential risk.
quotes.t: A Case for Empirical Cause Prioritization

quotes.c: Cost-effectiveness estimates for GiveWell top charities, and therefore GiveWell’s recommendations 6 , depend heavily on controversial questions about population ethics. I believe GiveWell takes an incorrect stance here, and it ought to give more weight to the total view. But more importantly, donors should be aware of how questions of population ethics affect the expected value of different interventions.
quotes.m: I believe GiveWell takes an incorrect stance here, and it ought to give more weight to the total view.
quotes.sum: GiveWell's charity rankings rely on contested views about whether creating additional lives has moral value, and the author argues it should favor the total view more.
quotes.t: GiveWell's Charity Recommendations Require Taking a Controversial Stance on Population Ethics

quotes.c: We then researched the top eight more deeply, with a keen idea to turn them into concrete charity ideas rather than amorphous interventions. When re-ranking, we came up with a top five, and wrote up more detailed reports -- SMS immunization reminders , tobacco taxation , iron and folic acid fortification , conditional cash transfers , and a poverty research organization . A key aspect to this narrowing was also talking to relevant experts, which we wish we did earlier on in the process as it could quickly eliminate unpromising options.
quotes.m: A key aspect to this narrowing was also talking to relevant experts, which we wish we did earlier on in the process as it could quickly eliminate unpromising options.
quotes.sum: The author describes narrowing possible charity interventions through research, ranking, and consultation with relevant experts.
quotes.t: Using a Spreadsheet to Make Good Decisions: Five Examples

quotes.c: I used to think one should be pessimistic about any intervention or idea that doesn’t involve helpful “feedback loops” (trying something, seeing how it goes, making small adjustments, and trying again many times) or useful selective processes (where many people try different ideas and interventions, and the ones that are successful in some tangible way become more prominent, powerful, and imitated). I was highly skeptical of attempts to make predictions and improve the world based primarily on logic and reflection, when unaccompanied by strong feedback loops and selective processes.
quotes.m: I was highly skeptical of attempts to make predictions and improve the world based primarily on logic and reflection, when unaccompanied by strong feedback loops and selective processes.
quotes.sum: Karnofsky says he became more open to doing good through logic, evidence, and scientific reasoning even without tight real-world feedback loops.
quotes.t: Three Key Issues I’ve Changed My Mind About

quotes.c: We may particularly care about learning value in a way that this framework doesn’t capture. Perhaps we expect an intervention to tell us something useful in the long term, but we don’t know what, so we have a hard time pinning down the impact of this learning. We could instead represent this by factoring in learning value to our final estimate.
quotes.m: Perhaps we expect an intervention to tell us something useful in the long term, but we don’t know what, so we have a hard time pinning down the impact of this learning.
quotes.sum: The author argues that decisions should account for the value of what an intervention can teach us, even when that learning is hard to quantify.
quotes.t: Evaluation Frameworks (or: When Importance / Neglectedness / Tractability Doesn't Apply)

quotes.c: Now, if we take these two axioms for granted, I come to the following conclusion: We must build an ASI that is aligned with human values, fully knowing that it will seize control over humanity. The alternative (wait until somebody accidentally creates an ASI and hope for the best) is less desirable, as that ASI will probably be misaligned.
quotes.m: We must build an ASI that is aligned with human values, fully knowing that it will seize control over humanity.
quotes.sum: The author argues that humanity should deliberately build an aligned superintelligence even though it would take control of society, because an accidental one would likely be misaligned.
quotes.t: Why We MUST Build an (aligned) Artificial Superintelligence That Takes Over Human Society - A Thought Experiment

quotes.c: The median LessWronger is a thirty year-old white man from the U.S.A. They're monogamous, straight, not looking for a romantic partner. They're an atheist democrat from a Christian family, and they've been in the community for about six years. They don't go to meetups, but they do consider themself an Effective Altruist and part of the ACX community.
quotes.m: They're an atheist democrat from a Christian family, and they've been in the community for about six years.
quotes.sum: A community survey portrays the typical LessWrong participant as a 30-year-old American white man, atheist, Democrat, and connected to Effective Altruism.
quotes.t: 2022 Survey Results

quotes.c: Now another question (and I would argue a very different question) is should you invest in collecting additional evidence? Well there I think you should apply the same approach, and that's what standard decision theory would suggest. You invest in additional evidence, if the cost of collecting that evidence is less than the expected value of the evidence. What's the expected value of the evidence? There might be a pure science value and I don't want to dismiss that, but from a utilitarian perspective it would be the probability that the additional evidence will change the future decision, times the expected value of changing the decision if it does so.
quotes.m: You invest in additional evidence, if the cost of collecting that evidence is less than the expected value of the evidence.
quotes.sum: The author argues that gathering more evidence should be treated as an investment: do it when its expected benefit exceeds its cost.
quotes.t: Michael Kremer: How much evidence is enough?

quotes.c: I think effective altruism often runs into questions about self-care and boundaries, and might have a few things to learn from social work.
quotes.m: effective altruism often runs into questions about self-care and boundaries
quotes.sum: Effective altruism should take self-care and personal boundaries seriously, potentially learning from social work.
quotes.t: Burnout and self-care

quotes.c: These standardised representations of poverty can give the impression that the situation is hopeless. In 2012, Oxfam released the results of a 2,000-person survey showing that negative images of poverty had become so pervasive as to lose purpose. A full 75% of those surveyed described themselves as ‘completely desensitized’ to images showing hunger, drought and disease. While 75% did believe it was possible to end hunger in places like Africa, only 20% believed they could play an active role in achieving this outcome. This kind of paralysis is exactly what we want to avoid.
quotes.m: This kind of paralysis is exactly what we want to avoid.
quotes.sum: Graphic, hopeless portrayals of poverty can desensitize people and make them feel unable to help, so advocates should avoid them.
quotes.t: Guidelines on depicting poverty

quotes.c: So I’d like there to exist a more formal process by which we can ensure that people taking action under the banner of effective altruism are acting in accordance with EA values, and strengthening rather than damaging the movement. I think that this is vital if the EA community is going to grow substantially and reach its full potential. If we did this successfully, this process would avoid feelings that EA is run by mob rule, it would ensure that bad behaviour is nipped in the bud, rather than growing to the point where the community spends hundreds of hours dealing with it, and it would give allegedly bad actors a transparent and fair assessment.
quotes.m: I’d like there to exist a more formal process by which we can ensure that people taking action under the banner of effective altruism are acting in accordance with EA values, and strengthening rather than damaging the movement.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that EA needs a formal, transparent process to hold people using its name accountable to community values.
quotes.t: Setting Community Norms and Values: A response to the InIn Open Letter

quotes.c: This study shows that it is really hard to create a good study. Even going into making the study knowing the past mistakes of studies and committing a lot of resources to avoid making those mistakes, it is still possible to repeat those mistakes. The first mission of any future study should be to get an adequate sample size -- something that we have now tried and failed at six times in a row.
quotes.m: The first mission of any future study should be to get an adequate sample size -- something that we have now tried and failed at six times in a row.
quotes.sum: The author says animal-advocacy ad studies have repeatedly been too small to give reliable answers, and future research must prioritize adequate sample sizes.
quotes.t: More Thoughts (and Analysis) on the Mercy For Animals Online Ads Study

quotes.c: First, the migrant crisis is a much greater global catastrophic risk than Trump could possibly be. Second, Trump opposes mass migration and increases the chance that nationalist movements will sweep the open-borders, globalist EU governments from power. The original post points out that nationalist powers taking over in Europe would fundamentally change it, which is true. However, the current trajectory of Europe is much worse.
quotes.m: the migrant crisis is a much greater global catastrophic risk than Trump could possibly be.
quotes.sum: The author argues that mass migration is a larger catastrophic threat than Trump and endorses nationalist electoral victories as a corrective.
quotes.t: A Different Take on President Trump

quotes.c: I'm unsure how large the shift from earning to give to direct work should be, but if you're undecided between the two, then (1) find out your specific options and reassess (i.e. compare specific job offers rather than broad classes) (2) ask where you have the greatest comparative advantage compared to the community, then if still undecided (3) consider leaning towards direct work.
quotes.m: ask where you have the greatest comparative advantage compared to the community
quotes.sum: If choosing between donating money and taking direct-impact work, compare concrete options and favor the path where your skills add the most beyond what others can do.
quotes.t: 6 common mistakes in the effective altruism community

quotes.c: I will first discuss the case against worldview diversification. When seeking to maximize expected positive impact, without being worried about the “risk” of doing no good, there is a case that we should simply put all available resources behind the worldview that our best-guess thinking favors.
quotes.m: there is a case that we should simply put all available resources behind the worldview that our best-guess thinking favors.
quotes.sum: He argues that if the goal is maximum expected impact, funders may be justified in concentrating all resources on their best-supported worldview rather than diversifying.
quotes.t: Worldview Diversification

quotes.c: I haven’t had many role models in my life, but I think Stephanie has been the major influence in my life that’s role model-like. I think of her as a mentor and have been inspired to take things more seriously, to pay more attention to how I think and to try to think in better ways by her. Her level of commitment to not letting the world die is extremely impressive to me and makes me want to tap into that commitment within myself more.
quotes.m: Her level of commitment to not letting the world die is extremely impressive to me and makes me want to tap into that commitment within myself more.
quotes.sum: The author admires a mentor’s intense commitment to preventing humanity’s extinction and wants to share that seriousness.
quotes.t: EA Interview Series, February 2016: John Salvatier

quotes.c: An even worse problem is that the Republican Party seems distinctly less interested in registering voters. (I think the sort of people who need help registering tend to vote Democrat?) I was unable to find a single Republican group that was registering voters in Madison – I’m not sure if that’s unique to us or if that’s a more general problem.
quotes.m: I think the sort of people who need help registering tend to vote Democrat?
quotes.sum: The author says voter-registration outreach may disproportionately help Democratic voters because Republican groups appear less engaged in it.
quotes.t: Voter Registration As an EA Group Meetup Activity

quotes.c: A few years ago, I was torn between focusing on global poverty and focusing on animal liberation. I’m increasingly persuaded that animal liberation – the question that affects the vast majority of the mammals and birds on this planet and could determine the future of the planet’s wild animals – is the question where I should spend my time.
quotes.m: I’m increasingly persuaded that animal liberation – the question that affects the vast majority of the mammals and birds on this planet and could determine the future of the planet’s wild animals – is the question where I should spend my time.
quotes.sum: The author says animal liberation should take priority over poverty work because it affects most mammals and birds and may shape wild animals' future.
quotes.t: The Poor Meat Investor Problem

quotes.c: We’re likely smart enough to exclude interventions that are likely to be quite inferior from a scale perspective , like farm sanctuaries , we still likely face a large range of potential cost-effectiveness. While we don’t know yet if the shape is logarithmically distributed like it appears to be for global health interventions[3], it seems to me that a lot of the interventions that “smart money” would pick include the possibility of no impact (being actually worthless) and net negative impact[4] (actively causing more harm per each dollar spent), even before considering their possible far-future effects.
quotes.m: a lot of the interventions that “smart money” would pick include the possibility of no impact (being actually worthless) and net negative impact[4] (actively causing more harm per each dollar spent)
quotes.sum: Animal advocacy may be less reliably cost-effective than global health because many plausible interventions could do nothing or make outcomes worse.
quotes.t: Global poverty could be more cost-effective than animal advocacy (even for non-speciesists)

quotes.c: Since the strategy derived from the data scientist’s information exceeds the value of our existing strategy by 3,600 estimated lives saved. Since we’d value this at $10.8M, funding the data scientist is clearly worth it even given the 5% error rate. However, notably the study is not as worthwhile as perfect information (which we valued at $27M).
quotes.m: Since we’d value this at $10.8M, funding the data scientist is clearly worth it even given the 5% error rate.
quotes.sum: The author argues that research improving cause priorities should be funded when its expected benefits exceed its costs, using estimated lives and dollars.
quotes.t: How should we prioritize cause prioritization?

quotes.c: Predictions matter because they separate the signal from the noise. Anyone can make a vague proclamation that sometime in the future something good or bad will happen; it’s the people who put definitive dates and measurable claims on these statements that make it possible to evaluate whether they were actually right or wrong, and figure out what we should do next.
quotes.m: Predictions matter because they separate the signal from the noise.
quotes.sum: Argues that altruistic groups should make measurable, time-bound predictions so they can test claims and learn what works.
quotes.t: Effective Altruism Prediction Registry

quotes.c: When we say “we ought not level New York City”, we’re really saying “In order to avoid killing people, we ought not level New York City” or perhaps even “we morally ought not level New York City”. If we insist that “we ought not level New York City” with no goal applied in a floating ought simpliciter form, we should (in order that we analyze meta-ethics correctly) envision some sort of ERROR 404 GOAL NOT FOUND whenever we try to wrap our head around it.
quotes.m: we should (in order that we analyze meta-ethics correctly) envision some sort of ERROR 404 GOAL NOT FOUND whenever we try to wrap our head around it.
quotes.sum: Moral “ought” claims only make sense relative to some goal; a goal-free, absolute obligation is a conceptual error.
quotes.t: End-Relational Theory of Meta-ethics: A Dialogue

quotes.c: With that said, I believe that potential risks have now received enough attention – some of which has been unfortunately exaggerated in my view – that premature regulation and/or intervention by government agencies is already a live risk. I’d be interested in the possibility of supporting institutions that could provide thoughtful, credible, public analysis of whether and when government regulation/intervention would be advisable, even if it meant simply making the case against such things for the foreseeable future. I think such analysis would likely improve the quality of discussion and decision-making, relative to what will happen without it.
quotes.m: premature regulation and/or intervention by government agencies is already a live risk.
quotes.sum: Karnofsky argues that advanced AI could have enormous consequences soon, while warning that exaggerated risk claims could lead to premature government regulation.
quotes.t: Potential Risks from Advanced Artificial Intelligence: The Philanthropic Opportunity

quotes.c: The key change is that we are no longer trying to incentivize honesty. We realized that trying to be incentive-compatible made the process much more expensive, for both us and the sellers. We also realized that the incentives were never going to be perfect or even great, once we had a dynamic process with more than one buyer.
quotes.m: The key change is that we are no longer trying to incentivize honesty.
quotes.sum: The author says an impact-purchasing process has stopped trying to make honesty incentive-compatible because doing so was too costly and could not work well in a dynamic market.
quotes.t: Final Round of the Impact Purchase

quotes.c: Fallacy #3 is particularly dangerous for people who've read a lot about the dangers of overconfidence. Right now, we're down to two remaining stages in Nate's "six stages of doom" for Trump, accumulating the remaining delegates and winning the convention. The prediction markets assign 74% probability that Trump passes through both of them. So the conditional probabilities must look something like 90% probability that Trump accumulates enough delegates, and then 80% probability that Trump wins the convention given those delegates.
quotes.m: The prediction markets assign 74% probability that Trump passes through both of them.
quotes.sum: The author argues that breaking an uncertain outcome into multiple stages can misleadingly make a likely overall result look implausible.
quotes.t: The Multiple Stage Fallacy

quotes.c: Sometimes community members actually say "we want to maximise the number of QALYs". I think we should stop doing this. Instead say something more like: "we want to maximise the number of people who have good lives", or just "maximise the good we do" and then if someone asks what "good" means, you can say it's people having happy or flourishing lives.
quotes.m: "we want to maximise the number of people who have good lives"
quotes.sum: He argues that the movement should describe its goal in human terms—helping more people have good, happy, flourishing lives—rather than maximizing QALYs.
quotes.t: We care about WALYs not QALYs

quotes.c: Of course, there will be variation in how involved people get with any movement. Some people will keep their engagement with effective altruism at a fairly casual level—perhaps telling friends and family about an excellent charity. Others will become deeply involved, committing much more of their time and money. People will shift between levels as their beliefs and life circumstances change, perhaps as they become more committed or develop health problems.
quotes.m: Others will become deeply involved, committing much more of their time and money.
quotes.sum: Effective altruism should accommodate varying levels of involvement, since people’s capacity and commitments change over time.
quotes.t: Against segregating EAs

quotes.c: Of course, doing such an analysis is a bit reductive and the raw numbers might not be good enough to capture all the ways in which the EA movement grows, especially on key metrics we might care about, like growing existing EAs, growing donation totals, coming up with new EA ideas that improve the movement as a whole, and creating significant career changes. Still, I think having this analysis could be helpful for deciding where to invest in the EA movement.
quotes.m: Still, I think having this analysis could be helpful for deciding where to invest in the EA movement.
quotes.sum: The author argues that measuring movement growth can help EA decide where to invest, despite the limits of reducing growth to data.
quotes.t: Is EA growing? A concrete study idea to find out (and a $100 offer for implementation)

quotes.c: This is a small, vague subset of the more intensive coordination I hope EAs, especially earn-to-givers, embrace in the future. I hope we develop a coordinated system of tracking charity funding gaps, financial information, and track records. I think value-aligned donors should consider forming donor blocs that work together and divide labor to reduce redundant and low-quality cause/charity prioritization investigations.
quotes.m: I think value-aligned donors should consider forming donor blocs that work together and divide labor to reduce redundant and low-quality cause/charity prioritization investigations.
quotes.sum: The author argues that aligned donors should coordinate, share funding data, and form blocs to make charity choices more efficiently.
quotes.t: Talk about donations earlier and more

quotes.c: I think this makes complete sense if you think we live in a world where the main conflict is between humans and nature, people and nature, which is a classic story archetype, because empowerment helps us to deal, clearly, with natural disasters like supervolcanoes, asteroids, diseases and pandemics. If we're smarter we can come up with vaccines more quickly, and we can prevent them from spreading. Wild animal suffering is another thing we could deal with if humans were better empowered, and so on, and so on. So in our people versus nature world, I think this theory is very compelling.
quotes.m: So in our people versus nature world, I think this theory is very compelling.
quotes.sum: The author argues that making people more capable has broad long-run benefits because it helps humanity manage natural threats, including pandemics and animal suffering.
quotes.t: Robert Wiblin: Making sense of long-term indirect effects

quotes.c: There have been vivid false projections of AI in the past , and we’re aware that today’s projections of future AI could look misguided in retrospect. This is a risk I think we should accept, given our philosophy of hits-based giving . Overall, I think it is appropriate to act as though there is at least a 10% chance of “transformative AI” within the next 20 years; as though this “10%” figure is somewhat stable/robust ; and as though we can be quite confident that the probability is at least 1%.
quotes.m: Overall, I think it is appropriate to act as though there is at least a 10% chance of “transformative AI” within the next 20 years
quotes.sum: A prominent funder argues that it is reasonable to act on a substantial chance that AI will transform society within 20 years, despite past forecasting failures.
quotes.t: Some Background on Our Views Regarding Advanced Artificial Intelligence (Open Philanthropy)

quotes.c: Most ideologies aren’t very explicitly defined (at least not beyond the groves of the academy), which facilitates drift. Witness, e.g. the drift of the term “liberal” (which is left-wing in the US, but right-wing in Scandinavia). To avoid such drift we need to discuss and emphasize the meaning of “Effective altruism” over and over again.
quotes.m: To avoid such drift we need to discuss and emphasize the meaning of “Effective altruism” over and over again.
quotes.sum: The author argues that EA should repeatedly define itself clearly to prevent its meaning from drifting like other political labels.
quotes.t: Effective Altruism’s fact-value separation as a weapon against political bias

quotes.c: Unless we’re fundamentally risk-averse, diversifying this way makes no sense. We are not trying to maximize the odds we at least accomplish something good, we’re trying to maximize expected value. If criminal justice has higher expected value than x-risk, we should make all our grants there (up to the point of diminishing marginal returns)–not make any lower-expected-value bets.
quotes.m: We are not trying to maximize the odds we at least accomplish something good, we’re trying to maximize expected value.
quotes.sum: A large donor should concentrate funding on whichever cause has the highest expected value, rather than diversify to improve the chance of some success.
quotes.t: How Should a Large Donor Prioritize Cause Areas?

quotes.c: It's well worth small amounts of effort to fight identity ossification of this sort early and often, if the efforts are effective. Identities are powerful , and we should actively manage them. I fear these processes will decrease cause selection quality.
quotes.m: Identities are powerful , and we should actively manage them.
quotes.sum: The author argues that EA should actively prevent people from becoming too attached to a single cause identity, because it can worsen decisions about where to help.
quotes.t: How we can make it easier to change your mind about cause areas

quotes.c: For all of the intellectual and material effort effective altruism puts into expanding the moral circle, the lesson of this paper is that we should bring caution to confidence that our circle is wide enough. And we ought not let this caution falter over time. There may exist universes of invisible harm, and beneficiaries we may remain unaware of for decades or centuries.
quotes.m: There may exist universes of invisible harm, and beneficiaries we may remain unaware of for decades or centuries.
quotes.sum: The author argues that efforts to broaden moral concern should remain humble because vast harms or beneficiaries may still be unseen.
quotes.t: "Allkind"

quotes.c: With legacy donations, you only get the money a long way in the future. If you persuade someone who's 40 with a life expectancy of 80, you'll get it in about 40 years. If you persuade someone who's 20, you'll get it in about 60 years, or perhaps longer. With normal fundraising, you get the money pretty fast - often nearly immediately, or otherwise over a couple of years.
quotes.m: With legacy donations, you only get the money a long way in the future.
quotes.sum: Legacy fundraising delays donations for decades, unlike ordinary fundraising, which provides money quickly.
quotes.t: Is legacy fundraising actually higher leverage?

quotes.c: Right now, EAs focus primarily on global poverty, animal welfare, reducing existential risk, and meta activities to improve the first three . However, some EAs are interested in looking for more . What other important causes might we be overlooking?
quotes.m: What other important causes might we be overlooking?
quotes.sum: The author argues that effective altruists may be overlooking worthwhile causes that create small benefits for many people.
quotes.t: Do EAs underestimate opportunities to create many small benefits?

quotes.c: It’s possible that spreading concern for wild animals will have a massive effect on the far future; but it’s not at all clear that ACE research will ever have this effect, even if it does research on reducing wild animal suffering. I discuss my general concerns with values spreading in “On Values Spreading” . Even so, I believe ACE has a decent chance of being the most effective charity.
quotes.sum: The author says expanding concern for wild animals could greatly shape the long-term future and argues that funding animal-charity research may be highly effective.
quotes.t: My Cause Selection: Michael Dickens

quotes.c: Partly due to demand from some members of the EA community, we’ll be experimenting with doing more theoretical research on effective altruism. This comes in two main categories: ‘crucial considerations,’ or ideas that have the potential to radically change how we evaluate our options; and ‘cause prioritisation’, or research on how to figure out which cause-areas one ought to focus on. We believe that this work is both extremely important and extremely hard to do, and will assess our progress on this front on an ongoing basis.
quotes.m: We believe that this work is both extremely important and extremely hard to do, and will assess our progress on this front on an ongoing basis.
quotes.sum: CEA says it will expand theoretical work on ideas that could radically alter priorities and on deciding which causes deserve focus.
quotes.t: Some Organisational Changes at the Centre for Effective Altruism

quotes.c: There are other important considerations related to the pace of progress in artificial intelligence that I did not consider. For example, the rate of progress—and where the progress happens—could affect: What country or organization obtains advanced capabilities first, which could positively or negatively affect overall risk. It could also affect the attitudes with which advanced AI is developed; for example, in today’s relatively stable and peaceful geopolitical environment, people seem particularly likely to prioritize safety before deploying advanced AI, relative to a possible world where geopolitics is more unstable and the incentives favor deploying advanced AI as soon as possible.
quotes.m: What country or organization obtains advanced capabilities first, which could positively or negatively affect overall risk.
quotes.sum: The pace and location of AI progress may determine who gets advanced AI first and whether geopolitical incentives favor safety or rapid deployment.
quotes.t: Differential Technological Development: Some Early Thinking

quotes.c: It’s possible that we luck out and it turns out the Orthogonality Thesis and the Doomsday Argument and Mind Crime are just philosophical curiosities that have no practical bearing in our earthly engineering efforts, that the AGI or Emulation will by default fall into an attractor basin which implements some form of MaxiPok with details that it only grasps after CEV or the Crypto, and we will be Ok. It is possible, and it is more likely than that our efforts will end up being the decisive factor. We need to focus our actions in the branches where they matter though.
quotes.m: It is possible, and it is more likely than that our efforts will end up being the decisive factor.
quotes.sum: The author argues that human efforts are more likely than luck to determine whether advanced AI has a good outcome.
quotes.t: My Coming of Age as an EA: 12 Problems with Effective Altruism

quotes.c: There are certainly good reasons to think 80K’s argument is correct -- there is already a lot of money in EA through Good Ventures and other high net-worth individuals and there is a potential that existing earning-to-give EAs may start donating much more soon. I’m excited how much the EA movement might grow through more direct work. However, I think we are still a ways off until earning-to-give people start reliably funding the remaining 85% of the movement.
quotes.m: However, I think we are still a ways off until earning-to-give people start reliably funding the remaining 85% of the movement.
quotes.sum: He argues that more people with high earning potential should consider donating professionally, because donor careers still do not reliably fund most of the movement.
quotes.t: Peter Hurford thinks that a large proportion of people should earn to give long term

quotes.c: The EA movement will still change its extension quite a few times until it maybe reaches a more stable desired world state. But no matter how long and how stable, how convergent it ends up being at the end of the day, it will always be open to further scrutiny and change.
quotes.m: it will always be open to further scrutiny and change.
quotes.sum: The author argues that EA should be understood as an evolving movement whose aims and membership remain open to revision.
quotes.t: Effective Altruism as an intensional movement

quotes.c: As has become clear, the interactions between EA and religion are not without tension, and any future attempts at outreach must be mindful of this. There are tensions specific to each religion, but also those that might pose difficulties for religion in general. Most notably, EA may be perceived as being in competition with religion: for charitable funds, and for belief systems. Indeed, as many regard EA as something of an “non-denominational religion”, religious groups may believe that EA could draw people away from religious devotion and towards a more EA-oriented lifestyle.
quotes.m: EA may be perceived as being in competition with religion: for charitable funds, and for belief systems.
quotes.sum: The author argues that effective altruism can compete with religious communities for donations, beliefs, and personal commitment, complicating outreach.
quotes.t: Effective Altruism and Religious Faiths: Mutually Exclusive Entities, or an Important Nexus to Explore?

quotes.c: If the reported effects are real and the suggested interpretation is correct, I think it would be a big deal. To put this in perspective, carbon dioxide concentrations in my room vary between 500 and 1500 ppm depending on whether I open the windows. The experiment reports cognitive effects for moving from 600 and 1000 ppm, and they are relatively large compared to interindividual differences.
quotes.m: The experiment reports cognitive effects for moving from 600 and 1000 ppm, and they are relatively large compared to interindividual differences.
quotes.sum: The author says that if reported findings are correct, ordinary indoor carbon-dioxide levels may have surprisingly large effects on cognition.
quotes.t: What is up with carbon dioxide and cognition? An offer

quotes.c: Somehow, meta-work became it’s own cause in this list, but I think that’s a mistake. Meta-work isn’t a cause, it’s a meta-cause, and it’s supposed to make the above actual-causes go better. To understand the meta-impact that meta-work has, it’s important to understand the object-level causes and have opinions on which one is best.
quotes.m: Meta-work isn’t a cause, it’s a meta-cause, and it’s supposed to make the above actual-causes go better.
quotes.sum: He argues that movement-building should serve concrete causes rather than become an end in itself.
quotes.t: EA risks falling into a "meta trap". But we can avoid it.

quotes.c: I place myself in the evidence camp. One of the strengths of evidence-based medicine in my view is that it realises the limits of our rationality. It realises that, actually, we are VERY bad at working out how to maximise expected utility through abstract reasoning so we should actually test stuff empirically to find out what works. It also allows consensus-building by decreasing uncertainty.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people are poor at calculating the best outcomes through abstract reasoning and should rely more on empirical testing.
quotes.t: Why effective altruism used to be like evidence-based medicine. But isn’t anymore

quotes.c: I think the argument that we should focus on doing lots of good rather than fixing harms we cause could drive destructive thoughtlessness about personal behavior, so I’m wary about making it too frequently. I’m most worried about this concern.
quotes.sum: She argues that treating good deeds as offsets for harms one causes can encourage careless personal behavior and conflicts with EA values.
quotes.t: Ethical offsetting is antithetical to EA

quotes.c: Respecting those we interact with and avoiding deception, coercion, and other behavior that violates common-sense ethics. In my view, arrogance is at its most damaging when it involves “ends justify the means” thinking. I believe a great deal of harm has been done by people who were so convinced of their contrarian ideas that they were willing to violate common-sense ethics for them (in the worst cases, even using violence).
quotes.m: In my view, arrogance is at its most damaging when it involves “ends justify the means” thinking.
quotes.sum: He argues that pursuing unconventional, high-risk ideas must still be constrained by ordinary ethics and rejection of coercion or deception.
quotes.t: Hits-based Giving

quotes.c: The latter two are particularly worrisome for those who, like me, want EA to change the attitudes of society as a whole. The movement will struggle to do this while it’s perceived as being elitist. More worryingly, I think the latter two are legitimate concerns to have about EA.
quotes.m: The movement will struggle to do this while it’s perceived as being elitist.
quotes.sum: The author wants EA to change society's attitudes but says credible concerns about elitism undermine that ambition.
quotes.t: EA's Image Problem

quotes.c: I have wanted to hear people's 'testimonies' for a long time (what I've heard this kind of thing called in evangelical religious movements - activist and political movements I've been around have called it something like 'getting involved'). I think these are important as you're able to see why people are here, and you're able to see how other people you're talking might be better encouraged to join in.
quotes.m: I think these are important as you're able to see why people are here, and you're able to see how other people you're talking might be better encouraged to join in.
quotes.sum: The author says personal origin stories can help explain why people join EA and how to encourage others to participate.
quotes.t: Many winding roads: an EA origin story

quotes.c: But squandering this privilege by pretending I don't have it would not help anyone except me . It might make me feel better, but me feeling better about my privilege is not the point. I could be a good hippie and spend my days volunteering at the local library and my evenings making pottery in my basement. No one could accuse me of making things worse, but I would hardly be making things better for people in extreme need. I think we should be less like Tolstoy barefoot in the woods, and more like Jane Addams using her wealth, connections, education, and skills for the benefit of others.
quotes.m: I think we should be less like Tolstoy barefoot in the woods, and more like Jane Addams using her wealth, connections, education, and skills for the benefit of others.
quotes.sum: Personal simplicity or moral purity is less important than using one's advantages, money, and skills to materially help people in extreme need.
quotes.t: An embarrassment of riches

quotes.c: Yet, it somehow seems to be true that billions or trillions of beings are having morally relevant experiences right now , and had them in the past, and (many times) more could have morally relevant experiences in the future. My emotions are not well-equipped to deal with this; they can't really understand numbers bigger than a three or experiences longer than an hour (true story) (I may be unusually incompetent in this regard, but probably not by many orders of magnitude).
quotes.m: My emotions are not well-equipped to deal with this; they can't really understand numbers bigger than a three or experiences longer than an hour (true story) (I may be unusually incompetent in this regard, but probably not by many orders of magnitude).
quotes.sum: The author says human emotions cannot grasp the scale of morally important experiences, so doing good requires acting beyond what one can emotionally understand.
quotes.t: Impossible EA emotions

quotes.c: Because quality risk is such a diverse category, I’ll use widening our moral circles as an example of how we could increase the expected value of the far future given we continue to exist, mainly because it’s what I see as most promising and have considered most fully. By this, I mean, “Increasing the extent to which we accommodate the interests of all sentient individuals, rather than just those who are most similar to us or have the most power in society.” It seems that narrow moral circles and a lack of concern for all sentient beings could lead civilization to be much worse, given it continues to exist, posing a substantial quality risk.
quotes.m: It seems that narrow moral circles and a lack of concern for all sentient beings could lead civilization to be much worse, given it continues to exist, posing a substantial quality risk.
quotes.sum: The author argues that preventing a surviving civilization from having narrow moral concern may be as important as preventing extinction.
quotes.t: Some considerations for different ways to reduce x-risk

quotes.c: If our choices were perceived as largely arbitrary, opaque, and instinctive (as they would likely appear if we made one-off grants rather than systematically thinking through all our options in the cause), people seeking funding might cease to become honest peers and move in the direction of trying to figure out how to relate to us in order to get funding. This risk exists to some degree in any case, but I think it would be greatly magnified if people had the sense they could get funding from us while not having much idea of how.
quotes.m: people seeking funding might cease to become honest peers and move in the direction of trying to figure out how to relate to us in order to get funding.
quotes.sum: Karnofsky argues that opaque grantmaking would turn community peers into people trying to manage relationships to win funding.
quotes.t: Why the Open Philanthropy Project isn't currently funding organizations focused on promoting effective altruism

quotes.c: We often only remember what we see as the essential pieces of an experience, not everything surrounding it. Participants asked about a recent theater experience, they only remembering the theater as being what's on stage, not the cold, the parking, the noise, and the interlude. Because accurate predictions are contingent on accurate memories, it’s hard to get the final step right if the first one is in the wrong direction.
quotes.m: Because accurate predictions are contingent on accurate memories, it’s hard to get the final step right if the first one is in the wrong direction.
quotes.sum: People mispredict how experiences will feel because memory leaves out mundane details that shape the actual experience.
quotes.t: 4 Common (Hedonic) Prediction Failures and How to Fix Them

quotes.c: There is a tension between ‘taking arguments seriously’ and ‘deferring to common sense’. Effective altruism only weakly converges with common sense morality, and thus we should expect their recommendations to diverge. On the other hand, that something lies far from common sense morality is a pro tanto reason to reject it. This is better acknowledged openly: “I think the best action by the lights of EA is to research wild animal suffering, but all things considered I will do something else, as how outlandish this is by common sense morality is a strong reason against it”.
quotes.m: On the other hand, that something lies far from common sense morality is a pro tanto reason to reject it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that EA should admit when its conclusions conflict with common sense and treat that conflict as evidence against them.
quotes.t: Beware surprising and suspicious convergence

quotes.c: People find the repugnant conclusion repugnant because they are not mentally capable of aggregating small experiences over lots of people; see also Torture vs. Dust Specks and its followup Circular Altruism .
quotes.sum: The author argues that resistance to the repugnant conclusion reflects people's inability to add up many small experiences across large populations.
quotes.t: On Values Spreading

quotes.c: I think about what else I could be doing instead of reading. Reading is great, but in many cases experience can be a better teacher. Moreover, picking up some experience can help me understand and apply the lessons in books better. I try to adopt a "doing-reading" loop, where I read something, act upon it, then read another something, etc., continuing to iteratively improve in whatever skill I'm after.
quotes.m: I try to adopt a "doing-reading" loop, where I read something, act upon it, then read another something, etc., continuing to iteratively improve in whatever skill I'm after.
quotes.sum: The author argues that reading should be paired with action and reflection so that advice is tested and turned into improved skills.
quotes.t: How to Read

quotes.c: We’ve thought a fair amount about the question of whether we ought to prioritize deep expertise or breadth in our philanthropy . That is, holding staff and budget constant, should we make deep commitments to a small number of focus areas, or keep tabs on a larger number of areas and make grants opportunistically, i.e. when outstanding opportunities arise? We’re quite undecided on this question, and we’re currently seeking to experiment with both approaches.
quotes.sum: A funder should weigh specialization in a few causes against broadly seeking unusually strong grant opportunities, and test both approaches.
quotes.t: Key Questions about Philanthropy, Part 2: Choosing Focus Areas and Hiring Program Staff

quotes.c: It’s worth noting that the criticism of “rewarding the measurable, rather than the important” has often been leveled at GiveWell’s work on top charities . I have long felt that focusing on the measurable is quite appropriate when (a) serving individual donors seeking somewhere they can give without having to invest a lot of time in learning; (b) working on issues related to global health and development, where higher-risk/higher-reward approaches have a history of coming up empty . However, the world of scientific research is very different. In this environment, it seems to me that insisting on accountability to meaningful short-term metrics could easily do more harm than good.
quotes.m: In this environment, it seems to me that insisting on accountability to meaningful short-term metrics could easily do more harm than good.
quotes.sum: Measurable results can be a good standard for charity, but demanding short-term metrics may harm fundamental scientific research.
quotes.t: Breakthrough Fundamental Science

quotes.c: Or is it more important to be honest about your moral beliefs and make some progress toward them, even if you don’t get everything done as well as you would like to?
quotes.m: Or is it more important to be honest about your moral beliefs and make some progress toward them, even if you don’t get everything done as well as you would like to?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether people should honestly pursue their moral commitments even when they cannot meet every ideal.
quotes.t: Aim high, even if you fall short

quotes.c: Imagine a country of 1,000 people. A new policy is proposed that will benefit 990 people by $1, but will cost the remaining ten people $10. The net benefit to society is $990 - 10*$10 = $880, a clear win, but these sorts of policies often don't happen. That's because the ten people who are harmed are strongly incentivised to work together to lobby the government against the policy. It's much harder for the 990 people to coordinate, and each individual stands to gain only $1.
quotes.m: The net benefit to society is $990 - 10*$10 = $880, a clear win, but these sorts of policies often don't happen.
quotes.sum: Policies that benefit most people can fail because a small group facing concentrated losses can organize more effectively than a large group with small gains.
quotes.t: Random idea: crowdsourcing lobbyists

quotes.c: But I think supporting the continuation of humanity and the socialization of the next generation can be considered a pretty basic part of human life. I understand that you may really dislike children. But understand that if you don't want children in your presence or at your event, it's not only the child you exclude. It's me.
quotes.m: But understand that if you don't want children in your presence or at your event, it's not only the child you exclude. It's me.
quotes.sum: Events that exclude children also exclude parents, and communities should treat raising and socializing the next generation as basic human activities.
quotes.t: On making spaces friendlier to parents

quotes.c: “Academia is too focused on knowledge for its own sake; we need to get it to think more about practical solutions and treatments.” I believe this attitude undervalues (A)-(B) and understates how important general insights and tools can be.
quotes.m: I believe this attitude undervalues (A)-(B) and understates how important general insights and tools can be.
quotes.sum: He argues that pressure for immediately practical medical research can wrongly discount the value of basic knowledge and general-purpose scientific tools.
quotes.t: The Path to Biomedical Progress

quotes.c: For us, the key question is what we, as the funder, are positioned to do better than others. We believe it makes sense to be active where we can offer something (besides money) that our grantees don’t have. But we want to avoid micro-managing grantees, who have more knowledge of their issues and their capabilities than we do.
quotes.m: We believe it makes sense to be active where we can offer something (besides money) that our grantees don’t have.
quotes.sum: A funder should contribute expertise beyond money where it adds value, while avoiding micromanagement of grantees who know their work better.
quotes.t: Key Questions about Philanthropy, Part 1: What Is the Role of a Funder?

quotes.c: Let’s say that I’m a Democrat, and my friend is a Republican. We both plan on donating $100 to our respective candidates. But after discussing it, we realise that this is a pretty pointless waste of money, and instead we agree to each put our $100 towards a charity recommended by Givewell.
quotes.m: We both plan on donating $100 to our respective candidates. But after discussing it, we realise that this is a pretty pointless waste of money, and instead we agree to each put our $100 towards a charity recommended by Givewell.
quotes.sum: The author argues that political opponents can redirect campaign donations to highly rated charities, producing more social good.
quotes.t: $5 billion in moral trade surplus?

quotes.c: Alternatively, we might affect what the future cared about. Under some types of Singleton, virtually any ethical debate could become a very pressing issue: we want to make sure the right side is preserved and propagated. Maybe it is important to persuade people that animals are morally valuable now so that an AI will care about them (though perhaps CEV obviates the need for this.) Or maybe we need to make sure the future Hegemon cares enough about art so the lightcone isn’t deprived of it.
quotes.m: Under some types of Singleton, virtually any ethical debate could become a very pressing issue: we want to make sure the right side is preserved and propagated.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a future all-powerful ruler or AI could permanently preserve today’s moral choices, making present ethical persuasion unusually consequential.
quotes.t: Permanent Societal Improvements

quotes.c: One may be more interested not in the absolute expected value of a something, but how it compares to something else. This problem gets harder when comparing across diverse cause areas: one intuition may be that a more speculative estimate should be discounted when 'up against' a more robust estimate when comparing two causes or two interventions.
quotes.m: This problem gets harder when comparing across diverse cause areas: one intuition may be that a more speculative estimate should be discounted when 'up against' a more robust estimate when comparing two causes or two interventions.
quotes.sum: The author discusses how to compare uncertain expected-value estimates across causes, especially human versus animal welfare.
quotes.t: Expected value estimates you can take (somewhat) literally

quotes.c: I don't think individuals should follow this 10-20% allocation though. Rather, individuals should try to move the overall balance more in the optimal direction. So, if you think the overall allocation should be 10-20%, then you should probably allocate most of your resources to meta activities (perhaps holding back ~25% for object level activities for learning and signalling).
quotes.m: individuals should try to move the overall balance more in the optimal direction.
quotes.sum: Individuals should direct their work toward neglected support activities when those activities are underfunded overall, rather than copying the ideal average allocation.
quotes.t: Why we need more meta

quotes.c: I think it suffers from the similar philosophical and implementation problems to anything CEV-like though - who knows what the wise dead people would have thought about low-fidelity ems, or nanobots distributing morphine to prevent wild animal suffering, or any of the other puzzles that may confront future society. You need to extrapolate and you need to aggregate opinions. And you need to choose the right people to start with.
quotes.m: You need to extrapolate and you need to aggregate opinions. And you need to choose the right people to start with.
quotes.sum: The author argues that designing AI around humanity's ideal values requires controversial choices about whose values count and how to extrapolate them.
quotes.t: Comments on Ernest Davis's comments on Bostrom's Superintelligence

quotes.c: Many people think of effective altruism as some sort of sacrifice -- you have to give up income and time in some sort of moral obligation to make the world a better place. I think this approach is misguided. Instead, I think being an EA is the best choice I've ever made for myself, personally and selfishly.
quotes.m: Instead, I think being an EA is the best choice I've ever made for myself, personally and selfishly.
quotes.sum: The author argues that effective altruism is not a personal sacrifice but has made his own life better and more enjoyable.
quotes.t: EA is the best choice I've ever made

quotes.c: I suspect this is underrated right now because the EA community is fairly atheist-heavy, but Harvard Effective Altruism has always gotten a great response to EA ideas from religious service groups. Even for atheists you could become a pseudo-religious leader like Greg Epstein . Again, this is a natural place that could benefit from the EA perspective since people are already looking for ways to improve the world.
quotes.m: Even for atheists you could become a pseudo-religious leader like Greg Epstein .
quotes.sum: The author suggests EA advocates could work through religious service groups or take on quasi-religious leadership roles to spread EA ideas.
quotes.t: Spitballing EA career ideas

quotes.c: If what matters most is that we maximize humanity’s future potential and some of our actions are expected to reduce existential risk in not-ridiculously-small ways, what it is best to do is primarily determined by how our actions are expected to reduce existential risk.
quotes.m: what it is best to do is primarily determined by how our actions are expected to reduce existential risk.
quotes.sum: He argues that, if maximizing humanity's future potential matters most, choices should chiefly be guided by their effect on existential risk.
quotes.t: A relatively atheoretical perspective on astronomical waste

quotes.c: Clearly explaining our reasoning and evidence. If you see a claim that isn’t backed up by a link or citation, you can assume there’s no further justification.
quotes.m: If you see a claim that isn’t backed up by a link or citation, you can assume there’s no further justification.
quotes.sum: The author argues that claims should be treated as unsupported unless they come with linked evidence or citations.
quotes.t: An epistemology for effective altruism?

quotes.c: It’s harder to change your career ‘role’ than your cause later in your career. For instance, if you become a great salesperson, it’s relatively easy to transition into an organisation that works on a different cause, but much harder to become great at some other skill. This means that early in your career it’s more important to figure out what types of roles suit you than what cause to support early in your career.
quotes.m: This means that early in your career it’s more important to figure out what types of roles suit you than what cause to support early in your career.
quotes.sum: Early-career people should prioritize developing a role-specific skill over choosing a cause, because skills are harder to switch later.
quotes.t: Two interviews with Holden

quotes.c: These awards are being made in exchange for certificates of impact. Here's how it works: you tell us about something good you did. We offer you some money. Rather than considering a complicated counterfactual ("How well will this money be spent if I don't take it?"), we encourage you to accept our offer if and only if you would be willing to undo the humanitarian impact of your project in exchange for the money.
quotes.sum: He proposes paying people for verified humanitarian impact, using whether they would undo the benefit for the payment as the acceptance test.
quotes.t: $10k of Experimental EA Funding

quotes.c: Cost-effectiveness is one of the most morally important issues in global health. This claim will be surprising to many, since conversations about the ethics of global health usually focus on more traditional moral issues such as justice, equality, and freedom. While these issues are also important, they are often overshadowed by cost-effectiveness.
quotes.m: Cost-effectiveness is one of the most morally important issues in global health.
quotes.sum: Ord argues that cost-effectiveness should be treated as a central moral issue in global health, often outweighing justice, equality, and freedom in practice.
quotes.t: The Moral Imperative Towards Cost-effectiveness

quotes.c: The first of these is if it helps to change course. If we are moving steadily in the wrong direction, we would do well to change our course, and this has a larger benefit the earlier we do so. For example, perhaps effective altruists are building up large resources in terms of specialist labour directed at combatting a particular existential risk, when they should be focusing on more general purpose labour.
quotes.sum: Argues that existential-risk work should prioritize early research that can redirect the movement toward more effective long-term strategies.
quotes.t: The timing of labour aimed at reducing existential risk

quotes.c: Unlike much basic research, this sort of work seems generally to have a very specific medical application in mind, and I believe that companies are often able to monetize the value created by new technologies they develop (especially drugs). Therefore, when looking at this kind of “translational science,” I think it is fair to ask: “If this research is generating more expected value than it costs, why isn’t industry investing in it? Why the need for nonprofit funds?”
quotes.m: “If this research is generating more expected value than it costs, why isn’t industry investing in it? Why the need for nonprofit funds?”
quotes.sum: He argues that nonprofit funding for applied medical research needs a stronger justification when drug companies could potentially profit from it.
quotes.t: Translational Science and the “Valley of Death”

quotes.c: The question of what discount rate EAs should have is very important, and very tricky. I really have absolutely no idea what the correct answer is.
quotes.m: I really have absolutely no idea what the correct answer is.
quotes.sum: MacAskill says choosing how much to discount the value of the future is important but that he does not know the right answer.
quotes.t: On discount rates

quotes.c: Generalist GiveWell staff (everyone we currently employ should be thought of as a generalist) gather information on many different causes, through methods including interviewing those with relevant expertise, and seek to understand different causes’ importance, tractability, and “crowdedness” at a high level.
quotes.m: seek to understand different causes’ importance, tractability, and “crowdedness” at a high level.
quotes.sum: GiveWell says its generalist staff compare causes by importance, tractability, and how neglected they are.
quotes.t: Exploring Life Sciences Funding

quotes.c: Economic behavior can help make efficient, robust decisions. You don’t need to give up on altruism to get those benefits. And conversely, altruism can grease the wheels of trade. I think economic altruism is a good attitude towards many interactions between nice people.
quotes.m: You don’t need to give up on altruism to get those benefits.
quotes.sum: He argues that altruism and market-style economic decision-making can reinforce each other, rather than being opposing approaches.
quotes.t: Economic altruism

quotes.c: Expertise would also be an advantage for following a grant, learning from it and continuing to help grantees as they progress. However, it seems quite possible to me that the best grantees tend to be self-driven and improvisatory, such that following them closely wouldn’t add value to what they’re doing, and would largely serve to assuage our own anxiety without doing much to increase our impact.
