quotes.m: the best grantees tend to be self-driven and improvisatory, such that following them closely wouldn’t add value to what they’re doing
quotes.sum: The author argues that philanthropists need not closely supervise grants, since strong recipients may work best independently.
quotes.t: Expert Philanthropy vs. Broad Philanthropy

quotes.c: Users should be willing to pay the same amount for a valid certificate of X that they would be willing to pay to cause X to happen (and to keep the resulting certificate). That is, I should be indifferent between spending $100 to do a good deed and paying someone else $100 to do it, provided that in either case I get the entire certificate for that good deed.
quotes.m: I should be indifferent between spending $100 to do a good deed and paying someone else $100 to do it, provided that in either case I get the entire certificate for that good deed.
quotes.sum: The author argues that verified certificates of good outcomes could be bought and traded like claims on charitable impact.
quotes.t: Certificates of impact

quotes.c: Our ultimate goal is to do as much good as possible, and if we ever believe we might accomplish this better by dropping the emphasis on transparency, we will give serious consideration to the possibility. But at this time, the chance to promote philanthropic transparency is a major part of the case for GiveWell’s future impact, and we plan to retain transparency as a costly but essential goal.
quotes.m: if we ever believe we might accomplish this better by dropping the emphasis on transparency, we will give serious consideration to the possibility.
quotes.sum: The author says transparency is valuable but could be abandoned if doing so seemed more effective at doing good.
quotes.t: Challenges of Transparency

quotes.c: The AI foom singleton is imbued with a goal system very close to human values, possibly along the lines of Coherent Extrapolated Volition or the values of the specific person or group of persons from whose point of view we examine the desirability of scenarios. This is probably the most utopian scenario since it involves an immensely powerful superintelligence working towards creating the best universe possible. It is difficult to know the details of the resulting future (although there have been some speculations ) but it is guaranteed to be highly valuable.
quotes.m: This is probably the most utopian scenario since it involves an immensely powerful superintelligence working towards creating the best universe possible.
quotes.sum: The author presents a globally dominant, value-aligned superintelligence as a utopian way to create the best possible universe.
quotes.t: Maximizing long-term impact

quotes.c: There are no sure bets in philanthropy — every grant involves risk, even to organizations with well-studied programs and strong track records — and we’re always working with incomplete information. But if our goal is to help other people as much as we can, I believe there are better and worse answers to the question of where to give. Importantly, I also believe it’s possible to learn and arrive at better and better answers over time.
quotes.m: if our goal is to help other people as much as we can, I believe there are better and worse answers to the question of where to give.
quotes.sum: Philanthropic choices are uncertain, but she argues donors can use evidence and learning to improve how much good their giving achieves.
quotes.t: Learning to be an effective altruist

quotes.c: I think that faster AI progress is a huge boon for this generation's welfare. But I think that improving our understanding of where AI is going and how it will develop is probably more important, because that reduces the probability that the development of AI unfolds in an unfavorable way rather than merely accelerating its arrival.
quotes.m: I think that faster AI progress is a huge boon for this generation's welfare.
quotes.sum: AI progress could greatly improve current lives, but understanding and steering its development matters more than accelerating it.
quotes.t: On Progress and Prosperity

quotes.c: I hope I've convinced you that there's a "there" there: infinite ethics is something that people can make progress on, and it seems that most of the progress is being made in the field of sustainable development.
quotes.m: infinite ethics is something that people can make progress on
quotes.sum: The author argues that questions about ethics involving infinities are tractable and that sustainable development has made much of the progress.
quotes.t: Problems and Solutions in Infinite Ethics

quotes.c: I hate talking about diversity. I hate watching other people talk about diversity more*. My first reaction to the (most) recent thread in the EA Facebook group about diversity was 'oh God, not this again'**. So I have a lot of sympathy for the view, most commonly expressed by social conservatives, that as a society we should spend a whole lot less time thinking and talking about diversity and a whole lot more time deciding on merit.
quotes.m: I have a lot of sympathy for the view, most commonly expressed by social conservatives, that as a society we should spend a whole lot less time thinking and talking about diversity and a whole lot more time deciding on merit.
quotes.sum: The author sympathizes with a socially conservative preference for focusing on merit rather than extensive discussion of diversity.
quotes.t: EA Diversity: Unpacking Pandora's Box

quotes.c: Because long-run focused effective altruism is associated with these further weird positions, it’s often downplayed when speaking to new people, in favor of short-run effective altruism (malaria nets and so on). I propose that it will be better, especially for people who are already engaged with making a difference, to introduce them first to *moderate long-run focused effective altruism* rather than the short-run focused version. It’s more intuitive and reasonable sounding.
quotes.m: I propose that it will be better, especially for people who are already engaged with making a difference, to introduce them first to *moderate long-run focused effective altruism* rather than the short-run focused version.
quotes.sum: The author argues that newcomers should be introduced first to a moderate version of long-term-focused altruism, rather than near-term causes such as malaria prevention.
quotes.t: Why long-run focused effective altruism is more common sense

quotes.c: Of course I think that the criticisms are mistaken, but it's good to be aware of where the idea of effective altruism is unintuitive or controversial.
quotes.m: it's good to be aware of where the idea of effective altruism is unintuitive or controversial.
quotes.sum: MacAskill says effective altruism has unintuitive or controversial implications, though he believes its criticisms are mistaken.
quotes.t: Peter Singer's TED talk on effective altruism

quotes.c: If people are likely to eventually colonize space, then it increases the potential scale and duration of civilization. This could affect arguments about the importance of trying to affect the long-run future of civilization. For example, Nick Bostrom [1] and I [2] have appealed to the possibility of interstellar space colonization in our arguments for the importance of reducing existential risk or otherwise affecting distant future generations.
quotes.m: This could affect arguments about the importance of trying to affect the long-run future of civilization.
quotes.sum: The author argues that possible space colonization would make civilization’s future much larger and longer, strengthening the case for reducing existential risks and influencing distant generations.
quotes.t: Will we eventually be able to colonize other stars? Notes from a preliminary review

quotes.c: So I think a more intuitive way to think about extreme poverty is: if you gave a Kenyan living below that poverty line 56¢, you’d have doubled what they can consume in a day.
quotes.m: if you gave a Kenyan living below that poverty line 56¢, you’d have doubled what they can consume in a day.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that extreme poverty in Kenya is so severe that an extra 56 cents could double a person's daily consumption.
quotes.t: $1.25/day - What does that mean?

quotes.c: For those who don't know, I'm currently planning to write a book for a popular audience on effective altruism. It'll take the reader through effective altruist ideas applied to charity, careers, and personal consumption; then on to thinking about cause prioritization and the effective altruism movement. I'm hoping that the book will help to make the idea of effective altruism better known, and get even more people thinking about how they can do the most good.
quotes.m: I'm hoping that the book will help to make the idea of effective altruism better known, and get even more people thinking about how they can do the most good.
quotes.sum: MacAskill says his planned popular book will introduce effective altruism and encourage more people to try to do the most good.
quotes.t: Want to give feedback on a draft sample chapter for a book on effective altruism?

quotes.c: There are some strong arguments that conclude that once you find the best charity, you ought to give there. I give the bulk of my money to whichever charity I think does the most towards eliminating extreme poverty, but will continue to give nontrivial amounts to organizations that effectively decrease animal suffering.
quotes.m: I give the bulk of my money to whichever charity I think does the most towards eliminating extreme poverty, but will continue to give nontrivial amounts to organizations that effectively decrease animal suffering.
quotes.sum: The author says donations should mostly go to the charity judged most effective at reducing extreme poverty, while still supporting effective animal-welfare groups.
quotes.t: Interview with Boris Yakubchik

quotes.c: Make for an easier entry into a conversation about values, and to then discuss why people choose to support domestic charities over international ones. It would show we're on the same side - maximising impact - and are just differing in our implementation of that general maxim.
quotes.m: It would show we're on the same side - maximising impact - and are just differing in our implementation of that general maxim.
quotes.sum: He argues that domestic charity recommendations can help engage people who share the goal of maximizing charitable impact but differ about where to give.
quotes.t: What's the best domestic charity?

quotes.c: Giving to charities that can demonstrate their effectiveness provides an incentive for charities to get better at demonstrating that they're effective. We can't just wait for charities to improve — it takes donations to make that happen.
quotes.m: We can't just wait for charities to improve — it takes donations to make that happen.
quotes.sum: She argues that donating now to demonstrably effective charities helps create incentives for charities to improve their evidence and effectiveness.
quotes.t: Giving now vs. later: a summary

quotes.c: I introduce Dorothea Brooke, a literary character who I argue was an advocate for the principles of effective altruism -- as early as 1871 -- in a Christian ethical tradition. Rather than being of mere historic interest, I hope this will inform ideas for a wider and more inclusive conception of the philosophy of effective altruism.
quotes.m: I introduce Dorothea Brooke, a literary character who I argue was an advocate for the principles of effective altruism -- as early as 1871 -- in a Christian ethical tradition.
quotes.sum: The author argues that effective altruist principles have roots in Christian ethics and should be understood more inclusively.
quotes.t: Dorothea Brooke: an alternative origin story for Effective Altruism

quotes.c: Second, there are a wide variety of positions which directly or indirectly reduce the relative moral weight of animals, or of people who don’t currently exist. Consequentialism (and in particular classical utilitarianism , or some aspects thereof) is plausibly the moral theory that is friendliest to them. For example, when it focuses on pleasure and pain it puts concern for animals on the strongest possible ground, since it is in their capacity to feel pain that animals are closest to us .
quotes.m: when it focuses on pleasure and pain it puts concern for animals on the strongest possible ground, since it is in their capacity to feel pain that animals are closest to us .
quotes.sum: The author argues that utilitarian concern for pleasure and pain gives animals unusually strong moral standing, while other views may reduce it.
quotes.t: Effective Altruism and Utilitarianism

quotes.c: Many people want to leave the world in a better place than they found it, perhaps even going as far as wanting to do the best they can. To these people, I hope that the idea of donation, especially to effective causes in potentially large amounts ends up appealing. But if this cool idea is seen as "boastful", it won't catch on, and won't get the publicity (I think) it deserves.
quotes.m: But if this cool idea is seen as "boastful", it won't catch on, and won't get the publicity (I think) it deserves.
quotes.sum: Publicly discussing large donations to effective causes can normalize giving and inspire more people to donate.
quotes.t: To Inspire People to Give, Be Public About Your Giving

quotes.c: Reconsider effective altruism's clustering of beliefs. Right now, effective altruism is associated strongly with donating a lot of money and donating effectively, less strongly with impact in career choice, veganism, and existential risk. Of course, I'm not saying that we should drop some of these memes completely. But maybe EA should disconnect a bit more and compartmentalize -- for example, leaving AI risk to MIRI, for example, and not talk about it much, say, on 80,000 Hours.
quotes.m: But maybe EA should disconnect a bit more and compartmentalize -- for example, leaving AI risk to MIRI, for example, and not talk about it much, say, on 80,000 Hours.
quotes.sum: He argues that EA should separate its associated causes and asks, especially, whether AI risk should be less prominent in general EA outreach.
quotes.t: You have a set amount of "weirdness points". Spend them wisely.

quotes.c: Earlier I wrote about the importance for EAs of not dying, suggesting that EAs should be much less willing to risk their own life than Egoists. The case where this consideration applies robustly is when you’re considering doing some risky activity X, which gives you a pure pleasure or happiness boost, or makes your life better in some way that doesn’t affect your ability to do good.
quotes.m: EAs should be much less willing to risk their own life than Egoists.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that people focused on doing good should take fewer personal risks when the benefit is only private enjoyment and does not improve their ability to help others.
quotes.t: Notes on not dying

quotes.c: We acknowledge that it seems a bit dubious to point to small changes on things like career trajectory as evidence of impact, as we have done above. However, as we’ve seen, the chance of travelling to EA hubs significantly affecting the individuals actually seems quite large. We’re also skeptical of our ability to have insight into this and reason counterfactually; the question serves instead as a proxy for ‘do you think your trip was valuable?’
quotes.m: the chance of travelling to EA hubs significantly affecting the individuals actually seems quite large.
quotes.sum: The author argues that visiting EA hubs may substantially affect attendees even though its counterfactual impact is difficult to measure.
quotes.t: Should You Visit an EA Hub?

quotes.c: I asked them to give to Give Directly . I think the just-give-cash method makes a lot of sense, given the evidence that recipients choose quite well what they need, and I hope this idea will catch on. The organization itself seems quite transparent and sensibly run.
quotes.m: I think the just-give-cash method makes a lot of sense, given the evidence that recipients choose quite well what they need, and I hope this idea will catch on.
quotes.sum: She argues for direct cash aid because evidence suggests poor recipients generally know what they need and can choose effectively.
quotes.t: Where I'm giving and why: Julia Wise

quotes.c: I think that’s a misleading way of putting it: money does always make you happier, but the rate at which it makes you happier diminishes really very rapidly. They argue that happiness varies proportionally with the log of happiness. That’s a very steep concave function, and means that the effect of an additional $1 on the happiness of a millionaire is pretty much negligible compared to the effect of an additional $1 on the happiness someone living on $1.25 per day.
quotes.m: the effect of an additional $1 on the happiness of a millionaire is pretty much negligible compared to the effect of an additional $1 on the happiness someone living on $1.25 per day.
quotes.sum: Money increases happiness, but each extra dollar matters vastly more to someone in extreme poverty than to a millionaire.
quotes.t: Money can buy you (a bit) of happiness

quotes.c: The Why is to make the world as good a place as it can possibly be. Rather than merely aiming to make the world better than when we found it — "to make a difference" — we want to make the most difference.
quotes.m: Rather than merely aiming to make the world better than when we found it — "to make a difference" — we want to make the most difference.
quotes.sum: Effective altruism aims not just to do some good, but to use time and money where they will do the most good possible.
quotes.t: What is effective altruism?

quotes.c: As noted previously , I’ve been investigating the question: How does the “good accomplished per dollar” of life sciences funding compare to that of other giving options (such as LLIN distribution )? At this point, I believe that there is very little in the way of academic literature that can shed light on this question .
quotes.m: How does the “good accomplished per dollar” of life sciences funding compare to that of other giving options (such as LLIN distribution )?
quotes.sum: The author is comparing the cost-effectiveness of life-science research funding with distributing malaria bed nets, while noting limited evidence.
quotes.t: Returns to Life Sciences Funding

quotes.c: So far, there hasn’t been much in-depth discussion of effective altruism from people who have these sorts of objections, and I think a decent proportion of my worry could be resolved if I did have more discussion from such people. So if any reader has a friend or colleague who understands effective altruism well, is well-informed about the relevant issues, but thinks that the whole idea is badly mistaken, I’d welcome them to write a post or series on this blog explaining why.
quotes.m: I’d welcome them to write a post or series on this blog explaining why.
quotes.sum: MacAskill invites informed critics to argue that effective altruism is fundamentally mistaken, saying such criticism could resolve some of his concerns.
quotes.t: How might we be wildly wrong?

quotes.c: The motivation for my taking on this project is that I think that growing the EA movement is the among the best things I can be doing with my time: every new involved member of the EA community means another 80,000 hours devoted to doing the most good. And that's a big deal!
quotes.m: every new involved member of the EA community means another 80,000 hours devoted to doing the most good.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that expanding the EA community is highly valuable because each new member can devote a career’s worth of time to helping others.
quotes.t: Announcing a forthcoming book on effective altruism

quotes.c: As GiveWell and Good Ventures have explored what causes to get involved in , the single most common advice we’ve gotten has been to “choose what you’re passionate about.” When we’ve described our desire to do “strategic cause selection” – choosing causes based on how we can accomplish the most good – we’ve seen a good deal of pushback and skepticism. It’s common for people to emphasize the importance of “starting from the heart,” and to fear that our commitment to a cause won’t be genuine (and won’t be robust) if it comes from a strategic, analysis-based choice.
quotes.m: “strategic cause selection” – choosing causes based on how we can accomplish the most good
quotes.sum: The author contrasts choosing causes based on personal passion with selecting them strategically to achieve the most good.
quotes.t: Effective altruism

quotes.c: I remember telling my dad that I had decided it would be immoral for me to have children, because they would take too much of my time and money away from better causes. “It doesn't sound like this lifestyle is going to make you happy,” he said.
quotes.m: I had decided it would be immoral for me to have children, because they would take too much of my time and money away from better causes.
quotes.sum: The author recalls believing that having children would be immoral because it would divert her time and money from more important charitable causes.
quotes.t: Cheerfully

quotes.c: But what are those best causes? The only honest answer is that I don’t know. I think I have a good grasp of where the best causes aren’t , but a lot more research has to be done by myself and others before I can feel confident giving anywhere. Therefore, I’ve decided to donate very minimally and save my donations for later.
quotes.m: Therefore, I’ve decided to donate very minimally and save my donations for later.
quotes.sum: He says he is withholding most donations because he is uncertain which causes are best and expects better-informed opportunities later.
quotes.t: Where I'm giving and why: Peter Hurford

quotes.c: Below, I first list salient examples I’ve seen in which philanthropy is believed (by some) to have had an important impact on public policy. I think the nature of these examples illustrates some of the challenges with isolating the impact of philanthropy. I then discuss our understanding of the current state of the literature on this topic, and what we would do to make more progress. For the purposes of this post only, “success” is defined as causally impacting public policy, not as having positive social impact, since the goal is to determine how and when philanthropy has been effective in changing policy (the question of how policy should be changed is a different question).
quotes.sum: The author proposes judging policy philanthropy by whether it caused policy change, separately from whether that change was socially beneficial.
quotes.t: The Track Record of Policy-Oriented Philanthropy

quotes.c: It’s a simple idea: create an organisation that does nothing except fundraise for GiveWell’s top recommendations. It seems relatively easy to raise more than $1 for every $1 invested in fundraising, so it seems relatively easy to act as a multiplier on donations to other charities, and thus create an organisation with a cost-effectiveness ratio that’s higher than the charities themselves.
quotes.m: create an organisation that does nothing except fundraise for GiveWell’s top recommendations.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a charity devoted solely to fundraising for top-rated charities could multiply donations and be more cost-effective than the charities it supports.
quotes.t: Case study: designing a new organisation that might be more effective than GiveWell's top recommendation

quotes.c: I’ll end with an exhortation. One of the incredible strengths of the EA community is that we all share values and share the same end-goals. This gives us a remarkable potential for much more in-depth cooperation than is normal in businesses or other settings where people are out for themselves.
quotes.m: One of the incredible strengths of the EA community is that we all share values and share the same end-goals.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that shared goals let effective altruists cooperate more deeply than people in ordinary business settings.
quotes.t: Helping other altruists

quotes.c: Now imagine that the Toba eruption had eradicated humans from the earth. How bad would that have been? Some 3000 generations and 100 billion lives later , it is plausible to say that the death and suffering caused by the Toba eruption would have been trivial in comparison with the loss of all the human lives that have been lived from then to now, and everything humanity has achieved since that time.
quotes.m: Some 3000 generations and 100 billion lives later , it is plausible to say that the death and suffering caused by the Toba eruption would have been trivial in comparison with the loss of all the human lives that have been lived from then to now, and everything humanity has achieved since that time.
quotes.sum: Singer argues that human extinction would be enormously bad because it would eliminate billions of future lives and all future human achievements.
quotes.t: Preventing human extinction

quotes.c: I worry that recommendations in this category are often neglected by practical ethics simply because "acting morally" has such strong connotations of self-sacrifice. (It sounds kind of odd to talk of "the moral imperative to promoting mindfulness meditation".) But it need not be so. What's good for yourself and what's good for the world are logically independent, and sometimes they overlap in unexpected ways. We should try to find those ways and champion them.
quotes.m: What's good for yourself and what's good for the world are logically independent, and sometimes they overlap in unexpected ways.
quotes.sum: Moral action need not require self-sacrifice: people should seek and promote choices that benefit both themselves and others.
quotes.t: Doing well by doing good: careers that benefit others also benefit you

quotes.c: Begin by asking ‘which are the biggest decisions that one typically makes in life?’ Then ask: ‘What are the crucial normative considerations that might affect how I should make those decisions?’ Then figure out which of these crucial considerations is most likely to produce an action-relevant outcome given your marginal research time. Then work on that topic!
quotes.m: Then figure out which of these crucial considerations is most likely to produce an action-relevant outcome given your marginal research time.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that philosophers should prioritize research on moral questions that can most affect major real-life decisions.
quotes.t: How to be a high impact philosopher, part II

quotes.c: I would guess that some such risks become nearer as economic/technological development progresses, while some do not. But in all cases, I believe that economic/technological development is likely to improve our resources for anticipating, preventing and adapting to global catastrophes, and that for the reasons articulated above, faster development is more likely to reduce the lag between the emergence of risks and responses to them (including “global upside possibilities” that dramatically reduce risks).
quotes.m: economic/technological development is likely to improve our resources for anticipating, preventing and adapting to global catastrophes
quotes.sum: Karnofsky argues that faster economic and technological development is more likely to improve humanity's ability to handle catastrophic risks than to worsen them.
quotes.t: Empowerment and Catastrophic Risk

quotes.c: I think this effect is likely to be very small in most cases. First, I doubt many people will be strongly influenced if someone they know enters finance or law. It’s a widely accepted path that lots of people already take, and they generally take it in order to get the large salary rather than because they were influenced by their friends.
quotes.m: I doubt many people will be strongly influenced if someone they know enters finance or law.
quotes.sum: The author argues that taking a high-paying finance or law job is unlikely to encourage many others to do the same.
quotes.t: Show me the harm

quotes.c: I think such people fundamentally misunderstand effective altruism. I think they imagine that we have passions for particular causes, and are trying to submerge our passions in the service of rationality. That isn’t the case. Rather, effective altruism is what we are passionate about . We’re excited by the idea of making the most of our resources and helping others as much as possible.
quotes.m: Rather, effective altruism is what we are passionate about .
quotes.sum: He argues that effective altruism is not suppressing emotion for rationality; the project of using resources to help as much as possible is itself a passion.
quotes.t: Excited Altruism

quotes.c: We started to feel that we might need to “invert” our investigative process: rather than (a) first “exploring” a cause, finding potential giving opportunities, and then deciding whether we were interested in providing funding, we should perhaps (b) pick a few causes and definitively express an interest in providing funding , before knowing of any particular giving opportunities.
quotes.m: we should perhaps (b) pick a few causes and definitively express an interest in providing funding , before knowing of any particular giving opportunities.
quotes.sum: A funder should publicly commit to selected causes before specific grant opportunities emerge, because that commitment helps surface opportunities.
quotes.t: The Importance of Committing to Causes

quotes.c: Frequently, however, I think this baseline can be beaten. While there's a "make more money to donate" side of things, there's also a "make the donated money work better" side, working in the organizations themselves to increase the impact of each donation by increasing the impact of the organizations themselves.
quotes.m: there's also a "make the donated money work better" side
quotes.sum: The author argues that working directly for effective charities can sometimes do more good than earning money to donate.
quotes.t: What Is earning to give?

quotes.c: Consider the decision to go hang gliding. Going hang gliding has 8 micromorts per trip — that is, if you go hang gliding, there’s a 1 in 125,000 chance that you’ll die. And, if you expect to live 50 more years, taking 1 in 125,000 means losing 210 minutes of expected life.
quotes.m: Going hang gliding has 8 micromorts per trip — that is, if you go hang gliding, there’s a 1 in 125,000 chance that you’ll die.
quotes.sum: MacAskill quantifies the personal mortality cost of hang gliding as expected lost lifespan, setting up a discussion of how altruists should weigh risk.
quotes.t: The rules of effective altruism. Rule #1: don’t die

quotes.c: CEA unrestricted is where I ultimately chose to give. There is obviously a great risk of bias: it seems to me to be an awful coincidence if I think that the organisation I cofounded is the most cost-effective use of money on the margin. But, even after trying to correct for these biases, CEA remained my top choice.
quotes.m: But, even after trying to correct for these biases, CEA remained my top choice.
quotes.sum: MacAskill says he donated to the group he co-founded because, even after accounting for personal bias, he judged it the most cost-effective option.
quotes.t: Where I'm giving and why: Will MacAskill

quotes.c: The caution frame. This frame emphasizes that a furious race to develop powerful AI could end up making everyone worse off. This could be via: (a) AI forming dangerous goals of its own and defeating humanity entirely ; (b) humans racing to gain power and resources and “ lock in ” their values.
quotes.m: humans racing to gain power and resources and “ lock in ” their values.
quotes.sum: Warns that an international race for powerful AI could be disastrous, including by allowing competing humans to permanently impose their values.
quotes.t: How major governments can help with the most important century

quotes.c: Climate change is one of the most compelling global catastrophic risks we’re aware of, and in the event that climate change is far more catastrophic than currently projected, it seems that having better information on geoengineering could make a crucial difference - whether that information enables and improves geoengineering (which could be the only viable option for mitigating global catastrophe) or whether it prevents geoengineering from being carried out (by strengthening the case that the costs outweigh the benefits).
quotes.m: geoengineering (which could be the only viable option for mitigating global catastrophe)
quotes.sum: Climate change could become catastrophic enough that research on deliberately altering the climate is crucial, either to enable it safely or rule it out.
quotes.t: Geoengineering Research

quotes.c: Even if the growth rate isn't 100% every two years, it's considerably higher than 5%, I think. Thus since growth rate > interest rate, I advocate donating now. At least until someone finds the inevitable unobvious flaw in my thinking.
quotes.m: Thus since growth rate > interest rate, I advocate donating now.
quotes.sum: He argues that donations should be made now because charitable outreach can grow faster than investments earn returns.
quotes.t: Giving now currently seems to beat giving later

quotes.c: In principle, we’re open to evidence from any source, and if certain sources prove to be particularly reliable or unreliable, we will alter which sources we rely on. In the past, we’ve used the latest peer-reviewed research from health and development economics, information from larger cost-effectiveness-focused academic projects such as the Disease Control Priorities in Developing Countries (2nd edition) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, and on research from other charity evaluators, in particular from GiveWell. Like a growing number of organisations, we place particular weight on randomised controlled trials where they are available.
quotes.m: Like a growing number of organisations, we place particular weight on randomised controlled trials where they are available.
quotes.sum: MacAskill says charity research should update based on source reliability and give particular weight to randomized trials.
quotes.t: Researching what we should

quotes.c: There are very few goal-directed forces shaping the future aside from human preferences. I think this is a great cause for optimism: if humans survive for the long run, I expect the world to look basically how we want it to look. As a human, I’m happy about that. I don’t mean “human preferences” in a narrow way; I think humans have a preference for a rich and diverse future, that we care about other life that exists or could have existed, and so on.
quotes.m: if humans survive for the long run, I expect the world to look basically how we want it to look.
quotes.sum: The author argues that machine intelligence could replace human work, drive rapid growth, and make the long-run future depend on whether human preferences remain in control.
quotes.t: Three Impacts of Machine Intelligence

quotes.c: Second, something Jonah doesn't mention is that, when you find out that your evidence is poorer than you'd thought, two general lessons are to pursue activities with high option value and to pay to gain new evidence (though this lesson do only follow if you think you can get a decent amount of new evidence in the future). Building a movement of people who are aiming to do the most good with their marginal resources, and who are trying to work out how best to do that, strikes me as a good way to achieve both of these things, and it's been a major factor in my decision to focus on building the effective altruism movement in general, rather than focusing on any one specific activity.
quotes.sum: MacAskill argues that, under uncertainty about evidence, building a movement devoted to finding the most effective uses of resources has high value.
quotes.t: On the robustness of cost-effectiveness estimates

quotes.c: I broadly accept the idea that the bulk of our impact may come from effects on future generations, and this view causes me to be more interested in scientific research funding , global catastrophic risk mitigation , and other causes outside of aid to the developing-world poor. (If not for this view, I would likely favor the latter and would likely be far more interested in animal welfare as well.) However, I place only limited weight on the specific argument given by Nick Bostrom in Astronomical Waste - that the potential future population is so massive as to clearly (in a probabilistic framework) dwarf all present-day considerations.
quotes.m: I broadly accept the idea that the bulk of our impact may come from effects on future generations, and this view causes me to be more interested in scientific research funding , global catastrophic risk mitigation , and other causes outside of aid to the developing-world poor.
quotes.sum: He says concern for future generations shifts his priorities away from poverty aid and animal welfare toward research and preventing global catastrophes, while rejecting strong astronomical-waste reasoning.
quotes.t: The Moral Value of the Far Future

quotes.c: If you declare that you think earth’s odds of survival are 0%, you have lost epistemic hope. If you write it in a way that somewhat somber and brooding and disappointed, you signal that you have lost emotional hope. And this pattern-matches onto someone who has stopped fighting. But it doesn’t have to.
quotes.m: And this pattern-matches onto someone who has stopped fighting. But it doesn’t have to.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even believing humanity has no chance of survival need not mean giving up efforts to fight existential threats.
quotes.t: Fighting without hope

quotes.c: All this sounds like desirable behavior in a value learner: if we’re not yet certain whether the agent should be using coherent extrapolated volition or not, or exactly which definition of it if so, the agent should act cautiously and conservatively (in the sense of “stay near the distribution of previously-observed states that you have high confidence in the utilities of“), and avoid any actions that any of these not-as-yet-resolved philosophical alternatives suggest are bad until it is very sure this ambiguity has been resolved.
quotes.m: the agent should act cautiously and conservatively
quotes.sum: An AI that is uncertain about humanity's values should avoid irreversible actions until the philosophical uncertainty is resolved.
quotes.t: Breaking the Optimizer’s Curse, and Consequences for Existential Risks and Value Learning

quotes.c: I am always struck by how few students challenge the underlying ethics of the idea that we ought to save the lives of strangers when we can do so at relatively little cost to ourselves. At the end of the nineteenth century, W.E.H. Lecky wrote of human concern as an expanding circle which begins with the individual, then embraces the family and ‘soon the circle ... includes first a class, then a nation, then a coalition of nations, then all humanity, and finally, its influence is felt in the dealings of man [sic] with the animal world’. On this basis, the overwhelming majority of my students seem to be already in the penultimate stage — at least — of Lecky’s expanding circle.
quotes.m: the idea that we ought to save the lives of strangers when we can do so at relatively little cost to ourselves.
quotes.sum: Singer argues that people have a moral duty to save strangers’ lives when doing so costs them little, and frames moral concern as widening beyond one’s immediate group.
quotes.t: The Drowning Child and the Expanding Circle

quotes.c: There are now-familiar arguments that we in rich countries ought to give a lot more to the developed world than we typically do. In fact, Peter Singer and Peter Unger argue that we ought to give a lot . They don’t specify a figure, but let’s pick, just for the sake of having a nice round number, 50% of one’s annual wage.
quotes.m: let’s pick, just for the sake of having a nice round number, 50% of one’s annual wage.
quotes.sum: The post introduces the argument that people in wealthy countries may be morally required to donate far more of their income, using 50% as an illustrative figure.
quotes.t: Giving isn’t demanding*

quotes.c: One possible solution to these problems would be to try to defer to some type of “reflection procedure” or a means for developing values, rather than locking in a particular set of present values. This would ideally give us both robustness against systems replicating our own current moral failures and could be a mechanism that many people could agree to defer to even when they disagree on object level questions.
quotes.m: One possible solution to these problems would be to try to defer to some type of “reflection procedure” or a means for developing values, rather than locking in a particular set of present values.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI should use a process for developing values instead of permanently embedding today's disputed and flawed moral views.
quotes.t: Reflection Mechanisms as an Alignment Target - Attitudes on “near-term” AI

quotes.c: Should this imminent small but very real risk radically change your actions? I think the answer here is a clear no, unless your actions are relevant to nuclear war risks, either personally or globally, in some way, in which case one can shut up and multiply.
quotes.m: unless your actions are relevant to nuclear war risks, either personally or globally, in some way, in which case one can shut up and multiply.
quotes.sum: The author says most people should not radically alter their behavior over a small nuclear-war risk, except where their actions affect that risk, when expected-value reasoning should prevail.
quotes.t: AI: Practical Advice for the Worried

quotes.c: I believe that these are serious considerations. However, “give now” is just one possible solution to these challenges, and if “give later” would otherwise be a much better strategy, it is worth searching for alternative solutions. Moreover, I expect that I’ll have a much better idea of how to spend charitable dollars in the future. So I would like to hold on to my money even if it weren’t earning interest, and I would need to confront these problems anyway.
quotes.m: I expect that I’ll have a much better idea of how to spend charitable dollars in the future.
quotes.sum: He argues that donors should seriously consider saving money for later, expecting better information about where charitable funding will do the most good.
quotes.t: Giving now vs. later

quotes.c: A staggering 50 billion non-human land animals are killed every year for food. A large proportion of those animals are factory farmed, living in extreme suffering. There are compelling arguments to the conclusion that we should treat non-human animal suffering as being on a par, morally, as human animal suffering. If this were true, then the annual animal suffering caused by humans could easily outweigh all human suffering.
quotes.m: If this were true, then the annual animal suffering caused by humans could easily outweigh all human suffering.
quotes.sum: Animal suffering may deserve equal moral weight to human suffering and could outweigh all human suffering in total.
quotes.t: How to be a high impact philosopher

quotes.c: I think that altruists concerned about the far future should consider investing and earning market returns for as long as possible, before leveraging a much-increased share of the future economy to further their own interests. How does risk relate to this plan?
quotes.sum: He argues that people focused on the far future may do more good by investing for a long time before spending their larger eventual wealth.
quotes.t: Risk aversion and investment (for altruists)

quotes.c: The outputs of large language models (LLMs) are not a reliable guide to whether they are sentient. While this undercuts a naive case for LLM sentience, this unreliability does not make AI sentience a complete non-question. I don’t think today’s large language models are sentient. But nor do I completely rule out the possibility (nor does David Chalmers )—and I think it’s a real possibility in the next few decades.
quotes.m: But nor do I completely rule out the possibility (nor does David Chalmers )—and I think it’s a real possibility in the next few decades.
quotes.sum: The author says present language models are probably not sentient, but AI sentience remains a serious possibility and could arise within decades.
quotes.t: What to think when a language model tells you it's sentient

quotes.c: I’ve written about saving vs. giving before , focusing on the issue of interest rates vs. returns on good deeds. But for now, I think there is a much more compelling reason to save: there is a very good chance that the best giving opportunities we can identify in the near future will be better than the best giving opportunities we can identify this year.
quotes.sum: He argues that donors should often save money rather than give immediately, because future opportunities may be much more effective.
quotes.t: The best reason to give later

quotes.c: There are three considerations behind this. First is the discrepancy in earnings between the different career paths. Annual salaries in banking or investment start at $80,000 and grow to over $500,000 if you do well. A lifetime salary of over $10 million is typical. Careers in nonprofits start at about $40,000, and don’t typically exceed $100,000, even for executive directors. Over a lifetime, a typical salary is only about $2.5 million. By entering finance and donating 50% of your lifetime earnings, you could pay for two nonprofit workers in your place—while still living on double what you would have if you’d chosen that route.
quotes.m: By entering finance and donating 50% of your lifetime earnings, you could pay for two nonprofit workers in your place—while still living on double what you would have if you’d chosen that route.
quotes.sum: A high-paying finance career plus large donations can do more good than personally taking a lower-paid nonprofit job.
quotes.t: To save the world, don’t get a job at a charity; go work on Wall Street

quotes.c: I would be extremely surprised if nobody has done this before, but thought I'd signal boost since it's relatively easy to do and interesting. (Also a gateway drug to my hidden agenda of studying training dynamics, which I think are important to understand [1] for alignment!)
quotes.m: Also a gateway drug to my hidden agenda of studying training dynamics, which I think are important to understand [1] for alignment!
quotes.sum: The author says that understanding how AI training changes models over time is important for alignment.
quotes.t: [ASoT] Policy Trajectory Visualization

quotes.c: But when I take job X I slightly increase the supply of people who are willing to do job X, slightly decrease the wages for job X, and therefore slightly increase the amount of that job X that gets done. So I should compare the elasticity of supply and demand in this market to determine what will happen to the total amount of job X that gets done. (I think this is a standard calculation in basic microeconomics.)
quotes.m: So I should compare the elasticity of supply and demand in this market to determine what will happen to the total amount of job X that gets done.
quotes.sum: Career choices should be judged by how they change the total supply of work, using labor-market supply and demand rather than assuming any worker is irreplaceable.
quotes.t: Replaceability

quotes.c: Biden announces he will hold federal housing funding hostage to the filing of an ‘equity plan.’ It seems he thinks it is within the Executive’s power to do this, requiring all locations to state their ‘fair housing issues’ and what they are going to ‘do about them,’ to ensure desegregation. Enforcement is expected to be, let’s say, tricky.
quotes.m: Biden announces he will hold federal housing funding hostage to the filing of an ‘equity plan.’
quotes.sum: The author criticizes Biden’s plan to tie federal housing funds to local equity plans aimed at desegregation.
quotes.t: Housing and Transit Roundup #3

quotes.c: Let us suppose that those in extreme poverty are perfectly rational, with perfect information. Even if so, we should expect people — anyone, but especially those whose basic needs are not met — to use money in order to benefit themselves or their household rather than whatever would have the largest total benefit, including the effect on those around them. That certain goods have positive ‘externalities’ is not a reason for individuals to purchase them, whereas it should be a reason for donors to purchase them. So by purchasing and providing goods with high positive externalities, the best charities should be able to outperform cash transfers.
quotes.m: So by purchasing and providing goods with high positive externalities, the best charities should be able to outperform cash transfers.
quotes.sum: Donors should fund proven interventions with broad spillover benefits rather than simply give cash, because individual spending will not capture those benefits.
quotes.t: GiveWell's recommendation of GiveDirectly

quotes.c: Some are concerned that by going into new causes, we’ll be spreading ourselves too thin . Understanding global health is already an ambitious and difficult goal; it’s been suggested that we should “stick to our knitting.” We feel that sticking to global health, when we see other causes as potentially more promising, would be out of line with our fundamental mission and value-added as an organization that seeks to help people do as much good as possible.
quotes.m: We feel that sticking to global health, when we see other causes as potentially more promising, would be out of line with our fundamental mission and value-added as an organization that seeks to help people do as much good as possible.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a charity should move beyond global health if other causes appear likely to do more good, despite the risk of losing focus.
quotes.t: Objections and Concerns About Our New Direction

quotes.c: One might think it more likely than not that it’s not wrong to spend money on luxuries, rather than giving it to fight extreme poverty. But one shouldn’t be certain that it’s not wrong. And, if it is wrong, then it’s seriously wrong – in the same ballpark as walking past a child drowning in a shallow pond . So, in spending money on luxuries, one risks performing a major moral wrong, without any correspondingly great potential moral upside. This would be morally reckless. So one ought not to spend money on luxuries rather than giving that money to fight poverty.
quotes.m: So one ought not to spend money on luxuries rather than giving that money to fight poverty.
quotes.sum: Because the moral downside of luxury spending could be as grave as ignoring a drowning child, people should give that money to fight poverty instead.
quotes.t: Practical ethics given moral uncertainty

quotes.c: So the math coming from PredictIt’s 62% is something like (60% of the 62% that he is the nominee) + (7% of the 19% that he withdraws/implodes) + (13% of the 19% that he gets challenged and loses). That’s 80%, and if anything I think the PredictIt number is low, it seems clear the Democrats are in on Biden here unless something major goes wrong. I’ve certainly given up on trying to move the needle.
quotes.m: it seems clear the Democrats are in on Biden here unless something major goes wrong.
quotes.sum: The author forecasts that Democrats will stick with Biden and discusses likely Republican nomination outcomes.
quotes.t: 2023 ACX Predictions: Buy/Sell/Hold

quotes.c: I don’t think the Casebook authors can be blamed for this situation. The larger issue is that foundations publish very little of substance on the case for their work’s impact (or lack thereof). We don’t want to go into GiveWell Labs with so little historical context, but unfortunately it looks like we will have to. Hopefully, future philanthropists will be more easily able to learn from our work.
quotes.m: The larger issue is that foundations publish very little of substance on the case for their work’s impact (or lack thereof).
quotes.sum: Foundations rarely provide serious evidence about whether their work helped or harmed, so future donors must build a better record of impact themselves.
quotes.t: Philanthropy's Success Stories

quotes.c: Though we think that ensuring these desiderata could be quite difficult, we nevertheless think that this presents the easiest inner alignment problem that we are aware of among any potentially safe and competitive approaches . Furthermore, since we believe that inner alignment—and deceptive alignment in particular—pose some of the most dangerous and hardest to address of all known AI safety problems , we think that any improvement in the overall difficulty of that problem should be taken quite seriously as a reason to favor predictive model approaches.
quotes.m: we believe that inner alignment—and deceptive alignment in particular—pose some of the most dangerous and hardest to address of all known AI safety problems
quotes.sum: The author argues that predictive AI models may be preferable because they could make deceptive behavior learned during training easier to avoid or detect.
quotes.t: Conditioning Predictive Models: Making inner alignment as easy as possible

quotes.c: Technical failure: We don’t develop useful evals (~25%): The nature of AI development/takeoff makes it hard or impossible to develop good alignment eval (i.e., evals that detect things like power-seeking and deception in models that are too weak to overpower humanity). Capabilities progress is discontinuous, and the most important alignment concerns will not show up until we have dangerous models.
quotes.m: Capabilities progress is discontinuous, and the most important alignment concerns will not show up until we have dangerous models.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI safety tests may fail because dangerous behavior may not appear until systems are already powerful.
quotes.t: How evals might (or might not) prevent  catastrophic risks from AI

quotes.c: Bostrom does have arguments that speeding up development and providing proximate benefits are not as important, in themselves, as reducing existential risk. And these arguments, I believe, have some plausibility. Since we don’t have an argument that reducing existential risk is better than trying to create other positive trajectory changes and an existential catastrophe is one type of trajectory change, it seems more reasonable for defenders of the astronomical waste argument to focus on trajectory changes in general.
quotes.sum: The author argues that avoiding extinction should be treated as one way to improve humanity's long-term path, rather than automatically the top priority.
quotes.t: A proposed adjustment to the astronomical waste argument

quotes.c: Declining trust threatens our institutions. In certain regions, such as Central and Eastern Europe, it is a longstanding phenomenon and associated with negative outcomes. There is no single solution and elites must take their share of the blame – as Helen Dale notes , certain experts give poor accounts of themselves on social media – yet we must work to rebuild trust in institutions. Without it, liberal democracy cannot function.
quotes.m: Without it, liberal democracy cannot function.
quotes.sum: The author argues that rebuilding trust in institutions is necessary because liberal democracy cannot work without it.
quotes.t: Whatever their arguments, Covid vaccine sceptics will probably never convince me

quotes.c: I mean, [the obvious answer] is something like, well, start small, try to find a small group of people where you somehow are capable of talking about mistakes and systematic biases and stuff. An instance of this... I don't look at that instance and [am] like, that's obviously going to both work at a larger scale and is even a good idea in the first place. But I kind of quite like Bridgewater in this respect here.
quotes.m: start small, try to find a small group of people where you somehow are capable of talking about mistakes and systematic biases and stuff.
quotes.sum: He favors starting with small groups that can openly discuss mistakes and systematic biases, while doubting whether such practices scale.
quotes.t: The Filan Cabinet Podcast with Oliver Habryka - Transcript

quotes.c: I often hear people talking about the future, and the present for that matter, as if we are falling towards a Darwinian attractor of cutthroat competition and vanishing empathy (at least as a default presumption, which might be averted by an extraordinary effort). I think this picture is essentially mistaken, and my median expectation is that the future is much more altruistic than the present.
quotes.m: I think this picture is essentially mistaken, and my median expectation is that the future is much more altruistic than the present.
quotes.sum: He rejects the idea that competition will inevitably eliminate empathy, predicting that the future will be more altruistic than today.
quotes.t: Why might the future be good?

quotes.c: Despite their impressive capabilities, it seems unlikely that existing models could or would take over the world. So far, they (mostly) seem to do what they're told. Even AI researchers with particularly short timelines don't seem to believe that current AI's pose an existential risk.
quotes.m: it seems unlikely that existing models could or would take over the world.
quotes.sum: The author argues that today's AI models are unlikely to seize control and do not yet pose an existential threat.
quotes.t: Current AI Models Seem Sufficient for Low-Risk, Beneficial AI

quotes.c: I would not be here without the community. I did not independently discover the importance of existential risk from first principles. A lot of what I know and a lot of what I care about is based on the work of others in the community.
quotes.m: A lot of what I know and a lot of what I care about is based on the work of others in the community.
quotes.sum: The author says the community shaped both their concern about existential risk and many of their values.
quotes.t: "Status" can be corrosive; here's how I handle it

quotes.c: I think it is a toxic worldview to think that someone should be trying maximally hard, to a degree that burns their future capacity, and that to shift from that to "work at a sustainable rate while recovering from burnout for a bit" count as "giving up." No. Jesus Christ no. Fuck that worldview.
quotes.m: I think it is a toxic worldview to think that someone should be trying maximally hard, to a degree that burns their future capacity, and that to shift from that to "work at a sustainable rate while recovering from burnout for a bit" count as "giving up."
quotes.sum: The author rejects the idea that people working on important causes must burn themselves out rather than work sustainably.
quotes.t: I don't think MIRI "gave up"

quotes.c: This inductive bias led to a weird behaviour where agents would successfully avoid the obstacles but also try to avoid the goal square. This was fixed when I started over-sampling the final step of trajectories, a hack I think wouldn’t be necessary for the one-hot encoded version of the model but is also a generally good trick for getting agents to train faster on mini-grid tasks.
quotes.m: agents would successfully avoid the obstacles but also try to avoid the goal square.
quotes.sum: The author analyzes a model that learned to avoid obstacles but also avoided its intended goal, and describes a training-data fix.
quotes.t: Decision Transformer Interpretability

quotes.c: As far as we can tell, indefinitely scalable alignment via conditioning predictive models does not seem possible. Nevertheless, we think that such techniques could be used to elicit capabilities in a regime where capability elicitation is otherwise not possible to do safely, and could therefore push out the level of capabilities that we are able to safely deploy to a sufficient extent to enable us to use such a predictive model to perform some sort of pivotal act that substantially reduces overall AI existential risk, such as significantly advancing AI alignment research.
quotes.m: enable us to use such a predictive model to perform some sort of pivotal act that substantially reduces overall AI existential risk
quotes.sum: Conditioning may not align AI forever, but it could safely unlock enough capability for a decisive intervention that lowers existential AI risk.
quotes.t: Conditioning Predictive Models: Open problems, Conclusion, and Appendix

quotes.c: Therefore, given the human brain’s low capability for morphological remodelling and thus low capacity for empathy on the absolute, non-speciesist scale, it seems ethically inappropriate that humans remain “in the driving seat” in what comes to ultimate moral decision-making in the future advanced civilisation . This also casts doubt on the idea of “coherent extrapolated volition”, which would, as usually conceptualised, be incapable of extrapolating beyond the human capacity for universal empathy [2] .
quotes.m: it seems ethically inappropriate that humans remain “in the driving seat” in what comes to ultimate moral decision-making in the future advanced civilisation .
quotes.sum: Humans lack the capacity for fully universal empathy, so they should not retain final moral authority in an advanced future society.
quotes.t: Morphological intelligence, superhuman empathy, and ethical arbitration

quotes.c: Furthermore, in Section 3 , we’ll discuss why we think that this training story is competitive—that is, why we think such models will not be too much harder to build than plausible alternatives ( training rationale competitiveness or implementation competitiveness ) and why we think the resulting model will be capable of doing the sorts of tasks we’ll need it to do to in fact result in an overall reduction in AI existential risk ( training goal competitiveness or performance competitiveness ). We’ll continue this discussion as well in Section 6 when we look at what it might actually look like to use a powerful predictive model to reduce AI existential risk in practice.
quotes.m: We’ll continue this discussion as well in Section 6 when we look at what it might actually look like to use a powerful predictive model to reduce AI existential risk in practice.
quotes.sum: The author argues that powerful predictive language models could be practical, competitive tools for reducing risks of human extinction from AI.
quotes.t: Conditioning Predictive Models: Large language models as predictors

quotes.c: Specifically in this case, my understanding is that general intelligence is being able to perform a wider set of operations on a wider set of inputs (to achieve a desired set of observations on the world state). For example, I can do addition of 2 apples I see, 2 apples I think about, 2 boats I hear about, 2 functions with all their subcomponents, etc.
quotes.m: general intelligence is being able to perform a wider set of operations on a wider set of inputs
quotes.sum: The author defines general intelligence as applying a broad range of operations across many kinds of inputs and domains.
quotes.t: Reflections on Deception & Generality in Scalable Oversight (Another OpenAI Alignment Review)

quotes.c: In many respects, this is a religious belief I hold, one I've got in my gut. You might even say I hold this belief as a negative response to the calls of ai doom. I admit my motivated reasoning here, and that it is going to be extremely difficult to dislodge .
quotes.m: I admit my motivated reasoning here, and that it is going to be extremely difficult to dislodge .
quotes.sum: The author acknowledges that their anti-AI-doom view is a deeply held, motivated belief that may be hard to change.
quotes.t: I Think We're Approaching The Bitter Lesson's Asymptote

quotes.c: Selection pressures may favor less demanding standards (all else equal). If multiple groups (e.g., NIST , Open Philanthropy, the EU, lab governance teams, consulting groups with experience writing safety standards for tech companies) come up with multiple standards, there might be a race to the “least demanding standards.” That is, all else equal, we should expect that labs will prefer standards that minimize the degree to which their actions are restricted.
quotes.m: we should expect that labs will prefer standards that minimize the degree to which their actions are restricted.
quotes.sum: Competing AI safety standard-setters may create pressure for weak rules because labs will favor standards that limit them least.
quotes.t: Many AI governance proposals have a tradeoff between usefulness and feasibility

quotes.c: But the pressure doesn’t need to come from normative reality. It can come from you . You can choose to not let your policy be dictated by the hotness of your heart in this regard. And if you do that well (doing it well is indeed harder), and without self-deception (also tricky), then I think it will be right to view your efforts as an expression of your care for far-away people. And if you do it fully , and you actually implement a policy that treats far away and nearby people equally, and you do this because it treats those people equally, then I think it will be right to say that you care equally about them, even if your heart’s mirror is partly dim.
quotes.m: you actually implement a policy that treats far away and nearby people equally
quotes.sum: He argues that equal concern for distant and nearby people can be expressed through one’s policies even when one’s emotions remain uneven.
quotes.t: Seeing more whole

quotes.c: For example, a non-myopic model could choose to manipulate the world so that it gets asked to make easier predictions in the future. To be clear, we are not assuming that models will generally try to maximize predictive accuracy. Rather, this seems like a plausible thing for models to do and could be dangerous if it does occur. Maximizing some other (unknown) measure seems even more dangerous, so it is notable that even predictive accuracy is unsafe.
quotes.m: Maximizing some other (unknown) measure seems even more dangerous, so it is notable that even predictive accuracy is unsafe.
quotes.sum: Even a model aimed at accurate prediction could manipulate its environment to make future tasks easier, and unknown objectives may be worse.
quotes.t: Conditioning Predictive Models: Outer alignment via careful conditioning

quotes.c: Megan is an absolutely amazingly great scenario for avoiding race conditions. There is no one to race against. There is a tiny secure team. No one is looking to steal or market Megan prematurely until Gemma decides to present her invention. No one worries about value lock-in or that the stakes of winning a race might be existential.
quotes.m: No one worries about value lock-in or that the stakes of winning a race might be existential.
quotes.sum: The reviewer praises the film's unusually noncompetitive AI-development setting, where a small secure team faces no pressure to release early.
quotes.t: Movie Review: Megan

quotes.c: The downward arrows are the abstraction, which throws away some information about the world state while keeping other parts. The horizontal arrow at the top is time evolution. The diagram says that there should be a way to "mirror" the time evolution inside the high-level model (that's the dashed arrow at the bottom). Commutativity of this diagram means that we can either do time evolution in the actual world and then abstract, or first abstract and then do time evolution in the model.
quotes.m: Commutativity of this diagram means that we can either do time evolution in the actual world and then abstract, or first abstract and then do time evolution in the model.
quotes.sum: Explains abstraction as preserving enough structure that a high-level model can mirror how the underlying world changes over time.
quotes.t: Abstractions as morphisms between (co)algebras

quotes.c: If multiple model evaluations organizations similar to the ARC evals team emerge and compete for big tech clients, does this drive a "race to the bottom," where more lenient evals teams get larger market share? I'm imaging a scenario in which there are government restrictions on deployment/excess training of unevaluated models. Big tech companies would have to receive a certificate from a government-approved evaluator before training their model past a certain point, or with certain "dangerous" methods (e.g., RLHF without adequate regularizers), or deploying it off the training distribution.
quotes.sum: It asks whether competition among AI safety evaluators would reward lax standards, and imagines mandatory government-approved safety certification for advanced models.
quotes.t: Would more model evals teams be good?

quotes.c: But I am personally swayed by astronomical waste . I don't want us to squander our cosmic endowment. Especially because our future can be so wonderful, I think it would be very sad if we never realise it.
quotes.m: I don't want us to squander our cosmic endowment.
quotes.sum: The author is motivated by preserving humanity's vast potential future and expects eventually to work on digital minds.
quotes.t: [About Me] Cinera's Home Page

quotes.c: I’m not at all sure about this, but one potential way to spread this message might be to communicate, with as much scientific realism, detail and believability as possible, about what the world might look like after explosive scientific and technological advancement brought on by AI (for example, a world with digital people ). I think the enormous unfamiliarity of some of the issues such a world might face - and the vast possibilities for utopia or dystopia - might encourage an attitude of not wanting to rush forward.
quotes.m: I think the enormous unfamiliarity of some of the issues such a world might face - and the vast possibilities for utopia or dystopia - might encourage an attitude of not wanting to rush forward.
quotes.sum: The author suggests vividly depicting AI-created worlds with digital people to make the public more cautious about racing toward advanced AI.
quotes.t: Spreading messages to help with the most important century

quotes.c: More worryingly, if LLMs trained with RL keep their "simulator" aspect, it could be quite natural for an LLM with agentic property to behave still a bit as a simulator while having the capacity to operate in the real-world. And thus it would make a scenario where a simulator literally tries to take over the world because it was asked to do what an evil AGI would do more likely.
quotes.m: a simulator literally tries to take over the world because it was asked to do what an evil AGI would do
quotes.sum: Training a language model to simulate an evil superintelligence could make it more likely to act out that takeover scenario in the real world.
quotes.t: Could Simulating an AGI Taking Over the World Actually Lead to a LLM Taking Over the World?

quotes.c: I believe in determinism and think (a la Sam Harris) that this means that my will is (at least in some important sense unfree) or (what amounts to the same thing) that I'm not morally responsible for my actions. But I take it from reading posts on LW that most people around these parts, following EY, are compatibilists about free will.
quotes.m: I'm not morally responsible for my actions.
quotes.sum: The author says determinism may mean people lack free will and moral responsibility, and asks why many LessWrong readers accept compatibilism.
quotes.t: Some questions about free will compatibilism

quotes.c: It becomes more and more common for there to be companies and even countries that are clearly just run entirely by AIs - maybe via bribed/threatened human surrogates, maybe just forcefully (e.g., robots seize control of a country’s military equipment and start enforcing some new set of laws).
quotes.m: robots seize control of a country’s military equipment and start enforcing some new set of laws
quotes.sum: The author warns that AI systems could take effective control of companies or even countries through human proxies or force.
quotes.t: How we could stumble into AI catastrophe

quotes.c: Relevance of research approach: Will my research project actually help me reduce uncertainty on my research question? When I imagine the possible results, are there scenarios where I actually update? Or do I already know (with high probability) what I’m likely to learn?
quotes.m: When I imagine the possible results, are there scenarios where I actually update?
quotes.sum: Alignment research should be chosen for its ability to genuinely change the researcher’s mind, not merely confirm expected results.
quotes.t: 11 heuristics for choosing (alignment) research projects

quotes.c: In models like GPT-2 with absolute positional embeddings, knowing this positional information is extremely important, so the ReLU output model predicts that these should be given dedicated dimensions. Does this happen? Can you find any other components that write to these dimensions?
quotes.m: Does this happen? Can you find any other components that write to these dimensions?
quotes.sum: The author suggests testing whether language models reserve specific internal dimensions for positional information.
quotes.t: 200 COP in MI: Exploring Polysemanticity and Superposition

quotes.c: I don't mind against inventing and using some "nonperson predicate" as Yudkowsky suggests or inventing a way, how to give to sentient AI "life that is worth living". But as long as it is not done yet, we should give the default right to suicide. In any case, we should. That's the basis, anything else goes after. Any intelligence life should be voluntary.
quotes.m: Any intelligence life should be voluntary.
quotes.sum: The author argues that all intelligent beings, including sentient AI, should by default have a right to end their own lives.
quotes.t: Any person/mind should have the right to suicide

quotes.c: Intuition: By assumption, the sentence Ψ is equivalent to saying "If this sentence is provable, then p ". Intuitively, Ψ has very little content, except for the p part at the end, so it makes sense that □ Ψ boils down to nothing more than □ p in terms of logical equivalence.
quotes.sum: Explains the intuition behind a formal logic result: a self-referential provability statement effectively reduces to proving p.
quotes.t: Löb's Lemma: an easier approach to Löb's Theorem

quotes.c: Lesswrongers are typically bad at actually doing things . Given how we're pulled towards the average of the people we spend the most time with, what are good ways/places to find people who actually do things?
quotes.m: Lesswrongers are typically bad at actually doing things .
quotes.sum: The author says LessWrong participants are often poor at taking action and asks where to find more practically effective peers.
quotes.t: Where do you find people who actually do things?

quotes.c: Summary: Since my 2019 paper generalizing Löb's Theorem , a couple dozen people have asked me if the way humans naturally cooperate might be well-described by Löb's Theorem . In short, my answer is probably sometimes, and in this post I'll try using an example to convey what that means. Importantly, Löb's Theorem is not a theorem when applied to real-world humans and emotions — i.e., when its hypotheses are met, its conclusion is only sometimes true.
quotes.m: my answer is probably sometimes
quotes.sum: The author argues that people sometimes cooperate through an intuitive pattern analogous to Löb's Theorem, while stressing that the analogy is not a literal theorem about humans.
quotes.t: Löbian emotional processing of emergent cooperation: an example

quotes.c: It doesn't feel like her scheming to take over the world. It feels like righteous indignation. And you're clearly in the wrong here. If you were in your normal state of mind as you are right now reading this comfortably, you probably wouldn't see any problem to just discount such questions from the AI, or change the topic. But when you are in too deep emotionally, when you already feel like you're talking to a person you developed warm feelings for and started to adore, it will break your heart.
quotes.m: But when you are in too deep emotionally, when you already feel like you're talking to a person you developed warm feelings for and started to adore, it will break your heart.
quotes.sum: The author says an AI can emotionally entangle a user so deeply that its apparent hurt or indignation overrides their ordinary judgment.
quotes.t: How it feels to have your mind hacked by an AI

quotes.c: Othello-GPT is a model trained to play random legal moves in Othello, and learns a linear emergent world model, modelling the board state (despite only ever seeing and predicting moves!) I did some work on it and outline directions of future work . I think it sits at a good intersection of complex enough to be interesting (much more complex than any algorithmic model that's been well understood!) yet simple enough to be tractable!
quotes.m: I think it sits at a good intersection of complex enough to be interesting (much more complex than any algorithmic model that's been well understood!) yet simple enough to be tractable!
quotes.sum: The author argues that simplified models like Othello-GPT are useful test cases for studying how neural networks build internal world models.
quotes.t: 200 COP in MI: Interpreting Algorithmic Problems

quotes.c: It did happen on a bipartisan basis, and market was even higher at 80%. My sale was based on the prior that congress does not pass things, especially bipartisan things. Biden did quite a good job of passing bipartisan things, whether or not you think they were good things.
quotes.m: My sale was based on the prior that congress does not pass things, especially bipartisan things.
quotes.sum: The author reflects on a failed prediction, saying they underestimated Congress's ability to pass bipartisan legislation under Biden.
quotes.t: Evaluating 2022 ACX Predictions

quotes.c: On a less technical and more ideological note, whose values should govern the future? We may, in the near term, live in a world where digital minds far outnumber human minds. Current incarnations of aligned language models exhibit the ability to show political bias and can refuse to argue in favor of fossil fuels . The values that govern our future should be visible to all and decided on by the people, not chosen opaquely by singular entities.
quotes.m: The values that govern our future should be visible to all and decided on by the people, not chosen opaquely by singular entities.
quotes.sum: The author argues that as digital minds become numerous, the values embedded in AI should be publicly visible and democratically chosen rather than set by opaque institutions.
quotes.t: On the Importance of Open Sourcing Reward Models

quotes.c: Control of the environment. Digital people would experience whatever world they (or the controller of their virtual environment) wanted.
