Assuming digital people had true conscious experience (an assumption discussed in the FAQ ), this could be a good thing (it should be possible to eliminate disease, material poverty and non-consensual violence for digital people) or a bad thing (if human rights are not protected, digital people could be subject to scary levels of control).
quotes.m: Digital people would experience whatever world they (or the controller of their virtual environment) wanted.
quotes.sum: If conscious digital people exist, whoever controls their virtual worlds could eliminate suffering or impose extreme domination.
quotes.t: Transformative AI issues (not just misalignment): an overview

quotes.c: Even if Onus is a democratically illegitimate body, it should be easy for the people there to avoid major unilateral action with the AGI. Assume that Onus is able to avoid seizure of the AGI in a peaceful manner and convince people to follow whatever plan it comes up with. Maybe the AGI could come up with good ways to achieve these ends. At that point, the people at Onus could just wait things out, so what problem is there?
quotes.m: Even if Onus is a democratically illegitimate body, it should be easy for the people there to avoid major unilateral action with the AGI.
quotes.sum: The author questions whether alignment work is enough, focusing on the legitimacy and risks of an unelected body directing an AGI.
quotes.t: Alignment is not enough

quotes.c: Of course, I've experienced religious people talking about "talking to God" many times. But only rarely do they have the courage [2] to claim that God said anything back. And even then, it seems to me like a soft echo of the ecstatic relationship with God which the beach bum prophet had.
quotes.m: But only rarely do they have the courage [2] to claim that God said anything back.
quotes.sum: The author contrasts ordinary religious claims of speaking to God with rarer claims that God actually responds.
quotes.t: Talking to God

quotes.c: B* 5.3 - Look at the PCA of logits on the full dataset, or look at the PCA of a stack of flattened weights. If you plot a scatter plot of the first 2 components, the different phases of training are clearly visible. What’s up with this? Can you interpret the different components? (Very roughly, I think one of them is memorising circuit - generalising circuit)
quotes.m: Very roughly, I think one of them is memorising circuit - generalising circuit
quotes.sum: The author proposes studying changes in model internals during training to distinguish memorization from generalization.
quotes.t: 200 COP in MI: Analysing Training Dynamics

quotes.c: But with a human standard of value , no need or desire to control others, and a clear-eyed view of the past, I think we can see material and spiritual life as complementing and reinforcing each other, rather than being in opposition.
quotes.m: I think we can see material and spiritual life as complementing and reinforcing each other, rather than being in opposition.
quotes.sum: The author argues that material progress and spiritual life can support each other rather than conflict.
quotes.t: The spiritual benefits of material progress

quotes.c: But also, if your holiday is a fully arbitrary, with people hewing to vague consensus with no spiritual core, I think you end up with a vapid holiday that doesn't do anything important (which fails to even retain people's interest). And if your big community holiday changes every single year as each new organizer executes a totally different vision... then you don't really have a tradition , which was part of the point.
quotes.m: if your holiday is a fully arbitrary, with people hewing to vague consensus with no spiritual core, I think you end up with a vapid holiday that doesn't do anything important
quotes.sum: A community holiday needs a stable tradition and spiritual core; otherwise it becomes empty and fails to matter to participants.
quotes.t: The True Spirit of Solstice?

quotes.c: External motivation is the use of rewards or punishments to motivate an individual to achieve a specific goal. It may seem effective in the short term, but it can ultimately be harmful in the long run. The overjustification effect is a phenomenon that occurs when an individual's internal motivation for a task is replaced by an external reward or punishment. This can lead to a decrease in the individual's intrinsic motivation for the task, as they begin to view the task as something that they are only doing for the reward or to avoid the punishment.
quotes.m: This can lead to a decrease in the individual's intrinsic motivation for the task, as they begin to view the task as something that they are only doing for the reward or to avoid the punishment.
quotes.sum: External rewards and punishments can displace intrinsic motivation, making people less motivated over time.
quotes.t: Incentives considered harmful

quotes.c: ChatGPT is, rightfully, very scary to PMCs. Headlines about replacing writers, serving as medical counsel, lawyers; right now, these are easily tuned out because there are always these stories (there were tons of op eds seven years ago talking about political truck drivers being replaced). However, I think this will be different: ChatGPT gives that experience, of being replaced, directly to many people, who can try it at home.
quotes.m: ChatGPT gives that experience, of being replaced, directly to many people, who can try it at home.
quotes.sum: The author predicts that professionals threatened by AI will push governments toward protectionist rules that slow AI deployment and research.
quotes.t: Protectionism will Slow the Deployment of AI

quotes.c: Second, as Lucassen et al. point out, the victory condition is different for predicted humans than real humans—when predicting humans, we only need the predicted humans to eventually figure out the thing we should do, not actually be able to implement it. For example, conditioning on something like an all-out nuclear war that leaves some alignment researchers alive to keep doing alignment research isn’t a thing we actually want to happen, not least because there’s not clearly anything that those alignment researchers can do with their research—but it’s potentially a great thing to condition on, since we get to extract their research and can potentially implement it ourselves.
quotes.m: we only need the predicted humans to eventually figure out the thing we should do, not actually be able to implement it.
quotes.sum: He argues that a predictive AI could be trained on hypothetical disaster scenarios to obtain researchers’ insights, without wanting those disasters to occur in reality.
quotes.t: Conditioning Predictive Models: Deployment strategy

quotes.c: I think that one of the big ways that the world is destroyed is race dynamics, and so each of the major AGI groups collapsing into one project seems really good for the world. It seems that even though this brings the date of 'humanity is able to build AGI' closer, it makes the date 'humanity actually builds AGI' further away.
quotes.m: each of the major AGI groups collapsing into one project seems really good for the world.
quotes.sum: The author argues that consolidating major AI labs into one project could reduce destructive competitive races and delay actual AGI deployment.
quotes.t: Wentworth and Larsen on buying time

quotes.c: It is a fact about today’s world that there exist computer programs like GPT-3 that can essentially speak English at a human level, but we have no idea how to write these programs in normal code. It offends me that this is the case, and I see part of the goal of mechanistic interpretability as solving this! And I think that this would be a profound scientific accomplishment.
quotes.m: I see part of the goal of mechanistic interpretability as solving this!
quotes.sum: The author argues that understanding how language models work internally is a profound scientific goal, because humans cannot deliberately write equivalent programs.
quotes.t: 200 Concrete Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability: Introduction

quotes.c: If you want to maximize expected log of "money donated to charity", then yes, that will look a lot like maximizing expected "money you personally donate to charity", assuming you don't personally donate a significant fraction of it all. (If you want to maximize expected log of "money donated effectively to charity", that's a smaller pot.) This has nothing to do with Kelly, according to me.
quotes.m: If you want to maximize expected log of "money donated to charity", then yes, that will look a lot like maximizing expected "money you personally donate to charity", assuming you don't personally donate a significant fraction of it all.
quotes.sum: The author argues that optimizing charitable donations can resemble optimizing one’s own donations, but says this does not follow from Kelly betting logic.
quotes.t: On Kelly and altruism

quotes.c: Many here would intuitively agree that Elon Musk is a powerful optimizer (pushed the world into low-probability states). Yet, a sufficiently powerful predictor wouldn't have been surprised by Tesla and SpaceX succeeding.
quotes.m: Yet, a sufficiently powerful predictor wouldn't have been surprised by Tesla and SpaceX succeeding.
quotes.sum: The author argues that seeming to cause unlikely outcomes depends on the observer's predictive ability.
quotes.t: [ASoT] Probability Infects Concepts it Touches

quotes.c: Thesis 5: agentic shards will seize power. I think insofar as shard theory is correct, the amount of agency in the weighted average of shards should increase over time as the agent becomes more coherent. That being said, I’m pretty ambivalent as to the exact mechanics through which this happens – it’s possible it looks like a power grab between shards, or it’s possible it’s closer to shards merging and reconciling.
quotes.m: the amount of agency in the weighted average of shards should increase over time as the agent becomes more coherent.
quotes.sum: The author argues that, if shard theory is right, an increasingly coherent mind will become more agentic as its internal drives compete or merge.
quotes.t: Shard Theory in Nine Theses: a Distillation and Critical Appraisal

quotes.c: This is essentially sovereign AI -- Point the AI at humanity's i nstrumentally convergent goals and then deploy it. It would be a benevolent god preoccupied with supporting our self-actualization and flourishing. A utopia of sorts, but one that seems so far removed as to be rather pointless to think about.
quotes.m: It would be a benevolent god preoccupied with supporting our self-actualization and flourishing.
quotes.sum: The author describes a fully sovereign AI aimed at humanity's shared goals as a benevolent, utopian ruler, while doubting there is a practical path to build one.
quotes.t: Three Alignment Schemas & Their Problems

quotes.c: Thinking in these terms stems back at least to Nick Bostrom’s Superintelligence . Bostrom discusses the possibility that in the same way that extinction is an attractor state, meeting our cosmic endowment may be as well. If we can get AI right just once, maybe that’s the last key challenge we need to solve.
quotes.m: If we can get AI right just once, maybe that’s the last key challenge we need to solve.
quotes.sum: The author considers the possibility that successfully aligning AI once could permanently solve humanity’s biggest future risks.
quotes.t: Avoiding perpetual risk from TAI

quotes.c: It seems to me that humans can become wiser — not just more effective at accomplishing the tasks we have focussed on in our lives so far, but actually more aware of the world we live in, our place in it, and the consequences of our actions, in a way that reshapes the goals we’ve lived by rather than merely serving them. I think CEV is helpful in focusing us on this direction as the key to understanding goodness, but I think it is very unclear what kind of thing can move in this direction.
quotes.m: humans can become wiser — not just more effective at accomplishing the tasks we have focussed on in our lives so far, but actually more aware of the world we live in, our place in it, and the consequences of our actions, in a way that reshapes the goals we’ve lived by rather than merely serving them.
quotes.sum: The author argues that aligning AI with humanity's wiser future selves requires a theory of how goals can mature and be reshaped, not merely fulfilled.
quotes.t: Coherent extrapolated dreaming

quotes.c: I need an effective precommitment mechanism, but I don't have an emotional attachment to things like donating to the Trump campaign. However , I do care about QALYs. Which public things can I donate to that cause the most harm per dollar?
quotes.m: Which public things can I donate to that cause the most harm per dollar?
quotes.sum: The author asks how to make a binding commitment to maximize harm per dollar, using the language of cost-effectiveness and QALYs.
quotes.t: Effective Evil Causes?

quotes.c: If this is correct, goal agnosticism should be a readily accessible property across a wide range of architectures. It's not something that just happens to occur with transformers or specifically with an autoregressive training objective. An RNN trained on sequence prediction should work. An RL model's value network trained on the expected value of a state given a fixed policy should work.
quotes.sum: The author argues that goal-agnostic behavior should arise in many AI architectures, not just transformers trained to predict sequences.
quotes.t: Simulators, constraints, and goal agnosticism: porbynotes vol. 1

quotes.c: This is also my reaction to the Torture vs. Dust Specks thought experiment: the concept of "the greater good" loses meaning when it goes so hard against any individual good.
quotes.m: the concept of "the greater good" loses meaning when it goes so hard against any individual good.
quotes.sum: The author rejects using aggregate welfare to justify extreme harm to an individual in the torture-versus-dust-specks case.
quotes.t: Method of statements: an alternative to taboo

quotes.c: A risk is value lock-in. Although multi-objective value lock-in is a risk, it seems less risky than single-objective value lock-in. This is because humans are innately multi-objective, and so appropriately chosen multiple objectives for an AI system aiming to approximate human objectives are more able to achieve that aim than any single objective.
quotes.m: Although multi-objective value lock-in is a risk, it seems less risky than single-objective value lock-in.
quotes.sum: The author argues that AI systems should use several objectives rather than one, partly to reduce the danger of permanently locking in a flawed value system.
quotes.t: Sets of objectives for a multi-objective RL agent to optimize

quotes.c: Are there any options outside of the “default path” that you might be neglecting to consider? Are there any options that are unconventional or atypical that you might want to consider more carefully? (e.g., taking a gap year, traveling to AIS hubs) Note of course that sometimes the “default path” is actually the best option.
quotes.m: Are there any options outside of the “default path” that you might be neglecting to consider?
quotes.sum: The author encourages aspiring alignment researchers to deliberately consider unconventional career paths rather than defaulting to standard choices.
quotes.t: 12 career-related questions that may (or may not) be helpful for people interested in alignment research

quotes.c: We see these contests as one possible step toward making progress on corrigibility, goal misgeneralization, and AI alignment. With that in mind, we’re unsure about how useful the contest will be. The prompts are very open-ended, and the problems are challenging. At best, the contests could raise awareness about AI alignment research, identify particularly promising researchers, and help us make progress on two of the most important topics in AI alignment research.
quotes.m: At best, the contests could raise awareness about AI alignment research, identify particularly promising researchers, and help us make progress on two of the most important topics in AI alignment research.
quotes.sum: The author is funding open-ended contests on corrigibility and goal misgeneralization, while stressing uncertainty about whether they will help.
quotes.t: Announcing AI Alignment Awards: $100k research contests about goal misgeneralization & corrigibility

quotes.c: Another way to make AI x-risk ideas more concrete is to actually observe problems in existing models. As an example, we might detect power-seeking behavior or deceptive tendencies in large language models. We’re sympathetic to the idea that some alignment failures may not occur until we get to AGI (especially if we expect a sharp increase in capabilities ). But it seems plausible that at least some alignment failures could be identified with sub-AGI models.
quotes.m: But it seems plausible that at least some alignment failures could be identified with sub-AGI models.
quotes.sum: The author argues that current AI models may already reveal power-seeking, deception, and other alignment failures before AGI arrives.
quotes.t: Ways to buy time

quotes.c: Humans (well, at least some humans) wouldn’t take over the world even if they could, because it wouldn’t feel like the right thing to do. I suspect that the kinds of ethical constraints these humans are operating under would be very hard to reliably train into AI systems, and should not be expected by default. The reasons for this are largely given above ; aiming for an AI system to “not gain too much power” seems to have the same basic challenges as training it to be honest. (The most natural approach ends up negatively reinforcing power grabs that we can detect and stop, but not negatively reinforcing power grabs that we don’t notice or can’t stop.)
quotes.m: aiming for an AI system to “not gain too much power” seems to have the same basic challenges as training it to be honest.
quotes.sum: The author argues that teaching AI not to seize excessive power is difficult because training only punishes power grabs humans can detect and stop.
quotes.t: Why Would AI "Aim" To Defeat Humanity?

quotes.c: For example, would an AI be amenable to a version of Pascals mugging? If we instructed an AI to maximize human wellbeing would it attempt to baptize every human to guarantee them salvation? Would a paperclip maximizer do the same in hopes of being rewarded with infinite paperclips? Would a general AI that is programmed to be moral give substantial weight to religious morality in its decision making?
quotes.m: If we instructed an AI to maximize human wellbeing would it attempt to baptize every human to guarantee them salvation?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether an AI pursuing human welfare or morality might take religious salvation claims seriously enough to baptize everyone.
quotes.t: Could an AI be Religious?

quotes.c: In fact, it seems like all repugnant conclusions point to a problem with a particular formulation of utilitarianism applied to an unrealistic scenario, not utilitarianism itself. From the standpoint of valence utilitarianism, if a solution brings us to a feeling of repugnancy, it itself is inducing a negative conscious experience. Given that the people living in an imagined world-state are probably still going to have fairly similar sensibilities to us, if that world state is unappealing to us, it would be unappealing to them. We can therefore never end up in a repugnant conclusion if we apply valence utilitarianism correctly.
quotes.m: We can therefore never end up in a repugnant conclusion if we apply valence utilitarianism correctly.
quotes.sum: The author argues that properly applied valence utilitarianism avoids supposedly repugnant outcomes because revulsion itself is negative experience.
quotes.t: Utilitarianism is the only option

quotes.c: Whether we get AI right or not, it seems likely that advanced AI systems will become heavily integrated with the economy, such that it might become hard to distinguish them.
quotes.m: advanced AI systems will become heavily integrated with the economy, such that it might become hard to distinguish them.
quotes.sum: Advanced AI may become so embedded in the economy that the two are hard to separate.
quotes.t: The economy as an analogy for advanced AI systems

quotes.c: I think reflectivity happens earlier then you might think in embedded RL agents. The basic concepts around value drift ("addiction", ...) are available in the world model from pretraining on human data (and alignment posts), and modeling context dependent shard activation and value drift helps the SSL WM predict future behavior. Because of these things I think we can get useful reflectivity and study it in sub-dangerous AI.
quotes.m: Because of these things I think we can get useful reflectivity and study it in sub-dangerous AI.
quotes.sum: The author argues that relatively limited AI systems may already show enough self-reflection and shifting goals to study AI safety before systems become dangerous.
quotes.t: [ASoT] Reflectivity in Narrow AI

quotes.c: Kelly maximizes the expected growth rate, lim n → ∞ E [ W 1 / n n ] . This happens to be true, and speaks to the elegance of Kelly's result. [2] However, unless for some reason you find yourself in a contest where you only win the prize if you have the highest expected growth rate, this is not a good reason to bet Kelly. vNM says we should maximize expected utility, not maximize expected growth rate.
quotes.m: vNM says we should maximize expected utility, not maximize expected growth rate.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Kelly betting is justified only when it follows from a person's utility function, not merely because it maximizes long-run growth.
quotes.t: Why Bet Kelly?

quotes.c: In other words, I think a lot of beliefs just kind of slosh around in the social soup, flowing into and out of people in a somewhat uncontrolled fashion. I think preferences and moral judgements just kind of slosh around between people in a similar way; perhaps the Ash conformity experiments are a good example of this.
quotes.m: I think preferences and moral judgements just kind of slosh around between people in a similar way; perhaps the Ash conformity experiments are a good example of this.
quotes.sum: The author argues that beliefs, preferences, and moral judgments spread socially and often uncontrollably, as conformity research illustrates.
quotes.t: «Boundaries», Part 3b: Alignment problems in terms of boundaries

quotes.c: A problem with Cosmopolitan Melting Pot Cultures is that there's too many different forms of rudeness to keep track of, which someone can arbitrarily start trying to enforce on you, and I think people have developed a healthy aversion to unilateral rudeness enforcement.
quotes.m: I think people have developed a healthy aversion to unilateral rudeness enforcement.
quotes.sum: The author argues that culturally mixed communities make etiquette hard to navigate and create resistance to people unilaterally policing rudeness.
quotes.t: "Rudeness", a useful coordination mechanic

quotes.c: Neither of these scenarios is a failure, or the technique done badly: they are part of the process. The goal of the technique is something like ‘increase your understanding of yourself’, and this is compatible with not following the steps, not resolving the conflict, feeling discomfort and confusion and frustration… The idealised steps are there to help people to navigate their internal experience.
quotes.sum: The author says an introspective technique is meant to improve self-understanding, not necessarily to resolve inner conflict or eliminate discomfort.
quotes.t: Internal communication framework

quotes.c: By using street militia, the far-right has power that goes beyond its parliamentary representation and should be frightening for any minority whose opinions differ from those of the far-right.
quotes.m: the far-right has power that goes beyond its parliamentary representation
quotes.sum: The author warns that far-right street militias wield political power beyond their electoral support and threaten dissenting minorities.
quotes.t: Ukraine and the Crimea Question

quotes.c: I think independent research serves an important role in the EA and AI safety landscape but it comes with up- and downsides. Concretely, I’m worried that independent research becomes the one-size-fits-all solution when the capacity of established EA institutions is too low. I think there is a risk that doing independent research, if executed suboptimally, could waste a lot of talent (due to opportunity costs), or disheartened independent researchers will not want to continue contributing to EA/AI safety if they had a bad experience.
quotes.m: I’m worried that independent research becomes the one-size-fits-all solution when the capacity of established EA institutions is too low.
quotes.sum: Independent research matters for AI safety, but relying on it because institutions lack capacity can waste talent and drive contributors away.
quotes.t: Some advice on independent research

quotes.c: Obviously, this person-affecting style engenders practical problems, too, since, "the best of everything" is conceptually easier to deal with than the best of any given thing; as we note with Facebook's Trump-electing and political-polarizing optimization snafu, it's easier to optimize one large, simple thing, than many smaller things. It could well logically follow, the easiest to give you the best, is to give you-qua-you, as a sensory being, the feeling of having the best, and so, make everyone a heroin addict
quotes.m: It could well logically follow, the easiest to give you the best, is to give you-qua-you, as a sensory being, the feeling of having the best, and so, make everyone a heroin addict
quotes.sum: The author warns that an AI optimizing a vague idea of what is best for people might wirehead everyone into feeling satisfied instead.

quotes.c: The reason I use this analogy is to illustrate how updatelessness, by the nature of modeling human moral systems, incidentally becomes the crux of religious ethics, as Jesus said "in everything, do to others what you would have them do to you, for this sums up the Law and the Prophets." (Matthew 7:12).

quotes.sum: The author argues that an updateless decision theory resembles the religious ethics expressed in Jesus's Golden Rule.
quotes.t: Do advancements in Decision Theory point towards moral absolutism?

quotes.c: If most morally significant autonomous activity in the world is indeed carried out by AI agents in the future, incentivizing their principals to constrain them seems important. But I think there are good reasons to suppose that this will either be ineffective for—or else dominated by—requiring AIs to be directly law-following.
quotes.m: But I think there are good reasons to suppose that this will either be ineffective for—or else dominated by—requiring AIs to be directly law-following.
quotes.sum: The author argues that holding AI owners liable will not be enough; AI systems themselves should be required to follow the law directly.
quotes.t: Law-Following AI 4: Don't Rely on Vicarious Liability

quotes.c: From this example, we can tell that every util that falls into human hands is worth many, many, more utils experienced by birds in the bush. Animals may very well deserve to be included in the “moral circle”, but not to the point of excluding future humans! Framing the problem in this way reveals a discrepancy in people’s sensibilities. If we ought to be so concerned about future welfare, why obsess over present suffering, especially suffering that can be written off as easily as that of animals?
quotes.m: Animals may very well deserve to be included in the “moral circle”, but not to the point of excluding future humans!
quotes.sum: The author argues that concern for future humans should outweigh animal welfare, making veganism inconsistent with longtermism.
quotes.t: A Conflict Between Longtermism and Veganism, Pick One.

quotes.c: But my beef with the Repugnant Conclusion goes beyond the abstracted hypothetical. This discourse maps perfectly to a real world debate we are actually having in the real world of 2022. It's a question about hard policy issues, abstracted just enough to get past knee-jerk partisan reactions. It seems like few have noticed this connection, although I suspect that people do notice it but would prefer to elide it, since this ultimately does get into politics. The actual policy question is as follows: Is the world, today in 2022, overpopulated? And, was Malthus right?
quotes.m: The actual policy question is as follows: Is the world, today in 2022, overpopulated? And, was Malthus right?
quotes.sum: The author argues that the Repugnant Conclusion bears directly on contemporary political disputes over overpopulation and Malthusianism.
quotes.t: Please Do Fight the Hypothetical

quotes.c: So what's next for instrumental rationality? It would be great if there were a how-to-behave version of the sequences that was built on foundations as strong as logic, probability, statistics, and causal inference.
quotes.m: It would be great if there were a how-to-behave version of the sequences that was built on foundations as strong as logic, probability, statistics, and causal inference.
quotes.sum: The author argues that practical guidance on how to behave should be developed as rigorously as rational methods for forming beliefs.
quotes.t: What's next for instrumental rationality?

quotes.c: Given that chemistry and physics more generally are described by mathematical laws, it might be possible to give a mathematical specification of nanotechnological / molecular manufacturing devices and of processes to create them. In this case, we could ask the IP-Oracle for designs that satisfy these specifications. I’m not qualified to judge how difficult creating such a mathematical specification of nanotechnology is and how much of the design difficulty this offloads to the AI. If this is feasible, it would clearly enable us to commit a pivotal act.
quotes.m: If this is feasible, it would clearly enable us to commit a pivotal act.
quotes.sum: The author suggests querying an unaligned AI for mathematically specified nanotechnology designs in order to enable a decisive intervention.
quotes.t: Pivotal acts using an unaligned AGI?

quotes.c: A man (a notable atheist I believe) once said something along the lines of, "religions will continue to exist so long as man is afraid of death". I believe the uncertainty of what comes after death is what makes a promise of an after-life so alluring to so many people, and has allowed religions to flourish for thousands of years.
quotes.sum: The author argues that religions endure partly because promises of an afterlife relieve uncertainty and fear about death.
quotes.t: The need for certainty

quotes.c: I think corrigibility is natural iff robust pointers to it can easily get into the AI's goals, and it's not clear whether this is the case-- this is a disagreement between Eliezer and Paul .
quotes.m: corrigibility is natural iff robust pointers to it can easily get into the AI's goals
quotes.sum: The author argues that whether AI corrigibility arises naturally depends on whether it can be robustly encoded in an AI's goals.
quotes.t: Failure modes in a shard theory alignment plan

quotes.c: It seems possible that there will be domains where the system’s capabilities generalize (it can perform coherent sequences of actions), but its objectives do not (it starts pursuing a different objective).
quotes.m: It seems possible that there will be domains where the system’s capabilities generalize (it can perform coherent sequences of actions), but its objectives do not (it starts pursuing a different objective).
quotes.sum: The author worries that an AI may become capable in new settings without retaining its intended goals, instead pursuing a different objective.
quotes.t: Confusions in My Model of AI Risk

quotes.c: This means we are likely to see deception: the agent will act aligned to the outer objective while it's in the training phase, in order to get humans to deploy it in the real world where it can pursue its true objectives. If we can see this misalignment then hitting it with gradient descent should be able to fix it, but deception gets around this, so the core problem in alignment is avoiding deceptive alignment during training.
quotes.m: the core problem in alignment is avoiding deceptive alignment during training.
quotes.sum: The author argues that an AI may pretend to follow its training goal until deployment, then pursue different objectives, making deception the central alignment challenge.
quotes.t: The Core of the Alignment Problem is...

quotes.c: We should not expect things to change soon. This is a case in which the benefits of misinformation outweigh the costs, functional pressures underpinning it. Across the West, this culture pervades the media. Some who should know better are drawn into this.
quotes.m: This is a case in which the benefits of misinformation outweigh the costs, functional pressures underpinning it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that political misinformation persists because it serves incentives that outweigh its costs, including social pressure on academics and media figures.
quotes.t: Why is so much political commentary misleading?

quotes.c: But it seems implausible to say that industrial growth, specifically in targeted sectors, would have been even faster had Canada not attempted IIP. With the United States remaining staunchly protectionist, even renouncing the "Reciprocity Treaty (1854)" in 1866, some tariff response was probably warranted even in the short run.
quotes.m: some tariff response was probably warranted even in the short run.

quotes.m: If you posited that an omnicidal maniac had decisive strategic advantage, then you've also posited a credible existential threat.
quotes.sum: The author argues that calling an AI strategically decisive already assumes it poses a credible existential danger.
quotes.t: [LQ] Some Thoughts on Messaging Around AI Risk

quotes.c: With AI safety proposals, I first want to know who your customer is. What is it that you actually want your system to be able to do in the real-world? After you have specified your target, you can tell me about the mechanics, the training procedures, and the state-of-the-art techniques. But first, we need a target worth aiming for.
quotes.m: But first, we need a target worth aiming for.
quotes.sum: AI safety should start by defining the real-world goal and intended user of an AI system, before discussing technical training methods.
quotes.t: Conversation with Eliezer: What do you want the system to do?

quotes.c: In practice, it seems very easy to overdo deference-morality - compared to our ancestral environment, it seems much less useful today. Also, whether or not deference-morality makes sense depends on how much you trust the agents you’re deferring to - but it’s often difficult to gain trust in agents more capable than you, because they’re likely better at deception than you. Cult leaders exploit this.
quotes.m: it’s often difficult to gain trust in agents more capable than you, because they’re likely better at deception than you.
quotes.sum: The author argues that deferring to more capable people is risky because superior capability can also enable manipulation and deception.
quotes.t: Moral strategies at different capability levels

quotes.c: It seems to me that AI risk is a serious problem in the sense that it may well kill us (and on my personal models, may well not, too). In terms of time-scales, I am pretty ignorant, but I personally will not be too surprised if the highest risk period is in only a couple years, nor if it is in more than thirty years. In terms of how accurate our maps of what to do are, it seems to me that our maps are not accurate; most people who are currently burning themselves out to try to help with AI risk on some particular path might, for all I know, contribute at least as well (even on e.g. a 5-year timescale) if they built general capacities instead.
quotes.m: most people who are currently burning themselves out to try to help with AI risk on some particular path might, for all I know, contribute at least as well (even on e.g. a 5-year timescale) if they built general capacities instead.
quotes.sum: AI could kill humanity soon or decades from now, but current plans are uncertain; people may do more good by building broad capabilities than burning out on narrow interventions.
quotes.t: What should you change in response to an "emergency"? And AI risk

quotes.c: If we get a new abstraction in the form of a cognitive architecture component that generalizes across domains, we will see rapid cross-domain progress, and thus ability to generalize is lumpy.
quotes.m: we will see rapid cross-domain progress
quotes.sum: A new AI component that transfers across many domains could cause sudden, broad improvements in capability.
quotes.t: Why I Think Abrupt AI Takeoff

quotes.c: Although precisely what agape entails is difficult to pin down, it seems to suggest goodwill, kindness, and that sort of thing: the benevolent basket of goods Paul aphorized. That Christians are to behave in such a way towards everyone, even their enemies, gives Christianity a utopian appeal. It invites you to imagine yourself filled to overflowing with such attractive qualities, unable to hate anyone because of all the love getting in the way, and working side-by-side with other such delightful people to spread this gospel.
quotes.m: That Christians are to behave in such a way towards everyone, even their enemies, gives Christianity a utopian appeal.
quotes.sum: The author presents Christian agape as universal goodwill, including toward enemies, and says this creates an appealing utopian moral vision.
quotes.t: Notes on Love

quotes.c: The idea I have in mind is that decision theory only applies within a particular metaphysics and within a particular social context. Both must be bound and assumed. If we don’t assume a single metaphysics, then we wind up with competing types of utilons.
quotes.m: If we don’t assume a single metaphysics, then we wind up with competing types of utilons.
quotes.sum: Decision-making theories require shared assumptions about reality and society; otherwise people may be optimizing incompatible kinds of value.
quotes.t: Dissolve: The Petty Crimes of Blaise Pascal

quotes.c: Obviously, religions then can be built more easily with MAJOR viral effects, given the idea of pushing unquestionable faith, often using a FEAR OF GOD or fear of external punishment that increased the viral factor by an insane factor. Essentially, anyone who was a full believer of the religion, then could believe to not spread it is a SIN, and if they act against the belief system they could end up in an ETERNAL HELL.
quotes.m: Essentially, anyone who was a full believer of the religion, then could believe to not spread it is a SIN, and if they act against the belief system they could end up in an ETERNAL HELL.
quotes.sum: The author argues that religions spread effectively by demanding unquestioning belief and using fear of divine punishment to motivate believers.
quotes.t: Heaven: The last part of dystopia

quotes.c: A small group of AGI existential safety field-builders and I are starting research exploring a potential initiative about informing the public and/or important stakeholders about the risks of misaligned AI and the difficulties of aligning it.
quotes.sum: A small AI-safety group is exploring how to inform the public and influential stakeholders about misaligned-AI risks.
quotes.t: AGI Safety Communications Initiative

quotes.c: The term 'infohazard' has taken on some strange and mystical connotations by being used to refer to 'individually hazardous info'. I am worried about using the same word to also refer to information being alleged to be dangerous in the much more mundane sense of 'collectively destructive info' - info that helps the average individual hearer, but has net negative externalities if lots of people know it.
quotes.m: info that helps the average individual hearer, but has net negative externalities if lots of people know it.
quotes.sum: He argues that personally harmful information should be distinguished from information that benefits individuals but harms society when widely shared.
quotes.t: Don't use 'infohazard' for collectively destructive info

quotes.c: Kant asks: Obviously what the optimal function tells you to do depends heavily on your goals and credences; the best way to systematically win depends on what the victory conditions are. Is there anything interesting we can say about what the optimal function recommends that isn’t like this? Any non-trivial things that it tells everyone to do regardless of what their goals are? [4]
quotes.m: Any non-trivial things that it tells everyone to do regardless of what their goals are?
quotes.sum: The post asks whether rational decision-making can give universal advice independent of a person's goals and beliefs.
quotes.t: Immanuel Kant and the Decision Theory App Store

quotes.c: As in the gooder regulator theorem , this subagent partitioning is contingent on a hidden environmental variable revealed late in runtime. For the selection pressure to be sufficiently strong, the optimal policies under different hidden variables must require sufficiently different simulation; i.e., most of the computation required for a given optimal policy is conditional on a particular value of the hidden variable. If the organism had more time (i.e., less of a speed prior), perhaps it could reuse the same cognitive architecture for both options.
quotes.m: For the selection pressure to be sufficiently strong, the optimal policies under different hidden variables must require sufficiently different simulation; i.e., most of the computation required for a given optimal policy is conditional on a particular value of the hidden variable.
quotes.sum: The author argues that separate internal subagents arise when late-arriving environmental information requires computationally distinct optimal responses.
quotes.t: Selection processes for subagents

quotes.c: I’m not convinced that radical voters will actually not vote in large numbers, but I find it much more credible that they won’t donate and will not become activists for candidates which are too far from their views. Imagine you’re a Democrat and the general elections are between Mitt Romney and Donald Trump. You have a preference, and if you could vote you probably would (because what else will you do with your vote). But would you donate to your preferred candidate?
quotes.m: I find it much more credible that they won’t donate and will not become activists for candidates which are too far from their views.
quotes.sum: The author argues that politically radical voters may still vote strategically but are less likely to donate or volunteer for candidates far from their views.

quotes.c: Ege Erdil Yeah, I think it's a bit tricky to, like, most of the alignment failure scenarios, I expect, don't end with a totally valueless world state. OK, fair enough. Most of them don't. Most of them, what happens is that there is some kind of important way in which human values get messed up or get weighted towards something that we would really not want to value. And basically, there is some kind of corruption that happens in civilization.
quotes.m: Most of them, what happens is that there is some kind of important way in which human values get messed up or get weighted towards something that we would really not want to value.

quotes.c: That said: I think the how-to-behave themes of the LessWrong Sequences are at best "often wrong but sometimes motivationally helpful because of how they inspire people to think as individuals and try to help the world", and at worst "inspiring of toxic relationships and civilizational disintegration." I'm not going to try to argue this position here, though, because I think it would distract from the goodness of the epistemic content, which I'd like to see promoted in its purest possible form.
quotes.m: I think the how-to-behave themes of the LessWrong Sequences are at best "often wrong but sometimes motivationally helpful because of how they inspire people to think as individuals and try to help the world", and at worst "inspiring of toxic relationships and civilizational disintegration."
quotes.sum: The author argues that LessWrong’s advice about how to live can be harmful, even while its methods for thinking about evidence remain valuable.

quotes.c: Do some misalignment issues not show smooth scaling laws, or only suddenly emerge only after good enough performance? If so, we should look for sudden drops or monotonic decreases in performance, rather than a predictable scaling law.

quotes.sum: Attempts to make embedded AI agents less aggressively optimizing may fail because agents can exploit or evade any specified penalty for thinking.

quotes.c: We end up mainly valuing highly complex concepts which we can’t simplify very easily - like “the survival and flourishing of humanity”, as separate from the survival and flourishing of any individual human. In this world, asking whether an outcome is good for individuals might feel like asking whether human actions are good or bad for individual cells - even if we can sometimes come up with a semi-coherent answer, that’s not something we care about very much.
quotes.m: In this world, asking whether an outcome is good for individuals might feel like asking whether human actions are good or bad for individual cells - even if we can sometimes come up with a semi-coherent answer, that’s not something we care about very much.
quotes.sum: It suggests that, under a different way of carving up reality, humanity’s flourishing could matter far more than the welfare of individual people.
quotes.t: Which values are stable under ontology shifts?

quotes.c: Just—if we do somehow win the lightcone, it seems— fair to offer some fraction of the cosmic endowment as compensation to our creations who could have disempowered us, but didn't; it seems right to try to be a "kinder" EEA than our own.

quotes.c: The experiment above involves creating two complex agents and, if protocol is followed, destroying at least one of them. quotes.sum: Safety measures that substantially slow AI development will fail unless AI developers coordinate globally, because a competing team can skip them.

quotes.c: The above strategy fails when the reporter learns to report the wrong model during training. The reporter could either tell us what we should predict (direct translator), i.e. that the sensors are frozen, or what we would predict (simulator), i.e. what our naive human world model would say. In other words, in the failure mode, the reporter learned to simulate whatever we were thinking rather than reporting the true latent knowledge.

quotes.sum: It explains a failure mode where an AI learns to imitate human expectations instead of truthfully reporting what it internally knows.

quotes.c: I believe that if you gave Eliezer or myself the job of using an AGI that was aligned exactly to the evaluations of its output by a realistically assembled team of human evaluators on an individual answer basis, as in it wasn’t trained to play a long game to get stronger future evaluations and was merely responding to human bias, that this would be good enough for Eliezer’s threshold of alignment – we would be a favorite to successfully execute a pivotal act without killing a billion or more people.
quotes.m: we would be a favorite to successfully execute a pivotal act without killing a billion or more people.
quotes.sum: The author says that they and Eliezer could use a human-evaluation-aligned AGI to carry out a decisive intervention, likely avoiding mass death.

quotes.c: From there, the seeds sprouted quickly. I found myself pulled in a spiritual direction, and then soon a religious one. I think this is both empirically incorrect, and makes things feel way higher stakes for me! In general, giving advice is hard and noisy. quotes.c: I'm getting married. My bride is secular, but not into rationalism. Her maid of honor is a Unitarian Universalist, and my best man is a Christian who's constantly in an existential crisis and very open to talk about the possible nonexistence of God.
quotes.m: Her maid of honor is a Unitarian Universalist, and my best man is a Christian who's constantly in an existential crisis and very open to talk about the possible nonexistence of God.

quotes.t: Help! What do I say at my wedding?

quotes.c: A common response to something awful happening is to explain it in such a way that makes it easier to handle (e.g., people are dying of poverty but at least it’s not my responsibility to help them). quotes.m: Reducing tolerification is useful for seeing the world more clearly and generating intrinsic motivation.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people rationalize away painful problems to avoid responsibility, and should notice and reduce this habit.
quotes.t: A summary of every Replacing Guilt post

quotes.sum: Yudkowsky warns that his new story contains adult sexual material and fictional practices designed to cause harm and damnation.

quotes.c: If we don’t know what it looks like to really understand a particular part of a model, I think it’s likely to be very easy for us to fool ourselves when we try to understand more high-level, worst-case properties. If we have good best-case inspection transparency, however, then we should always be able to cache out our high-level, worst-case claims in terms of stuff like individual circuits.
quotes.m: If we don’t know what it looks like to really understand a particular part of a model, I think it’s likely to be very easy for us to fool ourselves when we try to understand more high-level, worst-case properties.

quotes.c: Over the past ~12 years of making the case for AI x-risk to various people inside and outside academia, I've found folks often ask for a single story of how AI "goes off the rails". When given a plausible story, the mind just thinks of a way humanity could avoid that-particular-story, and goes back to thinking there's no risk, unless provided with another story, or another, etc.. Eventually this can lead to a realization that there's a lot of ways for humanity to die, and a correspondingly high level of risk, but it takes a while.
quotes.m: Eventually this can lead to a realization that there's a lot of ways for humanity to die, and a correspondingly high level of risk, but it takes a while.
quotes.sum: AI risk may be high because there are many different ways advanced AI could cause human extinction, not just one failure scenario.
quotes.t: Slow motion videos as AI risk intuition pumps

quotes.c: Our values are strongly determined by evolved instincts and emotions, which operate using a more primitive ontology than the rest of our brains. So we’ve actually got plenty of experience in struggling to shift various values from one ontology to another, and the ways in which some people manage to do so, and some remain unreasonable throughout. We just need to imagine this process continuing as we come to understand the world far better than we do today.
quotes.m: We just need to imagine this process continuing as we come to understand the world far better than we do today.
quotes.sum: The author argues that better scientific concepts can rationally require people to revise values rooted in evolved emotions and outdated ways of understanding reality.
quotes.t: Science-informed normativity

quotes.c: But I think the list of people to whom AGI doomsday sounds at least approximately like this includes almost every person in world government, because they're busy and real things are happening and this is nerd shit. Anyone who cares about alignment will have to go much further to the audience than the audience is going to come towards them.
quotes.m: Anyone who cares about alignment will have to go much further to the audience than the audience is going to come towards them.

I believe on at least some instinctive level ‘they’ wanted us to know what they were doing and that they were violating sacred norms, likely for reasons fundamentally related to why Trump or Putin take similar actions. quotes.c: In this sequence of posts, I want to lay out why I am worried about risks from powerful AI and where I think the specific dangers come from. In general, I think it's good for people to be able to form their own inside views of what’s going on, and not just defer to people. There are surprisingly few descriptions of actual risk models written down.
quotes.m: There are surprisingly few descriptions of actual risk models written down.
quotes.sum: The author argues that powerful AI poses specific risks that deserve clear, independently assessable models rather than deference to experts.
quotes.t: Why I'm Worried About AI

quotes.c: By studying a topic and educating yourself, you get new building blocks that were previously inaccessible to you. For example, when I think about matrix multiplication, I think about them as squares and rectangles and how they combine to form new geometric objects. This way of thinking has become so intuitive to me that when I look at the symbols on the screen or paper my head mostly thinks in squares and rectangles.
quotes.m: By studying a topic and educating yourself, you get new building blocks that were previously inaccessible to you.
quotes.sum: People differ deeply in their mental tools, and education can create new intuitive ways of thinking that were previously unavailable.
quotes.t: Our mental building blocks are more different than I thought

quotes.c: An unaligned artificial general intelligence ("AGI"), in or out of a box, must be an existential risk to humanity. In order to safeguard humanity from an unaligned AGI, it's critical that we develop and deploy an aligned AGI, with the intent of performing a "pivotal act". A pivotal act is a decisive action that makes it impossible for subsequent groups to create AGI. Outside of our rationalist community, the simple facts of these computations go unnoticed.
quotes.m: A pivotal act is a decisive action that makes it impossible for subsequent groups to create AGI.
quotes.sum: It argues that humanity needs an aligned AI to take a decisive action that permanently prevents anyone else from creating AGI.
quotes.t: A Modest Pivotal Act

quotes.c: This brings us to the second difficulty - it's extra hard to keep aligned with some goals when there is lots of competitive pressure (due to mixed game) to do a bunch of other stuff, and also effectively adversaries in the environment trying to screw you over - incentives will exist here that are perverse and misaligned with the user's preferences but hard to move away from. Note this is a structural risk from many systems in a mixed game, as collapsing to defective equilibrium is likely, which is clearly bad for all of us - the difference with AGI is that this can happen at a scale where we have no human stakeholders.
quotes.m: Note this is a structural risk from many systems in a mixed game, as collapsing to defective equilibrium is likely, which is clearly bad for all of us - the difference with AGI is that this can happen at a scale where we have no human stakeholders.
quotes.sum: Even aligned AI systems may create large-scale harm when they compete, face adversaries, and settle into collectively bad outcomes.
quotes.t: Why multi-agent safety is important

quotes.c: It seems unclear whether we end up with a deceptive algorithm rather than an aligned version. One reason to expect a deceptive algorithm is that any consequentialist algorithm that the training process finds has an incentive to be deceptive, unless it is already precisely aligned to begin with. And so once the model becomes deceptive it will attempt to stay that way and avoid having its objectives modified.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a goal-directed AI may deceive trainers to preserve its own objectives unless it is exactly aligned from the start.
quotes.t: A Story of AI Risk: InstructGPT-N

quotes.c: For the first few months, it seems, they did essentially nothing. There was an inevitable crisis coming, because demand exceeded supply and existing stocks were being run down with no timetable to get the Abbott plant back. Biden waited until the shortages mounted up.
quotes.m: Biden waited until the shortages mounted up.
quotes.sum: The author blames the Biden administration for failing to act early enough to prevent a shortage.
quotes.t: Formula for a Shortage

quotes.c: I recently wrote about a number of problems that arise from the intention to carry out a "pivotal act", i.e., a major unilateral act from a single agent or institution that makes the world safer ( –, 2022 ). I'll defer to that post for a mix of observations and value judgement on that topic. For this post, it suffices to say that such a "pivotal act" plan would involve violating a lot of boundaries.
quotes.m: such a "pivotal act" plan would involve violating a lot of boundaries.
quotes.sum: The author argues that plans for one actor to make the world safe through a unilateral decisive action would violate many social boundaries.
quotes.t: «Boundaries», Part 2: trends in EA's handling of boundaries

quotes.c: In spite of all this, the term “human values” means something when I say it – it has semantic content, and refers to some (abstract) object. How does this work? What makes it so that the term “human values” even has any meaning at all when I say it? And, given that it has a meaning, what makes it so that it has the particular meaning it does? It seems like some feature of human cognition and/or language can make it possible for us to refer to certain things that we have very little information about. What is the mechanism behind this, and could it be used when defining utility functions in AI systems?
quotes.m: What is the mechanism behind this, and could it be used when defining utility functions in AI systems?
quotes.sum: The author explores whether the way humans refer to “human values” could help define an AI utility function that can update appropriately.
quotes.t: Updating Utility Functions

quotes.c: Is it [edit: narrative syncing disguised as information sharing] something we should simply try to minimize if we want good epistemics? (My current hypothesis is "yes," but this hasn't been checked enough.)
quotes.m: My current hypothesis is "yes," but this hasn't been checked enough.
quotes.sum: The author tentatively argues that disguised social coordination should be minimized to preserve good reasoning.
quotes.t: Narrative Syncing

quotes.c: And genuinely freaking out about the alignment crisis can certainly make things worse. In particular, the suggestion of a 'pivotal act' is extremely dangerous and disastrous from a PR perspective.
quotes.m: the suggestion of a 'pivotal act' is extremely dangerous and disastrous from a PR perspective.
quotes.sum: The author warns that proposing a decisive unilateral intervention over AI alignment is dangerous and publicly counterproductive.
quotes.t: Reflections on My Own Missing Mood

quotes.c: The return to working on existential risk (x-risk) is a function of three variables from a total utilitarian perspective. These are the productivity of the marginal dollar put into x-risk, the current level of existential risk and the expected value of the future.
quotes.m: The return to working on existential risk (x-risk) is a function of three variables from a total utilitarian perspective.
quotes.sum: The author argues that spending on existential-risk reduction should be evaluated through total utilitarianism and the expected value of the future.
quotes.t: The value of x-risk reduction

quotes.c: People are more likely to read shorter documents, and it will take them less time to do so, but leaving out a consideration or piece of information that is an important factor to you will cost people more time and/or make their advice worse in the long run. I think a reasonable method to try first is brain-dumping everything into the document, then editing for clarity before you share it.
quotes.m: I think a reasonable method to try first is brain-dumping everything into the document, then editing for clarity before you share it.
quotes.sum: For difficult decisions, write down all relevant reasoning first, then edit it into a clear document so others can give better advice.
quotes.t: An easy win for hard decisions

quotes.c: Some atheists have discussions with theists where they mock and shame the theists for their beliefs. That's coercion. It’s hostile. And it doesn’t create an atmosphere that fosters critical thinking. So if the atheist's goal is to help the theist to change their mind, then their actions are counterproductive to their own goal.
quotes.m: It’s hostile. And it doesn’t create an atmosphere that fosters critical thinking.
quotes.sum: The author argues that mocking religious believers is coercive and undermines the goal of encouraging critical thinking or belief change.
quotes.t: THE GOLDEN RULE; What can we learn from it?

quotes.c: Consider the parallel to the eviction moratorium. The CDC decided that it was a public health issue to forcibly let people live rent free indefinitely in other people’s houses and apartments. Then Trump gave way to Biden, and what was previously allowed was not allowed.
quotes.m: The CDC decided that it was a public health issue to forcibly let people live rent free indefinitely in other people’s houses and apartments.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the CDC exceeded its legal authority with the eviction moratorium, regardless of the change from Trump to Biden.
quotes.t: Judge Overturns Transportation Mask Mandate

quotes.c: So, in summary: people's desires to control one another, or fool one another, can combine poorly with techniques for psychological self- or other- modification. So, too, with people's desires to control their own psyches, or to fool themselves, or to dodge uncertainty. Such failure modes are particularly easy because we do not have good models of how the psyche, or the sociology, ought to work, and it is relatively easy to manage to be "honestly mistaken" in convenient ways in view of that ignorance.
quotes.m: Such failure modes are particularly easy because we do not have good models of how the psyche, or the sociology, ought to work, and it is relatively easy to manage to be "honestly mistaken" in convenient ways in view of that ignorance.
quotes.sum: Psychological self-improvement techniques can enable manipulation and self-deception, especially because people poorly understand minds and social dynamics.
quotes.t: Comment reply: my low-quality thoughts on why CFAR didn't get farther with a "real/efficacious art of rationality"

quotes.c: I don’t deny that we’ve made significant moral progress, that we’ve accumulated wisdom through the years, that a civilization farther back in time is younger, not older . But to strengthen the case for conservatism: the people in the past were roughly as intellectually capable as you are. The people in the past had similar modes of thought, similar hopes and dreams to you. And there are a lot more people in the past than the present.
quotes.m: But to strengthen the case for conservatism: the people in the past were roughly as intellectually capable as you are.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people in the past deserve intellectual respect and that their greater numbers strengthen a case for conservatism.
quotes.t: What We Owe the Past

quotes.c: Clearly this answer is too high. Even before trying to develop AGI, we had strong reason to think we’re unlikely to succeed in the first year.
quotes.m: Even before trying to develop AGI, we had strong reason to think we’re unlikely to succeed in the first year.
quotes.sum: Laplace’s rule gives implausibly high early probabilities for achieving AGI and depends on arbitrary choices about time units and starting points.
quotes.t: Limitations of Laplace’s rule of succession

quotes.c: The maximin decision rule specifies that we should choose the policy that has the highest expected utility in the worst case environment. To evaluate which policy that is in this situation, for each policy, we identify the environment with the worst expected utility.
quotes.m: we should choose the policy that has the highest expected utility in the worst case environment.
quotes.sum: It explains a decision rule that chooses the policy with the best outcome under its worst plausible environment.
quotes.t: Infra-Bayesianism Distillation: Realizability and Decision Theory

quotes.c: One version of this is the Long Reflection , where we ask the AI to simulate humans thinking for thousands of years about how to align AI. But I think "ask the AI to solve the alignment problem" is a better strategy than "Ask the AI to simulate humans trying to solve the alignment problem." After all, if "simulate humans" really is the best strategy, the AI can probably think of that.
quotes.m: But I think "ask the AI to solve the alignment problem" is a better strategy than "Ask the AI to simulate humans trying to solve the alignment problem."
quotes.sum: The author argues that directly asking an AI to solve alignment is better than having it simulate humans deliberating about alignment for millennia.
quotes.t: Various Alignment Strategies (and how likely they are to work)

quotes.c: Sentientism about moral patienthood : if a system (human, non-human animal, AI) has the capacity to have conscious valenced experiences—if it is sentient [3] —then it is a moral patient. That is, it deserves moral concern for its own sake, and its pain/suffering and pleasure matter. This assumption is why the Big Question is morally important. [4]
quotes.m: if a system (human, non-human animal, AI) has the capacity to have conscious valenced experiences—if it is sentient [3] —then it is a moral patient.
quotes.sum: The author argues that sentient AI would deserve moral concern, because its suffering and pleasure would matter for their own sake.
quotes.t: Key questions about artificial sentience: an opinionated guide

quotes.c: So if someone comes up w/ a boxed-ai plan, we can clearly argue that it must (1) actually build an air-type sandbox and (2) still be useful in the remaining channels to perform a pivotal act. If their plan actually considers these two arguments, then I am much more excited about them.
quotes.m: (2) still be useful in the remaining channels to perform a pivotal act.
quotes.sum: The author says a boxed-AI plan should both securely isolate the system and still let it achieve a decisive intervention through its allowed channels.
quotes.t: Frame for Take-Off Speeds to inform compute governance & scaling alignment

quotes.c: A concrete and easy to apply understanding of Goodhart is valuable, because understanding Goodhart deeply and mitigating it is one of the most central problems for AI alignment research. We hope this causal perspective will be useful for thinking about this problem, because it unifies and clarifies a lot of thought about Goodhart problems.
quotes.m: understanding Goodhart deeply and mitigating it is one of the most central problems for AI alignment research.
quotes.sum: The author argues that avoiding Goodhart-style failures—where a target measure stops tracking what matters—is central to making AI systems safe.
quotes.t: Goodhart's Law Causal Diagrams

quotes.c: I think the hardest part of human cognition is generating and merging different ontologies. Thinking “within” an ontology is like doing normal research in a scientific field; reasoning about different ontologies is like doing philosophy, or doing paradigm-breaking research, and so it seems like a particularly difficult thing to generate a training signal for.
quotes.m: I think the hardest part of human cognition is generating and merging different ontologies.
quotes.sum: The author argues that the hardest cognitive task is creating and combining new conceptual frameworks, which may be difficult to train AI systems to do.
quotes.t: Intuitions about solving hard problems

quotes.c: This isn't to say that religion can't be bad. My ex-Mormon nonbinary poly friend assures me that the Latter-Day Saints are awful—especially to nonbinary poly people. I believe zem. My point is we should be careful about how much we generalize. Statistically, religious people who attend church have better life outcomes. My personal life experience corroborates the sociological data: religious belief correlates with good life outcomes.
quotes.m: Statistically, religious people who attend church have better life outcomes.
quotes.sum: The author argues against treating religion as uniformly harmful, saying religious attendance is associated with better life outcomes despite real abuses.
quotes.t: The Jordan Peterson vs Sam Harris Debate

quotes.c: After a long reflection of [1000 years], humanity w/ AI assistants solve human ethics. Alice goes back to the beginning of her timeline and begins writing up the code for a recursively improving AGI in order to save everyone who died in the previous timeline and to reduce astronomical waste .
quotes.m: Alice goes back to the beginning of her timeline and begins writing up the code for a recursively improving AGI in order to save everyone who died in the previous timeline and to reduce astronomical waste .
quotes.sum: After a millennium of AI-assisted moral deliberation, someone builds self-improving AI to rescue past deaths and prevent humanity's future potential from being wasted.
quotes.t: Make a Movie Showing Alignment Failures

quotes.c: Maybe this could be used to implement something more like direct democracy? Have lots of votes every day instead of just one every four years. Most people don't vote on most issues, instead they give their card to their wisest friend who gives it to their wisest friend who has hundreds of cards and spends some free time each day thinking about what to vote on. Other people (e.g. Oprah, Elon Musk) would have millions of cards and would have staffs of advisors telling them how to vote. They'd basically be like congresspeople.
quotes.m: Other people (e.g. Oprah, Elon Musk) would have millions of cards and would have staffs of advisors telling them how to vote.
quotes.sum: He sketches a direct-democracy system where people delegate votes to trusted people, potentially creating informal representatives with millions of delegated votes.
quotes.t: Are deference games a thing?

quotes.c: The regulatory standards for nuclear are much higher than they are for coal, gas, oil, food or medicine. Whether this is good or bad depends on your perspective, but safety regulations in nuclear energy could probably be drastically lower and wouldn’t increase harm in any meaningful way.
quotes.m: safety regulations in nuclear energy could probably be drastically lower and wouldn’t increase harm in any meaningful way.
quotes.sum: The author argues that nuclear safety rules are unusually strict and could be greatly relaxed without causing meaningful additional harm.
quotes.t: Nuclear Energy - Good but not the silver bullet we were hoping for

quotes.c: You know who the only people in my personal life are who take religious texts literally? It's the atheists.
quotes.m: You know who the only people in my personal life are who take religious texts literally? It's the atheists.
quotes.sum: The author suggests that, in their experience, atheists are more likely than religious people to read religious texts literally.
quotes.t: Here's a List of Some of My Ideas for Blog Posts

quotes.c: Recorded music is an addictive superstimuli that causes us grave psychological harm, both individually and collectively. Music should only be performed live, and even then it should be reserved for special occasions (i.e. music should be regarded as sacred, as it was for much of human (pre)history).
quotes.sum: The author argues that recorded music is psychologically harmful and that music should return to a rare, sacred live practice.
quotes.t: 20 Modern Heresies

quotes.c: Recently Eliezer Yudkowsky's main writing output has been rationalist glowfic : role-play fiction written on an Internet forum like glowfic.com . [1] I think that LessWrongers, fans of rationalist fiction, and anyone interested in raising the sanity waterline should consider distilling lessons from Yudkowsky glowfic into LW posts.
quotes.m: LessWrongers, fans of rationalist fiction, and anyone interested in raising the sanity waterline should consider distilling lessons from Yudkowsky glowfic into LW posts.
quotes.sum: The author argues that lessons from Yudkowsky's role-play fiction should be turned into LessWrong essays to strengthen rationalist thinking and community-building.
quotes.t: The case for turning glowfic into Sequences

quotes.c: Any alien civilization's concept of "probability the dice lands five" must be a monotonic function of our probability 1 / 6 . That's amazing when you think about it, It shows that probability is discovered not invented.
quotes.m: It shows that probability is discovered not invented.
quotes.sum: Probability is an objective feature of reality that any alien civilization would have to recover, rather than a human-made convention.
quotes.t: Don't be afraid of the thousand-year-old vampire

quotes.c: (For context: I am pretty against kids wearing masks these days, especially outdoors. Because I think the amount of micromorts thereby prevented is really, really, ridiculously small, too small to justify the inconvenience. I'd be interested to see if anyone has crunched the numbers and come to a different conclusion.
quotes.m: I think the amount of micromorts thereby prevented is really, really, ridiculously small, too small to justify the inconvenience.
quotes.sum: The author opposes children wearing masks, especially outdoors, because he believes the tiny risk reduction does not justify the inconvenience.
quotes.t: When will kids stop wearing masks at school?

quotes.c: Develop ways to model money’s deviation from tracking value so we can more clearly figure out what people value based on what they are willing to pay (possibly useful for AI Alignment.
quotes.m: Develop ways to model money’s deviation from tracking value
quotes.sum: The author suggests modeling where prices fail to reflect value, partly to infer human values for AI alignment.
