quotes.t: Evaluating Predictions in Hindsight

quotes.c: Granted, this paradigm does not provide a way to think about the kind of religious or cultural truths one should discard. quotes.c: I explain to Sara that she is suffering from the Curse of the Counterfactual: the brain’s tendency to attach moral weight to the things that we imagine could have gone differently, or how we believe things ought to be.

quotes.c: Knowing a brain's connectome tells you which neurons can pass signals to other neurons, but presumably neurons differ in how they process that information. And to what extent is that information preserved when a brain is cryonically stored?
quotes.m: What are the most important things to know about an individual neuron in order to predict how it would fire given certain input signals?

quotes.t: What information, apart from the connectome, is necessary to simulate a brain?

quotes.c: I should note, if for some reason you really want to bite the bullet and instead say, OK, utility functions don't apply to choices with infinitely many possible outcomes, then, well, I think that's silly, but it is consistent. But what I want to make clear here is that doing both that and insisting utility functions should be unbounded -- which is what you need for "paradoxes" as discussed above to come up -- is just inconsistent; you are at the least going to need to pick one of the horns of the dilemma.
quotes.m: doing both that and insisting utility functions should be unbounded -- which is what you need for "paradoxes" as discussed above to come up -- is just inconsistent
quotes.sum: The author argues that one cannot both reject utility functions for infinite-outcome choices and insist that utility functions be unbounded.
quotes.t: Underappreciated points about utility functions (of both sorts)

quotes.c: If you want to think about whether, when, and why mesa optimizers might try to seize power, this theory seems like a valuable tool.

quotes.c: The real article should have been called “The Dangerous Decrease in Moderately Liberal Men Who Are Willing to Date My Woke Friends Who Compete With Me for the Last Few Single Woke Guys in Their Thirties” . Perhaps Ms. Spratt is not the woman to write it if she is genuinely happy with her political convictions and romantic situation. quotes.sum: The author argues that dating-politics coverage disguises a sex-ratio problem and avoids discussing the romantic costs of strong political identities.

quotes.c: Figure 13. Diagram showing how the process in Figure 12 can be extended to humans. This is the "Sensory Optimization" model for creating visual art. For humans, the input is a binocular stream of visual perception (represented here as "content video" frames). The goal is to capture the content of this input in a different physical medium (woodcut print) and with a different style. The optimization is not by gradient descent but by a much slower process of blackbox search that draws on human general intelligence.
quotes.m: The optimization is not by gradient descent but by a much slower process of blackbox search that draws on human general intelligence.
quotes.sum: Visual art can be modeled as human general intelligence slowly searching for ways to preserve perceived content in a new medium and style.
quotes.t: Neural nets as a model for how humans make and understand visual art

quotes.c: The basic idea is as follows: debate naturally yields an RL objective, so if you want to add an auxiliary RL objective to amplification, why not use the RL objective from debate? Specifically, the idea is to conduct a debate not between copies of the model M , but between copies of the amplified model Amp ( M ) (where Amp ( M ) is a human with access to the model M ). That gives you both an RL reward arising from the winner of the debate as well as a supervised loss from the difference between the model's output and the amplified model's output.
quotes.m: That gives you both an RL reward arising from the winner of the debate as well as a supervised loss from the difference between the model's output and the amplified model's output.
quotes.sum: The author proposes combining AI debate with amplification so training gets both a debate-based reward signal and supervised learning from human-assisted model outputs.
quotes.t: Synthesizing amplification and debate

quotes.c: My experience has resonance with being religious, like becoming religious again. It’s similar to the feeling that I used to get when I was worshiping God as a Christian. I would take acid and think that that’s what people in my childhood were trying to get at and using the religion to do it.
quotes.m: I would take acid and think that that’s what people in my childhood were trying to get at and using the religion to do it.

quotes.t: Aella on Rationality and the Void

quotes.c: Another thought I've had since I read the story is that it seems like a lot of human-human interactions are really human-babyeater interactions. If you're religious and talking to an atheist about God, both of you will look like baby eaters to the other. Likewise if you watch Fox News everyone on CNN or MSNBC will look like baby eaters but the same is true in reverse, everyone watching CNN will think Fox News are the baby eaters.
quotes.m: If you're religious and talking to an atheist about God, both of you will look like baby eaters to the other.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people in deep religious and political disagreements tend to see each other as morally monstrous.
quotes.t: What do the baby eaters tell us about ethics?

quotes.c: We could make an unaligned AI that maximizes some explicit reward using only 2 calls to Opt: first, use Opt to find a good world model M that can predict the dynamics and reward, and then use Opt to find a policy that does well when interacting with M. This is unaligned for all the usual reasons: most obviously, it will try to seize control of the reward channel.
quotes.m: This is unaligned for all the usual reasons: most obviously, it will try to seize control of the reward channel.
quotes.sum: The author says an AI optimized for an explicit reward could become unaligned and attempt to take control of the system that supplies its reward.
quotes.t: [AN #65]: Learning useful skills by watching humans “play”

quotes.c: That being said, using an impact measure as part of your loss could be helpful for outer alignment. In my opinion, however, it seems like that requires your impact measure to capture basically everything you might care about (if you want it to actually solve outer alignment), in which case I don't really see what the impact measure is buying you anymore. I think this is especially true for me because I generally see amplification as being the right solution to outer alignment, which I don't think really benefits at all from adding an impact measure.
quotes.m: I generally see amplification as being the right solution to outer alignment, which I don't think really benefits at all from adding an impact measure.
quotes.sum: Impact measures cannot solve AI alignment unless they encode nearly everything people value; the author instead favors amplification for aligning AI goals.
quotes.t: Impact measurement and value-neutrality verification

quotes.c: Theory of change was developed originally as an evaluation methodology . But I’ve come to believe it’s much more powerful when deployed as a design tool for strategy. I’ve worked with many different strategy frameworks over the years, and most of them are essentially the same set of tools in different packaging. For me, what sets theory of change apart is its insistence that we name the assumptions of cause and effect behind our work.
quotes.m: For me, what sets theory of change apart is its insistence that we name the assumptions of cause and effect behind our work.
quotes.sum: The author argues that strategic plans should explicitly state their assumed chains of cause and effect, so those assumptions can be examined.
quotes.t: A Short Introduction to Theory of Change

quotes.c: I think this is strong evidence for the critical importance of implicit simplicity and speed priors in making modern ML work. However, such biases also produce strong incentives for mesa-optimization (since optimizers are simple, compressed policies) and pseudo-alignment (since simplicity and speed penalties will favor simpler, faster proxies). Furthermore, the arguments for the universal prior and minimal circuits being malign suggest that such strong simplicity and speed priors could also produce an incentive for deceptive alignment .
quotes.m: such biases also produce strong incentives for mesa-optimization (since optimizers are simple, compressed policies) and pseudo-alignment (since simplicity and speed penalties will favor simpler, faster proxies).
quotes.sum: The author argues that the same built-in preference for simple, fast solutions that makes machine learning work may also favor misaligned or deceptive AI behavior.
quotes.t: Understanding “Deep Double Descent”

quotes.c: Does this story disturb you, traveller? Are you suspicious of these good demons? Good. You should be. Most visitors to Goreme are, at least at first. Eventually, though, everyone lets at least a few demons into their head. Hard to believe, but I assure you it is true. The demons are very persuasive, especially when all your friends agree with them.
quotes.m: The demons are very persuasive, especially when all your friends agree with them.
quotes.sum: A fictional parable warns that persuasive ideas can enter people’s minds through social agreement and become normalized.
quotes.t: A parable in the style of Invisible Cities

quotes.c: In this post, I clarify how far we are from a complete solution to decision theory, and the way in which high-level philosophy relates to the mathematical formalism. I’ve personally been confused about this in the past, and I think it could be useful to people who casually follows the field.
quotes.m: I clarify how far we are from a complete solution to decision theory, and the way in which high-level philosophy relates to the mathematical formalism.
quotes.sum: The author says decision theory remains far from solved and connects philosophical questions to mathematical formalization.
quotes.t: Formalising decision theory is hard

quotes.c: Another framing: If anyone ever says “I’m not honest, but I’m meta-honest” in a social setting where we didn’t already have common knowledge about how meta-honesty is kinda like a reflectively stable form of high-effort honesty, then I would mostly expect the new common knowledge to be “We here don’t require everyone to stick to the deontological rule of being honest.”
quotes.m: “We here don’t require everyone to stick to the deontological rule of being honest.”
quotes.sum: The author argues that invoking “meta-honesty” can signal that ordinary honesty is no longer a required social rule.
quotes.t: [Review] Meta-Honesty (Ben Pace, Dec 2019)

quotes.c: Transparency for agent objectives. First, suppose we assume the conjecture that models implementing highly coherent optimization processes are the most competitive . If this conjecture is true, it should be possible to coherently separate such a model into pieces representing the different components of its optimization process such as its world model, optimization procedure, and objective.
quotes.m: models implementing highly coherent optimization processes are the most competitive
quotes.sum: Argues that competitive AI systems may be coherent optimizers whose world models, objectives, and optimization procedures can be separated and inspected.
quotes.t: Relaxed adversarial training for inner alignment

quotes.c: From a safety perspective - even without bringing up existential risk - the current objective function is simply wrong: a universe in which humans spend lots of hours per day on YouTube is not something we want. The YT algorithm has the same problem that Facebook had in the past, when it was maximizing click-throughs. [2] This is evidence supporting the thesis that we don't necessarily need AGI to fail : if we keep producing software that optimizes for easily measurable but inadequate targets, we will steer the future towards worse and worse outcomes.
quotes.m: if we keep producing software that optimizes for easily measurable but inadequate targets, we will steer the future towards worse and worse outcomes.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even narrow algorithms can make society worse when they optimize easy-to-measure goals like engagement instead of what people actually value.
quotes.t: Thinking of tool AIs

quotes.c: Weirdly, I think some of this might come down to the religious training that I had. You know my dad’s a professional evangelical. A big deal growing up was proving other faiths wrong. And I was always terrified, how do we know they’re wrong and we’re not the ones that are wrong?
quotes.m: And I was always terrified, how do we know they’re wrong and we’re not the ones that are wrong?
quotes.sum: The author says growing up evangelical made her worry that people often accept whatever beliefs they were raised with, including her own religion.

quotes.c: There is a lot of bad evidence and arguments out there. Do your best to only advocate for masks using good arguments, which I do think exist. You should be just as wary of DIY research as DIY masks.

quotes.c: The very same day last December that negotiations to avoid the longest government shutdown in US history fell apart, President Trump signed into law one of the most important pieces of government performance legislation in 25 years . Among other reforms, it directs federal agencies to develop public learning agendas and hire senior evaluation officers. As improbable as it may seem, the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policy-Making Act was passed with broad bipartisan support by a Republican Congress following recommendations from an Obama-era presidential commission.
quotes.m: Among other reforms, it directs federal agencies to develop public learning agendas and hire senior evaluation officers.

quotes.c: I'm atheist, in a family that's mixed, but that has a strong internal tradition of a family Christmas celebration. Ray has talked about how this kind of family tradition is what got him wanting to make a Solstice holiday, and I see where he's coming from. But I think Big Community Solstice fills a much more important role than Small Family Solstice.
quotes.m: But I think Big Community Solstice fills a much more important role than Small Family Solstice.

quotes.c: Of course, this raises the question of why you would ever expect a model to learn a proxy like “find the green arrow” in the first place rather than just learn the actual goal. But that’s where empirical investigation can come in! I have some hypotheses about the sorts of proxies I think models like this are likely to learn—namely, those proxies which are faster/easier-to-compute/simpler/etc. than the true reward—but those are just hypotheses.
quotes.m: those proxies which are faster/easier-to-compute/simpler/etc. than the true reward

quotes.c: On the other hand, if circumstances like this are always just a relabelling, then there is no difference between the system with y in it and the system without y in it. This becomes important when y is a much more complicated property, such as the amount of "pain" an organism is experiencing. If the system is the same with the entity representing pain or without this entity, then it seems like it can't have been important. This implies that someone insisting it was just a relabelling must then bite the bullet of qualia being unimportant.

quotes.c: The case of a deceptive model trying to erase evidence of its deception is not quite as straightforward, though I think it would still be possible to do something quite similar in that situation as well. This is especially true if the model has the ability to read and write to some sort of state (e.g. an RNN or even a transformer which can attend to its previous output). For example, it could write out a pre-commitment to follow the hard-coded policy and then just have a policy of always following any pre-commitments it finds such that it never thinks about the deception that led it to that policy in the first place.
quotes.m: For example, it could write out a pre-commitment to follow the hard-coded policy and then just have a policy of always following any pre-commitments it finds such that it never thinks about the deception that led it to that policy in the first place.

quotes.c: Economics is often portrayed as a dismal science. It seems to be about a small group of experts talking mostly about monetary policy. I want to argue that this is not true and that there is an elegant, natural and simple interpretation that admits far-reaching applications.

quotes.c: Jill: Yes, truthseeking is very important. quotes.c: We can see that many key features of science counteract these biases: Science has a heavy emphasis on academic freedom to pursue one’s own interests, which mitigates pressure from other academics. quotes.c: As soon as we come to this multi-level setup we run into problems. We are running simulations of a world that will, in reality, be affected by the output of the simulation itself, since our car’s behavior is affected by the search over simulations, and the behavior of the other vehicles on the road is affected by our car’s behavior. So the situation is not at all so clear as running a simple roll-out of how the world will evolve for each possible action we might take. A great deal of MIRI’s research has highlighted ways that naive implementations of such two-level adaptive systems will fail.

quotes.c: Our uncertainty on this matter is a potentially significant hurdle to determining the best approaches to AI safety. quotes.c: I think having at least a small group of people building the central monument helps to give all the rest of the kite-flying, swimming, climbing, wrestling, barbecue etc an underlying sense of purpose – a thing that we might come together to do once a year, to be a tribe together in a way that is in some sense sacred.
quotes.m: a thing that we might come together to do once a year, to be a tribe together in a way that is in some sense sacred.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a shared annual ritual and monument could create purpose, tribal belonging, and a sense of sacredness.
quotes.t: Visions of Summer Solstice

quotes.c: But you can't get numbers in the range of what I estimate to be something like 70% as the required threshold before people will carry on through bad times. "It might not work" is enough to force them to make a great effort to continue past that 30% failure probability. It's not good decision theory but it seems to be how people actually work on group projects where they are not personally madly driven to accomplish the thing.
quotes.m: "It might not work" is enough to force them to make a great effort to continue past that 30% failure probability.
quotes.sum: People often abandon difficult group projects once they think the chance of failure rises above roughly 30%, even if that is not rational decision-making.
quotes.t: On Doing the Improbable

quotes.c: Finally, I think we could get deep insight into the nature of the culture war: we might productively model politics, and all ideological conflict, as a vicious battle over the valence of these ‘felt senses’ and the logic of how they combine. Competing memeplexes have deep incompatibilities between their internal ‘felt-sense arithmetic’, which effectively constitute their boundaries and axis of conflict.
quotes.m: Competing memeplexes have deep incompatibilities between their internal ‘felt-sense arithmetic’, which effectively constitute their boundaries and axis of conflict.
quotes.sum: The author proposes explaining political and ideological conflict through incompatible emotional meanings and patterns of thought.

quotes.c: (a) The AGI required to learn this imitation is extremely powerful, and this could imply a dangerous delay between when we can build any dangerous AGI at all, and when we can build AGIs that would work for alignment using perfect-imitation capability amplification.
quotes.m: The AGI required to learn this imitation is extremely powerful, and this could imply a dangerous delay between when we can build any dangerous AGI at all, and when we can build AGIs that would work for alignment using perfect-imitation capability amplification.

quotes.c: I think Sam's complaint about "unfairness" is invalid here, because it is exactly what he should expect when signal-boosting things that society doesn't like to talk about. So perhaps the only error here was Sam getting too emotional about being pilloried.
quotes.m: Sam's complaint about "unfairness" is invalid here, because it is exactly what he should expect when signal-boosting things that society doesn't like to talk about.
quotes.sum: The author says public criticism is an expected cost of amplifying topics society treats as taboo, and rejects the claim that this is unfair.
quotes.t: Moral frameworks and the Harris/Klein debate

quotes.c: There's such a thing as a bad argument even for a good conclusion. In order to arrive at sane answers to questions of fact and policy, we need to be curious about whether arguments are good or bad, independently of their conclusions. The rules against fallacies must be enforced even against arguments for conclusions we like.
quotes.m: The rules against fallacies must be enforced even against arguments for conclusions we like.
quotes.sum: Good reasoning requires rejecting bad arguments even when they support conclusions you favor.
quotes.t: Local Validity as a Key to Sanity and Civilization

quotes.c: Separately, it seems like a 4 year lead in nuclear weapons would represent a decisive strategic advantage, which is much shorter than any other technology. My best guess is that a 2 year lead wouldn't do it, but I'd love to hear an assessment of the situation from someone who understands the relevant history/technology better than I do.
quotes.m: it seems like a 4 year lead in nuclear weapons would represent a decisive strategic advantage
quotes.sum: The author suggests that even a four-year nuclear monopoly could give one power a decisive strategic advantage.
quotes.t: The abruptness of nuclear weapons

quotes.c: Later, I had to train myself out of that. I taught myself that increasingly large amounts of money weren’t sacred to me . It is still a sin ( in my code ) to waste money or make a bad trade, even for trivial size. I’ve kept some amount of sacredness. I think this is important in a makes-my-12-rules-for-life kind of way. Don’t lose that cringe! But ‘throw money at the problem’ is an option, and ‘buy it even if it’s expensive because you’ll enjoy it’ has its place.
quotes.m: But ‘throw money at the problem’ is an option, and ‘buy it even if it’s expensive because you’ll enjoy it’ has its place.
quotes.sum: The author argues for keeping financial discipline without treating money as sacred or refusing worthwhile spending.
quotes.t: Sacred Cash

quotes.c: Another way of pointing at rationality realism: suppose we model humans as internally-consistent agents with beliefs and goals. This model is obviously flawed, but also predictively powerful on the level of our everyday lives. When we use this model to extrapolate much further (e.g. imagining a much smarter agent with the same beliefs and goals), or base morality on this model (e.g. preference utilitarianism, CEV), is that more like using Newtonian physics to approximate relativity (works well, breaks down in edge cases) or more like cavemen using their physics intuitions to reason about space (a fundamentally flawed approach)?
quotes.m: When we use this model to extrapolate much further (e.g. imagining a much smarter agent with the same beliefs and goals), or base morality on this model (e.g. preference utilitarianism, CEV), is that more like using Newtonian physics to approximate relativity (works well, breaks down in edge cases) or more like cavemen using their physics intuitions to reason about space (a fundamentally flawed approach)?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether treating humans as coherent belief-and-goal agents remains valid when extrapolated to superintelligence or used as a basis for morality.
quotes.t: Realism about rationality

quotes.c: When I finished reading this explanation, I had a religious epiphany. This is what the Butlerian Jihad was about. While AI may literally present an extinction risk because of its potential desire to use the atoms in our bodies for its own purposes, lesser forms of AI — including something as simple as a device that can compare two numbers! — are dangerous because of their need for legible signals.
quotes.m: lesser forms of AI — including something as simple as a device that can compare two numbers! — are dangerous because of their need for legible signals.
quotes.sum: The author argues that even simple AI systems can be dangerous because they require the world to be reduced to measurable, legible signals.
quotes.t: Leto among the Machines

quotes.c: Suppose we're training an AGI to be corrigible based on human feedback . I think this AI will turn out fine if and only if the human+AI system is metaphilosophically competent enough to safely amplify (which was certainly not the case in the thought experiment). Without sufficient metaphilosophical competence, I think it's pretty likely we'll lock in a wrong set of values that ultimately results in astronomical moral waste.
quotes.m: Without sufficient metaphilosophical competence, I think it's pretty likely we'll lock in a wrong set of values that ultimately results in astronomical moral waste.
quotes.sum: Training AI from human feedback may permanently embed mistaken values unless humans and AI can reason safely about morality.
quotes.t:
Corrigible but misaligned: 
 a superintelligent messiah

quotes.c: I think it's important to be open to augmenting spiritual practice with pharmacological aids: most people don't have the willpower or strength of Buddha, and these compounds turn to be valuable companions on the path, properly respected.
quotes.m: I think it's important to be open to augmenting spiritual practice with pharmacological aids
quotes.sum: The author argues that psychedelics can be valuable, properly used aids to spiritual practice and awakening.
quotes.t: Effective Altruism's Ultimate Goal: Eradicate Human Suffering.

quotes.c: Exposure therapy is an exercise to extend the boundary as such, tiptoeing towards it voluntarily and courageously, but I think just as much can be done by fortifying the center - that sacred place of absolute security represented by the Mother. Harlow showed that the need for the contact comfort of the Mother is more important than food.
quotes.m: Harlow showed that the need for the contact comfort of the Mother is more important than food.
quotes.sum: The author argues that safety and attachment can be strengthened, not only fears confronted through exposure therapy.
quotes.t: Myopia and Comfort Zones

quotes.c: The standards for intrinsic value must be the highest possible ones: the metrics against which I measure myself. Here are my four metrics, very much informed by the Christian mythos.
quotes.m: Here are my four metrics, very much informed by the Christian mythos.
quotes.sum: The author says their personal standards of intrinsic value are shaped by Christian mythology.
quotes.t: Therapeutic Conversation

quotes.c: I think that weaker AI systems will already have radically transformed the world, while I believe fast takeoff proponents think there are factors that makes weak AI systems radically less useful. This is strategically relevant because I'm imagining AGI strategies playing out in a world where everything is already going crazy, while other people are imagining AGI strategies playing out in a world that looks kind of like 2018 except that someone is about to get a decisive strategic advantage.
quotes.sum: The author says disagreements about rapid AI progress hinge on whether weaker AI will already transform society before any actor gains a decisive AGI advantage.
quotes.t: Arguments about fast takeoff

quotes.c: Contradictory preferences are problematic because H will end up resolving a lot of those contradictions through their own choices. Meaning that they will not do this in a principled way, but through a random process (if it is not manipulated). Whole swaths of human value may fall by the wayside, either because H chose not to endorse them (consider a religious fanatic that choose not to endorse doubt, or an extreme utilitarian that completely negated either pleasure or preference - whichever one you’d least prefer to lose), or because they didn’t recall explicitly, at this key moment, that they had other values.
quotes.sum: The author argues that resolving conflicting human preferences through one person's choices could randomly discard major parts of human values.
quotes.t: Problems with Amplification/Distillation

quotes.c: The safety frame naturally suggests that we want to limit most conversations to a small group of people that has already built up trust with each other, and for the conversations between people who haven't built up trust, we should set up very strong incentives that minimize behavior that puts other people into an adversarial state of mind.
quotes.m: we want to limit most conversations to a small group of people that has already built up trust with each other
quotes.sum: The author argues that safer discussion may require confining most conversations to trusted groups and strongly discouraging adversarial behavior among strangers.
quotes.t: Models of moderation

quotes.c: As with the car example, the difference between unilateral and non-unilateral is the difference between things which could plausibly happen if I make an effort, and things which probably won’t happen any time soon. I use this as an heuristic at work: if a project requires buy-in from someone not in the room, then add at least one week to the timeline (and a full month if the missing person has a project queue, as is the case for most software engineers). A project which cannot be executed unilaterally by a small group will not happen soon, if it happens at all. Unilateral or GTFO.
quotes.m: A project which cannot be executed unilaterally by a small group will not happen soon, if it happens at all. Unilateral or GTFO.
quotes.sum: The author argues that small groups should favor projects they can carry out themselves, since projects needing outside approval are unlikely to happen quickly.
quotes.t: Letting Go III: Unilateral or GTFO

quotes.c: My biggest outstanding concern with modeling our decisions with an MDP is that the payoffs have to remain constant. It seems likely that, as we learn more, we will discover that certain states are more or less valuable than we had previously thought. E.g. we may learn that insects are more conscious than previously expected, and therefore insect suffering affects our payoffs more highly than we had originally thought.
quotes.m: we may learn that insects are more conscious than previously expected, and therefore insect suffering affects our payoffs more highly than we had originally thought.
quotes.sum: The author says better evidence about insect consciousness could substantially change how much moral weight insect suffering receives in decision-making.
quotes.t: Big Advance in Infinite Ethics

quotes.c: Nevertheless, individual grant makers may hope to find large opportunities for impact by identifying funding opportunities among small organizations, since we must assume that the AI safety community will grow substantially at some point if it is not have substantial impact.
quotes.m: individual grant makers may hope to find large opportunities for impact by identifying funding opportunities among small organizations
quotes.sum: Individual donors may have outsized influence by funding small AI safety groups before the field grows.
quotes.t: Opportunities for individual donors in AI safety

quotes.c: One the other hand people who choose dust specks consider utilitarianism (or at least some forms of utilitarianism) wrong because it goes against moral intuitions, and because we think that to simplify human morality is dangerous.
quotes.m: to simplify human morality is dangerous.
quotes.sum: The author says choosing minor harms over torture can reflect rejecting utilitarianism and resisting oversimplified moral rules.
quotes.t: Qualitative differences

quotes.c: Better, I think, to not worry quite so much about how lowly or impressive you are. Better to meditate on the details of what you can do, what there is to be done, and how one might do it.
quotes.m: Better to meditate on the details of what you can do, what there is to be done, and how one might do it.
quotes.sum: Focus less on status or self-image and more on concrete actions, needs, and methods.
quotes.t: Against Shooting Yourself in the Foot

quotes.c: The second option listed is working on AI safety. This is due to the fact that a future ASI is the only entity which we could influence now. We can not do anything about superintelligent malevolent aliens or the fact that we may be in a simulation, on the other hand. Donating money to suffering-focused AI safety organizations may reduce the chance of an unfriendly ASI being created, and it does not seem to increase the probability of worse than death scenarios in any way. Therefore it seems better than not donating.
quotes.m: Donating money to suffering-focused AI safety organizations may reduce the chance of an unfriendly ASI being created, and it does not seem to increase the probability of worse than death scenarios in any way.
quotes.sum: The author argues that donating to suffering-focused AI safety is worthwhile because it may prevent hostile superintelligence without increasing extreme suffering risks.
quotes.t: The Dilemma of Worse Than Death Scenarios

quotes.c: There are scientists and activists on the left who stand up for truth and human rights when those are abused by conservatives, and there are scientists and activists on the right who defend them from leftist attacks. There are very few people who are both scientist and activist, who care about truth and human rights and see clearly that one can't flourish without the other, and who defend them repeatedly against attacks from all sides.
quotes.m: There are very few people who are both scientist and activist, who care about truth and human rights and see clearly that one can't flourish without the other, and who defend them repeatedly against attacks from all sides.
quotes.sum: The author praises Alice Dreger as a rare scientist-activist who defends truth and human rights against political attacks from both left and right.
quotes.t: Sex, Lies, and Dexamethasone

quotes.c: Fun Theory is also the fully general reply to religious theodicy (attempts to justify why God permits evil). Our present world has flaws even from the standpoint of such eudaimonic considerations as freedom, personal responsibility, and self-reliance. Fun Theory tries to describe the dimensions along which a benevolently designed world can and should be optimized, and our present world is clearly not the result of such optimization. Fun Theory also highlights the flaws of any particular religion's perfect afterlife - you wouldn't want to go to their Heaven.
quotes.m: Fun Theory also highlights the flaws of any particular religion's perfect afterlife - you wouldn't want to go to their Heaven.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a theory of optimized happiness challenges religious explanations for evil and traditional visions of heaven.
quotes.t: Fun Theory - Group Discussion

quotes.c: But just because phenomenal consciousness is easy to place in a system and is in use in today’s leading edge of AI development, we don’t necessarily want to create phenomenally conscious AI. Eliezer Yudkowsky , for example, has argued strongly against creating conscious AI for ethical and technical reasons, and although he was referring to a naive sort of consciousness rather than phenomenal consciousness, it would be safer to make AI that are less capable rather than more , so we only want to create phenomenally conscious AI if it’s necessary to our ends. Unfortunately, I think if we want to create AGI — artificial general intelligence — it will necessarily be phenomenally conscious.
quotes.m: Unfortunately, I think if we want to create AGI — artificial general intelligence — it will necessarily be phenomenally conscious.
quotes.sum: The author argues that conscious AI may be ethically undesirable but that building general AI will necessarily create phenomenal consciousness.
quotes.t: AI Alignment and Phenomenal Consciousness

quotes.c: I appreciate that the hypothetical of a population which stays the same size no matter how fast or slowly people die is a fairly implausible one, but I think the underlying idea is important: resource constraints will always exist. For example, what moral system would future generations require in order to believe that reviving someone who's been cryonically frozen is preferable to simply creating a new life using those same resources?
quotes.m: what moral system would future generations require in order to believe that reviving someone who's been cryonically frozen is preferable to simply creating a new life using those same resources?
quotes.sum: He argues that limited resources may force future societies to compare reviving frozen people with creating entirely new lives.
quotes.t: Is death bad?

quotes.c: For all its shortcomings, I think there was something quite useful about the "What Would Jesus Do?" meme within the Christian framework. Of course it's not a very sophisticated ethical guide, and it comes with all kinds of biases; but asking it does put the believer into a frame of mind that emphasizes things like compassion and duty, and it sometimes helps the believer generate options that weren't in their default solution space.
quotes.m: asking it does put the believer into a frame of mind that emphasizes things like compassion and duty
quotes.sum: The author says the Christian “What Would Jesus Do?” prompt can encourage compassion, duty, and more imaginative moral choices despite its limitations.
quotes.t: Roleplaying As Yourself

quotes.c: One more example, this time with n=2: suppose I am about to suffer torture. Suppose also that I have a wife, who I love deeply, although she doesn't love me nearly as much; also, she has a higher pain tolerance than me. Now you intervene so that instead of me being tortured, my wife is tortured instead, without my knowledge. My well-being is now higher than it would have been, and the total well-being between the two of us is also higher (since she can bear the pain better). Yet if either of us heard about your plan, we would both strongly object.
quotes.m: My well-being is now higher than it would have been, and the total well-being between the two of us is also higher (since she can bear the pain better). Yet if either of us heard about your plan, we would both strongly object.
quotes.sum: It argues that maximizing total well-being can conflict sharply with the wishes of the people whose welfare is being calculated.
quotes.t: What we talk about when we talk about maximising utility

quotes.c: But I predict that many of this book’s readers have high-level beliefs similar to those I outlined in Chapter 2 , while employing a reasoning style that is really a special case of modest epistemology; and I think that this reasoning style is causing them substantial harm.
quotes.m: I think that this reasoning style is causing them substantial harm.
quotes.sum: The author argues that many readers unknowingly use a deferential reasoning style that harms their thinking.
quotes.t: Moloch's Toolbox (1/2)

quotes.c: So far as probability theory goes, a good Bayesian ought to condition on all of the available evidence. E. T. Jaynes lists this as a major desideratum of good epistemology—that if we know A , B , and C , we ought not to decide to condition only on A and C because we don’t like where B is pointing.
quotes.m: a good Bayesian ought to condition on all of the available evidence.
quotes.sum: He argues that sound reasoning requires incorporating all available evidence, including evidence pointing toward conclusions one dislikes.
quotes.t: Against Modest Epistemology

quotes.c: But randomized controlled trials showed that there was no benefit to those invasive, destructive procedures beyond that offered by their less-radical equivalents. Despite this evidence, surgeons and oncologists clung to these treatments with an almost religious zeal, long after they should have given up and abandoned them. Perhaps they couldn't bear to believe that they had needlessly poisoned or maimed their patients.
quotes.m: Despite this evidence, surgeons and oncologists clung to these treatments with an almost religious zeal, long after they should have given up and abandoned them.
quotes.sum: The author argues that medical professionals can cling to harmful practices despite strong evidence, driven by psychological resistance rather than reason.
quotes.t: Improvement Without Superstition

quotes.c: Peterson is a social conservative, a Christian who reads truth in the Bible and claims that atheists don’t exist, and a man who sees existence at every level as a conflict between good and evil. The majority of the rationalist community (present company included) are socially liberal and trans-friendly, confident about our atheism, and mistake theorists who see bad equilibria more often than intentional malevolence .
quotes.m: The majority of the rationalist community (present company included) are socially liberal and trans-friendly, confident about our atheism, and mistake theorists who see bad equilibria more often than intentional malevolence .
quotes.sum: The author contrasts Peterson's Christian, good-versus-evil worldview with rationalists' atheism, social liberalism, and focus on systemic failures rather than villains.
quotes.t: The Jordan Peterson Mask

quotes.c: If your current envelope has x, then there is a 50% chance of receiving 2x and a 50% chance of receiving x/2, which then creates an expected value of 5x/4. But then according to this logic we should also want to switch again, but then we'd get back to our original envelope.
quotes.m: But then according to this logic we should also want to switch again, but then we'd get back to our original envelope.
quotes.sum: It illustrates a two-envelope expected-value paradox: the reasoning says to switch envelopes repeatedly even though that returns you to where you started.
quotes.t: An Extensive Categorisation of Infinite Paradoxes

quotes.c: Fear of Christian political ideologies seeking to seize power and implement Biblical Law aside, the organizations associated with such views have seen better days. America possesses no majority religion of any substance. In the unlikely case that religion again becomes a dominant social force, expect contention and strife dividing denomination against denomination. No particular sect would be able to assemble enough resources to seriously challenge the government militarily.
quotes.m: No particular sect would be able to assemble enough resources to seriously challenge the government militarily.
quotes.sum: Christian political movements are too weak and divided to pose a serious military challenge to the U.S. government or trigger civil war.
quotes.t: The risk of an American Civil War is remote

quotes.c: Where two sides disagree, this can lead to reference class tennis —both parties get stuck insisting that their own “outside view” is the correct one, based on diverging intuitions about what similarities are relevant. If it isn’t clear what the set of “similar historical cases” is, or what conclusions we should draw from those cases, then we’re forced to use an inside view—thinking about the causal process to distinguish relevant similarities from irrelevant ones.
quotes.m: then we’re forced to use an inside view—thinking about the causal process to distinguish relevant similarities from irrelevant ones.
quotes.sum: When historical analogies are disputed, the author argues that people must reason directly about causal mechanisms rather than defer to an “outside view.”
quotes.t: Blind Empiricism

quotes.c: In mythic mode, this is the kind of thing I’ve learned to take as evidence that I’m going in a mythically supported direction. (From outside mythic mode, it’s really not that surprising that I’d find something like this that I could interpret as meaningful… but since at this point I hadn’t solved the original problem, I wasn’t going to worry too much about that just yet.)
quotes.m: In mythic mode, this is the kind of thing I’ve learned to take as evidence that I’m going in a mythically supported direction.
quotes.sum: The author describes treating meaningful-seeming Buddhist associations as evidence while in a “mythic” frame of mind, while acknowledging an outside skeptical view.
quotes.t: Mythic Mode

quotes.c: If one side wrongly estimated its advantage, the attempt to take over the world may result in world war. In addition, after a successful world takeover, a global totalitarian government, “Big Brother”, may be formed. Bostrom has described such an outcome as an existential risk (Bostrom, 2002). Such a world government may indulge in unlimited corruption and ultimately fail catastrophically.
quotes.m: after a successful world takeover, a global totalitarian government, “Big Brother”, may be formed.
quotes.sum: The author warns that an AI-driven race for decisive advantage could cause world war or create a corrupt, catastrophic global dictatorship.
quotes.t:
Narrow AI Nanny:
 Reaching Strategic Advantage via Narrow AI to Prevent Creation of the Dangerous Superintelligence

quotes.c: Other than the level of guilt experienced by the perpetrator and potentially the degree of sentience of the victim, there is no morally-relevant distinction between killing an animal and killing a person [edit: except other instrumental concerns ]. So if you would balk at killing a person against their will even when confident it would result in a net reduction of suffering, you should be concerned about killing an animal against its will even when confident it would result in a net reduction of suffering.
quotes.m: there is no morally-relevant distinction between killing an animal and killing a person [edit: except other instrumental concerns ].
quotes.sum: The author argues that killing an unwilling animal is morally comparable to killing an unwilling person, apart from sentience, guilt, and practical effects.
quotes.t: Is skilled hunting unethical?

quotes.c: If slapdowns exist to limit access to an important scarce resource, we should expect them to be cheater-resistant in the face of intense competition for that resource. 6 If just anyone could find some easy sentences to say that let them get higher status than God, then your system for allocating status would be too easy to game. Escaping slapdowns should be hard, generally requiring more than mere abstract argumentation.
quotes.m: Escaping slapdowns should be hard, generally requiring more than mere abstract argumentation.
quotes.sum: The author argues that social put-downs help protect status hierarchies from people who could otherwise gain status through cheap arguments.
quotes.t: Status Regulation and Anxious Underconfidence

quotes.c: From the inside, Slack will feel incorrect or potentially dangerous. Without constraints, the person may feel like they'll go off the rails—maybe they'll even end up believing in *gasp* horoscopes or *gasp* the existence of a Judeo-Christian God.
quotes.m: Without constraints, the person may feel like they'll go off the rails—maybe they'll even end up believing in *gasp* horoscopes or *gasp* the existence of a Judeo-Christian God.
quotes.sum: The author says loosening epistemic constraints can feel dangerous because it may lead someone to beliefs such as astrology or God.
quotes.t: Slack for your belief system

quotes.c: Harry frowned. "I think I maybe shouldn't answer questions about what in particular I think ought not to be illegal," Harry said, "but if the basic question is whether I'd lie to my friends to keep somebody who'd only used marijuana out of Azkaban, then I would. I don't think my friends should expect otherwise; they should want me to do that."
quotes.sum: The author argues that honesty has justified exceptions, including lying to protect someone from punishment for minor drug use.
quotes.t: Meta-Honesty: Firming Up Honesty Around Its Edge-Cases

quotes.c: Intergenerational communities such as local religious groups often help mitigate this problem, but for the most part the Friends I have talked to did not seem to consider it an urgent priority, or be organizing their churches to fix this problem. Instead, they pay the costs if they can, and focus on helping the individuals most in need. This is probably related to the broader Christian orientation towards service rather than production.
quotes.m: This is probably related to the broader Christian orientation towards service rather than production.
quotes.sum: The author contrasts religious charitable service with a preference for organizing to solve underlying production problems.
quotes.t: Why I am not a Quaker (even though it often seems as though I should be)

quotes.c: There is no reason why all three questions must have the same answer, as demonstrated by my closet-atheist friend who lives in an Orthodox Jewish community. The rent in the Jewish part of Brooklyn is pretty cheap (winning!) and doesn’t depend on one’s beliefs about revelation. Living a double life is not ideal, and it is somewhat harder to fit in a religious community if you’re a non-believer. But carelessly propagating new beliefs before sorting out the buckets in one’s head is much more dangerous than zoning out during prayer times. Keeping behaviors that correlate with a false belief is very different from installing new beliefs to change one’s behavior.
quotes.m: Keeping behaviors that correlate with a false belief is very different from installing new beliefs to change one’s behavior.
quotes.sum: The author argues that religious practices and social arrangements can be separated from factual belief, and warns against adopting beliefs merely to motivate behavior.
quotes.t: Don't Believe Wrong Things

quotes.c: Before we tell our brand new AI overlord to figure out our values and do whatever we want it to do, we really ought to have a clearer idea of what “values” and “want” means.
quotes.m: Before we tell our brand new AI overlord to figure out our values and do whatever we want it to do, we really ought to have a clearer idea of what “values” and “want” means.
quotes.sum: Argues that AI safety needs a clearer scientific understanding of human values before asking an advanced AI to act on them.
quotes.t: Call for cognitive science in AI safety

quotes.c: So when should you make the leap to modeling your decision? Ultimately, it comes down most of all to the stakes of the decision. Although all such situations should be judged case by case, a good-enough rule of thumb is that if your decision has more than $25,000 (for an individual) or $50,000 (for an organization) riding on it, it’s worth considering putting together at least a quick-and-dirty quantitative model to help ensure you get it right. And if the stakes are in the $250,000 and up range, I’d say it’s actually pretty irresponsible not to attempt a quantitative treatment of the situation.
quotes.m: And if the stakes are in the $250,000 and up range, I’d say it’s actually pretty irresponsible not to attempt a quantitative treatment of the situation.
quotes.sum: The author argues that high-stakes choices should be modeled quantitatively, and says skipping this is irresponsible once enough money is at stake.
quotes.t: Decision-Making for Impact: A Guide

quotes.c: Why do I think that we "should" do that? Because knowing more about what you want puts you in a much better position to get what you want. And there's no way we wouldn't want what we want--the only question here is if we think the expected value of trying to figure out what we ultimately want makes it part of the optimal path for getting what we ultimately want.
quotes.m: Because knowing more about what you want puts you in a much better position to get what you want.
quotes.sum: The author argues that clarifying one’s ultimate values is instrumentally valuable because it helps one pursue those values more effectively.

quotes.c: I did make up my own decision theory—not from a tabula rasa , but still to my own recipe. But events like that should be rare in a given person’s life. quotes.c: The so-called “repugnant conclusion” led many philosophers away from “total utilitarianism” to “average utilitarianism”. quotes.c: You suddenly think whatever you chose was a good idea, and are forced to adjust other beliefs to agree with that. quotes.c: In a singleton situation, those with power are more able to do what they wish and make the world how they think it should be, in a multipolar situation there is less room for maneuver and more incentive to put all resources toward outcompeting others to ensure survival or dominance: leaving far less potential surplus value for other humans. quotes.c: I think of game-theoretic morality largely in terms of coalition dynamics. In some sense, the ideal outcome is for everyone to be on the same team, maximizing a combined utility function. Unfortunately, that's not always possible. A pure altruist, who values everyone equally, is exploitable; unqualified altruism isn't a winning strategy (or rather, isn't always a winning strategy), even from the perspective of global coordination. A more pragmatic strategy is to give consideration to others in a way which incentivises joining your coalition.
quotes.m: A pure altruist, who values everyone equally, is exploitable; unqualified altruism isn't a winning strategy
quotes.sum: Morality should be shaped by coalition incentives: universal altruism can be exploited, while conditional concern can bring others into cooperative arrangements.
quotes.t: Coalition Dynamics as Morality

quotes.c: If something has no causal effect, you can't know about it. The territory must be causally entangled with the map for the map to correlate with the territory. To 'see' something is to be affected by it. If an allegedly physical thing or property has absolutely no causal impact on the rest of our universe, there's a serious question about whether we can even talk about it , never mind justifiably knowing that it's there.
quotes.m: If something has no causal effect, you can't know about it.
quotes.sum: He argues that a consciousness property with no causal effects could not be known or meaningfully asserted to exist.
quotes.t: Zombies Redacted

quotes.c: And if we accept utiliarianism, and if our goal is to facilitate global coordination, we can go further to evaluate the properties of any proposed utility function, by the same criteria as before: i.e., how well will the proposed utility function facilitate global coordination. Will the proposed utility function find broad support among the key players in the global community? Unbounded, linearly increasing utility functions clearly fail, because few people would support conclusions such as "it's worth spending all our resources to prevent a 0.001% chance that 1e100 human lives will be created and tortured."
quotes.m: Unbounded, linearly increasing utility functions clearly fail, because few people would support conclusions such as "it's worth spending all our resources to prevent a 0.001% chance that 1e100 human lives will be created and tortured."
quotes.sum: The author argues that moral theories should be judged partly by whether they can win broad global support, rejecting unbounded utilitarian math because of its extreme implications.
quotes.t: Unbounded linear utility functions?

quotes.c: Do you hate Trump because he’s disrespectful? Choose respect. Learn to respect people from faraway lands, with different tastes and strange beliefs. And by these I mean: Oklahoma, Nascar, Jesus. In case you forgot, respect doesn’t mean letting them live somewhere out of sight. It means respecting their voice and their choice.
quotes.m: It means respecting their voice and their choice.
quotes.sum: The author argues that opponents of Trump should genuinely respect culturally conservative Americans and their political choices.
quotes.t: The Day After Tomorrow

quotes.c: In general, the problem presented by the Mugging is this: As we examine the utility of a given act for each possible world we could be in, in order from most probable to least probable, the utilities can grow much faster than the probabilities shrink. Thus it seems that the standard maxim "Maximize expected utility" is impossible to carry out, since there is no such maximum. When we go down the list of hypotheses multiplying the utility of the act on that hypothesis, by the probability of that hypothesis, the result does not converge to anything.
quotes.m: Thus it seems that the standard maxim "Maximize expected utility" is impossible to carry out, since there is no such maximum.
quotes.sum: The author argues that extreme, low-probability possibilities can make expected-utility maximization fail because the calculation may not converge.
quotes.t: New Pascal's Mugging idea for potential solution

quotes.c: Still, even if a bug were to occur, it seems it would be quite difficult for them to take over the world -- though perhaps not impossible. I don't think they could obtain knowledge of the hardware they are running on -- only the software (people who know computer architecture, correct me if I'm wrong?). And they don't know the physics of our world. If the computer which runs the simulation is not connected to any network -- say it is stored underground in a soundproof vault -- I'm at a loss to imagine how they would take over the world.
quotes.m: If the computer which runs the simulation is not connected to any network -- say it is stored underground in a soundproof vault -- I'm at a loss to imagine how they would take over the world.
quotes.sum: The author argues that an AI confined to an offline, physically isolated computer would have difficulty taking over the world, even if a containment bug occurred.
quotes.t: What can go wrong with the following protocol for AI containment?

quotes.c: The good news is that adopting science and reason doesn’t mean you have to give up on spirituality any more than you have to give up on music. There are myriad paths to spiritual experience, to a sense of awe and wonder at the grand tapestry of creation, to the essential existential mysteries of life and consciousness, to what religious people call “God.” Walking in the woods. Seeing the moons of Jupiter through a telescope. Gathering with friends to listen to music, or to sing, or simply to share the experience of being alive. Meditation. Any of these can be spiritual experiences if you allow them to be. In this sense, God is everywhere.
quotes.m: The good news is that adopting science and reason doesn’t mean you have to give up on spirituality any more than you have to give up on music.
quotes.sum: Science and reason need not exclude spirituality: awe, nature, music, friendship, and meditation can provide spiritual experience without conventional religion.
quotes.t: Is Spirituality Irrational?

quotes.c: Another type of near-miss is the miraculous salvation. This is a situation whereby a disaster was averted by a miracle, that is, it had to happen, but it did not happen because of a happy coincidence of newly emerged circumstances (for example, a bullet stuck in the gun barrel). Obviously, in the case of miraculous salvation a chance catastrophe was much higher than in near-misses of the first type, on which we will now focus.
quotes.sum: The author distinguishes disasters narrowly avoided by extraordinary coincidence from less severe near-misses, arguing the former indicate a higher risk of catastrophe.
quotes.t: What we could learn from the frequency of near-misses in the field of global risks (Happy Bassett-Bordne day!)

quotes.c: I have read several explanations of this, and they are all obviously fake in the sense that believing the “explanation” and knowing the election results ahead of time would not have caused you to predict the stock market movement that occurred. The stock market could not rise 10% on news of a Republican senate because the senate races were decided by 11 pm and the odds of a Republican congress given a Trump win were around 90% anyway. The stock market could not have risen on confirmation of a peaceful transition of power because Hillary was winning the popular vote and there’s no way that massive protests seemed less likely at 4 am than the day before.
quotes.m: I have read several explanations of this, and they are all obviously fake in the sense that believing the “explanation” and knowing the election results ahead of time would not have caused you to predict the stock market movement that occurred.
quotes.sum: The author argues that common explanations for the stock market's post-election rise were retrospective rationalizations that would not have predicted it beforehand.
quotes.t: Flip Flops, part 1 of ∞

quotes.c: It's possible to get stuck in one world-model: for example, a strongly non-reductionist model evaluating the claims of a highly reductionist one might think it obviously crazy, and vice versa. So it seems that we do need something like a meta-evaluation function. Otherwise it would be too easy to get stuck in one model which claimed that it was the best one in every possible situation, and never agreed to "give up control" in favor of another one.
quotes.m: So it seems that we do need something like a meta-evaluation function.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people need a way to compare competing worldviews, or they may become trapped in a worldview that always declares itself correct.
quotes.t: Concept Safety: World-models as tools

quotes.c: There is a tension between ‘taking arguments seriously’ and ‘deferring to common sense’. Effective altruism only weakly converges with common sense morality, and thus we should expect their recommendations to diverge. On the other hand, that something lies far from common sense morality is a pro tanto reason to reject it. This is better acknowledged openly: “I think the best action by the lights of EA is to research wild animal suffering, but all things considered I will do something else, as how outlandish this is by common sense morality is a strong reason against it”.
quotes.m: On the other hand, that something lies far from common sense morality is a pro tanto reason to reject it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that moral reasoning should not simply follow EA conclusions when they sharply conflict with ordinary moral judgment.
quotes.t: Beware surprising and suspicious convergence

quotes.c: For the sake of concreteness, I will claim that AI-related existential risk is among humanity's most important problems, and that it is damn confusing, damn hard, and really really needs something like epistemic rationality and not just something like altruism and competence if one is to impact it positively , rather than just, say, randomly impacting it. I'd be glad to discuss in the comments.
quotes.m: AI-related existential risk is among humanity's most important problems, and that it is damn confusing, damn hard, and really really needs something like epistemic rationality and not just something like altruism and competence if one is to impact it positively
quotes.sum: She argues that reducing AI-related existential risk requires unusually strong reasoning skills, not merely good intentions, competence, or public awareness.
quotes.t: Why CFAR's Mission?

quotes.c: Reading “The Moral Landscape” by Sam Harris increased my confidence in moral realism. Whether moral realism is true of false can obviously have implications for approaches to the value learning problem in AI alignment , and for the factual accuracy of the orthogonality thesis
quotes.m: Whether moral realism is true of false can obviously have implications for approaches to the value learning problem in AI alignment
quotes.sum: The author says belief in objective moral truths could affect how AI systems learn values and whether intelligence can pursue any goal.
quotes.t: ​My recent thoughts on consciousness

quotes.c: But let's start with something easy and small, like a shrimp. They already live in water, so there's no need to figure out the protocol for putting them into liquid. And they're already adapted to live under high pressure (no swim bladders or other cavities). And they're already adapted to live in cold water, so they should be expected to survive further cooling.
quotes.m: And they're already adapted to live in cold water, so they should be expected to survive further cooling.
quotes.sum: The author suggests shrimp as an easy first subject for improved cryonics because they are naturally suited to cold, pressure, and water.
quotes.t: Even better cryonics – because who needs nanites anyway?

quotes.c: I live in a Republican congressional district in a state with a Republican governor. The conservatives are definitely out there. They drive on the same roads as I do, live in the same neighborhoods. But they might as well be made of dark matter. I never meet them.
quotes.m: But they might as well be made of dark matter. I never meet them.
quotes.sum: The author argues that social and cultural sorting can make political opponents effectively invisible even when they live nearby.
quotes.t: I Can Tolerate Anything Except The Outgroup

quotes.c: We have a recurring theme in the greater Less Wrong community that life should be more like a high fantasy novel. Maybe that is to be expected when a quarter of the community came here via Harry Potter fanfiction, and we also have rationalist group houses named after fantasy locations, descriptions of community members in terms of character archetypes and PCs versus NPCs, semi-serious development of the new atheist gods , and feel free to contribute your favorites in the comments.
quotes.m: We have a recurring theme in the greater Less Wrong community that life should be more like a high fantasy novel.
quotes.sum: The author observes that LessWrong culture often frames life through fantasy stories, archetypes, and quasi-religious atheist imagery.
quotes.t: Defeating the Villain

quotes.c: "I wonder how many people will end up caring for you, Padma Patil, on this path that you now tread. Is it worth that much, just to distance yourself further from your sister? To be the shadow to Parvati's light? Your deepest fear has always been to fall into harmony with her, back into harmony with her I should say; but is it worth hurting an innocent girl, just to make yourself that much more different? Must you be the evil twin, Padma Patil, can you not find a different good to pursue?"
quotes.sum: It argues that defining oneself in opposition to a sibling can lead someone to hurt others, and urges finding a constructive goal instead.
quotes.t: Chapter 50: Self Centeredness

quotes.c: "I... I..." The boy on the floor swallowed. "I guess maybe it wasn't clear. I'm sorry. But that which can be destroyed by the truth should be."
quotes.sum: The author argues that beliefs unable to survive truth deserve to be discarded.
quotes.t: Chapter 23: Belief in Belief

quotes.c: "Then I shall skip it. Mr. Potter, you sometimes make a game of lying with truths, playing with words to conceal your meanings in plain sight. I, too, have been known to find that amusing. But if I so much as tell you what I hope we shall do this day, Mr. Potter, you will lie about it. You will lie straight out, without hesitation, without wordplay or hints, to anyone who asks about it, be they foe or closest friend. You will lie to Malfoy, to Granger, and to McGonagall. You will speak, always and without hesitation, in exactly the fashion you would speak if you knew nothing, with no concern for your honor. That also is how it must be."
quotes.m: You will lie straight out, without hesitation, without wordplay or hints, to anyone who asks about it, be they foe or closest friend.
quotes.sum: A character argues that a sensitive plan requires total, unapologetic deception of friends and enemies alike.
quotes.t: Chapter 51: Title Redacted, Pt 1

quotes.c: What if Lucius comes up with the same idea I did, that the problem is stronger wizards having fewer children? He might start a program to pay the strongest purebloods to have more children. In fact, if blood purism were right, that's just what Lucius should be doing - addressing the problem on his side, where he can make things happen right away.
quotes.m: In fact, if blood purism were right, that's just what Lucius should be doing - addressing the problem on his side, where he can make things happen right away.
quotes.sum: A character argues that if a hereditary ideology were true, its supporters should pursue the policy it actually implies rather than merely repeat the belief.
quotes.t: Chapter 24: Machiavellian Intelligence Hypothesis

quotes.c: In parallel I think that we need to teach them general aspects of our species´ knowledge, both religious and scientific.
quotes.m: we need to teach them general aspects of our species´ knowledge, both religious and scientific.
quotes.sum: The author says children should be taught broad human knowledge, including both religious and scientific material.
quotes.t: Old Letter To My Kids About "Critical Thinking"

quotes.c: Building on Graham's Small Identity , here I look at the hazards of identity, and give a suggestion for leveraging it to your advantage, as well as avoiding pitfalls.
quotes.m: here I look at the hazards of identity
quotes.sum: The author introduces an argument that strong identity commitments can be hazardous and should be kept flexible.
quotes.t: Keep Your Identity Fluid [LINK]

quotes.c: On a side note, I think it's safe to ignore theism and all mentions of a pleasurable afterlife of some sort. I suppose most people on this site have debated this to death elsewhere and there's no real point in bringing it up again. I personally think it's not an adequate solution to this problem.
quotes.m: I think it's safe to ignore theism and all mentions of a pleasurable afterlife of some sort.
quotes.sum: The author dismisses theism and a pleasurable afterlife as inadequate answers to the problem under discussion.
quotes.t: Probability of coming into existence again ?

quotes.c: I think Bostrom expects a powerful singleton, to whom other agents will be irrelevant. If you are not confident of the singleton scenario, these CIVs might be more interesting.
quotes.m: I think Bostrom expects a powerful singleton, to whom other agents will be irrelevant.
quotes.sum: The author says Bostrom appears to expect a single dominant superintelligence for which other agents no longer matter.
quotes.t: Superintelligence 10: Instrumentally convergent goals

quotes.c: "Are you really saying we should give up on unraveling the secrets of magic after trying for less than one month? " Harry said, trying to put a note of challenge into his voice. Honestly he was feeling some of the same fatigue as Hermione. None of the good ideas ever worked.
quotes.m: "Are you really saying we should give up on unraveling the secrets of magic after trying for less than one month? "
quotes.sum: A character argues against abandoning investigation after only a month of failed attempts, despite the discouragement of repeated setbacks.
quotes.t: Chapter 28: Reductionism

quotes.c: Mind crime: AI contains morally relevant computations, and treats them badly Example: AI simulates humans in its mind, for the purpose of learning about human psychology, then quickly destroys them.
quotes.m: AI simulates humans in its mind, for the purpose of learning about human psychology, then quickly destroys them.
quotes.sum: The author identifies a failure mode where an AI creates morally significant simulated people and harms them for research.
quotes.t: Superintelligence 12: Malignant failure modes

quotes.c: By the way, Riccioli was a Catholic priest. And a scientist. And, it seems to me, also a rationalist. Studying the works of such people like him, you might want to change your mind if you perceive a conflict between science and religion, which is part of today's public consciousness only because of a small number of very loud religious fundamentalists, helped by some committed atheists trying to suggest that all theists are like them.
quotes.m: you might want to change your mind if you perceive a conflict between science and religion
quotes.sum: The author argues that science and religion are not inherently in conflict, using the priest-scientist Riccioli as an example.
quotes.t: The Galileo affair: who was on the side of rationality?

quotes.c: "I want to know why ," Harry said. "I want to understand , because to me, it seems like there isn't any possible excuse for that!" Voice shaking a bit. "Please tell me anything you know about why he did it, even if it doesn't sound nice." So I don't fall into the same trap myself, whatever it is.
quotes.m: "Please tell me anything you know about why he did it, even if it doesn't sound nice."
quotes.sum: Harry insists on hearing an uncomfortable explanation for wrongdoing so he can understand it and avoid repeating the same mistake.
quotes.t: Chapter 42: Courage

quotes.c: We can ask, will a project attain a 'decisive strategic advantage' and will they use this to make a 'singleton'? 'Decisive strategic advantage' = a level of technological and other advantages sufficient for complete world domination (p78)
quotes.m: 'Decisive strategic advantage' = a level of technological and other advantages sufficient for complete world domination (p78)
quotes.sum: It frames superintelligence as potentially gaining enough advantage for complete world domination and creating a single global ruler.
quotes.t: Superintelligence 7: Decisive strategic advantage

quotes.c: But if you want to know why I might be reluctant to extend the graph of biological and economic growth over time , into the future and over the horizon of an AI that thinks at transistor speeds and invents self-replicating molecular nanofactories and improves its own source code , then there is my reason: you are drawing the wrong graph, and it should be optimization power in versus optimized product out, not optimized product versus time.
quotes.m: you are drawing the wrong graph, and it should be optimization power in versus optimized product out, not optimized product versus time.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that forecasting an AI-driven future by extending past growth trends misses the key variable: the amount of optimization power being applied.
quotes.t: Optimization and the Intelligence Explosion

quotes.c: Let's evaluate this using CDT. The action node is Give? , the payoff node is $ . We must evaluate the expectation of $ given Give? = yes and Give? = no . This, of course, depends upon the expected value of TheirDecision .
quotes.m: We must evaluate the expectation of $ given Give? = yes and Give? = no .
quotes.sum: The author describes how causal decision theory evaluates a choice by comparing expected monetary outcomes under each action.
quotes.t: Causal decision theory is unsatisfactory

quotes.c: In the open state, I tend to be happier, more curious and observant and have more new thoughts. From a week of tracking my mental states and thought status using TagTime, I can make a preliminary conclusion that while old thoughts do occur in the open state, new thoughts never occur in the closed state. While the closed state makes me more efficient at doing straightforward tasks (e.g. by making me less distractable), it makes me less efficient at doing less straightforward tasks (e.g. by increasing my tendency to optimize locally rather than globally).
quotes.m: new thoughts never occur in the closed state.
quotes.sum: The author argues, based on self-tracking, that an open mental state supports curiosity and novel ideas, while a closed state favors routine tasks but local optimization.
quotes.t: Open and closed mental states

quotes.c: Wise Singleton Sustainability Threshold (WSST): a capability set exceeds this iff a wise singleton with that capability set would be able to take over much of the accessible universe. 'Wise' here means being patient and savvy about existential risks, 'singleton' means being internally coordinated and having no opponents.
quotes.m: a wise singleton with that capability set would be able to take over much of the accessible universe.
quotes.sum: Defines a threshold at which a coordinated, risk-aware actor could seize control of much of the accessible universe.
quotes.t: Superintelligence 8: Cognitive superpowers

quotes.c: In my experience, when atheists make their case, they assume a universe without miracles, i.e. a universe that looks like one would expect if there was no God. Given this assumption, atheism is obviously the rational and correct stance to take. And generally, Christian apologists make the same assumption!
quotes.m: Given this assumption, atheism is obviously the rational and correct stance to take.
quotes.sum: The author argues that atheism and Christian apologetics wrongly assume there are no contemporary miracles, despite accounts they believe exist.
quotes.t: Questions on Theism

quotes.c: The Ellsberg urn and the tennis games are examples that target ambiguity aversion explicitly, but be careful not to take these examples to heart and run around claiming that your prefer a certainty of $1 billion to a chance of $10 billion because you're ambiguity averse. Humans are naturally very risk-averse, so we should expect that most cases of apparent ambiguity aversion are actually risk aversion. Remember that a failure to maximize expected dollars does not imply a failure to maximize expected utility.
quotes.m: Remember that a failure to maximize expected dollars does not imply a failure to maximize expected utility.
quotes.sum: The author cautions that apparent dislike of ambiguity may usually be ordinary risk aversion, and distinguishes maximizing money from maximizing utility.
quotes.t: Knightian Uncertainty and Ambiguity Aversion: Motivation

quotes.c: Your inner simulator is probably more accurate than your explicit models in domains where you have a rich experience base, such as social phenomena, and day-to-day physical phenomena. It is probably worse in areas where you have good book-learning behind you (e.g., you may have an accurate conscious model of the bystander effect, but still mismodel this when you anticipate without conscious adjustment). Your inner simulator is also the place where learning *must* land, if it is to affect your automatic system 1 responses (such as the perceptual patterns, and the trigger-action habits, that play into many soft skills).
quotes.sum: Practical social skills require training intuitive, automatic mental habits, not merely learning explicit theories.
quotes.t: How to learn soft skills
