quotes.c: Well... there's a couple of senses in which it seems imaginable. It's important to remember that imagining things yields info primarily about what human brains can imagine. It only provides info about reality to the extent that we think imagination and reality are systematically correlated for some reason.
quotes.m: It's important to remember that imagining things yields info primarily about what human brains can imagine.
quotes.sum: Imagination is evidence mainly about what humans can conceive, not about reality, unless there is a reason to think the two are correlated.
quotes.t: Causal Reference

quotes.c: So what's wrong with CT? Well, first it's clear that a lot of the evidence provided for CT doesn't count. Obviously, we cannot accept the existence of "high-quality philosophical arguments" or the ability to "explain sociological phenomena" without that information actually being provided. Likewise, CT's "noteworthy results in [...] everyday lives" aren't actually documented -- we have to take Ander's word for it that these things occurred.
quotes.m: a lot of the evidence provided for CT doesn't count.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Connection Theory makes unsupported claims and relies on undocumented evidence and personal testimony.
quotes.t: A Critique of Leverage Research's Connection Theory

quotes.c: Do you regularly ask, “What are the causes of my beliefs? Why do I think this? What’s the source?”
quotes.m: “What are the causes of my beliefs? Why do I think this? What’s the source?”
quotes.sum: The author recommends routinely examining the origins and evidence behind one's own beliefs.
quotes.t: Curiosity checklist: Looking for feedback

quotes.c: I'm not a Christian, but I definitely want to know if Christianity is true so I can stop taking the Lord's name in vain and hopefully get to heaven. (Please don't contact me about Christianity though, I've already thought about it a lot and judged it too improbable to be worth spending additional time thinking about.) Point is, it's hard to see how having more accurate knowledge could hurt .
quotes.m: Point is, it's hard to see how having more accurate knowledge could hurt .
quotes.sum: The author uses Christianity as an example to argue that more accurate beliefs are generally beneficial.
quotes.t: 6 Tips for Productive Arguments

quotes.c: While compulsory voting has an interesting appeal , I generally think people should be free to decline to participate for whatever reason if they want to. Indeed, given people's overconfidence and under-informed approach to issues (for which I don't blame them and for which I am also at fault), many people may have a moral imperative to not vote .
quotes.m: many people may have a moral imperative to not vote .
quotes.sum: The author argues that poorly informed, overconfident people may sometimes be morally better off abstaining from voting.
quotes.t: Yes, Voting is Rational, So Please Go Vote!

quotes.c: However, my priorities have changed, and I’m starting to really value the extra leverage prestige can bring me. I plan to start a Less Wrong/ 80,000 Hours club at whatever university I end up attending. I would have access to more intelligent, interested people at Stanford than at, say, UC Irvine. Perhaps more importantly, the club itself would have a better standing in the outside world if it were founded in Stanford.
quotes.m: I’m starting to really value the extra leverage prestige can bring me.
quotes.sum: The author says elite university prestige would give her more leverage and help a LessWrong/80,000 Hours student group recruit and gain outside credibility.
quotes.t: Admissions Essay Help?

quotes.c: You might next try the answer that for a statement to be meaningful, there must be some way reality can be which makes the statement true or false; and that since the universe is made of atoms, there must be some way to arrange the atoms in the universe that would make a statement true or false. E.g. to make the statement "I am in Paris" true, we would have to move the atoms comprising myself to Paris. A literateur claims that Elaine has an attribute called post-utopianism, but there's no way to translate this claim into a way to arrange the atoms in the universe so as to make the claim true, or alternatively false; so it has no truth-condition, and must be meaningless.
quotes.m: there's no way to translate this claim into a way to arrange the atoms in the universe so as to make the claim true, or alternatively false; so it has no truth-condition, and must be meaningless.
quotes.sum: It argues that a claim is meaningful only if some possible physical state of reality could make it true or false.
quotes.t: The Useful Idea of Truth

quotes.c: The money it would take to sign up for cryonics, though not large, is enough to buy several centuries of healthy life each year if given to givewell's top malaria charities. Since on average I expect to live another 50-60 years without cryonics, the investment would need to increase the expected value of my lifespan by at least 5,000 years at minimum to be morally acceptable to me.
quotes.m: the investment would need to increase the expected value of my lifespan by at least 5,000 years at minimum to be morally acceptable to me.
quotes.sum: The author says cryonics is morally unjustified unless it offers an enormous expected lifespan gain, because its cost could instead save many lives through malaria charities.
quotes.t: Cryonics priors

quotes.c: Extrapolating results on personal identity from C. elegans to humans is not ideal. If the results are biased in one direction, we should expect more redundancy in mammalian neural systems than there are in nematode ones, because mammals have so many more brain cells.
quotes.m: we should expect more redundancy in mammalian neural systems than there are in nematode ones, because mammals have so many more brain cells.
quotes.sum: The author cautions that findings about identity preservation in nematode brains may not generalize to humans, whose neural systems likely have more redundancy.
quotes.t: Brief response to kalla724 on preserving personal identity with vitrification

quotes.c: Carter’s resolution of the Mere Addition Paradox makes a great deal of sense, as it manages to avoid every single repugnant and counterintuitive conclusion that Total and Average Utilitarianism draw by themselves while still being completely logically consistent. In fact, I think that most people who reject the Repugnant Conclusion will realize that this was their True Rejection all along.
quotes.m: Carter’s resolution of the Mere Addition Paradox makes a great deal of sense, as it manages to avoid every single repugnant and counterintuitive conclusion that Total and Average Utilitarianism draw by themselves while still being completely logically consistent.
quotes.sum: The author endorses Carter’s population-ethics theory as a coherent way to reject the Repugnant Conclusion without accepting other counterintuitive outcomes.
quotes.t: Alan Carter on the Complexity of Value

quotes.c: Hypothetical: the recent $15mm Series A funding of Vicarious by Good Ventures and Founders Fund sets off a wave of $450mm in funded AGI projects of approximately the same scope, over the next ten years. Let's estimate a third of that goes to paying for man-years of actual, low-level, basic AGI capabilities research. That's about 1500 man-years. Anything which can show something resembling progress can easily secure another few hundred man-years to continue making progress.
quotes.m: Anything which can show something resembling progress can easily secure another few hundred man-years to continue making progress.
quotes.sum: The author warns that early AGI investment could trigger a self-reinforcing wave of funding for basic AI capability research.
quotes.t: Heading off a near-term AGI arms race

quotes.c: The incentive for e.g. taking advantage of sperm banks is automatic in this system - you can either pay a bunch of money to have a kid with your current husband, or you can be paid thousands of dollars and get free child care to be inseminated by the sperm of a Nobel winner who never had to diet. I think that, in practice, the basic test of a system like this would be whether it could get people to go over the inconvenience threshold of actually using sperm banks and egg donors.
quotes.m: you can either pay a bunch of money to have a kid with your current husband, or you can be paid thousands of dollars and get free child care to be inseminated by the sperm of a Nobel winner
quotes.sum: He argues that paying people and providing child care could make them choose sperm or egg donors selected for exceptional traits.
quotes.t: Constructing fictional eugenics (LW edition)

quotes.c: Or contrast: "I'm upset" -> "I'm upset because I think the other person is looking down on me" -> "I'm upset because the person's tone of voice sounds like people who looked down on me in high school". This is related to the incredibly important skill, search for the historical causes of your thoughts, rather than their justifications.
quotes.m: search for the historical causes of your thoughts, rather than their justifications.
quotes.sum: The author argues that rational self-understanding means tracing feelings to their historical causes rather than inventing after-the-fact justifications.
quotes.t: SotW: Be Specific

quotes.c: By the pigeonhole principle (you can't fit 3 pigeons into 2 pigeonholes) there must be some joint probability distributions which cannot be represented in the first causal structure. This means the first causal structure is falsifiable; there's survey data we can get which would lead us to reject it as a hypothesis.
quotes.m: This means the first causal structure is falsifiable; there's survey data we can get which would lead us to reject it as a hypothesis.
quotes.sum: Causal models make testable predictions, so data can rule out a proposed explanation of how variables are connected.
quotes.t: Causal Diagrams and Causal Models

quotes.c: Thus, the "circular" arguments given above are actually valid Bayesian inferences. But there is a reason that we consider A to be a fallacy, while B sounds valid. Since the intepretation (the Bible is the word of God, 3-cm tracks are signatures of electrons) logically requires the hypothesis, the probability of the interpretation cannot be higher than the probability of the hypothesis. If we assign the existence of God a very low prior belief, then we must also assign a very low prior belief to the interpretation of the Bible as the word of God.
quotes.m: If we assign the existence of God a very low prior belief, then we must also assign a very low prior belief to the interpretation of the Bible as the word of God.
quotes.sum: The author argues that circular religious arguments can be modeled as Bayesian inference, but weak priors for God also make Bible-based interpretations unlikely.
quotes.t: Fallacies as weak Bayesian evidence

quotes.c: Thus it is a worthwhile exercise to practice deflating the word 'true' out of any sentence in which it appears. (Note that this is a special case of rationalist taboo .) For example, instead of saying, "I believe that the sky is blue, and that's true! " you can just say, "The sky is blue", which conveys essentially the same information about what color you think the sky is.
quotes.m: Thus it is a worthwhile exercise to practice deflating the word 'true' out of any sentence in which it appears.
quotes.sum: The author recommends stripping vague truth-claims from language and stating direct beliefs instead, as a way to notice inconsistencies between stated and intuitive beliefs.
quotes.t: Rationality: Appreciating Cognitive Algorithms

quotes.c: Visualizing all 4 quadrants of this binary proposition - the world is like A and I believe A, the world is like B and I believe A, etc. - should, in principle, emotionally confirm the truth of the proposition: "If it will be cold, I want to believe it's cold; if it's not cold, I want to believe it's not cold; let me not become attached to beliefs I may not want."
quotes.m: If it will be cold, I want to believe it's cold; if it's not cold, I want to believe it's not cold; let me not become attached to beliefs I may not want.
quotes.sum: The author recommends mentally rehearsing both possibilities to avoid becoming emotionally attached to a preferred belief.
quotes.t: SotW: Avoid Motivated Cognition

quotes.c: This is a potentially very powerful measure - an AI wanting to take over the world would have to do while ensuring that it only uses facts that were going to be important anyway (and uses them in precisely the right amounts, and prevents the human reaction from disrupting this setup, and leaving open the same spread of possible future worlds dependent on variations in current evidence, etc...) It seems an immense challenge even for a super intelligent AI. Generally, the more coarse grained the AI's vision is, the more useful this measure becomes.
quotes.m: It seems an immense challenge even for a super intelligent AI.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a reduced-impact constraint could make an AI takeover extremely difficult, even for a superintelligent system.
quotes.t: The mathematics of reduced impact: help needed

quotes.c: This is the basis for why we're so willing to chase after lost miners or Baby Jessica no matter the monetary cost, but turn a blind eye to the mass unknown starving in the developing world. Indeed, the person doesn't even need to be particularly identified, though it does help.
quotes.m: we're so willing to chase after lost miners or Baby Jessica no matter the monetary cost, but turn a blind eye to the mass unknown starving in the developing world.
quotes.sum: People readily spend to help identifiable victims but neglect large numbers of unnamed people starving in poorer countries.
quotes.t: Why Don't People Help Others More?

quotes.c: I've just been thinking (a dangerous pastime, I know) and remembering my religious days, and one of the things that made me so anxious back then, and made adopting atheism so gratifying, what the sheer drought of information. I had so many, so many questions, and there were no satisfying answers to be found.
quotes.m: I had so many, so many questions, and there were no satisfying answers to be found.
quotes.sum: The author recalls finding religion distressingly unable to answer their questions, and experiencing atheism as relief.
quotes.t: Fiction: A Setting Justifying the Epistemic Aggressiveness Of A Religion Stand-in

quotes.c: And that's unfortunate, in my view, as movies are probably the most prevalent and influential art form for the general public, and because many people will form their views on abstract concepts based on the percepts that movies provide (related to the issue of generalizing from fictional evidence ). One need only glance over the examples on the tvtropes page " Hollywood Atheist " to see that movies and television aren't exactly putting the best foot forward for our kind.
quotes.m: many people will form their views on abstract concepts based on the percepts that movies provide
quotes.sum: The author says film strongly shapes public beliefs, and argues that movies and television portray atheists poorly.
quotes.t: Non-theist cinema?

quotes.c: Claim #1 might provoke a yawning "Yes, of course..." from many scientists and philosophers, but both claims are currently heretical in the field of Jesus Studies, which shows many signs of being an unsound research program in general. The book is written for a mass audience, but is also aimed at historians in general. It is, as far as I know, the first book to lay out the detailed case for why historians should be using Bayesian methods.
quotes.m: It is, as far as I know, the first book to lay out the detailed case for why historians should be using Bayesian methods.
quotes.sum: The author argues that scholarship on Jesus is methodologically unsound and says historians should use Bayesian reasoning.
quotes.t: Mini-review: 'Proving History: Bayes' Theorem and the Quest for the Historical Jesus'

quotes.c: More generally: Posts or comments advocating or 'asking about' violation of laws that are actually enforced against middle-class people (e.g., kidnapping, not anti-marijuana laws) may at the admins' option be censored on the grounds that it makes LW look bad and that anyone talking about a proposed crime on the Internet fails forever as a criminal (i.e., even if a proposed conspiratorial crime were in fact good, there would still be net negative expected utility from talking about it on the Internet; if it's a bad idea, promoting it conceptually by discussing it is also a bad idea; therefore and in full generality this is a low-value form of discussion).
quotes.m: even if a proposed conspiratorial crime were in fact good, there would still be net negative expected utility from talking about it on the Internet
quotes.sum: The author argues that LessWrong may censor discussion of real-world crimes because public discussion is harmful even if the crime itself could hypothetically be worthwhile.
quotes.t: New censorship: against hypothetical violence against identifiable people

quotes.c: Secondly, I don't think it is honest or sane to insist on the reality of God but exempt any opinions from testing against reality just because they relate to God in some way. It's almost redundant to point out the atrocities that have been carried out on the pretext of slightly different interpretations of religious doctrine between tribal sub-groups of Christianity. Absent that, some other pretext might have been used, but even so if there is to be any stable common ground between hotly disputed opinions, reality must be it.
quotes.m: if there is to be any stable common ground between hotly disputed opinions, reality must be it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that religious beliefs should be tested against reality, rather than exempted from scrutiny, because reality is the only stable ground for resolving disputes.
quotes.t: Being a Realist (even if you believe in God)

quotes.c: In short: the New Year is a great time to do some life review and planning. How are things going? How was the past year? Do a thorough personal review to find out. What are you going to do next year? Make a plan. How can you increase your chances of success? Take all of your plans, projects, and goals and optimize them based on what you have learned on Less Wrong.
quotes.m: Take all of your plans, projects, and goals and optimize them based on what you have learned on Less Wrong.
quotes.sum: The author urges readers to systematically review their lives, make plans, and optimize their goals using LessWrong-style ideas.
quotes.t: How to get the most out of the next year

quotes.c: And much the same way that a lot of craziness stems, not so much from "having a wrong model of the world", as "not bothering to have a model of the world", a lot of personal effectiveness isn't so much about "having the right goals" as "bothering to have goals at all" - where unpacking this somewhat Vassarian statement would lead us to ideas like "bothering to have something that I check my actions' consequences against, never mind whether or not it's the right thing" or "bothering to have some communication-related urge that animates my writing when I write, instead of just sitting down to log a certain number of writing hours during which I feel rewarded from rearranging shiny words".
quotes.m: a lot of personal effectiveness isn't so much about "having the right goals" as "bothering to have goals at all"
quotes.sum: The author argues that effectiveness comes less from selecting perfect goals than from actively checking actions against goals and consequences.
quotes.t: Urges vs. Goals: The analogy to anticipation and belief

quotes.c: I find sunk costs have a large effect in the board game "Go" (so that beginners are instructed "not to throw good stones after bad"), and I assume it also does in poker, but both of those games are too long and too full of distractors to be used in a simple demo.
quotes.m: both of those games are too long and too full of distractors to be used in a simple demo.
quotes.sum: The author is looking for a simple game or demonstration that clearly teaches people to avoid letting sunk costs distort decisions.
quotes.t: [Question] Do you know a good game or demo for demonstrating sunk costs?

quotes.c: I actually updated -- thereafter, I didn't fish for coins in my wallet anymore -- but still didn't admit it in the original argument.
quotes.m: I actually updated -- thereafter, I didn't fish for coins in my wallet anymore -- but still didn't admit it in the original argument.
quotes.sum: The author describes changing his behavior after being persuaded, while failing to acknowledge the update during the argument.
quotes.t: How to enjoy being wrong

quotes.c: "So," you say, after the first dozen times you ask the Oracle a question and it returns an answer that you'd have to take on faith, "we'll just specify in the utility function that the plan should be understandable."
quotes.m: the Oracle a question and it returns an answer that you'd have to take on faith
quotes.sum: The author argues that even an AI designed as a question-answering tool may give plans humans cannot independently understand or verify.
quotes.t: Reply to Holden on 'Tool AI'

quotes.c: If we set the two equations equal to each other, we can solve for the value for P that would make both strategies equally viable, expected value wise. That value is 50.05%. So as long as we are confident that Omega has a better than 50.05% chance at predicting our choice, the expected value formula says we can expect to earn more from one-boxing.
quotes.m: So as long as we are confident that Omega has a better than 50.05% chance at predicting our choice, the expected value formula says we can expect to earn more from one-boxing.
quotes.sum: It argues that, in Newcomb’s problem, one-boxing has higher expected value if Omega predicts choices with more than 50.05% accuracy.
quotes.t: The Expected Value Approach to Newcomb's Problem

quotes.c: The students failed to see the correct answer because they weren't thinking creatively enough. While the correct approach in this situation is indeed to notice your confusion, a worthwhile approach still could be to list all the possible solutions you think could be the answer. (And of course only list real solutions that you actually understand, not fake ones.)
quotes.m: The students failed to see the correct answer because they weren't thinking creatively enough.
quotes.sum: The author argues that rational thinking requires noticing confusion and creatively generating real alternative explanations.
quotes.t: Magic Tricks Revealed: Test Your Rationality

quotes.c: Me: "Because even though I, in my mortal uncertainty, will eventually be wrong about all sorts of things if I make enough statements one after another, this fact can't be used to increase the probability of arbitrary statements beyond what my prior says they should be, because then my prior would sum to more than 1. There must be some kind of required condition for taking a hypothesis seriously enough to worry that I might be overconfident about it -"
quotes.m: this fact can't be used to increase the probability of arbitrary statements beyond what my prior says they should be, because then my prior would sum to more than 1.
quotes.sum: Argues that uncertainty and possible overconfidence do not justify treating arbitrary, extremely unlikely claims as serious possibilities.
quotes.t: Pascal's Muggle: Infinitesimal Priors and Strong Evidence

quotes.c: If you are already an atheist that does not believe in ghosts, what can you learn from rationality? I'd love to be wrong about lots of things but my problem is, I think I'm right.
quotes.m: I'd love to be wrong about lots of things but my problem is, I think I'm right.
quotes.sum: The author asks what rationality can offer someone who is already atheist and feels confident in their beliefs.
quotes.t: What can we gain from rationality?

quotes.c: Eliezer's post on Torture vs. Dust Specks [ Here ] has generated lots of discussion as well as what Eliezer describes as interesting [ ways ] of [ avoiding ] the question. We will do no sort of thing in this post, we will answer the question as intended; I will interpret that eye specks is cumulatively greater suffering than the suffering of 50 years.
quotes.m: I will interpret that eye specks is cumulatively greater suffering than the suffering of 50 years.
quotes.sum: The author accepts that a vast accumulation of tiny harms can outweigh fifty years of torture.
quotes.t: Do the people behind the veil of ignorance vote for "specks"?

quotes.c: Now I'm pretty sure that the God of the Bible is man-made and Jesus of Nazareth was probably a failed prophet , but I don't have good reasons to reject the supernatural all together. I'm working through the sequences, but this process is slow.
quotes.m: I'm pretty sure that the God of the Bible is man-made and Jesus of Nazareth was probably a failed prophet
quotes.sum: The author rejects the biblical God and likely rejects Jesus's prophecy, while remaining uncertain whether anything supernatural exists.
quotes.t: Exclude the supernatural? My worldview is up for grabs.

quotes.c: In this allegory, Blainetology is presented as intentionally frustrating because it seems so reasonable and logical despite being so silly. What of the inference that a magic trick is most likely to be explicable by slight of hand instead of actual magical powers? It's an entirely unproven inference, yet we use it every time we see a magician preform. If there's one thing I would want those who invoke supernatural powers to explain, it would be to answer why it is reasonable to inference to a trick with magicians, but not with things like consciousness or the origin on the universe?
quotes.m: It's an entirely unproven inference, yet we use it every time we see a magician preform.
quotes.sum: The author defends reductionist skepticism: unexplained phenomena should not automatically be treated as evidence of supernatural causes.
quotes.t: The Magician: A Reductionist's Allegory

quotes.c: The standard story makes concessions to it, as social conservatives believe morals should be taught to children using behaviorist principles ("Spare the rod and spoil the child"). This is the theory of ethics endorsed by "Walden Two" and warned against by "A Clockwork Orange". And it is the theory of ethics so badly abused by the former Soviet Union, among other tyrannical governments.
quotes.m: And it is the theory of ethics so badly abused by the former Soviet Union, among other tyrannical governments.
quotes.sum: The author criticizes teaching morality through behaviorist conditioning, associating it with coercive social control and authoritarian abuse.
quotes.t: Morality is not about willpower

quotes.c: My friend is a skeptical theist. She, for instance, scoffs mightily at Camping's little dilemma/psychosis but then argues from a position of comfort that Rapture it's a silly thing to predict because it's clearly stated that no one will know the day. And then she gives me a confused look because the psychological dissonance is clear.
quotes.m: And then she gives me a confused look because the psychological dissonance is clear.
quotes.sum: The author criticizes a theist friend for dismissing a Rapture prediction while preserving the underlying belief.
quotes.t: Remaining human

quotes.c: More broadly, given even a small chance that the future of AI will end up in some first-mover scenario, it's worth asking, "what can we do to prevent some small group of humans (the SIAI, a secret conspiracy of billionaires, a secret conspiracy of Google employees, whoever) from steering a first-mover scenario in a direction that's beneficial to themselves and perhaps their blood relatives, but harmful to the rest of humanity?"
quotes.sum: The author warns that a group that gets an early AI advantage could steer its benefits toward itself and its relatives at everyone else's expense.
quotes.t: Why a Human (Or Group of Humans) Might Create UnFriendly AI Halfway On Purpose

quotes.c: No, seriously, why is it that non-religious movements seem to lack this oomph, this particular eagerness, that the religious are often portrayed bearing? There's untapped human potential, here, friends, and we're letting it go to waste. Reversed stupidity is not intelligence. So, how do we infuse this kind of zeal, of enthusiasm, into, say, the Less Wrong brand of Secular Humanism?
quotes.m: So, how do we infuse this kind of zeal, of enthusiasm, into, say, the Less Wrong brand of Secular Humanism?
quotes.sum: The author argues that secular humanism and LessWrong should cultivate some of religion’s emotional zeal and ability to motivate followers.
quotes.t: "The Book Of Mormon" or Belief In Belief, The Musical

quotes.c: I've noticed during my thoughts on the issue that I seem to be biased against Christianity- although raised in a Christian household, I have noticed that I become more tense when reading effective arguments for Christianity and more relaxed when reading good arguments against it- I also feel strongly tempted to pull out books which I know give good arguments against Christianity.
quotes.sum: The author notices an emotional bias against Christianity and a tendency to seek arguments against it.
quotes.t: Requesting advice

quotes.c: When I started going to the Vancouver meetup, it wasn't really happening. I got inspired by the "communities need heroes" thing and started to just make it happen. It worked. You really do need someone holding the bottom line. When I fail to make things happen, other people don't reliably step in, things just stop happening. This one keeps getting drilled into me. I still seem to have an aversion to seizing power and stepping on toes, but I'm starting to see that it's really ok. Go ahead and seize power. Be the benevolent dictator. People like it.
quotes.m: Go ahead and seize power. Be the benevolent dictator. People like it.
quotes.sum: The author argues that local communities need a person willing to take control, even as a “benevolent dictator,” to keep things functioning.
quotes.t: What I Learned About Meetup Organization

quotes.c: I think you'd intuitively think that only a fool would cling to certainty so much that he or she wouldn't be willing to take what is an almost guaranteed 24 million. Why is it okay to give up certainty on some bets and not others, regardless of what expected utility says?
quotes.m: Why is it okay to give up certainty on some bets and not others, regardless of what expected utility says?
quotes.sum: Questions why people value certainty inconsistently across gambles, even when expected utility favors the riskier choice.
quotes.t: The Allais Paradox and the Dilemma of Utility vs. Certainty

quotes.c: I wouldn't say that everyone who called themselves a behaviorist had religious motivations. But perhaps there was a dangerous synergy between his rationalist doctrine, and a parasitic religious one.
quotes.m: But perhaps there was a dangerous synergy between his rationalist doctrine, and a parasitic religious one.
quotes.sum: The author suggests that a behaviorist's rationalism may have reinforced a harmful religious doctrine.
quotes.t: Religious Behaviorism

quotes.c: Assume, too kindly, that your estimates are unbiased. And suppose you use this decision procedure many times, for many different decisions, and your estimates are unbiased. It seems reasonable to expect that on average you will receive the estimated expected value of each decision you make in this way.
quotes.m: It seems reasonable to expect that on average you will receive the estimated expected value of each decision you make in this way.
quotes.sum: It sets up the intuitive belief that repeatedly choosing options with unbiased estimates should deliver the estimated value on average.
quotes.t: The Optimizer's Curse and How to Beat It

quotes.c: Now suppose that R was shown to be formally independent of ZFC in the sense that for some axiom A0, ZFC+A0 implies P=NP and ZFC+~A implies P!=NP. This would resolve the mathematical question of P versus NP but the question Q seems like a prima facie concrete question with a definitive yes or no answer that does not rely for its substance on M or ZFC or any other epistemic construct. It would seem that we must have missed something in our description of reality, M.
quotes.m: It would seem that we must have missed something in our description of reality, M.
quotes.sum: The author argues that if P versus NP were independent of ZFC, this would reveal a flaw in our model of reality rather than make the question genuinely unanswered.
quotes.t: What independence between ZFC and P vs NP would imply

quotes.c: In “Tsuyoku Naritai!”, Yudkowsky is making reference to the more general Jewish concept of yeridas hadoros , or “descent of the generations,” which generally refers to the notion that people become less-and-less spiritual with succeeding generations, and the ancient past is therefore associated with sacred origins, rather than with more primitive stages of a progressive, evolutionary scale. Yudkowsky’s views on Judaism’s approach to knowledge and progress are based primarily, I think, on three misunderstandings concerning yeridas hadoros.
quotes.m: Yudkowsky’s views on Judaism’s approach to knowledge and progress are based primarily, I think, on three misunderstandings concerning yeridas hadoros.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Yudkowsky misunderstands a Jewish idea about spiritual decline across generations when discussing knowledge and progress.
quotes.t: Ontologial Reductionism and Invisible Dragons

quotes.c: Now, perhaps not so obviously, could it be people have some incentives to say and even believe or at least try to believe things that are obviously wrong even to people of their tribe (political/religious/ect. affilation)? Why would something like this arise? My mind at this point wandered to conspicuous consumption .
quotes.m: could it be people have some incentives to say and even believe or at least try to believe things that are obviously wrong even to people of their tribe
quotes.sum: The author wonders whether people may adopt obviously false beliefs as a form of social signaling, analogous to conspicuous consumption.
quotes.t: The importance of Not Getting the Joke

quotes.c: A generic rallying cry of “Science!”, “Humanism!” or “Rationality!” is not a satisfying answer to the problems of Death and Global Suffering and Existential Risk. It’s not satisfying on an artistic level, an intellectual level or a tribal level. Having specific ideas about how to steer the future is what gives our group a unique identity. Caring too much about that identity is dangerous, but it can also be extremely motivational.
quotes.m: Having specific ideas about how to steer the future is what gives our group a unique identity.
quotes.sum: Shared, concrete visions for directing the future give the rationalist community identity and motivation, though excessive attachment to that identity is risky.
quotes.t: The Value (and Danger) of Ritual

quotes.c: I presently believe that the cluster of existential risk efforts that have well-considered expected value which is within a few orders of magnitude of the one that appears to have the highest expected value is larger than it may initially seem. There are often large error bars surrounding the expected value of a given intervention on account of the model uncertainty leading to assessment of the expected value of the intervention varying heavily with new data.
quotes.m: There are often large error bars surrounding the expected value of a given intervention on account of the model uncertainty leading to assessment of the expected value of the intervention varying heavily with new data.
quotes.sum: Existential-risk projects that look less cost-effective may be comparable once uncertainty in impact estimates is considered.
quotes.t: Efficient philanthropy: local vs. global approaches

quotes.c: In this framework, the greater X is, the lower the expected value of Action A. This syncs well with my intuitions: if someone threatened to harm one person unless you gave them $10, this ought to carry more weight (because it is more plausible in the face of the "prior" of life experience) than if they threatened to harm 100 people, which in turn ought to carry more weight than if they threatened to harm 3^^^3 people (I'm using 3^^^3 here as a representation of an unimaginably huge number ).
quotes.sum: The author argues that extraordinary claims of enormous stakes should be discounted using prior experience, rather than taken literally in expected-value calculations.
quotes.t: Why We Can't Take Expected Value Estimates Literally (Even When They're Unbiased)

quotes.c: Almost all instances of the word "true" can be eliminated from the sentences in which they appear by applying Tarski's formula. For example, if you say, "I believe the sky is blue, and that's true!" then this can be rephrased as the statement, "I believe the sky is blue, and the sky is blue." For every "The sentence 'X' is true" you can just say X and convey the same information about what you believe - just talk about the territory the map allegedly corresponds to, instead of talking about the map.
quotes.m: For every "The sentence 'X' is true" you can just say X and convey the same information about what you believe - just talk about the territory the map allegedly corresponds to, instead of talking about the map.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people should usually state what they think is the case rather than add the abstract label “true” to a sentence.
quotes.t: Only say 'rational' when you can't eliminate the word

quotes.c: This class - a religious class I took as an atheist in order to achieve an unrelated goal - turned out to be one of the most important classes I have ever taken in my life. It taught me an important meta-skill I have used to great effect ever since.
quotes.m: It taught me an important meta-skill I have used to great effect ever since.
quotes.sum: The author says an unexpectedly valuable religious class taught them a broadly useful meta-skill.
quotes.t: Build Small Skills in the Right Order

quotes.c: As stipulated, your afterlife accounts for at least 99% of your utility if follow-thru (and hence chr ) is true. If we suppose that the length of time for which God rewards us in Heaven or torments us in Hell has an exponential distribution, and we are considering only the part of that distribution where >= 99% of your utility is in the afterlife, then almost certainly p(chr) * U(Christianity | chr) > (1-p(chr)) * U(atheism | not(chr)). It now appears we should accept Pascal's wager.
quotes.m: It now appears we should accept Pascal's wager.
quotes.sum: The author uses probability and expected utility to argue that even a small chance of Christianity being true makes Pascal's wager rational.
quotes.t: Pascal's wager re-examined

quotes.c: In this essay I talk about what I believe about rather than what I care about. What I care about seems like an entirely emotional question to me. I cannot Shut Up And Multiply about what I care about. If I do, in fact, Shut Up and Multiply, then it is because I believe that doing so is right.
quotes.m: I cannot Shut Up And Multiply about what I care about.
quotes.sum: The author argues that moral concern is emotional and cannot simply be dictated by aggregating outcomes; doing so would itself require a prior belief that it is right.
quotes.t: A Defense of Naive Metaethics

quotes.c: I suspect that forgetfulness is the single largest hindrance to me improving my rationality. This isn't something I've seen others report on LessWrong, so I'm suspicious that I'm in some kind of self-serving spiral, or that I'm doing something obvious wrong.
quotes.m: I suspect that forgetfulness is the single largest hindrance to me improving my rationality.
quotes.sum: The author wonders whether poor memory is their main obstacle to becoming more rational, while questioning whether that belief is self-serving.
quotes.t: I want a better memory.

quotes.c: Jehova's Witnesses aim to interpret the Bible literally , which is in some sense admirable because that is the only way it can serve much to constrain one's anticipations about reality. By contrast, if one aims to interpret a religious text only "metaphorically", then there are so many possible meanings that it does essentially nothing to constrain one's anticipations.
quotes.m: if one aims to interpret a religious text only "metaphorically", then there are so many possible meanings that it does essentially nothing to constrain one's anticipations.
quotes.sum: The author argues that literal readings are more epistemically meaningful because they make testable predictions, while metaphorical readings can evade constraint by reality.
quotes.t: List of literally false statements in the Bible

quotes.c: What I learned, even when reading Christian scholars, shocked me . The gospels were written decades after Jesus' death, by non-eyewitnesses. They are riddled with contradictions, legends, and known lies. Jesus and Paul disagreed on many core issues. And how could I accept miracle claims about Jesus when I outright rejected other ancient miracle claims as superstitious nonsense?
quotes.m: And how could I accept miracle claims about Jesus when I outright rejected other ancient miracle claims as superstitious nonsense?
quotes.sum: The author describes rejecting Christianity after applying the same skeptical standards to its miracle claims that they applied to other religions' claims.
quotes.t: A Rationalist's Tale

quotes.c: We're trying to reduce existential risk -- to increase the odds that an eventual Singularity is good, from the perspective of humane values. To do this, we need more rational, effective people -- people who can train to do the needed research, who can fund that or other work, and who can otherwise exert influence toward good outcomes.
quotes.m: To do this, we need more rational, effective people -- people who can train to do the needed research, who can fund that or other work, and who can otherwise exert influence toward good outcomes.
quotes.sum: The author says reducing existential risk requires cultivating rational, effective people who can research, fund, and influence a humane technological future.
quotes.t: Mini-camp on Rationality, Awesomeness, and Existential Risk (May 28 through June 4, 2011)

quotes.c: Nevertheless, it seems quite reasonable to write Bayesian algorithms, and indeed to expect them to perform optimally on average. But can we formalize and prove a result along these lines? Does someone know of existing work in this direction?
quotes.m: Nevertheless, it seems quite reasonable to write Bayesian algorithms, and indeed to expect them to perform optimally on average.
quotes.sum: The author suggests Bayesian algorithms should perform best on average and asks whether this can be formally proved.
quotes.t: rationality for turing machines

quotes.c: Of course, if we have global government, its main goal should be prevention of global catastrophe. But we do not have global government and most people hate the idea. I find it irrational. But discussion about global goverment is pure theoretical one, because I do not see peaceful ways of its creation. If friendly AI take over the world ve will became global government de facto.
quotes.m: If friendly AI take over the world ve will became global government de facto.
quotes.sum: The author argues that opposition to world government is irrational and suggests a friendly AI taking over could create one in practice.
quotes.t: [MORESAFE] Prevention of the global catastrophe and human values

quotes.c: It would be really convenient if rationality, the meme-cluster that we most enjoy and are best-equipped to participate in, also happened to be the best for winning at life. In case it turns out that life is not quite so convenient, maybe we should be a little humbler about our grand experiment. Even if we have good reason to assert that mainstream religious thinking is flawed, maybe we should be slower to advise people to give up the health benefits (footnote 15) of belonging, emotionally, to one or another religious community.
quotes.m: maybe we should be slower to advise people to give up the health benefits (footnote 15) of belonging, emotionally, to one or another religious community.
quotes.sum: The author argues that rationalists should be humbler and not casually urge people to leave religious communities that provide belonging and health benefits.
quotes.t: An Outside View on Less Wrong's Advice

quotes.c: But hold on. Even a moral code defined in terms of the preferences of Washoe the chimpanzee is objective3. So not only is Bill's claim that only God-based morality can be objective3 false (because Harris' moral theory is also objective3), but also it's trivially easy to come up with a moral theory that is 'objective' in Craig's (apparent) sense of the term (that is, objective3).
quotes.m: Even a moral code defined in terms of the preferences of Washoe the chimpanzee is objective3.
quotes.sum: The author argues that defining morality through God does not uniquely make it objective, because any fixed preference-based moral code could qualify.
quotes.t: Pluralistic Moral Reductionism

quotes.c: I think it might be a valuable exercise to spend an hour practicing rationalist mindfulness, constantly asking yourself, "What am I currently doing that is not rational?" as though you had to find something to fulfill your obligation to an LW meetup.
quotes.m: "What am I currently doing that is not rational?"
quotes.sum: He recommends repeatedly questioning your own actions to identify what you are doing irrationally.
quotes.t: Constantly ask what you're currently doing that is irrational

quotes.c: Death is something that still seems to be solidly in the hands of religious and spiritual types as a discussion topic. I’m hoping that this post (in addition to not being too rambling) can provide some impetus for people to challenge that in daily life.
quotes.m: Death is something that still seems to be solidly in the hands of religious and spiritual types as a discussion topic.
quotes.sum: The author argues that rationalist communities should offer open, nonreligious ways to discuss grief and support people after death.
quotes.t: Rationality, Community, and Death

quotes.c: This is the way the term "faith" is used by religious people when they argue against the primacy of reason, as demonstrated in these quotes , which is the context I am concerned with. (It's also the meaning used by atheists arguing against religious faith, eg. Sam Harris in The End of Faith .)
quotes.sum: The author distinguishes religious faith from reason, focusing on uses of faith that reject reason's primacy.
quotes.t: Faith and theory

quotes.c: Real life is not a morality tale, and I don't know if I'd prophesy that the instant you get too much awesome and not enough rationality, the group will be punished for that sin by going off and trying to read auras. But I think I would prophesy that if you got too large and insufficiently reasonable, and if you lost sight of your higher purposes and your dreams of world optimization, the first major speedbump you hit would splinter the group.
quotes.m: if you got too large and insufficiently reasonable, and if you lost sight of your higher purposes and your dreams of world optimization, the first major speedbump you hit would splinter the group.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that a growing rationalist group needs to retain reason and ambitious world-improving goals or it will fracture under pressure.
quotes.t: Epistle to the New York Less Wrongians

quotes.c: Imagine you’re at a Less Wrong meetup when out of nowhere Eliezer Yudkowsky proposes his torture versus dust specks problem . Years of bullet-biting make this a trivial dilemma for any good philosopher, but suddenly you have a seizure during which you vividly recall all of those history lessons where you learned about the horrible things people do when they feel justified in being blatantly evil because of some abstract moral theory that is at best an approximation of sane morality and at worst an obviously anti-epistemic spiral of moral rationalization.
quotes.m: the horrible things people do when they feel justified in being blatantly evil because of some abstract moral theory
quotes.sum: The author warns that abstract moral theories and habitual “bullet-biting” can rationalize plainly evil actions.
quotes.t: Metacontrarian Metaethics

quotes.c: For those associated with primarily religious communities (still or in the past), do you have any suggestions about how to engage on-the-fly discussions? For example, I've thought than an elevator-pitch about my non-belief would be helpful... but I have found that previous conversations almost always degrade into pointless debate. How might I clearly express my stance while avoiding the pitfall of purposeless ruffled feathers?
quotes.m: How might I clearly express my stance while avoiding the pitfall of purposeless ruffled feathers?
quotes.sum: A recent nonbeliever asks how to discuss leaving religion with religious acquaintances without turning conversations into unproductive arguments.
quotes.t: Recent de-convert saturated by religious community; advice?

quotes.c: Person 1: According to model A (e.g. some Fermi calculation with probabilities coming from certain reference classes), pursuing course of action X will reduce existential risk by 10 -5 ; existential risk has an opportunity cost of 10 25 DALYs (*), therefore model A says the expected value of pursuing course of action X is 10 20 DALYs. Since course of action X requires 10 9 dollars, the number of DALYs saved per dollar invested in course of action X is 10 11 . Hence course of action X is 10 10 times as cost-effective as the most cost-effective health interventions in the developing world.
quotes.m: Hence course of action X is 10 10 times as cost-effective as the most cost-effective health interventions in the developing world.
quotes.sum: A speculative calculation says that reducing tiny existential risks can appear vastly more cost-effective than global-health aid.
quotes.t: Model Uncertainty, Pascalian Reasoning and Utilitarianism

quotes.c: Wow, 5%!?! If I convert that into "There is a 5% probability that the God of the Bible exists and will send me to hell" , I feel scared. But I know how to cheer myself up: I just say, "No way, the chance I'll end up in hell MUST be less than 5%. After all, the God of the Bible is CLEARLY just a big, mean alpha-monkey and... [ rehearse all the atheistic arguments here ]" .
quotes.m: "There is a 5% probability that the God of the Bible exists and will send me to hell" , I feel scared.
quotes.sum: The author reflects on assigning probabilities to atheism and how even a small chance of biblical hell feels emotionally frightening.
quotes.t: How confident is your atheism?

quotes.c: Tim McGrew, author of this excellent annotated bibliography on Bayesian reasoning , recently co-authored with his wife Lydia a Bayesian defense of the resurrection of Jesus . I interviewed Lydia for my podcast, here . Atheist Richard Carrier has leveled some objections to their article, but his objections are weak .
quotes.m: Atheist Richard Carrier has leveled some objections to their article, but his objections are weak .
quotes.sum: The author endorses a Bayesian argument for Jesus's resurrection and dismisses an atheist critic's objections.
quotes.t: A Bayesian Argument for the Resurrection of Jesus

quotes.c: Does anyone know of work that attempts to build a theorem prover by learning-from-examples? I'm imagining extracting a large corpus of theorems from back issues of mathematical journals, then applying unsupervised structure discovery techniques from machine learning to discover recurring patterns.
quotes.m: I'm imagining extracting a large corpus of theorems from back issues of mathematical journals, then applying unsupervised structure discovery techniques from machine learning to discover recurring patterns.
quotes.sum: The author asks whether theorem proving could be automated by learning recurring structures from a large corpus of published mathematical proofs.
quotes.t: Automated theorem proving by learning from examples

quotes.c: So it seems that, if we maximize expected total utility with time discounting, we need not even consider expansion beyond our planet. Even the inevitable extinction of all life in the Universe from being restricted to one planet scarcely matters in any rational utility calculation.
quotes.m: Even the inevitable extinction of all life in the Universe from being restricted to one planet scarcely matters in any rational utility calculation.
quotes.sum: The author argues that discounting future utility can make even universal extinction seem insignificant in a rational calculation.
quotes.t: Rationalists don't care about the future

quotes.c: Interesting to reconsider the events of " To lead, you must stand up " in this light. It makes more sense if you read it as "None of those people had instincts saying it was a good idea to declare themselves the leader of the monkey tribe, in order to solve this particular coordination problem where 'do nothing' felt like a viable option" instead of "nobody had the initiative".
quotes.sum: It argues that apparent passivity in a group may come from an instinct not to seize leadership, rather than a simple lack of initiative.
quotes.t: Are You a Paralyzed Subordinate Monkey?

quotes.c: Science has long questioned theism by examining design flaws in the nature. However, it seems to me that some science followers don't like being questioned about the scientific methodology. Just like theists don't like being questioned about existence of God.
quotes.m: some science followers don't like being questioned about the scientific methodology. Just like theists don't like being questioned about existence of God.
quotes.sum: The author argues that some defenders of science resist scrutiny of scientific methods much as theists resist questioning God.
quotes.t: Ideological bullies?

quotes.c: Suppose my results really are representative of most people’s intuitions. Something other than the large population of lives barely worth living makes the repugnant conclusion scenario repugnant. Depending on what it is, we might find that intuition more or less worth overruling. For instance if it is just a disrespect for lowly people, we might prefer to give it up.
quotes.m: For instance if it is just a disrespect for lowly people, we might prefer to give it up.
quotes.sum: The author argues that revulsion toward the “repugnant conclusion” may rest on contempt for people with modest wellbeing, and so may deserve to be discarded.
quotes.t: Mediocre masses are not what’s repugnant

quotes.c: One consideration is that FOOM hasn't already happened -- at least not here on Earth. If the smallest FOOM seed were very small (like a few hundred bytes) then we would expect evolution to have already bumped into it at some point. Although evolution is under no specific pressure to produce a FOOM, it has probably produced over the last few billion years all the interesting computations up to some minor level of complexity, and if there were a FOOM seed among those then we would see the results about us.
quotes.m: If the smallest FOOM seed were very small (like a few hundred bytes) then we would expect evolution to have already bumped into it at some point.
quotes.sum: The author argues that evolution's failure to produce an intelligence explosion suggests the smallest self-improving AI seed is not extremely simple.
quotes.t: Size of the smallest recursively self-improving AI?

quotes.c: First, consider the evangelical atheist community to which I belong . There is a tendency for lay atheists to write "refutations" of theism without first doing a modicum of research on the current state of the arguments. This can get atheists into trouble when they go toe-to-toe with a theist who did do his homework.
quotes.m: There is a tendency for lay atheists to write "refutations" of theism without first doing a modicum of research on the current state of the arguments.
quotes.sum: The author criticizes atheists who attack religious arguments without adequately researching them first.
quotes.t: The Neglected Virtue of Scholarship

quotes.c: Thus, for the past six months, several times a day, I've interrupted my thoughts and put them back on an “ask questions” track. (“Grrr, he said my argument was dishonest... Wait, is he right? What should it look like if he is?”; “I notice I feel hopeless about this paper writing. Maybe there’s something I should do differently?”) It's helping. I'm building the habit of interrupting myself when I'm "thinking" without trying to find something out, or taking actions that I expect won't accomplish anything.
quotes.m: I'm building the habit of interrupting myself when I'm "thinking" without trying to find something out, or taking actions that I expect won't accomplish anything.
quotes.sum: The author recommends deliberately turning unproductive reactions and rumination into concrete questions that could update beliefs or guide useful action.
quotes.t: Use curiosity

quotes.c: I think it's flinching away from the pain of the decision to do the work - the momentary, immediate pain of (1) disengaging yourself from the (probably very small) flow of reinforcement that you're getting from reading a random unimportant Internet article, and (2) paying the energy cost for a prefrontal override to exert control of your own behavior and begin working.
quotes.m: I think it's flinching away from the pain of the decision to do the work
quotes.sum: Procrastination comes from avoiding the immediate discomfort of starting work, even when working would be less painful overall.
quotes.t: Working hurts less than procrastinating, we fear the twinge of starting

quotes.c: Nevertheless, I find it compelling to say that I became a skeptic (and from there a rationalist and consequentialist) because from an early age I attended two different religious schools at the same time.
quotes.m: I became a skeptic (and from there a rationalist and consequentialist) because from an early age I attended two different religious schools at the same time.
quotes.sum: The author says being educated in both Christian and Jewish settings led them toward skepticism, rationalism, and consequentialism.
quotes.t: The Benefits of Two Religious Educations

quotes.c: Shouldn't we focus on engineered/controlled value drift rather than preventing it entirely? is that possible to program into an AI? somehow I don't think so. It seems to me that the whole premise of a single benevolent AI depends to a large extent on the similarity of basic human drives, supposedly we're so close to each other it's not a big deal to prevent value drift.
quotes.m: the whole premise of a single benevolent AI depends to a large extent on the similarity of basic human drives
quotes.sum: The author doubts that AI value drift can be deliberately controlled and questions whether a single benevolent AI could rely on shared human motivations.
quotes.t: wireless-heading, value drift and so on

quotes.c: The third and fourth explanations fit well with my experiences. My existential angst didn't fade until I purged my brain's religious cobwebs and started improving my life. These things happened at about the same time, so I can't tell whether three or four fits better.
quotes.m: My existential angst didn't fade until I purged my brain's religious cobwebs and started improving my life.
quotes.sum: The author says abandoning religious beliefs, alongside improving their life, relieved their existential anxiety.
quotes.t: The Meaning of Life

quotes.c: Most of the time, your objective in communicating is to reduce ambiguity. You lay out your thoughts in order, package them securely, and hope that they survive however many translations it takes until they can be reassembled in the same order inside someone else's mind. A word that means more than one thing is, in that context, a navigational hazard; it has too many degrees of freedom, so more information must be included to constrain it, lock in the single intended meaning. Unintended potential interpretations are dangerous noise.
quotes.m: Unintended potential interpretations are dangerous noise.
quotes.sum: The author says ordinary communication aims to eliminate ambiguity so the listener reconstructs exactly the intended meaning.
quotes.t: Write It Like A Poem

quotes.c: I personally would never litter on purpose, yet I often skip voting because it seems like it doesn't make a difference. Is voting rational? How do you justify voting or not voting? My post was non-partisan so I'm soliciting non-partisan comments, trying to focus on the theory behind voting in general.
quotes.m: Is voting rational? How do you justify voting or not voting?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether voting is rational when one person's vote seems unlikely to affect the outcome.
quotes.t: Why should you vote?

quotes.c: Try to be precise in your propositions. Saying "I believe in God. 99% sure." isn't informative because we don't quite know which God you're talking about. A deist god? The Christian God? Jewish?
quotes.m: Saying "I believe in God. 99% sure." isn't informative because we don't quite know which God you're talking about.
quotes.sum: The author argues that confidence claims about God are meaningless unless the specific proposition is defined precisely.
quotes.t: The Irrationality Game

quotes.c: I.e., Eliezer's posts describe parts of an art for cases such as "free will" in which the initial question is confused, and must be dissolved rather than answered. He also notes the virtue of sustained effort .
quotes.m: the initial question is confused, and must be dissolved rather than answered.
quotes.sum: The author says some philosophical questions, such as free will, are confused and should be dissolved rather than answered.
quotes.t: Branches of rationality

quotes.c: Such risk-avoidant goals would, I think, be more likely to be achieved by averaging (although I haven't done the math). But they do not maximize expected utility. They suffer risk-avoidance bias, by construction.
quotes.m: But they do not maximize expected utility.
quotes.sum: The author argues that averaging values may reduce risk but is biased because it does not maximize expected utility.
quotes.t: Averaging value systems is worse than choosing one

quotes.c: It seems that one disguised empirical question scientists are asking, when they ask “Is X real, or just a handy predictive device?” is the question: “will I still get accurate predictions, when I use X in a less circumscribed or compartmentalized manner?”
quotes.m: “will I still get accurate predictions, when I use X in a less circumscribed or compartmentalized manner?”
quotes.sum: Scientific claims that something is real can be tested by whether the concept keeps making accurate predictions beyond its original, narrow use.
quotes.t: Were atoms real?

quotes.c: I argue that many techniques for epistemic rationality, as taught on LW, amount to techniques for reducing compartmentalization. I argue further that when these same techniques are extended to a larger portion of the mind, they boost instrumental, as well as epistemic, rationality.
quotes.m: when these same techniques are extended to a larger portion of the mind, they boost instrumental, as well as epistemic, rationality.
quotes.sum: The author argues that reducing mental compartmentalization improves both accurate beliefs and practical decision-making.
quotes.t: Compartmentalization in epistemic and instrumental rationality

quotes.c: But it seems like explicitly modeling when your friend is and isn't accurate, and when explicit models have and haven't led you to good actions, should at least help.
quotes.m: explicitly modeling when your friend is and isn't accurate, and when explicit models have and haven't led you to good actions, should at least help.
quotes.sum: Explicitly tracking when people and reasoning models have been accurate may improve judgment.
quotes.t: Making your explicit reasoning trustworthy

quotes.c: I agree with SarahC’s point that humans seem predisposed to impute essences everywhere. Still, discussions about whether there’s a magical essence “free will” seem to pop up more often than discussions about whether there’s a magical essence “carpet”, “ocean”, “California”, or “female”. I mean, folks are interested in these other questions, and they have discussions about what meaning to use and how much that meaning cleaves nature at its joints, but they don’t generally expect a separate sort of essence that has causal powers and isn’t made out of atoms.
quotes.m: folks are interested in these other questions, and they have discussions about what meaning to use and how much that meaning cleaves nature at its joints, but they don’t generally expect a separate sort of essence that has causal powers and isn’t made out of atoms.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people wrongly treat free will as a special nonphysical essence, unlike ordinary concepts whose meanings can be analyzed without invoking magic.
quotes.t: If reductionism is the hammer, what nails are out there?

quotes.c: The American Anthropological Association has apparently decided to ditch the word "science", arguably so they can promote political messages without hindrance from empirical data.
quotes.m: The American Anthropological Association has apparently decided to ditch the word "science", arguably so they can promote political messages without hindrance from empirical data.
quotes.sum: The author argues that an anthropology association may be abandoning science in order to promote political messages without empirical constraints.
quotes.t: Anthropologists and "science": dark side epistemology?

quotes.c: Christopher Hitchens is probably dying of cancer. Hitchens is a well known author, journalist and militant atheist. Having read much of his work I believe he is also a very high IQ rationalist who enjoys being provocative.
quotes.m: Hitchens is a well known author, journalist and militant atheist.
quotes.sum: The author frames the dying atheist Christopher Hitchens as a provocative, high-IQ rationalist seeking advanced medical advice.
quotes.t: Christopher Hitchens and Cryonics

quotes.c: Religious discrimination is illegal in many parts of the world, and I think that's probably a good thing. Still, keeping this at the object level (no meta-rules or veils of ignorance) it seems to me that discriminating against religious people is fine. I'm curious what other people think.
quotes.m: it seems to me that discriminating against religious people is fine.
quotes.sum: The author says that, despite supporting legal protections, they think discrimination against religious people can be acceptable when judged directly rather than by general rules.
quotes.t: A hypothetical candidate walks into a hypothetical job interview...

quotes.c: I'm writing a paper on how simple or complicated intelligence is, and what implications that has for AI forecasting. In that context: adopt Shane Legg's measure of intelligence (i.e., let "intelligence" measure a system's average goal-achievement across the different "universe" programs that might be causing it to win or not win reward at each time step, weighted according to the universe program's simplicity).
quotes.m: I'm writing a paper on how simple or complicated intelligence is, and what implications that has for AI forecasting.
quotes.sum: The author proposes using a formal, simplicity-weighted definition of intelligence to study what intelligence means for AI forecasts.
quotes.t: Help request: What is the Kolmogorov complexity of computable approximations to AIXI?

quotes.c: Because I take astronomical waste seriously and believe in shutting up and multiplying, I believe that reducing existential risk is ultimately more important than developing world aid. I would very much like it if there were a highly credible existential risk charity.
quotes.m: I believe that reducing existential risk is ultimately more important than developing world aid.
quotes.sum: The author argues that preventing existential catastrophe matters more than aid to people in the developing world, based on expected-value reasoning about the far future.
quotes.t: Transparency and Accountability

quotes.c: Jim wanted to get his act together and really help the world, not diddle around reading shiny-fun blog comments. But his discussion of how to “really help the world” seemed to me to contain a number of errors[1] -- errors enough that, if he cannot sort them out somehow, his total impact won’t be nearly what it could be. And they were the sort of errors LW could have helped with.
quotes.m: And they were the sort of errors LW could have helped with.
quotes.sum: The author argues that LessWrong can help people identify reasoning errors that would otherwise limit how much good they do.
quotes.t: Goals for which Less Wrong does (and doesn't) help

quotes.c: I'm writing the section of the rationality book dealing with hindsight bias, and I'd like to write my own, less racially charged and less America-specific, version of the Hindsight Devalues Science example - in the original, facts like "Better educated soldiers suffered more adjustment problems than less educated soldiers. (Intellectuals were less prepared for battle stresses than street-smart people.)" which is actually an inverted version of the truth, that still sounds plausible enough that people will try to explain it even though it's wrong.
quotes.m: which is actually an inverted version of the truth, that still sounds plausible enough that people will try to explain it even though it's wrong.
quotes.sum: He seeks plausible-sounding false claims to illustrate hindsight bias: people readily invent explanations for claims that fit expectations even when they are wrong.
quotes.t: Request:  Interesting Invertible Facts

quotes.c: Many folk here on LW take the simulation argument (in its more general forms) seriously. Many others take Singularitarianism 1 seriously. Still others take Tegmark cosmology (and related big universe hypotheses) seriously. But then I see them proceed to self-describe as atheist (instead of omnitheist, theist, deist, having a predictive distribution over states of religious belief, et cetera), and many tend to be overtly dismissive of theism.
quotes.m: But then I see them proceed to self-describe as atheist (instead of omnitheist, theist, deist, having a predictive distribution over states of religious belief, et cetera), and many tend to be overtly dismissive of theism.
quotes.sum: The author questions why people open to speculative cosmology still identify firmly as atheists and dismiss theism.
quotes.t: Theists are wrong; is theism?

quotes.c: To illustrate thought structuring, I use the example of Edward de Bono's " six thinking hats " mnemonic. With Edward de Bono's "six thinking hats" method you metaphorically put on various colored "hats" (perspectives) and switch "hats" depending on the task.
quotes.m: With Edward de Bono's "six thinking hats" method you metaphorically put on various colored "hats" (perspectives) and switch "hats" depending on the task.
quotes.sum: The author presents the “six thinking hats” method as a way to structure reasoning by deliberately switching perspectives.
quotes.t: Sequential Organization of Thinking: "Six Thinking Hats"

quotes.c: College fraternity brothers are, on the whole, not the most rational of people. (I say this as a current Yale student.) Rationalists are supposed to win . DKE is clearly winning; the members of DKE are collectively far more powerful than the entire atheist movement, despite having far fewer members. What is going on here?
quotes.m: DKE is clearly winning; the members of DKE are collectively far more powerful than the entire atheist movement, despite having far fewer members.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a cohesive Yale fraternity has more collective power than a much larger atheist movement, challenging the idea that rational people naturally prevail.
quotes.t: How Irrationality Can Win: The Power of Group Cohesion

quotes.c: "Wrong", you say, "no new information has been injected here, I have simply pointed out how to reason rationally. Two rational agents cannot take the same information and arrive at different probability assignments, and thinking clearly does not constitute new information. Your previous estimate was irrational, full stop."
quotes.sum: The author presents a strict rationalist view: agents with the same information should reach the same probability judgments.
quotes.t: When does an insight count as evidence?

quotes.c: In absence of further context, the beliefs of somebody coming from a very different worldview inevitably seem absurd independently of whether or not they're well grounded.
quotes.m: the beliefs of somebody coming from a very different worldview inevitably seem absurd independently of whether or not they're well grounded.
quotes.sum: People often dismiss beliefs from very different worldviews as absurd before understanding the reasoning behind them.
quotes.t: Reflections on a Personal Public Relations Failure: A Lesson in Communication

quotes.c: According to Christianity, belief makes you stronger and better. The Bible claims that people who believe are substantially better off both while living and after death. So if a self modifying decision maker decides for a second that the Christian faith is accurate, won't he modify his decision making algorithm to never doubt the truth of Christianity? Given what he knows, it is the best decision.
quotes.m: So if a self modifying decision maker decides for a second that the Christian faith is accurate, won't he modify his decision making algorithm to never doubt the truth of Christianity?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether a self-modifying AI that briefly accepts Christianity would rationally alter itself so it can never question that belief.
quotes.t: Question about self modifying AI getting "stuck" in religion

quotes.c: Does it matter if you experienced pain in the past, but you don't remember? (And there are no other side-effects, etc etc). At one point in Accelerando , Charles Strauss describes children that routinely decapitate and disembowel each other, only to be repaired (bodily and memory-wise) by the friendly local AI. This struck me as awful, but I'm suspicious of my intuition.
quotes.m: This struck me as awful, but I'm suspicious of my intuition.
quotes.sum: The author argues that pain remains bad even if it is later erased from memory, while questioning how much to trust that intuition.
quotes.t: Does it matter if you don't remember?

quotes.c: Now, is there a God? Your answer should be of the form "My estimate of the likelihood that there is a God is X%". Don't style yourself as an atheist, believer, or agnostic. Assess the evidence at your disposal (science, scriptures, what you where told…), then give your number.
quotes.m: Don't style yourself as an atheist, believer, or agnostic. Assess the evidence at your disposal (science, scriptures, what you where told…), then give your number.
quotes.sum: The author argues that belief in God should be expressed as a numerical probability based on evidence, rather than as a religious identity.
quotes.t: "Is there a God" for noobs

quotes.c: It’s been argued before that we like to say ‘ sacred values ‘ like human life are infinitely valuable. Ascribing infinite value to something that you don’t really sacrifice everything for risks being too obviously hypocritical. Do we claim ineffability to hide this hypocrisy?
quotes.m: Ascribing infinite value to something that you don’t really sacrifice everything for risks being too obviously hypocritical.
quotes.sum: The author questions whether calling human life infinitely valuable conceals a gap between stated sacred values and actual willingness to sacrifice.
quotes.t: Why is reductionism rude?

quotes.c: Since truth doesn’t depend on who is asking -- and since our feelings about the truth often do depend -- it can help to ask what an outside observer would say. Instead of asking “Am I right in this dispute with my friend?” ask: “If I observed this from the outside, and saw someone with my track record and skillset, and someone else with my friend’s track record and skillset, disagreeing in this manner -- who would I think was probably right?”.
quotes.m: Since truth doesn’t depend on who is asking -- and since our feelings about the truth often do depend -- it can help to ask what an outside observer would say.
quotes.sum: The author argues that disagreements should be evaluated from an outside view of each person's track record, rather than through personal feelings of being right.
quotes.t: Navigating disagreement: How to keep your eye on the evidence

quotes.c: Now to contrast with my non-religious friends; this isn’t universally true, but I’ve seen a trend of general negative-ness. This attitude can be self-directed, i.e. complaining about work or school or relationships without any effort to find solutions. I know some very unhappy people, and it seems insane to me that they just sit back and take it, month after month. The negative attitude can also be directed outwards into biting sarcasm and rude, judgemental comments about others. This often comes from people who seem happy enough with their own lives. Maybe I didn’t notice this as much before I started going to church, where it became obvious in its absence.
quotes.m: Maybe I didn’t notice this as much before I started going to church, where it became obvious in its absence.
quotes.sum: The author says nonreligious acquaintances seem more negative and contrasts this with the more positive atmosphere they perceive at church.
quotes.t: Positive Thinking

quotes.c: This brings be all the way back to the much-loved quotation, "that which can be destroyed by the truth should be". Now there are several ways to interpret the quote but at least one interpretation implies the existence of a simple isomorphism from true beliefs to good decisions. Personally, I can think of lots of things that could be destroyed by the truth but should not be.
quotes.m: Personally, I can think of lots of things that could be destroyed by the truth but should not be.
quotes.sum: The author rejects the idea that true beliefs automatically produce good decisions, arguing that some things truth could destroy should be preserved.
quotes.t: That which can be destroyed by the truth should *not* necessarily be

quotes.c: “Empirical tests” here can include your own direct observations, friends’ anecdotes, published controlled studies, and anything else in the world that should look different, if [received wisdom / your own impression] is true. Many folks just throw up their hands or take a vote when they see folks that disagree with one another; but sorting out the evidence is a learnable skill.
quotes.m: Many folks just throw up their hands or take a vote when they see folks that disagree with one another; but sorting out the evidence is a learnable skill.
