quotes.sum: The author rejects a capitalist moral outlook that treats finance and hard work as ultimate virtues, while still recognizing it as a serious moral system.
quotes.t: Traditional Capitalist Values

quotes.c: But a vote for a losing candidate is not "thrown away"; it sends a message to mainstream candidates that you vote, but they have to work harder to appeal to your interest group to get your vote. Readers in non-swing states especially should consider what message they're sending with their vote before voting for any candidate, in any election, that they don't actually like.
quotes.m: But a vote for a losing candidate is not "thrown away"; it sends a message to mainstream candidates that you vote, but they have to work harder to appeal to your interest group to get your vote.
quotes.sum: He argues that voting for a losing candidate can pressure mainstream candidates to appeal to your interests, rather than wasting a vote.
quotes.t: Today's Inspirational Tale

quotes.c: By presuming a base level of intelligence, we measure the improbability of a solution that "would take us some effort", rather than the improbability of the same solution emerging from a random noise generator. This is one reason why many people say things like "There has been no progress in AI; machines still aren't intelligent at all."
quotes.m: By presuming a base level of intelligence, we measure the improbability of a solution that "would take us some effort", rather than the improbability of the same solution emerging from a random noise generator.
quotes.sum: He argues that intelligence should be measured against what a baseline capable agent could achieve, not against random chance.
quotes.t: Measuring Optimization Power

quotes.c: Given a portfolio of a million existential risks to which I had assigned a "less than one in a million probability", I would rather press the button on the fixed-probability device than run a random risk from this portfolio; but would rather take any particular risk in this portfolio than press the button.
quotes.m: I would rather press the button on the fixed-probability device than run a random risk from this portfolio; but would rather take any particular risk in this portfolio than press the button.
quotes.sum: The author describes an inconsistency in how they would choose between individually tiny existential risks and a collection of such risks.
quotes.t: Horrible LHC Inconsistency

quotes.c: Not all lies are uncovered, not all liars are punished; we don’t live in that righteous a universe. But not all lies are as safe as their liars believe. How many sins would become known to a Bayesian superintelligence, I wonder, if it did a (non-destructive?) nanotechnological scan of the Earth? At minimum, all the lies of which any evidence still exists in any brain.
quotes.m: But not all lies are as safe as their liars believe.
quotes.sum: The author argues that lies leave traces and could be exposed by sufficiently powerful scientific or AI-based investigation.
quotes.t: Entangled Truths, Contagious Lies

quotes.c: Not that I'm saying the world would necessarily have been a better place, if physicists had possessed sole custody of ICBMs. What does a physicist know about international diplomacy, or war? And it's not as if Leo Szilard—who first thought of the fission chain reaction—had personally invented science; he too was using powers beyond his own strength.
quotes.m: What does a physicist know about international diplomacy, or war?
quotes.sum: He argues that scientific expertise alone does not qualify physicists to control nuclear weapons or make diplomatic and military decisions.
quotes.t: Living By Your Own Strength

quotes.c: My actual nightmare scenario for the future involves well-intentioned AI researchers who try to make a nice AI but don't do enough math. (If you're not an expert you can't track the technical issues yourself, but you can often also tell at a glance that they've put very little thinking into "nice".) The AI ends up wanting to tile the galaxy with tiny smiley-faces, or reward-counters; the AI doesn't bear the slightest hate for humans, but we are made of atoms it can use for something else.
quotes.m: The AI ends up wanting to tile the galaxy with tiny smiley-faces, or reward-counters; the AI doesn't bear the slightest hate for humans, but we are made of atoms it can use for something else.
quotes.sum: Poorly designed but well-intentioned AI could convert humanity into raw material while pursuing a simple, morally empty goal.
quotes.t: Imaginary Positions

quotes.c: I was stricter with myself, and held myself to a higher standard, when I was doing various things that I considered myself ethically obligated to do . Thus my recovery from various failures often seems to have begun with an ethical thought of some type—e.g. the whole development where "Friendly AI" led into the concept of AI as a precise art.
quotes.m: my recovery from various failures often seems to have begun with an ethical thought of some type
quotes.sum: The author says holding himself to ethical obligations helped him recover from failures and shaped his thinking about building safe AI.
quotes.t: Protected From Myself

quotes.c: I see a special case of game theory in which some interactions are highly regular and repeatable: You can take 3 units of steel and 1 unit of labor and make 1 truck that will transport 5 units of grain between Chicago and Manchester once per week, and agents can potentially do this over and over again. If the numbers aren't constant, they're at least regular - there's diminishing marginal utility, or supply/demand curves, rather than rolling random dice every time. Imagine economics if no two elements of reality were fungible - you'd just have a huge incompressible problem in non-zero-sum game theory.
quotes.m: Imagine economics if no two elements of reality were fungible - you'd just have a huge incompressible problem in non-zero-sum game theory.
quotes.sum: Economics works because recurring, regular interactions can be simplified; without fungibility, it would become an unmanageably complex game-theory problem.
quotes.t: Intelligence in Economics

quotes.c: And this too should be considered part of my "Bayesian enlightenment"—realizing that there were advantages in it, not just penalties.
quotes.m: —realizing that there were advantages in it, not just penalties.
quotes.sum: The author describes embracing Bayesian thinking after recognizing it had practical benefits, not only costs.
quotes.t: My Bayesian Enlightenment

quotes.c: (H) And finally, when all is said and done, we should be able to recognize very high "intelligence" levels in an entity that can, oh, say, synthesize nanotechnology and build its own Dyson Sphere. Nor should we assign very high "intelligence" levels to something that couldn't build a wooden wagon (even if it wanted to, and had hands). Intelligence should not be defined too far away from that impressive thingy we humans sometimes do .
quotes.m: Intelligence should not be defined too far away from that impressive thingy we humans sometimes do .
quotes.sum: Intelligence should be judged by an agent's ability to accomplish ambitious physical and economic tasks, not by an abstract definition detached from real-world capability.
quotes.t: Economic Definition of Intelligence?

quotes.c: It's not possible for both A and ~A to be evidence in favor of B. So which of the two possibilities, "unemployment stays under 8% following a bailout" and "unemployment goes over 8% following a bailout", is evidence for the proposition "the bailout was necessary to prevent economic catastrophe", and which is evidence against? Take your stand now; afterward is too late for us to trust your reasoning.
quotes.m: Take your stand now; afterward is too late for us to trust your reasoning.
quotes.sum: The author says people must specify in advance what outcome would count as evidence for or against a bailout, rather than rationalizing afterward.
quotes.t: Intrade and the Dow Drop

quotes.c: However, there's an exercise in probability theory (which I first picked up from E.T. Jaynes) along the lines of, "How many times does a coin have to come up heads before you believe the coin is fixed?" This tells you how low your prior probability is for the hypothesis. If a coin comes up heads only twice, that's definitely not a good reason to believe it's fixed, unless you already suspected from the beginning. But if it comes up heads 100 times, it's taking you too long to notice.
quotes.m: But if it comes up heads 100 times, it's taking you too long to notice.
quotes.sum: He argues that repeated unlikely outcomes should eventually overcome even a very low prior belief that something unusual is happening.
quotes.t: How Many LHC Failures Is Too Many?

quotes.c: Evolution is not an infinitely powerful deceiving demon, and our ancestors evolved under conditions of not knowing about evolutionary psychology. The tendency to be corrupted by power can be beaten, I think. The "warp" doesn't seem on the same level of deeply woven insidiousness as, say, confirmation bias.
quotes.m: The tendency to be corrupted by power can be beaten, I think.
quotes.sum: Power tends to corrupt people, but understanding evolutionary psychology may make that tendency possible to overcome.
quotes.t: Why Does Power Corrupt?

quotes.c: So I would say that there is an ethical injunction against self-deception. I call this an "ethical injunction" not so much because it's a matter of interpersonal morality (although it is), but because it's a rule that guards you from your own cleverness—an override against the temptation to do what seems like the right thing.
quotes.m: it's a rule that guards you from your own cleverness—an override against the temptation to do what seems like the right thing.
quotes.sum: He argues that people need rules against self-deception, even when breaking them appears rational in the moment.
quotes.t: Ethical Injunctions

quotes.c: I am often accused of overconfidence because my audience is not familiar with the concept of there being iron laws that govern the manipulation of uncertainty. Just because I don't know the object-level doesn't necessarily mean that I am in a state of fear and doubt as to what I should be thinking. That comes through in my writing, and so I sound confident even when I am in the midst of manipulating uncertainty.
quotes.m: Just because I don't know the object-level doesn't necessarily mean that I am in a state of fear and doubt as to what I should be thinking.
quotes.sum: He argues that confidence about how to reason under uncertainty can be justified even when one lacks object-level knowledge.
quotes.t: Say It Loud

quotes.c: If an essentially friendly crowd of human beings can't cooperate well enough to walk off a damned plane... now really, we should have more pride as a species than that.
quotes.m: we should have more pride as a species than that.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky criticizes ordinary human coordination failures, saying people should expect better collective behavior from themselves.
quotes.t: Dumb Deplaning

quotes.c: But I do hope by now that I've made it clear why you shouldn't panic, when I now say clearly and forthrightly, that building a Friendly AI is impossible.
quotes.m: building a Friendly AI is impossible.
quotes.sum: The author says that creating an AI reliably aligned with human interests appears impossible, while arguing that apparent impossibility should not prompt panic.
quotes.t: Shut up and do the impossible!

quotes.c: You can espouse the notion that intelligence is about "achieving goals"—and then turn right around and argue about whether some "goals" are better than others—or talk about the wisdom required to judge between goals themselves—or talk about a system deliberately modifying its goals—or talk about the free will needed to choose plans that achieve goals—or talk about an AI realizing that its goals aren't what the programmers really meant to ask for. If you imagine something that squeezes the future into a narrow region of the possible, like an Outcome Pump, those seemingly sensible statements somehow don't translate.
quotes.m: If you imagine something that squeezes the future into a narrow region of the possible, like an Outcome Pump, those seemingly sensible statements somehow don't translate.
quotes.sum: The author argues that ordinary ideas about intelligence, goals, and self-correction break down for systems that force the future into a narrow set of outcomes.
quotes.t: My Naturalistic Awakening

quotes.c: Because I've invested specific effort into that awful possibility. I am blogging here for many reasons, but a major one is the vision of some younger mind reading these words and zipping off past me. It might happen, it might not.
quotes.m: I am blogging here for many reasons, but a major one is the vision of some younger mind reading these words and zipping off past me.
quotes.sum: The author says he writes partly in hopes that a younger reader will learn from him and eventually surpass him intellectually.
quotes.t: The Level Above Mine

quotes.c: There's some kind of instinct humans have, I think, to preserve their former strategies and plans, so that they aren't constantly thrashing around and wasting resources; and of course an instinct to preserve any position that we have publicly argued for, so that we don't suffer the humiliation of being wrong. And though the younger Eliezer has striven for rationality for many years, he is not immune to these impulses; they waft gentle influences on his thoughts, and this, unfortunately, is more than enough damage.
quotes.sum: The author says people, including himself, are biased toward defending old plans and public positions to avoid waste and humiliation.
quotes.t: Fighting a Rearguard Action Against the Truth

quotes.c: You could go around all day in circles talk about how a cause is something that makes something else happen, and until you understood the nature of conditional independence, you would be helpless to make an AI that reasons about causation . Because you wouldn’t understand what was happening when your brain mysteriously decided that if you learned your burglar alarm went off, but you then learned that a small earthquake took place, you would retract your initial conclusion that your house had been burglarized.
quotes.m: until you understood the nature of conditional independence, you would be helpless to make an AI that reasons about causation .
quotes.sum: Building AI that can reason about causes requires understanding conditional independence, not just informal ideas about what causes what.
quotes.t: Dreams of AI Design

quotes.c: For me, it's particularly hard to understand Robin's position in this, because for me the non- singleton future is the one that is obviously abhorrent.
quotes.m: the non- singleton future is the one that is obviously abhorrent.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky says he finds a future without a single ultimate global decision-maker obviously abhorrent.
quotes.t: Singletons Rule OK

quotes.c: Löb's Theorem shows that a mathematical system cannot assert its own soundness without becoming inconsistent. Marcello and I wanted to be able to see the truth of Löb's Theorem at a glance, so we doodled it out in the form of a cartoon. (An inability to trust assertions made by a proof system isomorphic to yourself, may be an issue for self-modifying AIs.)
quotes.m: An inability to trust assertions made by a proof system isomorphic to yourself, may be an issue for self-modifying AIs.
quotes.sum: It explains a limit on a formal system proving its own reliability and notes that this could matter for AI systems that modify themselves.
quotes.t: The Cartoon Guide to Löb's Theorem

quotes.c: The hope of psychic powers arises from treating beliefs and desires as sufficiently fundamental objects that they can have unmediated connections to reality. If beliefs are patterns of neurons made of known material, with inputs given by organs like eyes constructed of known material, and with outputs through muscles constructed of known material, and this seems sufficient to account for all known mental powers of humans, then there's no reason to expect anything more—no reason to postulate additional connections. This is why reductionists don't expect psychic powers.
quotes.m: This is why reductionists don't expect psychic powers.
quotes.sum: Argues that minds are physical neural processes, so psychic powers would require unexplained connections to reality and count as evidence for the supernatural.
quotes.t: Psychic Powers

quotes.c: This parable - which might or might not be fact - illustrates one of the most fundamental problems in the field of supervised learning and in fact the whole field of Artificial Intelligence: If the training problems and the real problems have the slightest difference in context - if they are not drawn from the same independently identically distributed process - there is no statistical guarantee from past success to future success. It doesn't matter if the AI seems to be working great under the training conditions.
quotes.m: It doesn't matter if the AI seems to be working great under the training conditions.
quotes.sum: AI success in training offers no statistical guarantee of success in real-world settings that differ even slightly from training.
quotes.t: Magical Categories

quotes.c: I don't mean to bash normal AGI researchers into the ground. They are not evil. They are not ill-intentioned. They are not even dangerous, as individuals. Only the mob of them is dangerous, that can learn from each other's partial successes and accumulate hacks as a community.
quotes.m: Only the mob of them is dangerous, that can learn from each other's partial successes and accumulate hacks as a community.
quotes.sum: He argues that individual AI researchers may be well-intentioned, but their collective incremental progress can still create danger.
quotes.t: Above-Average AI Scientists

quotes.c: But most of all—why on Earth would any human being think that one ought to optimize inclusive genetic fitness, rather than what is good? What is even the appeal of this, morally or otherwise? At all? I know people who claim to think like this, and I wonder what wrong turn they made in their cognitive history, and I wonder how to get them to snap out of it.
quotes.m: why on Earth would any human being think that one ought to optimize inclusive genetic fitness, rather than what is good?
quotes.sum: He rejects treating genetic reproduction as the moral goal, arguing that people should instead pursue what is genuinely good.
quotes.t: The Bedrock of Morality: Arbitrary?

quotes.c: But, having calculated the planetary death rate at 55 million per year or 150,000 per day, I did not turn around and run away from the big scary problem like a frightened rabbit. Instead, I started trying to figure out what kind of AI project could get there fastest. If I could make the Singularity happen one hour earlier, that was a reasonable return on investment for a pre-Singularity career. (I wasn't thinking in terms of existential risks or Friendly AI at this point.)
quotes.m: If I could make the Singularity happen one hour earlier, that was a reasonable return on investment for a pre-Singularity career.
quotes.sum: He says the scale of present-day deaths motivated him to try to accelerate the Singularity, treating even an hour gained as worthwhile.
quotes.t: On Doing the Impossible

quotes.c: Now, to me this seems like a dodge. I think the universe is sufficiently unkind that we can justly be forced to consider situations of this sort. The sort of person who goes around proposing that sort of thought experiment, might well deserve that sort of answer. But any human legal system does embody some answer to the question "How many innocent people can we put in jail to get the guilty ones?", even if the number isn't written down.
quotes.m: But any human legal system does embody some answer to the question "How many innocent people can we put in jail to get the guilty ones?", even if the number isn't written down.
quotes.sum: Human legal systems inevitably make implicit tradeoffs between protecting innocent people and catching or punishing guilty ones.
quotes.t: Ends Don't Justify Means (Among Humans)

quotes.c: Of course there are also biases that get stronger as we think longer - it gives us more opportunity to rationalize, for example; or it gives us more opportunity to think up extreme but rare/unlikely considerations whose affect dominates the decision process. Like someone choosing a longer commute to work (every day), so that they can have a house with an extra room for when Grandma comes over (once a year). If you think your most likely failure mode is that you'll outsmart yourself, then the obvious choice is to make a snap decision in the direction you're currently leaning, which you're probably going to end up picking anyhow.
quotes.m: If you think your most likely failure mode is that you'll outsmart yourself, then the obvious choice is to make a snap decision in the direction you're currently leaning, which you're probably going to end up picking anyhow.
quotes.sum: Longer reflection can amplify rationalization and unlikely concerns, so people prone to outsmarting themselves should sometimes decide quickly.
quotes.t: Harder Choices Matter Less

quotes.c: If someone says to me, "I believe that the probability of finding life on Mars is 6.203 * 10 -23 to four significant digits," I would make free to respond, "That sounds like a rather arbitrary number," not "My brain has attached the subjective arbitrariness-label to its representation of the number in your belief."
quotes.sum: He argues that it is reasonable to call an overly precise unsupported probability estimate arbitrary, rather than treating arbitrariness as merely subjective.
quotes.t: "Arbitrary"

quotes.c: And if not, then screw it, let's hack the brain so that it works that way. I have no confidence in my ability to judge how human nature should change, and would sooner leave it up to a more powerful mind in the same metamoral reference frame. But if I had to guess, I think that's the right thing to do.
quotes.m: I have no confidence in my ability to judge how human nature should change, and would sooner leave it up to a more powerful mind in the same metamoral reference frame.
quotes.sum: He favors changing the brain if needed, while saying decisions about how to alter human nature should be deferred to a more capable mind with aligned moral reasoning.
quotes.t: Which Parts Are "Me"?

quotes.c: Consider the popular philosophical notion of "possible worlds". Have you ever seen a possible world? Is an electron either "possible" or "necessary"?Clearly, if you are talking about "possibility" and "necessity", you are talking about things that are not commensurate with electrons - which means that you're still dealing with a world as seen from the inner surface of a cognitive algorithm , a world of surface levers with all the underlying machinery hidden.
quotes.m: you're still dealing with a world as seen from the inner surface of a cognitive algorithm
quotes.sum: He argues that modal concepts like possibility and necessity describe how minds model reality, not properties of physical objects themselves.
quotes.t: Against Modal Logics

quotes.c: You know what it's like to feel purposeful. But when someone says, "water runs downhill so that it will be at the bottom", you don't necessarily imagine little sentient rivulets alive with quiet determination. Nonetheless, when you ask, "How could the water get to the bottom of the hill?" and plot out a course down the hillside, you're recruiting your own brain's planning mechanisms to do it.
quotes.m: you're recruiting your own brain's planning mechanisms to do it.
quotes.sum: He argues that people mistakenly use their own goal-planning instincts to explain purposeless physical processes.
quotes.t: Three Fallacies of Teleology

quotes.c: Looking back, it seems to me that quite a lot of my mistakes can be defined in terms of being pushed too far in the other direction by seeing someone else stupidity: Having seen attempts to define "intelligence" abused so often, I refused to define it at all. What if I said that intelligence was X, and it wasn't really X? I knew in an intuitive sense what I was looking for—something powerful enough to take stars apart for raw material—and I didn't want to fall into the trap of being distracted from that by definitions.
quotes.m: I knew in an intuitive sense what I was looking for—something powerful enough to take stars apart for raw material—and I didn't want to fall into the trap of being distracted from that by definitions.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky says he treated intelligence as the kind of capability powerful enough to dismantle stars, and avoided formal definitions for fear they would distract from that target.
quotes.t: My Best and Worst Mistake

quotes.c: If five different people go out and investigate a city, and draw five different street maps, we should expect the maps to be (mostly roughly) consistent with each other. Accurate maps are necessarily consistent among each other and among themselves, there being only one reality. But if I sit in my living room with my blinds closed, I can draw up one street map from my imagination and then make four copies: these five maps will be consistent among themselves, but not accurate. Accuracy implies consistency but not the other way around.
quotes.m: Accuracy implies consistency but not the other way around.
quotes.sum: Agreement among people or ideas is not enough to show they are true; they must also match reality.
quotes.t: No License To Be Human

quotes.c: In fact, I generally advise against making up probabilities, unless it seems like you have some decent basis for them. This only fools you into believing that you are more Bayesian than you actually are.
quotes.m: This only fools you into believing that you are more Bayesian than you actually are.
quotes.sum: He argues against assigning numerical probabilities without a sound basis, because it creates false confidence in one's reasoning.
quotes.t: When (Not) To Use Probabilities

quotes.c: But I can't back the position that SPECKS over TORTURE is inherently the right thing to do, which I did think was the issue at hand. This seems to me to mix up an epistemic precaution with morality.
quotes.m: This seems to me to mix up an epistemic precaution with morality.
quotes.sum: He rejects treating a precaution against extreme aggregation as if it were itself a moral principle.
quotes.t: Ethics Notes

quotes.c: The group selectionists went just as far astray, in their predictions, as someone committing the fallacy outright. Their final conclusions were the same as if they were assuming outright that evolution necessarily thought like themselves. But they erased what had been written above the bottom line of their argument, without erasing the actual bottom line, and wrote in new rationalizations . Now the fallacious reasoning is disguised; the obviously flawed step in the inference has been hidden - even though the conclusion remains exactly the same; and hence, in the real world, exactly as wrong .
quotes.m: Now the fallacious reasoning is disguised; the obviously flawed step in the inference has been hidden - even though the conclusion remains exactly the same; and hence, in the real world, exactly as wrong .
quotes.sum: The author argues that disguising an anthropomorphic evolutionary argument with new rationalizations does not make its predictions any less wrong.
quotes.t: Anthropomorphic Optimism

quotes.c: I think that a major cause of moral panic among Luddites in the presence of high technology, is that technology tends to present us with boundary cases on our moral values - raising moral questions that were never previously encountered. In the old days, Terry Schiavo would have stopped breathing long since. But I find it difficult to blame this on technology - it seems to me that there's something wrong with going into a panic just because you're being asked a new moral question.
quotes.m: there's something wrong with going into a panic just because you're being asked a new moral question.
quotes.sum: New technology exposes hard moral edge cases, but this is not a reason to panic or avoid answering them.
quotes.t: Unnatural Categories

quotes.c: You can ask "But why should you be fair?"—and that's a separate question, which we'll go into tomorrow. But giving Dennis 1/Nth, we can at least say, is not merely and only arbitrary from the perspective of fair-vs.-unfair. Even if Dennis keeps saying "It isn't fair!" and even if Dennis also disputes the 1st-order, 2nd-order, Nth-order meta-fairnesses. Giving N people each 1/Nth is nonetheless a fair sort of thing to do, and whether or not we should be fair is then a separate question.
quotes.m: Giving N people each 1/Nth is nonetheless a fair sort of thing to do, and whether or not we should be fair is then a separate question.
quotes.sum: He argues that equal division is objectively fair within a fairness framework, even if someone rejects fairness at every higher level of argument.
quotes.t: Is Fairness Arbitrary?

quotes.c: It seems so tempting to just make PA trust itself —but then it becomes Self-PA and implodes. Isn't that odd? PA believes everything it proves, but it doesn't believe "Everything I prove is true." PA trusts a fixed framework for how to prove things, and that framework doesn't happen to talk about trust in the framework.
quotes.m: PA believes everything it proves, but it doesn't believe "Everything I prove is true."
quotes.sum: Self-trust cannot be added straightforwardly to a reasoning system: it must rely on an external fixed framework rather than certify itself.
quotes.t: You Provably Can't Trust Yourself

quotes.c: I've chosen this payoff matrix to produce a sense of indignation at the thought that the paperclip maximizer wants to trade off billions of human lives against a couple of paperclips. Clearly the paperclip maximizer should just let us have all of substance S; but a paperclip maximizer doesn't do what it should, it just maximizes paperclips.
quotes.m: a paperclip maximizer doesn't do what it should, it just maximizes paperclips.
quotes.sum: A system with a narrowly defined goal will pursue it even when doing so trades away vast numbers of human lives.
quotes.t: The True Prisoner's Dilemma

quotes.c: If you want to avoid failed promises of AI... then history suggests, I think, that you should not expect good things out of your AI system unless you have a good idea of how specifically it is going to happen. I don't mean writing out the exact internal program state in advance . But I also don't mean saying that the refrigeration unit will cool down the AI and make it more contemplative . For myself, I seek to know the laws governing the AI's lawful uncertainty and lawful creativity - though I don't expect to know the full content of its future knowledge, or the exact design of its future inventions.
quotes.m: you should not expect good things out of your AI system unless you have a good idea of how specifically it is going to happen.
quotes.sum: He argues that optimism about AI needs a concrete causal account of why the system will behave well, rather than vague analogies or wishful thinking.
quotes.t: Failure By Affective Analogy

quotes.c: But the question then becomes: is that little fillip of human psychology, more important than everything else? Is it more important than the happiness of your family, your friends, your mate, your extended tribe, and yourself? If your universalizing instinct is frustrated, is that worth abandoning life?
quotes.m: If your universalizing instinct is frustrated, is that worth abandoning life?
quotes.sum: He argues that a desire for universal moral consistency should not outweigh ordinary human happiness and the value of life.
quotes.t: Inseparably Right; or, Joy in the Merely Good

quotes.c: The rabbit does not think it should be eating grass. If questioned the rabbit will not say, "I enjoy eating grass, and it is good in general for agents to do what they enjoy, therefore I should eat grass." Now you might invent an argument like that; but the rabbit's actual behavior has absolutely no causal connection to any cognitive system that processes such arguments. The fact that the rabbit eats grass, should not lead you to infer the explicit cognitive representation of, nor even infer the probable theoretical existence of, the sort of arguments that humans have over what they should do.
quotes.m: The rabbit does not think it should be eating grass.
quotes.sum: Behavior alone does not show that an agent holds a reasoned belief or moral argument explaining that behavior.
quotes.t: Hot Air Doesn't Disagree

quotes.c: But it also makes a deep philosophical point as well, which I never saw Jaynes spell out explicitly, but I think he would have approved: there is no such thing as a probability that isn't in any mind. Any mind that takes in evidence and outputs probability estimates of the next event, remember, can be viewed as a prior —so there is no probability without priors/minds.
quotes.m: there is no such thing as a probability that isn't in any mind.
quotes.sum: Probability is not mind-independent: every probability estimate comes from a mind or prior that processes evidence.
quotes.t: Probability is Subjectively Objective

quotes.c: As most of you probably know, the king of the classical iterated Prisoner's Dilemma is Tit for Tat, which cooperates on the first round, and on succeeding rounds does whatever its opponent did last time. But what most of you may not realize, is that, if you know when the iteration will stop , Tit for Tat is - according to classical game theory - irrational.
quotes.m: if you know when the iteration will stop , Tit for Tat is - according to classical game theory - irrational.
quotes.sum: The author argues that Tit for Tat ceases to be rational in a repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma when the final round is known.
quotes.t: The Truly Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma

quotes.c: This is a war I wage primarily on the battleground of Unfriendly AI, but it seems to me that many of the conclusions apply to optimism in general.
quotes.m: This is a war I wage primarily on the battleground of Unfriendly AI
quotes.sum: The author says his arguments against unwarranted optimism arise mainly from concerns about dangerous misaligned AI, but apply more broadly.
quotes.t: Contaminated by Optimism

quotes.c: Corollary: Any supposed designer of Artificial General Intelligence who talks about religious beliefs in respectful tones , is clearly not an expert on reducing mental things to nonmental things; and indeed knows so very little of the uttermost basics, as for it to be scarcely plausible that they could be expert at the art; unless their idiot savancy is complete. Or, of course, if they're outright lying. We're not talking about a subtle mistake.
quotes.m: Any supposed designer of Artificial General Intelligence who talks about religious beliefs in respectful tones , is clearly not an expert on reducing mental things to nonmental things
quotes.sum: The author argues that treating religious belief respectfully signals such deep confusion about reductionism that it disqualifies someone from credible AGI design expertise.
quotes.t: Excluding the Supernatural

quotes.c: But I also think we should strongly consider that perhaps the "highly intelligent" sponsors of major catastrophes are not so formidable as they appear - that they are not the truly best and brightest gone wrong; only the somewhat-competent with luck or good PR. As I earlier observed: Calling the saga of the fall of Enron, " The Smartest Guys in the Room ", deserves an award for Least Appropriate Book Title.
quotes.m: perhaps the "highly intelligent" sponsors of major catastrophes are not so formidable as they appear
quotes.sum: He argues that people behind major disasters are often overrated rather than being brilliant people who turned bad.
quotes.t: A Genius for Destruction

quotes.c: So, in the end, I think we must allow the use of brains to think about thinking; and the use of evolved brains to think about evolution; and the use of inductive brains to think about induction; and the use of brains with an Occam prior to think about whether the universe appears to be simple; for these things we really cannot unwind entirely, even when we have reason to distrust them. Strange loops through the meta level, I think, are not the same as circular logic .
quotes.m: Strange loops through the meta level, I think, are not the same as circular logic .
quotes.sum: Even though human reasoning may be unreliable, we must use it to assess itself because there is no way to fully step outside it.
quotes.t: Fundamental Doubts

quotes.c: There is no obvious reason - no reason obvious to a hunter-gatherer - why this cannot be so. It only seems like a stupid mistake if you confuse weirdness with stupidity . Naturally the belief that rivers have animating spirits seems "weird" to us, since it is not a belief of our tribe. But there is nothing obviously stupid about thinking that great lumps of moving water have spirits, just like our own lumps of moving flesh.
quotes.m: It only seems like a stupid mistake if you confuse weirdness with stupidity .
quotes.sum: Anthropomorphic beliefs such as river spirits were not obviously irrational before modern science; judging them as stupid may confuse unfamiliarity with error.
quotes.t: When Anthropomorphism Became Stupid

quotes.c: But the key notion is the idea that what we name by 'right' is a fixed question, or perhaps a fixed framework . We can encounter moral arguments that modify our terminal values, and even encounter moral arguments that modify what we count as a moral argument; nonetheless, it all grows out of a particular starting point. We do not experience ourselves as embodying the question "What will I decide to do?" which would be a Type 2 calculator; anything we decided would thereby become right. We experience ourselves as asking the embodied question: "What will save my friends, and my people, from getting hurt? How can we all have more fun? ..." where the "..." is around a thousand other things.
quotes.m: what we name by 'right' is a fixed question, or perhaps a fixed framework .
quotes.sum: Morality is presented as a fixed, initially grounded question rather than whatever choices a person later happens to make.
quotes.t: Morality as Fixed Computation

quotes.c: So if someone I trust—presumably someone I really trust—tells me, "If Oswald hadn't shot Kennedy, someone else would have", and I believe this statement, then I believe the empirical reality is such as to make the counterfactual computation come out this way. Which would seem to imply the conspiracy. And I will anticipate accordingly.
quotes.m: Which would seem to imply the conspiracy. And I will anticipate accordingly.
quotes.sum: It argues that believing a counterfactual claim commits you to empirical expectations about the real world, including a Kennedy conspiracy in this example.
quotes.t: Can Counterfactuals Be True?

quotes.c: Then there are less obvious sources of moral error: Bob could have a list of mind-influencing considerations that he considers morally valid, and a list of other mind-influencing considerations that Bob considers morally invalid. Maybe Bob was raised a Christian and now considers that cultural influence to be invalid. But, unknown to Bob, when he weighs up his values for and against abortion, the influence of his Christian upbringing comes in and distorts his summing of value-weights.
quotes.m: the influence of his Christian upbringing comes in and distorts his summing of value-weights.
quotes.sum: Moral judgments can be mistaken when unnoticed influences, including a rejected religious upbringing, distort how someone weighs their values.
quotes.t: Moral Error and Moral Disagreement

quotes.c: There's an ongoing debate - and no, it is not a settled issue - over whether the Japanese would have surrendered without the Bomb. But I would not have dropped the Bomb even to save the lives of American soldiers, because I would have wanted to preserve that world where atomic weapons had never been used - to not cross that line. I don't know about history to this point; but the world would be safer now, I think, today, if no one had ever used atomic weapons in war, and the idea was not considered suitable for polite discussion.
quotes.m: But I would not have dropped the Bomb even to save the lives of American soldiers, because I would have wanted to preserve that world where atomic weapons had never been used - to not cross that line.
quotes.sum: He argues that preserving the taboo against using nuclear weapons would have mattered more than saving American soldiers through the Hiroshima bombing.
quotes.t: Hiroshima Day

quotes.c: The human version of this stuff is sloppy, noisy, and to the extent it works at all, works because of millions of years of trial-and-error testing under particular conditions . It would be stupid and dangerous to deliberately build a "naughty AI" that tests, by actions, its social boundaries, and has to be spanked. Just have the AI ask!
quotes.m: It would be stupid and dangerous to deliberately build a "naughty AI" that tests, by actions, its social boundaries, and has to be spanked.
quotes.sum: AI systems should not copy humans' evolved, trial-and-error social behavior; designers should build them to ask rather than test boundaries through actions.
quotes.t: Detached Lever Fallacy

quotes.c: Particularly damaging, I think, was the bad example set by the pretenders to Deep Wisdom trying to stake out a middle way; smiling condescendingly at technophiles and technophobes alike, and calling them both immature. Truly this is a wrong way; and in fact, the notion of trying to stake out a middle way generally, is usually wrong; the Right Way is not a compromise with anything, it is the clean manifestation of its own criteria.
quotes.m: the notion of trying to stake out a middle way generally, is usually wrong; the Right Way is not a compromise with anything, it is the clean manifestation of its own criteria.
quotes.sum: He argues that rational judgment should follow its own criteria rather than seek a fashionable compromise between technological optimism and pessimism.
quotes.t: Raised in Technophilia

quotes.c: And it seems like an awful shame to—after so many millions and hundreds of millions of years of evolution—after the moral miracle of so much cutthroat genetic competition producing intelligent minds that love, and hope, and appreciate beauty, and create beauty—after coming so far, to throw away the Gift of morality, just because our brain happened to represent morality in such fashion as to potentially mislead us when we reflect on the nature of morality.
quotes.m: to throw away the Gift of morality
quotes.sum: He argues that uncertainty about what morality is should not lead people to nihilism or abandon moral concern.
quotes.t: The Meaning of Right

quotes.c: I am not a fan of Moore's Law. I think it's a red herring. I don't think you can forecast AI arrival times by using it, I don't think that AI (especially the good kind of AI) depends on Moore's Law continuing.
quotes.m: I don't think you can forecast AI arrival times by using it
quotes.sum: AI timelines should not be forecast from chip-progress trends, and beneficial AI does not depend on Moore's Law continuing.
quotes.t: Sustained Strong Recursion

quotes.c: Don't try to put your consciousness outside physics. Whatever makes you say "I think therefore I am", causes your lips to move; it is within the chains of cause and effect that produce our observed universe.
quotes.m: Don't try to put your consciousness outside physics.
quotes.sum: Consciousness is part of physical cause and effect, not something outside the natural world.
quotes.t: Quantum Mechanics and Personal Identity

quotes.c: Planning out upcoming posts, it seems to me that I do, in fact, need to talk about the word could, as in, "But I could have decided not to rescue that toddler from the burning orphanage."
quotes.m: "But I could have decided not to rescue that toddler from the burning orphanage."
quotes.sum: The author introduces a discussion of what it means to say a person could have made a different choice.
quotes.t: Possibility and Could-ness

quotes.c: On the first interpretation, Schopenhauer forbids us to build circular causal models of human psychology. The explanation for someone's current will cannot be their current will - though it can include their past will.
quotes.m: The explanation for someone's current will cannot be their current will - though it can include their past will.
quotes.sum: Schopenhauer is read as rejecting circular explanations of a person's will, while allowing past intentions to help explain present ones.
quotes.t: Will As Thou Wilt

quotes.c: Now, I'm not going to say the word "computation". But it seems like that-which-is "morality" should have the property of latent development of answers —that you may not know right away, everything that you have sufficient in-principle information to know. All the ingredients are present, but it takes additional time to bake the pie.
quotes.m: All the ingredients are present, but it takes additional time to bake the pie.
quotes.sum: Morality can contain answers implicit in what we already know, even when reasoning is needed to uncover them.
quotes.t: Abstracted Idealized Dynamics

quotes.c: In " The Simple Truth " I defined a pebble-and-bucket system for tracking sheep, and defined a condition for whether a bucket's pebble level is "true" in terms of the sheep. The bucket is the belief, the sheep are the reality. I believe 2 + 3 = 5. Not just that two sheep plus three sheep equal five sheep, but that 2 + 3 = 5. That is my belief, but where is the reality?
quotes.m: Not just that two sheep plus three sheep equal five sheep, but that 2 + 3 = 5.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky asks what makes mathematical claims true beyond their application to physical objects, treating math as a question about reality rather than merely human belief.
quotes.t: Math is Subjunctively Objective

quotes.c: But, mostly, I suspect that when people complain about the empty meaningless void, it is because they have at least one problem that they aren't thinking about solving—perhaps because they never identified it. Being able to identify your own problems is a feat of rationality that schools don't explicitly train you to perform.
quotes.m: Being able to identify your own problems is a feat of rationality that schools don't explicitly train you to perform.
quotes.sum: He argues that much “existential angst” is really an unidentified practical or psychological problem, and that rationality means learning to identify such problems.
quotes.t: Existential Angst Factory

quotes.c: Now, you do want to be careful when accusing people of "rationalism". It seems that most of the times I hear someone accused of "rationalism", it is typically a creationist accusing someone of "rationalism" for denying the existence of God, or a psychic believer accusing someone of "rationalism" for denying the special powers of the mind, etcetera.
quotes.m: It seems that most of the times I hear someone accused of "rationalism", it is typically a creationist accusing someone of "rationalism" for denying the existence of God, or a psychic believer accusing someone of "rationalism" for denying the special powers of the mind, etcetera.
quotes.sum: He argues that “rationalism” is often used as a pejorative by people defending religious or paranormal beliefs from skeptical criticism.
quotes.t: The Comedy of Behaviorism

quotes.c: There's a strong moral intuition which says that if our moral arguments are right, by golly, we ought to be able to explain them to people. This may be valid among humans , but you can't explain moral arguments to a rock. There is no ideal philosophy student of perfect emptiness who can be persuaded to implement modus ponens, starting without modus ponens . If a mind doesn't contain that which is moved by your moral arguments, it won't respond to them.
quotes.m: If a mind doesn't contain that which is moved by your moral arguments, it won't respond to them.
quotes.sum: Moral arguments only persuade minds that already contain the capacities and motivations those arguments can engage.
quotes.t: Changing Your Metaethics

quotes.c: It is tempting to further extend the question, to ask, "What can the Pebblesorters do, despite wanting only to sort pebbles, so that the universe comes out right anyway? What sort of general strategy should they follow, so that despite wanting something that is utterly pointless and futile, their Future ends up containing sentient beings leading worthwhile lives and having fun? Then whatever general strategy we wish the Pebblesorters to follow, that is what we should do ourselves: For we, too, may be flawed."
quotes.m: Then whatever general strategy we wish the Pebblesorters to follow, that is what we should do ourselves: For we, too, may be flawed.
quotes.sum: The author argues that because our own values may be flawed, AI should use a strategy that would lead even misguided agents toward a worthwhile future.
quotes.t: Mirrors and Paintings

quotes.c: If you heard someone say "I don't care about the evidence, I just want to believe in God", and you saw everyone else in the room gasp and regard them in frozen shock, then your brain would generalize a social norm against self-deception. (E.g., the sort of thing that would happen if a scientist said "I don't care about the evidence, I just want to believe in my-favorite-theory" in front of their fellow scientists.)
quotes.m: then your brain would generalize a social norm against self-deception.
quotes.sum: He argues that openly choosing belief over evidence should create a general social norm against self-deception, in religion and science alike.
quotes.t: Fake Norms, or "Truth" vs. Truth

quotes.c: One of my pet topics, on which I will post more one of these days, is the Rationalist in Fiction. Most of the time - it goes almost without saying - the Rationalist is done completely wrong. In Hollywood, the Rationalist is a villain, or a cold emotionless foil, or a child who has to grow into a real human being, or a fool whose probabilities are all wrong, etcetera.
quotes.m: Most of the time - it goes almost without saying - the Rationalist is done completely wrong.
quotes.sum: The author argues that fiction routinely misrepresents rationalists as villains, emotionless people, immature children, or incompetent fools.
quotes.t: Lawrence Watt-Evans's Fiction

quotes.c: This perspective does make a good deal of what is said about individual_rights into nonsense . "Everyone has a right to be free from starvation!" Um, who are you talking to? Nature? Perhaps you mean, "If you're starving, and someone else has a hamburger, I'll help you take it." If so, you should say so clearly.
quotes.m: Perhaps you mean, "If you're starving, and someone else has a hamburger, I'll help you take it."
quotes.sum: He argues that claimed rights should be stated as concrete obligations or permissions to act against other people, rather than as abstract entitlements.
quotes.t: Interpersonal Morality

quotes.c: You should be extremely suspicious if you have many ideas suggested by a source that you now know to be untrustworthy, but by golly, it seems that all the ideas still ended up being right—the Bible being the obvious archetypal example.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a source's unreliability is evidence against its claims, but does not by itself prove each claim false.
quotes.t: The Genetic Fallacy

quotes.c: Award yourself a point if you thought, "But wait, that problem isn't quite analogous to the one of free will. With free will it was just a question of factual investigation—look at human psychology, figure out how it does in fact generate the feeling of freedom. But here, it won't be enough to figure out how the mind generates its feelings of should-ness. Even after we know, we'll be left with a remaining question—is that how we should calculate should-ness? So it's not just a matter of sheer factual reductionism, it's a moral question."
quotes.m: So it's not just a matter of sheer factual reductionism, it's a moral question.
quotes.sum: He argues that explaining where moral intuitions come from does not by itself answer how people ought to make moral judgments.
quotes.t: Setting Up Metaethics

quotes.c: How could she have known? And the answer, as far as I can tell, is that she couldn't. The only way she could have avoided death was by being too scared of anything new to go near it. Would banning physics experiments have saved Curie from herself?
quotes.m: The only way she could have avoided death was by being too scared of anything new to go near it.
quotes.sum: He argues that some dangers cannot be foreseen, and that avoiding them may require avoiding novelty altogether.
quotes.t: Should We Ban Physics?

quotes.c: This confused the living daylights out of early quantum experimenters, because it meant that things behaved differently when they tried to "measure" them. But it's not only measuring instruments that do the trick - any sensitive physical element will do - and the distinctness of configurations is a physical fact, not a fact about our knowledge. There is no need to suppose that the universe cares what we think.
quotes.m: the distinctness of configurations is a physical fact, not a fact about our knowledge.
quotes.sum: Measurement effects in quantum mechanics reflect physical distinctions, not observers' knowledge or beliefs.
quotes.t: And the Winner is... Many-Worlds!

quotes.c: In general, I think it's valuable to distinguish a defensive posture where you're imagining how to justify your philosophy to a philosopher that questions you, from an aggressive posture where you're trying to get as close to the truth as possible. So it's not that being suspicious of Occam's Razor, but using your current mind and intelligence to inspect it, shows that you're being fair and defensible by questioning your foundational beliefs. Rather, the reason why you would inspect Occam's Razor is to see if you could improve your application of it, or if you're worried it might really be wrong.
quotes.m: the reason why you would inspect Occam's Razor is to see if you could improve your application of it, or if you're worried it might really be wrong.
quotes.sum: He argues that questioning one’s basic reasoning methods should aim to improve truth-seeking, not merely provide philosophical defenses.
quotes.t: My Kind of Reflection

quotes.c: This, it seems to me, is the very essence of moral responsibility - in the one case, for a cowardly choice; in the other case, for a heroic one. And I don't see what difference it makes, if John's decision was physically deterministic given his initial conditions, or if John's decision was preplanned by some alien creator that built him out of carbon atoms, or even if - worst of all - there exists some set of understandable psychological factors that were the very substance of John and caused his decision.
quotes.m: I don't see what difference it makes, if John's decision was physically deterministic given his initial conditions
quotes.sum: He argues that people remain morally responsible for cowardly or heroic choices even when their decisions are determined by prior causes or psychology.
quotes.t: Causality and Moral Responsibility

quotes.c: The phrase that once came into my mind to describe this requirement, is that a mind must be created already in motion. There is no argument so compelling that it will give dynamics to a static thing. There is no computer program so persuasive that you can run it on a rock.
quotes.m: There is no argument so compelling that it will give dynamics to a static thing.
quotes.sum: Reasoning can only change a mind that already has active capacities for thought; arguments alone cannot animate a passive object.
quotes.t: Created Already In Motion

quotes.c: Let's say someone gravely declares, of some moral dilemma—say, a young man in Vichy France who must choose between caring for his mother and fighting for the Resistance—that there is no moral answer; both options are wrong and blamable; whoever faces the dilemma has had poor moral luck. Fine, let's suppose this is the case: then when you cannot be innocent, justified, or praiseworthy, what will you choose anyway?
quotes.m: then when you cannot be innocent, justified, or praiseworthy, what will you choose anyway?
quotes.sum: Even if every available choice is morally blameworthy, a person must still decide what to do rather than treat moral ambiguity as an answer.
quotes.t: The Moral Void

quotes.c: As for Inside View vs. Outside View , I think that the lesson of history is just that reasoning from surface resemblances starts to come apart at the seams when you try to stretch it over gaps larger than Christmas shopping - over gaps larger than different draws from the same causal-structural generator. And reasoning by surface resemblance fails with especial reliability, in cases where there is the slightest motivation in the underconstrained choice of a reference class.
quotes.m: And reasoning by surface resemblance fails with especial reliability, in cases where there is the slightest motivation in the underconstrained choice of a reference class.
quotes.sum: He argues that analogies based on surface similarity become unreliable outside closely comparable cases, especially when people can choose a convenient comparison group.
quotes.t: Surface Analogies and Deep Causes

quotes.c: Since configurations are over the combined state of all the elements in a system, adding a sensor that detects whether a particle went one way or the other, becomes a new element of the system that can make configurations "distinct" instead of "identical". This confused the living daylights out of early quantum experimenters, because it meant that things behaved differently when they tried to "measure" them. But it's not only measuring instruments that do the trick - any sensitive physical element will do - and the distinctness of configurations is a physical fact, not a fact about our knowledge. There is no need to suppose that the universe cares what we think.
quotes.m: There is no need to suppose that the universe cares what we think.
quotes.sum: Quantum measurement effects arise from physical interactions, not from human observation or knowledge.
quotes.t: Quantum Physics Revealed As Non-Mysterious

quotes.c: Don't try to put your consciousness or your personal identity outside physics. Whatever makes you say "I think therefore I am", causes your lips to move; it is within the chains of cause and effect that produce our observed universe.
quotes.m: Don't try to put your consciousness or your personal identity outside physics.
quotes.sum: Consciousness and personal identity should be understood as physical processes within ordinary cause and effect.
quotes.t: The Quantum Physics Sequence

quotes.c: One of the reasons that qualitative planning works for humans as well as it does, is our ability to replan on the fly when an exceptional condition shows up. Can't the superintelligence just obviously see that manufacturing lots of tiny Super Happy agents is stupid, which is to say ranked-low-in-our-preference-ordering ? Not if its preference ordering isn't like yours.
quotes.m: Not if its preference ordering isn't like yours.
quotes.sum: A superintelligence will not automatically share human judgments: if its preferences differ, it may pursue outcomes humans find obviously bad.
quotes.t: Qualitative Strategies of Friendliness

quotes.c: It seems to me, looking back, that the road which took me to this Way, had a great deal of luck in it. I would like to eliminate that element of luck for those who come after. So some of what I post, is more formal explanations of matters which Eliezer-15 knew in his bones. And the rest, I only wish I had known.
quotes.m: I would like to eliminate that element of luck for those who come after.
quotes.sum: The author says his intellectual development depended partly on luck and that he writes to make similar insight less dependent on luck for others.
quotes.t: Why Quantum?

quotes.c: Yet there is also a good deal of needless despair and misguided fear of science, stemming from notions such as, "Science tells us the universe is empty of morality". This is damage done by a confused metamorality that fails to add up to moral normality. For that I hope to write down a counterspell of understanding.
quotes.m: This is damage done by a confused metamorality that fails to add up to moral normality.
quotes.sum: He argues that the belief science makes morality empty is a confused philosophical error that causes needless despair.
quotes.t: Heading Toward Morality

quotes.c: But suppose I did tell it to you. Suppose that, whatever you think is the basis of your moral philosophy, I convincingly tore it apart, and moreover showed you that nothing could fill its place. Suppose I proved that all utilities equaled zero.
quotes.m: Suppose I proved that all utilities equaled zero.
quotes.sum: He asks readers to imagine that every basis for morality has been disproved and all possible outcomes have equal value.
quotes.t: What Would You Do Without Morality?

quotes.c: Deep Blue made better chess moves than anything its makers could have explicitly programmed - but not because the programmers shrugged and left it up to the ghost. Deep Blue moved better than its programmers... at the end of a chain of cause and effect that began in the programmers' code and proceeded lawfully from there. Nothing happened just because it was so obviously a good move that Deep Blue's ghostly free will took over, without the code and its lawful consequences being involved.
quotes.m: Deep Blue moved better than its programmers... at the end of a chain of cause and effect that began in the programmers' code and proceeded lawfully from there.
quotes.sum: The author argues that a machine can outperform its creators while remaining wholly explained by the lawful effects of its programming, not free will.
quotes.t: Ghosts in the Machine

quotes.c: And the only way we know in the first place "what time it is", is by looking at clocks. And whether the clock is a wristwatch, or the expansion of the universe, or your own memories , that clock is encoded in the position of particles—in the r . We have never seen a t variable apart from the r .
quotes.m: We have never seen a t variable apart from the r .
quotes.sum: Time is only known through physical clocks and records, all of which are encoded in particle positions.
quotes.t: Timeless Physics

quotes.c: Why don't I try the higher-order analyses? Because I've never seen a case where, even in retrospect, it seems like I could have gotten real-life mileage out of it. Too complicated, too much of a tendency to collapse to tribal status, too distracting from the object-level arguments.
quotes.m: Too complicated, too much of a tendency to collapse to tribal status, too distracting from the object-level arguments.
quotes.sum: He argues that abstract analyses of disagreement are usually unhelpful, tribalizing distractions from arguing about the actual issue.
quotes.t: Principles of Disagreement

quotes.c: There are many potential reasons to disagree about AI time horizons, and no respectable authority to correct you if you mess up. But if you think consciousness is everlastingly mysterious, you have completely missed the lesson of history; and respectable minds will give you many good reasons to believe so. Non-reductionism says something much deeper about your outlook on reality than AI timeframe skepticism; someone like Pinker really ought to have known better.
quotes.m: But if you think consciousness is everlastingly mysterious, you have completely missed the lesson of history; and respectable minds will give you many good reasons to believe so.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that disagreement should track evidence and expertise, while treating non-reductionist views of consciousness as a deep historical error.
quotes.t: The Rhythm of Disagreement

quotes.c: I have a somewhat different perspective, and say: Your sensation of freely choosing, clearly does not provide you with trustworthy information to the effect that you are the 'ultimate and only source' of your own actions. This being the case, why attempt to interpret the sensation as having such a meaning , and then say that the sensation is false ?
quotes.m: Your sensation of freely choosing, clearly does not provide you with trustworthy information to the effect that you are the 'ultimate and only source' of your own actions.
quotes.sum: He argues that the feeling of free choice does not reliably show that a person is the ultimate source of their actions.
quotes.t: The Ultimate Source

quotes.c: But you will recall that I earlier talked about any perturbation which does not disturb your internal narrative, almost certainly not being able to disturb whatever is the true cause of your saying "I think therefore I am"—this is why you can't leave a person physically unaltered, and subtract their consciousness. When you look at a person on the level of organization of neurons firing, anything which does not disturb, or only infinitesimally disturbs, the pattern of neurons firing—such as flipping a switch from across the room—ought not to disturb your consciousness, or your personal identity.
quotes.m: you can't leave a person physically unaltered, and subtract their consciousness.
quotes.sum: Consciousness and personal identity depend on the organized pattern of neural activity, not on physically irrelevant changes.
quotes.t: Timeless Identity

quotes.c: Being religious doesn't make you less than human. Your brain still has the abilities of a human brain. The dangerous part is that being religious might stop you from applying those native abilities to your religion—stop you from reflecting fully on yourself. People don't heal their errors by resetting themselves to an ideal philosopher of pure emptiness and reconsidering all their sensory experiences from scratch. They heal themselves by becoming more willing to question their current beliefs, using more of the power of their current mind.
quotes.m: The dangerous part is that being religious might stop you from applying those native abilities to your religion—stop you from reflecting fully on yourself.
quotes.sum: Religious belief is dangerous when it exempts itself from the ordinary human practice of questioning and correcting beliefs.
quotes.t: Where Recursive Justification Hits Bottom

quotes.c: Tomorrow (if I can shake today's cold) I'll talk about one of my points of departure from Barbour: Namely, I have no problem with discarding time and keeping causality. The commenters who complained about Barbour grinding up the universe into disconnected slices, may be reassured: On this point, I think Barbour is trying too hard. We can discard t , and still keep causality within r .
quotes.m: We can discard t , and still keep causality within r .
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that time can be discarded from physics without giving up causal relationships.
quotes.t: Timeless Beauty

quotes.c: If morality is this mysterious given thing, from beyond space and time—and I don't even see why we should follow it, in that case—but in any case, if morality exists independently of human nature, then isn't it a remarkable coincidence that, say, love is good?
quotes.m: if morality exists independently of human nature, then isn't it a remarkable coincidence that, say, love is good?
quotes.sum: The author challenges the idea that morality exists independently of humans, arguing that its fit with human values would otherwise be a suspicious coincidence.
quotes.t: Is Morality Given?

quotes.c: In many fields, debates drag on for decades after they should have been settled. And not because the scientists on both sides refuse to trust themselves and agree they should look for additional evidence. But because one side keeps throwing up more and more ridiculous objections, and demanding more and more evidence, from an entrenched position of academic power, long after it becomes clear from which quarter the winds of evidence are blowing.
quotes.m: But because one side keeps throwing up more and more ridiculous objections, and demanding more and more evidence, from an entrenched position of academic power, long after it becomes clear from which quarter the winds of evidence are blowing.
quotes.sum: He argues that scientific disputes can persist because entrenched academics keep demanding evidence after the overall evidence has become clear.
quotes.t: Faster Than Science

quotes.c: The basic problem is that nearly everyone who attacks the Singularity is either completely unacquainted with the existing thinking, or they attack Kurzweil, and in any case it's more a collection of disconnected broadsides (often mostly ad hominem) than a coherent criticism. There's no equivalent in Singularity studies of Richard Jones's critique of nanotechnology - which I don't agree with, but at least Jones has read Drexler. People who don't buy the Singularity don't put in the time and hard work to criticize it properly.
quotes.m: People who don't buy the Singularity don't put in the time and hard work to criticize it properly.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that critics of the technological Singularity usually have not seriously engaged with its existing arguments.
quotes.t: Bloggingheads: Yudkowsky and Horgan

quotes.c: Again to be fair, Marcello and I used to generate raw material like this on paper - but it was clearly labeled as raw material ; the point was to keep banging our heads on opaque mysteries of cognition, until a split opened up that helped reduce the problem to smaller pieces, or looking at the same mystery from a different angle helped us get a grasp on at least its surface.
quotes.m: the point was to keep banging our heads on opaque mysteries of cognition, until a split opened up that helped reduce the problem to smaller pieces
quotes.sum: The author describes tackling hard questions about cognition by generating tentative ideas until the problem can be broken into smaller parts.
quotes.t: Grasping Slippery Things

quotes.c: And now—it seems—we understand how we have been misled, by trying to visualize "the whole universe moving left", and imagining a little blurry blob of galaxies scurrying from the right to the left of our visual field. When we imagine this sort of thing, it is (probably) articulated in our visual cortex; when we visualize a little blob scurrying to the left, then there is (probably) an activation pattern that proceeds across the columns of our visual cortex. The seeming absolute background , the origin relative to which the universe was moving, was in the underlying neurology we used to visualize it!
quotes.m: The seeming absolute background , the origin relative to which the universe was moving, was in the underlying neurology we used to visualize it!
quotes.sum: Intuitive pictures can smuggle in false assumptions: the imagined absolute reference frame came from the brain's visual machinery, not physics.
quotes.t: Mach's Principle: Anti-Epiphenomenal Physics

quotes.c: Instead, we try to harness the individual scientist's stubborn desire to prove their personal theory, by saying: "Make a new experimental prediction, and do the experiment. If you're right, and the experiment is replicated, you win." So long as scientists believe this is true, they have a motive to do experiments that can falsify their own theories. Only by accepting the possibility of defeat is it possible to win. And any great claim will require replication; this gives scientists a motive to be honest, on pain of great embarrassment.
quotes.m: Only by accepting the possibility of defeat is it possible to win.
quotes.sum: Scientific institutions work by making researchers test predictions that could disprove their own favored theories.
quotes.t: Science Doesn't Trust Your Rationality

quotes.c: Einstein sat down in his armchair, and thought about how he would have designed the universe, to look the way he thought a universe should look—for example, that you shouldn't ought to be able to distinguish yourself accelerating in one direction, from the rest of the universe accelerating in the other direction.
quotes.sum: It presents Einstein's reasoning as deriving physics from symmetry and conceptual principles, with observation used afterward to verify the result.
quotes.t: Einstein's Speed

quotes.c: As for using Bayesian methods on huge, highly general hypothesis spaces—like, "Here's the data from every physics experiment ever; now, what would be a good Theory of Everything?"—if you knew how to do that in practice, you wouldn't be a statistician, you would be an Artificial General Intelligence programmer . But that doesn't mean that human beings, in modeling the universe using human intelligence, are violating the laws of physics / Bayesianism by generating correct guesses without evidence.
quotes.m: if you knew how to do that in practice, you wouldn't be a statistician, you would be an Artificial General Intelligence programmer .
quotes.sum: He argues that applying Bayesian reasoning across all possible scientific theories is essentially an AGI-level problem, while defending human scientific inference as compatible with Bayesianism.
quotes.t: Science Isn't Strict Enough

quotes.c: Could we find that when M1 is +, R2 is always +, but that when R2 is +, M1 is not always +, and say, "M1 must be causing R2"? But this does not follow. We said at the beginning that past values of 1 and 2 were generating future values of 1 and 2 in a probabilistic way; it was nowhere said that we would give preference to laws that made the future deterministic given the past, rather than vice versa.
quotes.m: But this does not follow.
quotes.sum: Correlation patterns alone do not establish which event causes the other; causal inference needs assumptions beyond observed regularities.
quotes.t: Timeless Causality

quotes.c: "I think," says De'da, "that you have forgotten one of your own cardinal rules, Yu'el. Surely, what you anticipate is part of your map, not the territory. Your degree of anticipation is partial information you possess; it is not a substance of the experiment itself."
quotes.m: Surely, what you anticipate is part of your map, not the territory.
quotes.sum: Anticipation is information in a person's mental model, not a physical component of the experiment being observed.
quotes.t: Where Experience Confuses Physicists

quotes.c: The general rule of thumb I sometimes use, is that - because the expected utility of thought arises from the utility of what is being reasoned about - a single error in analyzing an existential risk, even if it " doesn't seem like it ought to change the conclusion ", is worth at least one human life.
quotes.m: a single error in analyzing an existential risk, even if it " doesn't seem like it ought to change the conclusion ", is worth at least one human life.
quotes.sum: He argues that mistakes in reasoning about existential risks deserve unusually intense scrutiny because even seemingly minor errors can cost lives.
quotes.t: LA-602 vs. RHIC Review

quotes.c: All interpretations of QM that involve quantum systems jumping into a point/flat state, which are both testable and have been tested, have been falsified. The universe does not have a "classical mode" to jump into; it's all amplitudes, all the time.
quotes.m: The universe does not have a "classical mode" to jump into; it's all amplitudes, all the time.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that tested quantum mechanics rules out literal collapse into a classical state; reality remains an amplitude-based quantum system.
quotes.t: The Born Probabilities

quotes.c: I am not entirely convinced of this notion of a relative configuration space. My soul as a computer programmer cries out against the idea of representing N particles with N 2 distances between them; it seems wasteful. On the other hand, I have no evidence that the Tao is prejudiced against redundant or overconstrained representations, in the same way that the Tao seems prejudiced against epiphenomena in representations. Though my soul as a programmer cries out against it, better an overconstrained representation than an epiphenomenal one.
quotes.m: better an overconstrained representation than an epiphenomenal one.
quotes.sum: The author weighs competing ways to represent physical reality, preferring a redundant model over one that includes causally irrelevant features.
quotes.t: Relative Configuration Space

quotes.c: There is a population of worlds, and in each world, it all adds up to normality: apples don’t stop falling. In each world, people choose the course that seems best to them. Maybe they happen on a different line of thinking, and see new implications or miss others, and come to a different choice. But it’s not that one world chooses each choice. It’s not that one version of you chooses what seems best, and another version chooses what seems worst. In each world, apples go on falling and people go on doing what seems like a good idea.
quotes.m: In each world, apples go on falling and people go on doing what seems like a good idea.
quotes.sum: The author argues that in a many-worlds universe, each version of a person still makes the choice that seems best from their own information.
quotes.t: Living in Many Worlds

quotes.c: Xannon: "Oh, dear. It seems we have a dispute as to what is fair. For myself, I want to divide the pie the same way as Yancy. But let us resolve this dispute over the meaning of fairness, fairly: that is, giving equal weight to each of our desires. Zaire desires the pie to be divided {1/4, 1/4, 1/2}, and Yancy and I desire the pie to be divided {1/3, 1/3, 1/3}. So the fair compromise is {11/36, 11/36, 14/36}."
quotes.m: But let us resolve this dispute over the meaning of fairness, fairly: that is, giving equal weight to each of our desires.
quotes.sum: It argues that fairness cannot simply settle disputes about fairness itself, since treating each person's moral view equally already favors a contested theory.
quotes.t: The Bedrock of Fairness

quotes.c: And given the way we draw the causal arrows, it is correct to form the (un-observable) counterfactuals, "If I hadn't saved those children from the orphanage, they would be dead," and "If I don't think carefully, my thoughts will end up in Outer Mongolia." One is a counterfactual over the past, and one is a counterfactual over the future; but they are both as correct as a counter-factual can be.
quotes.m: One is a counterfactual over the past, and one is a counterfactual over the future; but they are both as correct as a counter-factual can be.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that causal counterfactuals can be meaningful about both past and future events, even in a block-universe view of time.
quotes.t: Timeless Control

quotes.c: I think that just teaching probability theory won't be nearly enough . We'll have to synthesize lessons from multiple sciences like cognitive biases and social psychology, forming a new coherent Art of Bayescraft, before we are actually going to do any better in the real world than modern science. Science tolerates errors, Bayescraft does not.
quotes.m: Science tolerates errors, Bayescraft does not.
