quotes.sum: He argues that probability theory is insufficient and that science should be replaced or improved by a stricter practical discipline of Bayesian reasoning.
quotes.t: Changing the Definition of Science

quotes.c: Yet as implausible as I find consciousness-causes-collapse, it at least gives us a picture of reality. Sure, it’s an informal picture. Sure, it gives mental properties ontologically basic status. You can’t calculate when an “experimental observation” occurs or what people “know,” you just know when certain probabilities are obviously zero.
quotes.m: Yet as implausible as I find consciousness-causes-collapse, it at least gives us a picture of reality.
quotes.sum: He argues that even an implausible consciousness-based account of quantum collapse is preferable to an interpretation that offers no intelligible picture of reality.
quotes.t: Quantum Non-Realism

quotes.c: I say again that the question “What kind of information does the configuration’s structure incorporate?” has experimental consequences . You can deduce, from experiment, the way that reality itself must be treating configurations.
quotes.m: You can deduce, from experiment, the way that reality itself must be treating configurations.
quotes.sum: The author argues that questions about what information physical structures contain can be tested experimentally.
quotes.t: Joint Configurations

quotes.c: When we look back and ask, “How could the early quantum scientists have done better , even in principle?” it seems that the insights they needed were philosophical ones.
quotes.m: it seems that the insights they needed were philosophical ones.
quotes.sum: The author argues that early mistakes in quantum science required philosophical, not merely technical, insights to avoid.
quotes.t: Where Philosophy Meets Science

quotes.c: Just remember that this business of single paths through time is not fundamentally true. It's merely a good approximation for modeling a sofa. The classical hallucination breaks down completely by the time you get to the atomic level.
quotes.m: The classical hallucination breaks down completely by the time you get to the atomic level.
quotes.sum: Classical intuitions about objects following one path through time are useful approximations, not fundamental reality.
quotes.t: Feynman Paths

quotes.c: The blob of amplitude in which you find yourself, where you see the Sensor's dial in some particular position, will have a sub-distribution over actual Atom positions that falls off according to (1) the initial amplitude distribution for the Atom, analogous to the prior; and (2) the amplitude for the Sensor's dial (and the rest of the Sensor!) to end up in our part of configuration space, if the Atom started out in that position. (That's the part analogous to the likelihood function.) With a Sensor at all sensitive, the amplitude for the Atom to be in a state noticeably different from what the Sensor shows, will taper off very sharply.
quotes.m: With a Sensor at all sensitive, the amplitude for the Atom to be in a state noticeably different from what the Sensor shows, will taper off very sharply.
quotes.sum: The author explains quantum measurement as Bayesian-style updating: a sensitive sensor makes atom states inconsistent with its reading very unlikely.
quotes.t: Decoherence is Pointless

quotes.c: That, I think, is how you make incremental progress on these kinds of problems—by working with incomplete theories that have wrong elements clearly labeled "WRONG!" Academics, it seems to me, have a bias toward publishing only theories that they claim to be correct—or even worse, complete—or worse yet, coherent. This, of course, rules out incremental progress on really difficult problems.
quotes.m: Academics, it seems to me, have a bias toward publishing only theories that they claim to be correct—or even worse, complete—or worse yet, coherent.
quotes.sum: He argues that difficult problems require openly using incomplete theories with clearly marked flaws, rather than waiting for polished and coherent ones.
quotes.t: Which Basis Is More Fundamental?

quotes.c: First, let it be said that I do indeed hold that "reductionism", according to the meaning I will give for that word, is obviously correct; and to perdition with any past civilizations that disagreed .
quotes.m: "reductionism", according to the meaning I will give for that word, is obviously correct; and to perdition with any past civilizations that disagreed .
quotes.sum: The author forcefully states that reductionism is obviously correct and dismisses civilizations that rejected it.
quotes.t: Reductionism

quotes.c: An analogy: When a doctor says, "Hey, I think that virus X97 is causing people to drip green slime," you don't respond: "Aha, but you haven't explained the exact chain of causality whereby this merely physical virus leads to my experience of dripping green slime... so it's probably not a virus that does it, but a bacterium!"
quotes.m: you haven't explained the exact chain of causality whereby this merely physical virus leads to my experience of dripping green slime... so it's probably not a virus that does it, but a bacterium!
quotes.sum: He argues that an incomplete explanation of how physical processes produce experience is not evidence against the physical explanation.
quotes.t: The Conscious Sorites Paradox

quotes.c: “ Also ,” says Nohr, raising his voice, “you’ve given no justification for why there’s only one surviving world left by the collapse, or why the collapse happens before any humans get superposed, which makes your theory really suspicious to a modern physicist. This is exactly the sort of untestable hypothesis that the ‘One Christ’ crowd uses to argue that we should ‘teach the controversy’ when we tell high school students about other Earths.”
quotes.m: This is exactly the sort of untestable hypothesis that the ‘One Christ’ crowd uses to argue that we should ‘teach the controversy’ when we tell high school students about other Earths.
quotes.sum: A fictional physicist criticizes a collapse theory as unjustified and untestable, comparing its advocates to creationist-style demands to “teach the controversy.”
quotes.t: If Many-Worlds Had Come First

quotes.c: The squared moduli of ( 1 + 0 i ) and ( 0 − i ) are both 1, so the magic measuring tool should tell us that the ratio of squared moduli is 1. Way back up at the level where physicists exist, we should find that Detector 1 goes off half the time, and Detector 2 half the time.
quotes.m: Detector 1 goes off half the time, and Detector 2 half the time.
quotes.sum: Explains that equal squared quantum amplitudes imply two detectors should each register a photon half the time.
quotes.t: Configurations and Amplitude

quotes.c: Perhaps I should say, "you should assign unaltered prior probability to additional invisibles", rather than saying, "do not believe in them." But if you think of a belief as something evidentially additional, something you bother to track, something where you bother to count up support for or against, then it's questionable whether we should ever have additional beliefs about additional invisibles.
quotes.m: it's questionable whether we should ever have additional beliefs about additional invisibles.
quotes.sum: The author argues that claims about things that can no longer be observed may not deserve separate evidential beliefs.
quotes.t: Belief in the Implied Invisible

quotes.c: So if a mind is arriving at true beliefs, and we assume that the second law of thermodynamics has not been violated, that mind must be doing something at least vaguely Bayesian - at least one process with a sort-of Bayesian structure somewhere - or it couldn't possibly work .
quotes.m: that mind must be doing something at least vaguely Bayesian
quotes.sum: The author argues that any mind reliably reaching true beliefs must contain some roughly Bayesian process.
quotes.t: Searching for Bayes-Structure

quotes.c: From a normative perspective, it seems to me that if we should reject the crackpot angels in the first scenario, even without being able to distinguish the two theories experimentally , then we should also reject the angels of established science in the second scenario, even without being able to distinguish the two theories experimentally.
quotes.m: we should also reject the angels of established science in the second scenario, even without being able to distinguish the two theories experimentally.
quotes.sum: He argues that science should reject unnecessary supernatural-style explanations even when experiments cannot distinguish them from alternatives.
quotes.t: Decoherence is Falsifiable and Testable

quotes.c: Contrast this probabilistic situation to the qualitative reasoning where I just believe that snow is white, and believe that I believe that snow is white, and believe "'snow is white' is true", and believe "my belief '"snow is white" is true' is correct", etc. Since all the quantities involved are 1, it's easy to mix them up.
quotes.m: Since all the quantities involved are 1, it's easy to mix them up.
quotes.sum: Argues that treating beliefs as all-or-nothing makes it easy to confuse a claim’s truth with confidence in that claim.
quotes.t: Qualitatively Confused

quotes.c: Because they have no motivation for writing the hymn except a vague feeling that since churches have hymns, they ought to have one too. And, on a purely artistic level, that puts them far beneath genuine religious art that is not an imitation of anything, but an original expression of emotion.
quotes.m: Because they have no motivation for writing the hymn except a vague feeling that since churches have hymns, they ought to have one too.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky criticizes humanists who imitate religious rituals, arguing that genuine religious art comes from authentic emotion rather than copying churches.
quotes.t: Is Humanism A Religion-Substitute?

quotes.c: Mystery exists in the mind, not in reality. If I am ignorant about a phenomenon, that is a fact about my state of mind, not a fact about the phenomenon itself. All the more so, if it seems like no possible answer can exist: Confusion exists in the map, not in the territory. Unanswerable questions do not mark places where magic enters the universe. They mark places where your mind runs skew to reality.
quotes.m: Confusion exists in the map, not in the territory.
quotes.sum: Mystery and unanswerable questions reflect flaws in human thinking, not supernatural gaps in reality.
quotes.t: Wrong Questions

quotes.c: The media thinks that only the cutting edge of science is worth reporting on. How often do you see headlines like “General Relativity still governing planetary orbits” or “Phlogiston theory remains false”? So, by the time anything is solid science, it is no longer a breaking headline.
quotes.m: So, by the time anything is solid science, it is no longer a breaking headline.
quotes.sum: The author argues that reliable, settled science is ignored by news media, while speculative frontier findings get disproportionate attention.
quotes.t: The Beauty of Settled Science

quotes.c: Similarly, I don't see the use of a telescope as circular logic, but as reflective coherence; for every systematic way of arriving at truth, there ought to be a rational explanation for how it works.
quotes.sum: The author argues that reliable ways of learning truth should have rational explanations, using telescopes as an example of mutually supporting evidence rather than circular reasoning.
quotes.t: Reductive Reference

quotes.c: So let me state then, very clearly, on behalf of any and all physicists out there who dare not say it themselves: Many-worlds wins outright given our current state of evidence. There is no more reason to postulate a single Earth, than there is to postulate that two colliding top quarks would decay in a way that violates Conservation of Energy. It takes more than an unknown fundamental law; it takes magic.
quotes.m: Many-worlds wins outright given our current state of evidence.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that current evidence decisively favors the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics and that alternatives require implausible assumptions.
quotes.t: Many Worlds, One Best Guess

quotes.c: The work of Luigi Galvani and Hermann von Helmholtz suggests that the activities of neurons are electrochemical in nature, rather than mechanical pressures as previously believed. Nonetheless, we think an analogy with Babbage's 'Analytical Engine' suggests that a vastly complicated network of neurons could similarly exhibit thoughtful properties.
quotes.m: a vastly complicated network of neurons could similarly exhibit thoughtful properties.
quotes.sum: The author argues that thought could emerge from a sufficiently complex network of electrochemical neurons, by analogy with a mechanical computing engine.
quotes.t: Brain Breakthrough! It's Made of Neurons!

quotes.c: Now here's the question—and yes, it is a little unkind, but I think it needs to be asked: Presumably most readers of these novels see themselves in the protagonist's shoes, fantasizing about their own acquisition of sorcery. Wishing for magic. And, barring improbable demographics, most readers of these novels are not scientists.
quotes.m: Presumably most readers of these novels see themselves in the protagonist's shoes, fantasizing about their own acquisition of sorcery.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky challenges fantasy readers who want magical power while not wanting the real-world scientific work that could create transformative power.
quotes.t: If You Demand Magic, Magic Won't Help

quotes.c: The universe is not wavering between using particles and waves, unable to make up its mind. It’s only human intuitions about quantum mechanics that swap back and forth. The intuitions we have for billiard balls, and the intuitions we have for crests and troughs in a pool of water, both look sort of like they’re applicable to electrons, at different times and under different circumstances. But the truth is that both intuitions simply aren’t applicable .
quotes.m: But the truth is that both intuitions simply aren’t applicable .
quotes.sum: Human intuitions drawn from everyday objects and waves do not accurately describe quantum reality.
quotes.t: Quantum Explanations

quotes.c: So if you're going to have an Aristotelian proverb at all, the proverb should be, not "I can define a word any way I like," nor even, "Defining a word never has any consequences," but rather, "Definitions don't need words."
quotes.m: Definitions don't need words.
quotes.sum: The author argues that useful definitions should identify concepts rather than merely assign labels.
quotes.t: Empty Labels

quotes.c: If you close your eyes and concentrate on your inward awareness, you will begin to form thoughts, in your internal narrative, that go along the lines of "I am aware" and "My awareness is separate from my thoughts" and "I am not the one who speaks my thoughts, but the one who hears them" and "My stream of consciousness is not my consciousness" and "It seems like there is a part of me which I can imagine being eliminated without changing my outward behavior."
quotes.m: "It seems like there is a part of me which I can imagine being eliminated without changing my outward behavior."
quotes.sum: It examines why introspection can make people feel there is a separate inner observer that could be removed without changing behavior.
quotes.t: Zombies! Zombies?

quotes.c: As for the paradox, there isn't one. The appearance of paradox comes from thinking that the probabilities must be properties of the cards themselves. The ace I'm holding has to be either hearts or spades; but that doesn't mean that your knowledge about my cards must be the same as if you knew I was holding hearts, or knew I was holding spades.
quotes.m: The appearance of paradox comes from thinking that the probabilities must be properties of the cards themselves.
quotes.sum: Probability describes an observer's state of knowledge, not an intrinsic property of the cards or events themselves.
quotes.t: Probability is in the Mind

quotes.c: In classical mechanics, violating Conservation of Momentum is provably impossible. So any Excel spreadsheet calculated according to the rules of classical mechanics must necessarily show that no reactionless thrust exists - unless your machine is complicated enough that you have made a mistake in the calculations.
quotes.m: any Excel spreadsheet calculated according to the rules of classical mechanics must necessarily show that no reactionless thrust exists
quotes.sum: He argues that a calculation cannot prove a machine violates a known physical law; apparent proof almost certainly contains an error.
quotes.t: Perpetual Motion Beliefs

quotes.c: The equivalent of the Zombie World, for questions of identity/continuity, is the Soul Swap World. The allegation is that the Soul Swap World is microphysically identical to our own; but every five minutes, each thread of consciousness jumps to a random new brain, without the brains changing in any third-party experimentally detectable way. One second you're yourself, the next second you're Britney Spears.
quotes.m: One second you're yourself, the next second you're Britney Spears.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky uses a hypothetical undetectable “soul swap” to argue about whether personal identity depends on anything beyond physical brain states.
quotes.t: Identity Isn't In Specific Atoms

quotes.c: The one comes to you and says: "I believe with firm and abiding faith that there's an object in the asteroid belt, one foot across and composed entirely of chocolate cake; you can't prove that this is impossible." But, unless the one had access to some kind of evidence for this belief, it would be highly improbable for a correct belief to form spontaneously . So either the one can point to evidence, or the belief won't turn out to be true.
quotes.m: So either the one can point to evidence, or the belief won't turn out to be true.
quotes.sum: Correct beliefs need evidence; without it, a belief being true would be an unlikely accident rather than knowledge.
quotes.t: GAZP vs. GLUT

quotes.c: Clearly our machine learner is not very general. Why not allow it to represent all possible concepts, so that it can learn with the greatest possible flexibility?
quotes.m: Why not allow it to represent all possible concepts, so that it can learn with the greatest possible flexibility?
quotes.sum: The author asks whether a machine learner should be able to represent every possible concept to maximize its flexibility.
quotes.t: Superexponential Conceptspace, and Simple Words

quotes.c: Once I realized that someone, somewhere in the expanses of space and time, already knows the answer to any answerable question—even biology questions and history questions; there are other decoherent Earths—then I realized how silly it was to think as if the joy of discovery ought to be limited to one person.
quotes.m: I realized how silly it was to think as if the joy of discovery ought to be limited to one person.
quotes.sum: The author argues that discovery need not lose its value just because equivalent people elsewhere may already know the answer.
quotes.t: Joy in Discovery

quotes.c: When you actually see an electron trapped in a little electron trap, what's really going on, is that the cloud of amplitude distribution that includes you and your observed universe, can at least roughly factorize into a subspace that corresponds to that little electron, and a subspace that corresponds to everything else in the universe. So that the physically real amplitude distribution is roughly the product of a little blob of amplitude-factor in the subspace for that electron, and the amplitude-factor for everything else in the universe.
quotes.m: the physically real amplitude distribution is roughly the product of a little blob of amplitude-factor in the subspace for that electron, and the amplitude-factor for everything else in the universe.
quotes.sum: He argues that an apparently individual electron is really an approximately separable part of one universal quantum amplitude distribution.
quotes.t: No Individual Particles

quotes.c: This academic paradigm, I think, was mostly a deranged legacy of behaviorism, which denied the existence of thoughts in humans, and sought to explain all human phenomena as "reflex", including speech. Behaviorism probably deserves its own post at some point, as it was a perversion of rationalism; but this is not that post.
quotes.m: Behaviorism probably deserves its own post at some point, as it was a perversion of rationalism; but this is not that post.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that behaviorism wrongly denied human thoughts and reduced speech and other behavior to reflexes.
quotes.t: Words as Mental Paintbrush Handles

quotes.c: I have already remarked that nothing is inherently mysterious —nothing that actually exists, that is. If I am ignorant about a phenomenon, that is a fact about my state of mind , not a fact about the phenomenon; to worship a phenomenon because it seems so wonderfully mysterious, is to worship your own ignorance; a blank map does not correspond to a blank territory, it is just somewhere we haven't visited yet, etc. etc...
quotes.m: to worship a phenomenon because it seems so wonderfully mysterious, is to worship your own ignorance
quotes.sum: Mystery belongs to the observer's ignorance, not to reality; treating unexplained things as wondrous mistakes a blank mental map for the world.
quotes.t: Joy in the Merely Real

quotes.c: A neural network needs a learning rule. The obvious idea is that when two nodes are often active at the same time, we should strengthen the connection between them—this is one of the first rules ever proposed for training a neural network, known as Hebb's Rule.
quotes.m: A neural network needs a learning rule.
quotes.sum: Explains the basic idea behind Hebbian learning: strengthen neural connections between units that activate together.
quotes.t: Neural Categories

quotes.c: "Why do I think I have free will?", in contrast, is guaranteed answerable. You do, in fact, believe you have free will. This belief seems far more solid and graspable than the ephemerality of free will. And there is, in fact, some nice solid chain of cognitive cause and effect leading up to this belief.
quotes.m: You do, in fact, believe you have free will.
quotes.sum: He argues that instead of debating an abstract, possibly confused question about free will, one should explain the causal origins of one's belief in it.
quotes.t: Righting a Wrong Question

quotes.c: Oh, but arguing the real question would require work. You'd have to actually watch the wiggin to see if he reached for the ketchup. Or maybe see if you can find statistics on how many green-eyed black-haired people actually like ketchup. At any rate, you wouldn't be able to do it sitting in your living room with your eyes closed. And people are lazy.
quotes.m: Oh, but arguing the real question would require work.
quotes.sum: He argues that people avoid empirical questions because checking facts takes work, preferring verbal disputes they can conduct without evidence.
quotes.t: Sneaking in Connotations

quotes.c: For a start: You must at least be able to admit to yourself which ideas scare you, and which ideas you are attached to. But this is a substantially less difficult test than fairly counting the evidence for an idea that scares you. Does it help if I say that I have occasion to use this technique myself?
quotes.m: fairly counting the evidence for an idea that scares you.
quotes.sum: He argues that rational thinking requires noticing emotional attachments and fairly weighing evidence even for frightening ideas.
quotes.t: Leave a Line of Retreat

quotes.c: Thus the category "human" grows richer, and adds more and more characteristics; and when Diogenes finally presents his plucked chicken, we are not fooled: This plucked chicken is obviously not similar to the other "featherless bipeds".
quotes.m: This plucked chicken is obviously not similar to the other "featherless bipeds".
quotes.sum: Categories gain meaning from many overlapping similarities, not merely from a simple verbal definition.
quotes.t: Similarity Clusters

quotes.c: As there are at least some values of Y that tell us about Z (and vice versa) there must be mutual information between the two variables; and so you will find—I am confident, though I haven't actually checked—that calculating the entropy of YZ yields less total uncertainty than the sum of the independent entropies of Y and Z. H(Y,Z) = H(Y) + H(Z) - I(Y;Z) with all quantities necessarily nonnegative.
quotes.m: H(Y,Z) = H(Y) + H(Z) - I(Y;Z) with all quantities necessarily nonnegative.
quotes.sum: It explains that when two facts reveal something about each other, their combined uncertainty is lower than if they were independent.
quotes.t: Mutual Information, and Density in Thingspace

quotes.c: But if the holes for secret knowledge are not filled by true beliefs, they will be filled by false beliefs. There is nothing but science to learn—the emotional energy must either be invested in reality , or wasted in total nonsense, or destroyed. For myself, I think it is better to invest the emotional energy; fun should not be needlessly cast away.
quotes.m: There is nothing but science to learn—the emotional energy must either be invested in reality , or wasted in total nonsense, or destroyed.
quotes.sum: People crave hidden, meaningful knowledge; he argues that science should satisfy that desire or it will be diverted into cults and false beliefs.
quotes.t: To Spread Science, Keep It Secret

quotes.c: The Great Stories are not eternal, because the human species, Homo sapiens sapiens, is not eternal. I most sincerely doubt that we have another thousand years to go in our current form. I do not say this in sadness: I think we can do better .
quotes.m: I most sincerely doubt that we have another thousand years to go in our current form. I do not say this in sadness: I think we can do better .
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky expects humanity to change beyond its current biological form within a millennium and sees that as an improvement, not a loss.
quotes.t: Savanna Poets

quotes.c: Definitions can't be expected to exactly match the empirical structure of thingspace in any event, because the map is smaller and much less complicated than the territory. The point of the definition "feathered flying things" is to lead the listener to the bird cluster, not to give a total description of every existing bird down to the molecular level.
quotes.m: The point of the definition "feathered flying things" is to lead the listener to the bird cluster, not to give a total description of every existing bird down to the molecular level.
quotes.sum: Definitions are useful pointers to real-world clusters, not exact descriptions that must cover every exception.
quotes.t: The Cluster Structure of Thingspace

quotes.c: It is conceptually possible to you that 235757 is prime, because you don't know any better. But it isn't logically possible that 235757 is prime; if you were logically omniscient, 235757 would be obviously composite (and you would know the factors). That that's why we have the notion of impossible possible worlds, so that we can put probability distributions on propositions that may or may not be in fact logically impossible.
quotes.m: That that's why we have the notion of impossible possible worlds, so that we can put probability distributions on propositions that may or may not be in fact logically impossible.
quotes.sum: It distinguishes what seems possible to an uninformed person from what is logically possible, defending reasoning under logical uncertainty.
quotes.t: Hand vs. Fingers

quotes.c: So I reply: "I think it has to do with admiration of craftsmanship: work going in and wonder coming out. What the included items have in common is the similar aesthetic emotions that they inspire, and the deliberate human effort that went into them with the intent of producing such an emotion."
quotes.m: What the included items have in common is the similar aesthetic emotions that they inspire, and the deliberate human effort that went into them with the intent of producing such an emotion.
quotes.sum: He argues that categories should reflect an underlying common pattern, here admiration for deliberate craftsmanship that produces wonder.
quotes.t: Where to Draw the Boundary?

quotes.c: As I remarked earlier , when a large yellow striped object leaps at me, I think "Yikes! A tiger!" not "Hm... objects with the properties of largeness, yellowness, and stripedness have previously often possessed the properties 'hungry' and 'dangerous', and therefore, although it is not logically necessary, auughhhh CRUNCH CRUNCH GULP."
quotes.m: when a large yellow striped object leaps at me, I think "Yikes! A tiger!"
quotes.sum: He argues that useful reasoning relies on immediate, meaningful concepts rather than detached lists of abstract properties.
quotes.t: Feel the Meaning

quotes.c: People cling to their intuitions , I think, not so much because they believe their cognitive algorithms are perfectly reliable, but because they can't see their intuitions as the way their cognitive algorithms happen to look from the inside.
quotes.m: they can't see their intuitions as the way their cognitive algorithms happen to look from the inside.
quotes.sum: People mistake intuitions for direct answers because they cannot recognize them as the subjective output of mental algorithms.
quotes.t: How An Algorithm Feels From Inside

quotes.c: And then there's the most important word of all to Taboo. I've often warned that you should be careful not to overuse it, or even avoid the concept in certain cases. Now you know the real reason why. It's not a bad subject to think about. But your true understanding is measured by your ability to describe what you're doing and why, without using that word or any of its synonyms.
quotes.m: But your true understanding is measured by your ability to describe what you're doing and why, without using that word or any of its synonyms.
quotes.sum: He argues that genuine understanding requires explaining an idea without relying on its usual label or synonyms.
quotes.t: Replace the Symbol with the Substance

quotes.c: The conventional theory for explaining this is "psychological reactance", social-psychology-speak for "When you tell people they can't do something, they'll just try even harder." The fundamental instincts involved appear to be preservation of status and preservation of options. We resist dominance, when any human agency tries to restrict our freedom.
quotes.m: We resist dominance, when any human agency tries to restrict our freedom.
quotes.sum: People resist restrictions on their freedom because they instinctively protect their status and available options.
quotes.t: Scarcity

quotes.c: A bit of physics occurred, and lo, the entropy of Y went to 0, but the entropy of X went to log 2 (7) = 2.8 bits. So entropy was transferred from one system to another, and decreased within the Y subsystem; but due to the cost of bookkeeping, we didn't bother to track some information, and hence (from our perspective) the overall entropy increased.
quotes.m: due to the cost of bookkeeping, we didn't bother to track some information, and hence (from our perspective) the overall entropy increased.
quotes.sum: He explains apparent entropy growth as an effect of limited bookkeeping: information is shifted or omitted from the observer's accounting.
quotes.t: The Second Law of Thermodynamics, and Engines of Cognition

quotes.c: A simpler interpretation is that people are using the (demonstrated) similarity heuristic as a proxy for the probability that a disease spreads, and this heuristic is (demonstrably) asymmetrical.
quotes.m: people are using the (demonstrated) similarity heuristic as a proxy for the probability that a disease spreads
quotes.sum: People may judge how likely a disease is to spread by relying on an intuitive, asymmetric sense of similarity rather than probability.
quotes.t: Typicality and Asymmetrical Similarity

quotes.c: People who argue that atheism is a religion "because it states beliefs about God" are really trying to argue (I think) that the reasoning methods used in atheism are on a par with the reasoning methods used in religion, or that atheism is no safer than religion in terms of the probability of causally engendering violence, etc... What's really at stake is an atheist's claim of substantial difference and superiority relative to religion, which the religious person is trying to reject by denying the difference rather than the superiority(!)
quotes.sum: The author argues that calling atheism a religion is an attempt to deny atheism’s claimed superiority in reasoning and social consequences.
quotes.t: Disguised Queries

quotes.c: But surely there is a social imperative to use words in a commonly understood way? Does not our human telepathy, our valuable power of language, rely on mutual coordination to work? Perhaps we should voluntarily treat dictionary editors as supreme arbiters—even if they prefer to think of themselves as historians—in order to maintain the quiet cooperation on which all speech depends.
quotes.m: Does not our human telepathy, our valuable power of language, rely on mutual coordination to work?
quotes.sum: The author examines whether clear, shared language requires voluntarily following common dictionary usage.
quotes.t: The Argument from Common Usage

quotes.c: Logical truths are true in all possible worlds, and so never tell you which possible world you live in - and anything you can establish "by definition" is a logical truth.
quotes.sum: Definitions alone cannot establish facts about the world; they only state logical relationships between concepts.
quotes.t: 37 Ways That Words Can Be Wrong

quotes.c: Sometimes fallacies of compression result from confusing two known things under the same label—you know about acoustic vibrations, and you know about auditory processing in brains, but you call them both "sound" and so confuse yourself. But the more dangerous fallacy of compression arises from having no idea whatsoever that two distinct entities even exist . There is just one mental folder in the filing system, labeled "sound", and everything thought about "sound" drops into that one folder.
quotes.m: But the more dangerous fallacy of compression arises from having no idea whatsoever that two distinct entities even exist .
quotes.sum: He argues that a serious reasoning error occurs when people use one concept for distinct things without realizing the distinction exists.
quotes.t: Fallacies of Compression

quotes.c: And suppose I reply, "But I saw Socrates out in the fields with some herbologists; I think they were trying to prepare an antidote. Therefore I don't expect Socrates to keel over after he drinks the hemlock—he will be an exception to the general behavior of objects in his cluster: they did not take an antidote, and he did."
quotes.m: Therefore I don't expect Socrates to keel over after he drinks the hemlock—he will be an exception to the general behavior of objects in his cluster: they did not take an antidote, and he did.
quotes.sum: Uses Socrates and an antidote to illustrate reasoning from specific causal evidence rather than a broad generalization.
quotes.t: Arguing "By Definition"

quotes.c: Intensional definitions don't capture entire intensions; extensional definitions don't capture entire extensions. If I point to just one tiger and say the word "tiger", the communication may fail if they think I mean "dangerous animal" or "male tiger" or "yellow thing". Similarly, if I say "dangerous yellow-black striped animal", without pointing to anything, the listener may visualize giant hornets.
quotes.m: Intensional definitions don't capture entire intensions; extensional definitions don't capture entire extensions.
quotes.sum: Definitions based on examples or descriptions can both fail to convey everything a concept means.
quotes.t: Extensions and Intensions

quotes.c: And then there's the business of the strange value that people attach to certainty. Again, I don't have my books, but I believe that one experiment showed that a shift from 100% probability to 99% probability weighed larger in people's minds than a shift from 80% probability to 20% probability.
quotes.m: a shift from 100% probability to 99% probability weighed larger in people's minds than a shift from 80% probability to 20% probability.
quotes.sum: People may irrationally prize absolute certainty more than much larger changes in probability.
quotes.t: Zut Allais!

quotes.c: So while I don't mean to update on imaginary evidence, I would predict a positive result for the experiment: I would expect them to find that mere labeling had power over all things, at least in the human imagination.
quotes.m: I would expect them to find that mere labeling had power over all things, at least in the human imagination.
quotes.sum: The author argues that simply assigning labels can shape how people perceive almost anything, not only other humans.
quotes.t: Categorizing Has Consequences

quotes.c: Get together a pack of soi-disant futurists and ask them if they believe we'll have Artificial Intelligence in thirty years, and I would guess that at least half of them will say yes. If you leave it at that, they'll shake hands and congratulate themselves on their consensus. But make the term "Artificial Intelligence" taboo, and ask them to describe what they expect to see, without ever using words like "computers" or "think", and you might find quite a conflict of expectations hiding under that featureless standard word.
quotes.m: But make the term "Artificial Intelligence" taboo, and ask them to describe what they expect to see, without ever using words like "computers" or "think", and you might find quite a conflict of expectations hiding under that featureless standard word.
quotes.sum: He argues that apparent agreement about AI often conceals incompatible expectations, and that people should explain predictions without relying on vague labels.
quotes.t: Taboo Your Words

quotes.c: If you don't do either, then clearly you do not really believe that you know anything the prediction markets don't. (Or you don't understand expected utility , or your utilities over final outcomes drop off improbably fast in the vicinity of your current wealth minus fifty bucks - you don't have to bet the full $250.) It is free money, going now for anyone who genuinely thinks they know better than the prediction markets what will happen next.
quotes.m: It is free money, going now for anyone who genuinely thinks they know better than the prediction markets what will happen next.
quotes.sum: He argues that anyone who thinks they can predict better than a market should prove it by betting, unless the stakes meaningfully strain their finances.
quotes.t: Buy Now Or Forever Hold Your Peace

quotes.c: It's clear that the function of mapping reality is performed strictly by Outer Chalmers. The whole business of producing belief representations is handled by Bayesian structure in causal interactions . There's nothing left for the Inner Chalmers to do, but bless the whole affair with epiphenomenal meaning. Where now 'meaning' is something entirely unrelated to systematic map-territory correspondence or the ability to use that map to navigate reality.
quotes.m: There's nothing left for the Inner Chalmers to do, but bless the whole affair with epiphenomenal meaning.
quotes.sum: He argues that consciousness adds no explanatory role to how beliefs track reality, which is instead handled by causal Bayesian processes.
quotes.t: Zombie Responses

quotes.c: But when a large yellow striped feline-shaped object leaps out at me from the shadows, I think, "Yikes! A tiger!" Not, "Hm... objects with the properties of largeness, yellowness, stripedness, and feline shape, have previously often possessed the properties 'hungry' and 'dangerous', and thus, although it is not logically necessary, it may be an empirically good guess that aaauuughhhh CRUNCH CRUNCH GULP."
quotes.m: "Yikes! A tiger!"
quotes.sum: Words such as “tiger” package learned predictions, letting people make fast practical inferences rather than laboriously listing observed traits.
quotes.t: Words as Hidden Inferences

quotes.c: You could reason, perhaps, as follows: "All things I have observed which wear clothing, speak language, and use tools, have also shared certain other properties as well, such as breathing air and pumping red blood. The last thirty 'humans' belonging to this cluster, whom I observed to drink hemlock, soon fell over and stopped moving. Socrates wears a toga, speaks fluent ancient Greek, and drank hemlock from a cup. So I predict that Socrates will keel over in the next five minutes."
quotes.m: So I predict that Socrates will keel over in the next five minutes.
quotes.sum: Uses Socrates drinking hemlock to illustrate reasoning by observed patterns and category-based prediction.
quotes.t: The Parable of Hemlock

quotes.c: Unreasonable? I am a rationalist: what do I care about being unreasonable? I don't have to conform to a particular ritual of cognition. I don't have to take only box B because I believe my choice affects the box, even though Omega has already left. I can just... take only box B.
quotes.m: I don't have to conform to a particular ritual of cognition.
quotes.sum: The author argues that rationality should mean choosing what works, not following a prescribed ritual of reasoning.
quotes.t: Newcomb's Problem and Regret of Rationality

quotes.c: Trusting that algebra, correctly used, will not carry you to an absurd result, is not a matter of blind faith. When we see apparent evidence against algebra's trustworthiness, we should also take into account the massive evidence favoring algebra which we have previously encountered. We should take into account our past experience of seeming contradictions which turned out to be themselves flawed.
quotes.m: When we see apparent evidence against algebra's trustworthiness, we should also take into account the massive evidence favoring algebra which we have previously encountered.
quotes.sum: Past evidence should outweigh a seemingly decisive contradiction, prompting a search for an error rather than abandonment of established mathematics.
quotes.t: Trust in Bayes

quotes.c: The problem with the Allais Paradox is the incoherent pattern 1A > 1B, 2B > 2A. If you need $24,000 for a lifesaving operation and an extra $3,000 won't help that much, then you choose 1A > 1B and 2A > 2B. If you have a million dollars in the bank account and your utility curve doesn't change much with an extra $25,000 or so, then you should choose 1B > 1A and 2B > 2A. Neither the individual choice 1A > 1B, nor the individual choice 2B > 2A, are of themselves irrational. It's the combination that's the problem.
quotes.m: Neither the individual choice 1A > 1B, nor the individual choice 2B > 2A, are of themselves irrational. It's the combination that's the problem.
quotes.sum: He argues that the Allais paradox is irrational only when a person's two lottery choices form an inconsistent pair, not because either choice is always wrong alone.
quotes.t: Allais Malaise

quotes.c: "The truth," you say, "is that the way my people see the world is so different from yours, that you can't even imagine what I think is the truth. I've painted no pictures, taken no photographs; all I've done is look at you, and nothing happens when I look at you, that doesn't happen when anyone else looks at you. But you are being constantly photographed, all the time, and you never had any soul to begin with: this is the truth."
quotes.m: But you are being constantly photographed, all the time, and you never had any soul to begin with: this is the truth.
quotes.sum: A dialogue contrasts a traditional belief in souls with a radically different, naturalistic account of identity and observation.
quotes.t: Three Dialogues on Identity

quotes.c: Albert: "But I wouldn't even have to tell you about the robot operation. You wouldn't notice. If you think, going on introspective evidence, that you are in an important sense "the same person" that you were five minutes ago, and I do something to you that doesn't change the introspective evidence available to you, then your conclusion that you are the same person that you were five minutes ago should be equally justified. Doesn't the Generalized Anti-Zombie Principle say that if I do something to you that alters your consciousness, let alone makes you a completely different person, then you ought to notice somehow?"
quotes.m: Doesn't the Generalized Anti-Zombie Principle say that if I do something to you that alters your consciousness, let alone makes you a completely different person, then you ought to notice somehow?
quotes.sum: He argues that a change which genuinely altered someone's consciousness or identity should leave some difference in what they can notice from the inside.
quotes.t: The Generalized Anti-Zombie Principle

quotes.c: Years ago, I was speaking to someone when he casually remarked that he didn’t believe in evolution. And I said, “This is not the nineteenth century. When Darwin first proposed evolution, it might have been reasonable to doubt it. But this is the twenty-first century. We can read the genes. Humans and chimpanzees have 98% shared DNA. We know humans and chimps are related. It’s over. ”
quotes.m: We know humans and chimps are related. It’s over.
quotes.sum: He argues that modern genetic evidence makes disbelief in evolution no longer reasonable.
quotes.t: But There's Still A Chance, Right?

quotes.c: But when it comes to messy gene expression networks, we've already found the hidden beauty - the stable level of underlying physics. Because we've already found the master order, we can guess that we won't find any additional secret patterns that will make biology as easy as a sequence of cubes. Knowing the rules of the game, we know that the game is hard.
quotes.m: Knowing the rules of the game, we know that the game is hard.
quotes.sum: Physics may explain biology's foundations without making biological systems easy to predict or engineer, because computation and evolutionary history still create complexity.
quotes.t: Is Reality Ugly?

quotes.c: Where does religion come from? It appears to be a human universal, and to have its own emotion backing it - the emotion of religious faith. Religion often involves costly sacrifices, even in hunter-gatherer tribes - why does it persist? What selection pressure could there possibly be for religion?
quotes.m: What selection pressure could there possibly be for religion?
quotes.sum: The author asks why religion is universal and costly, framing it as an evolutionary puzzle requiring an explanation.
quotes.t: A Failed Just-So Story

quotes.c: As I recently remarked , if you say, "Many times I have witnessed the turning of the seasons, and tomorrow I expect the Sun will rise in its appointed place in the east," then that is not a certainty . And if you say, "I expect a purple polka-dot fairy to come out of my nose and give me a bag of money," that is not a certainty. But they are not the same shade of uncertainty, and it seems insufficiently narrow to call them both "faith".
quotes.m: But they are not the same shade of uncertainty, and it seems insufficiently narrow to call them both "faith".
quotes.sum: The author argues that ordinary predictions and fantastical claims are both uncertain, but differ sharply in how justified they are, so neither should simply be called faith.
quotes.t: Expecting Beauty

quotes.c: I've never been a fan of the notion that we should (normatively) have a discount rate in our pure preferences - as opposed to a pseudo-discount rate arising from monetary inflation, or from opportunity costs of other investments, or from various probabilistic catastrophes that destroy resources or consumers. The idea that it is literally, fundamentally 5% more important that a poverty-stricken family have clean water in 2008, than that a similar family have clean water in 2009, seems like pure discrimination to me - just as much as if you were to discriminate between blacks and whites.
quotes.m: The idea that it is literally, fundamentally 5% more important that a poverty-stricken family have clean water in 2008, than that a similar family have clean water in 2009, seems like pure discrimination to me - just as much as if you were to discriminate between blacks and whites.
quotes.sum: He argues that future people’s welfare should not count less simply because it occurs later, treating pure time discounting as discriminatory.
quotes.t: Against Discount Rates

quotes.c: I think the most important lesson to take away from Asch’s experiments is to distinguish “expressing concern” from “disagreement.” Raising a point that others haven’t voiced is not a promise to disagree with the group at the end of its discussion.
quotes.m: Raising a point that others haven’t voiced is not a promise to disagree with the group at the end of its discussion.
quotes.sum: People should raise unvoiced concerns without treating that as a commitment to oppose the group’s eventual conclusion.
quotes.t: On Expressing Your Concerns

quotes.c: If you were looking at a diagram like the one above, but you knew for a fact that the other people in the experiment were honest and seeing the same diagram as you, and three other people said that C was the same size as X, then what are the odds that only you are the one who’s right? I lay claim to no advantage of visual reasoning—I don’t think I’m better than an average human at judging whether two lines are the same size. In terms of individual rationality, I hope I would notice my own severe confusion and then assign >50% probability to the majority vote.
quotes.m: In terms of individual rationality, I hope I would notice my own severe confusion and then assign >50% probability to the majority vote.
quotes.sum: He argues that when trustworthy peers unanimously disagree with your perception, rationality means treating their agreement as strong evidence that you are mistaken.
quotes.t: Asch's Conformity Experiment

quotes.c: Ordinarily I prefer to discuss politics indirectly, rather than directly. Politics varies from government to government. Better to talk about human universals - cognitive biases that can be nailed down and examined in the laboratory - malfunctions of sanity that appear wherever humans go. Then it's up to you to apply the knowledge to your own political situation.
quotes.m: Better to talk about human universals - cognitive biases that can be nailed down and examined in the laboratory - malfunctions of sanity that appear wherever humans go.
quotes.sum: The author favors discussing universal cognitive biases over direct political commentary, leaving readers to apply the lessons locally.
quotes.t: Posting on Politics

quotes.c: This pattern of belief is very hard to justify from a Bayesian perspective. It is just the same hypothesis in both cases. Even if, in the second case, I announce an experimental method and my intent to actually test it, I have not yet experimented and I have not yet received any observational evidence in favor of the hypothesis.
quotes.sum: He argues that planning a test is not evidence: beliefs should not be updated until observations actually arrive.
quotes.t: Rational vs. Scientific Ev-Psych

quotes.c: This is what creates the impression of a mathematical universe that is "out there" in Platonia, a universe which humans are exploring rather than creating . Our definitions teleport us to various locations in Platonia, but we don't create the surrounding environment. It seems this way, at least, because we don't remember creating all the wonderful things we find.
quotes.m: Our definitions teleport us to various locations in Platonia, but we don't create the surrounding environment.
quotes.sum: Mathematics can feel like an independently existing world because definitions lead us to structures whose consequences we did not consciously invent.
quotes.t: Beautiful Math

quotes.c: When I look back at my own personal journey toward rationality—not just humanity's historical journey—well, I grew up believing very strongly that I ought to be rational. This made me an above-average Traditional Rationalist a la Feynman and Heinlein, and nothing more. It did not drive me to go beyond the teachings I had received. I only began to grow further as a rationalist once I had something terribly important that I needed to do. Something more important than my pride as a rationalist, never mind my life.
quotes.m: I only began to grow further as a rationalist once I had something terribly important that I needed to do.
quotes.sum: Rationality alone is not enough, he argues; people need a deeply important goal to overcome conformity and pursue truth beyond inherited ideas.
quotes.t: Something to Protect

quotes.c: Meanwhile, yes, I sometimes do mention "cryonics" as the archetype for a socially weird belief which happens to be true. No matter what I use as an example of "socially weird but true", some people are going to disagree with it. Otherwise it wouldn't be an example. And weird-but-true is certainly an important topic in rationality - otherwise there would be a knockdown argument against ever dissenting .
quotes.m: And weird-but-true is certainly an important topic in rationality - otherwise there would be a knockdown argument against ever dissenting .
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that rational thinking must allow dissent and socially unusual beliefs that may nevertheless be true.
quotes.t: My Strange Beliefs

quotes.c: So it seems there’s an asymmetry between argument and authority. If we know authority we are still interested in hearing the arguments; but if we know the arguments fully, we have very little left to learn from authority.
quotes.m: If we know authority we are still interested in hearing the arguments; but if we know the arguments fully, we have very little left to learn from authority.
quotes.sum: He argues that direct arguments are ultimately more informative than authority, even when authority is useful evidence.
quotes.t: Argument Screens Off Authority

quotes.c: As I have remarked before , it seems worthwhile to distinguish "faith" that the sun will rise in the east just like the last hundred thousand times observed, from "faith" that tomorrow a green goblin will give you a bag of gold doubloons. When first-order arithmetic has been observed to be internally consistent over the last ten million theorems proved in it, and you see a seeming proof of inconsistency, it is, perhaps, reasonable to double-check the proof.
quotes.m: it seems worthwhile to distinguish "faith" that the sun will rise in the east just like the last hundred thousand times observed, from "faith" that tomorrow a green goblin will give you a bag of gold doubloons.
quotes.sum: He argues that confidence should track repeated evidence, not blind belief, including when trusting mathematics.
quotes.t: Trust in Math

quotes.c: Cultishness is quantitative, not qualitative. The question is not, “Cultish, yes or no?” but, “How much cultishness and where?” Even in Science, which is the archetypal Genuinely Truly Noble Cause, we can readily point to the current frontiers of the war against cult-entropy, where the current battle line creeps forward and back.
quotes.m: Cultishness is quantitative, not qualitative.
quotes.sum: The author argues that cult-like dynamics come in degrees, including within science, and should be examined through authority and institutional bias.
quotes.t: Every Cause Wants To Be A Cult

quotes.c: Just as you can’t always experiment today, you can’t always check the calculations today. 2 Sometimes you don’t know enough background material, sometimes there’s private information, sometimes there just isn’t time. There’s a sadly large number of times when it’s worthwhile to judge the speaker’s rationality. You should always do it with a hollow feeling in your heart, though, a sense that something’s missing.
quotes.m: There’s a sadly large number of times when it’s worthwhile to judge the speaker’s rationality.
quotes.sum: When claims cannot be checked directly, judging how rational the speaker is can be necessary, but should feel like an imperfect substitute for verification.
quotes.t: Hug the Query

quotes.c: Your instinctive willingness to believe something will change along with your willingness to affiliate with people who are known for believing it—quite apart from whether the belief is actually true. Some people may be reluctant to believe that God does not exist, not because there is evidence that God does exist, but rather because they are reluctant to affiliate with Richard Dawkins or those darned “strident” atheists who go around publicly saying “God does not exist.”
quotes.m: Your instinctive willingness to believe something will change along with your willingness to affiliate with people who are known for believing it—quite apart from whether the belief is actually true.
quotes.sum: The author argues that people often accept or reject beliefs based on whom those beliefs socially associate them with, rather than on evidence.
quotes.t: Reversed Stupidity Is Not Intelligence

quotes.c: If Nature is one way, the likelihood of the data coming out the way we have seen will be one thing. If Nature is another way, the likelihood of the data coming out that way will be something else. But the likelihood of a given state of Nature producing the data we have seen, has nothing to do with the researcher's private intentions. So whatever our hypotheses about Nature, the likelihood ratio is the same, and the evidential impact is the same, and the posterior belief should be the same, between the two experiments.
quotes.m: the likelihood of a given state of Nature producing the data we have seen, has nothing to do with the researcher's private intentions.
quotes.sum: The author argues that evidence should change beliefs identically regardless of a researcher's intentions, because intentions do not alter the likelihood of observed data.
quotes.t: Beautiful Probability

quotes.c: Yet the map is not the territory: If I say that I am 99% confident that 2 + 2 = 4, it doesn’t mean that I think “2 + 2 = 4” is true to within 99% precision, or that “2 + 2 = 4” is true 99 times out of 100. The proposition in which I repose my confidence is the proposition that “2 + 2 = 4 is always and exactly true,” not the proposition “2 + 2 = 4 is mostly and usually true.”
quotes.m: The proposition in which I repose my confidence is the proposition that “2 + 2 = 4 is always and exactly true,” not the proposition “2 + 2 = 4 is mostly and usually true.”
quotes.sum: He argues that confidence measures uncertainty in one's beliefs, not the degree to which a mathematical fact itself is true.
quotes.t: Infinite Certainty

quotes.c: Even in reading popular works on science, there is yet power. You don't want to end up like those poor souls in that recent interview (I couldn't Google) where a well-known scientist in field XYZ thinks the universe is 100 billion years old. But it seems to me that there's substantially more power in pushing until you encounter some basic math. Not complicated math, just basic math.
quotes.m: But it seems to me that there's substantially more power in pushing until you encounter some basic math.
quotes.sum: The author argues that real scientific understanding requires pushing beyond popular explanations until one reaches basic mathematical foundations.
quotes.t: The Simple Math of Everything

quotes.c: There is an interaction here, a confluence of folly, between the evolutionary psychology of politics as a football game , and the evolutionary psychology of trying to side with the winner. The media - I am not the first to observe this - report on politics as though it is a horse race. Good feelings about a candidate are generated, not by looking over voting records, but by the media reporting excitedly: "He's pulling ahead in the third stretch!"
quotes.m: Good feelings about a candidate are generated, not by looking over voting records, but by the media reporting excitedly: "He's pulling ahead in the third stretch!"
quotes.sum: He argues that horse-race media coverage makes voters support whoever appears to be winning rather than evaluating candidates' records.
quotes.t: Stop Voting For Nincompoops

quotes.c: But then it occurred to me that I'd never explained why a simple utility function wouldn't be enough. We are a thousand shards of desire, as I said in " Thou Art Godshatter ". Only that first required discussing " Evolutionary Psychology ", which required explaining that human minds are " Adaptation-Executers, not Fitness-Maximizers ", plus the difference between " Protein Reinforcement and DNA Consequentialism ".
quotes.m: We are a thousand shards of desire, as I said in " Thou Art Godshatter ".
quotes.sum: Human motivation cannot be reduced to one simple goal: people contain many evolved, partly conflicting desires.
quotes.t: Fake Fake Utility Functions

quotes.c: What is the meaning of eating chocolate? That's between you and your moral philosophy. Personally, I think chocolate tastes good, but I wish it were less harmful; acceptable solutions would include redesigning the chocolate or redesigning my biochemistry.
quotes.m: acceptable solutions would include redesigning the chocolate or redesigning my biochemistry.
quotes.sum: The author treats changing one’s own biology as an acceptable way to reduce the harms of enjoying chocolate.
quotes.t: Adaptation-Executers, not Fitness-Maximizers

quotes.c: But these studies on the halo effect of attractiveness should make us suspicious that there may be a similar halo effect for kindness, or intelligence. Let’s say that you know someone who not only seems very intelligent, but also honest, altruistic, kindly, and serene. You should be suspicious that some of these perceived characteristics are influencing your perception of the others.
quotes.m: You should be suspicious that some of these perceived characteristics are influencing your perception of the others.
quotes.sum: The author warns that seeing someone as smart or kind can bias us into assuming they have other virtues too.
quotes.t: The Halo Effect

quotes.c: If I claim to value art for its own sake, then would I value art that no one ever saw? A screensaver running in a closed room, producing beautiful pictures that no one ever saw? I'd have to say no. I can't think of any completely lifeless object that I would value as an end, not just a means. That would be like valuing ice cream as an end in itself, apart from anyone eating it. Everything I value, that I can think of, involves people and their experiences somewhere along the line.
quotes.m: Everything I value, that I can think of, involves people and their experiences somewhere along the line.
quotes.sum: He argues that happiness is not the only value, but that what people value ultimately concerns people and their experiences rather than lifeless objects.
quotes.t: Not for the Sake of Happiness (Alone)

quotes.c: Actually, I think Shermer's falling prey to correspondence bias by supposing that there's any particular correlation between Rand's philosophy and the way her followers formed a cult. Every cause wants to be a cult .
quotes.m: Every cause wants to be a cult .
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that Objectivism's cult-like follower behavior was not uniquely caused by Ayn Rand's philosophy, because all causes tend toward cult dynamics.
quotes.t: Guardians of Ayn Rand

quotes.c: I have previously emphasized that the evolution-of-foxes works at cross-purposes to the evolution-of-rabbits; there is no unitary Evolution God to praise for every beauty of Nature. Azathoth has ten million hands. When you conjure, you don't get the evolution, the Maker of Butterflies. You get an evolution, with characteristics and strength that depend on your exact conjuration.
quotes.m: You get an evolution, with characteristics and strength that depend on your exact conjuration.
quotes.sum: Evolution is not a single benevolent force; any evolutionary process produces outcomes shaped by its specific setup and incentives.
quotes.t: Conjuring An Evolution To Serve You

quotes.c: “It’s not vacuous,” I say. “Here’s an analogy: The logician Alfred Tarski once said that the assertion ‘Snow is white’ is true if and only if snow is white. If you can understand that, you should be able to see why an empty bucket is magical if and only if the pastures are empty of sheep.”
quotes.m: The logician Alfred Tarski once said that the assertion ‘Snow is white’ is true if and only if snow is white.
quotes.sum: It uses an analogy to argue that truth is about whether beliefs match the external world, not whether they fit other beliefs.
quotes.t: The Simple Truth

quotes.c: And yet... I think the Inquisition's attitude toward truth played a role. The Inquisition believed that there was such a thing as truth, and that it was important; well, likewise Richard Feynman. But the Inquisitors were not Truth-Seekers. They were Truth- Guardians.
quotes.m: But the Inquisitors were not Truth-Seekers. They were Truth- Guardians.
quotes.sum: He argues that believing truth matters is not enough: authoritarian enforcers can see themselves as protecting truth rather than genuinely seeking it.
quotes.t: Guardians of the Truth

quotes.c: Yet if you need to know about the forest for any pragmatic reason - if there is anything you plan on doing with the knowledge - then the answer is no longer a matter of mutual agreement. If, for example, you need to know whether landmines will be set off by the tree falling, then you cannot make the land mines explode or unexplode by any possible amount of agreement about the meaning of the word "sound". You can get the whole world to agree, one way or the other, and it still won't make a difference.
quotes.m: You can get the whole world to agree, one way or the other, and it still won't make a difference.
quotes.sum: Practical consequences are not determined by social agreement about words; reality stays the same regardless of consensus.
quotes.t: Purpose and Pragmatism

quotes.c: Sam Harris came closer when he put the accusing finger on faith. If you don’t place an appropriate burden of proof on each and every additional nice claim, the affective resonance gets started very easily. Look at the poor New Agers. Christianity developed defenses against criticism, arguing for the wonders of faith; New Agers culturally inherit the cached thought that faith is positive, but lack Christianity’s exclusionary scripture to keep out competing memes.
quotes.m: If you don’t place an appropriate burden of proof on each and every additional nice claim, the affective resonance gets started very easily.
quotes.sum: He argues that treating faith as inherently good weakens standards of evidence and can fuel self-reinforcing belief spirals.
quotes.t: Uncritical Supercriticality

quotes.c: With intense positive affect attached to the Great Thingy, the resonance touches everywhere. A believing Communist sees the wisdom of Marx in every hamburger bought at McDonald’s; in every promotion they’re denied that would have gone to them in a true worker’s paradise; in every election that doesn’t go to their taste; in every newspaper article “slanted in the wrong direction.” Every time they use the Great Idea to interpret another event, the Great Idea is confirmed all the more. It feels better—positive reinforcement—and of course, when something feels good, that, alas, makes us want to believe it all the more.
quotes.m: It feels better—positive reinforcement—and of course, when something feels good, that, alas, makes us want to believe it all the more.
quotes.sum: Strong positive feelings about an ideology can make people interpret every experience as evidence that it is true.
quotes.t: Affective Death Spirals

quotes.c: I am your hero! I am your master! Learn my arts, Seek my way. Learn as I learned, Seek as I sought. Envy me! Aim at me! Rival me! Transcend me! Look back, Smile, And then — Eyes front! I was never your city, Just a stretch of your road.
quotes.m: I was never your city, Just a stretch of your road.
quotes.sum: A celebrated teacher should be treated as a temporary guide to learn from and eventually surpass, not as a permanent authority or destination.
quotes.t: The Litany Against Gurus

quotes.c: The deeper the deletion, the stricter the test. If all proofs of the Pythagorean Theorem were deleted from my mind, could I re-prove it? I think so. If all knowledge of the Pythagorean Theorem were deleted from my mind, would I notice the Pythagorean Theorem to re-prove? That’s harder to boast, without putting it to the test; but if you handed me a right triangle with sides of length 3 and 4, and told me that the length of the hypotenuse was calculable, I think I would be able to calculate it, if I still knew all the rest of my math.
quotes.m: If all knowledge of the Pythagorean Theorem were deleted from my mind, would I notice the Pythagorean Theorem to re-prove?
quotes.sum: He distinguishes remembering a proof from independently recognizing a mathematical problem and reconstructing its solution.
quotes.t: Truly Part Of You

quotes.c: When I observe failures of explanation, I usually see the explainer taking one step back, when they need to take two or more steps back. Or listeners assume that things should be visible in one step, when they take two or more steps to explain. Both sides act as if they expect very short inferential distances from universal knowledge to any new knowledge.
quotes.m: Both sides act as if they expect very short inferential distances from universal knowledge to any new knowledge.
quotes.sum: People often fail to explain or understand ideas because they underestimate how many reasoning steps separate common knowledge from a new conclusion.
quotes.t: Expecting Short Inferential Distances

quotes.c: As the case of cryonics testifies, the fear of thinking really different is stronger than the fear of death. Hunter-gatherers had to be ready to face death on a routine basis—hunting large mammals, or just walking around in a world that contained predators. They needed that courage in order to live. Courage to defy the tribe’s standard ways of thinking, to entertain thoughts that seem truly weird—well, that probably didn’t serve its bearers as well.
quotes.m: the fear of thinking really different is stronger than the fear of death.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that humans are evolutionarily more afraid of socially strange beliefs than of death, using cryonics as evidence.
quotes.t: Lonely Dissent

quotes.c: You'll notice that my first post, on the Two-Party Swindle , worried about the tendency of voters to lose themselves in emotion and identify with "their" professional politicians. If you think the chief benefit of living in a democracy is the hope of getting Your-Favorite-Legislation passed, then you might abandon yourself in adulation of a professional politician who wears the colors of Your-Favorite-Legislation. Isn't that the only way you can get Your-Favorite-Legislation, the most important thing in the world, passed?
quotes.m: the tendency of voters to lose themselves in emotion and identify with "their" professional politicians.
quotes.sum: He warns that voters who treat democracy mainly as a route to favored laws can become emotionally devoted to partisan politicians.
quotes.t: The American System and Misleading Labels

quotes.c: Evolution doesn't operate on particular individuals; individuals keep whatever genes they're born with. Evolution operates on a reproducing population, a species, over time. There's a natural tendency to think that if an Evolution Fairy is operating on the species, she must be optimizing for the species. But what really changes are the gene frequencies, and frequencies don't increase or decrease according to how much the gene helps the species as a whole. As we shall later see, it's quite possible for a species to evolve to extinction.
quotes.sum: Evolution selects changes in gene frequencies, not what benefits a species overall, so evolution can even drive a species extinct.
quotes.t: Evolving to Extinction

quotes.c: When Ayn Rand ’s long-running affair with Nathaniel Branden was revealed to the Objectivist membership, a substantial fraction of the Objectivist membership broke off and followed Branden into espousing an “open system” of Objectivism not bound so tightly to Ayn Rand. Who stayed with Ayn Rand even after the scandal broke? The ones who really, really believed in her—and perhaps some of the undecideds, who, after the voices of moderation left, heard arguments from only one side. This may account for how the Ayn Rand Institute is (reportedly) more fanatical after the breakup than the original core group of Objectivists under Branden and Rand.
quotes.m: The ones who really, really believed in her—and perhaps some of the undecideds, who, after the voices of moderation left, heard arguments from only one side.
quotes.sum: Group splits can leave behind the most committed believers and remove moderating voices, making the remaining movement more extreme.
quotes.t: Evaporative Cooling of Group Beliefs

quotes.c: Which is to say: The very fact that a religious person would be afraid of God withdrawing Its threat to punish them for committing murder, shows that they have a revulsion of murder which is independent of whether God punishes murder or not. If they had no sense that murder was wrong independently of divine retribution, the prospect of God not punishing murder would be no more existentially horrifying than the prospect of God not punishing sneezing.
quotes.m: they have a revulsion of murder which is independent of whether God punishes murder or not.
quotes.sum: Religious fear that God might stop punishing murder reveals a moral revulsion toward murder that exists independently of divine commands.
quotes.t: Fake Morality

quotes.c: I thought it deserved a sharper presentation, for the benefit of the popular audience that Gould deluded; and a clear-cut example of Gould's "work", to show what the fuss is about. Many academic writers on Gould could not speak as sharply as Gould deserved. As I have no fear for my own reputation, I will say it plainly: One way or another, knowingly or unknowingly, Gould deceived the trusting public and committed the moral equivalent of deliberate scientific fraud.
quotes.m: One way or another, knowingly or unknowingly, Gould deceived the trusting public and committed the moral equivalent of deliberate scientific fraud.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that Stephen J. Gould misled the public so seriously that it was morally comparable to deliberate scientific fraud.
quotes.t: Beware of Stephen J. Gould

quotes.c: Closely related is the illusion of transparency : We always know what we mean by our words, and so we expect others to know it too. Reading our own writing, the intended interpretation falls easily into place, guided by our knowledge of what we really meant. It’s hard to empathize with someone who must interpret blindly, guided only by the words.
quotes.m: It’s hard to empathize with someone who must interpret blindly, guided only by the words.
quotes.sum: People overestimate how clearly their intended meaning comes across because they already know what they meant.
quotes.t: Illusion of Transparency:  Why No One Understands You

quotes.c: This also illustrates the point I was trying to make in Einstein's Arrogance : With large answer spaces, nearly all of the real work goes into promoting one possible answer to the point of being singled out for attention. If a hypothesis is improperly promoted to your attention—your sense of aesthetics suggests a beautiful way for Nature to be, and yet natural selection doesn't involve an Evolution Fairy who shares your appreciation—then this alone may seal your doom, unless you can manage to clear your mind entirely and start over.
quotes.m: If a hypothesis is improperly promoted to your attention—your sense of aesthetics suggests a beautiful way for Nature to be, and yet natural selection doesn't involve an Evolution Fairy who shares your appreciation—then this alone may seal your doom, unless you can manage to clear your mind entirely and start over.
quotes.sum: He argues that appealing but unsupported explanations can mislead thinkers, who must discard intuitive stories and rebuild their reasoning from evidence.
quotes.t: The Tragedy of Group Selectionism

quotes.c: Richard Feynman once said that if you really understand something in physics you should be able to explain it to your grandmother. I believed him. I was shocked to discover it wasn't true.
quotes.m: I was shocked to discover it wasn't true.
quotes.sum: Yudkowsky argues that even genuine understanding may be hard to communicate, because teachers can misread feedback and overestimate what others grasp.
quotes.t: Double Illusion of Transparency

quotes.c: This suggests—to say the very least—that we should be more careful when we expose ourselves to unreliable information, especially if we’re doing something else at the time. Be careful when you glance at that newspaper in the supermarket.
quotes.m: Be careful when you glance at that newspaper in the supermarket.
quotes.sum: The author argues that casually encountering unreliable information can mislead us, so people should be more cautious about media exposure.
quotes.t: Do We Believe Everything We're Told?

quotes.c: This 1 bit per generation has to be divided up among all the genetic variants being selected on, for the whole population. It's not 1 bit per organism per generation, it's 1 bit per gene pool per generation. Suppose there's some amazingly beneficial mutation making the rounds, so that organisms with the mutation have 50% more offspring.
quotes.m: It's not 1 bit per organism per generation, it's 1 bit per gene pool per generation.
quotes.sum: Natural selection has a limited amount of information it can accumulate each generation across an entire population.
quotes.t: Natural Selection's Speed Limit and Complexity Bound

quotes.c: Suppose there's a box containing a million dollars. The box is locked, not with an ordinary combination lock, but with a dozen keys controlling a machine that can open the box. If you know how the machine works, you can deduce which sequences of key-presses will open the box. There's more than one key sequence that can trigger the button. But if you press a sufficiently wrong sequence, the machine incinerates the money. And if you don't know about the machine, there's no simple rules like "Pressing any key three times opens the box" or "Pressing five different keys with no repetitions incinerates the money."
quotes.m: if you don't know about the machine, there's no simple rules like "Pressing any key three times opens the box" or "Pressing five different keys with no repetitions incinerates the money."
quotes.sum: Uses a high-stakes lock analogy to argue that correct general rules require understanding the underlying mechanism, not superficial patterns.
quotes.t: Leaky Generalizations

quotes.c: As you read this, some young man or woman is sitting at a desk in a university, earnestly studying material they have no intention of ever using, and no interest in knowing for its own sake.
